rows.title: Sources of ancient Indian history - archaeological, literary, foreign accounts; dating methods
sub: Group-II S1-1: Sources of ancient Indian history - archaeological, literary and foreign accounts

secs.t: Foreign accounts - author, country, ruler visited, chronological order

x: Exam angle: arrange travellers chronologically; match work - author - language.
Exam angle: "pair not correctly matched" - the wrong pair both in 2018 and 2019 was
I-Tsing - Ashoka
The Periplus was written by an anonymous Greek sailor around 60 CE and contains information on Indian Ocean ports and Andhra–Rome trade.
I-Tsing was a Chinese traveller of the late seventh century who studied at Nalanda and wrote about Buddhist monastic life.
Al-Biruni, a scholar from
Khwarizm in Central Asia
, wrote Kitab-ul-Hind, also called Tahqiq-i-Hind, in Arabic.
The correct sequence is Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang and Al-Biruni, moving from the Mauryan period through the Gupta and Harsha periods to the eleventh century.
Deimachus, Dionysius, Ptolemy and Strabo
are among the Greek or Roman writers associated with ancient accounts of India.
Megasthenes’ Indica belongs to the 4th century BCE and is associated with the first foreign mention of the Andhras, 30 forts and urban habitation.
Hiuen Tsang’s 7th-century account states that the
Sriparvata vihara lacked patronage
The Periplus was written in Greek by an anonymous Greek sailor, Geography by Ptolemy, and Natural History by Pliny in Latin.
Ptolemy's Geography refers to Masolia and its textiles, Ben Ra as Vengi, Kantakossyla, and the ports Bharukachha, Sopara and Kalyani.

secs.t: Inscriptions - issuer, language, script, key word

x: Exam angle: wrong pair in APPSC 2012 was
Rudradaman - Nanaghat
(correct: Junagadh).
The
Hathigumpha inscription
of Kharavela of Kalinga records his campaigns and mentions Tamil kingdoms.
The Nasik Prashasti praises Gautamiputra Satakarni as the destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
The
Naneghat inscription
, issued by Queen Naganika, is an important source for the early history of the Satavahana family.
The
Myakadoni inscription
of Pulumavi III provides the basis for the Karnataka-homeland theory of the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Literary works - author and period

x: Exam angle: "Rajatarangini was composed by" - match work with author and dynasty.
Vishakhadatta
wrote Mudrarakshasa, which deals with Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya's struggle against the Nandas.
The
Vayu, Vishnu and Matsya Puranas
contain genealogical lists of the Satavahanas.
The Puranas provide genealogical material, identify Pulomavi III as the last Satavahana, and the Vayu Purana refers to the Andhra people.
Arthashastra belongs to the Mauryan context, Gathasaptasati to the Satavahana period, Harshacharita to the age of Harsha, and Rajatarangini to the 12th century.

secs.t: Religious literature as source - Buddhist and Jain

x: The Sri Lankan chronicles illuminate Mauryan history, Andhra Buddhism and Sangam chronology, while Jain texts and Smritis provide information on Andhra traditions and Gupta-age social and legal institutions.
Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa
are Sri Lankan Pali chronicles that provide the Gajabahu-Senguttuvan synchronism used in dating the Sangam age.
The Aitareya Brahmana gives the earliest literary reference, the Mahabharata associates the Andhras with the Kauravas, and Buddhist texts use the term Andhakaratta.

secs.t: Earliest inscriptions - script and decipherment

x: Kharosthi was a right-to-left north-western script, represented in the Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts, and its decipherment drew on bilingual Indo-Greek coins.
Andhrapatha first appears epigraphically in the
Maidavolu copper plates of Pallava Sivaskandavarma
, composed in Prakrit and dated to about 300 CE.
Tamil-Brahmi or Tamizhi is dated to approximately
the 3rd century BCE
, supporting the early chronology of the Sangam corpus.

secs.t: Archaeologists, surveyors and historians

x: John Marshall
, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of the Indus Valley Civilisation in 1924.
James Burgess is associated with
the Buddhist stupas of Amaravati and Jaggayyapeta
and with surveys of western Indian cave temples.
The correct order is Brahmi decipherment in 1837, Walter Elliot’s Amaravati work in 1845, discovery of Nagarjunakonda in 1926, and Wheeler’s Arikamedu excavation in 1945.

secs.t: Coins as source

x: Punch-marked coins were recently found at Balirajgarh in
Madhubani district of Bihar
Ship-motif coins of
Vasisthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri
indicate the importance of maritime trade during the Satavahana period.
The cited account associates ship-motif coins with Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni and states that no later ruler issued them.

secs.t: Dating methods - principle

x: Radiocarbon dating
measures the decay of carbon-14 in organic remains.
Dendrochronology determines age by counting annual growth rings in trees.
Thermoluminescence measures the light released when pottery or other burnt material is heated; the radiation absorbed since its last firing is thereby assessed.
Counting annual tree rings is the principle of dendrochronology, not stratigraphy.

secs.t: AP sources - Amaravati, Bhattiprolu, Nagarjunakonda, Alluru

x: The
inscriptions and stupas
of Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda are key sources for the history of ancient Andhra.
The 13th Major Rock Edict of Ashoka lists the Andhras among the peoples within the
Mauryan Empire
Indica is regarded as the first foreign work to mention the Andhras, and Ashoka's Thirteenth Major Rock Edict names them.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Megasthenes, the Periplus, Ptolemy and Pliny all provide information relevant to ancient Andhra; the associated references are about 30 Andhra forts, Koddura, Masulia and Satavahana Andhra respectively.
Inscriptions are regarded as the most reliable source, and foreign accounts supplement the record where Indian texts are silent.
The copied inscriptions span the
Satavahana to Vijayanagara periods

rows.title: Sources for the history of Andhra - inscriptions, coins, literature and foreign accounts
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-1

secs.t: Inscriptions of Andhra - dynasty, language and what each records

x: Exam angle: Manchikallu + Mayidavolu = Pallavas; Alluru = multiple gifts (Karle, Veerapuram, Ramagiri were the distractors, G2 2017).

The Nagarjunakonda inscription records Santamula’s foundation of the kingdom; Alluru records donations and feudatory status; Manchikallu records the Pallava conquest; Mayidavolu records Pallava rule over Andhrapatha.
Jaggayyapeta records Buddhist donations, Gurazala belongs to the dynasty’s last phase, and Manchikallu records Simhavarman’s conquest of Vijayapuri.

secs.t: Literary sources on Andhra - text and what it reveals

x: The Matsya Purana mentions 30 Satavahana kings and a period of 456 years.
These Jatakas refer to the Andhra region and state that Kharavela was defeated by the Asmaka king Satakarni.
Gathasaptasati is associated with Hala, written in Prakrit, consists of 700 verses, and reveals social life and early Telugu words.
Both Kashikhandam and Haravilasam, associated with Srinatha, reveal sea trade during the Reddi period.

secs.t: Copper-plate grants - donor, donee, land and tax details

x: Copper-plate grants generally record a king granting a village or land to Brahmins, together with tax exemptions.
Vishnukundin grants measured land in ‘
nivartanas
The Mayidavolu plates are Prakrit copper-plate grants issued by Pallava Sivaskandavarman and also contain the earliest inscriptional use of ‘Andhrapatha’.

secs.t: Archaeological sources - stupa sites and habitation mounds

x: Salihundam, Guntupalli and Jaggayyapeta are stupa sites.
Kotilingala, Kondapur and Gudiwada Dibba are associated with habitation or mint evidence, while the other options mix categories.
Gudiwada Dibba is a habitation mound showing occupation from the Mauryan to the Satavahana period.
All four classifications are correct.

secs.t: Roman coin hoard find-spots in Andhra

x: Peddabankur yielded coins of Augustus and Tiberius; Gutiparti yielded a coin of Claudius; Yeleswaram and Akkinapally are in Nalgonda; and Nagavarappadu is in Khammam.
The gold coin of Constantine found at Kudali Sangameswaram is dated to the period

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both statements are true, and the need to verify foreign accounts against the Puranas, Prakrit inscriptions and coins explains why they are used cautiously.
The finds of punch-marked coins and Greek-inscribed seals at Rajghat are associated with the Banaras Hindu University area at Varanasi.
Arikamedu is identified as a Roman trade centre on the east coast, while Rajghat at Varanasi is associated with punch-marked coins and Greek-inscribed seals.

rows.title: Stone Age cultures - Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic, Chalcolithic sites of India

secs.t: FIRST evidence → site/region

x: Mayiladumparai in Krishnagiri district
of Tamil Nadu has yielded the earliest AMS-dated iron evidence in India, dated to 2172 BCE.
H. D. Sankalia associated the first harvesting of rice in Andhra with the Iron, or Megalithic, Age.
Lehuradeva in Uttar Pradesh provides evidence of early rice cultivation dating to about
6500 BCE
; Koldihwa is another associated site.

secs.t: AP Stone Age sites → phase

x: Billasurgam caves in Kurnool district belong to the Palaeolithic phase and have yielded stone tools, rare bone tools and animal fossils.
Kurnool caves and Jwalapuram are Upper Palaeolithic sites, Nagarjunakonda has Lower Palaeolithic tools and microliths, and Yerragondapalem has quartzite blades.
Robert Bruce Foote
is regarded as the pioneer of Andhra Pradesh prehistory and is associated with Billasurgam and the Pennar region.

secs.t: Palaeolithic tool techniques and sites

x: The Middle Palaeolithic is characterized by flake tools, prepared cores such as the Levallois technique, scrapers, borers and points.
Patne
, along with Kurnool caves, Jwalapuram and Baghor I and III, is associated with Upper Palaeolithic blades and bone tools.
The Sohan valley lies in Pakistan Punjab, followed broadly by Didwana in Rajasthan, Hunsgi in Karnataka and Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu.

secs.t: Megalithic burials - types and AP sites → district

x: Megalithic burials were marked by large stones and commonly contained grave goods such as weapons, tools and pottery; several local names were used for them in Andhra Pradesh.
A cist is a stone-slab box chamber; a dolmen is a table-like chamber; a sarcophagus is a clay or terracotta coffin; and a menhir is an upright memorial stone.

secs.t: Mesolithic sites and microlith centres → region

x: Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama are Mesolithic sites in the
Ganga plain of Uttar Pradesh
, particularly the Pratapgarh region.
Lekhahia and Baghai Khor are rock-shelter sites in the Vindhyas of Uttar Pradesh.
Giddaluru, Nagarjunakonda and Kondapur are Andhra microlith centres, and their discovery is associated with Robert Bruce Foote.

secs.t: Rock art - Bhimbetka and painting themes

x: The rock shelters of Bhimbetka were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003.
Bhimbetka shows continuous habitation extending from the Lower Palaeolithic period to medieval times.

Bhimbetka contains Upper Palaeolithic art in about 300 caves and shelters, while its Mesolithic art includes hunting and basket-carrying scenes and later became more static after contact with Malwa's Chalcolithic farmers.

secs.t: Neolithic sites → region and distinctive find

x: Mehrgarh is associated with early farming and mud-brick houses, Burzahom with pit dwellings and dog burials, Chirand with bone and antler tools, and Utnoor with ash mounds.
Gufkral is associated with Kashmir's pit dwellings, Koldihwa with early rice in Uttar Pradesh, and Utnoor with ash mounds in Telangana.
Eastern Neolithic sites are associated with
pointed-butt celts and shouldered axes
, showing links with South-East Asia.

secs.t: Chalcolithic cultures of India → type site

x: Ahar-Banas 2800–1500 BCE, Kayatha 2450–1700 BCE, Malwa 1900–1400 BCE and Jorwe about 1400–700 BCE.
Chalcolithic cultures were not confined to a single period: some preceded the Harappan civilisation, many followed it and some overlapped with it.

Ahar is associated with south-eastern Rajasthan and sites such as Ahar and Gilund; Malwa with Madhya Pradesh and Navdatoli, Eran and Kayatha; and Jorwe with Maharashtra and Inamgaon, Nevasa and Daimabad.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Karivalamvanthanallur shows occupation passing directly from the Microlithic to the Iron/Early Historic age, without a Neolithic or Chalcolithic phase.
Panayal in
Kasaragod, Kerala
, is associated with a megalithic rock-cut burial chamber.
Karivalamvanthanallur
in Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, is noted for a sequence from the Microlithic directly to the Iron Age, skipping the Neolithic stage.

rows.title: Pre-historic cultures of Andhra - Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and Megalithic sites
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-2

secs.t: Palaeolithic sites - river valley and district

x: Robert Bruce Foote discovered the relevant Palaeolithic tools and also found Palaeolithic tools at Pallavaram near Chennai.
The Billa Surgam caves are in Kurnool district, now Nandyal, and have yielded stone and bone tools.
The
Kurnool caves and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi
are identified as the only Indian Upper Palaeolithic bone-tool sites in this context.

secs.t: Mesolithic / Microlithic implement centres

x: The Mesolithic is also called the Microlithic period, and its tools were produced by flaking and chipping.
The tools are described as resembling South Indian and Caspian microliths.

secs.t: Neolithic-Chalcolithic sites - present district/state and features

x: Utnur is in Mahbubnagar, Palavoy in Anantapur, Ramapuram in Kurnool, and Sanganakallu–Tekkalakota in Bellary, Karnataka.
Utnur in Mahbubnagar, Telangana, is associated with a Neolithic ash mound.
All three pairs are correctly matched.
Patapadu
is the standard site associated with Chalcolithic evidence in Andhra Pradesh, particularly painted pottery.

secs.t: Tools by stage - type and raw material

x: Lower Palaeolithic tools were handaxes, cleavers and choppers; Middle Palaeolithic tools included flakes and scrapers; Upper Palaeolithic tools included blades and bone tools; Mesolithic tools were microliths.

The sequence proceeds from quartzite and limestone in the Lower Palaeolithic through chert-based materials, silica-rich stone and bone, Mesolithic microlithic materials, and finally copper in the Chalcolithic.

secs.t: Megalithic phase - pottery, iron, habitation sites

x: The Megalithic culture in this context is identified with the Iron Age, and black-and-red ware is its characteristic pottery.
Glass mirrors
were not included in the list.
Nagarjunakonda
was identified as a centre among the Megalithic habitation sites.
The other groups contain Palaeolithic, Neolithic-Chalcolithic or cave sites.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: AMS dating at Mayiladumparai has placed the Iron Age in South India at approximately
2100 BCE
, earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
All three combinations are correct.
Manchirevula is associated with
Hyderabad
and has yielded Upper Palaeolithic petroglyphs and a quartz tool.

rows.title: Pre-Harappan and Early Harappan cultures - Mehrgarh, Amri, Kot Diji, Kalibangan-I

secs.t: Early farming sites - earliest settled life, Stone Age-to-Harappan continuity

x: Mehrgarh is located in Baluchistan near the Bolan Pass and is associated with the earliest settled life in the subcontinent.
Mehrgarh
, dating to about 7000 BCE, provides evidence of the earliest agriculture, domestication and pottery in the subcontinent.
Mehrgarh shows Stone Age-to-Harappan continuity, Kili Gul Muhammad lies in the Quetta valley, and Rana Ghundai lies in the Zhob-Loralai valley.

secs.t: Early Harappan cultures → type site

x: The Early or Pre-Harappan phase is dated to approximately
in the current periodisation.
The Early Harappan phase is called the
Regionalisation Era
and corresponds to the Hakra phase.
Kot Diji
in Sindh was a fortified pre-Harappan settlement destroyed by fire and yielded many stone implements.
Mitathal
is associated with the pre-Harappan, Mature Harappan and Late Harappan phases.

secs.t: Kalibangan-I findings

x: Kalibangan is located in Rajasthan on the
Ghaggar
Kalibangan means “
black bangles
The pre-Harappan level at Kalibangan yielded the earliest known ploughed field, whose criss-cross furrows indicate mixed cropping.
The Mature-phase fire altars came later, not in the earlier pre-Harappan level.
B.
B. Lal and B. K. Thapar
excavated Kalibangan from 1961 to 1969.

secs.t: Transition from Early to Mature Harappan - continuity debate

x: Pottery and buildings at Kalibangan and Kot Diji anticipate Mature Harappan forms, supporting gradual and internal urbanisation.
All three statements are correct and indicate technological, architectural and symbolic continuity before the Mature Harappan phase.

John Marshall proposed indigenous evolution; E. J. H. Mackay suggested migration from Sumer; Mortimer Wheeler supported diffusion from West Asia; regional evolution from Mehrgarh is the current consensus.

secs.t: Crops, animals and crafts at Mehrgarh by period

x: Period I, the aceramic Neolithic phase around 7000 BCE, yielded barley and wheat along with sheep, goats and cattle.
Pottery began in
Period II
, which is also associated with cotton.
Copper working, wheel-made painted pottery and beads appear in
Period III and later
phases at Mehrgarh.

secs.t: Excavator of each early site

x: Amri was excavated by N. G. Majumdar in 1929 and later by J.-M. Casal.
Kot Diji was associated with Ghurye’s discovery and F. A. Khan’s 1955 work; Banawali with R. S. Bisht; Mitathal with Suraj Bhan; and Rana Ghundai with E. J. Ross.
W. A. Fairservis
excavated both Kili Gul Muhammad and Damb Sadaat.

secs.t: Pottery traditions of the Early Harappan phase

x: Northern Black Polished Ware
is not one of them.
The Early Harappan phase had distinct regional traditions, while Mature Harappan pottery became more uniform.

secs.t: Burial practices at Mehrgarh

x: At Mehrgarh, the dead were often buried under or near houses in a flexed position, accompanied by ornaments, tools and sometimes goats as grave goods.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rakhigarhi covers approximately 550 hectares and shows continuous occupation from the
Early to the Mature Harappan phase
Haryana protected Tighrana and Mitathal in
Bhiwani
district.
Evidence from Mehrgarh and Early Harappan sites supports local growth and regional evolution, rather than an exclusively Mesopotamian origin.

rows.title: Indus Valley Civilization - discovery, chronology, geographical extent, boundary sites
sub: Group-II S1-2: Salient features of the Indus Valley Civilization - extent, chronology and major sites

secs.t: Site → river and present state/district - Indian vs Pakistani sites

x: Exam angle: "Kalibangan is located in" - answer
Hanumangarh
Mohenjodaro lies in Sindh province of Pakistan, near Larkana, on the Indus River.
Lothal lies at the Bhogava–Sabarmati confluence in Ahmedabad district of Gujarat, near the head of the Gulf of Cambay.
Kalibangan is in Hanumangarh, Rajasthan; Ropar is on the Sutlej in Punjab; and Alamgirpur is on the Hindon in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh.
Rakhigarhi is in Hisar district, Banawali in the Hisar–Fatehabad region, Mandi in Muzaffarnagar and Dholavira in Kutch.
The
Ghaggar–Hakra system
had the highest concentration of settlements, with about 250 sites, of which six were cities.

secs.t: Site → discoverer/excavator and year

x: Exam angle: "Excavator of Lothal" -
S.R. Rao
R. D. Banerji
excavated Mohenjodaro in 1922; later work was associated with Mackay, K. N. Dikshit and Marshall.
N. G. Majumdar excavated Chanhudaro, Y. D. Sharma Ropar, J. P. Joshi Surkotada and R. S. Bisht Banawali.
Charles Masson described the ruins during 1826–38, railway ballast use occurred in 1857, J. Fleet published seals in 1912 and Sahni found Harappa in 1921–22.
The excavation years were Harappa—1921, Mohenjodaro—1922, Chanhudaro—1931 and Lothal—1954.

secs.t: Harappan vs non-Harappan sites

x: Sutkagendor
was a Harappan westernmost coastal town or port on the Makran coast.
Alamgirpur
, a Late Harappan site in Meerut district of Uttar Pradesh, is identified as the easternmost Harappan site.
Surkotada is a fortified Harappan site in Kutch associated with horse bones; the interpretation is disputed.
Kot Diji
has both pre-Harappan and Harappan levels.

secs.t: Other names - Mesopotamian name, local names

x: Lothal is known as Mini Harappa, not the City of the Dead.
Mohenjodaro
means ‘Mound of the Dead’.
Kalibangan means ‘black bangles’.

secs.t: Boundary sites

x: Manda
in Jammu and Kashmir is regarded as the northern boundary site.
Manda is the northern site, Daimabad the southern site, Alamgirpur the eastern site and Sutkagendor the western site.
The civilisation is estimated in the material to have covered about 1.3 million square kilometres and supported about five million people.
The
Harappan Civilisation
is described as the largest Bronze Age civilisation by area, extending over roughly 1.3 million square kilometres.

secs.t: Chronology and origin theories → scholar

x: The Late Harappan phase, dated to 1900–1300 BCE, is associated with
de-urbanisation and the OCP and Cemetery-H cultures
Kot Diji, Amri and Sothi-Siswal
are associated with the Early Harappan phase, which was characterised by village settlements.
John Marshall proposed 3250–2750 BCE on the basis of cross-dating with Mesopotamian evidence.
D. P. Agrawal's radiocarbon-based dating placed the civilisation approximately in

secs.t: Naming debate and non-Aryan character

x: The term Harappan is preferred because Harappa was the first site found and the civilisation extended well beyond the Indus valley.
The Mature Harappan culture was urban, whereas the Rigvedic culture was predominantly pastoral.
The stated comparison is: Indus Valley—urban, Rigvedic—pastoral, Later Vedic—agrarian and Medieval—landlordism.

secs.t: Largest sites, recent excavations, UNESCO status

x: Haryana is stated to have
seven
protected Harappan sites: Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Bhirrana, Kunal, Siswal, Mitathal and Tighrana.

Dholavira is the only Harappan site on the World Heritage List, Rakhigarhi remains tentative, Mohenjo-daro has been a UNESCO site since 1980, and Tighrana and Mitathal received Haryana’s protection in June 2026.
Harappa was discovered in 1921, Mohenjo-daro became a UNESCO site in 1980, Dholavira later became the first IVC site on the UNESCO list, and Tighrana and Mitathal were protected in June 2026.

secs.t: Site-specific findings

x: Lothal
has yielded rice husks, fire altars, a Persian Gulf seal and an ivory scale, in addition to its bead-making activity.
Mohenjodaro
has yielded the bronze Dancing Girl, the Priest-King, the Pashupati seal, the Great Bath, the Great Granary and an assembly hall.
Lothal
is associated with the dockyard, bead factory, rice husk, fire altars, Persian Gulf seal and terracotta ship.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Harappan Civilization was the largest of the contemporary Bronze Age civilizations—Egypt and Mesopotamia—when compared by area.
Dholavira
was the first Indus Valley Civilization site to be included on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Mound 7 yielded 56 skeletons, including a woman approximately 4,600 years old, and the skeletons were transferred to the Anthropological Survey of India, Kolkata, under an MoU.

rows.title: IVC town planning - grid layout, citadel and lower town, drainage, Great Bath, granaries
sub: Group-II S1-3: IVC town planning, drainage, granaries and the Great Bath

secs.t: Granaries → site and structure type

x: Exam angle: "The great granary has been found at" -
Mohenjodaro
The Great Granary, regarded as the largest building at the site, was found at
Mohenjodaro
Harappa had two rows of six granaries each near the river, together with circular working platforms and single-roomed barracks.
Lothal
had a warehouse on a raised platform beside the dock; seal impressions were also associated with the warehouse.

secs.t: Town planning hallmarks - grid, orientation, divisions

x: Exam angle: statement questions - "same size bricks for all constructions" and "houses mostly single-storey" are both
false
Organised town planning, including grid-patterned streets and civic divisions, is a hallmark of the Indus Valley Civilization.
The Harappan grid plan consisted of north–south and east–west streets crossing at right angles, dividing cities into blocks; main streets were about 30 feet or 10 metres wide.

secs.t: Great Bath - site, size, materials, waterproofing

x: The Great Bath was situated
on the citadel mound
of Mohenjodaro.
The Great Bath measured approximately 12 metres by 7 metres and was about 2.4 metres deep.
The Great Bath was built with burnt bricks set in gypsum mortar and was waterproofed with a layer of bitumen.
The Great Bath had flights of steps at its north and south ends.

secs.t: Building materials - burnt vs mud brick, brick ratio

x: The standard brick ratio was 1:2:4 in the order of thickness, width and length.
Burnt bricks were common, while mud bricks were used for fillings, platforms and at Kalibangan.
House bricks measured about 7 × 14 × 28 cm and city-wall bricks about 10 × 20 × 40 cm.

secs.t: Houses - courtyard, wells, bathrooms, doors

x: Rooms around a central courtyard and bathrooms connected to drains were features of houses, while staircases indicate that some houses were multi-storeyed.
Doors and windows generally opened onto side lanes rather than main streets, indicating concern for privacy.
Wells were found inside houses or neighbourhoods, and
Mohenjodaro
is noted for having the greatest number of wells.

secs.t: Citadel and lower town - sites and exceptions

x: Dholavira
was divided into a citadel, a middle town and a lower town; the citadel itself included a castle and bailey.
Kalibangan had a fortified lower town, Lothal had both divisions in one enclosure, and Sutkagendor had a citadel and lower city.
The western citadel stood on a raised, fortified platform and contained public buildings, while the eastern lower town was associated with commoners’ houses.

secs.t: Drainage - covered drains, manholes, soak pits

x: The planned drainage system
is regarded as the most advanced feature of Indus Valley Civilization towns.
Wastewater generally moved from house drains into street drains and then into soak pits or main channels.
Covered drains had manholes for maintenance, were built with burnt bricks and terracotta pipes, and used street slopes for natural flow.

secs.t: Special structures → site

x: The dockyard, whose function has also been debated as possibly an irrigation tank, is associated with
Lothal
Fire altars have been identified at Kalibangan, including seven such altars, and at Lothal.
The largest inscription is the ten-sign signboard found at the
North Gate of Dholavira
The stadium or ceremonial ground at Dholavira measured approximately
283 × 47 metres

secs.t: Dholavira - three-part plan, water harvesting, rock-cut features

x: Dholavira had giant reservoirs supplied through bunds, check-dams and channels, along with dams and embankments.
Dholavira had
a stadium or ceremonial ground and a signboard inscription
in addition to its reservoirs and related hydraulic works.
Dholavira used sandstone and limestone blocks for major construction and had partly rock-cut reservoirs, while Mohenjodaro and Harappa are contrasted with it for baked-brick construction.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Dholavira had 16 reservoirs covering about 10 per cent of the site, and the largest measured approximately 73 × 29 metres.
Standardisation of bricks, grid planning and drainage points to civic authority and considerable early engineering skill.
The absence of clearly identified palaces or temples does not disprove civic authority; standardised urban planning instead suggests it.

rows.title: Major Harappan sites and their signature finds - Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Chanhudaro, Lothal, Dholavira, Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi, Surkotada, Rangpur

secs.t: Water management finds → site

x: Dholavira
had 16 reservoirs, dams, embankments and stepwells cut in sandstone, demonstrating an elaborate water-management system.
Dholavira's reservoirs covered about 10 per cent of the site, its largest was approximately 73 × 29 metres, and Mohenjodaro had the most wells.
Lothal is associated with an artificial tidal dockyard, though some interpretations identify it as an irrigation tank.

secs.t: Largest sites and current relevance

x: The genetic finding has been interpreted as pointing towards indigenous ancestry and challenging the Aryan-invasion view.
The National Maritime Heritage Complex is being developed at Lothal in Gujarat.
The
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
is developing the complex as Asia's largest maritime heritage museum.
India and
the Netherlands
signed an MoU concerning the National Maritime Heritage Complex in 2026.

secs.t: Site-specific seals and sculptures

x: The Bronze Dancing Girl is one of the best-known sculptures discovered at
Mohenjodaro
Harappa has yielded a red sandstone male torso, a bronze dog chasing a deer, and bullock carts.
The Pashupati seal is from Mohenjodaro, the ship on a seal from Lothal, carts with seated drivers from Chanhudaro, and the red sandstone male torso from Harappa.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The latest reported excavation yielded five complete skeletons of individuals aged about 30–40 years and three fragmentary burials.

rows.title: IVC economy - agriculture, crops, domesticated animals, internal and external trade, Meluhha
sub: Group-II S1-4: IVC economy - agriculture, crafts, trade, seals, weights and measures

secs.t: External trade partners - Meluhha, Dilmun, Magan and their modern identification

x: Exam angle: "In ancient times the Indus region was known as" → Meluhha; distractors Dilmun, Makan, Surkotada.
Harappan seals, beads and weights are reported from Oman, Bahrain, Iraq, Iran and Egypt, indicating extensive external trade links.
Copper came from Khetri and Oman, tin from Afghanistan, gold from Kolar and Afghanistan, and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan through Shortughai.

secs.t: Animals known and unknown - domesticated vs wild

x: Exam angle: "Which animal was not known to the Indus people" → Horse.
Exam angle: "Which animal is not depicted on Harappan seals" → Horse.
The unicorn is the most common seal motif; cow and lion are absent from seals; and a horse figure has been reported from Lothal terracotta.

secs.t: Metals known and unknown → source region

x: Exam angle: "Which metal has not been found at Harappan sites" → Iron.
Carnelian and agate came from Saurashtra, steatite from south Rajasthan, chert from Rohri, and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan through Shortughai.
Khetri supplied copper, Shortughai supplied lapis lazuli from Badakhshan, Kolar supplied gold, and the Saurashtra coast and Balakot supplied shells.

secs.t: Trade evidence - boat models, dockyard, Indus seals abroad, Persian Gulf seal

x: The Lothal dockyard was brick-lined, measured approximately 218 m by 37 m, had sluice gates and lay in the Bhal region of Gujarat.
Indus seals have been found at Susa, Ur, Nippur, Failaka and Bahrain, demonstrating contacts beyond the Indus region.
The cylinder seals at Mohenjodaro and reserved slip ware at Harappa are evidence of Mesopotamian contacts.

secs.t: Crops cultivated → site of evidence; FIRST cotton cultivation

x: Wheat is evidenced at Harappa and Mehrgarh, barley at Banawali, rice at Lothal and Rangpur, and garlic at Balu.
Lothal has yielded rice husks dated to about 2500 BCE, regarded as the earliest evidence of rice cultivation in Gujarat.
Wheat, barley, peas, sesame and mustard
are among the crops cultivated by the Harappans.

secs.t: Crafts and industries → centre

x: Bead-making was concentrated at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Kalibangan; shell work at Nageshwar, Balakot and Lothal; copper and bronze work at Harappa, Mohenjodaro and Lothal; and spinning and weaving at Mohenjodaro and Chanhudaro.
Chanhudaro had factories producing beads, bangles, shell ornaments, metal objects, seals and toys.
Kerala-no-dhoro is associated with salt production, Kot Bala with the earliest furnace, and Kuntasi with ivory, copper and bead workshops.

secs.t: Agricultural evidence - ploughed field, terracotta plough, irrigation debate

x: Kalibangan
has yielded the earliest evidence of a ploughed field with furrows and mixed cropping.
Terracotta plough models were found at Banawali and Bahawalpur, a clay plough at Rakhigarhi, well irrigation at Allahdino, and reservoirs at Dholavira.
Wells at Allahdino, reservoirs at Dholavira and flood irrigation are evidenced, whereas conclusive evidence of canal irrigation is absent.

secs.t: Internal trade - raw material source areas → material sourced

x: South Rajasthan was a source of steatite.
Sutkagendor on the Makran coast of Baluchistan, near the Iran border, is regarded as the
westernmost Harappan site

secs.t: Seals - material, shape, motifs, find sites, uses

x: Exam angle: bull seal → Mohenjodaro.
The unicorn is the most common motif; square seals combine animals and inscriptions, rectangular seals carry only inscriptions, and a button seal was found at Lothal.
Some accounts, including the cited examination treatment, identify the
humpless bull
as the commonest animal represented on Harappan seals, while the unicorn is also widely identified as the most common motif.

secs.t: Weights and measures - chert weights, binary/decimal, scale finds

x: Exam angle: "In which IVC city was a scale discovered" -
Lothal
Exam angle: "In which city was a scale discovered" → Lothal; ivory scale → Lothal.
The ivory scale or balance was found at Lothal, the shell scale at Mohenjodaro, the copper scale at Harappa, and the shell angle-measuring object in Saurashtra.

secs.t: Ports and trading posts linked with West Asia

x: Shortughai was located in Afghanistan and functioned as a trading colony for lapis lazuli; it was not on the Sindh coast.
Lothal had a brick-lined tidal dockyard measuring 218 m by 37 m, equipped with sluice gates and linked to the Gulf of Khambhat.
Sutkagendor, situated on the Makran coast of Balochistan, was the westernmost Indus site and served as a port on the Dasht river.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Indus Valley Civilization is associated with the first cotton cultivation, Lothal with the world's earliest tidal dockyard, and Kalibangan with the earliest ploughed field.
The discovery supports the view of Dilmun as
a trade hub linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilization
The 2026 compilations specifically repeated the Lothal dockyard, the Persian Gulf seal, and the Meluhha–Dilmun–Magan trade table.

rows.title: IVC seals, weights and measures, Harappan script (undeciphered features)

secs.t: Seals and sealings - material, shapes, uses, value as the main source

x: Exam angle: long-distance communication → "seals and sealings"; distinctive feature of IVC → seals.
Since the Harappan script remains unread, seals are regarded as the most distinctive artefacts and an important source of information about Harappan society.
Seals and sealings
served as a means of long-distance communication, in addition to their commercial and identity-related functions.

secs.t: Weights - material, shape, numerical system

x: Lower denominations followed the binary sequence 1:2:4:8:16:32:64, after which decimal multiples such as 160, 320 and 640 were used.
The distribution of similar weights over about 8,00,000 square kilometres suggests
central regulation and standardized trade
practices.
Ivory weight balances are associated with Mohenjodaro and Lothal, chert trade weights have been reported from Rakhigarhi, and Harappan weights were generally cubical.

secs.t: Harappan script - direction, decipherment status, number of signs, pictographic nature

x: Harappan inscriptions were generally written from
right to left
, as indicated partly by cramped spacing at the left end.
Estimates of the number of Harappan signs range from about 400 to 700, while around 400 signs are commonly cited.
Harappan signs occur on seals, tablets, pottery, copper plates and tools.

secs.t: Decipherment attempts → scholar

x: The Proto-Dravidian hypothesis is associated with Iravatham Mahadevan and Asko Parpola; the Indo-Aryan view with S.R. Rao; Proto-Munda has weak linguistic support; and the isolate view considers decipherment impossible for now.
S.R. Rao
proposed the Indo-Aryan or early Sanskrit interpretation, which remains a minority view.

secs.t: Longest inscription and Dholavira signboard

x: J. Fleet noticed the unknown symbols in 1912; Dholavira was excavated by R.S. Bisht in 1990; it entered the UNESCO list in 2021; and the Rakhigarhi report belongs to the later 2026 reporting context.
Rakhigarhi
is on the Tentative List, whereas Dholavira is the only Harappan site on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Uniform seals and weights indicate
standardisation and regulated trade
across the Harappan cultural region.
The language underlying the undeciphered script remains debated, particularly between Dravidian and Indo-Aryan interpretations.
The Indus script is considered one of the world’s earliest writing systems, although it remains undeciphered.

rows.title: IVC society and polity - social stratification debate, burial practices, absence of temples/palaces

secs.t: Burial practices → site (extended, pot, joint/double, fractional; R-37, Cemetery-H, Sanauli, Lothal, Kalibangan)

x: Exam angle: double burial → Lothal; Sanauli → human burials.
Rakhigarhi Mound 7 is a burial plot from which
56 skeletons were recovered
, including the remains of a woman approximately 4,600 years old.
Harappa is associated with the R37 cemetery, Mohenjodaro with fractional burial, and Ropar with a dog buried alongside a man.

secs.t: Social stratification evidence - house sizes, citadel vs lower town, burial goods

x: Single-roomed barracks are reported at
Harappa
and form part of the evidence for variation in building types and living arrangements.
There is no textual evidence for a rigid caste system in the Harappan civilisation; caste is considered to have crystallised in the Later Vedic period.
Female skeletons at Rakhigarhi were found with jasper and agate beads and shell bangles.

secs.t: Polity debate - priest rule, merchant class, city-state vs centralised state

x: The priest-rule interpretation draws on the citadel, Great Bath and steatite Priest-King.
Trade-driven uniformity, together with the absence of identifiable kings and palaces, has been used to argue for merchant elites or civic administrators.
The city-state argument points to the existence of several large cities without a clearly identified single capital.

secs.t: Uniformity as evidence of central authority - bricks, weights, seals, planning

x: All four features—standard brick proportions, binary weights, uniform seals and grid planning—are cited as evidence of Harappan-wide standardisation.
Grid-plan towns and related standardisation extended across approximately
8,00,000 square kilometres
The
construction of walls, platforms and reservoirs
indicates the mobilisation and coordination of labour on a considerable scale.
Both statements are true, and the widespread standardisation of construction, measurement, sealing and urban planning provides the principal basis for inferring central authority.

secs.t: Absence of monumental temples/palaces - interpretations

x: The statement that Harappan cities possessed great palaces and temples is incorrect.
One interpretation is that worship occurred in domestic or open-air settings and that political power was not personalised in a king.
The Great Bath
, along with structures such as granaries and pillared halls, is interpreted as a civic public structure.

secs.t: Dress, ornaments and cosmetics

x: Harappan ornaments used materials such as gold, silver, ivory, copper, lapis lazuli, carnelian and faience.
Chanhudaro is associated with lipstick, while bronze mirrors, ivory combs and collyrium sticks were used as cosmetic or grooming items.
Harappan depictions and artefacts indicate varied hairstyles, and men with trimmed beards and shaved upper lips are described.

secs.t: Pastimes - toys, dice, games

x: Cubical dice, similar in form to modern dice, have been found at
Harappa
Terracotta toy carts, animals, marbles, rattles, whistles and spinning tops are reported.
Chanhudaro is associated with a
toy factory
and is also noted for lipstick and shell craft.
All four are included among the proposed Harappan pastimes and cultural activities, although hunting and fishing are specifically regarded as speculative.

secs.t: Warfare and weapons - scarcity debate

x: Maces, axes, spears, and bows and arrows made of copper and bronze are all associated with Harappan weapons.
Harappan weapons are relatively few and simple, leading to the usual interpretation of a comparatively peaceful society.
The huddled skeletons at Mohenjodaro were once read as massacre victims but are now interpreted as representing
multiple burials

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Harappan social and political interpretations are inferred mainly from material remains, and the script has not supplied the names of rulers.
Harappan polity is characterised as corporate in comparison, while the Later Vedic polity is described as a hereditary monarchy with declining Sabha and Samiti.
Mound 7 yielded 56 skeletons, including a woman approximately 4,600 years old, and the remains were transferred under an MoU for anthropological study.

rows.title: IVC art and craft - bronze Dancing Girl, Priest-King, terracotta figurines, bead-making, pottery

secs.t: Bead-making → centres + materials

x: Exam angle: bead industry located at → Chanhudaro.

Chanhudaro had a bead-making factory, Lothal had bead workshops and exported carnelian beads, Kalibangan was a bead-making centre, and Rakhigarhi had a gemstone factory with over 3,000 semi-precious stones.
Indus bead-makers used
carnelian, agate, jasper, steatite, lapis lazuli, faience and gold
Carnelian came from Saurashtra, carnelian beads were exported to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf, and Lothal had bead workshops associated with this trade.

secs.t: Pottery - colour, design motifs, perforated jars

x: Indus pottery was wheel-made; red pottery with black painted designs was typical, alongside plain red and painted red-and-black varieties.
Perforated jars had a large hole at the base and several small holes over the wall, probably for straining liquor.
Harappan pottery was predominantly red ware decorated with black painted designs.

secs.t: Lost-wax (cire perdue) technique - which objects

x: In the lost-wax process, a wax model is coated with clay, heated to remove the wax, filled with molten metal, and finally freed by removing the clay mould.
The Dancing Girl, the copper dog and bird of Lothal, and the bronze bull of Kalibangan are associated with the lost-wax technique.

secs.t: Terracotta figurines - mother goddess, animals, toy carts

x: The great humpless bull, Chanhudaro toy carts, whistles, rattles, birds, gamesmen and discs are associated with them.
These terracotta representations have been associated with
Gujarat and Kalibangan

secs.t: Metal crafts - copper, bronze, gold, silver objects

x: The dog chasing a deer is a bronze object from Harappa; the dog and bird are copper objects from Lothal; the bull or ox is from Kalibangan; and the larger animal group is from Daimabad.
Copper, bronze and silver vessels, gold and silver necklaces at Allahdino, and a gold foundry with an active furnace at Rakhigarhi are all documented features.

secs.t: Seal carving as art - motifs

x: The
unicorn
was the most common animal motif on Indus steatite seals; bull, elephant, tiger and rhinoceros were also represented.
Indus seals were commonly made of steatite, displayed animal and Pashupati motifs, and carried short script lines.

secs.t: Faience and shell work → site

x: Shell-working evidence is associated with Nageshwar, Balakot and Lothal, while Chanhudaro had a shell-ornament factory.
Shell bangles have been reported from
Rakhigarhi
burials.
Faience was used for
beads, bangles and glazed ware
, and its association with mosaic glass provides an early clue to glass-making.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: NCERT is to restore the original image of the Dancing Girl in its new Class 9 Art textbook.
The naturalistic quality of bronze and stone sculpture indicates advanced metallurgical skill and craft specialisation.

rows.title: IVC religion - Pashupati seal, Mother Goddess, tree and animal worship, fire altars
sub: Group-II S1-5: IVC society, religion, art and the Harappan script

secs.t: Animal and bird worship - humped bull, unicorn, birds held sacred

x: The humped bull, mythical unicorn, elephant and tiger are identified as sacred animals in the Harappan religious tradition.
Pigeons and doves
were regarded as sacred birds in the Harappan religious tradition.
Both the humped bull motif and the horned-deity motif are stated to have appeared first in the
Early Harappan phase

secs.t: Tree worship - species depicted on seals

x: Exam angle: tree shape found on Indus seals → Pipal.
The
pipal
is the most depicted tree on Indus seals and appears in ritual scenes with human figures.
The pipal motif is traced to the Early Harappan phase and is shown in ritual scenes.

secs.t: Pashupati seal and horned deity - site, animals, posture, identification debate

x: Exam angle: the Indus people worshipped → Shiva.
The
deer
is represented below the central Pashupati figure, while the elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo occur around it.
A horned deity on a terracotta cake was found at
Kalibangan
; a clay mask of a horned god is also associated with Kalibangan and Gujarat.

secs.t: Mother Goddess figurines - distribution and interpretation

x: The terracotta female figurines are associated with fertility symbolism and are interpreted as evidence of
a fertility cult
Mother Goddess figurines have been found at Harappa, Kot Diji, Kalibangan and sites in Gujarat.
The Mother Goddess and Pashupati evidence together indicates the worship of both female and male deities.
Mother Goddess figurines
were the most important clay figures of the Indus Civilization.

secs.t: Nature of Harappan religion - secular vs religious, absence of temples, idol worship

x: Harappan religion was nature- and fertility-oriented and included the Mother Goddess, pipal and animals.
The civilization is described as predominantly secular, with religious elements present but not dominant.

All four statements are supported: figurines and images indicate idol worship; the Great Bath suggests ritual purification; yoga and meditation were practised; and belief in ghosts and evil forces is indicated.

secs.t: Fire altars - sites where found

x: Kalibangan
yielded a row of seven fire altars.
Both the assertion and reason are true.

secs.t: Phallic and yoni stone worship

x: Lingam and yoni symbols and round or pierced stones at Harappa are interpreted as fertility objects and possible early Shaivite elements.
Pits with animal remains may indicate sacrificial rituals, but this interpretation is speculative.

secs.t: Amulets, charms and burial customs - afterlife beliefs

x: The placement of pottery, ornaments, mirrors, beads and food with the dead indicates a belief in an afterlife and also reflects status differences.
Kalibangan has yielded
extended burials in oval pits, pot burials in circular pits and symbolic graves
Sonauli is associated with burials containing coffins and chariots, belonging to the Late Harappan or Copper Hoard phase.

secs.t: Continuities in later Hinduism

x: The Harappan Pashupati figure is regarded as a possible antecedent of the later Hindu representation of Shiva as Pashupati.
The association of Kalibangan fire altars with Vedic yajna remains debated and is not definitive.
Rig Vedic religion featured male nature gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna and open-air yajnas, with no temples or idols.

secs.t: Art → site + material

x: Exam angle: "Dancing Girl is made of" -
bronze
(the recorded key "1" is a key-position error).
The Dancing Girl is from Mohenjodaro and is bronze; the Priest-King is from Mohenjodaro and is steatite; the nude male torso is Harappan red sandstone; and the dancer torso is Harappan sandstone.
The Priest-King is from Mohenjodaro; the nude male torso and dog chasing a deer are from Harappa; and the copper dog and bird are from Lothal.

secs.t: Palaces and temples - secular or religious, classes, polity

x: Planned cities and drains suggest municipal governance, while the exact political structure remains uncertain.
No horse-drawn chariots have been found as clear evidence of Harappan warfare, and the proposed four-fold division is speculative.
Fortified citadels suggest the presence of some ruling group, but its nature—possibly priestly or merchant—is not conclusively established.

secs.t: Toys, games, ornaments and cosmetics

x: Terracotta cart
s, whistles, rattles, birds, animals, gamesmen and discs are among the known Harappan toys and game objects.
Lipstick has been identified at
Chanhudaro
Mirrors and combs were known.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both statements are true, and the undeciphered nature of Harappan records is a principal reason why the proto-Shiva interpretation remains debated rather than proven.
Rakhigarhi is noted as the only Harappan site with ancient DNA in the cited account, along with evidence of a gold foundry and gemstone factory.
The rare cylindrical steatite seal with an alligator motif and five Harappan signs is associated with
Rakhigarhi

rows.title: Decline of the IVC - competing theories; Late Harappan cultures (Cemetery-H, Jhukar, Rangpur)
sub: Group-II S1-6: Decline of the Indus Valley Civilization - theories and Late Harappan cultures

secs.t: Late Harappan material traits - tool materials, pottery, settlement pattern

x: Late Harappan cultures used stone and copper tools, lacked complicated-casting metal objects, and developed varied regional pottery styles.
Cemetery H corresponds to the Harappa region of Punjab; Jhukar to Sindh; Rangpur to Gujarat; and the Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase to Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
The Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase is identified in the table with
Ochre Coloured Pottery
(OCP).

secs.t: Late Harappan sites and cultures → region

x: Exam angle: Dadheri is a Late Harappan site of → Punjab.
Bara is associated with Punjab in India, not Maharashtra.
Jhangar is linked with Sindh and Amri, Dadheri with Punjab, Daimabad with Maharashtra, and Alamgirpur with Uttar Pradesh.
Rangpur and Rojdi are Late Harappan sites in
Gujarat
; Rangpur is associated with the Rojdi culture.

secs.t: Decline theories → proponent / study

x: Exam angle: IIT Kharagpur study group - continuous low rainfall for
900 years
Mortimer Wheeler
proposed the Aryan invasion explanation in 1947; the theory is now generally rejected.
The current consensus favours a gradual, multi-causal decline over approximately 200 years, with considerable regional variation; the sudden-catastrophe model is rejected.
Deoria Tal pollen evidence indicates a sharp weakening of the summer monsoon about 4,200 years ago, known as the 4.2 ka event.
The current consensus rejects a single sudden catastrophe and favours a gradual, multi-causal decline.

secs.t: Evidence cited for each theory - skeletons, silt, dried rivers

x: The huddled skeletons were traditionally cited as evidence of invasion or massacre, although they are now interpreted as multiple burials without archaeological proof of invasion.
The Rig Veda post-dates the decline, and the skeletons do not constitute archaeological proof of an Aryan invasion.
The Ghaggar-Hakra system contained the densest cluster of settlements and later dried up under the effects of tectonic shifts and reduced rainfall.

secs.t: Ochre Coloured Pottery culture and Copper Hoards - link debate

x: Copper Hoards are often found with OCP in the
Ganga-Yamuna Doab
, forming the basis of their commonly proposed association.

secs.t: Continuity into Chalcolithic and Vedic cultures

x: The identification of Ghaggar-Hakra with the Rigvedic Sarasvati is an argument used by scholars supporting continuity between Late Harappan and Vedic cultural traditions.
Bhagwanpura provides evidence of overlap through a 13-roomed house containing Late Harappan pottery and Painted Grey Ware.
The absence of horse, chariot and iron supports the pre-Vedic argument, while fire altars and pipal worship are cited by the continuity view.

secs.t: Direction of settlement shifts after the decline

x: Post-urban settlement shifts were mainly
eastward towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and southward towards Gujarat and the Deccan

secs.t: Mortimer Wheeler's invasion theory and its rejection

x: Mortimer Wheeler
proposed the invasion theory in 1947, attributing the decline to Aryan invaders.
Wheeler cited skeletons found at Mohenjodaro and Indra’s epithet Purandara, meaning ‘fort-breaker’, in support of the invasion theory.
All three statements are among the major grounds for rejecting Wheeler’s invasion explanation: lack of archaeological evidence, the later date of the Rig Veda and reinterpretation of the skeletons.

secs.t: De-urbanisation - gradual vs sudden

x: The decline was gradual, extending over about 200 years, and its timing differed across regions.
The decline of cities was accompanied by the emergence of smaller rural settlements and movement towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, Gujarat and the Deccan.

secs.t: Continuity of Harappan traits

x: Pipal worship, Mother Goddess worship and ritual bathing are cited as possible continuities.
Ritual bathing is regarded as a possible Harappan continuity reflected in later
temple tanks and ghats
Bead-making in Gujarat, red ware with black designs, dish-on-stand vessels and bullock carts are all cited as traits continuing into later cultures.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Deoria Tal pollen study links the decline with the 4.2 ka aridity event, particularly a monsoon failure and drought conditions.
Both statements are true, and the lack of invasion evidence together with the gradual, regionally varied decline directly explains why the invasion theory is inadequate as a single explanation.

rows.title: Aryan question - Original Home theories (Max Muller, Tilak, Avinash Chandra Das); archaeological correlates

secs.t: Linguistic and epigraphic evidence - Indo-European family, Boghazkoi inscription, Avesta

x: Exam angle: "Which inscription names Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatyas?" - Boghazkoi (distractors: Mansehra, Shahbazgarhi, Junagadh, Ecbatana, Behistun).
Vedic Sanskrit belongs to the
Indo-European
language family, whose geographical spread includes Europe, Asia and the Middle East.
The Boghazkoi treaty invokes the Vedic deities
Indra, Mitra, Varuna and Nasatyas
Both statements are true, and the linguistic and conceptual parallels between the Avesta and Rigveda explain why they are linked to a common Indo-Iranian stock.

secs.t: Meaning of 'Arya' - ethnic vs linguistic group; classical Sanskrit sense

x: Exam angle: options "ethnic group / nomadic people / speech group / superior race" - answer: speech group.
‘Arya’ originally meant noble or of high birth and later acquired the sense of persons of noble lineage and social standing.
The term denotes a linguistic-cultural group and does not necessarily denote a biologically superior race.

secs.t: Original home theories → proponent + book

x: Exam angle: match-the-following of homeland, scholar and book (Tilak-Arctic is the favourite pair).
Dayananda Saraswati associated the homeland with Tibet, Penka with Europe or Germany on physical type, and P. Giles with Hungary and the Danube valley on linguistic grounds.
Max Muller proposed Central Asia, B. G. Tilak the Arctic region, Dayanand Saraswati Tibet and A. C. Das the Sapta Sindhu theory.

secs.t: Archaeological correlates - horse, spoked wheel, Andronovo, BMAC, Gandhara Grave culture

x: Arguments for migration rely significantly on evidence relating to horses and spoked-wheel chariots, along with changes in pottery, burials and settlements.
Harappans are described as using solid wheels, while spoked-wheel chariots form part of the archaeological argument associated with Aryan migration.
The relationship between Painted Grey Ware archaeology and Later Vedic textual geography remains an open question; Vedic archaeology is not settled on this issue.

secs.t: Aryan migration vs indigenous debate - genetic studies (Rakhigarhi DNA)

x: Vedic-Sarasvati continuity
, claims regarding Harappan-script decipherment and astronomical dating of the Rigveda are among the arguments of the Indigenous or Out of India theory.
Romila Thapar and Upinder Singh represent a synthesis in which small groups migrated, achieved elite dominance and underwent cultural assimilation, without a simple invasion or replacement model.

secs.t: Aryan-Harappan relationship - chronological and cultural comparisons

x: Max Muller, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Avinash Chandra Das are associated with theories on the original home of the Aryans.
Harappan cultural transmission is associated with seals and script, while the Rigvedic tradition was transmitted orally through hymns.
B.B. Lal’s identification of the Sarasvati and the proposed Painted Grey Ware–Vedic link form important bases for the continuity argument.

secs.t: Dasas and Dasyus - references in Rigveda

x: The Dasas and Dasyus are distinguished: the Dasas were regarded as a branch of early Aryans, while the Dasyus were original inhabitants.
The Dasyus were regarded as original inhabitants who possibly practised phallus worship and did not raise cattle for dairy.
The Panis are described as another non-Aryan group associated with
cattle-holding and trade

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rakhigarhi is in Hisar district and covers approximately 550 hectares.
Rakhigarhi is described as the largest known Harappan settlement and is situated on the seasonal Drishadvati river.
The racial conception of the Aryan was a colonial idea.
Genetics remains contested and has not settled all disputes.

rows.title: Rig Vedic (Early Vedic) period - geography of Sapta Sindhu, rivers, tribes, Battle of Ten Kings

secs.t: Rivers by prominence - most mentioned, naditama, Afghan links

x: Sindhu
, identified with the Indus, is the river mentioned most often in the Rigveda.
Sarasvati
is described as ‘naditama’, or the best of rivers, and is also called Saubhagyadayini in the relevant tradition.
Kubha, Krumu, Gomati and Suvastu are identified with the Kabul, Kurram, Gomal and Swat rivers and indicate links with Afghanistan.

secs.t: Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings) - site, victor, king, priests

x: The Bharatas, led by
Sudas of the Tritsu family
, defeated the opposing confederacy in the Dasarajna.
The battle may reflect actual competition among tribal confederacies, but the Rigveda is religious poetry rather than a straightforward chronicle.
The traditional explanation identifies the rivalry between the priests
Vasishtha and Vishvamitra
as the cause of the conflict.

secs.t: Tribes → Panchajana grouping and odd-one-out

x: Exam angle: "Which tribe is not in the Panchajana?" - Kikata.
The five tribes of the Panchajana were
Yadus, Turvasas, Anus, Druhyus and Purus
The name Bharatavarsha is traced to the Bharata tribe.

secs.t: Physical features - Himavant, Mujavant, samudra debate

x: Himavant denotes the Himalayas, Mujavant is a Hindu Kush mountain associated with Soma, Dhanva means desert land and Rigvedic Samudra can mean a collection of water.
In the Rigveda, Samudra may refer to a collection of water and is not necessarily evidence of knowledge of the open sea in every occurrence.
The Rigvedic term Samudra has a debated, broad meaning, whereas the later Satapatha Brahmana mentions the eastern and western seas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sapta Sindhu geography places the Early Vedic heartland in Punjab, Haryana and adjoining north-western areas before the later eastward movement.
The Early Vedic core lay in Punjab–Haryana, while the Later Vedic core shifted eastward to the Ganga–Yamuna Doab, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, including Kosala and Videha.

rows.title: Early Vedic polity - rajan, sabha, samiti, vidatha, gana; nature of tribal chiefdom
sub: Group-II S1-7: Early Vedic (Rig Vedic) age - geography, tribes, polity (sabha, samiti, rajan)

secs.t: Nature of early Vedic polity - tribal chiefdom (jana, vis, grama) vs later kingdom

x: The early Vedic hierarchy proceeded from Jana, the tribe, to Vis, the clan, Grama, the village, and Kula, the family.
The term Janapada is absent in the Rigveda, reflecting the predominantly tribal rather than territorial character of early Vedic polity.
Jana is mentioned approximately
275 times
in the Rigveda, underlining the importance of the tribe in early Vedic political organisation.

secs.t: Vedic assemblies → composition and function; Prajapati's daughters

x: Exam angle: judicial assembly = Sabha; "daughters of Prajapati" and "separate institutions" = Atharvaveda (not Rigveda).
Exam angle: "judicial assembly" = Sabha; "earliest/most-mentioned assembly" = Vidatha; "Veda treating Sabha and Samiti as separate" = Atharvaveda.
Vidatha represented the whole tribe, Samiti the general tribal members, Sabha the elders and elites, and Gana a military troop or group of tribesmen.
Vidatha
is mentioned 122 times in the Rigveda, compared with nine references to Samiti and eight to Sabha.

secs.t: Officials → role

x: Gramani was the village head and could also lead fighting groups.
Purohita was the chief priest and adviser, Senani the army commander, Vrajapati the pasture officer and Spasa the spy.
Spasa
referred to spies employed by the king.
Kulapa or Kulapati
was the head of the Kula, or family.

secs.t: Rajan - election/hereditary debate, duties, balis

x: Monarchy was the usual form and succession often passed within the family, but the office was not strictly hereditary and the Samiti had a role in selection.
Kingship was generally not considered divine, but the Puru king Trasadasyu was exceptionally described as ardhadeva, or demi-god.
Sena was a temporary militia organised into units such as
Sardha, Vrata and Gana

secs.t: Women in assemblies - participation evidence

x: Women participated in the Sabha and Vidatha, female members of the Sabha were called Sabhavati, and the Atharvaveda records women's participation in the Samiti.
Sabhavati was the term used for women members or participants in the Sabha.
The increasing restriction of the assemblies to nobles and Brahmanas explains the exclusion of women in the later Vedic period.

secs.t: Warfare - gavishti, weapons, chariots

x: ‘Gavishti’ literally refers to the
search for cows
and denotes cattle raids, which were a common form of warfare in the Rig Vedic period.
Horse-drawn chariots, bronze weapons and the military units Sardha, Vrata and Gana are all associated with early Vedic warfare.
Early Vedic conflicts included intra-Aryan struggles as well as wars against the Dasas and Dasyus.

secs.t: Absence of standing army and regular tax system

x: The Sena was a temporary militia, and no regular tax-collecting machinery existed.
Bali was a voluntary offering.
There were no specialised officers for justice; disputes were settled through
community consensus or mediators such as the Madhyamasi

secs.t: Rig Vedic rivers - ancient and modern names

x: Exam angle: pairs of ancient/modern names; Vitasta-Chenab and Asikni-Jhelum are classic wrong pairs.
The standard Sapta Sindhu list comprises
Sindhu, Vitasta, Asikni, Parushni, Vipas, Sutudri and Sarasvati
Sapta Sindhu covered eastern Afghanistan, the north-western frontier region, Punjab, Haryana and the fringes of western Uttar Pradesh, forming the early Vedic heartland.

secs.t: Tribes - Panchajana, Bharatas, Purus

x: The five tribes of Panchajana were
Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa and Puru
The Bharatas were associated with Bharatavarsha, while Tritsus, Krivis and Srinjayas were other tribes; Divodasa defeated Sambara and Panis were associated with cattle concealment.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The assemblies are considered early democratic or proto-participatory elements because they contained traces of elective participation within a tribal order.
The Later Vedic period saw hereditary territorial kingship, the ratnins, regular taxation and royal sacrifices including Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Ashvamedha.
‘Andhra’ first appears later in the Aitareya Brahmana, in connection with the Sunahshepa story; it does not appear first in the Rig Veda.

rows.title: Early Vedic society and economy - pastoralism, gavishti, varna origins, position of women
sub: Group-II S1-8: Early Vedic society, economy and the position of women

secs.t: Pastoral economy - wealth and cow-derived terms

x: Exam angle: "Aghanya refers to - cows"; "most valuable property in early Rigvedic period - cow".
The Early Vedic economy was mainly pastoral, with cattle-keeping combined with secondary agriculture, constituting a mixed economy.
Cattle, sheep, goats, horses, dogs and asses were kept, whereas
buffalo
was not prominent.
Gavishti means a search for cows and came to denote
war
or a cattle raid.

secs.t: Position of women - seers, marriage customs, niyoga

x: Exam angle: "Which is not Rig Vedic?" - Gargi.
Gargi
was a later Vedic scholar associated with Upanishadic dialogue, whereas Apala, Ghosha and Vishvavara were Rigvedic women seers.
The Aitareya Brahmana reflects the later patriarchal attitude by describing daughters as
a source of misery
Early Vedic society was patriarchal and preferred sons, yet women received education, participated in sacrifices and assemblies, and could own cattle.

secs.t: Crop and food terms → meaning; implements, irrigation

x: Exam angle: match crop terms (RPSC 2021 paired Yava with "millet" as the only option left - the standard meaning is barley).
Rice
was rare or late in the Rigvedic context and became prominent in Later Vedic texts.
Mudga means mung bean, Godhuma means wheat, Ikshu means sugarcane and Vrihi means rice.
Datra was a sickle, Titau a sieve and Supra a winnowing fan.

secs.t: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

x: Exchange in the early Vedic period was conducted mainly through barter, as coins had not yet come into use.
Nishka was a gold ornament in the Rigveda and later came to denote a unit of value or gold piece.
The Panis were traders, were associated with cattle wealth, and were condemned as greedy and non-Aryan groups who hid cattle.

secs.t: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

x: The Purusha Sukta describes Brahmana as originating from the mouth, Kshatriya from the arms, Vaishya from the thighs and Shudra from the feet.
Arya and Dasa varna reflected a cultural, linguistic and partly colour-based distinction between Vedic groups and conquered local groups; it was not yet a rigid caste system.
The Rig Vedic hymn describing a poet, a physician father and a mother who ground corn illustrates that occupation was not strictly birth-bound.

secs.t: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

x: Sapatni
was the term used for the wife in the early Vedic family context.
Kula means family, Grama village, Vis clan and Jana tribe.
Gotra is absent in the Rigveda, is first named in the Atharvaveda, and gotra exogamy is a Later Vedic development.
Jana is mentioned 275 times in the Rigveda, while the term Janapada does not occur there.

secs.t: Occupations and crafts

x: Takshan was a carpenter, Karmara a metal worker, Hiranyakara a goldsmith and Bhishak a physician.
Charmamna referred to a tanner, while Bhishak was the physician.
Ayas in the Rigveda referred to
copper or bronze
Weaving was known, with women undertaking much of it.
Vaya
was the term associated with a weaver.

secs.t: Food, drink and pastimes

x: The Soma plant was associated with the
Mujavant mountains
and was used to prepare the sacred drink Soma.
Milk and milk products, barley preparations and meat on occasions
formed part of the early Vedic diet.
The gambler's hymn is found in
Rigveda X.34
and is associated with the pastime of dicing.

secs.t: Rig Vedic religion - nature of worship and the major gods

x: Exam angle: statement sets - "Prithvi was mother of all gods" is wrong (that is
Aditi
); Dyaus = Zeus/Jupiter is right.
Rig Vedic worship involved hymns and yajnas in the open air and aimed mainly at material benefits such as cattle, sons and victory.
Early Vedic religion personified forces of nature, was dominated by male gods and commonly sought material benefits such as cattle, progeny and victory.

secs.t: Tax - bali

x: In the early Vedic period, bali was a voluntary offering or tribute made by tribesmen to the rajan and could also include war booty.
In the Later Vedic period, bali became compulsory and existed along with bhaga, the one-sixth share of produce, and shulka.
The
bhagadugha
was associated with the collection of the later Vedic levies, including bali, bhaga and shulka.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Early Vedic economy was pastoral and associated with yava, while the Later Vedic economy became agrarian and was associated with rice and wheat.
The shift from a cattle-based tribal economy to an agrarian territorial society contributed to the emergence of territorial kingship and a more established varna hierarchy.
The evidence is mixed: texts praise women seers, and education and assembly rights existed, but society remained patriarchal and displayed son-preference.

rows.title: Later Vedic period - eastward expansion, iron (krishna ayas), Painted Grey Ware culture
sub: Group-II S1-9: Later Vedic age - eastward expansion, iron, rise of kingship and rituals

secs.t: Pottery sequence of Indian protohistory - order and period

x: Exam angle: "Pottery of 1000-600 BC in the Gangetic plain" = Painted Grey Ware.
Exam angle: "pottery of the Gangetic plain 1000-600 BC" = PGW; list questions exclude NBPW.
Black and Red Ware occurs from the Chalcolithic period onwards, is known in the Later Vedic context, and is associated with the Megalithic or Iron Age cultures of South India.
The bowls and dishes of Painted Grey Ware were probably used by the
rising upper strata

secs.t: Iron - earliest evidence, dating, Vedic metal terms

x: Exam angle: BPSC 2022 asked when iron use began, with options of 6,000-12,000 years ago; the key was "none of the above".
Exam angle: BPSC 2022 "when did iron use begin" - answer "none of the above" (options 6,000/9,000/12,000 years ago did not fit).

Mayiladumparai is linked with the 2172 BCE AMS date; Sivagalai with iron and paddy dated to about 2953 BCE; Thirumalapuram with an early–mid third-millennium BCE urn chamber; and Adichanallur with urn burials.

secs.t: Eastward expansion - Videgha Madhava legend, Sadanira, Kuru-Panchala

x: Videgha Madhava and Gautama Rahugana followed Agni Vaishvanara as it burnt the forests eastward from the Sarasvati towards the Sadanira.
The movement proceeded from Punjab into the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, including Kurukshetra and the Delhi-upper Doab, and then towards Kosala, Kashi and Videha by about 600 BCE.
Kuru-Panchala occupied the Delhi-Meerut area, had Hastinapur as its capital, formed the cultural centre of the Aryan world, and the Kurus resulted from the Bharata-Puru union.

secs.t: Painted Grey Ware sites → region

x: These sites are located respectively in Meerut, Etah, Bareilly and Kurukshetra, with the latter in Haryana.
Painted Grey Ware sites were found mainly in the upper Ganga basin, not exclusively in the lower Indus basin.
Copper found at the Painted Grey Ware sites was possibly obtained from
Khetri in Rajasthan

secs.t: Agriculture expansion - new crops, ploughs, rice

x: Rice and wheat became chief crops, rice had ritual importance, barley continued, and double cropping was mentioned.
Ploughs could be drawn by 6, 8, 12 and even
24 oxen
, indicating the increasing scale of agricultural operations.
Iron ploughshares, axes and hoes, along with iron and fire used for clearing forests, supported agricultural expansion.

secs.t: Later Vedic texts as sources

x: The Samaveda contains musical versions of Rigvedic hymns; the Yajurveda gives ritual procedures; the Atharvaveda contains spells and charms; and the Upanishads discuss Atman, Brahman, Karma and Moksha.
The
Atharvaveda
is regarded as the latest Veda and includes spells, charms against disease and elements of folk practice.
The Yajurveda gives ritual procedures in prose, is connected with the Adhvaryu priest, and has Krishna and Shukla branches.

secs.t: Settlements - villages vs early towns

x: Settlements were mainly villages with mud and wattle houses.
True towns emerged after the Vedic period during the Northern Black Polished Ware phase, including Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur.
Iron-working, copper work, weaving, leatherwork, pottery and carpentry expanded.
Shresthins point to merchant groups.

secs.t: Ratnins, revenue officials and taxes

x: Exam angle: "Bhagadugha" = revenue collector (distractors: gambling officer, messenger, forest officer).
The
Ratnahavimshi
rite involved offerings at the houses of the Ratnins and honoured the king’s twelve functionaries.
The APP list of twelve Ratnins includes
Parivakti
along with Purohita, Rajan, Mahishi, Senani, Bhagadugha, Sangrahitri, Suta, Kshata, Govikartana, Gramani and Akshavapa.

secs.t: Later Vedic gods rising in importance

x: Prajapati
, regarded as the creator, became the supreme god during the Later Vedic period.
Both statements are true, and the increasing ritualism of Later Vedic worship explains the emergence of the Upanishadic critique.
Vishnu
rose as the preserver in the later Vedic period, despite being a minor deity in the Rigveda.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Mayiladumparai date of 2172 BCE and the Sivagalai date of about 2953 BCE push the evidence for Indian iron use far earlier than the Gangetic date of about 1000 BCE.
The extent to which Painted Grey Ware archaeology corresponds to the geography described in Later Vedic texts remains an open question.
BHU opened 22 sealed boxes containing more than 10,000 artefacts from
Rajghat in Varanasi
, also known as Kashi.

rows.title: Later Vedic polity - rise of territorial kingship; rajasuya, ashvamedha, vajapeya; the ratnins

secs.t: Rise of territorial kingship - janapada, rashtra, titles

x: The term
rashtra
, meaning territory, first appears in this political context and reflects the rise of territorial kingship.
The Aitareya Brahmana names Rajya, Bhojya, Swarajya, Vairajya and Samrajya.
The broad sequence is the territorial transformation from Jana to Janapada, the rise of hereditary kingship, the disappearance of Vidatha, and the continued but restricted role of Sabha and Samiti.

secs.t: Royal sacrifices → purpose

x: Rajasuya was a consecration conferring supreme power, Ashvamedha involved a horse sacrifice and asserted supremacy over other kings, while Vajapeya included a chariot race against the king’s kinsmen.
Ashvamedha symbolised royal supremacy and unquestioned control over the territory traversed by the sacrificial horse, and it is discussed in both Brahmanas.
Large Shrauta sacrifices required numerous priests and substantial dakshina, thereby increasing Brahmanical influence and strengthening the ritual basis of royal power.

secs.t: Fate of sabha, samiti and vidatha

x: Sabha and Samiti continued but came under the control of chiefs and wealthy nobles; the Samiti lost power, while the Sabha retained a judicial role.
Women were excluded from the Later Vedic assemblies.

secs.t: Taxes - bali, shulka, bhaga (nature, collector)

x: Bali became a regular tribute, Bhaga was the king’s share of produce, and Shulka was a customs duty or toll.

The sources present two textbook views: one notes emerging standing elements such as chariot warfare, iron weapons and professional warriors, while another records the continued raising of tribal levies and absence of a fully standing army.

secs.t: Kingdoms of the period

x: King Janaka was associated with
Videha
, located in North Bihar beyond the Sadanira or Gandak.
The Kuru–Panchala alliance dominated the upper Ganga valley, while Kosala, Kashi and Videha rose in the east.
The sequence proceeds from tribal jana units to territorial janapadas, then to hereditary territorial kingship and finally to larger Mahajanapadas.

secs.t: Theory of divine origin of kingship - Aitareya/Shatapatha Brahmana

x: The Aitareya Brahmana gives an early account in which the gods, suffering defeat at the hands of the Asuras, selected a king as their war leader.
The Shatapatha Brahmana linked the king to Prajapati, the creator god.
Royal rituals such as Rajasuya and Vajapeya helped connect kingship with divine sanction and legitimacy.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Regular bali-bhaga-shulka and the presence of ratnins reflect the consolidation and institutionalisation of hereditary territorial monarchy in the Later Vedic period.

The sequence was Early Vedic elective chieftainship, followed by Later Vedic hereditary territorial monarchy and declining assemblies, culminating in the rise of the Mahajanapadas in the 6th century BCE.
