rows.title: Later Vedic society - four varnas, ashrama system, gotra, decline in the status of women
sub: Group-II S1-10: Later Vedic society - varna system, ashramas, changing status of women

secs.t: Samskaras and the eight forms of marriage

x: Exam angle: "marriage by purchase of bride" =
Asura
; capture = Rakshasa.
In the Brahma form, the father gave his daughter, along with gifts, to
a learned man of good conduct
Fraternal polyandry is associated with the Khas, sororal polygyny concerns sisters, group marriage involves several men and women, and polygyny is permitted for Muslims.
Gandharva is based on mutual consent, Rakshasa on force, Paishacha is the lowest form, and Asura involves bride price.

secs.t: Four varnas and the emergence of caste

x: Exam angle: "caste as a new form of social organisation" questions test that varna rigidified after the Rig Vedic phase.
The later Vedic fourfold order consisted of
Brahmana, Rajanya or Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra
The Purusha Sukta in the Tenth Mandala of the Rigveda contains the first statement of the fourfold varna order.
Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas were collectively called Dvija, or twice-born, because of their entitlement to Upanayana.

secs.t: Ashrama system - four stages and pancha mahayajna

x: Exam angle: "Pancha Mahayajna performed in which ashrama?" - Grihastha.

The first three Ashramas were prevalent in later Vedic times; the Chhandogya Upanishad refers to the first three, Sannyasa was added later, and the Jabala Upanishad gives the earliest listing of all four.
Brahmacharya involved Vedic study, Grihastha involved household duties, Vanaprastha involved gradual withdrawal, and Sannyasa involved complete detachment.

secs.t: Gotra and kinship terms

x: Gotra exogamy prohibited intra-gotra marriage, while caste endogamy and sapinda restrictions formed additional elements of the North Indian kinship pattern.
Irawati Karve
analysed sapinda and gotra rules and divided India into four kinship zones in Kinship Organization in India, published in 1953.
Gotra literally means ‘
cow-pen
’ and later came to denote lineage from a common male ancestor.

secs.t: Education - gurukula, upanayana, teachers

x: Exam angle: "mantra in the Kshatriya upanayana" = Trishtubh.
Upanayana was the sacred-thread initiation into Vedic study and was available to the Brahmana, Kshatriya and Vaishya varnas, but not to Shudras and women.
The
Shatapatha Brahmana
gives an elaborate description of the Upanayana ceremony.
Chudakarma
was the tonsure ceremony, traditionally performed in the third year.

secs.t: Purusharthas - four goals of life

x: Trivarga comprises
Dharma, Artha and Kama
, the first three Purusharthas.
Dharma, Artha and Kama formed the earlier trivarga in the Later Vedic-Sutra phase.
Dharma means duty, Artha wealth, Kama desire and Moksha liberation.

secs.t: Status of women

x: The status of women declined through loss of Upanayana, restricted education and exclusion from several religious and public activities; education did not become more widely available.
The
Aitareya Brahmana
presents the daughter as a source of misery and the son as the protector, reflecting the declining status of women.
References to
child marriage and sati
appear in accounts of the declining status of women in Later Vedic society.

secs.t: Occupational groups and guilds

x: Vaishyas engaged in farming, trade and craft production and paid tribute.
The
Shatapatha Brahmana
contains the first reference to money-lending.
A gana was a guild-like body of Vaishyas, and its head was called a
Shreshthin
Upadhyaya was a teacher who taught the Veda or Vedanga for a livelihood, not the head of a Vaishya gana.

secs.t: Untouchability - earliest references

x: The
Chhandogya Upanishad
contains an early reference to the Chandala as a despised birth.
Later Vedic society witnessed discrimination against Shudras and Chandalas, but untouchability as a formal rule is associated with the post-Vedic Dharmasutras.

secs.t: Teachers and priests

x: An Acharya initiated the pupil through upanayana and taught the whole Veda without accepting a fee.
The Hotri recited the Rigveda, whereas the Udgatri chanted the Samaveda.
Hotri was the Rigveda reciter, Udgatri the Samaveda chanter, Purohita the family or royal priest and adviser, and Adhvaryu the Yajurveda priest performing sacrificial acts.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Later Vedic period witnessed the fixing of Varna and gotra rules rather than their absence.
The fixing of
Varna, gotra, samskaras and ashramas
formed the later Dharmashastra social order and provided the institutional background against which Buddhist and Jain protest developed.
Early Vedic society had flexible occupation and varna distinctions, while Later Vedic varna became birth-based.

rows.title: Vedic literature - four Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, Vedangas, Sutras
sub: Group-II S1-11: Vedic literature - Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, Vedangas

secs.t: Earliest literary references to the Andhras

x: Exam angle: "first literary reference to Andhras" = Aitareya Brahmana; "Andhakaratta" = Jain texts.
Vishvamitra cursed the fifty sons who refused to accept Sunahshepa to become
non-Aryan peoples
, including the Andhras, Pundras and Pulindas.
Megasthenes’ Indica describes the Andhras as possessing
30 fortified towns and a large army
Ashoka’s
Rock Edict XIII
names the Andhras among the peoples within his empire.

secs.t: Grammar and Vedanga works → author; six Vedangas

x: Katyayana composed the Varttika, critical notes on Panini’s grammar.
Nirukta is the earliest extant work on
etymology
and is associated with Yaska.
Shiksha is phonetics, Kalpa is rituals, Chandas is metrics and Jyotisha is astronomy.
The six Vedangas are
Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Chandas and Jyotisha
Nyaya is associated with Gautama, Vaisheshika with Kanada, Sankhya with Kapila and Purva Mimamsa with Jaimini.

secs.t: Sutras - Shrauta, Grihya, Dharma, Sulba

x: Grihya, Dharma and Sulba Sutras respectively concern domestic rites, law and social practice, and altar construction.
Baudhayana
is one of the authors associated with the Sulba Sutras; Apastamba, Katyayana and Manava are also associated with them.
Baudhayana
’s Sulbasutra contains the rule corresponding to the theorem now known as the Pythagoras theorem.

secs.t: Veda → Brahmana, Aranyaka, Upanishad, priest

x: The Rigveda was recited by the Hotri, Samaveda chanted by the Udgatri, Yajurveda executed by the Adhvaryu and Atharvaveda supervised by the Brahman priest.
Aranyakas are ‘forest texts’, generally concluding parts of the Brahmanas and forming a bridge from ritualism to philosophical speculation.
The Shatapatha Brahmana mentions
the Great Flood
, besides describing the eastward spread of culture.

secs.t: Upanishads - dialogues, principal ones, relation to Puranas

x: The Upanishads are called Vedanta, meaning the ‘end of the Veda’, both in sequence and philosophical culmination.
The Upanishads are anti-ritualistic philosophical texts that teach Atman–Brahman identity and discuss karma, samsara and moksha.
These are three important dialogue traditions associated respectively with the Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya and Katha Upanishads.
The Upanishads are Shruti texts, whereas the Puranas belong to Smriti and are later, legend-based works.

secs.t: National mottos and famous verses → source

x: The prayer beginning ‘Asato ma sadgamaya’ and ‘Tamaso ma jyotirgamaya’ occurs in the
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
The Gayatri Mantra occurs in the
Third Mandala
of the Rigveda and is attributed to Vishvamitra in praise of Savitri.

secs.t: Rigveda structure

x: The Early Vedic period is generally placed around
, although some comparative tables use the narrower range 1500–1100 BCE.
Mandala VI is associated with Bharadvaja, Mandala VII with Vasishtha and the Battle of Ten Kings, Mandala IX with Soma and Mandala X with the Purusha Sukta and Nasadiya hymn.

Rigvedic references to rivers, tribes and settlements broadly correspond with archaeological evidence, but the religious text must be interpreted critically rather than treated as a literal chronicle.
The first and tenth Mandalas are later additions, the hymns seek practical blessings, and the text shows similarities with the Iranian Avesta.

secs.t: Shakhas and recensions

x: The Krishna, or Black, Yajurveda mixes mantras and prose, whereas the Shukla, or White, Yajurveda contains mantras separately.
The Shukla Yajurveda has the Vajasaneyi Samhita, including the Madhyandina and Kanva recensions, and the Shatapatha Brahmana.
The Krishna Yajurveda is represented by the
Taittiriya, Maitrayani, Kathaka and Kapishthala
traditions.
The surviving recension of the Rigveda is the Shakala, also called Shakalya, recension.

secs.t: Four Vedas - content, branches, priests, Upaveda

x: The
Samaveda
consists mainly of Rigvedic hymns set to melodies called saman and is regarded as the root of Indian music.
The Yajurveda contains ritual formulas and prose instructions, is associated with the Adhvaryu priest, and has Dhanurveda as its Upaveda.
The Samaveda sets mostly Rigvedic verses to saman melodies for chanting by the Udgatri.

secs.t: Epics, Puranas and Smritis

x: The Mahabharata is described as having been compiled over a long period extending from about the
10th century BCE to the 4th century CE
The Ramayana contains approximately 24,000 verses and is described as having been composed in five stages beginning from the 5th century BCE.
Manusmriti is regarded as the earliest Smriti, and Vijnaneshwara’s Mitakshara is a commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rigvedic hymns are invocations addressed to the devas, whereas Yajurvedic mantras are connected with the conduct of yajna.
The Eastern Chalukya inscriptions from Cheepurupalli and Nidamarru praise Brahmin scholars learned in the Vedas and Vedangas.
The Harappan script remains undeciphered and does not provide deciphered textual records, while Later Vedic culture is known through texts preserved in an oral tradition.

rows.title: Vedic religion, ritual and philosophy; the six orthodox schools (shad-darshanas)

secs.t: Six orthodox schools → founder, key text, order

x: The Nyaya school is associated with the Nyaya Sutra.
Samkhya
is regarded as the oldest of the six orthodox schools.
The traditional pairs are Nyaya–Vaisheshika, Samkhya–Yoga and Mimamsa–Vedanta.
All three statements correctly describe the core orientations of Nyaya, Vaisheshika and Purva Mimamsa.

secs.t: Doctrine → school; astika vs nastika

x: Exam angle: odd-one-out lists mix one nastika school (Charvaka/Ajivika) among the six astikas.
Satkaryavada is a principal doctrine of
Samkhya
, holding that the effect pre-exists in the cause.
Astika
denotes the systems that accept Vedic authority, including the six orthodox darshanas.
Charvaka, Buddhism, Jainism and Ajivika
reject the authority of the Vedas and are classified as nastika traditions.

secs.t: Rigvedic gods → domain, parallels, hymn counts

x: Varuna
was associated with water and cosmic order, and was regarded as the upholder of Rita and the ethically highest god.
Dyaus was the celestial father and sky deity, comparable to Jupiter or Zeus in Greek and Roman traditions.
Soma was associated with a plant and ritual drink, and
the entire Ninth Mandala of the Rigveda is devoted to Soma hymns

secs.t: Mimamsa and Vedanta exponents → school

x: Kumarila Bhatta and Prabhakara were exponents of
Purva Mimamsa
Ramanuja is associated with Vishishtadvaita.

secs.t: Yoga and Samkhya concepts

x: Samkhya teaches liberation through discriminating Purusha from Prakriti, while Yoga provides the practical discipline and method for achieving it.
Yama, niyama, asana, pranayama and pratyahara are the five bahiranga limbs.
Dharana, dhyana and samadhi constitute the inner or antaranga limbs of Ashtanga Yoga.
Yoga identifies discipline and meditation as the path to liberation.

secs.t: Rituals - yajna types, soma, domestic rites

x: The
Hotri
was the priest associated with the Rigveda.
The Adhvaryu was associated with the Yajurveda, whereas the Udgatri was associated with the Samaveda.
Agnistoma
was the regular Soma yajna.
Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Ashvamedha were royal sacrifices.
The
Grihya Sutras
governed domestic rites.

secs.t: Upanishadic philosophy

x: Atman, Brahman, Karma, Samsara and Moksha
are central concepts of Upanishadic philosophy.
Upanishadic thought criticised mechanical sacrifice and emphasised meditation and teaching through the guru–disciple relationship.
The
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
introduced the doctrine of transmigration, connected with the cycle of rebirth.
Both statements are true, and the criticism of mechanical sacrifice explains the Upanishadic turn towards meditation and instruction through a guru.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Upanishadic concepts formed the philosophical and spiritual basis of later Hinduism.
Vivekananda's Neo-Vedanta reworked and presented the
Advaita
Vedanta tradition in a modern form.
The Nanaghat record mentions Indra, Vasudeva, Surya, Chandra, Yama and Varuna.
Ikshvaku Santamula performed the Ashvamedha, Rajasuya and Vajapeya, and an Ashvamedha altar was found at Nagarjunakonda.

rows.title: The sixteen Mahajanapadas - list, capitals, monarchies vs ganasanghas (Anguttara Nikaya)
sub: Group-II S1-12: Causes for the rise of heterodox sects; the sixteen Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha

secs.t: Mahajanapada → capital

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2024 - Avanti-Ujjain, Kosala-Shravasti, Vatsa-Kaushambi, Anga-Champa; Assaka capital =
Bodhan
Magadha had Rajagriha or Girivraja as its earlier capital and Pataliputra as its later capital.
Kashi, Vajji and Kuru are correctly matched with Varanasi, Vaishali and Indraprastha respectively.
Avanti had Ujjayini as its northern capital and
Mahishmati
as its southern capital.
Panchala
was divided into northern Panchala, with Ahichchhatra as its capital, and southern Panchala, with Kampilya as its capital.

secs.t: Present region, rivers, map identification

x: Kamboja
was situated in the north-west frontier region and was noted for horse-breeding.
Eight Mahajanapadas lay in present-day Uttar Pradesh, and Assaka was the only one south of the Vindhyas.
Kashi was associated with the Ganga–Varuna confluence, Kosala with the Sarayu, Vatsa with the Yamuna and Avanti with the Sipra.

secs.t: Sources listing them

x: The Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya, a text of the Sutta Pitaka, lists the sixteen Mahajanapadas.
The Bhagavati Sutra is a Jain source and gives a different list of Mahajanapadas from the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya.
The Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a different list and includes eastern and southern names such as
Vanga, Malava and Ladha
or Radha.

secs.t: Ganasanghas vs monarchies

x: Gana-sanghas depended on contributions from members, while monarchies collected regular
Bali, Bhaga and Shulka
Vajji and Malla were gana-sanghas, and Kamboja was regarded as a later republic in the Arthashastra tradition.
Later Vedic polity became territorial, the kingship became hereditary, Vidatha disappeared, and regular revenues such as Bali, Bhaga and Shulka emerged.

secs.t: Rulers contemporary with the Buddha

x: Bimbisara, Prasenajit, Udayana and Pukkusati were associated with Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Gandhara respectively.
Avantiputra was associated with
Surasena
and is described as a disciple of the Buddha.
Vasavadatta, the daughter of
Chanda Pradyota
of Avanti, was associated with the famous romance of Udayana of Vatsa.
Bhasa's
Svapnavasavadatta
is the famous literary work associated with the romance of Udayana and Vasavadatta.

secs.t: Rivalries among the four powers

x: Chanda Pradyota of Avanti rivalled Bimbisara of Magadha and Udayana of Vatsa.
Kosala first annexed Kashi; Magadha subsequently acquired it through dowry and war.
Magadha did not remain subordinate; it ultimately emerged as the supreme power between the sixth and fourth centuries BCE.

secs.t: Magadha dynasties - order, rulers, Buddha's contemporaries, Nandas in Hathigumpha

x: Exam angle: "Bimbisara's dynasty" = Haryanka; "contemporary of Buddha" = Bimbisara.
Udayin built Pataliputra, Ajatashatru defeated the Vajjis, and Kalashoka was associated with the Second Buddhist Council.
Dhana Nanda
was the last Nanda ruler and was ruling Magadha when Alexander invaded north-western India.
Bimbisara, Prasenajit, Udayana and Pradyota were all contemporaries of the Buddha, ruling Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti respectively.

secs.t: Rise of Magadha - reasons, capitals, annexations

x: Fertile land, rainfall, iron ore, war elephants and the Ganga-Son river system together strengthened Magadha’s agricultural, military and transport advantages.
Ajatashatru defeated the Vajji confederacy after a sixteen-year war, aided by sowing dissension among the confederates.
Ajatashatru defeated Vajji, while Shishunaga destroyed Avanti; the Kosala conflict occurred during Ajatashatru's reign.

secs.t: Other heterodox sects - Ajivikas and Charvaka/Lokayata

x: Exam angle: "philosophy of the Charvakas" = Lokayata.
The Ajivikas followed Niyati, or strict fatalism, and rejected karma and free will.
Ashoka and Dasharatha
gifted the Barabar caves to the Ajivikas.
The
Majjhima Nikaya
records debates involving the Buddha, Jains and Ajivikas.
The Ajivika movement is associated successively with Nanda Vachcha, Kisa Sankichcha and Gosala, who was the third chief.

secs.t: Foreign invasions - Persian and Alexander

x: Cyrus
began the Achaemenid Persian expansion, while Darius I later annexed Punjab and Sindh.
Darius I annexed Punjab and Sindh around
516 BCE
during the Achaemenid period.
Alexander crossed the Indus in 326 BCE, fought Porus at the Hydaspes, faced his army’s refusal beyond the Beas, and died at Babylon in 323 BCE.

secs.t: Assaka/Asmaka - the Andhra-Telangana link

x: Assaka or Asmaka was the only Mahajanapada south of the Vindhyas and was situated on the Godavari.
Potana or Potali is identified with Bodhan in present-day Nizamabad district of Telangana.
The Suttanipata refers to
sage Bavari’s ashram on the Godavari in Assaka
, providing an early Andhra-region link in Buddhist literature.

secs.t: Causes for the rise of heterodox sects

x: Costly rituals, animal sacrifice, Sanskrit-centred religious practice and dissatisfaction with ritualism encouraged the rise of heterodox sects.
Mahavira and Buddha were Kshatriyas, and Kshatriya resentment of Brahmin dominance was one factor behind the rise of heterodox movements.
Vaishyas enriched by trade and money-lending sought higher social status and religious teachings that did not disapprove of their economic activities.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Banaras Hindu University
opened 22 boxes containing finds from the 1957–1969 Rajghat excavations.
The Rajghat artefacts indicate that Varanasi’s urban origins date to approximately
800 BCE
The Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha were linked with the second urbanisation, the emergence of the first large Indian state and the rise of heterodox sects amid economic change.
Monarchies generally permitted quicker decisions but could experience succession struggles, while gana-sanghas were collectively governed and could be slower and divided.

rows.title: Second urbanisation - NBPW, punch-marked coins, guilds (shreni), growth of towns

secs.t: Punch-marked coins

x: Punch-marked coins were called panas or karshapanas, carried various punched symbols and followed standard weights.
Karshapana or kahapana denoted a standard silver or copper punch-marked coin.
Pali texts
provide the first definite literary references to coins, including kahapana, nikkha, kamsa and kakanika.
Satavahanas initially used inherited punch-marked coins and subsequently issued die-struck coins in lead, potin, copper and silver.

secs.t: Chronology of economic firsts

x: AMS dating at Mayiladumparai places the evidence at about
2172 BCE

secs.t: Trade and merchant terms; routes

x: Setthi or Sedhi denoted a rich merchant-banker and domestic trader.
Gahapati, Vanija and Setthi are correctly matched.

secs.t: Towns of the period

x: Kaushambi
, the town associated with Vatsa, stood on the bank of the Yamuna and was fortified.
Ujjayini was located on the Sipra in Avanti and was referred to as Ozene by Ptolemy.
More than 60 towns flourished during the period from 600 to 300 BCE, including Pataliputra, Rajagriha, Shravasti, Varanasi, Vaishali, Champa, Kaushambi and Ujjayini.

secs.t: Northern Black Polished Ware

x: NBPW, dated approximately to 700–200 BCE, followed Painted Grey Ware and served as a hallmark of the second urbanisation.
Rajghat has pre-NBPW levels about 3,000 years old, along with punch-marked coins and Greek-inscribed seals.
The urban phase of Varanasi is dated to approximately
800 BCE
, while Rajghat also contains pre-NBPW levels about 3,000 years old.

secs.t: Causes of second urbanisation

x: All four factors contributed to the second urbanisation: iron technology, agricultural surplus, expanding trade and monetisation, and the formation of states with administrative capitals.
New merchant classes, especially Vaishyas, supported
Buddhism and Jainism
during the period of expanding towns, trade and state formation.

secs.t: Money-lending and banking terms

x: The
Satapatha Brahmana
contains the first reference to money-lending.
Kusidin
is the term used for a usurer in the Satapatha Brahmana.
Guild deposits at fixed interest, particularly those recorded in the Nashik inscription, demonstrate that guilds performed banking functions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Kotilingala, Dhulikatta and Kondapur were Satavahana trade centres, Sarthavahas were foreign-trade merchants, and Yajnasri Satakarni issued ship-mast coins.

src: Sources: CDI (Block01 Mahajanapadas > Urbanisation, Coinage, Introduction); UPSC (Ancient History p.44); CDX (AP History pp.21, 45-46); APP (AP History > Satavahana economy); APHQ (aph2019_36, aph2012_5); LENSD 8 Sep 2026, 23 Aug 2026; LENS Aug 2026 p.117; APPCA Jun 2026; PYQ keys (UPSC 2012/2026, RPSC 2018, UPPSC 2008/2010)

rows.title: Rise of Magadha - Haryankas (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru), Shishunagas, Nandas; causes of supremacy

secs.t: Ruler → contribution

x: Bimbisara conquered Anga, Ajatashatru defeated the Vajji confederacy, Udayin shifted the capital to Pataliputra, and Kalashoka is associated with the Second Buddhist Council.
Bimbisara conquered Anga, entered into matrimonial alliances, and was a contemporary of both Buddha and Mahavira.
Ajatashatru fought the Vajji confederacy for
sixteen years
and ultimately defeated it.

secs.t: Causes of Magadhan supremacy

x: Iron, river transport and eastern elephants contributed to Magadhan power.
Nearby iron ore supplied material for weapons and tools.
Alluvial soil and ample rainfall supported agriculture, while the Ganga and Son aided transport and trade.
Rajagriha was fortified by five hills, whereas Pataliputra functioned as a river fort.
Magadha's society was relatively unorthodox, with little Vedic hold.

secs.t: Nandas - titles, wealth, extent, references

x: Sarvakshatrantaka
means destroyer of Kshatriyas.
Greek writers described the Nandas as possessing a formidable army and great wealth.
Greek writers referred to
Dhana Nanda
by names rendered as Agrammes or Xandrames.
The Hathigumpha inscription credits a Nandaraja with an irrigation canal in Kalinga.
The Nandas are stated to have reached the
Deccan and Kalinga

secs.t: Capital shifts

x: Rajagriha was protected by hills.
Pataliputra stood at the confluence of the
Ganga and Son
, with the Gandak nearby.
Vaishali is associated with Shishunaga.

secs.t: Court and succession traditions

x: Buddhist texts preserve a patricide chain involving Bimbisara, followed by Ajatashatru and then Udayin.
Udayin was probably killed at the instigation of
Palaka of Avanti
Jivaka, the royal physician, was sent by Bimbisara to treat
Pradyota of Avanti
for jaundice.

secs.t: Matrimonial alliances of Bimbisara

x: Kosaladevi belonged to Kosala, Chellana to the Lichchhavi clan of Vaishali, and Khema to Madra in Punjab.
Kosaladevi, also referred to in connection with Mahakoshala, brought Kashi as dowry.
The alliances gave Magadha the revenue of Kashi and security on its western and northern sides.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Magadha's rise created the territorial and political base for the Mauryan Empire.
Kashi was associated with Brahmadatta and with Rajghat in present-day Varanasi.

rows.title: Jainism - Tirthankaras, life of Mahavira, Triratna, Panchamahavratas, anekantavada and syadvada
sub: Group-II S1-13: Emergence of Jainism - Mahavira, doctrines, Triratna, Panchamahavratas

secs.t: Tirthankaras - 1st, 20th, 22nd, 23rd, 24th: symbols and nirvana places

x: Exam angle: "24th Tirthankara" and "20th Tirthankara - Munisuvrat Swami" are direct one-liners.
Exam angle: "24th / 20th / 1st Tirthankara was..." and symbol-matching.
Rishabhadeva or Adinatha, the first Tirthankara, has the bull as his symbol and is believed to have attained moksha at Mount Kailash, also called Ashtapada.
Neminatha or Arishtanemi, the 22nd Tirthankara, is associated with the conch and is believed to have attained nirvana at Girnar in the Gujarat region.
Parshvanatha was born in the family of Asvasena and Vama at Varanasi, renounced at 30, attained enlightenment after 84 days of penance and lived about 250 years before Mahavira.
Rishabhadeva is associated with the bull, Munisuvrata with the tortoise, Neminatha with the conch and Vasupujya with the buffalo.

secs.t: Philosophical doctrines - exponent and meaning (syadvada, anekantavada, nayavada)

x: Exam angle: two traps - "preacher of Syadvada" = Kundakundacharya; "title Syadvadachala Simha" = Somadeva Suri.
Syadvada is the Jain theory of conditioned predication or relativity of truth.
Somadeva Suri authored
Yasastilaka Champu
and Nitivakyamrita.
Jainism is associated with Anekantavada, Syadvada and Nayavada; Buddhism with anatta and pratityasamutpada; Ajivikas with niyati; and Charvaka with materialism.

secs.t: Jain concepts and practices - jiva/ajiva, karma, kaivalya, sallekhana

x: Exam angle: "Santhara is a ritual of fasting to death amongst - Jains".
Jiva refers to the conscious soul, whereas Ajiva denotes non-conscious matter or non-living reality.
Kevala Jnana or Kaivalya is the state of omniscience attained by the soul after the removal of karmic bondage.
Jain liberation involves stopping the inflow of karma and shedding accumulated karma, or nirjara, through penance, ultimately leading to Kevala Jnana and the Siddha state.
Paryushana is the Jain festival, its last day Samvatsari is the day of forgiveness, Pratikramana is introspection, and Sallekhana is the ritual fast unto death.
Because Jain ahimsa extends to all forms of life, strict followers avoided agriculture since ploughing and related activities could injure organisms in the soil.

secs.t: Mahavira - birth, parents, clan, enlightenment, death, titles

x: Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, was the son of Siddhartha, and belonged to the Jnatrika clan.
Mahavira renounced worldly life at the age of 30 and subsequently undertook twelve years of rigorous asceticism.
Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana at Jrimbhikagrama, on the bank of the Rijupalika river, under a sal tree.
Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana at the age of 42, after twelve years of rigorous asceticism.
Makkhali Gosala was Mahavira’s companion for about
six years
before founding the Ajivika sect.

secs.t: Triratna - three jewels, Jain vs Buddhist versions

x: Exam angle: questions test which set belongs to which religion.
The Jain Ratnatraya consists of Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct and constitutes the path to moksha.

secs.t: Jainism and Buddhism compared

x: Jainism regards the soul as eternal and karma as material bondage.
Jainism follows a stricter interpretation of ahimsa, extending even to thought.
All four statements correctly describe the monastic traditions and textual languages or collections associated with Jainism and Buddhism.
Jainism uses the concept of kevala jnana, while Buddhism refers to nirvana or Buddhahood.

secs.t: Panchamahavratas - five vows and the fifth added by Mahavira

x: Parshvanatha
taught the four vows, collectively associated with chaturyama.
Brahmacharya
, or celibacy, was added by Mahavira as the fifth vow.
Jain householders observe Anuvratas, which include non-injury, non-stealing, non-adultery, truth and non-possession.

secs.t: Jainism in Andhra - early centres, inscriptions, royal patronage

x: Samprati, Ashoka's grandson, is associated with constructing a Jain basadi or vihara at Vaddamanu in Mahavira's name.
Danavulapadu is a Jain kshetra at Jammalamadugu in YSR Kadapa district, associated with Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III.
The Bhadrabahu–Chandragupta route to Shravanabelagola passed through Kurnool and Anantapur
, supporting the description of Rayalaseema as a Jain corridor.

secs.t: Contemporaries of Mahavira - rulers and teachers

x: Chetaka was a Lichchhavi ruler and the maternal uncle of Mahavira.
Gautama Buddha was the teacher of Buddhism, Makkhali Gosala led the Ajivika tradition, Ajita Kesakambalin represented materialism and Sanjaya Belatthiputta was associated with skepticism.
Parshvanatha preceded Mahavira and was not a contemporary teacher of his period.
Bimbisara and Ajatashatru were associated with Magadha, Udayana with Vatsa and Pradyota with Avanti.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Anekantavada recognises the many-sided nature of reality and is therefore cited as a basis of pluralism and tolerance.
Jain
ahimsa
significantly influenced Gandhi's philosophy and his emphasis on non-violence.
Jainism's severe austerities limited its mass appeal, while loss of royal patronage and the Digambara–Svetambara split contributed to its later decline.
Sallekhana is a Jain practice involving voluntary fasting unto death under prescribed spiritual conditions.

rows.title: Jain councils, Digambara-Svetambara split, Jain literature (Angas), spread and royal patrons
sub: Group-II S1-14: Jain councils, sects, literature, spread and royal patronage

secs.t: Royal patrons → dynasty

x: Kharavela was the second-century BCE king of Kalinga and a staunch Jain patron.
Chandragupta Maurya is traditionally described as a disciple of Bhadrabahu who migrated south and ended his life by sallekhana at Shravanabelagola.
Simuka or Srimukha is identified as the first Satavahana Jain patron; the Kalpa Pradeepa attributes 52 Jain temples to his 52 army chiefs.
Indra III built a Jain kshetra at Danavulapadu in Kadapa, not the Gommateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola.
The twelfth-century councils at Vallabhi and Mathura are associated with Chalukya
Kumarapala
, whose guru was Hemachandra.

secs.t: Jain canon - Angas, Upangas, Purvas, Agamas, language

x: Exam angle: odd-one-out - Jain texts (Acharanga, Bhagavati, Kalpasutra) vs Buddhist (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa, Divyavadana, Milindapanho).
Jain sacred texts are called
Agamas or Siddhanta
The fourteen Purvas were regarded as the earliest Jain texts, but they are now mostly lost.
The Svetambara canon includes twelve Angas, while Digambaras maintain that all the original Angas were lost and follow a separate canon.

secs.t: Jain works → author

x: Exam angle: Samayasara (asked 2008 and 2019), Yogasara (2017) - all Kundakundacharya.
The Tattvartha Sutra, associated with Umasvati, presents core Jain doctrines and is accepted in versions by both the Digambara and Svetambara traditions.
Appayacharya, also known as Appayaryudu, composed Jinendra Kalyanabhyudayamu and dedicated it to the Kakatiya ruler
Prataparudra

secs.t: Contributions of Jainism - language, literature, social base

x: Early Jains used
popular Prakrit
instead of Sanskrit to communicate their teachings widely.
Jains produced some of the earliest important Apabhramsa works and its first grammar; later Jain works appeared in Sanskrit and regional languages as well.
Jainism challenged birth-based hierarchy, emphasised conduct and action, and promoted vegetarianism in accordance with ahimsa.

secs.t: Jain sects → leader and differences

x: Digambaras are sky-clad, Svetambaras wear white robes, Sthanakvasis oppose idol worship, and Terapanthi was founded by Acharya Bhikshu.
Digambara doctrine holds that women must be reborn as men before attaining moksha; Svetambaras accept the possibility of liberation for women.
The Digambara tradition limited monkly possessions to a broom and water pot, while the Svetambara tradition recognised fourteen items including clothing.

secs.t: Jain councils → place, period, president, outcome

x: The second council at Vallabhi was held in 512 CE under Maitraka patronage and is associated with the written compilation of the canon and addition of the Upangas.
The first council belongs to about 300 BCE, the second to 512 CE, Gommateshwara to about 983 CE, and Vimala Shah’s Dilwara temple to 1031 CE.

secs.t: Spread - Karnataka, Gujarat, Tamil country

x: The famine tradition states that Bhadrabahu, the sixth Thera, travelled south with Chandragupta to
Shravanabelagola
in Karnataka.
Early Jain ascetic camps were located in the caves of the Erramala and Nallamala ranges.
Both statements are true, and the traditional southward migration of Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta helps explain the importance of Shravanabelagola as a Jain centre.

secs.t: Jain architecture and pilgrim sites → region

x: Dilwara is at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, Shravanabelagola is in Karnataka, Udayagiri-Khandagiri is in Odisha, and Sammed Shikhar is in Jharkhand.
Sammed Shikhar or Shikharji is situated on
Parasnath Hill
in Jharkhand and is associated with the nirvana of Parsvanatha.
Gommateshwara is the Bahubali statue at Shravanabelagola, associated with Chamundaraya and dated to about 983 CE.

secs.t: Jainism in AP - Ramatirtham, Vaddamanu, Nedumba Vasati, Potla Cheruvu

x: Potla Cheruvu belonged to the Eastern Chalukya period; the Kadalalaya Basadi was built in 1117 CE; Ganapatideva’s persecution came later; and Devaraya II’s Jinalaya belongs to a still later Vijayanagara context.
Ganapatideva’s persecution is mentioned in Siddeshwara Charitra, while the flight of a Jain monk to Hanamkonda from Rajaraja Narendra’s persecution is recorded in the Orugallu Kaifiyat.

secs.t: Jain centres in Andhra

x: Danavulapadu is associated with Rashtrakuta Indra III; Vijayawada with Ayyana Mahadevi’s Nedumbasadi; Munugodu with Pudvithilakavasati; and Ramatirtham with the Eastern Chalukya period.
Ramatirtham was an Eastern Chalukya-era Jain centre associated with Ugraditya.
Aryavatam is identified with
Bikkavolu
in the list of Jain centres.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The factors identified were loss of royal patronage, sectarian split, severe austerity, lack of missionary zeal and rival Bhakti revival.

The stated regional tradition associates Kalamukha/Vira Shaiva hostility with the persecution of Jains by Ganapatideva at Anmakonda, while Anmakonda also served as a refuge from Eastern Chalukya persecution.
The Samrat Samprati Museum was inaugurated at
Koba in Gujarat
to highlight Jain heritage.

rows.title: Buddhism - life of the Buddha, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Pratityasamutpada, Sangha
sub: Group-II S1-15: Emergence of Buddhism - Buddha's life, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path

secs.t: Events of the Buddha's life → place and present-day site

x: Exam angle: "first sermon" = Sarnath; birth-enlightenment-sermon-death match.
The Great Renunciation occurred when Siddhartha was 29 years old, accompanied by the charioteer Channa and the horse Kanthaka.
Gautama Buddha attained enlightenment at Uruvela under the Bodhi tree on the bank of the
Niranjana
River.
The five former companions were
Kondanna, Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama and Assaji
; they became arhats after the first sermon.
Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana at Kusinara at the age of 80, traditionally dated to 483 BCE; some accounts give an approximate alternative date.

secs.t: Core goal and teachings - nirvana, middle path, anatta, Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path

x: The Middle Path avoids both the extreme of severe asceticism and the opposite extreme of sensual indulgence.
Dukkha means suffering; Samudaya identifies craving as its cause; Nirodha is its cessation; and Magga is the path to cessation.
Prajna consists of Right View and Right Intention; Sila consists of Right Speech, Right Action and Right Livelihood; Samadhi consists of Right Effort, Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration.
Dhammachakra Pravartana, the first sermon at Sarnath, expounded
the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path

secs.t: Buddha's life - clan, family, teachers, converts, successor

x: All four statements correctly describe Siddhartha Gautama's clan, parents, foster mother, wife and son.
Siddhartha first studied under teachers including Uddaka Ramaputta, then renounced worldly life, practised austerities with five ascetics and finally attained enlightenment.
Siddhartha Gautama practised austerities for
six years
before abandoning them and attaining enlightenment at the age of 35.
“Appamadena sampadetha” means “
strive diligently
” and is associated with Buddha's last words.

secs.t: Epithets and titles of the Buddha

x: Jina, Kevalin and Nigantha Nataputta are all titles or designations associated with Mahavira, not the Buddha.

secs.t: Pratityasamutpada - twelve links in order

x: Pratityasamutpada
is the doctrine of dependent origination, according to which phenomena arise through causal conditions.
The first four links are Avidya, Samskara, Vijnana and Namarupa.
The fifth to eighth links are Shadayatana, Sparsha, Vedana and Trishna.
The final four links are Upadana, Bhava, Jati and Jara-marana.

secs.t: Triratna and ascetic terms

x: Parivrajaka means wandering ascetic, Shramana means an ascetic outside the Vedic fold, Upasaka means lay follower and Uposatha is the confession and rule-recitation observance.
Pravrajya means leaving lay life or going forth; Upasampada denotes full ordination.
Parajika denotes a grave monastic offence carrying expulsion from the order.

secs.t: Sangha - membership, women, Vinaya

x: The Sangha admitted persons above 15 irrespective of caste, but excluded certain categories such as criminals, lepers and those with infectious diseases.
Women were admitted after requests associated with
Ananda and Mahapajapati Gotami
, who became the first nun.
Buddhist monks traditionally shaved their heads, wore yellow or saffron robes and obtained food through daily alms.

secs.t: Buddhist doctrines - anatta, anicca, karma, pratityasamutpada

x: Anicca means impermanence, while Anatta teaches that there is no permanent, unchanging self or atman.
Buddhist karma is intention-based morality; the present state is linked to past actions, and rebirth continues until nirvana.
The raft analogy expresses Upaya, or skilful means, and indicates that teaching is a means of crossing over rather than a dogma to be clung to.

secs.t: Triratna of Buddhism

x: The Triratna consists of Buddha as teacher, Dhamma as teaching and Sangha as the order.

secs.t: Disciples and Sangha

x: Ananda was the personal attendant and recited the Sutta Pitaka; Upali recited the Vinaya Pitaka; Mahakassapa presided over the First Council; Subhadda was the last convert.
Sariputta and Mahamoggallana were chief disciples, and their relics are associated with
Sanchi

secs.t: Four Noble Truths (Arya Satya)

x: Samudaya identifies the cause of suffering, especially craving, ignorance and attachment.
All four statements correctly describe the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its causes, its cessation and the path to cessation.
Both statements are true, and the identification of Magga as the path to cessation directly explains why the Eightfold Path has this role.

secs.t: Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga)

x: Ethics consists of Right Speech, Right Action and Right Livelihood.
Samma-ditthi means Right View, Sankappa means Right Intention, Vaca means Right Speech and Samadhi means Right Concentration.
The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom, ethics and mental discipline exactly as stated in all three statements.
Kammanta means Right Action.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Anagarika Dharmapala
founded the Maha Bodhi Society in 1891 to work for the restoration of Bodh Gaya to Buddhist control.
All four statements correctly describe the rational, moderate and socially accessible nature of Buddhism, its rejection of Vedic ritual and caste, and the role of the organised Sangha in its spread.
In June 2026, the Ministry of Culture sent the relics of Sariputta and Mahamoggallana from Sanchi to
Mongolia

rows.title: Buddhist councils (four), Hinayana-Mahayana-Vajrayana, Tripitakas and Pali literature
sub: Group-II S1-16: Buddhist councils, Hinayana-Mahayana-Vajrayana, Tripitakas and the spread of Buddhism

secs.t: Buddhist councils → place, period, ruler, president, outcome

x: Exam angle: council-president matching and chronological order of venues.
At the First Buddhist Council, the Vinaya Pitaka was compiled through the recitation of Upali and the Sutta Pitaka through Ananda.
The Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali dealt with disputes regarding monastic rules, which eventually contributed to the division between the Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas.
The Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka was held on the advice of the monk
Parsva
and dealt with Sarvastivada disputes in Kashmir and Gandhara.
Moggaliputta Tissa
presided over the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra around 250 BCE.

secs.t: Philosophical schools → founder and doctrine

x: Nagarjuna
is regarded as the founder of the Madhyamika or Sunyavada school, which emphasises emptiness and the middle position between existence and non-existence.
Madhyamika philosophy is based on Sunyata, or emptiness, and seeks a middle position between the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Vaibhashika or Sarvastivada expresses the view that all exists, meaning that dharmas exist in the past, present and future.

secs.t: Nagarjuna - school, works, Sriparvata

x: The Maha Vihara, also called Parvata Vihara, at Sriparvata is associated with Satavahana ruler
Yajna Sri Satakarni
, who was contemporary and friendly with Nagarjuna.
Suhrlekha was a letter to a Satavahana king, I-tsing noticed its memorisation, and tradition connects Nagarjuna with the Fourth Council and 32 sects in Andhradesha.
The philosophical Nagarjuna founded Madhyamika and Sunyavada, whereas Siddha Nagarjuna is distinguished as the founder of Vajrayana at Sriparvata and is described as a Telugu native.

secs.t: Tripitakas → content and sub-texts

x: Patimokkha, Vibhanga and Khandhaka
are sub-texts of the Vinaya Pitaka, which deals with monastic discipline.
The Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with Buddhist philosophy in question-and-answer form and includes works such as Yamaka and Kathavatthu.
Majjhima means medium, and this Nikaya contains
medium-length discourses, including debates with Jains and Ajivikas
Milindapanha is framed as a dialogue between the Indo-Greek ruler Menander, called Milinda, and the Buddhist monk Nagasena.

secs.t: Buddhist scholars → work

x: Nagarjuna
is associated with the Madhyamika Karika tradition and wrote Suhrlekha.
Vasubandhu
wrote Abhidharmakosa and was the brother of Asanga.
Buddhaghosha composed Visuddhimagga at
Anuradhapura
Buddhaghosha was born near Guntur at Kota Nemapuri.
Dignaga wrote
Pramana Samuccaya
and is regarded as the father of Indian logic.
Dharmakirti
is known as the “Kant of India” and wrote Pramana Vartika and Nyaya Bindu.

secs.t: Buddhist texts → sect and language

x: Divyavadana
is a Sanskrit collection of Buddhist legends and is associated with the Mahayana tradition.
Avadanashataka is a
Sanskrit
work containing avadana tales.
Aryamanjushrimulakalpa
is a Sanskrit Mahayana-Vajrayana text containing historical data.
Mahavastu is a mixed Sanskrit-Prakrit biography of the Buddha.
Mahavamsa is a Pali Sri Lankan chronicle written by
Mahanama

secs.t: Sects - Hinayana vs Mahayana vs Vajrayana

x: Mahayana
emphasises the Bodhisattva who postpones nirvana for the welfare of all beings.
Vajrayana is characterised by mantras, mudras, mandalas and associated tantric practices.
The six paramitas are dana, sila, kshanti, virya, dhyana and prajna.
In Andhra, Hinayana was associated with Amaravati, Mahayana with Sriparvata and Vajrayana with Salihundam.
Nine of the eighteen sects existed in Andhra, Mahishasakas were the only Hinayana sect mentioned, and the three centres are associated with the stated traditions.

secs.t: Stupa architecture, chaitya vs vihara, stupas by location

x: A
chaitya
is a Buddhist prayer hall, whereas a vihara is a monastery or residence for monks.
Sanchi was built by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, encased in stone under the Shungas, and received UNESCO World Heritage status in 1989.
The four toranas of Sanchi are associated with the
Satavahanas
, although the stupa had earlier origins under Ashoka and was later encased under the Shungas.

secs.t: Spread abroad and decline in India

x: Ashoka’s mission to Sri Lanka is associated with
Mahendra and Sanghamitra
Mahayana entered Tibet in the seventh century and later merged with Vajrayana and the indigenous Bon tradition.
The
Gelug
school became dominant in Tibetan Buddhism by the fifteenth century.
Nalanda was sacked by
Bakhtiyar Khalji
during the Turkish raids.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Odisha’s Buddhist Diamond Triangle consists of
Ratnagiri, Udayagiri and Lalitagiri
in the Jajpur-Cuttack region.
The three Odisha sites form the Diamond Triangle, are associated with the Jajpur-Cuttack region, were added to UNESCO’s Tentative List, and represent all three yanas.
China insists on
the 1793 Golden Urn rule
in the Dalai Lama succession controversy.

rows.title: Spread and decline of Buddhism; Buddhist and Jain architecture - stupa, chaitya, vihara

secs.t: AP Buddhist sites → district, period, patron, features

x: Nagarjunakonda was an Ikshvaku capital, is situated on an island in the Nagarjuna Sagar, and contains over thirty stupas including evidence of a Sinhala vihara.
Amaravati, also known as Dhanyakataka, is placed in
Palnadu
district in the current arrangement; older books commonly refer to it as being in Guntur district.
Thotlakonda and Bavikonda are hilltop monasteries in Visakhapatnam district and are linked with Sri Lanka–Southeast Asia trade connections.
Nagarjunakonda is situated on an island in the
Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir
on the Palnadu side and is named after Acharya Nagarjuna.
Bavikonda, Thotlakonda and Bojjannakonda are
Buddhist hilltop monasteries near Visakhapatnam
, dating approximately to 200 BCE.

secs.t: Stupa architecture - parts; stupa vs chaitya vs vihara

x: Anda is the
hemispherical mound
of a stupa and symbolically represents the cosmos.
Dhatugarbha contains bodily relics, Paribhogika contains objects used by Buddha, and Uddeshika is memorial in character.
An Arama was a larger Buddhist complex containing
a stupa, vihara, chaitya and school
Ayaka pillars or Ayakapata are a distinctive
Andhra
feature; the Purna Kumbha is among their associated symbols.

secs.t: Buddhist literary names → present site, acharyas

x: The Buddhist literary name
Siddharthaka Chaitya
is identified with Guntupalli.
Dhanyakataka is Amaravati and Sriparvata is Nagarjunakonda.
The 1,500-room vihara at Sriparvata was associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni and the acharya Bhavaviveka.
Hiuen Tsang found Sriparvata without patronage in the seventh century CE.

secs.t: Oldest and largest stupas → builder, period

x: Piprahwa
in Uttar Pradesh, identified with ancient Kapilavastu, has an inscribed relic vessel linked to the Buddha’s kin and is dated among the earliest stupas, around the fifth century BCE.
Sanchi began as an Ashokan brick stupa in the third century BCE, received a stone casing under the Shungas and its toranas are associated with the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Recent excavations of Buddhist sites

x: Vaishya Tekri is believed to contain a Mauryan third-century BCE stupa associated with Ashoka’s wife Devi and possibly identified with Kanakagiri Vihara.
The Vaishya Tekri stupa is estimated to have a diameter of about 350 feet and a height of about 100 feet.
The 2013–14 excavations led by B. R. Mani indicated activity at Sarnath before the time of Ashoka.

secs.t: Buddhist and Jain cave sites → state and sect

x: Bhaja is in Maharashtra, Bagh in Madhya Pradesh, Udayagiri-Khandagiri in Odisha and Sittanavasal in Tamil Nadu.
Karle in Maharashtra contains a great chaitya, and Pulumavi II donated a village to the Mahasanghikas.
Ajanta has 25 viharas and four chaityas, Caves 9–10 are associated with the Satavahana phase, and Cave 10 contains the Svetagaja Jataka.

secs.t: Aniconic symbols → event

x: The Bodhi tree and the empty seat symbolise the
enlightenment
of Buddha.
The horse Kanthaka represents renunciation, the Dharmachakra represents the first sermon, and footprints, along with the stupa, represent parinirvana.
The first human-form representations of Buddha appeared in the 1st century CE, particularly in the Gandhara and Mathura schools.

secs.t: Monasteries and universities → scholars, patrons

x: Nalanda
is associated with a Gupta foundation under Kumaragupta I. Vikramashila and Odantapuri were associated with the Palas, while Vallabhi was associated with the Maitrakas.
Vikramashila was associated with Dharmapala, Valabhi with the Maitrakas, Odantapuri with Gopala, and Dhanyakataka/Sriparvata with Nagarjuna and Bhavaviveka.
Vikramashila
in Bihar was a major Vajrayana centre patronised by the Pala ruler Dharmapala.

secs.t: Spread and decline

x: Veerapurushadatta
is associated with the rebuilding of the Nagarjunakonda Maha Chaitya and with Sriparvata University.
Veerapurushadatta is described as hostile to Saivism, and the trampled Shivalinga sculpture reflects this hostility.
Mahadeva Bhikshu
is credited in the Mahavamsa tradition with taking Buddhism to Sri Lanka with 100,000 followers.
Pushyamitra Shunga, Shashanka and Mihirakula
are identified as hostile rulers associated with the decline of Buddhism.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sarnath was on the UNESCO
Tentative List
since 1998 and was nominated for the UNESCO list in 2025–26.
The ‘Discover Andhra’ campaign focused on the Buddhist circuit comprising Amaravati, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda.
The AP Tourism ‘Discover Andhra’ campaign focusing on the Buddhist circuit was reported in February 2026.
Srinatha’s
Haravilasam
describes sea trade under the Reddi kings.

rows.title: Other heterodox sects - Ajivikas (Makkhali Gosala), Charvaka/Lokayata materialism

secs.t: Charvaka/Lokayata - names, tenets, aphorisms, sources

x: Exam angle: name-matching (Lokayata, Barhaspatya) and "which school accepts only perception".
Charvaka philosophy is called
Lokayata
, meaning a materialist system concerned with the worldly sphere.
Charvaka identifies the conscious body with the soul and denies the survival of a separate soul after death.
The aphorism expresses the
Charvaka
rejection of an afterlife and its emphasis on material enjoyment during the present life.

secs.t: Ajivikas - founder, doctrine, lifestyle, patronage, caves

x: Exam angle: statement-sets - determinism
and
austerity true; "order of rebirth can be changed" false; caste discrimination false.
Ajivikas practised extreme asceticism, including nakedness, lying on nails, walking through fire and sitting in large earthen pots.
Ajivika ascetics were often called
Sudra sannyasins
, reflecting their organised ascetic identity outside orthodox Brahmanical structures.

secs.t: Heterodox teachers contemporary with the Buddha → doctrine

x: Akriyavada, associated with Purana Kassapa, held that actions have no moral consequence; even killing or charity produces neither merit nor demerit.
Pakudha Kaccayana
taught the doctrine of seven eternal, uncreated elements and denied the ultimate reality of killing and being killed.
Sanjaya Belatthiputta refused to affirm or deny propositions and is therefore associated with
scepticism or agnosticism

secs.t: Relations of Ajivikas with Mahavira and the Buddha

x: Gosala spent about six years as Mahavira’s companion and later broke away.
The
Majjhima Nikaya
records debates involving the Buddha, Jains and Ajivikas.

secs.t: Sources for heterodox sects

x: The Samannaphala Sutta, contained in the Digha Nikaya, presents Ajatashatru’s report of the views of the six teachers to the Buddha.
The
Bhagavati Sutra
, a Jain Anga, provides the fullest account of Gosala and his quarrel with Mahavira.
Ashokan edicts, Barabar cave inscriptions, the Bhagavati Sutra and the Samannaphala Sutta all provide evidence for the study of heterodox sects, including the Ajivikas.

secs.t: Decline of Ajivikas and Lokayata

x: The Ajivikas survived for nearly 2,000 years and disappeared around
the 14th century CE
in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
The heterodox traditions declined with the Puranic-Bhakti revival, including under the Pallavas, and because they lost royal patronage.
Lokayata left no surviving texts and is known mainly through the criticisms and refutations of opposing philosophical traditions.

secs.t: Comparison of heterodox views - karma, soul, fate, Vedas

x: Jainism treats karma as material bondage removable by penance, Buddhism views it through intention, and Ajivikas deny its power to alter destiny.
Jainism and Buddhism give importance to effort, Ajivika teaches Niyati or complete predetermination, and Charvaka has no separate doctrine of fate in the comparison.
The Shramana reaction, including Jainism, Buddhism, Ajivika and Charvaka currents, arose amid
urbanisation and Magadhan patronage
in the sixth century BCE.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Charvaka accepts only perception.
These sects reflect the intellectual ferment of the sixth century BCE and the religious pluralism of the Mauryan period.

rows.title: Persian and Macedonian invasions - Alexander's campaign, Battle of Hydaspes, effects on India

secs.t: Alexander's invasion - route, year, rulers who submitted or resisted

x: Exam angle: "which people's women fought Alexander" = Massaga; "first to submit" = Ambhi.
Alexander wanted to investigate the Greek geographers' puzzle concerning
the limits of the ocean
Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BC and entered India through the Khyber Pass in 326 BC.
The Malloi or Malavas
and other gana-sanghas fought Alexander during his retreat.

secs.t: Battle of Hydaspes - river, opponents, outcome

x: The Hydaspes was the Jhelum, called Vitasta in Sanskrit.
The battle was fought in 326 BC between Alexander and Porus.
Alexander was impressed by Porus's bravery
and restored his kingdom, which was later enlarged.
Alexander founded Bucephala, named after his horse, and Nicaea near the Hydaspes battlefield.

secs.t: Indian political situation at the invasion - Magadha, causes of success

x: The north-west was divided into small independent states, including Taxila, Porus's Punjab and Gandhara, rather than being united under one central power.
The huge army of the Nanda kingdom deterred Alexander from advancing farther east.
Alexander's success was attributed to the absence of a central power, his superior army and assistance from traitorous Indian rulers.

secs.t: Alexander's companions and Greek historians vs later envoys

x: Nearchus was Alexander's admiral; Onesicritus and Aristobulus were companions who left first-hand accounts; Deimachus was the later envoy to Bindusara.
Indian sources are silent on Alexander
, so the campaign is known mainly through Greek writers.
Greek writers used the name Sandrokottas for
Chandragupta Maurya
, helping establish the chronology of the early Mauryas around 322 BCE.

secs.t: Achaemenid invasion - ruler, territory annexed, Herodotus

x: Cyrus
, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, was the first Achaemenid ruler to campaign into the Indian north-west, particularly the Gandhara region.
Darius I
annexed Punjab and Sindh west of the Indus.
Punjab and Sindh west of the Indus were organised as
the twentieth satrapy
of the Achaemenid Empire.
Herodotus described the Indian satrapy as the most populous and fertile.

secs.t: Reason for Alexander's retreat - the Beas

x: War weariness, homesickness, disease and fear of the Nanda army contributed to the refusal.
Hyphasis was the Greek name for the
Beas
, beyond which Alexander's army refused to advance.
Alexander set up
twelve large stone altars
on the northern bank of the Beas before withdrawing.
After setting up the altars, Alexander withdrew down the Indus, while Nearchus led the fleet by sea.

secs.t: Persian influence - script, language, administration, art

x: Kharosthi
was derived from Aramaic, was written from right to left and was used in north-western India.
Ashoka's Kandahar edict used
Aramaic
, reflecting the north-western influence of the Persian administrative and script tradition.
Ashokan edicts reflect the Darius model through the terms lipi or dipi and the stylistic movement from third-person opening to first-person expression.

secs.t: Effects of the invasion - routes, satrapies, contact, politics

x: Alexander divided the conquered area into
three
parts, each placed under Greek governors.
The accounts of Onesicritus and Nearchus recorded observations on
Indian geography and society
The invasion destroyed several small north-western states and cleared the way for Chandragupta, who expelled the Greek satraps with Porus, also called Parvataka, as an ally.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Alexander's invasion is regarded as the first dated event of Indian history, and Greek accounts help fix the chronology of the Mauryas.
Persian contact during the sixth–fifth centuries BC left lasting influences on script and art, while Alexander's nineteen-month campaign left almost no lasting political mark.

src: Sources: UPSC (Ancient History p.2, p.79); CDI (Block02 Foreign Travellers - Later Graeco-Roman Texts; Block01 Mauryas - Chandragupta; Block01 Mahajanapadas - Nanda dynasty); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Mauryan Empire - Magadha's Rise; Mauryan Art - Achaemenid influence); CURRENT lane: none

rows.title: Sources for the Mauryas - Arthashastra, Indica of Megasthenes, Mudrarakshasa, edicts

secs.t: Literary work → author and content

x: Parishishtaparvan, a Jain work by Hemachandra, describes Chandragupta's conversion to Jainism under Bhadrabahu and his subsequent renunciation.
Vishakhadatta
wrote the Mudrarakshasa, which describes the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta.
Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa concern Ashoka and Buddhism in Lanka; Divyavadana and Ashokavadana contain Ashokan legends; Parishishtaparvan describes Chandragupta's Jain end; the Puranas give genealogies.

secs.t: Indica of Megasthenes

x: Fragments of Indica are preserved in the writings of Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny and Arrian.
Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra as
Palibothra
, also rendered in some accounts as Polibrotha.
Megasthenes' account included uncritical folklore, such as the story of gold-digging ants, and therefore must be used critically.
Strabo, following Megasthenes, stated that Indians did not know
writing

secs.t: Arthashastra - author, subject, rediscovery, topics

x: The Arthashastra deals with administration, economy, espionage, taxation, diplomacy, welfare, revenue and courts.
R. Shamasastry
rediscovered the Arthashastra at Mysore in 1905; it was published in 1909.
The Arthashastra consists of
15 books
, known as adhikaranas.
Both works are commonly compared for their realist approach to politics and their emphasis on ends-justify-means reasoning.

secs.t: Puranic sources

x: The Puranas provide Mauryan king lists and genealogies, with the
Vishnu Purana
being the one usually cited.

secs.t: Buddhist and Jain sources - ruler each covers

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
Jain sources associate Chandragupta with Bhadrabahu, Jainism and his death at
Shravanabelagola
Vamsatthapakasini
is identified as a commentary on the Mahavamsa.

secs.t: Epigraphic sources

x: James Prinsep first deciphered the Ashokan edicts in 1837.
The Greek-Aramaic edict was found at Shar-i-Kuna in the Kandahar region.
The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I is dated approximately to 150 CE and records the construction of the Sudarshana lake during Chandragupta Maurya's reign by the governor Pushyagupta.
The
Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela
is also cited for Mauryan references.

secs.t: Archaeological sources

x: The ruins of the 80-pillared hall of Pataliputra are located at
Kumrahar near Patna
The wide distribution of punch-marked coins and Northern Black Polished Ware indicates the
spread of Mauryan material culture
Ashokan pillars, stupas and viharas
are important archaeological remains associated with the Mauryan period.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: AP angle:
Indica is the first foreign mention of the Andhras (30 forts).
Criticism & debates:
Megasthenes' seven "castes" and no-slavery claim are known misreadings.

rows.title: Chandragupta Maurya and Bindusara - conquests, treaty with Seleucus, Chanakya
sub: Group-II S1-17: Mauryan Empire - sources, Chandragupta, Bindusara and Ashoka

secs.t: Greek names and identification - Sandrocottos

x: Sandrocottus or Sandrokottas, used by Greek writers, refers to
Chandragupta Maurya
Justin, Plutarch, Arrian and Strabo all used Greek forms of the name Chandragupta Maurya.
Sir William Jones
made the identification in 1793.
The identification fixed an important point in early Indian chronology and placed Chandragupta around
322 BCE
, contemporaneous with Alexander.

secs.t: Treaty with Seleucus Nicator

x: Seleucus I Nicator
, a general of Alexander, attempted to recover the north-west but was defeated by Chandragupta.
Seleucus made the attempt around
; the treaty is generally dated around 305 BCE.
All four pairs correctly identify the territories associated with the treaty: Aria with Herat, Arachosia with Kandahar, Paropanisadai with the Kabul valley and Gedrosia with Balochistan.

secs.t: Chanakya - names, office, role

x: The tradition describes Chanakya as raising an army, eliminating the Greek satraps, allying with Porus and finally besieging Pataliputra.
Chanakya’s alliance with Porus, referred to in some traditions as Parvataka or Parvartaka, formed part of the campaign against the Nandas.
Mudrarakshasa
narrates the political events surrounding Chandragupta’s rise and Chanakya’s role.

secs.t: Chandragupta's conquests

x: Pushyagupta
, Chandragupta’s governor in Saurashtra, constructed the Sudarshana lake.
All four statements are supported by the traditions and references associated with Chandragupta’s conquests and later life.
The Tamil poet Mamulanar refers to the southward expansion of the Mauryas.

secs.t: Greek ambassadors → Mauryan ruler

x: Exam angle: "Who first mentioned Andhra forts?" = Megasthenes.
Megasthenes
was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta’s court and wrote Indica.
Megasthenes recorded that the Andhras had thirty forts.
Deimachus
was sent by Antiochus I of Syria to the court of Bindusara.
Dionysius was sent by
Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt
to the court of Bindusara.

secs.t: Chandragupta Maurya - origin debate, first empire

x: Chandragupta’s reign is generally given as 324/321 to 297 BCE.
Mudrarakshasa, Devi Chandraguptam and the tenth-century Vamsatthapakasini are associated with traditions about Chanakya and Chandragupta.
The
Mauryas
under Chandragupta are regarded as the first pan-Indian empire, although some traditions also describe the Nandas as early empire-builders.

secs.t: Chandragupta and Jainism

x: Chandragupta is described in Jain tradition as a disciple of
Bhadrabahu
, the sixth Jain Thera.
Bhadrabahu
migrated south during the famine, and Chandragupta accompanied him.
Jain tradition states that Chandragupta abdicated, became an ascetic and died by Sallekhana, or fasting to death, at Shravanabelagola.
The famine tradition is linked with the division between the Digambara tradition associated with Bhadrabahu and the Svetambara tradition associated with Sthulabhadra.

secs.t: Bindusara - titles, contacts, religion

x: Simhasena was Bindusara’s birth name, but the pair is not correctly framed as a title relationship; Amitraghata was his title meaning ‘slayer of foes’.
Amitraghata means ‘
slayer of foes
’ or ‘slayer of enemies’; the Greek form was Amitrochates.
Bindusara is generally described as a patron of the
Ajivikas
, although some traditions indicate an inclination towards Jainism.

secs.t: Revolts at Taxila - princes sent

x: Taxila revolts were directed against oppressive officials; Susima failed, Ashoka was then sent, and Kunala handled another revolt during Ashoka’s reign.
Susima
, the eldest prince, was initially sent to Taxila but failed to suppress the revolt.

secs.t: Foreign envoys and Indica's descriptions

x: The original Indica has not survived; it is known through quotations by
Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus
Megasthenes divided Indian society into
seven
classes, including philosophers, farmers, soldiers and councillors.
Megasthenes described a 30-member municipal body organised into six boards at Palibothra.
Megasthenes claimed that India had no slaves, but the Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts indicate that slavery did exist.

secs.t: Chandragupta Maurya - rise, Kautilya, Seleucus, Sudarshana, Jain end

x: Chandragupta became ruler in 321 BC, defeated Seleucus in 305 BC, later died at Shravanabelagola, and Sudarshana lake was repaired by Rudradaman I much later.
Brahmanical traditions connect the name with Mura, described as a Shudra woman, whereas Buddhist and Jain traditions identify the Mauryas as Kshatriyas of the Moriya clan.

secs.t: Religion followed by Mauryan rulers

x: Bindusara is associated with Ajivika beliefs.
Samprati
is known as the 'Ashoka of Jainism' and is associated with Jainism.
The Barabar caves in Bihar are the oldest surviving rock-cut caves and are carved in granite.

secs.t: Extent - southern limits and Andhra

x: Rajula Mandagiri is a minor-edict site in
Kurnool
district.
Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras among peoples following Ashoka's Dhamma within his domain; the edict is dated approximately to 256 BCE.
The Satavahanas began as Mauryan feudatories, and the Andhras are described as already Buddhist by the time of Rock Edict XIII.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Chandragupta Maurya
was the first Mauryan ruler and the first ruler to establish a pan-Indian empire.
Megasthenes
was the first Greek envoy to an Indian court and visited the court of Chandragupta Maurya.
The Yerragudi edicts are associated with
Ashoka
and constitute important evidence of Mauryan presence in the Andhra region.

rows.title: Ashoka - accession, Kalinga War, Dhamma and its content, Dhamma Mahamatras

secs.t: Dhamma - principles, central idea, sources and the Buddhism debate

x: Pillar Edict II
defines Dhamma through the ideas of few faults and many good deeds, including mercy, charity, truthfulness and purity.
Ashoka was personally Buddhist, but his Dhamma incorporated ideas common to several sects and was therefore broader than sectarian Buddhism.
The Bhabru Edict shows Ashoka's personal devotion to the Three Jewels, and non-violence together with religious toleration formed the central idea.

secs.t: Ashoka and Buddhism - teacher, pilgrimage, Third Council, missions

x: According to the Sri Lankan tradition, the monk
Nigrodha
initiated Ashoka in his fourth regnal year.
Nigrodha is mentioned in the Sri Lankan tradition, Upagupta in the Divyavadana, and Samudra is included in the account associated with UPSC notes.
Mahinda and Sanghamitta went to Sri Lanka, Sona and Uttara to Suvarnabhumi, Majjhantika to Kashmir-Gandhara and Mahadeva to Mahishamandala.

secs.t: Welfare measures in the edicts

x: Rock Edict II refers to welfare measures in the Chola, Chera, Pandya and Satyaputra lands and in the realm of a Greek king.
Pillar Edict V, issued in Ashoka's 26th year, mentions restrictions on killing specified animals and burning forests, prohibition of cattle branding, and prisoner releases.
Pillar Edict IV granted condemned prisoners
a three-day respite
before execution.

secs.t: Ashoka - titles, viceroyalties, accession

x: Devanampiya means beloved of the gods, Piyadassi means of pleasing appearance, Buddhashakya Ashoka occurs at Maski and Dharmasoka occurs in a Sarnath inscription.
Ashoka acceded around 272 BCE, visited Bodh Gaya in the 11th regnal year, enlarged the Kanakamuni stupa in the 14th year and visited Lumbini in the 21st year.

secs.t: Kalinga War - motive, year, edict, extent

x: Major Rock Edict XIII
describes the Kalinga War, Ashoka's remorse and the human cost of the conflict.
Major Rock Edict XIII mentions approximately 1,00,000 people killed and 1,50,000 deported during the Kalinga War.
The Chola, Pandya, Chera, Satyaputra and Kerala lands in the far south were outside Ashoka's imperial territory.

secs.t: Dhamma officials and tours - regnal year

x: Ashoka undertook the Dhammayatra to Bodh Gaya in
the 11th regnal year
, replacing the earlier practice of viharayatra.

Dhamma Mahamatras were appointed in the 14th regnal year, as stated in Rock Edict V. The reference to the 13th year represents thirteen years after consecration and should not be confused with the regnal-year entry in the table.

secs.t: Later Buddhist legends - Ashokavadana, Mahavamsa

x: Upagupta
is portrayed as Ashoka’s guide in the Ashokavadana or Divyavadana tradition.
The Ashokavadana or Divyavadana, written in Sanskrit, associates Ashoka with Upagupta, the Taxila campaign and the legend of Chandashoka becoming Dharmashoka.
The Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa are Sri Lankan Pali accounts associated with Nigrodha and Mahinda, and the Mahavamsa depicts early Ashoka as cruel.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ashoka enlarged the Amaravati stupa that had been built by
Mahadeva
Mahadeva went to
Mahishamandala
after the Third Buddhist Council.
Rock Edict XIII names Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Magas, Antigonus Gonatas and Alexander of Epirus.
Ashoka is regarded as the first Indian king to address his people directly through inscriptions, which were written in Prakrit.

rows.title: Ashokan inscriptions - Major and Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts, sites, scripts, James Prinsep
sub: Group-II S1-19: Ashoka's Dhamma, edicts and their locations; Kalinga War

secs.t: Scripts and languages → region

x: Brahmi was used in most of India, Kharosthi in the north-west, Greek in Afghanistan, and Aramaic at Kandahar and Laghman.
Greek and Aramaic versions of Ashokan edicts occur in
Afghanistan
, particularly at Kandahar.
The edicts avoid naming the Eightfold Path, Four Noble Truths and Nibbana; they also do not mention sati or varna.
Shar-i-Kuna is at
Kandahar
in Afghanistan and contains a bilingual Greek–Aramaic edict.

secs.t: Name of the monarch - titles, edicts naming Ashoka, FIRST ruler

x: Devanampiya Piyadasi means ‘beloved of the gods, of pleasing looks’.
The expression ‘engraved by command of King Piyadassi’ occurs in Major
Rock Edict XIV
Besides Maski and Gujarra, the name Ashoka is also found at
Nittur and Udegolam
in Karnataka.
The Mahastupa at Kanaganahalli contains a portrait slab of Ashoka with his queen, bearing the label ‘Raya Asoko’.

secs.t: AP/Karnataka Minor Rock Edict sites → content

x: Exam angle: Bhattiprolu and Dhanyakataka are distractors - they are not Ashokan edicts.
Erragudi is associated with instruction in Dhamma, Rajula Mandagiri with the guru-disciple relationship, Maski with the name Ashoka, and Kanaganahalli with the ‘Raya Asoko’ portrait label.
‘Andhra-bhrityas’ is a Puranic term, and one interpretation identifies the Andhras of Rock Edict XIII with Satavahanas serving as Mauryan feudatories.

The Andhra-related evidence includes the Amaravati stupa tradition, the plaque bearing Ashoka’s name, the mention of Andhras in Rock Edict XIII, and the Erragudi and Rajula Mandagiri edicts in the Kurnool-Nandyal region.

secs.t: Major Rock Edict sites → present state

x: Exam angle: "Where has a Major Rock Edict been found?" - Girnar (Barabar has cave inscriptions; Allahabad and Delhi are pillar sites).
The Major Rock Edicts at
Shahbazgarhi
, and also at Mansehra, were written in Kharosthi script.
The Maski Minor Rock Edict names Ashoka and calls him ‘Buddhashakya Ashok’.
Kanaganahalli
in Karnataka has a Mahastupa with a portrait slab depicting Ashoka and his queen.

secs.t: Pillar edicts → site and content

x: The pillar edicts cluster in the Ganga plain because river transport facilitated movement of the heavy monoliths.
The Allahabad-Kosam pillar contains Pillar Edicts I–VI, the Schism Edict and the Queen's Edict concerning Karuvaki's gifts.
Delhi-Meerut and Lauriya Nandangarh contain Pillar Edicts I–VI, and the Allahabad-Kosam pillar later received Samudragupta's prashasti.

secs.t: Major Rock Edict number → subject

x: Major Rock Edict II
discusses medical care for men and animals and the planting of herbs and trees.
Rock Edict XII
advocates welfare of all sects and honouring the essence of all doctrines, expressing religious tolerance.
Major Rock Edict XIII records remorse for the Kalinga War, advocates Dhammavijaya, names Greek kings and mentions the Andhras.
At Dhauli and Jaugada, the Separate Kalinga Edicts replace Major
Rock Edicts XI–XIII
and address officers of Tosali and Samapa.
The Separate Kalinga Edicts instructed the officers to stop
unjust imprisonment and torture
and expressed the idea that all men were Ashoka's children.
The Bhabru inscription expresses faith in the
Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha
and recommends Buddhist texts.

secs.t: Decipherment - James Prinsep

x: James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837.
The
Delhi-Topra pillar edicts
were the first Ashokan edicts to be read.
The Maski edict, found in 1915, named Ashoka and thereby confirmed the identification of Devanampiya Piyadasi with Ashoka.
The Maski edict is important because it explicitly mentioned Ashoka’s name and confirmed his identity as Devanampiya Piyadasi.

secs.t: Moved pillars → who shifted them

x: Firoz Shah Tughlaq
shifted the Topra pillar from Ambala to Delhi and installed it at Firozabad.
The Maski edict is not a moved pillar.
The Kosam pillar was traditionally shifted by Akbar, and
Jahangir
later added his own inscription to it.

secs.t: Dhamma - principles, Mahamattas, yatras, epithets

x: Dhamma promoted kindness and charity and condemned violence, cruelty, anger, pride and jealousy.
Rock Edict V states that Dhamma Mahamattas were appointed 13 years after consecration, which is counted as Ashoka’s 14th regnal year.
Ashoka began Dhamma yatras from his 11th regnal year, starting with Bodh Gaya.
Dhamma yatras replaced royal pleasure tours and began with a visit to Bodh Gaya.

secs.t: Kalinga War - causes, consequences, edicts

x: Major Rock Edict XIII records approximately 1,00,000 killed, 1,50,000 taken captive, and many more deaths from famine and disease.
The Kalinga War produced remorse, encouraged Ashoka’s conversion to Buddhism and led him to prefer Dhammavijaya over military conquest.
The Separate Edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada replace
Major Rock Edicts XI–XIII
; Major Rock Edict XIII is omitted at these sites.

secs.t: Buddhist missions sent by Ashoka → region

x: Mahendra and Sanghamitra went to Sri Lanka; Sona and Uttara to Suvarnabhumi; Majjhantika to Kashmir-Gandhara; and Mahadeva to Mahisha Mandala.
Rakkhita was associated with Vanavasi, Yona Dhammarakkhita with Aparanta, Mahadhammarakkhita with Maharashtra, and Sona and Uttara with Suvarnabhumi.
Major Rock Edict XIII names Antiochus II of Syria, Ptolemy II of Egypt, Magas of Cyrene, Antigonus Gonatas of Macedonia and Alexander of Epirus.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ashokan edicts have been found in
India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan
; the CDI additionally includes Bangladesh in this geographical spread.
The form of the edicts shows a comparative relationship with the Persian inscriptions of Darius, including the change from third-person to first-person expression and the use of ‘lipi’ or ‘dipi’.
