rows.title: Mauryan administration - central, provincial and local; espionage, judiciary, revenue system
sub: Group-II S1-18: Mauryan administration - central, provincial, revenue, espionage and judiciary

secs.t: Mauryan officials → department

x: Pautavadhyaksha handled weights and measures, Sitadhyaksha crown lands and agriculture, and Panyadhyaksha commerce or state trade.
Panyadhyaksha was in charge of commerce, Akaradhyaksha of mines, Koshadhyaksha of the treasury and Lavanadhyaksha of salt.
Although Mauryan rule was highly centralised and has been described as paternal despotism, the king was not entirely unchecked.

secs.t: Kautilya's eighteen tirthas

x: Each of the eighteen tirthas received an annual salary of
12,000 panas
Dandapala was the head of
the army department
in Kautilya’s Mauryan list of tirthas.
These offices respectively headed the council, supervised forts, guarded frontiers and administered civil justice.
In the Mauryan list, Antapala was the frontier officer and warden of marches.

secs.t: Local officials → level

x: Rajukas handled land survey and assessment and had judicial powers, while Yuktas served as subordinate revenue or secretarial officers.
Megasthenes described Agronomoi as district officers responsible for roads, irrigation and land measurement.
Mahabaladhikrita, Mahadandanayaka and Mahasandhivigrahika
were Gupta titles, not Mauryan officials.
Bhagadugha and Sangrahitri
are Vedic titles, not Mauryan officials.

secs.t: Revenue terms → meaning

x: Hiranya was a cash tax, Setu covered income from gardens, orchards and root crops, and Vana was income from forests.
Other revenues included ferries, forests, mines, pastures, licence fees and fines.
The Rummindei pillar records exemption of Lumbini from bali and reduction of bhaga to one-eighth.
Megasthenes reported that evasion of the sales tax could attract the
death
penalty.

secs.t: Judiciary - courts, Pradvivaka, penalties

x: Dharmasthiya courts dealt with civil matters such as marriage, contracts and inheritance, while Kantakashodhana courts dealt with criminal matters.
The judicial ladder proceeded from the village court to Sangrahana, Dronamukha, Janapada and finally the king.
Punishments included fines, amputation, mutilation and death, and their severity varied by varna.
Civic offences such as
dumping dirt on roads
and creating public nuisance attracted fines.

secs.t: Saptanga theory - seven elements, in order

x: The first four elements in the standard order are Swami, Amatya, Janapada and Durga.
The fifth, sixth and seventh elements are Kosha, Danda or Bala, and Mitra respectively.
The standard theory contains seven elements and does not include
Shatru
Janapada denotes territory and people, Kosha the treasury, Danda or Bala the army or force, and Mitra an ally.

secs.t: Settlement hierarchy (largest to smallest)

x: Sthaniya consisted of 800 villages, Dronamukha 400, Kharvatika 200 and Sangrahana 10; therefore.

secs.t: Provincial administration - provinces and capitals

x: Pataliputra was the capital of Magadha/Prachya, Taxila of Uttarapatha, Ujjain of Avantirashtra and Suvarnagiri of Dakshinapatha.
The four statements of provincial structure are consistent with the Mauryan arrangement: four provinces, royal princes or governors as rulers, and Vish or Ahara as district units.
Pushyagupta Vaishya
served as governor of Saurashtra under Chandragupta Maurya.

secs.t: Megasthenes' city and army boards

x: The fifth committee supervised the sale or inspection of manufactured goods, while the sixth collected the sales tax.
The municipal organisation handled sanitation, water supply, roads and buildings, and comprised six committees with five members each.
Megasthenes attributed to Chandragupta an army of approximately 6,00,000 foot soldiers and 30,000 cavalry.

secs.t: Espionage - gudhapurushas

x: Gudhapurushas, or secret agents, operated under
the Mahamatrapasarpaa
Samstha were stationary secret agents, whereas Sanchara were wandering secret agents.
Samstha guises included Kapatika, Udasthita, Grihapatika, Vaidehaka and Tapasa.
Sanchara guises included Satri, Tikshna, Rasada and Parivrajika.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Mauryan Empire is regarded as
the first centralised bureaucratic empire in India
Suvarnagiri was connected with the Dakshinapatha, governed the Deccan and included Andhra within its administrative orbit.
The Arthashastra is understood to describe an ideal or normative administrative system.
Kautilya’s statement indicates that effective government cannot depend on the king alone.

rows.title: Mauryan economy, society and urban life; Mauryan art and architecture (pillars, Sarnath capital, Barabar caves, Didarganj Yakshi)
sub: Group-II S1-20: Mauryan socio-economic and religious conditions
Group-II S1-21: Mauryan art and architecture - pillars, capitals, caves and sculpture

secs.t: Mauryan art objects and monuments → site; oldest structures

x: Exam angle: "which of these are Mauryan" - Dhauli elephant, Didarganj Yakshi, Sanchi stupa, Kumrahar hall were all correct (APPSC G1 2024: all four).
Exam angle: "which was made earliest" and "which of these are Mauryan" sets.
The Dhauli elephant belongs to the third century BCE and is earlier than the Gupta Udayagiri Varaha, Pallava monuments at Mahabalipuram and the Lingaraja Temple.
The Mauryan age marked a shift from wood to
stone
as the main medium of artistic and architectural expression.

secs.t: Currency, ports and trade routes

x: Exam angle: "Mauryan silver coin was called" - Pana (not Niska, Kakini or Shatamana).
Mauryan imperial currency consisted mainly of punch-marked silver coins, often carrying symbols such as peacocks and hills.
Punch-marked silver panas or karshapanas go back to the Mahajanapada age, particularly the sixth century BCE.
Uttarapatha was the northern highway running from
Taxila through Pataliputra to Tamralipti
Uttarapatha connected Taxila and the Ganga valley, while Dakshinapatha was the southern route to the Deccan and passed through Assaka.

secs.t: Barabar and Nagarjuni caves - donor, sect, number, inscriptions

x: Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha constructed the caves primarily as shelters for Ajivika ascetics.
Lomas Rishi and Karna Chopar belong to Barabar, while Gopika belongs to Nagarjuni.
The Barabar and Nagarjuni hills are located in
Jehanabad
district of Bihar, near Gaya.
The Lomas Rishi entrance has the earliest known stone ogee, or horseshoe-shaped, arch.
The Lomas Rishi entrance copies a thatched wooden hut, known as the Parnashala style.

secs.t: Mauryan pillars - material, polish, capitals, Persian debate

x: Exam angle: "Persian influence" questions - similar in polish and edict idiom, different in base, shaft and lotus.
Mauryan pillars were monolithic, free-standing and circular, generally made of Chunar sandstone and finished with the characteristic Mauryan polish.
The highly lustrous surface of the pillars is known as
Mauryan polish
and gives the stone a metallic shine.

secs.t: Pataliputra palace and city - material, excavated sites

x: Megasthenes compared the Pataliputra palace with the palaces of
Susa and Ecbatana
Fa-Hien
, the Chinese pilgrim who travelled in the fifth century CE, expressed admiration for the remains of the palace.
Pataliputra was mainly a wooden city, although polished stone pillars were used in important structures.
Bulandibagh
yielded remains of the wooden palisade associated with the city of Pataliputra.

secs.t: Popular art - Yaksha/Yakshi findspots; court vs popular art

x: Yaksha and Yakshi sculptures arose from folk worship and represent popular art, while Mauryan pillars and monumental works are associated with court or royal patronage.
Yaksha and Yakshi figures are regarded as the earliest large-scale human sculptures in Indian art and originated in folk worship rather than royal patronage.
Yakshas were revered in
Jainism, Buddhism and Hinduism
, showing the broad religious spread of their worship.

secs.t: Society in the Arthashastra and Indica

x: Megasthenes described
seven
classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen or hunters, artisans, soldiers, overseers and councillors.
The Arthashastra recognised slavery arising through birth, sale, capture in war and judicial punishment.
A female slave who bore her master a son became free, and the son was entitled to the legal status of the master's son.
The Arthashastra used the term moksha for divorce in certain circumstances and permitted widow remarriage.

secs.t: Economy - state role in agriculture, mines, trade, crafts; sita land

x: Sita was crown land cultivated for the state, under the supervision of the Sitadhyaksha, often using slaves and hired labourers.
The Mauryan state exercised monopoly or strong control over mining, forestry, salt, liquor, arms and metallurgy.
The state supervised the sale of goods, usury prevailed in the absence of banking, and NBPW was typical Mauryan pottery.

secs.t: Megasthenes' classification of Indian society

x: Indica
of
Megasthenes
(Greek; envoy of
Seleucus
) divides society into
seven classes
: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers, councillors.
He said India had
no slaves;
also noted the Andhras' forts -
30 walled towns

secs.t: Slavery and labour

x: Karmakaras were hired wage labourers.
Vishti was unpaid forced labour imposed for the state.
The Arthashastra stated that
no Arya could be made a slave
Kautilya classified nine categories of slaves under the term
dasas
The son of a female slave who bore her master a child was entitled to the legal status of the master's son.

secs.t: Position of women in the Arthashastra

x: Stridhana was a woman's own property, including jewellery and resources for maintenance.
The Arthashastra recognised moksha for a wife deserted by her husband, permitted widow and long-deserted-wife remarriage, and records both anuloma and pratiloma inter-varna marriages.

secs.t: Education centres

x: Taxila
was the most famous centre of learning among Taxila, Ujjain and Varanasi.
Bhadrabahu's Kalpasutra belongs to the Mauryan age as represented in the educational and intellectual record of the period.

secs.t: Guilds (shrenis) and craft organisation

x: Good roads and state incentives encouraged crafts, while merchants, artisans and shrenis financed early Buddhist centres, including those in Andhra.
Shreshthis were
merchants
who, along with artisans and guilds, supported economic and religious institutions.
The Arthashastra included troops supplied by guilds, or shreni troops, among the
types of army

secs.t: Religious conditions

x: Mauryan religious conditions were broadly liberal and tolerant, allowing freedom of faith, while the state continued to protect the institutions of varna and ashrama.
Ashoka and Dasaratha donated the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves to the Ajivikas.
The Ashokan edicts mention neither varna nor sati, although they refer to groups such as dasas, Ajivikas and Nirgranthas.

secs.t: Stupas built by Ashoka

x: Tradition states that Ashoka redistributed the Buddha’s relics from the original eight stupas into 84,000 stupas.
The original brick stupa at Sanchi is associated with Ashoka, while its stone toranas bearing Jataka scenes were added during the Satavahana period.
Bharhut is noted for its sculpted railings containing
narrative scenes
The Dharmarajika stupas mentioned are located at
Sarnath and Taxila

secs.t: Pillar capitals → site

x: The four-lion capital with the Dharmachakra is from Sarnath, the bull from Rampurva, the single lion from Lauriya Nandangarh and the elephant from Sankisa.
The four lions placed back to back with the Dharmachakra constitute the
Sarnath
capital.
The single-lion capital is associated with Lauriya Nandangarh in Champaran.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Barabar complex is described as India’s oldest rock-cut structures, comprising four plus three caves known as Satghar, and having an Ajivika dedication.
Barabar represents the earliest rock-cut architecture, Lomas Rishi the earliest stone ogee arch, Sarnath the National Emblem, and Bhattiprolu Andhra Pradesh’s oldest stupa.
Vaishya Tekri may contain a third-century BCE stupa larger than Sanchi and has yielded punch-marked and cast Avanti coins.

rows.title: Decline of the Mauryan Empire - competing explanations
sub: Group-II S1-22: Decline of the Mauryan Empire

secs.t: Dynasty that succeeded the Mauryas - founder and manner of accession

x: Pushyamitra Sunga
founded the Sunga dynasty after overthrowing the Mauryas.
Pushyamitra, the Mauryan commander-in-chief, killed Brihadratha during a military review, thereby carrying out a military coup.
The Sunga dynasty is generally dated to
187 BC
, though some accounts give approximately 185 BCE.
The Mauryas were followed by the Sungas, who were subsequently succeeded by the Kanvas.

secs.t: Last Mauryan king - how the dynasty ended

x: Brihadratha ruled the eastern half of the declining Mauryan Empire from
Pataliputra
Brihadratha is described as the seventh king in succession after
Ashoka
The Mauryan Empire was already facing Indo-Greek pressure in the north-west during Brihadratha’s reign.

secs.t: Theories of decline → historian

x: Exam angle: match theory with historian; "which is NOT a cause" type.
H. C. Raychaudhuri
linked the decline to the weakening of military spirit following Ashoka’s pacifist policy after the Kalinga War.
Romila Thapar emphasised that an administration dependent on the king could collapse when a weak ruler succeeded him.

secs.t: Later Mauryan rulers - list and division of the empire

x: The Vishnu Purana lists seven successors of Ashoka, the empire probably split into western and eastern parts, and Brihadratha was the last ruler of the eastern line.
The usual list is Kunala, Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan and Brihadratha.
The Indo-Greeks had virtually replaced the western later Mauryas by about
180 BC

secs.t: Evidence cited for the financial crisis theory

x: The increased alloy content in later punch-marked silver coins has been interpreted as evidence of fiscal strain and debasement.
Spending on Dhamma missions and donations to the Buddhist Sangha was considered a burden on the treasury.
Such taxes were cited as evidence that the state was searching for additional revenue during a period of financial strain.

secs.t: Foreign threats after Ashoka

x: Bactrian or Indo-Greek invasions, including those associated with Demetrius and Menander, threatened the north-west.
Antiochus III crossed the Hindu Kush around 206 BC and took tribute from the local ruler
Subhagasena
The Great Wall diverted Scythian tribes towards the west and south, increasing pressure on regions near India while Mauryan frontier defence weakened.

secs.t: Regions that broke away after Ashoka

x: Jalauka in Kashmir, Kharavela and the Chedis in Kalinga, Yajnasena in Vidarbha, and the Indo-Greeks in the north-west.
The Satavahanas, earlier Mauryan feudatories, emerged as the breakaway power in the Andhra or Deccan region.
Yajnasena is associated with
Vidarbha
in the account of the regions that broke away after Ashoka.

secs.t: Pushyamitra Sunga - rituals and Buddhism debate

x: Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedhas, the Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva is associated with this tradition, and Patanjali is linked with his court.
Divyavadana describes Pushyamitra as a persecutor of Buddhists, but the growth of Sanchi and Bharhut under Sunga rule complicates that claim.
The Sunga core comprised
Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha and the Narmada valley

secs.t: Kanva dynasty - founder and succession

x: Vasudeva Kanva
, a Brahmana minister, killed the last Sunga ruler Devabhuti and seized power.
The succession was Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana and Susharman.
The four Kanva kings ruled approximately from 73 to 28 BC.
The last Kanva ruler, Susharman, was ended by the Andhras or Satavahanas.

secs.t: Indo-Greek incursions after the Mauryas

x: The Deccan was lost to the Satavahanas and was not continuously part of the Sunga core.
Malavikagnimitram records that
Vasumitra
, the grandson of Pushyamitra, defeated a Yavana army on the Sindhu river.
Menander's capital was
Sakala
, identified with Sialkot.
Menander, or Milinda, is associated with the debate with Nagasena recorded in the Milindapanho.

secs.t: Kharavela of Kalinga - Hathigumpha inscription

x: The Hathigumpha inscription provides a year-by-year record of Kharavela's reign.
The Hathigumpha inscription is located in the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves in
Odisha
Kharavela was a Jain ruler of the Chedi, or Mahameghavahana, line.
Kharavela raided Magadha and brought back the Jina image that the Nandas had taken.
Kharavela sent an army west while ignoring Satakarni.

secs.t: Rise of Satavahanas in the Deccan

x: Simuka, also known as Srimukha, is regarded as the founder of the Satavahana dynasty.
The Satavahanas began as Mauryan feudatories, are called Andhra-bhrityas in the Puranas, and united the Krishna-Godavari region.
The Satavahanas emerged as an independent power in the Deccan after the
decline of the Mauryan Empire
Bhojas, Maharathis and Rashtrikas
were feudatory chiefs who rose in the Deccan.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Historians do not accept one single explanation; contemporary interpretations stress structural weakness and weak successors, while also debating religious explanations.
Ashokan edicts at
Erragudi and Rajula Mandagiri
in Kurnool demonstrate Mauryan rule in Andhra.
Erragudi and Rajula Mandagiri are identified as the only Ashokan edict sites in Andhra Pradesh; Rajula Mandagiri lies in the Kurnool-Nandyal region, and Ashoka enlarged the Amaravati stupa.

rows.title: Early historic Andhra - Andhras in literature, Mauryan contact, early Buddhist centres
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-38

secs.t: Names for Andhra in early texts - Vedic, epic, Buddhist and Jain references

x: Exam angle: "Which text mentions Andhra Path?" - Vinayavatthu, not Suttanipata or the Jatakas.
The Rigveda has no reference to the Andhras, while the Mahabharata associates them with the Kaurava side and the Vayu Purana places them in the Deccan.
The
Aitareya Brahmana
contains the first literary mention of the Andhras, in the Sunahshepa story.

secs.t: Asokan edicts in Andhra - site, district and content

x: The Erragudi inscription is in present-day Nandyal district, uses Prakrit and Brahmi, and refers both to teachers inculcating Dhamma and Rajukas administering justice and welfare.
The 13th Major Rock Edict includes the Andhras among the peoples following Ashoka’s Dhamma and indicates that Andhra came under Ashoka after the Kalinga War.

secs.t: Recent ASI excavations of early historic sites in AP

x: Gudiwada Dibba
in Krishna district is an early historic mound showing continuous occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times.
Adurru in East Godavari district was a Mahasanghika Buddhist centre.
Excavations in the Nagarjunasagar valley provide material evidence for an early Andhra settlement, supporting the antiquity of Andhra as a distinct region.

secs.t: Buddhist literature place names - modern site

x: Siddharthaka Chaitya is identified with Guntupalli in Eluru district.
Andhranagari, also called Dhanyakataka, is identified with
Amaravati-Dharanikota on the Krishna
River.
The Serivanija Jataka refers to Andhapura or Andhakapura, a city reached by crossing the river
Telavaha
Sriparvata or Vijayapuri is identified with
Nagarjunakonda

secs.t: Jataka stories on Andhra - kingdom or ruler referred

x: The
Serivanija Jataka
refers to merchants trading to Andhapura.
All three pairs are correctly matched.
The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka states that Satakarni of Asmaka defeated
Kharavela of Kalinga

secs.t: Megasthenes on the Andhras - army, towns, forts

x: Megasthenes was the Greek ambassador of
Seleucus
at the Mauryan court.
Megasthenes’ Indica is the first foreign source to mention the Andhras.
Megasthenes stated that the Andhras possessed 30 forts, described as walled towns, and that they lived in towns.

secs.t: Andhra janapadas in Buddhist texts - capital and river

x: Assaka or Asmaka was a Mahajanapada on the Godavari, with Bodhan or Podana as its capital, and is named in the Anguttara Nikaya.
Assaka had its capital at Bodhan; Mulaka had its capital at Pratishthana; Andhra lay on the Dakshinapatha trade route; and Asmaka was another name for Assaka.

secs.t: Bavari legend and early Buddhist contact with the Godavari region

x: Bavari was a Brahmin teacher from
Kosala
who settled on the Godavari in Assaka territory.
Bavari sent
sixteen
disciples to meet the Buddha.
The Bavari legend is recorded in the Suttanipata, specifically in the Parayana-vagga.
The Bavari legend indicates that
Buddhist ideas had reached the Godavari region before Mauryan expansion
, showing early contact between the region and Buddhism.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true.
The Madhya Pradesh government is to resume digging at Vaishya Tekri near Ujjain, where a possible Mauryan stupa larger than Sanchi has been identified.
Devnimori is a Kshatrapa-period site in Gujarat.

rows.title: Sungas and Kanvas - Pushyamitra Sunga, Bharhut and Sanchi, Patanjali, the Besnagar pillar

secs.t: Sources for Pushyamitra's reign and the Yavana invasion → author

x: The
Gargi Samhita
records the Yavana advance on Saketa, Panchala, Mathura and Pataliputra.
Patanjali
authored the Mahabhashya, which contains references to the Yavana sieges of Saketa and Madhyamika.
Kalidasa's
Malavikagnimitram
presents Agnimitra as its principal hero and also refers to the Vidarbha conflict and Vasumitra's victory.
Mudrarakshasa concerns Chandragupta Maurya and the establishment of Mauryan power, not the Yavana invasion during Pushyamitra's reign.

secs.t: Pushyamitra Sunga - accession, Ashvamedhas, Buddhism debate

x: Pushyamitra is said to have defeated the Bactrian Greek ruler
Demetrius
after the Greeks challenged his sacrificial horse.
Buddhist art continued to flourish at Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya.
One tradition attributes destruction of the original Bodhi Tree to Pushyamitra and also records a similar act by Shashanka of Gauda in the seventh century CE.

secs.t: Besnagar (Heliodorus) pillar

x: Heliodorus was the ambassador of
the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas
at the court of the Sunga king Bhagabhadra.
The Besnagar monument is a
Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva
, and Heliodorus describes himself as a Bhagavata.
The pillar is early inscriptional evidence of Bhagavatism, an early form of Vaishnavism, and shows the assimilation of a foreigner into an Indian religious tradition.

secs.t: Sunga art - Bharhut, Sanchi, Bodh Gaya

x: The Sunga-period work at Sanchi included encasing Ashoka's brick stupa in stone and adding stone railings and toranas.
The Sanchi toranas carry narrative panels depicting Jataka stories and episodes from the Buddha's life.
Bharhut's inscriptions mention guilds of ivory workers and stone carvers who contributed to its construction and decoration.

secs.t: Dynastic succession - Maurya, Sunga, Kanva and later

x: The sequence is Maurya, Sunga, Kanva and Kushana.
Chandragupta founded the Mauryan dynasty.
Devabhuti was killed by his minister Vasudeva, who founded the Kanva dynasty.
The Puranas state that the Satavahanas defeated the Sunga and Kanva dynasties.

secs.t: Patanjali and the Mahabhashya

x: The Mahabhashya comments on Panini's Ashtadhyayi through
Katyayana
's Varttikas, forming the grammarian trio Panini–Katyayana–Patanjali.
Patanjali was a contemporary of Pushyamitra and is believed to have served as his
royal priest
The Sunga court encouraged a revival of classical Sanskrit, in contrast to Ashoka's prominent use of Prakrit.
The Manusmriti took early shape in this period and classified foreigners as
Vratya Kshatriyas

secs.t: Sunga rulers and origin

x: The Sunga kingdom lost its north-western territories to the Yavanas and the Deccan to the Satavahanas.
Vasumitra
was the son of Agnimitra and is described in Malavikagnimitram as having defeated the Yavanas on the Sindhu.
Bhojas, Maharathis and Rastrikas
are identified as powerful feudatories that rose during the Sunga period.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ashtamahasthana literally refers to the
eight
Buddhist sacred sites.
The Sunga period is associated with Brahmanical revival, the rise of Bhagavatism and the development of stone Buddhist art.

The debate contrasts the account in Divyavadana, which presents Pushyamitra as a persecutor, with archaeological evidence from Sanchi and Bharhut that does not support a simple, uniform persecution narrative.

rows.title: Indo-Greeks - Menander and Milindapanho, Indo-Greek coinage and its significance

secs.t: Indo-Greek ruler → contribution / coinage feature

x: Exam angle: "Sankarshana + Vasudeva on coins" = Agathocles, not Kushana or Gupta rulers.
Menander I
, also known as Milinda, is regarded as the greatest Indo-Greek ruler and is associated with the spread of Hellenistic culture.
Hermaius
was the last ruler of the line, and his defeat ended Greek supremacy south of the Hindu Kush.

secs.t: Menander and the Milindapanho

x: Menander I, or Milinda, is assigned a reign of approximately
Milindapanho, meaning “Questions of Milinda,” was written in
Pali
Nagasena
was the Buddhist monk associated with the discussion recorded in Milindapanho.
Gandhara art is associated with the Kushanas, the Junagadh rock inscription with Rudradaman I, Milindapanho with Menander, and the Taxila copper plate with Patika.

secs.t: Indo-Greek coinage - legends, portraits, metals, deities; FIRST claims

x: Indo-Greek coins are noted for realistic royal portraits, often showing rulers wearing helmets or diadems.
Indo-Greek coins were mainly made of silver and copper; gold coins were rare despite the Indo-Greeks’ FIRST claim regarding gold coinage in India.
Indo-Greek coins depicted Greek deities such as
Zeus, Athena and Heracles
, along with selected Indian religious figures and symbols.

secs.t: Indo-Greek administrative and cultural contributions

x: Hellenistic art contributed to the development of the Gandhara school, which flourished later under the
Kushanas
Yavanika was the term used for the
stage curtain
, reflecting a cultural contribution associated with the Indo-Greeks.
Hora refers to a horoscope and Romaka Siddhanta reflects Greek influence in astronomy.
The Smritis describe the Greeks absorbed into Indian society as
Vratya Kshatriyas

secs.t: Bactrian Greeks - origin and entry into India

x: Diodotus I
revolted against the Seleucids in the third century BCE and founded an independent Bactrian Greek kingdom.
Bactria was situated in
north Afghanistan
, where Greek settlers established themselves after Alexander’s campaigns.
The weak successors of
Ashoka
facilitated the southward movement of the Bactrian Greeks into India.
The raids are described as reaching Saketa and Madhyamika and extending towards Pataliputra.

secs.t: Heliodorus and Indo-Greek diplomatic ties

x: Heliodorus was from
Taxila
and served as the envoy of Antialcidas to Bhagabhadra.
The Besnagar Garuda pillar honours Vasudeva, and Heliodorus describes himself as a Bhagavata.
Megasthenes was associated with Seleucus I, Daimachos with Antiochus I’s mission to Bindusara, and Heliodorus with Antialcidas’s mission to Bhagabhadra.
Rock Edict XIII refers to Hellenistic kings and is evidence of
earlier Greek–Mauryan contacts

secs.t: End of Indo-Greek rule - successor powers

x: The Sakas replaced the Indo-Greeks first, followed by the Parthians or Pahlavas, and finally the Kushanas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Indo-Greek period is associated with Greek–Indian synthesis in Gandhara art, religious interaction through Heliodorus, and philosophical exchange through Milindapanho.
Indo-Greek coinage is especially noted for royal portraits and bilingual legends, while Kushana coinage is associated with large-scale gold and numerous deities.
The Kushanas were notable for large-scale gold coin issues, while the Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins, known as dinaras.

rows.title: Shakas, Parthians and Western Kshatrapas - Rudradaman I and the Junagadh inscription, Saka era

secs.t: Kshaharata inscriptions → issuer + content; Satavahana reconquest

x: The
Nasik cave inscription
records Ushavadatta’s deposit of 2,000 karshapanas in the weavers’ guild at Govardhana.
Ushavadatta
issued the Karle inscription recording the donation of a village to the monks of the Karle chaitya.
The Nasik Prashasti calls Gautamiputra Satakarni the destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas; Kushanas are not included in this description.

secs.t: Western Kshatrapas - Kshaharatas vs Kardamakas; coinage metals

x: The Kshaharatas were associated with the Western Deccan, whereas the Kardamakas ruled around Ujjain, Malwa and Kathiawar.
Ptolemy
records the clash between Chashtana and the Satavahana ruler Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
Numerous silver coins have been found in western India, and Kardamaka silver coins carried dates in the Saka era.
The recorded gold-to-silver ratio is 1:35, corresponding to one suvarna being equal to 35 karshapanas.

secs.t: Eras → starting year + founder; converting dates

x: The Common Era year is obtained by adding 78 to the Saka year: 125 + 78 =
203 CE
The Common Era equivalent is obtained by subtracting 57 from the Vikrama Samvat year: 200 − 57 = 143? Wait, under the stated conversion CE = Vikrama − 57, the correct value is 143 CE.

secs.t: Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I

x: Exam angle: "repaired Sudarshana lake in a 2nd-century Sanskrit rock inscription" =
Rudradaman
Pushyagupta built the lake, Tushaspha added canals under Ashoka, Rudradaman repaired it through Suvishakha, and Chakrapalita repaired it again during the Gupta period.
Rudradaman defeated Satakarni twice but spared him because of their close relationship, and Rudradaman’s daughter married Vasishthiputra Satakarni.

secs.t: Saka era as the national calendar

x: The Saka-based national calendar was adopted from
22 March 1957
In a leap year, 1 Chaitra falls on
21 March
; in a normal year it falls on 22 March.

secs.t: Chronology of foreign invaders

x: The sequence is Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Parthians and Kushanas.
Maues, also known as Moga, is regarded as the first prominent Saka king, around 80 BC.

secs.t: Shaka branches → region

x: Rajuvula and Sodasa belonged to the Mathura branch.
Mathura
, Ujjain and Girnar were important centres of Saka rule.
The Sakas were often at war with the
Satavahanas
, especially in western and upper Deccan regions.

secs.t: Parthians (Pahlavas)

x: Gondophares
is regarded as the greatest ruler among the Parthians or Pahlavas in India.
The Takht-i-Bahi inscription near Peshawar is associated with
Gondophares
Christian tradition states that
St Thomas
visited the court of Gondophares.

secs.t: Contributions - epigraphy, coinage, dress, military

x: These foreign ruling groups patronised the artistic centres of
Sanchi, Mathura and Gandhara
Trousers, long coats, helmets and boots
were features shared by the Shakas and Kushanas, along with a stronger cavalry tradition.
The satrap system was a form of provincial administration in which satraps governed territorial units.
The Shakas, Parthians and related foreign groups were absorbed into society as
Vratya Kshatriyas

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gautamiputra Satakarni
defeated Nahapana, the Kshaharata ruler, and restruck his coins as an assertion of Satavahana power.
Following Rudradaman I's defeat of Pulumavi, the Satavahana centre shifted from Pratishthana, or Paithan, to Amaravati.
The Nasik Prashasti is associated with
Gautamiputra Satakarni
and forms part of the evidence used to recall his achievements.

rows.title: Kushanas - Kujula Kadphises, Kanishka, era of 78 CE, Fourth Buddhist Council, Kushana coinage

secs.t: Kushana rulers → contribution + titles

x: Kujula Kadphises
, also known as Kadphises I, united the five Yuezhi clans and occupied the Kabul valley and Kashmir.
The Rabatak genealogy places Vima Taktu
between Kujula Kadphises and Vima Kadphises
Kanishka represented the zenith of Kushana power, and Huvishka was his successor with Mathura as an important centre.
Devaputra reflected Chinese influence, Shaonano Shao Persian influence, Kaisara the Roman Caesar tradition, and Maharaja the Indian tradition.

secs.t: Items introduced by Shakas and Kushanas

x: The Shakas and Kushanas improved cavalry and promoted the wider use of saddles and reins in riding.

secs.t: Fourth Buddhist Council

x: The Fourth Buddhist Council is generally dated to approximately
72 CE
The council formalised the Mahayana–Hinayana division, addressed Sarvastivada disputes, and used Sanskrit instead of the earlier Pali or Prakrit practice.
The correct sequence is the First Council at Rajagriha, the Second at Vaishali, the Third at Pataliputra and the Fourth at Kashmir.

secs.t: Kushana coinage - FIRST large-scale gold, deities, portraits

x: The Kushana gold dinara followed the Roman weight standard and weighed approximately 8 grams, equivalent to 120 grains.
Kushana coins depicted more than thirty deities from Greek, Iranian and Indian traditions, including Helios, Mithra and Shiva.
Kanishka is shown standing in a peaked helmet, long coat and boots and making a sacrifice at an altar.

secs.t: Kanishka's court scholars → work

x: Ashvaghosha
of Pataliputra composed Buddhacharita in Sanskrit and was also vice-president of the Fourth Buddhist Council.
Nagarjuna
is associated with Madhyamika philosophy and Suhrllekha, a letter addressed to a Satavahana king.
Vasumitra was president, Parshva encouraged Kanishka to convene the council, and Mathara is included in the court list.
I-tsing recorded that he saw students in India memorising Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha.

secs.t: Kanishka - capitals, extent, Rabatak, Sarnath, China

x: Kanishka's empire extended from the Oxus to the Ganga and included Kashgar, Khotan and Yarkand in the Tarim Basin.
The Rabatak inscription gives the succession as Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu, Vima Kadphises and Kanishka.
The Rabatak inscription names
Saketa, Kaushambi, Pataliputra, Sri-Champa and Ujjain
among the Indian cities under Kanishka.
The Sarnath inscription records that Friar Bala dedicated a Bodhisattva image in the third year of Kanishka.

secs.t: Rise of Mahayana and Buddha-image worship

x: The Kushanas helped move Buddhism from the Pali-Prakrit Hinayana tradition towards Sanskrit Mahayana.
Gandhara art shows strong Greek influence and commonly depicts the Buddha standing in pleated robes.
The first Buddha images date to the 1st century CE and are associated with the Gandhara and Mathura styles.
Mathura developed an indigenous style with seated meditating Buddhas shown with halos, while Amaravati is recognised for white limestone narrative panels.

secs.t: Era of 78 CE - founder debate and later name

x: Although the 78 CE era is commonly credited to Kanishka, some accounts credit
Gautamiputra Satakarni
with starting the Salivahana era.
The era became known as the Saka era because the Western Kshatrapas, who were Sakas, used it on their records and coins.
The era is also called Salivahana Saka and became India's national calendar in 1957.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The reported findings near Takshashila consist of rare
Kushana-era coins and lapis lazuli stones
The Kushanas acted as Silk Road intermediaries connecting
Han China, Rome and India
Kushana trade promoted a second wave of urbanisation involving centres such as Mathura, Taxila, Ujjain and Shravasti.
The Kushana period led into the Gupta age, forming an important bridge in the development of early Indian urban and cultural history.

rows.title: Schools of art - Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati compared

secs.t: Gandhara school - foreign influence, patron dynasty, region

x: Exam angle: "Indian + Greek features = ?" → Gandhara; "flourished under which dynasty?" → Kushanas.
The Gandhara school developed in the north-western frontier region, particularly around Peshawar, Taxila and the Swat Valley in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Gandhara art reflects Hellenistic
Greek, Roman and Persian
influences in combination with Indian artistic traditions.

secs.t: Art school → patron dynasty, material, theme

x: Gandhara is linked with the Kushanas; Mathura with the Kushanas and later Gupta age; Amaravati with the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus; and its mature phase with the Ikshvakus and Mahayana themes.
Amaravati was patronised by the Satavahanas and later the Ikshvakus; it used white limestone and depicted Jatakas, the life of the Buddha and narrative reliefs.

secs.t: Buddha image - first anthropomorphic depiction debate, earliest human images

x: Before anthropomorphic representation, the Buddha was worshipped aniconically through symbols including the throne, footprints, wheel, tree and stupa.
Hinayana is associated here with symbolic worship, while Mahayana encouraged the worship of Buddha images or idols.
Amaravati Ayakapatas show the Buddha through symbols, reflecting the aniconic tradition.
Standing Buddha images became prominent in the
Gupta phase
of the Mathura school.

secs.t: Mudras of the Buddha → event depicted

x: Bhumisparsha
mudra shows the right hand touching the earth, symbolising enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and calling the earth to witness against Mara.
The raised right palm in Abhaya mudra signifies
fearlessness and protection
; it is also associated with reassurance after enlightenment and the subduing of Nalagiri.
Varada mudra is shown with a lowered open palm and signifies
boon-giving or charity

secs.t: Depiction features compared - drapery, hair, halo, physique, narrative

x: Gandhara sculpture is marked by heavy, toga-like robes with deep folds, while Mathura sculpture commonly shows a transparent, clinging garment.
Gandhara commonly depicts wavy hair with a top-knot, whereas Mathura depicts a shaved head or snail-shell curls.
Mathura
is characterised by frontal, single icons, unlike Gandhara’s standing Buddha in Greek attire and Amaravati’s crowded narrative compositions.

secs.t: Amaravati school sites in AP

x: The mature or final phase of the Amaravati school occurred under the
Ikshvakus
and included Mahayana themes.
James Fergusson
publicised Amaravati art through his work Tree and Serpent Worship and called it the ‘Epitome of Indian architecture’.
Amaravati art influenced Sri Lanka, particularly Anuradhapura, South-East Asia and later Gupta art.

secs.t: Mathura school - Jain and Brahmanical images, Kushana royal portraits

x: The Mathura school was indigenous to the Ganga plains and was not restricted to Buddhism; it produced Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical images.
The Mathura school produced the earliest surviving iconic images of several Hindu deities, Jain Tirthankaras and Yaksha-Yakshi figures.
The headless standing statue of Kanishka is associated with
Mat near Mathura

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The campaign focuses on the Andhra Pradesh Buddhist circuit comprising
Amaravati, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda
Gandhara is foreign-influenced and Buddhist, Mathura is indigenous and multi-religious, while Amaravati is indigenous and narrative in the Satavahana-Ikshvaku context.
Amaravati is identified with ancient
Dhanyakataka
, where the Buddha is believed to have taught the Kalachakra.

rows.title: Satavahanas - origin debate, Simuka, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Nasik Prasasti, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
sub: Group-II M1-A-5: Satavahanas - origin, chronology and political history from Simuka to Yajnasri Satakarni
Group-II M1-A-6: Gautamiputra Satakarni and the Nasik Prasasti; Satavahana-Saka conflict

secs.t: Origin debate - Andhras vs Andhrabhrityas, original home theories

x: Exam angle: scholar → theory matching; "not the same" = Sukthankar.
The Satavahanas are described as having initially served as Mauryan feudatories and having established independence in the Deccan after the decline of the Mauryas.
Satavahana or
Shalivahana
is identified in the tradition as the legendary progenitor of the line.
All three statements correctly represent the views attributed to D.C. Sircar, K.A. Nilakanta Sastri and R.S. Sharma respectively.
B.S.L. Hanumantha Rao
held that the Satavahanas belonged to the original Andhra janapada.

secs.t: Inscription → issuer + ruler praised + findspot

x: The Naneghat inscription was issued by Devi Naganika, wife of Satakarni I. It records his victories, Vedic sacrifices, gifts to Brahmins and a Maharathi marriage connection.
The Nasik Prasasti was issued by Gautami Balasri, the mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni, during the reign of her grandson
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
Myakadoni, also called Mekadoni, is associated with the period of Pulumavi III and reflects the
final phase of Satavahana power in the Bellary region
Records of donations to caves during Pulumavi II’s reign are associated with
Karle and Bhaja
in western Maharashtra.
The Kanheri evidence identifies Vasishthiputra Satakarni’s queen as the daughter of
Rudradaman
, indicating a close Satavahana-Kardamaka relationship.

secs.t: Puranic and literary sources

x: The
Matsya Purana
contains the longest and most systematic list of Satavahana kings and is the principal Puranic basis for their political history.
Pliny wrote Natural History, Megasthenes recorded that the Andhras lived in towns, Ptolemy wrote Geography, and Somadeva Suri composed Kathasaritsagara.
Pulomavi III was the thirtieth and later Satavahana ruler, was defeated by Srisantamula, and is associated with Myakadoni in Bellary in his last days.

secs.t: Titles and roles → ruler; queens as regents

x: Satakarni I
bore the titles Dakshinapathapati and Apratihatachakra.
Shakasanhari was one of the titles of
Gautamiputra Satakarni
, reflecting his association with the defeat of the Shakas.
Kshatriya-darpa-mana-mardana
literally denotes the crusher of the pride of the Kshatriyas.
Devi Naganika acted as guardian and regent during the minority of her son.
All four statements correctly describe Naganika, including her royal lineage, regency, ritual role and association with the Naneghat inscription.

secs.t: Capitals, AP places, subordinate territories

x: Pratishthana was the principal western capital, while Dhanyakataka or Amaravati later became the eastern political, cultural and Buddhist centre.
Pratishthana is identified with
Paithan in Maharashtra
and was the principal western capital of the Satavahanas on the Godavari.
The eastern centre was shifted to Dhanyakataka or Amaravati under
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
after the attacks of Rudradaman.

secs.t: Metronymics of kings

x: Metronymics reflected the high status of royal women and respect for the mother, but Satavahana succession continued to be patriarchal.
Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra and Halamiputra
are maternal-gotra names prefixed to Satavahana kings' names.

secs.t: Founder, administration and last rulers

x: Satakarni II
is identified as the sixth ruler in the Satavahana dynastic sequence.
Yajna Sri Satakarni
is described as the greatest of the later Satavahana rulers.
The Puranic long chronology places Simuka approximately in 230–207 BCE
, while another chronology places the dynasty broadly from the first century BCE to the third century CE.
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi is placed as the twenty-fourth ruler and is associated with the Amaravati inscription.
Pulumavi III is identified as the last ruler in the Puranic sequence, whereas revival of maritime power and ship coins are associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni.

secs.t: Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, Sri Yajna Satakarni

x: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana and recovered Malwa, Saurashtra, Konkan and Nasik.
The Jogalthambi hoard contains
Nahapana
’s silver coins restruck by Gautamiputra Satakarni, providing evidence of Gautamiputra’s victory.
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
issued ship-motif coins and extended Satavahana rule into coastal Andhra.
Yajna Sri Satakarni is associated with the revival of maritime power, ship coins, patronage of Nagarjuna and the Nagarjunakonda Mahavihara.

secs.t: Literary traditions on Satavahana origins

x: The
Gathasaptasati
does not narrate the early history of the Satavahanas.
The Brihatkatha is attributed to
Gunadhya
and was written in Paisachi.
Katantra is associated with Sharvavarman and Kundala Satakarni.
Somadeva is associated with the Kathasaritsagara, and Jain and Dipavamsa traditions also discuss the origins.

secs.t: Position in the dynastic sequence

x: The sequence is Mauryas, Sungas, Kanvas and then Satavahanas.
Chutus are also included among the successors.
After the Vakatakas and other immediate successors, the later sequence mentioned is Chalukyas followed by Rashtrakutas.

secs.t: Titles of early rulers

x: Hala
, the seventeenth Satavahana ruler, bore the title ‘Kavivatsala’.
Vasishthiputra Pulumavi bore the titles ‘Dakshinapatheshwara’ and ‘
Navanagaraswami
Yajna Sri Satakarni
is associated with the title ‘Trisamudradhipati’ in the Banabhatta tradition.

secs.t: Nasik Prasasti - issuer, reign, language, titles

x: The Nasik Prasasti is in Prakrit prose and Brahmi script and records Gautamiputra’s expeditions, victories, empire and titles, including his destruction of Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
The Nasik Prasasti records gifts made by Gautami Balasri and her son to monks on the
Trirashmi hill
Gautami Balasri is described in the Nasik Prasasti as the wife of a
Rajarshi

secs.t: Inscriptions on Gautamiputra's achievements - site

x: The
Nasik inscription
records the military achievements of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
The Naneghat inscription is associated with Satakarni I and Naganika, not Gautamiputra.

secs.t: Social and religious claims in the Nasik Prasasti

x: Balasri’s account presents Gautamiputra’s line as
Brahmana
The Nasik Prasasti credits him with fostering Brahmin families, upholding varnashrama and stopping varna-sankara.
All three statements are associated with Gautamiputra’s Buddhist patronage.

secs.t: Territories conquered - regions named in the Nasik Prasasti

x: Anupa
represented the Narmada valley and its capital was Mahishmati.
Aparanta was North Konkan, Vidarbha was Berar, Akara was East Malwa and Avanti was West Malwa.
Mulaka was associated with the Godavari valley and Paithan area, along with Asika or Asaka.

secs.t: Later Satavahana-Kardamaka relations - Junagadh evidence

x: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman is a Sanskrit inscription dated approximately to
150 CE
The inscription claims that Rudradaman twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, but spared him because of a close relationship.
Ptolemy records clashes with Chashtana, while the Sanskrit Junagadh inscription identifies Satakarni as lord of Dakshinapatha.
Yajnasri Satakarni
later won back territory that had been lost by the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Satavahana period is significant for the public voice associated with its queens, as reflected by figures such as Naganika and Gautami Balasri.
The Satavahana homeland and chronology remain debated, while the Nasik Prasasti is the main source for Gautamiputra’s reign.
Gautamiputra is credited in the tradition with the Salivahana era of AD 78, but that attribution conflicts with the dates c. 106–130 CE assigned to his reign.
Simuka is placed around c. 230–207 BCE, Gautamiputra around c. 106–130 CE, Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription around 150 CE, and Yajnasri’s recovery occurred later.

rows.title: Satavahana administration, economy, coinage and Prakrit literature (Hala's Gathasaptasati)
sub: Group-II M1-A-7: Satavahana administration and the feudatory system
Group-II M1-A-8: Satavahana socio-economic conditions - varna, guilds, trade, ports and coinage
Group-II M1-A-10: Satavahana literature - Prakrit, Hala's Gathasaptasati, Gunadhya's Brihatkatha

secs.t: Literature → author; Gathasaptasati as social source, women contributors

x: Gathasaptasati was composed under
Hala
, the seventeenth Satavahana king, who bore the title Kavivatsala.
Gathasaptasati, or Sattasai, is an anthology of 700 gathas in Maharashtri Prakrit, dealing chiefly with love, rural life and nature.
Anulakshmi, Anupalabdha, Reva or Revati, and Madhavi are identified as women contributors to Gathasaptasati.
Gathasaptasati refers to sati, the absence of child marriage and the plight of wives of seafaring merchants.
All four features—sugar and jaggery, Brundagana, house-wall paintings and hanging of criminals—are included in the social picture associated with Gathasaptasati.
Brihatkatha is associated with Gunadhya, Katantra with Sarvavarma, Lilavati Parinayam with Kutuhala, and Harivijaya with Sarvasena.
Lilavati Parinayam by Kutuhala concerns
Hala’s marriage to the Sinhala princess Lilavati near the Bhimeswara temple at Saptagodavari
, identified with Draksharamam.

secs.t: Coinage - metals, ship-motif, bilingual and portrait coins

x: The recorded Satavahana coin metals are
lead, potin, copper, bronze and silver
Satakarni I
is credited with issuing the first silver coins among the Satavahanas.
The Kondapur mint in Medak is associated with the legend ‘Siri Chimuka Sata’.
The Satavahanas issued no gold coins in the cited account, although Roman gold coins circulated.
The bilingual silver portrait coins carried Prakrit on one side and a Dravidian language on the other.
Recorded Satavahana coin motifs include the elephant, horse, lion, camel, chaitya and dharmachakra.
The Ujjain symbol is described as
a cross with four circles
and appears on the reverse of Satavahana coins.
Iron coins with a copper coating are attributed to
the Shalankayanas
, not the Satavahanas.

secs.t: Administrative and military terms → meaning

x: Exam angle: "Katakas and Skandhavaras mean..." with distractors like tax-free monk villages or rock-cut areas.
Kataka denoted a permanent military camp, garrison or fortified administrative centre, generally located in cities.
Pliny mentions
1,00,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry and 1,000 elephants
in the Satavahana army.
The Satavahana army was described as Chaturanga bala—chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry—with archers also present.
Amaravati sculptures show infantry in front, cavalry and elephants on the flanks, and archers at the rear.

secs.t: Official language and script

x: Sanskrit became prominent under the Ikshvakus; Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription is the first complete Sanskrit inscription, while Nagabu and Vepuru occur in the Amaravati and Myakadoni inscriptions respectively.
Telugu script developed from Brahmi; Satavahana inscriptions used Prakrit and Brahmi; and differentiation from Kannada began during the Rashtrakuta–Eastern Chalukya age.
The Bhattiprolu inscriptions, dated approximately to 400 BCE in Guntur, use a variant of Brahmi and contain early Telugu place and personal names.

secs.t: Tax-free land grants - FIRST evidence

x: The Satavahanas made tax-free grants of villages or land to
Brahmanas and Buddhist monks
Tax-free land grants created rights and immunities that later formed a basis of
the early-medieval feudal order
Satakarni I gave
cows, land and gold
to Brahmins in connection with the Vedic sacrifices recorded in the inscription.

secs.t: Guilds → craft, interest rates, Indo-Roman ports

x: Exam angle: rate of interest (12%), which inscription (Nasik), which guild (Kolika = weavers; Padhika = butchers).
Shrenis organised traders and artisans of a particular craft and regulated work, quality, prices, wages and conduct.
Tailika denotes the oil guild, Kulara the potters, Gandhika the perfume traders and Sarthavaha the long-distance traders.
Padhika denoted butchers, Udayantrika or Adyantrika operated water-machines such as ghatiyantras, and Gandhika denoted perfumers; all three pairs are correctly matched.
The deposit carrying interest at three-fourths of one per cent per month was meant for
the other needs of monks
Pliny, writing in Latin in Natural History, referred to the drain of Roman gold and fine cloth.
Wine came from Italy and Arabia, silk and camphor from China, and gold from Malaya and Sumatra.

secs.t: Inland trade routes and centres

x: Iron ore was worked in the
Karimnagar–Warangal
area.
Pratishthana or Paithan was the capital and an inland trade centre situated on the
Godavari
Mahapatha nirmatalu
means builders or makers of great roads and is associated with the Satavahanas.
Guduru was known for fine cotton, Palnadu for diamonds, Vinukonda for metal, and Guntupalli for copper and iron.

secs.t: Society - metronymics, caste mobility, women donors, debates

x: Gautamiputra Satakarni
claimed the title or description Ekabrahmana and was associated with stopping varna-sankara, reflecting Brahmanical ideology amid social mobility.
Gautami Balasri donated a
vihara
, illustrating the role of women donors in Buddhist patronage.
Women donors, particularly royal women, were important patrons; Gautami Balasri is associated with a vihara, while the kings generally followed Vedic religion.

secs.t: Urban administration - Nigama Sabha, towns and Gahapati

x: The Nigama Sabha is referred to in the
Bhattiprolu inscription
Dhanyakataka
was among the major Satavahana towns, along with places such as Pratishthana, Vijayapuri, Nasik and Kondapur.
Barukaccha, Sopara, Kalyan and Govardhana
are included among the major Satavahana towns.

secs.t: Officers - Amatya, Mahamatra, Mahasenapati, Gulmika and others

x: Pattikapala
was responsible for drafting land-grant and gift inscriptions.
The Mantri Parishad assisted the Satavahana king in administration and governance.
Visvamatyas were consulted on major decisions; they were not keepers of royal stores.
A Gulmika headed a Gulma, a cluster of villages, and could supervise law and order.
Hereditary village offices encouraged feudal tendencies, while vetti referred to forced labour owed by villagers.

secs.t: Administrative units - Rashtra, Ahara, Grama and their heads

x: Rashtra was a province, Ahara a district or province, Vishaya a sub-division and Grama the village unit.
Distant Aharas were entrusted to Mahasenadhipatis, a Gramani could oversee five or ten villages, and a cluster of villages was called a Gulma.
Rajakambata referred to the core territory directly controlled by the king.

secs.t: Feudatories - Maharathis, Mahabhojas, Mahatalavaras

x: Maharathis were hereditary tax-collecting feudatories of the western Deccan.
The omission of the emperor’s name suggests that the Mahabhojas enjoyed a
near-independent position
within the Satavahana political structure.
The indicated order was Raja, followed by Mahabhoja, followed by Senapati.
Mahatalavaras or Mahasenadhipatis were generals entrusted with border provinces and later developed into feudal lords.

secs.t: Taxes and cesses - Bhaga, Kara, Deya-Meya

x: Bhaga was the king’s share of the harvest, fixed at one-sixth.
Karukara was the tax imposed on artisans and professionals.
Land revenue
was the chief source of Satavahana state income.

secs.t: Nature of kingship - succession and queen mothers

x: Satavahana kingship was hereditary and patriarchal, and it was comparatively decentralised; succession was not exclusively elective.
Satavahana rulers used
matronymics
, or names derived from the mother’s lineage or gotra.
Gautami Balasri issued the Nasik inscription during the reign of her grandson Pulumavi.

secs.t: Roman trade - exports, imports, coin hoards, decline

x: Fine textiles, muslin, pepper and ivory were exports, while wine and gold and silver coins were among the imports.
Roman coins have been found at
Bhattiprolu and Nagarjunakonda
Pliny complained that Roman gold was draining to India through trade, estimated at about 12.5 million denarii a year in one account.

secs.t: Varna and caste

x: The four-varna system, or chaturvarna, operated during the Satavahana period.
Gautamiputra Satakarni called himself
Ekabrahmana and Varnasankarya nirodhaka
, the stopper of the mixing of varnas.
Gandhikas were perfumers, not land surveyors.

secs.t: Trade centres and ports - by region

x: Maisolia was identified with Machilipatnam, Kantakossyla with Ghantasala, Koddura with the Gudur area, and Dhanyakataka with Amaravati/Dharanikota.
Koddura
, identified with the Gudur area in Krishna, was described in the Periplus as the only east-coast port.
Bharukachha, Sopara, Kalyan and Vyjayantipura
were the west-coast ports associated with Satavahana maritime expansion.
Bhavaviveka is described as the acharya at the
Sriparvatam vihara

secs.t: Agriculture

x: The Satavahanas expanded cultivation in the Krishna–Godavari basin.
Ghatiyantras used for lifting water were made by the
Udayantrika guild
Farm surplus fed urban growth and supported the expansion of trade and crafts.

secs.t: Women - status in inscriptions and literature

x: Naganika and Gautami Balasri issued inscriptions, and the use of matronymics indicates the social importance of maternal identity.
Independent donations by women, without naming husbands or fathers, are recorded at
Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati
The evidence includes women artisans and merchants, women poets in the Gathasaptasati, and the Kamasutra's reference to vetti or forced labour performed by women.

secs.t: Hala - title, anthology, language

x: Hala honoured Kumarila and Sripalita and compiled the Gathasaptasati in Maharashtri Prakrit.
Hala married Lilavati at the
Bhimeswara temple at Draksharamam
, in the Saptagodavari region.

secs.t: Gunadhya's Brihatkatha - language, legend, adaptations

x: Brihatkatha is described as having 7,000 verses in seven stories; its original is lost, and it mentions slavery.
All three statements form the traditional account: Gunadhya lost the dispute with Sarvavarma, wrote in Paishachi, and began burning the work after the king ignored it.
Kathasaritsagara was authored by Somadeva Suri, Brihatkatha Manjari by Kshemendra, and Brihatkatha Shloka Sangraha by Buddhasvami.

secs.t: Sarvavarma's Katantra - purpose and patron

x: Katantra was a short Sanskrit grammar prepared for Kuntala Satakarni so that the king could learn Sanskrit quickly.

secs.t: Later works on Satavahana kings - Kutuhala's Lilavati

x: Lilavati Parinayam narrates Hala's marriage to the Sinhala princess Lilavati at Draksharamam.
Lilavati Parinayam mentions Satavahana patronage of Nagarjuna, and Harshacharita gives Yajna Sri the title Trisamudradhipati, meaning lord of three seas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The newly found Satavahana-era Prakrit-Brahmi inscriptions were discovered in Gundaram Forest in Jayashankar Bhupalpally district of Telangana.
The Desi words in the Gathasaptasati are regarded as
the earliest traces of Telugu
, and the Satavahana period laid the foundation of the language.
The Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions from Egypt record trader names including
Cikai Korran, Kopan and Catan
, and date from the 1st to 3rd centuries CE.
Ashokan inscriptions belong to the 3rd century BCE, followed by Satavahana records, Tamil-Brahmi trader inscriptions of the 1st–3rd centuries CE, and Vijayanagara-period inscriptions.

rows.title: Satavahana art and architecture - Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, rock-cut caves (Karle, Bhaja, Nasik)
sub: Group-II M1-A-4: Buddhist sites of Andhra - Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Salihundam, Ghantasala
Group-II M1-A-11: Satavahana art and architecture - Amaravati school, stupas and rock-cut caves

secs.t: Amaravati stupa - phases, patrons, discovery, themes, relics, sculptures today

x: The Buddha’s bone powder was enshrined in a
copper urn
by Mahadeva Bhikshu.
Vasishthiputra Satakarni
is associated with the enlargement that added limestone sculptures and a stone railing or vedika.
The final enlargement is attributed to the Ikshvakus, while Acharya Nagarjuna is associated with construction of the enclosing wall or prakara.

secs.t: Nagarjunakonda - Sriparvata, Ikshvakus, excavation, submergence, museum

x: The
Ikshvaku queens
are specifically noted as major donors to Buddhist establishments at Nagarjunakonda.
Yajna Sri Satakarni built the 1,500-room
Sriparvata Sangharama
for Acharya Nagarjuna.
Longhurst
conducted the excavation of Nagarjunakonda from 1927 to 1931, after its discovery by A.R. Saraswati in 1926.
The February 2026 excavation report refers to the discovery of a
massive university complex
at Nagarjunakonda.

secs.t: Andhra stupa features - ayaka platforms and pillars

x: The lotus and bull represent birth, the horse the Great Renunciation, the Bodhi tree enlightenment and the Dharmachakra the first sermon.
Ayaka platforms and pillars are identified with the Andhra sites of Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Ghantasala, Bhattiprolu and Jaggayyapeta.
The phrase occurs in the Nagarjunakonda Ayaka inscription and refers to relics associated with the perfectly enlightened Buddha.

All four pairings are correct in the stated descriptions: Sanchi is the largest stupa in India, Kesariya the largest brick stupa, Bharhut the most ancient stupa in India and Amaravati the largest in Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Western Deccan rock-cut caves → site + type

x: Karle has the largest chaitya hall; Bhaja has early Buddhist caves; Nasik has viharas with Satavahana inscriptions; and Bedsa has a chaitya with bell-capital pillars.
The Nasik chaitya was funded by
Vishnudatta
, who donated 3,500 karshapanas.
Rock-cut work peaked in
the Sahyadris of the western Deccan
, including sites such as Nasik, Naneghat, Karle, Bhaja, Kanheri, Junnar and Ajanta.

secs.t: Chaitya hall plan - shape, pillars, facade

x: A chaitya hall is rectangular and ends in an apse; rows of pillars form side aisles and a stupa stands at the far apse end.
A chaitya is a prayer hall with a stupa, while a vihara is a monastery with cells around a central hall.
Karle is associated with the largest chaitya hall, 12 dance-couple sculptures and a village donated by Pulumavi II.

secs.t: Donors in inscriptions - merchants, guilds, women

x: ‘Tambaya Danamu’ is an inscriptional donation term found at
a Buddhist site in the Krishna district
Merchants, guilds, Yavanas and artisans
, including an artisan named Dimikudu, are recorded as donors.

secs.t: Satavahana sculpture themes - Jataka panels, Buddha symbols

x: The early phase represented the Buddha through symbols such as the Bodhi tree, empty throne, footprints, wheel and stupa rather than a human image.
Amaravati sculpture includes Jataka panels and scenes such as the Dharmachakra Parivartana and the Buddha at Gaya.
The Amaravati school influenced Buddhist art in
Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia

secs.t: Site-specific inscriptions - ruler or donor named

x: The Bhattiprolu relic-casket inscriptions name the ruler
Kubiraka
and refer to the Nigama-sabha.
Amaravati records mention Pulumavi II, Ikshvaku records at Nagarjunakonda mention Veerapurushadatta, and Yajnasri Satakarni is named as a donor at Chinaganjam.
Amaravati records mention Pulumavi II, the name ‘Nagabu’ and the stupa of the Chaitika Sangha.
At
Nagarjunakonda
and Jaggayyapeta, Ikshvaku records are associated with Veerapurushadatta, under whom Buddhism peaked.

secs.t: Ancient names and texts - modern site and sect

x: Purvasaila was centred at Dhanyakataka, Aparasaila at Sriparvata, Rajagirika at Guntupalli and Siddharthika at Gudivada.
Siddharthaka chaitya is associated with Guntupalli, not Nagarjunakonda.
Purvasaila, Aparasaila, Uttarasaila, Rajagirika and Siddharthika were five Chaitika branches of
the Mahasanghikas
, associated with Mahadeva Bhikshu.

secs.t: Buddhist acharyas - vihara associated

x: Nagarjuna was associated with Sriparvata/Nagarjunakonda and is linked with Madhyamika and Shunyavada.
Dinnaga
is identified as the father of Buddhist logic and is associated with work in the Andhra country.
Aryasangha is associated with Yogachara, Maitreyanatha with Vijnanavada, and Padmasambhava with the transmission of Vajrayana to Tibet.
Chittasuddhi Prakaranam
was written by Aryadeva, who was a disciple of Nagarjuna.

secs.t: Recent excavations and new finds

x: A new interpretation centre at Thotlakonda was opened on
1 March 2026
Thotlakonda was spotted through an aerial survey conducted by the Indian Navy.
The excavations found the main stupa, votive stupas, Satavahana coins and Roman coins.

secs.t: Discoverers and excavators

x: Colonel Colin Mackenzie
identified Amaravati in 1797.
The correct order is Mackenzie’s identification in 1797, Sewell’s excavations in 1877, Rea’s Bhattiprolu excavation in 1892, and Longhurst’s Nagarjunakonda work in 1927.

secs.t: Amaravati school - phases, material, themes, comparison

x: The Amaravati school developed from the 2nd century BCE to the 3rd century CE under Satavahana patronage.
Although it developed under Satavahana patronage, the Amaravati school reached its final, most mature phase under the
Ikshvakus
All four features are characteristic of the Amaravati school: narrative Buddhist reliefs, movement, emotional expression, floral and vegetal decoration, and the Buddha seated on a lotus in padmasana.

secs.t: Sculptural panels - Jatakas, Buddha-life scenes, phases of depiction

x: The early phase is aniconic, using the Bodhi tree, empty throne, footprints, wheel and stupa; the later phase depicts the Buddha in human form, seated on a lotus with dancing Gandharvas and Yakshas.
The Gathasaptasati states that people painted
mythological scenes
on the walls of houses.

secs.t: Amaravati sculptures - discoverer, dispersal, museums

x: The perimeter of the Amaravati stupa is stated to have been about
435 feet
The Amaravati stupa had an approximate height of
20 metres

secs.t: Terracotta, ivory and bead finds

x: Guilds of ivory workers made donations at Amaravati.
Kondapur yielded
terracotta figurines, beads and coins
Nelakondapalli is associated with a post-Satavahana mahastupa, bronze and marble Buddhas in the Amaravati style, and a sculptor’s workshop identified with V. V. Krishna Sastry.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The identified visitor markets are
Japan, Korea, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar
Buddhavanam is a 279-acre theme park at Nagarjuna Sagar in Nalgonda, Telangana, and it hosted Miss World 2025 contestants.
The Ikshvakus
built the earliest structural Hindu temples, while Satavahana chaitya-vihara forms provided an architectural base for later Hindu temple architecture.

rows.title: Satavahana religious conditions - Buddhism, Brahmanism and royal patronage
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Acharya Nagarjuna - works, philosophy, patron, place

x: Suhrullekha, a collection of letters of friendly advice, was addressed to
Yajna Sri Satakarni
Suhrullekha
, meaning ‘friendly letter’, is one of the works associated with Acharya Nagarjuna.
The Sriparvata vihara or Mahachaitya built for Nagarjuna is stated to have had 1,500 rooms.
Kathasaritsagara states that Nagarjuna was killed by a Satavahana prince, whereas Lilavati Parinayam refers to his patronage by a Satavahana king.

secs.t: Early Brahmanical shrines - Gudimallam

x: The Parasurameswara temple is at
Gudimallam
in the present Chittoor, now Tirupati, district, and contains the oldest Shivalinga of the Satavahana period.

secs.t: Brahmanism - Vedic sacrifices and the Naneghat inscription

x: The Naneghat inscription of Devi Naganika was in Prakrit; she was the wife of Satakarni I and daughter of Maharathi Tranakayiro.
The sons named in the inscription are
Vedasiri, Hakusiri and Kumara Satavahana
; Vedasiri is identified as the eldest.
The Nasik inscription calls Gautamiputra Satakarni
Agama nilaya
, meaning an abode of traditional learning.

secs.t: Buddhism - royal and queens' patronage

x: Buddhism relied more on public support than on royal support.
Gautami Balasri donated
a cave vihara at Nasik for the Bhadrayaniya sect
, reportedly for the recovery of her son.
Pulumavi II
donated a village to Mahasanghika monks at Karle.
Krishna donated a Nasik cave for shramanas and appointed a Dharma Mahamatra.

secs.t: Buddhist sects in Andhra - centres

x: The Chaityaka sect was founded by
Mahadeva Bhikshu
, regarded as the first Buddhist acharya in Andhra.
Chaityaka or Chaityakavada was centred on the worship of
chaityas
These sects were associated respectively with the Dhanyakataka hills, Sriparvatam and Nasik.
Tibetan tradition states that the Buddha preached at Amaravati at the request of King
Subendran

secs.t: Deities invoked in inscriptions - Vedic vs Bhagavata

x: The inscription invokes
Indra, Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Surya, Chandra, Yama and Varuna
, combining Vedic and Bhagavata elements.
Bhagavata religion was founded by Vasudeva-Krishna and centred at Mathura.
Bhagavata religion reached Andhra under Krishna, became the Vasudeva religion by Hala’s time, and Bhagavata symbols are noted in Gautamiputra’s inscriptions.

secs.t: Donors to the sangha - by category

x: Donors included kings, queens, officials, merchants, guilds such as ivory workers and coral dealers, artisans and independent women.
The deposit with the Govardhana weavers illustrates how guilds placed money on deposit and transferred the interest to Buddhist monks.
The Alluru inscription of the
Ikshvaku Virapurushadatta
records donations to many communities and institutions.

secs.t: Jainism in Satavahana Andhra - Kundakunda

x: Kundakundacharya was a Jain teacher associated with Konakondla and preached
Syadvada
Royal women patronised Buddhism and, according to the stated account, also patronised Jainism.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The period is characterised by religious pluralism, including Brahmanical practices such as the Ashvamedha and Buddhist centres such as Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda.
Prakrit, described as the people’s language, helped Buddhism communicate beyond elite circles and become a mass movement.
Yavana merchants are associated with funding caves at
Karle, Bhaja, Nasik, Junnar and Kanheri

rows.title: Ikshvakus - political history, Vasishthiputra Chamtamula and Virapurushadatta
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Rulers - period and contribution; last ruler

x: Chamtamula attempted to make the intelligentsia partners in agricultural development by giving land, ploughs, bullocks and cows.
The reign of
Virapurushadatta
is regarded as the golden age of Buddhism under the Ikshvakus, and his queens were important donors.
All three statements are included among the notable firsts associated with the Ikshvakus: early Hindu temples, dated inscriptions naming sculptors, and the recorded naming practice.

secs.t: Titles and Puranic names

x: Sri Parvatadhipati was a title of Virapurushadatta, while Gosatasahasra and Halasatasahasra were titles of Chamtamula.
The Puranas refer to the
Ikshvakus
as Sri Parvatiyas or Sri Parvatiya Andhras and as Andhrabhrityas.
B.S.L. Hanumantha Rao connected the name Ikshvaku with
ikshu, meaning sugarcane
The lion was the Ikshvaku symbol and Prakrit was their royal language.

secs.t: Capital - Vijayapuri

x: Vijayapuri, identified with modern Nagarjunakonda, lies in the Nagarjuna Sagar valley and was excavated by R. Subrahmanyam.
Excavations at Vijayapuri revealed an amphitheatre, possibly built with Roman help, and an Ashvamedha platform.

secs.t: Origin debate - descent claims, link to the Satavahanas

x: Gopalachari
is associated with the view that the Ikshvakus were Telugu or Andhra people, though the APP material also records a differing attribution to Caldwell.
Rapson and Buhler supported a North Indian origin; Vogel a Kannada origin; D.R. Bhandarkar a Kshatriya or mixed Kshatriya-Brahmin origin; and Gopalachari a Telugu/Andhra origin.
The Nagarjunakonda inscription is described as claiming Solar or Rama lineage from Ayodhya, with later claims of Shakya descent.

secs.t: Vedic sacrifices by Chamtamula

x: Chamtamula performed Ashvamedha, Vajapeya, Agnishtoma, Agnihotra and Rajasuya sacrifices.
An Ashvamedha platform was found at Nagarjunakonda, supporting the record of Chamtamula’s sacrifice.
Chamtamula invited Brahmins from northern regions, and the family worshipped Virupakshapati, identified with Shiva, and Mahasena, identified with Kartikeya.

secs.t: Matrimonial alliances

x: Rudrabhattarika was a princess of Ujjain, and the marriage connected the Ikshvakus with the Sakas or Western Kshatrapas.
Virapurushadatta’s other wives included Bhattidevi and Bapisri, while Rudrabhattarika was the princess of Ujjain.
Marriage with the maternal uncle’s daughter is a form of
cross-cousin marriage
and is cited as a southern custom among the Ikshvakus.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Ikshvakus are regarded as a bridge dynasty that brought the Amaravati school to its peak, built the first temples and moved Andhra towards an agrarian, Puranic order.
Many Roman coins have been found at
Nagarjunakonda
, indicating long-distance commercial connections.
Machilipatnam
is the 16th–17th century handloom port; it should not be confused with the Ikshvaku-period ports Motupalli and Ghantasala.

src: Sources: APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2, Ikshvaku dynasty); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.62, 64-65, 100); CDI (Block09 Ikshvaku Dynasty - introduction, conclusion); APHQ (G2 2017 Q11, 2019 Q5, 2025 Q3)

rows.title: Ikshvaku socio-economic conditions; role of royal women as donors
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Royal women donors → monument donated (Chamtisri, Bapisri, Chatisri, Kodabalisri, Rudradhara Bhattarika)

x: Exam angle: "the woman who served Buddhism most" =
Bodhisiri
(Bapisiri, Chantisiri, Adavi Chantisiri are the distractors).
Harmyasri, a sister of Sri Santamula, set up a pillar at the Maha Chaitya of the Aparamahavinaseliya sect for her
mother
Bapisri and Chatisri, queens of Virapurushadatta, made
independent pillar dedications at the Mahachaitya
Kodabalisri built a vihara for
Mahishasaka monks
; the record also associates her with a great stupa and vihara.

secs.t: Donative inscriptions at Nagarjunakonda - donor's relation to the king

x: Most records are Prakrit Ayaka-pillar inscriptions dated in Virapurushadatta's sixth regnal year.
Chamtisri's inscription invokes
long life, victory and prosperity
for Virapurushadatta.
Chamtisri held the titles
Mahatalavari and Mahadanapatni
, the latter referring to her position as wife of Pugiya chief Skandasri.
Different sources describe Bodhisri as Bodhisarma's daughter-in-law, niece-in-law or niece.

secs.t: Economy - trade, ports and foreign contacts in Ikshvaku records

x: Roman gold and silver coins found at Nagarjunakonda and a Roman-style amphitheatre at Vijayapuri indicate foreign contact.
Exports included
spices
, iron, coconuts and cotton textiles.
Ikshvaku coins carried the
Ujjain symbol, elephant and lion
; the lion was the royal emblem.
The recorded findspots of Ikshvaku coins include
Guntur, Krishna and Godavari
districts.

secs.t: Guilds and merchant donors in Ikshvaku inscriptions

x: Guilds were called
Nigamalu
; the spelling Negimalu also occurs.
Parnika Sreni consisted of betel-leaf traders, Poosika Sreni of sweetmeat traders, Sale of weavers and Telika of oil pressers.
Rathavasya donated to the
Nodageshwara temple
Nagarjunakonda was home to merchants and artisans
organised into guilds

secs.t: Society - varna, marriage customs recorded in inscriptions

x: Varna rules became stricter, Brahmadeya grants supported Brahmins, Shudras were the majority and a new landlord class emerged.
Kodabalisri's marriage to Vishnurudra Sivalananda Satakarni represented the Ikshvaku connection with the
Chutus
The inscriptions record the practice of sati, the use of matronymics such as Vasishthiputra and names derived from the grandfather, such as Ehuvala Santamula.

secs.t: Gifts recorded in Chamtamula's inscriptions - items and quantities

x: The title
Goshatasahasra Halashatasahasra
denotes the giver of hundreds of thousands of cows and ploughs.
Santamula performed the Ashvamedha, Vajapeya and Agnistoma sacrifices, and an Ashvamedha altar has been found at Nagarjunakonda.
The four sectors included administration and army, temples and festivals, poets and scholars, and gifts to religious bodies; some funds supported tanks and canals.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Ikshvaku period marks Andhra's movement from the Satavahana trade economy towards an agrarian, agrahara-based early medieval order.
The Buddhist heritage circuit
is placed first in the AP 'Discover Andhra' campaign, and Nagarjunakonda is identified as a key site.
The debate holds that women's general status declined, even though royal women continued to exercise religious and economic agency, including through patronage and donations.
