rows.title: Ikshvaku religious conditions - Buddhism at Nagarjunakonda, Brahmanical temples
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Religious policy by reign - Veerapurushadatta's peak, Ehuvala Chamtamula (Bodhisiri), Rudrapurushadatta

x: Exam angle: greatest patronage =
Veerapurushadatta
; Bodhisri's service = reign of
Ehuvala Chamtamula
. CDX lists Bodhisri under Virapurushadatta; the APPSC key follows Ehuvala.
The sculptures at Nagarjunakonda show a Shivalinga trampled underfoot, reflecting the strong Buddhist orientation associated with Virapurushadatta's reign.
Satavahana inscriptions are in Prakrit and Brahmi, while Ehuvala Santamula is associated with the first Sanskrit inscriptions of the Ikshvakus; Gummadi Darru indicates a Buddhist educational centre.

secs.t: Kings vs queens - attitude to Buddhism, patronage pattern, tutelary deity Hariti

x: The Ikshvaku pattern was one of dual patronage: most kings performed Vedic sacrifices, while royal women and wealthy lay women supported Buddhist stupas and viharas.
Puranic Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Shakti worship all flourished
under the Ikshvakus.
Skanda was identified with Kartikeya; Vishnu was worshipped as Narasimha; Hariti protected children; and Ganapati was the elephant-headed deity.

secs.t: Buddhist monasteries at Nagarjunakonda → sect (Aparasaila, Bahusrutiya, Mahisasaka, Mahaviharavasin)

x: The Maha Chaitya belonged to the Aparamahavinaseliya tradition; Bhatti Mahadevi or Ehuvala Santamula's vihara to the Bahushrutiyas; Kodabalisri's vihara to the Mahishasakas; and Bodhisri's Sinhala Vihara to the Mahaviharavasins.
Purvasailiya, Rajagirika and Siddharthika were among the Mahasanghika branches or related sects named.
Acharya Bhadanta Ananda was said to know
the Digha and Majjhima Nikayas
by heart.

secs.t: Mahachaitya - relic, donor (Bodhisiri), inscriptions

x: The expression ‘
Samma Sambudhasa dhatuvara parigahita
’ means that the excellent relics of the Buddha were enshrined.

Chamtisri rebuilt the Paravata Mahachaitya in Virapurushadatta's sixth year, and the structure had nine Ayaka pillars; the earlier monument was associated with Yajnasri Satakarni and Acharya Nagarjuna.
The pillar inscriptions named Chamtisri, Adavi Chamtisri, Harmyasri, Chathasri, Bapisri, Chatisri and Rudrabhattarika.

secs.t: Foreign Buddhist links - monasteries for foreign monks, countries in inscriptions, Itsing and Suhrllekha

x: The inscription named Kashmir, Gandhara, China, Chila(ta), Tosali, Aparanta, Vanga, Vanavasi, Yavana, Damila and Palura.
Ceylonese monks made Nagarjunakonda their base for Hinayana, strengthening the Sri Lankan Buddhist connection.

The earlier Paravata Mahachaitya associated with Yajnasri Satakarni preceded its rebuilding by Chamtisri; the Mahadeva Bhikshu tradition belongs to the Sri Lankan link, and Itsing visited around 700 CE later.

secs.t: Brahmanical shrines at Nagarjunakonda → deity (Sarvadeva, Pushpabhadraswami, Kartikeya)

x: The Sarvadeva shrine, also called Kumaraswami Sarvadevadivasa, was dedicated to
Kartikeya
The Pushpabhadraswami shrine was a Shaiva shrine with an elephant-back plan, begun by Virapurushadatta and completed by Ehuvala.
The Ashtabhuja Narayanaswami shrine was built by Shivasena, the commander of the Abhira king Vasusena.
Hariti was regarded as the mother goddess of children and was associated with a Saptamatrika shrine.

secs.t: Acharya Nagarjuna and Sriparvata - tradition, monastery, Sri Parvataswamy identified as Buddha (Kielhorn)

x: Sriparvata is identified with Nagarjunakonda, or Vijayapuri, and is traditionally called Dakshina Gaya.
Yajnasri Satakarni
built viharas and chaityas at Sri Parvatam for Nagarjuna.
Hiuen Tsang found the Sriparvata vihara
neglected
during his seventh-century visit.
Sriparvata refers to Nagarjunakonda or Vijayapuri, while Sriparvataswami was the family deity of the Vishnukundins and is identified with Srisaila Mallikarjuna.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In April 2026, the Palnadu Collector visited the Nagarjunakonda Museum, proposed a Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam boat service and pushed Swadesh Darshan works.
Buddhavanam, located next to Nagarjunakonda, is being developed under the
Integrated Buddhist Circuit
and was visited by Miss World contestants in May 2025.
Ashtabhuja Narayanaswami is regarded as the first Vaishnava temple in Andhra, while the Ikshvakus represented the last royal Buddhist zenith in Andhra.

Religious Conditions; Block09 Jainism and Buddhism in Andhra); APP (AP History Ancient Parts 1-2 > Ikshvaku Dynasty; Satavahana Buddhism); APHQ 2008, 2012, 2019; TH 2 Apr 2026; LENS May 2025 p.16; APPCA Feb 2026

rows.title: Ikshvaku art, architecture and literature
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Nagarjunakonda sculpture - comparison with Amaravati school, favourite themes, Buddha depiction

x: Nagarjunakonda was a main centre of the
Amaravati School
, which attained its mature phase under the Ikshvakus.
The Mandhata sculpture at Jaggayyapeta is regarded as the most important Ikshvaku sculpture and the
first depiction of a Chakravarti in Indian art
The carving of sculptors' names is associated with the
beginning of the Sculptor's Style
; Badantacharya at the Mahavihara is an example.

secs.t: Stupa and chaitya ground plans → examples at Nagarjunakonda

x: Dhatugarbha stupa
s were built over bodily relics of the Buddha or great monks, as in the case of the Maha Chaitya.

Bhattiprolu is associated with the oldest stupa in Andhra; Jaggayyapeta with a relic stupa and the Mandhata sculpture; Ghantasala with Kantakossyla; and Nagarjunakonda with the Ikshvaku centre and over 30 stupas.

secs.t: Secular structures excavated at Vijayapuri - types and purpose

x: The Kreeda Vedi was a sports arena, thought to have been built with Roman assistance, and it has been described as having no parallel elsewhere in India.
Kummakundam denotes
water tanks or bathing pools
excavated at Vijayapuri.
The 1954–1960 excavations uncovered the palace complex and Brahmanical temples constructed of brick.

secs.t: Language of Ikshvaku inscriptions - change over reigns, earliest Sanskrit record in Andhra

x: The earliest Sanskrit inscription of Andhra and South India is at the Swarna Devalayam, or Golden Temple, at Nagarjunakonda.
The inscription is dated to the 11th regnal year of Ehuvala Santamula.
Sanskrit replaced Prakrit in Ikshvaku inscriptional usage from the fourth century CE.
Bapi, Remmanaka, Adavi, Ehuvala and Anikki are Telugu words found in Ikshvaku records.

secs.t: Buddhist Sanskrit literature linked to Nagarjunakonda

x: Suhrllekha, along with Madhyamika works, is associated with
Acharya Nagarjuna
Sutralankara, in Sanskrit, is attributed to
Aryasangha
Visuddhimagga is a Pali work attributed to Buddhaghosha.
The panchangam mentioned in the Jain Dharmamrita comprises
tithi, vara and nakshatra
The eighth-century Kuvalayamala records the presence of foreign students at
Dhanyakataka and Nagarjunakonda

secs.t: Relocation of monuments - Nagarjuna Sagar project (1955), island museum, Anupu, Yeleswaram

x: Jawaharlal Nehru
laid the foundation stone of the Nagarjuna Sagar Project on 10 December 1955.
The Archaeological Survey of India used
salvage archaeology
to dismantle and rebuild monuments before submergence.
The monuments relocated to Anupu and Nagarjunakonda island are called
transplanted monuments
Anupu is situated on the bank of the
Krishna
and became one of the locations for transplanted monuments.

secs.t: Excavations → discoverer and excavators + years

x: The correct sequence is 1926 discovery, 1927–31 work of A. H. Longhurst, 1938 work of T. N. Ramachandran, and the 1954–60 rescue excavation.
R. Subrahmanyam
was among the excavators involved in the large rescue excavation of 1954–1960.
The habitation at Nagarjunakonda extends from the
Palaeolithic period up to 1960 CE

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Palnadu Collector
reviewed the Nagarjunakonda Museum and the Swadesh Darshan works.

Temple architecture is linked with the base of Dravida architecture; the Amaravati school was brought to its peak; the first Sanskrit inscription in South India is an inscriptional achievement; and the first sculptor signatures relate to sculptural practice.

rows.title: Vishnukundins - political history, Madhava Varma I and II
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Capitals and their shifts (Indrapalanagara, Amarapura, Denduluru, Bezawada) → ruler

x: Exam angle: "Amarapuri → Denduluru" =
Madhavavarma
B.S.L. Hanumantha Rao
identified Amarapura with Velpuru in Guntur, whereas another identification places it at Munnanuru.
Madhava Varma II
shifted the capital from Amarapuri to Denduluru because of constant Pallava wars and fortified Amarapuri.
Denduluru, also called Dendulurapura, was situated near
Vengi or Pedavegi
in Eluru district.

secs.t: Titles → ruler (Janasraya, Trikuta-Malayadhipati)

x: Madhava Varma II acquired the title Trikuta-Malayadhipati after defeating
the Anandagotrikas
Govinda Varma was Shadabhigna, Vikramendra Varma I was Mahakavi, and Indrabhattaraka Varma bore the title Satyasraya.
Trisamudradhipati belonged to Madhava Varma II; Shadabhigna to Govinda Varma; Paramamaheshwara to Indrabhattaraka Varma; and Sakala Bhuvana Rakshabharanaikashraya to Vikramendra Varma II.
Vikramendra Varma I
was associated with the titles Mahakavi and Parama Saugata.

secs.t: Rulers - chronological order and contribution

x: Indravarma
, who ruled from 358 to 370 CE, is described as the founder of the Vishnukundin dynasty and a Vakataka vassal.
These activities are associated with
Govinda Varma I
, whose rule also saw expansion into the Krishna-Godavari region and both sides of Sriparvata.
Vikramendra Varma I was the son of Madhava Varma II and a Vakataka princess, while Indrabhattaraka Varma was defeated by Ishanavarma and killed in the Kalinga war.

secs.t: Sequence of post-Ikshvaku dynasties - correct order Ikshvakus → Brihatpalayanas → Salankayanas → Vishnukundins

x: Exam angle: G2 2008 order question - answer
a, d, c, b
(Ikshvakus, Brihatpalayanas, Salankayanas, Vishnukundins).
After the Ikshvakus came the Brihatpalayanas or Pallavas in the relevant territories, followed by the Salankayanas, Vishnukundins and Eastern Chalukyas.
The Salankayana capital was Vengi or Pedavegi, they followed Vaishnavism, and Madhava Varma II conquered them.

secs.t: Origin debate - identification of Vishnukundi, original home

x: Most historians regard the Vishnukundins as Brahmins belonging to the Vishnukundina gotra, although alternative caste theories have also been proposed.
B.V. Krishna Rao regarded them as Brahmins; K. Gopalachari proposed an Agnikula Kshatriya origin; N. Venkataramanayya described them as Brahmins who adopted Kshatriya ways.
Early records and forts at Amrabad, Keesaragutta and Indrapalanagara point to Telangana as the original home.

secs.t: Inscriptions → ruler (Chikkulla, Ipur, Polamuru, Tummalagudem, Khanapur)

x: The Polamuru plates of Ramachandrapuram are attributed to
Madhava Varma IV
in the numbering followed by the source.
The Tummalagudem records include associations with Govinda Varma I and Vikramendra Varma II, a grant to Paramabhattarika’s vihara, and the first Sanskrit inscription found in Telangana.
The Velpuru pillar is associated with
Madhava Varma II
and records the installation of Ganapati in his 33rd year.

secs.t: Madhava Varma II - sacrifices performed, conquests

x: Madhava Varma II is credited with performing 11 Ashvamedhas, 16 Rajasuyas and one Purushamedha.
Madhava Varma II is said to have placed the conch of the Vasishthas of Devarashtra on his coins after defeating them.
The Bezawada inscription narrates that Madhava Varma II sentenced his own son to death after the prince’s chariot killed the son of a poor woman.

secs.t: Wars and decline - dynasties fought, power that ended their rule

x: The recorded sequence is the breakaway of Prithvi Maharaja, the killing of Indrabhattaraka, the defeat of Manchana Bhattaraka by Pulakeshin II in 624 CE, and then the foundation of the Eastern Chalukyas by Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
Pulakeshin II of the Badami Chalukyas
defeated Manchana Bhattaraka at Kunala near Kolleru in 624 CE, ending Vishnukundin rule.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Khanapur is in Satara, Maharashtra, and Ramatirtham is separately associated with Indravarma; they are not a pair belonging to the Guntur region.
Differences among sources concern the founder, numbering of rulers, dates and certain title attributions.
The APPSC keys follow the identifications Madhava Varma II as Janasraya and Madhava Varma II as Amarapuri leading to Denduluru.

src: Sources: CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.94, 100-106; APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Vishnukundin Dynasty); CDI (Block09 Salankayana Dynasty; Vishnukundin Dynasty); APHQ 2008, 2011, 2025

rows.title: Vishnukundin society, religion, administration and coinage
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Coinage - metal used, coating, symbols on coins, find-spots

x: Lion, Nandi, ship, trishula, conch and Sriparvata were mentioned as symbols;
lotus
was not included in the list.
Ship-marked coins and the title Trisamudradhipati point to the importance of
sea trade
A Roman gold coin of Constantine was found at
Kudali Sangameswaram near Alampur
Fa-hien
reported the use of cowrie shells, or gavvalu, as money.

secs.t: Administration - territorial units, officers, military organisation

x: Akshapataladhikrita kept records, Rajjuka measured land with ropes, Gulmika supervised border areas, and Phaladara measured grain and fixed the king's share.
Hastikosa was the elephant corps, Veerakosa was the infantry commander and Chhata was a spy.
The Polamuru plates record divine ordeals, Bhaga was one-sixth, and Vishti was forced labour, later called vetti in Telugu.

secs.t: Religion - Vedic sacrifices performed, family deity of the dynasty

x: Madhava Varma II was said to have performed 11 Ashvamedhas, 16 Rajasuyas and approximately 1,000 yagas.
Dantamukha Swami was installed at
Velpuru
in the 33rd year of Madhava Varma II.
Bhutagrahaka Swami was associated with Yama, Ramalingeswara temples were recorded at the four named places, and Dharmapuri became a Narasimha kshetra.

secs.t: Buddhism and Jainism - viharas and grants under Vishnukundin rule

x: Govinda Varma I founded the Govinda Vihara; Prithvimula and Harivarma were associated with the Gunapashapuram viharas; Vikramendra Varma II granted Irundhera; and the queen of Govinda Varma I founded the Paramabhattarika Mahadevi Vihara.
Jainism declined as Kapalika Shaivism rose; Jain shrines such as Srisailam were converted, and Kumarilabhatta attacked Jainism.

secs.t: Brahmana land grants (agraharas) - grant inscriptions, donee details

x: Mutukali or Mruthukali was granted as an agrahara to
Indravarma and Agnivarma
The Ipur plates mention
Agnisarma and Easwarasarma
as donees of gifts made to Brahmins.
The Ipur plates record gifts of
cows, gold and land
to Brahmins.
The feudalisation interpretation holds that tax-free Brahmadeyas with administrative rights created
a landed intermediary class

secs.t: Education - Ghatika centres, Brahmanical learning

x: Ghatikas were higher Sanskrit and Vedic colleges concerned with advanced Brahmanical learning.
The inscriptions of
Indrabhattaraka Varma
provide the first mention of Ghatikas in Andhra.
Indrabhattaraka Varma is credited with the Ghatikeshwara temple at
Keesara
The Ghatikas taught fourteen vidyas: four Vedas, six Vedangas, Mimamsa, Nyaya, Dharmashastra and Puranas.
Madhava Varma II bore the title
Vidyadvijaguru

secs.t: Literature - Janasraya Chhandovichiti authorship, Sanskrit works of Vikramendra Varma

x: The work is associated with Madhava Varma II through the title Janasraya, while an alternative view credits the poet Gunaswami with composing it in the king's name; its subject is prosody.
The Indrapalanagara plates call Vikramendra Varma I Mahakavi, but the sources do not name any surviving Sanskrit work by him.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The period witnessed a Vedic-Puranic revival, the temple and agrahara economy, and the first Hindu cave temples.
The period is described as one in which varna rules hardened, women's status declined, and practices such as child marriage and sati increased.

src: Sources: CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.100-109; APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Vishnukundin Dynasty: Administration, Economy, Society, Religion, Education); CDI (Block09 Vishnukundin Dynasty); APHQ 2025

rows.title: Vishnukundin art and architecture - Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda caves
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Cave temples → dynasty + deity (Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram, Bhairavakonda, Akkanna-Madanna)

x: The
Guptas
at Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh are credited with the earliest Hindu cave temples in India, whereas the Vishnukundins are associated with the first Hindu cave temples in the Telugu states.
Madhava Varma I is credited with the
Undavalli, Bhairavakonda and Mogalrajapuram
caves in the attribution followed by APP and CDX.

secs.t: Cave → present location, district, river

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2019 asked where Undavalli is; the key is
Vijayawada
. Its revenue district is Guntur.
Undavalli and Akkanna-Madanna are associated with the Krishna region, Mogalrajapuram is in present NTR district, and Keesaragutta is in Medchal-Malkajgiri district of Telangana.
Undavalli is located at Undavalli in Tadepalli mandal of Guntur district, in the Amaravati capital area near Vijayawada and Mangalagiri, on the Krishna bank.

secs.t: Bhairavakonda - eight caves, Nellore district, Shaivism, dynastic attribution debate

x: Bhairavakonda combines lion pedestals beneath the pillars with kumbha or pot capitals, and its Shaiva association is specifically linked to the Kapalika sect.
APP and CDX credit Madhava Varma I of the Vishnukundin dynasty, whereas APHQ dates the caves to the Pallava period of the seventh–eighth centuries CE.
The resemblance of Bhairavakonda to the
early Pallava caves of Mahabalipuram
is one reason for the Pallava-period attribution suggested by CDI.

secs.t: Undavalli - number of storeys, main sculpture, earlier religious use

x: Exam angle: LENS Aug 2026 test - "built by the
Cholas
as a Hindu temple, later Buddhist" is
false
; the true statements are the Krishna-bank location and the Ananta Padmanabha statue.
The centrepiece of Undavalli is a monolithic reclining Vishnu, identified as Ananta Padmanabha Swamy, approximately 5 metres or 16 feet long.

secs.t: Mogalrajapuram - number of caves, notable sculptures

x: Caves 1–3 contain sanctums behind a pillared mandapa and are associated with Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
Cave 4
at Mogalrajapuram is identified as the Durga cave and has Ardhanarishvara painted on its back wall.
Cave 5 is the largest cave at Mogalrajapuram and contains the
Shiva Tandava Nataraja
sculpture.
Trimurti figures are carved on the kapota, or eave, above the pillar capitals at Mogalrajapuram.

secs.t: Cave architecture features - pillar types, dwarapalas, shrine plans

x: The typical plan consists of a pillared mandapa or ardhamandapa in front of one or more garbhagriha cells cut into the rock.
Dwarapalas, or door guardians, flank the entrances to the shrine spaces, a feature also seen in contemporary Pallava caves.
Bhairavakonda has lion pedestals and pot capitals, Mogalrajapuram has a decorated kapota above the capitals, and Undavalli displays purnakumbha motifs.

secs.t: Comparison with Pallava rock-cut caves (Mahendravarman style)

x: The Vishnukundin caves are generally dated to the fourth–sixth centuries, with Undavalli in the fourth–fifth century, while Mahendravarman I’s Pallava caves belong to the seventh century.

Undavalli is notable for its storeyed plan, Bhairavakonda for lion pedestals and pot capitals, Pallava caves for simha-mukha pillars, and Bhairavakonda for the overlap of the two stylistic traditions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The two-day “Telugu Mahotsavam” at Undavalli Caves was held on
Minister
Kandula Durgesh
announced at the close of the festival that it would become an annual festival held in every region.
Undavalli Caves lie inside the Amaravati capital area, specifically in Tadepalli mandal.
The two-day Telugu Mahotsavam at the Undavalli caves was held on 29
July 2026

Legacy); CDX AP History Complete Notes pp.102, 108-109; APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Vishnukundin Dynasty > Architecture); APHQ 2012, 2019, 2025; LENSD 29 Jul 2026; LENS Aug 2026 pp.117, 124; CDCA Jul 2026 p.65; APPCA 15 Jul 2026; TH 17 Apr, 25-27 Jul 2026, 28 Apr 2026

rows.title: Andhra society and culture in the early period - varna, women, education and festivals
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-46

secs.t: Varna and caste - Brahmana, Kshatriya claims, emerging agricultural castes

x: Exam angle: statement pairs on "Vedic caste system + Satavahana role"; match sub-caste name → occupation.
Satavahana kings were associated with the enforcement of varna-dharma, granted tax-free villages to Brahmins, and the Nanaghat inscription mentions Brahmins trained in Vedic learning and ritual.
Greeks, Sakas, Pahlavas and Kushanas
adopted Indian names and faiths and were assimilated into the Kshatriya order.

secs.t: Women - status, education, property, social customs

x: Exam angle: Ikshvaku woman patron of Buddhism (Bodhisiri); matronymics; female poets of the Gathasaptasati.
The society was patriarchal and organised around joint families, yet women enjoyed considerable respect and participated in festivals, assemblies and public life.
Gautami Balasri funded a cave-vihara at Nasik, Bodhisiri was the greatest woman patron of Buddhism, and Chantisiri built the Mahachaitya at Nagarjunakonda.

secs.t: Education - viharas, Ghatikas, agraharas as centres

x: Nagarjunakonda developed as a leading centre of Buddhist learning in South India under Ikshvaku patronage.
Ghatikasthanas were
Vedic colleges
and were established by the Vishnukundins.
Govindavarma was described as shadabhigna, or a master of six sciences.
Indrabhattaraka Varma
is associated with the expression ‘Ghatika Vapta punyasancharya’ and was credited with founding ghatikas.

secs.t: Festivals and amusements - inscriptions and Gathasaptasati

x: Exam angle: "most important literary source of Satavahana society" → Gathasaptasati (not Puranas, Aitareya Brahmana or Dharmasutras).
The Gathasaptasati contains about 700 verses in Maharashtri Prakrit and discusses family, marriage, women, agriculture, trade, festivals and occupations.
Nagarjunakonda, the Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri, had an amphitheatre or stadium for
performances and games

secs.t: Food, dress and ornaments - sculptural evidence (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda)

x: Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda reliefs show men wearing a lower cloth and turban, while women are depicted with heavy anklets, bangles, girdles and necklaces.
Reliefs from
Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda
provide the principal visual evidence for dress and adornment in the Satavahana-Ikshvaku age.

secs.t: Marriage customs - inscriptions and literature

x: Anuloma was a higher-caste man–lower-caste woman union producing offspring termed Ugra, while Viloma or Pratiloma was the reverse union producing offspring termed Chandala.
Kathasaritsagara
mentions inter-caste marriages, showing that caste practices were not completely rigid at that stage.
Hala married the Sri Lankan princess Lilavati; Satakarni I married the daughter of Maharathi Tranakayira; and Vasishthiputra Satakarni married a daughter of Saka Rudradaman.

secs.t: Folk cults and popular worship - sculpture and inscriptions

x: The Vishnukundins were associated with the Shiva temple of Ramalingeswara and also repaired and built viharas; therefore, their activities were not exclusively Buddhist.
Vasishthiputra Chantamula, an Ikshvaku king, performed the
Asvamedha and Vajapeya
sacrifices.
Nagarjunakonda contained Buddhist establishments as well as Brahmanical shrines, including Pushpabhadraswami.
Amaravati reliefs show the worship of
nagas, yakshas and sacred trees
alongside Buddhist symbols.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Early Andhra combined the Vedic varna order with strong Buddhist patronage, and women played a major role in that patronage.
Kshatriya-status claims continued in the colonial period, including through the Vanniyakula Kshatriya Mahasabha of 1888 and the Akhil Bharatiya Kshatriya Mahasabha of 1897.

src: Sources: APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 - Satavahana and Vishnukundin society, religion, education); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.42-43); APHQ (aph2019_1, aph2019_3); CDCA 31 Jul 2026 p.61; TH 22 Apr 2026

rows.title: Sangam Age - the three Sangams, sources; Tolkappiyam, Ettuthogai, Pattupattu, Pathinenkilkanakku

secs.t: Sangam literature - language, aham and puram, material culture

x: Exam angle: statement questions - "devoid of material culture / no warrior ethic" are false.
Sangam literature comprises about 2,400 poems by several hundred poets, including women, and is regarded as one of the earliest bodies of secular literature in India.
Both Ettuthogai and Pattupattu contain poems classified under aham, dealing with interior or personal themes, and puram, dealing with exterior and public themes.

secs.t: Tamil works → author + subject

x: Tolkappiyam was written by Tolkappiyar, Tirukkural by Tiruvalluvar, Silappadikaram by Ilango Adigal and Manimekalai by Sittalai Sattanar.
Tolkappiyam
, attributed to Tolkappiyar, is the earliest extant Tamil work on grammar and poetics and also contains material on society and polity.
Silappadikaram, written by Ilango Adigal, is regarded as the first Tamil epic and tells the story of Kannagi and Kovalan through the motif of the anklet.

secs.t: Three Sangams → place + presiding scholar + surviving works

x: The traditional account places the first Sangam at Then Madurai, the second at Kapatapuram and the third at Madurai; all are described as being under Pandya patronage.
According to the traditional account, nothing survives from the First Sangam.
Agastya presided over the First Sangam; the Second is associated with Agastya and Tolkappiyar; and Nakkirar presided over the Third Sangam.

secs.t: Sangam anthologies - Ettuthogai, Pattupattu, Pathinenkilkanakku

x: Akananuru, Kalittogai and Paripadal are among the eight Ettuthogai anthologies.
Ettuthogai means the collection of eight anthologies, while Pattupattu consists of ten idylls.
Ettuthogai and Pattupattu together constitute the eighteen major works known as Melkanakku.
Pathinenkilkanakku comprises eighteen minor works, mainly on ethics and morals, includes Tirukkural and is largely regarded as post-Sangam.

secs.t: Twin epics - author, story, period

x: Ilango Adigal
, identified as the younger brother of Chera Senguttuvan, composed Silappadikaram.
Manimekalai relates how
the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi becomes a Buddhist nun
and reflects Buddhist philosophy.
Both Silappadikaram and Manimekalai are considered
post-Sangam works

secs.t: Other sources - classical accounts, Ashokan edicts, Hathigumpha

x: The anonymous Greek work
Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
provides information on ports, Muziris, pepper and Arikamedu.
Pliny’s Natural History refers to Chera spices, Pandya pearls, Chola muslin and the outflow or drain of Roman gold.
Ashokan inscriptions identify the
Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas
as southern neighbours of the Mauryan Empire; Satiyaputras and Keralaputras are also mentioned in Rock Edict II.

secs.t: Archaeological sources - Arikamedu, Kaveripattinam, Keezhadi

x: Arikamedu
, near Puducherry, was an Indo-Roman trading settlement and is described in the Periplus as the ‘market street of the Romans’.
Kaveripattinam or Puhar was a Chola port described in Pattinappalai as cosmopolitan and containing Yavana settlements.
Keezhadi is considered the most important Sangam urban excavation and indicates
South Indian urbanisation contemporary with the Gangetic Second Urbanisation

secs.t: Chronology debate of the Sangam corpus

x: The Sangam corpus is generally placed between approximately the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, or
300 BCE–300 CE
Tamil-Brahmi evidence establishes the early limit; the accepted Sangam span follows; the twin epics are later post-Sangam works; and the named traveller accounts are still later indirect evidence.
The legendary account of three Sangams and two submerged cities is traditional rather than historically established.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The documentation of approximately 30 mostly Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in Egyptian Theban tombs was reported in LENS in February 2026, while the July 2025 recap concerned the Tamil Nadu excavation and its archaeological finds.
Sangam Age sources are significant because they offer
the earliest detailed picture of South Indian society, economy and polity

src: Sources: CDI (Block02 Sangam Age - sources, literature, post-Sangam works); UPSC (Ancient History pp.130-131, 135); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.28, 47); APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Satavahana - literary sources on trade); APPCA (NextGen History CA 2026, Jun 2026); LENS Jul 2025 p.18; LENS Feb 2026 p.107

rows.title: Sangam kingdoms - Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas; Karikala, Senguttuvan, Nedunjeliyan

secs.t: Ruler → dynasty + achievement

x: Karikala Chola
won the Battle of Venni, defeating the Cheras, Pandyas and eleven chieftains.
Senguttuvan undertook a Himalayan expedition and obtained stone for the idol of Pattini or Kannagi.
Silappadikaram narrates Kovalan’s execution by the Pandya king, Kannagi’s burning of Madurai, Senguttuvan’s Himalayan expedition and his association with the Pattini cult.

secs.t: Kingdom → capital, port, emblem, river

x: The Chera emblem was the bow, the Chola emblem was the tiger, and the Pandya emblem was the fish; their associated rivers were Periyar, Kaveri and Vaigai respectively.
Chera, Chola and Pandya rulers were collectively called the
Muvendar
, meaning the three crowned kings.
The Cheras traded with Rome and are said to have built a temple of Augustus near Muziris.

secs.t: Polity terms → meaning; assemblies, ministers, army

x: Ko, Kon, Mannan and Vendan were terms used for the
king
Aimperunkulu was a
five-member advisory body
consisting of ministers, priests, commanders, envoys and spies.
Avai was the royal court, in which poets were also present.
Army commanders bore the title
Enadi
Sangam polity was a hereditary monarchy with subordinate chieftains, and the Velir were minor hill or forest chieftains.

secs.t: Battles → victor

x: At Vahaipparandalai,
nine chieftains submitted to Karikala
Nedunjeliyan of the Pandyas won at Talaiyalanganam and gained control over the Tamil country.

secs.t: Kallanai (Grand Anicut) - river, builder

x: Kallanai was constructed across the Kaveri and is attributed to Karikala Chola.
The remains were found in the Kollidam, a distributary of the Kaveri that branches off at the Upper Anicut or Mukkombu.

secs.t: Pattini cult - founder ruler

x: The Pattini cult centred on Kannagi, regarded as the
ideal wife
The Sri Lankan king Gajabahu is said to have attended the consecration of the Pattini idol.

secs.t: Chieftains - velir, the seven patrons

x: Nalli was one of the seven great patrons, not a minister of Aimperunkulu.
The Kadai ezhu vallals were
Pari, Kari, Ori, Pegan, Ay, Athiyaman and Nalli

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The seal shows the
Chola tiger with the Pandya two fish and the Chera bow
, marking Chola victory over both the Pandyas and Cheras.
The Leiden copper plates record Chola grants to the
Chulamanivarma vihara at Nagapattinam
Rivalry among the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, together with Roman trade, shaped early Tamil political organisation.
The Renati, Pottapi and Nellore Choda families claimed descent from
Karikala Chola

src: Sources: UPSC (Ancient History pp.135-136); CDI (Block02 Sangam Age - political organisation); IYB 2026 p.627; CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.150); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Telugu Chodas); APPCA (NextGen History CA 2026, Jun 2026); LENSD 15 Aug 2026; TH 18 May 2026

rows.title: Sangam society and economy - tinai concept, Indo-Roman trade, ports, religion; the Kalabhra interregnum

secs.t: Social groups → occupation/status (vellalar, arasar, vanigar, panar, parayar, kadaisiyar)

x: Exam angle: "Vellalars were rich peasants who formed the fourth caste"; distractors were poets, labourers and forest tribes.
The Tolkappiyam lists Arasar, Anthanar, Vanigar and Vellalar, with Vellalar as the fourth group.
Brahmins were present and respected, but the rigid varna system had not fully developed and social mobility was possible.

secs.t: Ports → kingdom + coast + classical names (Muziris, Korkai, Puhar/Kaveripattinam, Tondi, Arikamedu, Uraiyur)

x: Exam angle: Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were
ports
Korkai was a Pandya port on the east coast, noted for pearl fishing and the export of pearls and shells.
Puhar or Kaveripattinam was a Chola east-coast port where cotton, muslin and silk were traded and a Yavana quarter prospered.
Tamil ports traded with
Berenike and Myos Hormos
on the Egyptian Red Sea coast.

secs.t: Indo-Roman trade - items traded (Yavanapriya), amphorae, Roman coin hoards, embassies to Rome, Arikamedu excavations

x: Sweet wine
, gold and horses were among the imports from the Roman world, while muslin, ivory and precious stones were exports.
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, composed around 60 CE, is attributed to
an anonymous Greek merchant
and is a major source for Indo-Roman trade.
Tamil-Brahmi potsherds have been found at
Berenike, Quseir al-Qadim and the Valley of the Kings
in Egypt.

secs.t: Sangam customs and terms → meaning (vattakirutal, kalavu, karpu, uzhavar)

x: Kalavu denotes
pre-marital or secret love
, whereas Karpu denotes married life or wedded chastity.
Nadukal was a hero stone erected for a warrior who died in battle.

secs.t: Five tinais → landscape, occupation, deity

x: Marutam was associated with agriculture in riverine plains.
Neidal represented the coastal landscape and was associated with fishing and salt making; its deity was Varunan.
Murugan belongs to Kurinji, Mayon to Mullai, Vendan to Marutam and Varunan to Neidal.
The Tolkappiyam gives the five-fold division, including Kurinji, Mullai and Palai with their respective landscapes and deities.

secs.t: Religion - Murugan, Mayon, Korravai, hero stones (nadukal)

x: Seyon, identified with Murugan, was regarded as the chief Tamil deity in the Sangam tradition.
Murugan's six sacred abodes are known collectively as
Arupadai Veedu
Nadukal were set up for warriors who fell in battle and could contain carvings of their deeds and inscriptions.
Megalithic cist burials and urn burials are associated with the funerary practices referred to in this context.

secs.t: Women - poetesses (Avvaiyar etc.), sati, dancers

x: Avvaiyar, Nachchellaiyar and Kakkaipadiniyar are identified as women poets of Sangam literature.
Sati was practised in the upper strata, while widows led a hard life.
Viraliyar were dancers who performed at courts and received patronage from kings and nobles.

secs.t: Kalabhras - period, religious leanings, dark age debate, end

x: The period was called a dark age because later Brahmanical records depicted the Kalabhras negatively and surviving sources are scarce.
The newer view regards the Kalabhra period not simply as a dark age, but as a period marked by Jain-Buddhist literary activity.
The Kalabhra interregnum ended in the late sixth century through the efforts of the Pandya ruler Kadungon and the Pallava ruler Simhavishnu.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Roman coins have been found at Attirala in Kadapa, Salihundam in Srikakulam, Vijayawada, Vinukonda, Nagarjunakonda and Nellore; Kudali Sangameswaram also yielded a coin of Constantine.
Indo-Roman trade reached its peak during the Satavahana-Sangam age, from approximately the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE, and did not flourish after the Satavahanas.

rows.title: Gupta Empire - sources, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and the Allahabad Prasasti (Harishena)
sub: Group-II S1-23: Gupta Empire - sources, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II

secs.t: Titles and epithets → ruler (Kaviraja, Vikramaditya, Maharajadhiraja, Lichchhavi-dauhitra, Prithivyah Pratham Veer, Napoleon of India)

x: Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha used ‘Maharaja’, Chandragupta I first adopted ‘Maharajadhiraja’, and Kumaragupta I bore the title ‘Mahendraditya’.
Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka were imperial titles associated with the Gupta tradition. ‘
Dharmamahamatra
’ was an administrative designation associated with the Mauryan period, not a common Gupta imperial title.

secs.t: Samudragupta's campaigns - north vs south policy, southern kings defeated → kingdom (Vishnugopa, Hastivarman, Mahendra, Swamidatta), outcomes

x: Samudragupta followed the policy of grahana-moksha-anugraha in the south: the rulers were captured, released and restored as tributaries rather than being permanently annexed.
Samudragupta annexed territory in the north, restored southern rulers as tributaries, received tribute from frontier rulers and subdued forest kingdoms.
Mahendra was associated with Kosala, Vishnugopa with Kanchi, Hastivarman with Vengi and Swamidatta with Kottura.
The Allahabad Prasasti refers to
twelve
southern kings who were defeated and subsequently released and reinstated as tributaries.
Samudragupta performed an
Ashvamedha
to celebrate his military achievements and also issued Ashvamedha coins.
Some coins of Samudragupta depict him playing the veena, reflecting his association with music and culture.

secs.t: Allahabad Prasasti - author and his other works, language, other rulers' inscriptions on the same pillar

x: The Allahabad or Prayaga Prasasti is a
Sanskrit
eulogy of Samudragupta’s conquests.
The pillar bearing the Allahabad Prasasti also carries an inscription of Jahangir, along with Ashoka’s edicts and the Queen’s edict.
The Allahabad Prasasti celebrates Samudragupta’s military conquests, while Ashoka’s inscriptions on the same pillar convey a message associated with peace and dhamma.

secs.t: Chandragupta I - marriage alliance, era started, first Gupta coins, queens of Gupta kings

x: Exam angle: king-queen matching (UPPSC 2019: 3-1-2-4).
Chandragupta I
, who ruled approximately from 319 to 335 CE, is regarded as the real founder of the Gupta Empire.
Chandragupta I ruled South Bihar and parts of eastern Uttar Pradesh, including Saketa and Prayaga, with Pataliputra as his capital.
Kumaradevi was the queen of Chandragupta I. Duttadevi, Kuberanaga and Anantadevi were associated with Samudragupta, Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I respectively.
The first Gupta gold coins issued by Chandragupta I are the
King-Queen type
, depicting Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi in association with the Lichchhavis.

secs.t: Foreign contacts - Sri Lankan embassy to the Gupta court

x: Meghavarman, the Buddhist ruler of Sri Lanka, sent a mission to Samudragupta for permission to build a monastery and rest house at Bodh Gaya.
The mission of Meghavarman and the request concerning Bodh Gaya are recorded in
a Chinese source
Kushanas and Sakas paid homage, while rulers of Southeast Asia and Ceylon sent tribute.

secs.t: Gupta origin debate - caste, original home

x: The Guptas are described as originally Vaishyas who were later treated as Kshatriyas by Brahmanas; a Brahmana origin has also been proposed on the basis of the Dharana gotra.
Sri Gupta is stated to have ruled a small part of
North Bengal and South Bihar
The early Gupta territory was centred on
Magadha, Prayaga and eastern Uttar Pradesh

secs.t: Sources - inscriptions (Allahabad, Eran, Mehrauli, Bhitari, Junagadh of Skandagupta), coins, Puranas, Devichandraguptam

x: Parnadatta
, the governor of Skandagupta, was responsible for the repair of the Sudarshana lake, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription.
Devichandraguptam narrates the episode involving
Ramagupta, Dhruvadevi and Chandragupta II
Gupta coins, mostly gold, depict rulers, deities and rituals and thereby reveal royal titles, religious ideas, ritual practices and the prosperity of the period.

secs.t: Samudragupta's coins - types (lyrist, ashvamedha, archer)

x: The
lyrist or veena-player type
depicts Samudragupta as a poet-musician and supports the association of the title Kaviraja with him.
Samudragupta issued the Ashvamedha type after performing the Ashvamedha, or horse sacrifice.
The
King-Queen type
belongs to the coinage of Chandragupta I, whereas Samudragupta issued lyrist, Ashvamedha and archer types among others.

secs.t: Inscription → ruler + composer

x: Harishena
, the court poet of Samudragupta, composed the Allahabad Pillar inscription in Sanskrit on an Ashokan pillar.
The later record at Eran belongs to Bhanugupta and is dated to 510 CE.
The Mandsaur record belongs to the period of Kumaragupta I, under the feudatory Bandhuvarman, and was composed by Vatsabhatti.
The Bhitari inscription of Skandagupta records the
repulse of the Hunas

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The inscription is a chief source for information about the fourth-century Andhra regions and rulers of
Vengi, Pishtapura, Avamukta and Devarashtra
The Allahabad Pillar records Samudragupta’s conquests, while the Bhitari inscription records Skandagupta’s repulse of the Hunas.
Samudragupta is regarded as the greatest Gupta ruler because of the extensive conquests and political influence described in the Allahabad Prashasti.

rows.title: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, Kumaragupta, Skandagupta; the Hunas and Gupta decline
sub: Group-II S1-29: Decline of the Guptas; the Huna invasions

secs.t: Chronological order of Gupta rulers (Chandragupta I to Vishnugupta)

x: Exam angle: Samudragupta → Chandragupta II → Kumaragupta I → Skandagupta.
Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2018 answer - Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I, Skandagupta.
The Kali Era begins traditionally in 3102 BC, the Saka Era in 78 CE, and the Gupta Era is associated with Chandragupta I. Vikrama Samvat is traditionally associated with Vikramaditya, not Kanishka.

secs.t: Chandragupta II - titles and other names, Saka conquest evidence, silver coins, matrimonial alliances, Fa-Hien's visit, Navaratnas

x: Chandragupta II defeated the Saka ruler Rudrasimha III and annexed western Malwa and Gujarat, thereby reaching the western sea.
Chandragupta II married Kuberanaga, a Naga princess; his daughter Prabhavati married Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II; Dhruvadevi was married after Ramagupta’s killing.
Prabhavati Gupta’s marriage to Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II enabled Chandragupta II to exercise indirect control over the Vakataka kingdom.

secs.t: Huna invasions → Huna leader + Gupta reign invaded + Indian ruler who repelled each (Toramana, Mihirakula)

x: Exam angle: Kumaragupta I = first attack; Skandagupta = repulsed; Yashodharman = defeated Mihirakula.
Toramana occupied large parts of western and central India, while Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman, Narasimhagupta Baladitya and the Maukharis.

The Saka conquest of Chandragupta II preceded the first Huna attack in late Kumaragupta I’s reign; later Huna waves occurred under Skandagupta, followed by Toramana’s advance under the weaker successors.

secs.t: Skandagupta - invasions faced, inscriptions (Bhitari, Junagadh)

x: Skandagupta faced the Pushyamitras, particularly at the end of Kumaragupta’s reign, and the Hunas during his own reign.
The Bhitari pillar is located at Ghazipur in Uttar Pradesh and records Skandagupta’s victories over the Pushyamitras and Hunas.
Skandagupta’s gold coins depict him with
a bow and arrow, the Garuda standard and Lakshmi

secs.t: Ramagupta episode - source text, succession dispute

x: The Ramagupta episode is narrated in
Devichandraguptam
, attributed to Vishakhadatta.

All three statements describe the traditional Ramagupta episode: the elder brother agreed to surrender Dhruvadevi, after which Chandragupta II killed the Saka king, killed Ramagupta and married Dhruvadevi.

secs.t: Successor powers - Maukharis, Later Guptas, Maitrakas, Pushyabhutis, Aulikaras (Mandsaur prashasti)

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
The Later Guptas were associated with Magadha, the Maitrakas with Valabhi, the Pushyabhutis with Thanesar and later Kannauj, and the Aulikaras with Mandsaur.
The Maukharis, Maitrakas and Pushyabhutis were included.
Both groups of inscriptions come from the Aulikara area centred on Mandsaur in Malwa.
All four combinations are correct.

secs.t: Causes of Gupta decline - external, feudatory and economic explanations

x: Repeated Huna invasions
were an external cause of Gupta decline.
Hereditary governors contributed to the growth of autonomous feudatories rather than strengthening centralised imperial control.
Both statements are true, and the reduction of state revenue through land grants directly weakened the state's ability to maintain a professional army.
Vishnugupta
is identified as the last Gupta ruler, with his reign placed approximately between 540 and 550 CE.

secs.t: Kumaragupta I - institutions founded, threats faced, coins

x: Kumaragupta I was associated with Kartikeya worship, performed an Ashvamedha, issued relevant gold coin types and faced the Pushyamitras and the first Huna attack.
Kumaragupta I
issued new gold coin types showing Kartikeya and the king feeding a peacock.
All four are associated with Kumaragupta I. The Damodarpur copper plates are also notable for indicating guilds acting as banks.

secs.t: Yashodharman of Mandasor - role against the Hunas

x: Yashodharman was a
Gupta feudatory
in Malwa.
Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani are dated to approximately
532 CE
Yashodharman's victory did not revive the Gupta Empire; his own rise as a regional power undermined Gupta authority and reflected the wider process of political fragmentation.

secs.t: Inscriptions on the Hunas

x: The Eran boar inscription was built in Toramana's first regnal year and records Huna rule over Eran.
The Eran source refers to governors called Lokapala, the Bhitari pillar records Skandagupta's defeat of the Hunas, and the Junagadh inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.
The Eran inscription of Bhanugupta is dated to
510 CE
and is regarded as the earliest sati record mentioned here.

secs.t: Coinage debasement as evidence

x: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions after Skandagupta in western Malwa and Saurashtra is evidence that these areas were no longer under effective Gupta control.

secs.t: Rise of regional kingdoms

x: The Vakatakas were associated with northern Maharashtra and Vidarbha, and Harishena patronised Ajanta.
The Vakatakas were Brahmins, successors of the Satavahanas, contemporaries of the Guptas, and Rudrasena II married Prabhavati Gupta.
Madhava Varma II was the greatest Vishnukundin ruler, ruled around 440–495 CE, won over 100 battles and performed 11 Ashvamedhas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The break-up of Gupta authority marked a movement from a single empire to regional kingdoms and a more feudal political order.
The Kushans declined under pressure from the Sasanians together with the rise of an Indian power, while the Guptas similarly faced external invasions and the rise of regional powers.

rows.title: Gupta administration - feudalism debate, land grants, agraharas, revenue and local bodies
sub: Group-II S1-24: Gupta administration, land grants, revenue and the feudalism debate

secs.t: Land grants and agrarian structure - brahmadeya, agrahara, devagrahara, grantees, effects on tribal frontiers and peasantry

x: Brahmadeya was granted to Brahmanas singly or collectively, agrahara was tax-free land or a village given to Brahmanas, devagrahara was assigned to temples and monasteries, and secular grants went to officials or feudatories in lieu of salary.
Nivi dharma meant a trust, nivi dharma akshayana a perpetual endowment, aprada dharma enjoyment of income without alienation, and bhumichchhidranyaya ownership by the first reclaimer of waste land.

secs.t: Revenue and land terms → meaning (bhaga, bhoga, udranga, uparikara, halivakara, vishti, aprahata, kuliyavapa, dronavapa) - prescribed revenue share

x: Exam angle: Kuliyavapa and Dronavapa = land measurement.
Bhoga consisted of periodic supplies in kind, including fruits, firewood and flowers, made to the king.
Kshetra meant cultivable land, khila meant waste land, and vastu meant habitable land.
The law books prescribe one-sixth, while different references mention one-seventh or a range from one-fourth to one-sixth.

secs.t: Indian feudalism debate → historian (R.S. Sharma, D.C. Sircar, Harbans Mukhia, B.D. Chattopadhyaya) - essential elements, origin explanations

x: R.S. Sharma
argued that Indian feudalism crystallised through land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade and urban decay.
The evidence cited included the seventh-century
decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage
, shrinking towns and a closed village economy.
The essential elements are power based on control of land, lord–vassal ties and weak central authority.

secs.t: Administrative units → order + officer (bhukti, vishaya, vithi, grama)

x: The Vithi, particularly in eastern India, was associated with the Ayuktaka and other officials.
Bhukti was the provincial unit, Vishaya the district, Vithi a group of villages, and Grama the village unit.
The village headman’s consent was required for land transactions, indicating a role for local village authority.

secs.t: Nature of Gupta kingship - divine claims, centralisation vs decentralisation

x: Gupta rulers used the exalted titles Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka and made divine claims about kingship.
Samudragupta was equated with Kubera or Dhanada, Varuna, Indra and Yama or Antaka.
Gupta kingship was hereditary, but there was no firm rule of primogeniture.
Gupta administration relied substantially on feudatories and grantees, and it was considerably less centralised than Mauryan administration.

secs.t: Officials → function (kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika, mahadandanayaka, dandapashika)

x: The
Sandhivigrahika
was the minister responsible for peace and war.
The Dandapashika was the district police officer.
Kumaramatyas were senior or high-cadre officers, ranked with princes; ministers and commanders were chosen from them.
The
Akshapataladhikrita
kept royal records, whereas the Pustapala was the keeper of land-transfer records.

secs.t: Town administration → profession/rank (nagarashreshthi, sarthavaha, prathama kulika, prathama kayastha)

x: Exam angle: "Kayastha" = scribes.
The
Prathama kulika
represented the chief artisans or craft guilds on the town board.
The
Nagarashreshthi
, the chief banker or merchant, served as chairman of the town council or adhikarana.
Kayasthas were associated with scribal and official work; the Prathama kayastha represented the chief scribes on the town board.

secs.t: Judicial system - law books of the period (Narada, Brihaspati, Katyayana)

x: The period witnessed a clearer distinction between civil and criminal law; theft and adultery were criminal matters, while property disputes were civil matters.
Both statements are true, and the varna-based hierarchy explains why legal treatment was not uniform for all persons.

secs.t: Land types and measures

x: Kshetra means cultivated or fertile land, Khila means untilled waste land, Vastu means habitable house-site land, and Aprahata denotes uncultivated forest land in this classification.
Kulyavapa and Dronavapa were measures of land area, defined by the area that could be sown with one kulya and one drona of seed respectively.

secs.t: Vishti and peasant condition

x: Vishti was unpaid forced labour performed for the state or for the recipient of a land grant; in Telugu usage it is associated with vetti.
Peasant dependence was reflected in semi-servile status, tenant farming, sharecropping, tenancy at will and the burden of many taxes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The debate centres on R. S. Sharma’s land-grant thesis and the criticism that the absence of serfdom makes the European model of feudalism unsuitable or limited for India.
Satavahana and Ikshvaku brahmadeya grants barred royal officials from interfering in the granted areas.
Both statements are true, and the analytical significance of land grants in studying intermediaries and agrarian dependence explains their central place in the feudalism debate.

Sources: Group-II S1-24: CDI (Block02 The Guptas - administrative system, agrarian structure, taxation; Block01 Kushans Sunga Kanauj Contributions); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Gupta Political Organisation; Gupta-Era Terminology; Gupta Society; Harshavardhana and Post-Gupta Key Terms); UPSC (Ancient History p.115); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.35, 44, 73, 124)

rows.title: Gupta society and economy - varna and jati, position of women, Fa-Hien's account, trade decline
sub: Group-II S1-25: Gupta socio-economic conditions - Fa-Hien's account, trade, caste and women

secs.t: Trade decline - collapse of Roman trade, shift to Southeast Asian trade, urban decay debate, timing of decline

x: Exam angle: statement-type questions on the post-Gupta decline of trade and towns.
R. S. Sharma’s urban decay interpretation links the shrinking of commercial towns with rural self-sufficiency and scarcity of gold coins.
Sanghol, Hastinapur, Mathura, Shravasti and Kaushambi are identified as sites showing decline;
Pataliputra
is not included in this list.

Eastern Roman trade continued until about 550 CE; decline became visible in the post-Gupta period, stagnation is associated with c. 750–1000 CE, and recovery came with the Arab empire from the 10th century.

secs.t: Guilds and merchants - rule-making, banking functions, military role, autonomy, guild inscriptions → content (Dashpur/Mandsaur, Indore copper plate)

x: Exam angle: MPPSC 2024 and 2021 - Dashpur = first advertisement; composer is not "Bhava".
Exam angle: "NOT a feature of guilds" - the wrong option is always "non-autonomous bodies".
Guilds undertook charitable activities such as constructing temples, rest houses, assembly halls and gardens;
appointment of provincial governors
was not their function.
The Dashpur inscription concerns the silk-weavers’ guild and Sun temple; the Indore copper plate concerns the oil-men’s guild and temple lamp; the Damodarpur plates describe banking functions.

secs.t: Ports → region (Tamralipti, Bharuch, Kalyan, Ghantasala, Kadura, Chaul)

x: Tamralipti
, identified with Tamluk, was the chief eastern port in Bengal.
Bharuch or Barygaza was situated in
Gujarat
and was the largest port on the west coast.
Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul handled foreign trade, and Bharuch was the largest west-coast port.
Silk from China
was imported, whereas textiles, gems and spices were among the exports.

secs.t: Coinage - gold, silver and copper coin names, quality over time

x: The Gupta gold coins were called
dinaras
, and the Guptas issued them in the largest numbers.
Copper issues were few, later dinaras contained less gold, gold coins became scarce after the Gupta period, and cowries were used for ordinary exchange.
Later Gupta gold coins show debasement: their gold content declined and the proportion of alloy increased.

secs.t: Position of women - earliest sati inscription, child marriage, property rights, education

x: Women were generally denied education.
Women generally had no property rights, but they could control stridhana, consisting of marriage gifts.
The evidence indicates the absence of purdah rather than its general prevalence.

secs.t: Fa-Hien - route, ruler visited, observations on society, hospitals, Chandalas, administration

x: Fa-Hien travelled overland through Central Asia and Gandhara and returned by sea through Sri Lanka, including the port of Tamralipti on his return route.
Fa-Hien records that persistent rebellion could be punished by
cutting off the right hand
, although ordinary crimes were generally dealt with through fines.
Fa-Hien observed that the general population avoided meat, onion, garlic and liquor, whereas the Chandalas lived outside settlements and announced their approach by striking wood.

secs.t: Craft production centres → region (textiles, gems, handicrafts)

x: Silk weaving flourished in Lata in Gujarat until
the weavers moved to Mandsaur in Malwa
The Mehrauli pillar is associated with rust-free iron metallurgy, not silk weaving.
Gems, spices and textiles
were the main exports.
Silk weaving was practised in Lata and Malwa, Indian muslin was valued in Rome, and silk was imported from China.

secs.t: Varna and jati - new castes (Kayasthas), Chandalas, varna-jati relationship

x: Both statements are true, and the absorption of foreigners and tribes through land-grant processes explains the multiplication of jatis.
Chandalas were outside the four-varna order and lived outside settlements; untouchability intensified in relation to them.
Brahmanas
received brahmadeya land grants, which also strengthened their position in the social and agrarian order.

secs.t: Agriculture - Brihaspati/Amarasimha land types, irrigation (Sudarshana lake)

x: Urvara means fertile, usara barren, maru desert, and aprahata fallow land.
All four pairs are correctly matched in the glossary: kshetra was cultivable, khila waste, aprahata forest or uncultivated, and vastu habitable land.
The lake was first built by Pushyagupta under Chandragupta Maurya, repaired by Rudradaman, and repaired again under Skandagupta by Parnadatta.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Odisha's Baliyatra festival honours
Sadhaba mariners who sailed to Southeast Asia
Ghantasala and Kadura in Krishna district were Andhra's east-coast ports, while the Satavahana weavers' guild was known as Kolika Shreni.
Peasant obligations, including vishti or forced labour, formed the basis of
the urban decay and feudalism critique
of the Gupta economy.

rows.title: Gupta religion - Bhagavatism, Vaishnavism, Saivism; beginnings of temple architecture (Deogarh, Bhitargaon)
sub: Group-II S1-26: Gupta religious conditions - Vaishnavism, Saivism, Buddhism and Jainism

secs.t: Saivism and Shaktism - sects and their offshoots (Pashupata, Kapalika, Kalamukha), Shiva linga forms → earliest example site (Gudimallam)

x: Exam angle: both APPSC Kapalika keys exist - read the options (Pashupata vs Misra).
Shaktism involves the worship of mother goddesses such as
Durga, Amba, Kali and Chandi
The
linga, trident and bull
appeared as sectarian symbols on Gupta coins and seals.
Ekamukhalinga, showing one face of Shiva, is exemplified by
Udayagiri Cave 4 and Khoh
in Madhya Pradesh.

secs.t: Puranas - total number, composition period, principal Puranas

x: The Puranas were compiled over several centuries and received their final shape during the Gupta period, approximately the 4th to 6th centuries CE.
Arthashastra Purana
is not included in that list.
The pancha-lakshana of the Puranas consists of
creation, re-creation, genealogies, manvantaras and dynastic history

secs.t: Bhagavatism - originator, earliest worshippers of Vasudeva-Krishna, avatara concept, foreign patrons, Heliodorus pillar link

x: The Pancharatras were also called
Bhagavatas or Sattvatas
and formed part of the devotional tradition centred on Vasudeva-Krishna.
Bhagavatism preached
the avatara theory
of Vishnu, according to which Vishnu manifests in different forms.
The pillar at Besnagar was dedicated to Vasudeva, associated with Garuda, and was erected by Heliodorus, who identified himself as a Bhagavata, during the court of Bhagabhadra.

secs.t: Gupta royal religion - religious titles → first ruler to assume (Parama Bhagavata), dynastic emblem

x: Chandragupta II
is credited with being the first Gupta ruler to assume the title ‘Parama Bhagavata’, signifying devotion to Vishnu.
Coins of
Skandagupta
carry the Garuda standard, which was the Gupta royal emblem.
The Guptas patronised Bhagavatism, but Samudragupta also permitted Meghavarman to establish a monastery at Bodh Gaya.
Gupta Bhagavatism was based on
Karma, Bhakti and Ahimsa

secs.t: Temple plans and stages of evolution - Panchayatana layout, flat roof, shikhara beginnings, garbhagriha, mandapa

x: The architectural sequence was first-stage Sanchi and Tigawa, second-stage Nachna and Bhumara, and third-stage Deogarh and Bhitargaon.
The first stage, represented by Sanchi Temple 17 and Tigawa, had a square sanctum, flat roof, shallow four-pillared portico and low platform.
The third stage, represented by Deogarh and Bhitargaon, saw the disappearance of the flat roof, the emergence of a low square shikhara and the Panchayatana plan.

secs.t: Varaha panel at Udayagiri - ruler commemorated

x: The colossal Varaha panel at Udayagiri was carved under
Chandragupta II
, and the cave functioned as his personal temple.
The Varaha incarnation is shown lifting the earth from the sea or cosmic waters.

secs.t: Buddhism and Jainism under the Guptas - patronage evidence

x: Udayagiri in Madhya Pradesh has one Jain cave among its twenty caves, along with important Hindu religious sculpture.
Asanga was a Yogachara teacher, Vasubandhu wrote the Abhidharmakosa, Dinnaga founded Buddhist logic and Buddhaghosa wrote the Visuddhimagga.
Fa-Hien saw both Mahayana and Hinayana Buddhism active, but noted decay at Kapilavastu, Gaya and Kushinagar.
Buddhism lost royal patronage during the period, and the Huna ruler Mihirakula persecuted Buddhists.

secs.t: Puranic Hinduism - Puranas, idol worship, temple rituals

x: Hinduism became increasingly theistic and devotional, while temple-based idol worship became common and the earlier dominance of sacrificial Brahmanism declined.
The four Purusharthas are Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha.

secs.t: Religion → founder, text, symbol, centre

x: Exam angle: APPSC G2 2025 match - Jainism-Triratna, Buddhism-Ashtanga Margam, Saivism-Linga, Animism-Nature worship.
Jainism is associated with Mahavira and the Agamas, Buddhism with Gautama Buddha and the Tripitaka, Ajivika with Makkhali Gosala, and Saivism with the Linga.
Jainism is associated with Triratna, Buddhism with Ashtanga Marga, Vaishnavism with chakra, shankha and Garuda, and Saivism with the linga.

secs.t: Jainism under the Guptas - Vallabhi council, Mathura school

x: The Vallabhi council was held under
Devarddhi Kshamashramana
and resulted in the compilation of the Svetambara canon.
Mathura
was a major centre of Jain art, particularly for Tirthankara images.
Udayagiri has one Jain cave among its twenty caves, and Fa-Hien mentions Jainism.

secs.t: Religious tolerance - Buddhist and Jain gifts in Gupta records

x: The Sanchi inscription of Chandragupta II’s officer Amrakardava records a grant to a Buddhist vihara, demonstrating tolerance toward another faith.
The Kahaum pillar inscription of the Skandagupta period records Jain images, providing evidence of the continued presence and acceptance of Jainism.
Fa-Hien noted cordial Hindu-Buddhist relations during the Gupta period, despite observing decay at certain Buddhist centres.

secs.t: Shakti and Surya worship

x: Durga, Amba, Kali and Chandi
were worshipped as mother goddesses.
Gaja-Lakshmi
appears on seals, indicating the early presence of goddess and fertility-related worship.
Tantrism spread from the fifth century, emphasised ritual and feminine energy, admitted women and Shudras, and affected all four named religious traditions.
Surya and Shakti worship already appear in Hala’s Gathasaptasati.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Gupta age witnessed the standardisation of the iconography of Brahmanical, Jain and Buddhist deities.
Sirpur was the capital of Dakshina Kosala, flourished from the fifth to the twelfth century, accommodated four religious traditions, and has an approximately sixth-century brick Lakshmana temple.
The Salankayanas followed Vaishnavism, but their rulers also used Shaiva titles such as Parama Mahesvara.

rows.title: Gupta art, literature, science and technology - Kalidasa, Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Ajanta, Mehrauli pillar
sub: Group-II S1-27: Gupta art and architecture - temples, Ajanta, sculpture and coins
Group-II S1-28: Gupta literature, science and technology - Kalidasa, Aryabhata, Varahamihira

secs.t: Literary work → author (Kalidasa vs wrongly attributed works; Mudrarakshasa, Mrichchhakatika, Amarakosha, Panchatantra, Nitisara, Kamasutra, Bhasa)

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT by Kalidasa" - Mudrarakshasa, Mrichchhakatika, Kiratarjuniya are the usual distractors.
Devichandraguptam is attributed to
Vishakhadatta
and deals with events connected with Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi.
Hitopadesha is a later work based on the Panchatantra, while Bhasa predates Kalidasa and Charudatta is his best-known play in this context.
Naishadhiyacharita was composed by
Sriharsha
and deals with the story of Nala and Damayanti.
Kamandaka's
Nitisara
is identified as a Gupta-age treatise on polity.

secs.t: Scientists → field + contribution (Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Brahmagupta, Bhaskara I and II, Charaka, Dhanvantari)

x: Aryabhata stated that the Earth rotates on its axis, described it as spherical and gave scientific explanations for eclipses.
Aryabhata is noted for calculating an accurate value of pi, besides his work on place value and zero.
Brahmagupta formulated rules of arithmetic involving
zero and negative quantities
Bhaskara I wrote a commentary on
Aryabhatiya
and helped spread Aryabhata's school of astronomy.
Bhaskara I is associated with writing numbers in decimal place-value notation and using a circle for zero in 629 CE.
Bhaskara II belonged to the twelfth century and authored Siddhanta Shiromani, in addition to Lilavati.
Aryabhata is regarded as the first Indian scholar to treat mathematics as a distinct subject; Aryabhatiya contains a separate Ganitapada.

secs.t: Ajanta and Bagh paintings - religion, patrons, Jataka panels, famous panels, technique

x: The Ajanta caves were recorded by the British officer John Smith in 1819 while he was hunting tigers.
Ajanta has about 30 caves; Caves 9 and 10 contain the earliest paintings, and the later phase received Vakataka patronage under Harishena.
Ajanta contains themes from Jataka tales, secular life, Bodhi-tree worship and group dances.
Ajanta paintings were executed mainly in tempera on dry lime plaster, known as fresco secco, rather than true fresco on wet plaster.
Ajanta was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, among the early Indian sites to receive that status.
The Satavahana-era paintings came first, followed by the Vakataka phase, John Smith's recording in 1819, and UNESCO inscription in 1983.

secs.t: Astronomy and mathematics texts → author + subject + foreign influence

x: Panchasiddhantika summarises
five
siddhantas: Surya, Romaka, Paulisa, Vasishtha and Paitamaha.
Romaka Siddhanta is an astronomical work summarised by Varahamihira and reflects Roman-Greek influence, comparable to the Paulisa tradition.
Aryabhata gave the value of pi as approximately 3.1416 and explained the apparent motion of the heavens through the Earth's rotation on its axis.

secs.t: Place-value and decimal system - earliest use, zero, mathematician credited

x: The earliest epigraphic use of the place-value system is associated with the
Mankani plates of Gujarat, dated to AD 595–596
The Sankheda copper plate, dated 594 CE, is associated with an early dated epigraphic use of a place-value numeral.
Arab contact
carried the Indian decimal place-value notation to the Islamic world and subsequently to Europe.

secs.t: Navaratnas of Chandragupta II - names and field

x: Amarasimha is remembered as a lexicographer, especially for the Amarakosha.
The Navaratna list is a traditional association.
Chandragupta II ruled approximately from 380 to 413 CE, whereas Varahamihira lived around 505–587 CE; therefore, he lived later.
The sequence follows the fields as stated: poetry and drama, lexicography, astronomy and astrology, and Ayurveda.

secs.t: Mehrauli iron pillar - location, ruler, metallurgy

x: The inscription refers to the ruler as ‘
Chandra
’, generally identified with Chandragupta II.
The pillar is now at Mehrauli, was originally erected at Udayagiri near Vidisha, and its inscription records victories or authority in the North-West and Bengal.
The high-phosphorus iron is associated with the formation of a protective layer, helping the pillar resist corrosion for more than fifteen centuries.

secs.t: Sculpture - Sarnath, Mathura, Sultanganj Buddhas

x: Sarnath sculpture used polished Chunar buff sandstone and generally avoided heavy ornamentation.
The seated Buddha at Sarnath is characteristically shown in the
Dharmachakra mudra
, symbolising the turning of the wheel of the Dharma.
The Mathura tradition continued during the Gupta period, acquiring greater elegance and softness, and Gupta stone sculpture belongs to the Mathura school.

secs.t: Gupta temples → place + material

x: Bhitargaon = 5th-6th c. brick temple (UPPSC 2021, both statements true).
Bhitargaon in Kanpur district is a Brahmanical brick temple of the 5th–6th century CE and is noted for its terracotta panels.
The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh comprise twenty caves, including nineteen Hindu and one Jain cave, with Varaha and Shiva representations.
Sanchi 17 has a flat roof and four-pillar porch; Nachna has a covered ambulatory; Bhumara has flanking shrines; and Deogarh has a shikhara with a panchayatana plan.
Stage 1 had a square sanctum and flat roof; Stage 2 introduced the covered ambulatory and raised platform; Stage 3 developed the low square shikhara and high platform.

secs.t: Gupta coinage - dinara, silver after Saka conquest, coin types

x: The silver coins introduced after the Saka conquest were modelled on
Saka silver issues
The king-queen type belongs to Chandragupta I; tiger-slayer to Samudragupta; lion-slayer to Chandragupta II; and Garuda standard to Skandagupta.
Kumaragupta I issued coins depicting Kartikeya or the king feeding a peacock, as well as Ashvamedha coins.

secs.t: Bagh and other caves - Hallisaka, Udayagiri Varaha, Buddhist caves

x: The Bagh caves in Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh comprise nine Buddhist viharas, generally dated to the fifth–sixth centuries CE, and their paintings include secular and local themes.
The Hallisaka painting at Bagh is known for depicting
a joyous folk dance
The colossal Varaha at Udayagiri is a panel of Vishnu’s boar incarnation and reflects the Vaishnava orientation of the site.

secs.t: Classical age label - justification and criticism

x: All four developments are cited as grounds for regarding the Gupta period as a classical age.
All four conditions are cited as limitations of the Golden Age label.
The criticism highlights rigid caste distinctions, forced labour, declining trade and towns, and the falling status of women, showing that benefits were unevenly distributed.

secs.t: Kalidasa - dramas vs poems, plots, wrong attributions

x: Abhijnana Shakuntalam and Vikramorvashiyam are dramas; Kumarasambhava is a Mahakavya; and Meghaduta is a lyric poem.
Malavikagnimitram portrays the love of Agnimitra, a
Shunga king of Vidisha
, and Malavika.
Shringara Shataka is attributed to Bhartrihari, not Kalidasa.
Naishadhiyacharita
was written by Sriharsha, who belongs to the post-Gupta period.

secs.t: Dramatists → works

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
The Harishena associated with Brihatkatha Kosha was a different, later Jain author.
The two Harishenas were different persons.
Dandin wrote Dasakumaracharita and Kavyadarsha, while Bhatti wrote Ravanavadha.

secs.t: Grammar and lexicon → author

x: Amarakosha was written by Amarasimha, Chandra Vyakarana by Chandragomin, Prakrit Prakasha by Vararuchi, and Katantra by Sharvavarman.
Chandragomin was a
Buddhist
grammarian of the fifth century and is associated with Chandra Vyakarana.
Katantra is attributed to
Sharvavarman
and is associated with the Satavahana age.

secs.t: Medicine and veterinary texts → author

x: Hastyayurveda is attributed to Palakapya and deals with elephant diseases.
Palakapya is associated with Hastyayurveda, a veterinary text dealing with diseases of elephants.
Ancient physicians used iron and mercury preparations, performed operations such as lithotomy, and Navanitakam was a medical manual concerning metallic preparations.
Ashtanga Sangraha and Ashtanga Hridaya are associated with Vagbhata.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The earliest Ajanta paintings belong to the Satavahana phase and show a connection with the Amaravati style.
The Undavalli caves are in Guntur on the Krishna and feature Vishnukundina adaptation of Gupta rock-cut architecture, including the five-metre reclining Ananta Padmanabha Vishnu.
The Romaka and Paulisa Siddhantas show Greek input into Indian science, challenging the view that Indian scientific development was entirely isolated.
