rows.title: Vakatakas; Harshavardhana - sources (Harshacharita, Hiuen Tsang), Kannauj and Prayag assemblies, administration
sub: Group-II S1-30: Harshavardhana - sources, rise to power and conquests
Group-II S1-31: Harsha's administration, religion, patronage and the accounts of Hiuen Tsang and Banabhatta

secs.t: Harsha's own works vs works about him (Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda, Harshacharita, Kadambari)

x: Exam angle: "not written by Harsha" =
Harshacharita
Exam angle: "Which is NOT written by Harsha?" - the answer is
Harshacharita
(by Bana) or Kadambari; Bana is paired with Harsha, not the Guptas or Kanishka.
Harshacharita, written by Banabhatta, is
a semi-historical biography of Harsha
and an important literary source for his reign.
The Madhuban plate, Sonpat seal and Banskhera inscription are all sources for Harsha's reign; the Banskhera record is noted for bearing Harsha's signature.

secs.t: Court poets → patron + work (Banabhatta, Mayura, Matanga Divakara)

x: Vakpatiraja was associated with Yashovarman of Kannauj, not Harsha's court.
Mayura
, a court poet of Harsha, composed Suryashataka, a hymn to the Sun.

secs.t: Nalanda at the time of Harsha - founder, head, curriculum, Hiuen Tsang

x: Exam angle: statement sets mixing "founded by Harsha" / "Hiuen Tsang was chancellor" with the correct one (Silabhadra).
Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I in the Gupta period, was headed by Silabhadra in Harsha's time, and was an important Mahayana centre.
Nalanda had a difficult entrance examination, used Sanskrit as the medium of instruction and encouraged debate over lectures.
Nalanda accommodated about 10,000 students with free boarding; Hiuen Tsang studied and taught there; and Harsha built a multi-storied monastery at the institution.

secs.t: Harsha - titles, capitals, conquests, conflict with Pulakesin II

x: Harsha came to power in 606 CE at the age of 16, after the death of his brother Rajyavardhana.
Harsha used the titles Siladitya and
Sakalottarapathanatha
, meaning lord of all North India.
Dhruvasena II of Valabhi was made a vassal of Harsha and married Harsha's daughter.
Pulakesin II's
Aihole inscription
records his victory over Harsha on the Narmada.
Harsha died without an heir in 647 CE, bringing the Pushyabhuti line to an end.

secs.t: Hiuen Tsang - reign, route, places, Si-Yu-Ki, observations

x: Hiuen Tsang was a Chinese Buddhist monk popularly called the ‘
Prince of Pilgrims
’; some accounts also refer to him as the ‘King of Travelers’.
Si-Yu-Ki is regarded as
the longest and most detailed account of Central and South Asia
among the works associated with Hiuen Tsang.
Hiuen Tsang described the kingdom as well governed and free from revolts, but recorded that he himself was robbed twice.
Hiuen Tsang mentioned rigid caste distinctions, untouchables, the declining position of women and the rise of Brahmanism.
Hiuen Tsang praised Harsha, Pulakesin II of the Chalukyas and Narasimhavarman of the Pallavas.

secs.t: Vakatakas - founder, branches, Prabhavatigupta, Pravarasena, Ajanta

x: Pravarasena I was Vindhyashakti’s son, the only Vakataka ruler to take the title Samrat, and performed Vajapeya and Ashvamedha sacrifices.
Prabhavatigupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, married the Vakataka ruler
Rudrasena II
Prabhavatigupta’s regency enabled the Guptas to exercise indirect control over the Deccan through the Vakataka kingdom.
Harishena patronised Ajanta
Caves 16 and 17
through his minister Varahadeva.

secs.t: Post-Gupta kingdoms and Vardhana lineage

x: The Maukharis were associated with Grahavarman, Gauda with Sasanka, Kamarupa with Bhaskaravarman and Valabhi with Dhruvasena II.
Naravardhana
is identified as the founder of the Vardhana line in the late fifth or early sixth century; Prabhakaravardhana was its first great ruler.
Prabhakaravardhana was their father, Yashomati became sati in 605 CE, and Rajyavardhana was killed by Sasanka.

secs.t: Kannauj assembly and Prayag assembly

x: The Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen Tsang and propagated Mahayana, while the Prayag assembly was primarily a charitable gathering held periodically.
The assembly honoured Hiuen Tsang, propagated Mahayana and lasted 23 days in the stated account.
The Prayag assembly was held every five years, Harsha distributed his treasury while retaining only his clothes, and Hiuen Tsang attended the sixth assembly.

secs.t: Administration - feudatories, officials, revenue, land grants

x: Hiuen Tsang described
four
divisions of revenue: the king's use or administration, public servants, scholars and religious charity.
The four parts were assigned to the king's own use or state administration, public servants, scholars and religious activities including charity to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks.
Officials were commonly remunerated through land grants rather than cash, while samantas acknowledged Harsha's authority by sending tribute.

secs.t: Capitals - Thanesar to Kannauj; Maukharis and Grahavarman

x: Thanesar was Harsha's first capital, and Kannauj was the capital of the Maukharis.
Grahavarman was a Maukhari ruler and the husband of Rajyashri.
Devagupta of Malwa
killed Grahavarman and held Rajyashri at Kannauj.

secs.t: Allies and rivals

x: Bhaskaravarman
of Kamarupa, corresponding broadly to Assam, was an ally of Harsha.
Harsha and Bhaskaravarman allied against
Shashanka
of Gauda, whose capital was Karnasuvarna.
The Harsha era began in 606 CE, Harsha came to power in the same year, his conflict with Pulakesin II occurred later, and he died in 647 CE.

secs.t: Sources → type

x: Harshacharita is a literary Sanskrit biography, Si-Yu-Ki is a foreign account, Banskhera bears Harsha's signature and the Madhuban plate is an epigraphic land-grant record useful for chronology.
Si-Yu-Ki
is Hiuen Tsang's foreign account.
The
Aihole inscription
is a Chalukyan epigraphic source recording Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha on the Narmada.

secs.t: Harsha's religion - stages and sects patronised

x: Harsha was converted to Mahayana Buddhism under the influence of
Hiuen Tsang
; the influence of his sister Rajyashri is also noted.
Harsha adopted pro-Buddhist measures such as banning animal food and punishing the killing of living beings.
Harsha supported Mahayana Buddhism through measures such as monasteries and rest houses, while continuing to patronise Brahmanical scholars.

secs.t: Hiuen Tsang's account of Andhra (An-to-lo, Dhanyakataka)

x: Hiuen Tsang referred to Andhra as An-to-lo and identified
Vengi
as its capital.
Vengi had about 20 viharas and Dhanyakataka had about 20 Mahasanghika viharas.
The account records decline at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda, degeneration of some monasteries and lack of patronage at Sriparvata.
The tradition recorded by Hiuen Tsang stated that Buddha first visited Salihundam and then Dharanikota, identified with Dhanyakataka.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Hiuen Tsang's Andhra account is the principal evidence, while the cited explanation attributes the decline to Shaiva propaganda and associates Kumarila Bhatta with it.
Hiuen Tsang visited Andhra in 639–640 CE; Dhanyakataka had about 20 viharas; Harsha died in 647 CE; and Pulakesin II assumed the title Paramesvara.
The Aihole inscription is significant precisely because it records Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha at the Narmada and mentions the title Paramesvara.

units.title: Kanauj and their Contributions; South Indian Dynasties - Badami Chalukyas, Eastern Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Kalyani Chalukyas, Cholas, Hoysalas, Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Reddis

rows.title: Tripartite struggle for Kanauj - Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas; causes and outcome

secs.t: Participants → ruler in each phase

x: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were based initially in
Rajasthan-Gujarat and Avanti
, and later established themselves at Kannauj.
Vatsaraja, Dharmapala and Dhruva belonged respectively to the Pratihara, Pala and Rashtrakuta dynasties.
Mihira Bhoja
was a prominent Gurjara-Pratihara ruler who held Kannauj in the later phase of the struggle.
The struggle began when Gurjara-Pratihara ruler
Vatsaraja
, around 780–800 CE, clashed with Dharmapala and Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva.

secs.t: Rashtrakuta northern campaigns - rulers who crossed the Vindhyas

x: This description in the Sanjan plates refers to the northern campaign of Rashtrakuta ruler
Govinda III
Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III sacked Kannauj around 916 CE after defeating Pratihara ruler
Mahipala I
The Rashtrakuta campaigns brought booty and prestige, but the Rashtrakutas did not retain lasting control over the northern territories.

secs.t: Phases - sequence of Kanauj rulers installed and removed (Indrayudha, Chakrayudha)

x: The sequence was Vatsaraja's occupation, Dharmapala's installation of Chakrayudha, Nagabhata II's ousting of Chakrayudha, and the later Pratihara control under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I.
Dharmapala removed the Pratihara nominee
Indrayudha
and installed Chakrayudha as his puppet ruler at Kannauj.
In the third phase, Nagabhata II ousted Chakrayudha and defeated Dharmapala; subsequently, Govinda III defeated both and withdrew.

secs.t: Contending dynasties vs distractors

x: The correct sequence is Pallava Mahendravarman I, Pala Gopala, Pratihara Bhoja and Chola Parantaka I.
The
Pallavas
were not participants in the tripartite struggle.
Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas were the contending powers.

secs.t: Kannauj - ancient names and value as the cause

x: Mahodaya
, also expressed as Mahodaya Shri, was an ancient name associated with Kannauj.
After Harsha, Kannauj became a symbol of imperial sovereignty and was associated with the title of Samrat of North India.
Kannauj commanded the agrarian wealth of the Gangetic Doab and access to Arabian Sea trade through Gujarat, thereby bypassing the Arab-held Indus delta.

secs.t: Outcome - who held Kannauj, effects

x: Kannauj was finally held by the Pratiharas under Bhoja and Mahendrapala I, but no single power permanently retained it for a long period.
The exhaustion of the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, along with Pratihara decline after Indra III's raid, opened the way for new Rajput states such as the Chandelas and Chauhans.

secs.t: Sources - Sanjan plates, Gwalior prashasti, Khalimpur plates

x: The Sanjan plates are Rashtrakuta, the Gwalior prashasti is Pratihara, and the Khalimpur plates are Pala sources.
The Sanjan plates, issued during the reign of Rashtrakuta ruler Amoghavarsha I in 871 CE, describe
Govinda III's Himalayan campaign
The
Gwalior prashasti
of Mihira Bhoja records Nagabhata II's victories over Chakrayudha and Dharmapala.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The struggle demonstrates the shift of power to regional kingdoms during early medieval India.
Rashtrakuta ruler
Dhruva
defeated Vishnuvardhana IV of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, showing the parallel Deccan dimension of Rashtrakuta expansion.
Kannauj's primacy began under Harsha; Hiuen Tsang observed that Pataliputra had lost its earlier place to Kannauj.

rows.title: Palas of Bengal - Gopala, Dharmapala, Devapala; Nalanda and Vikramshila, Pala art

secs.t: Universities → founder + present location (Vikramashila, Odantapuri, Somapura, Jagaddala, Nalanda)

x: Somapura Mahavihara is located at Paharpur in Naogaon district of present-day Bangladesh.
Odantapuri was situated at Bihar Sharif in Nalanda district of Bihar and is described as having accommodated approximately 12,000 monks.
Vikramashila reached its zenith under
Ramapala
, although its foundation is attributed to Dharmapala.
Kumaragupta I founded Nalanda, Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura, and Ramapala founded Jagaddala.

secs.t: Gopala - founder, manner of accession, source

x: Gopala was elected by regional notables to bring an end to matsyanyaya, a period of anarchy, around the middle of the eighth century.
The
Khalimpur plate of Dharmapala
records the election of Gopala.
Gopala displaced the later Guptas in Magadha and the Khadgas in eastern Bengal, and he is associated with the construction of Odantapuri.

secs.t: Buddhist centres of learning - odd-one-out

x: Taxila
was an ancient centre in Gandhara and does not belong to the early-medieval Pala group.
Valabhi was known as a Hinayana centre during the time of Harsha.

secs.t: Pala contacts with Southeast Asia

x: Balaputradeva was a Shailendra ruler of
Suvarnadvipa or Suvarnabhumi
Pala-style bronze images found in Southeast Asia indicate maritime cultural exchange across the Bay of Bengal.

secs.t: Pala patronage of Buddhism - acharyas and Tibet

x: Shilabhadra was associated with Nalanda in Harsha's time; Shantarakshita went to Tibet and founded Samye; Atisha was linked with Vikramashila; and Sakya Sri Bhadra was associated with Jagaddala.

secs.t: Pala rulers → achievement

x: All three statements describe the recorded political and institutional activities of Dharmapala.
Mahipala I
, whose reign is placed around c. 977–1027, revived Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola.
Ramapala, c. 1072–1126, is described as the last strong Pala ruler.
The sequence is Gopala, Devapala, Mahipala I and Ramapala.

secs.t: Pala art - materials, manuscripts, artists

x: Pala art is known for bronze and black-stone or basalt sculpture and illustrated Buddhist manuscripts written on palm leaves.
Dhiman and his son Vitapala were noted artists associated with Pala art, as recorded by Taranatha.
Somapura had rich terracotta ornamentation and Vikramashila had terracotta panels on its walls.

secs.t: Literature - Ramacharita, Buddhist texts

x: Ramacharita was written by
Sandhyakar Nandi
and deals with Ramapala and the Kaivarta peasant revolt.
Buddhist texts were compiled at Nalanda under Dharmapala, while Jagaddala became associated with translating books into Tibetan.

secs.t: Successor dynasty in Bengal

x: The
Sena dynasty
succeeded the Palas in Bengal.
The sequence is Samantasena, Vijayasena, Ballalasena and Lakshmanasena.
Lakshmanasena was the last Sena ruler; Jayadeva was associated with his court, and Lakshmanasena was ousted by Bakhtiyar Khilji.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Palas were the last major royal patrons of Buddhism in India and supported its transmission to Tibet and Southeast Asia through institutions, teachers and maritime contacts.
Andhra's Dharmakirti taught at Nalanda and studied under the Nalanda head Dharmapala of Kanchi.

src: Sources: CDI (Block02 Early Educational Institutions - Odantapuri, Vikramshila, Jagaddala, Panchamahavihara); UPSC (Medieval History p.6, 7, 8); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Nalanda University); CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.91, 94)

rows.title: Gurjara-Pratiharas - Nagabhata I and II, Mihira Bhoja; resistance to Arab expansion

secs.t: Pratihara rulers → achievement + order; odd-one-out lists

x: Vatsaraja took Kannauj and defeated Dharmapala, but was later defeated by the Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva, marking the beginning of the tripartite struggle.
Kannauj was sacked by the Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III during the reign of
Mahipala I
, around 916 CE.
Besides the well-known Pala ruler Devapala, a later Gurjara-Pratihara king also bore the name Devapala and ruled approximately from c. 948 to c. 954.

secs.t: Mihira Bhoja - titles, parentage, capital, coins, extent, Sulaiman

x: Mihira Bhoja bore the title
Adivaraha
, reflecting his devotion to Vishnu; Adivaraha also appeared on his coins.
Mihira Bhoja's expansion was checked by
Sankaravarman of Kashmir, Rashtrakuta Krishna II and Pala Devapala
Sulaiman
, writing in the mid-ninth century, praised Mihira Bhoja's army, wealth and security and regarded his cavalry as the best in India.

secs.t: Rajashekhara - patrons, works vs wrongly attributed

x: Prabandhachintamani
was written by Merutunga, whereas Kavyamimamsa, Karpuramanjari and Viddhasalabhanjika were works of Rajashekhara.
Kavyamimamsa is a work on poetics, Karpuramanjari is a Prakrit play and Viddhasalabhanjika is by Rajashekhara.
Rajashekhara was the court poet of Mahendrapala I and was also associated with the court of Mahipala I.

secs.t: Origin debate - Gurjara identity, agnikula

x: The dynasty claimed descent from Lakshmana, who was regarded as Rama's
door-keeper
brother.
Gurjara has been interpreted either as the name of a tribe or people or as a reference to the region called Gurjaratra.
The Agnikula legend associates the
Pratiharas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras and Chauhans
with birth from the fire-pit at Mount Abu.

secs.t: Capitals - Bhinmal, Ujjain, Kanauj

x: The sequence was Bhinmal in early Rajasthan, followed by Ujjain or Avanti, and later Kannauj, also known as Mahodaya, from the time of Nagabhata II.
Nagabhata II
made Kannauj the capital of the Pratihara kingdom.

secs.t: Decline - raids and successor Rajput states

x: All three developments weakened the Pratihara power: Indra III raided Kannauj, Mahmud of Ghazni attacked it in 1018, and several feudatories became independent.
The
Chandelas, Chauhans, Paramaras and Chaulukyas
broke away as the Pratihara feudatory structure weakened.
The Pratihara temple style is stated to have peaked at
Khajuraho
, which is also a UNESCO site.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were the principal power that helped keep Arab rule confined to Sindh.
Sulaiman praised the Pratihara cavalry, while he named Amoghavarsha of the Rashtrakutas as one of the four great kings of the world.

src: Sources: UPSC (Medieval History p.4, 5); CDI (Block01 Kushans Sunga Kanauj Contributions - Tripartite Struggle; Block02 Historical Accounts of Foreign Travellers - Sulaiman; Block04 Advent of Islam)

rows.title: Rashtrakutas - Dantidurga, Govinda III, Amoghavarsha (Kavirajamarga), Krishna I

secs.t: Ruler → contribution / event

x: Dhruva was the first Rashtrakuta ruler to move north, defeated Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, and subdued the Eastern Chalukyas and the Gangas of Talakad.
Govinda III defeated Nagabhata II and Dharmapala and is said in the Sanjan plates to have reached the Himalayas.
The sequence is Dantidurga, Dhruva, Govinda III and Amoghavarsha I. Their approximate reign periods were 753–756, 780–793, 793–814 and 814–878 respectively.

secs.t: Literary work → author + language

x: Kavirajamarga is associated with Amoghavarsha I and is regarded as the earliest work on Kannada poetics.
Pampa wrote a Kannada Adipurana, Jinasena wrote a Sanskrit Adipurana, and Pampa is described as Telugu-origin or Telugu-born.
Ganitasarasangraha was written by
Mahaviracharya
and is identified as a Sanskrit mathematical work.
Nalachampu
, written by Trivikrama Bhatta in Sanskrit, is identified as the first champu.

secs.t: Founder - establishment, rituals, capital

x: Dantidurga performed the
Hiranyagarbha
ritual at Ujjain.
Dantidurga, whose reign is placed around 753–756 CE, was contemporary with Eastern Chalukya
Vijayaditya I

secs.t: Capitals - Elapura, Manyakheta

x: The early Rashtrakuta seat was in the Elapura region, Dantidurga’s inscription is in Ellora’s Dashavatara cave, and Amoghavarsha I built Manyakheta.
Manyakheta or Malkhed is in
Karnataka
and was built by Amoghavarsha I.

secs.t: Titles of rulers → ruler

x: Balhara, or Vallabharaja, was a title generally used for Rashtrakuta kings, not exclusively for Govinda III.
Viranarayana was one of the titles of
Amoghavarsha I

secs.t: Conflicts with Vengi, Pallavas and Cholas (Takkolam)

x: The Rashtrakuta–Vengi conflict continued for approximately 200 years and involved repeated struggles with the Eastern Chalukyas.
Vijayaditya II
is stated to have fought 108 battles against Rashtrakuta forces.
These facts describe important Rashtrakuta–Eastern Chalukya relations during the reigns of Dhruva and Amoghavarsha I.
At Takkolam in 949 CE, Krishna III defeated the Cholas under Parantaka I, and the Chola prince Rajaditya was killed.

secs.t: Court poets - Kannada Ratnatraya and patrons

x: Pampa was patronised by Arikesari II, Ponna by Krishna III, Ranna by Tailapa II, and Swayambhu was an Apabhramsha poet linked to the court.
The Kannada Ratnatraya consisted of
Pampa, Ponna and Ranna
, the three celebrated Kannada poets associated with major royal patrons.
Pampa was patronised by
Arikesari II
of the Vemulavada Chalukyas, who were Rashtrakuta feudatories.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pampa wrote Vikramarjuna Vijaya in Kannada, modelled Arjuna on Arikesari II, and is noted as a Telugu-born or Telugu-origin poet.
The Rashtrakuta period is described as a golden age of Kannada and as the zenith of rock-cut art, represented by the Kailasa temple at Ellora and Elephanta.
Sulaiman visited the court of
Amoghavarsha I
and considered him one of the four great kings of the world.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Rashtrakutas - Literature, Exam Value Additions; Block09 Rashtrakutas Literature; Block02 Sulaiman); UPSC (Medieval History p.8, 9, 44); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas); CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.110, 116, 117)

rows.title: Rashtrakuta administration, trade and religion; Kailasa temple at Ellora; Al-Masudi's account

secs.t: Kailasa temple at Ellora - ruler, technique, deity, features

x: Exam angle: "carved during the reign of" - Krishna I, not Dantidurga or Amoghavarsha.
The temple contains panels such as Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa, Mahishasuramardini and Shiva Nataraja, along with Ramayana, Mahabharata and Purana scenes.
The Rashtrakutas contributed to the Vesara synthesis, which combined Nagara and Dravida architectural features and became associated with the Deccan style.

secs.t: Ellora caves - number, district, three groups, chronology

x: Exam angle: cave count, the 12-17-5 split, and ordering of named caves.
Ellora’s location near the Elaganga and on the Ujjain–Deccan route also helps explain its cultural importance and religious diversity.
The Hindu caves were mainly associated with the Rashtrakutas, while the Jain caves are generally dated to the ninth and tenth centuries; later additions are credited in some accounts to the Yadavas.

secs.t: Elephanta caves - patron debate, Trimurti

x: Elephanta is near Mumbai, its patronage is debated with many historians favouring the sixth-century Kalachuris, and its famous image is the Trimurti.
The masterpiece of the Elephanta caves is the three-headed Shiva known as Trimurti or Maheshamurti.

secs.t: Religion - Jainism, Saivism, Vaishnavism, Buddhism

x: Jainism
reached a high point under Amoghavarsha I, who was a devout Jain and is described as having renounced the throne.
Rashtrakuta religious policy included Shaiva royal affiliation, patronage of Vaishnavism and Buddhism without persecution, and accommodation of Muslim Arab merchants in ports.
Trivikrama
composed Nalachampu, identified as the first Champu.

secs.t: Arab travellers → account and title for the king

x: Sulaiman
, who visited during the reign of Amoghavarsha I, ranked the Rashtrakuta king among the four great kings along with the Caliph, the Chinese emperor and the Byzantine emperor.
The ninth-century traveller Ibn Khurdadbeh called the Balhara
the greatest king of India
Balhara is the Arabic form of Vallabha or Vallabharaja, a Rashtrakuta royal title.

secs.t: Administration - rashtra, vishaya, bhukti and officials

x: Rashtra was headed by the Rashtrapati, Vishaya by the Vishayapati, Bhukti by the Bhogapati and Grama by the Gramakuta or gavunda.
Nad-gavundas were hereditary local officers of the nadu and assisted in the collection of revenue.
Dantidurga overthrew Chalukya ruler Kirtivarman II; therefore Kirtivarman II was not the ruler who overthrew Dantidurga.

secs.t: Trade - Arab merchants, ports, horse trade

x: Control of major trade routes
brought prosperity to the Rashtrakutas and connected them with Gujarat, the Arabian Peninsula and South India.
Cambay is also known as Khambhat and was one of the western ports associated with Rashtrakuta trade.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The twinning agreement signed by India and Jordan concerned
Petra and Ellora
, both UNESCO sites.
The Rashtrakuta era raised Kannada to a classical medium and gave Ellora its Hindu peak.
Krishna III helped Danarnava kill Ammaraja II in 970 CE and seize Vengi.
Nalachampu was written by
Trivikrama
and is regarded as the first Champu work.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Rashtrakutas exam table, Ellora caves; Block09 Rashtrakuta Religion, Art & Architecture); UPSC (Art & Culture p.23-24; Medieval History p.10); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Gupta cave architecture, Ellora); CDX (AP History p.120); VIS PT365 2026 p.100; LENS May 2025 p.16

rows.title: Badami (Vatapi) Chalukyas - Pulakesin I, Pulakesin II, Aihole inscription of Ravikirti

secs.t: Inscriptions of Pulakesin II → Andhra place names and events

x: Exam angle: "Which inscription of Pulakesin II calls Mangalagiri Mangalapura?"
The Maruturu and Kopparam inscriptions record Pulakesin II's defeat of Mahendravarman I and his securing of the territory between the Krishna and Godavari rivers.
The
Satara inscription
of 617 CE records Pulakesin II's appointment of his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana as viceroy of Vengi.

secs.t: Aihole inscription - author, language, date, poets, victories

x: The Aihole inscription refers to the celebrated poets
Kalidasa and Bharavi
The Aihole inscription lists victories over Harsha, the Kadambas, the Mauryas of Konkan and several other groups, but it does not record a
victory over the Guptas of Pataliputra
Kirtivarman I is described as the ‘night of doom’ to the
Nalas, Mauryas and Kadambas

secs.t: Pulakesin II - titles, eastern conquests, embassy, Chinese account

x: Pulakesin II assumed the title
Dakshinapatheshwara
, presenting himself as the lord of the southern route in contrast to Harsha's Uttarapatheshwara.
Pulakesin II conquered Kosala and Kalinga, marched to Vengi, defeated the Durjayas and appointed Kubja Vishnuvardhana there.
The embassy was exchanged with Khusrau II, and an Ajanta Cave 1 painting was once read as representing it; that identification is now questioned.

secs.t: Ruler → achievement

x: Pulakesin I founded the independent kingdom; Kirtivarman I expanded it and became the ‘night of doom’; Mangalesha ruled as regent and extended the territory; Vikramaditya I restored power after Pallava occupation.
Vikramaditya II
took Kanchi three times but spared it.
The Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal was built by Lokamahadevi, queen of Vikramaditya II.

secs.t: Capital - Vatapi

x: Vatapi is modern Badami, located in Bagalkot district of Karnataka.
Pulakesin I fortified Vatapi, as recorded in the Badami cliff inscription dated to
543 CE

secs.t: Pulakesin I's sacrifices

x: Pulakesin I performed the
Ashvamedha
The Vajapeya and Hiranyagarbha sacrifices were used by Chalukya kings to claim
Kshatriya status

secs.t: Succession war with Mangalesha

x: Kirtivarman I left minor sons, so his brother Mangalesha governed as regent.
After exile, Pulakesin II attacked and killed Mangalesha at
Elapattu-Simbige in the Bana territory
around 609-10 CE.

secs.t: End of the dynasty - successor power

x: The last ruler, Kirtivarman II, was overthrown by Dantidurga, who founded the Rashtrakuta power around 753-757 CE.
The Badami Chalukyas ruled approximately from
543 to 757 CE

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pulakesin II's Vengi conquest led to the Eastern Chalukya line, with Vishnuvardhana's appointment in 617 CE, independence in 624 CE and Pithapuram as capital.
The Pune copper plates of Eastern Chalukya
Vishnuvardhana II
, dated 669 CE, contain the first epigraphic reference to Guntur as Kumturu.
The Badami Chalukyas are significant for bridging North and South India, while the Aihole inscription is an important dated prasasti for their history.

src: Sources: UPSC (Medieval History p.25-26); CDI (Block03 Badami Chalukyas intro and exam table; Religious synthesis); CDX (AP History p.110-111, 113); APP (Indian History Part 1 > Harsha; AP History Ancient Part 1 & 2 > Eastern Chalukyas, cross-era fragments); APHQ (G2 2019); TH 25 Aug 2026

rows.title: Chalukya-Harsha and Chalukya-Pallava conflicts; Chalukya administration

secs.t: Chalukya-Harsha conflict - victor, river, source, title

x: The cited examination keys give 618 CE and 637 CE, while the chronological inference from the 634 CE Aihole record requires the event to predate that record.
The Aihole inscription of Pulakesin II, composed by Ravikirti, and Hiuen Tsang’s account confirm the conflict.
Pulakesin II was styled
Dakshinapatheshwara
, meaning lord of the south, in opposition to Harsha’s title Uttarapatheshwara.

secs.t: Women in administration - queens and princesses as governors

x: Vijayabhattarika, also known as Vijaya-mahadevi, was the queen of Chandraditya and governed while issuing land grants in her own name.
Lokamahadevi and Trailokyamahadevi
, queens of Vikramaditya II, commissioned the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal.
Akkadevi, a Kalyani Chalukya princess, governed the province of Kisukad.

secs.t: Chalukya-Pallava conflicts - rounds and rulers

x: The four rounds occurred in the order: Pulakesin II–Mahendravarman I, Pulakesin II–Narasimhavarman I, Vikramaditya I–the Pallavas, and Vikramaditya II–Nandivarman II.
Nandivarman II was involved in the fourth Chalukya-Pallava conflict, in which Kanchi was taken and spared.
Vikramaditya I
recovered Vatapi around 655 CE after its occupation by the Pallavas.
The Pallava occupation of Vatapi lasted
about 13 years
until Vikramaditya I recovered it.

secs.t: Battles → place + victor

x: Pullalur, near Kanchi, was fought around 618–619.
Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakesin II at Manimangala around 642 CE.
Paranjoti
was the Pallava general associated with Narasimhavarman I’s sack of Vatapi.

secs.t: Titles won in these wars → ruler

x: Narasimhavarman I
assumed the title Vatapikonda, meaning conqueror of Vatapi, after capturing the Chalukya capital.
Pulakesin II was styled Paramesvara, Narasimhavarman I was Vatapikonda, and Vikramaditya II was Kanchiyamkonda.
Vikramaditya II assumed the title Kanchiyamkonda after taking Kanchi during the reign of Nandivarman II.

secs.t: Chalukya occupation of Kanchi - ruler, inscription

x: Vikramaditya II entered Kanchi around 740 CE during Nandivarman II’s reign and left a Kannada inscription on a pillar.
Lokamahadevi’s
Virupaksha temple
at Pattadakal commemorates Vikramaditya II’s victory and copies the Kailasanatha temple of Kanchi.

secs.t: Chalukya administration - units, officials, feudatories

x: Vishayapati
was the official heading a Rashtra or Vishaya.
Agraharas were Brahmin land grants that spread widely, and mahajanas managed them.
R.S. Sharma termed the spread of agraharas the
proliferation of the feudal land grant system
In Rayalaseema, the Renati Chodas were initially feudatories of the early Pallavas and subsequently became feudatories of the Badami Chalukyas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The wars stimulated political activity in Rayalaseema, including
the rise of the Renati Chodas, Banas and Vaidumbas
The Pitikayagulla inscription indicates
post-Badami Chalukya influence in Rayalaseema
and is written in early Telugu script.
The rivalry lasted about a century and influenced Deccan and Tamil politics as well as temple art.

src: Sources: APP (Indian History Part 1 > Harsha's conquests, timeline); UPSC (Medieval History p.25-26, 29); CDI (Block03 Badami Chalukyas intro, Pattadakal; SOUTH INDIAN DYNASTIES); CDX (AP History p.111, 150); APPCA Jun 2026; TH 14 Jun 2026

rows.title: Badami Chalukya art - Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal (UNESCO); origin of the Vesara style

secs.t: Alampur Navabrahma temples - dynasty, style, district

x: The nine Navabrahma temples at Alampur were built by the
Badami Chalukyas
during the 7th–8th centuries CE.
The Navabrahma temples are associated with the Nagara style, particularly the curvilinear rekha shikhara.
Alampur is in present-day Jogulamba Gadwal district of Telangana, was earlier part of Mahabubnagar district, and is located in the Telugu region.

secs.t: Temple → site + shikhara style

x: Ravana Phadi is a rock-cut cave at Aihole without a tower.
Papanatha at Pattadakal is associated with the Nagara style.

secs.t: Aihole - epithet, early freestanding temples, Durga temple plan

x: The Lad Khan temple is rectangular, has a flat roof, uses stone grilles for light and contains twelve carved pillars in the mukha mandapa.
The Lad Khan temple is noted for having one of
the earliest massive bracket capital
s and is regarded as an early Chalukyan temple.
The Durga temple has an apsidal, or gajaprishtha, plan and a pillared gallery running around the shrine.

secs.t: Pattadakal - UNESCO status, styles, patron queens

x: Pattadakal was a royal coronation site, is associated with the coronation stone, represents the mature phase and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
Pattadakal displays Nagara and Dravida temple forms side by side and represents the mature phase of Chalukyan architecture.
Pattadakal is noted for Nandi mandapas, narrative friezes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Panchatantra, and polished pillars.

secs.t: Badami cave temples - numbers, deities, Jain cave

x: The four main Badami caves were excavated in sandstone around
Agastya lake
Badami has four principal sandstone caves dating broadly to the 6th–7th centuries; the earliest were made under Mangalesha, and the fourth cave is Jain.
Cave 3 is dedicated to Vishnu, is the largest cave at Badami and contains Mangalesha's inscription dated 578 CE.

secs.t: Architects and inscriptions naming them

x: The Meguti inscription identifies Ravikirti, a poet and composer, while the Virupaksha inscriptions name Gunda Anivaritachari and Sarvasiddhi Acharya as architects.
Ravikirti was the
poet and composer
named in the Aihole Meguti inscription, not the architect of the temple.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The sequence proceeds from the rock-cut caves of Badami to the experimental structural temples of Aihole and finally to the mature architectural phase at Pattadakal.
The sequence moves from Badami's rock-cut architecture through Aihole's experiments to Pattadakal's mature forms, after which the Eastern Chalukyas carried the Vesara or Chalukyan style into Andhra.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Badami Chalukyas - Vesara style, Pattadakal, exam table; SOUTH INDIAN DYNASTIES); UPSC (Art & Culture p.37, 44; Medieval History p.31); APP (Indian History Part 1 > temple styles, Lad Khan; Chola > Dravida; AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas); APHQ (G2 2008 Navabrahma)

rows.title: Pallavas - Simhavishnu, Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I Mamalla, Nandivarman II

secs.t: Mahendravarman I - titles, Mattavilasa Prahasana, conversion, cave temples

x: The
Mandagapattu
cave temple carries the celebrated claim that it was constructed without brick, timber, metal or mortar.
Mamandur
, along with Mandagapattu, Mahendravadi and Dalavanur, is associated with Mahendravarman I’s cave temples.
Mahendravarman I lost the Krishna-Godavari region to the Chalukya ruler
Pulakesin II
, as indicated by the Maruturu and Kopparam inscriptions.

secs.t: Early Pallava charters and Andhra links

x: The Mayidavolu plates were issued by Sivaskandavarman as yuvaraja, the Hirahadagalli plates record his sacrifices, and the Manchikallu inscription is associated with Simhavarman’s conquest of Vijayapuri.
The Manchikallu inscription records the Pallava conquest of Vijayapuri after the defeat of the
Ikshvakus
Pallava
Simhavarman
defeated the last Ikshvaku ruler Rudrapurushadatta, an event associated with the establishment of Pallava rule in the Krishna valley.

secs.t: Pallava ruler → political event + chronology

x: Sivaskandavarman is linked with Kanchi coming under Pallava control; Vishnugopa faced Samudragupta; Simhavishnu defeated the Kalabhras; and Narasimhavarman I took Vatapi.
The main line runs from Simhavishnu to Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I, Paramesvaravarman I, Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), and finally Nandivarman II.
Simhavishnu ruled approximately from 575 to 600 CE.

secs.t: Origin debate and territory

x: Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital, and the Pallava dynasty is generally placed approximately between 275 and 897 CE.
The major theories mentioned are Parthian or Pahlava origin, Andhra origin and local Tamil origin in Tondaimandalam.
The Andhra-origin theory draws support from early Prakrit charters found in the Krishna-Guntur region and the Pallavas’ replacement of the Ikshvakus there.

secs.t: Kanchi as centre of learning - Ghatika, Dandin, Bharavi, Mayurasharman

x: A Ghatika was a higher learning centre where scholars gathered, generally attached to temples.
According to the Talagunda inscription, Mayurasharman, a Brahmin student at
the Kanchi Ghatika
, was insulted by a Pallava horseman and subsequently took up arms and founded the Kadamba kingdom.
Hiuen Tsang visited Kanchi around
640 CE
and praised Narasimhavarman alongside Harsha and Pulakesin II.

secs.t: Narasimhavarman I - titles, Chalukya wars, Sri Lanka expeditions

x: Narasimhavarman I bore the titles Mamalla, meaning great wrestler, and Vatapikonda, meaning conqueror of Vatapi.
Narasimhavarman I defeated and killed Pulakesin II at Manimangala in 642 CE and captured or sacked Vatapi through his general Paranjoti.
Narasimhavarman I sent two naval expeditions to Sri Lanka to restore his ally, Prince Manavarma.

secs.t: Nandivarman II - accession, religious patronage

x: After the death of Paramesvaravarman II around 731 CE, ministers and nobles selected Nandivarman II, a twelve-year-old from a collateral line.
Nandivarman II was an ardent Vaishnavite and is associated with the construction of the Vaikuntha Perumal temple at Kanchi.
Nandivarman II temporarily lost Kanchi to the Chalukya ruler
Vikramaditya II

secs.t: Later Pallavas and end of the dynasty

x: The sequence is Dantivarman, Nandivarman III, Nripatunga and Aparajita.
Aditya I Chola
killed Aparajita, bringing the Pallava dynasty to an end around 897–898 CE.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pallava rule was important for Dravida temple architecture, the spread of Grantha-derived scripts, and the growth of Alvar and Nayanar Bhakti traditions.
The Mayidavolu and Manchikallu records are associated with Andhra, and the Renati Chodas are identified as early Pallava feudatories.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Pallavas intro, 4 stages; Block09 Pallavas Andhra - Religion, Rathas); UPSC (Medieval History p.26, 31-32); APHQ (G2 2019, 2025, 2000); APP (AP History Ancient Part 1 > Ikshvakus - Rudrapurushadatta; Part 2 > fragments); CDX (AP History p.108, 111, 147, 150)

rows.title: Pallava art and architecture - Mandagapattu inscription, Mahabalipuram rathas, Shore Temple, Kailasanatha

secs.t: Mahabalipuram monuments → patron

x: The Pancha Rathas, Varaha Mandapa and Mahishasuramardini Cave are attributed to
Narasimhavarman I
, also known as Mamalla.
The Pancha Rathas are monolithic granite monuments named after the five Pandavas and Draupadi, and their forms imitate earlier wooden and structural traditions.
The Shore Temple is structural, has two Shiva shrines and one Vishnu shrine, and is identified with the surviving temple of the Seven Pagodas tradition.

secs.t: Four phases of Pallava architecture → ruler + example

x: Pallava architecture evolved from rock-cut pillared mandapas to monolithic rathas and mandapas, and subsequently to structural temples.

The Mahendra phase is represented by Mandagapattu and Mahendravadi; the Mamalla phase by the Pancha Rathas; the Rajasimha phase by the Shore Temple and Kailasanatha; and the later phase by Vaikuntha Perumal.
The Nandivarman/Aparajita phase is associated with smaller structural temples such as Vaikuntha Perumal, not the earliest rock-cut cave temples.

secs.t: UNESCO Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram - comparison with Ajanta

x: Mahabalipuram represents Pallava Hindu architecture, whereas Ajanta represents Buddhist cave paintings and rock-cut monastic architecture.
Ajanta was inscribed in 1983, contains 25 viharas and 4 chaityas, has Jataka paintings, and was found in 1819 by John Smith.
Ajanta consists mainly of cave paintings and rock-cut monasteries in a cliff, whereas Mahabalipuram is noted for open-air reliefs, monolithic rathas and a structural temple.

secs.t: Mandagapattu inscription - claim, materials

x: The inscription famously states that the temple was made without brick, timber, metal or mortar, marking an important stage in South Indian rock-cut architecture.
The inscription is associated with
the beginning of rock-cut cave temples in South India
under Mahendravarman I.
Dvarapalakas
, or guardian figures, are found at the entrance and later became common in South Indian temples.

secs.t: Kailasanatha and Vaikunthaperumal temples, Kanchi

x: Kailasanatha contains Shiva sculptures, influenced Chola temple architecture, and was completed by Mahendravarman III.
Vaikuntha Perumal is a Vishnu temple with a storeyed sanctum and panels depicting Pallava history.
Vikramaditya II's Kannada inscription is on Kailasanatha, and the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal was modelled on Kailasanatha.

secs.t: Pallava sculpture and painting - Sittannavasal, Panamalai

x: Pallava sculpture evolved from rigid forms towards graceful, dynamic and naturalistic representations and included narrative panels.
Sittannavasal in Pudukkottai, Tamil Nadu, is a Jain cave known for murals, including the depiction of a lotus pond.
Sittannavasal was once credited to Mahendravarman I, but an inscription records a ninth-century Pandya renovation.
Panamalai contains a Rajasimha-period painting of
Parvati
in the Talagirishvara Temple.

secs.t: Pallava rock-cut temples in Andhra → which dynasty's caves

x: The caves at Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda are attributed to the
Vishnukundins
, who imitated the Pallava cave style in the Telugu lands.
Undavalli is a multi-storeyed Vishnukundin complex on the Krishna in Guntur district with a monolithic reclining Anantasayana Vishnu; its attribution is not Chola.
Mogalrajapuram, attributed to the Vishnukundins, contains Shiva and Vishnu shrines and displays an early ardhamandapa and garbhagriha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pallava rathas contributed the vimana and ardhamandapa forms to early Andhra temples, while Vishnukundin caves imitated Pallava style.
The Pallavas are regarded as pioneers of Dravida temple architecture.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Pallavas - Art & Sculpture, 4 stages, Mains value addition; Block09 Pallavas Rathas, Vishnukundin rock-cut caves); UPSC (Art & Culture p.35, 45, 48); APHQ (G2 2000, 2008, 2012, 2025); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > fragments; Indian History Part 1 > Ajanta); CDX (AP History p.58, 108); LENS Aug 2026 p.124

rows.title: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi - Kubja Vishnuvardhana, dynastic history, patronage of Telugu (Nannaya)
sub: Group-II M1-A-19: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi - Kubja Vishnuvardhana and the dynastic history

secs.t: Ruler → title + contribution (Kubja Vishnuvardhana to Rajaraja Narendra)

x: The Eastern Chalukyas were founded as a branch of the
Badami Chalukyas
after Pulakeshin II conquered the Vengi region.
Pulakeshin II
conquered Vengi and appointed his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana as its viceroy.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana became viceroy in 617 CE and declared independence in
624 CE
The Kopparam plates refer to
Kubja Vishnuvardhana
by the title “Yuvaraja.”.
Jayasimha Vallabha I
bore the title “Samastha Bhuvanashraya.”.
All three statements are associated with Chalukya Bhima I: the 360 battles, a 30-year reign and the construction of the Pancharamas.
The Pithapuram inscription of Mallappadeva records the tradition of Chalukya Bhima I fighting 360 battles.
Panduranga, the commander of
Gunaga Vijayaditya III
, issued the Addanki inscription.
Tripura Martya Maheshwara was the title of Gunaga Vijayaditya III, not Amma I. Saktivarman I, Rajaraja Narendra and Vimaladitya are correctly matched as shown.
Rajaraja Narendra bore the title “
Kavyageetha Priyudu
”; Rajarajanarayana and Baraganda Bhairava were also associated with him.
The Telugu Choda ruler
Jatachoda Bhima
killed Danarnava and seized Vengi until Danarnava’s sons recovered it with Chola assistance.

secs.t: Temples → ruler + style (108 Saiva temples, Pancharamas, Draksharama, Biccavolu)

x: Exam angle: "108 Shaivalayas" → Vijayaditya II, not Kubja or Vishnuvardhana III/IV.
The Bikkavolu Shiva temples of
Mukteshwara, Vijayeshwara and Chandrashekhara
are attributed to Gunaga Vijayaditya III.
The Bhimeswara temples at Draksharama and Samalkot, also called Chalukya Bhimavaram, are associated with
Chalukya Bhima I
Bhimarama
and Draksharama are included among the key Pancharama temples mentioned in the Eastern Chalukya tradition.

secs.t: Nannaya and other Telugu figures → patron + collaborator

x: Nannaya Bhattaraka is regarded as Adi Kavi because Andhra Mahabharatamu is considered the first major Telugu literary work.
Nannaya's Andhra Mahabharatamu follows the Champu style, which combines verse and prose.
Narayana Bhattu bore the title
Ashtabhasha Kavisekhara
The
Kalamalla inscription
, dated approximately to 575 CE and associated with Renati Choda Dhananjaya, predates Nannaya.

secs.t: Queens and Jain patronage (Nedumba Vasati, Ayyana Mahadevi, Potla Cheruvu)

x: Chamekamba
, a courtesan during the reign of Ammaraja II, secured the Kaluchumbarru grant for a Jain temple.
Potla Cheruvu was a popular Jain centre during this period.
Vishnuvardhana III
granted Mushikonda to the Jains, illustrating the dynasty's religious tolerance.
Kundavva was a Chola princess and the queen of Vimaladitya; she was the mother of
Rajaraja Narendra

secs.t: Official language, religious sect favoured, mother goddess

x: The matronymic Hariti-putra was also used by the
Satavahanas, Ikshvakus and Kadambas
, indicating a southern cultural connection.
Kushmandini was the mother goddess worshipped by the early Chalukyas.

secs.t: Court titles and towns developed → person (Gandharva-vidya-visarada, Kandukuru → Bejawada)

x: Vijayaditya III, or Gunaga Vijayaditya, developed Kandukuru as another Bejawada.
Pithapuram, or Pishtapura, was the first capital under Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
Jayasimha Vallabha I
shifted the capital from Pithapuram to Vengi, identified with Pedavegi.

secs.t: Chronological order of Andhra dynasties

x: The Magallu inscription is noted as the first inscription mentioning the
Kakatiyas
The Eastern Chalukyas ruled approximately from 624 to 1075 CE.

secs.t: Wars with Rashtrakutas - rulers and battles

x: Vishnuvardhana IV supported Govinda III, was defeated by Dhruva, and strengthened the relationship through Dhruva's marriage to Sheela Mahadevi.
The 108 temples commemorated Vijayaditya II's victories, traditionally connected with his 108 battles fought over 12 years.
Vimaladitya married both Kundavva and Melama, while Rajaraja Narendra married Ammanga Devi, the daughter of Rajendra Chola.
Rajaraja Narendra, the son of Kundavva, was supported by
Rajendra I
. Vijayaditya VII, the son of Melama, was supported by Kalyani Jayasimha II.
Vimaladitya was crowned in May 1011, Rajaraja Narendra in 1022, the Kalidindi conflict followed, and the battle of Koppam occurred in 1053.

secs.t: Capitals and inscriptions → ruler (Pishtapura, Vengi, Rajamahendravaram; end of the line)

x: Kubja Vishnuvardhana used Pithapuram as the first capital, Jayasimha Vallabha I used Vengi, and Rajamahendravaram was associated with Amma I and Rajaraja Narendra.
Vengi, corresponding to Pedavegi near Eluru, was the capital under
Jayasimha Vallabha I
The Kopparam copper plates dated to 631 CE describe Kubja Vishnuvardhana as
Yuvaraja
The Nandampudi inscription records Rajaraja Narendra's grant to Narayana Bhattu, written by Nannaya, and the Korumelli plates are also associated with Rajaraja Narendra.

secs.t: Titles → ruler

x: Exam angle: title-to-king matching; the Kiranapuram/Achalapuram/Kandukur triplet is the favourite distractor trap.
The titles Tribhuvanankusa and Samasta Bhuvanashraya are associated with
Jayasimha I and Vishnuvardhana III
The APPSC key identifies
Kiranapuram, Achalapuram and Kandukur
as the three cities.
Chalukya Bhima was associated with Kollabhiganda, Saktivarma I with Chalukya Chandra, Vimaladitya with Rajamartanda, and Rajaraja Narendra with Rajarajanarayana.

secs.t: Copper-plate grants → ruler

x: Kopparam is associated with Kubja Vishnuvardhana, Vipparla with Jayasimha I, Chekurru with Ammaraja I, and Chipurupalli names the scholar Madhavasharma.
In the copper-plate grant association, the Kopparam plates are attributed to
Pulakesin II

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 1075 CE date excludes the later Chalukya-Chola phase, whereas the 1189 CE interpretation includes that phase in the dynastic reckoning.

Kubja Vishnuvardhana was the first king of the Eastern Chalukya line; Kulothunga I inherited the Chalukya kingdom in 1075 CE; Jayangondar recorded the Kalinga campaign; and the Vengi court laid the base for Telugu literature.

rows.title: Eastern Chalukya administration, society and religious conditions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Court scholars and artists - titles and works → holder/author

x: Chellavva
, also called Challavva, held the title “Gandharva-vidya-visarada” and served as a court singer and dancer.
Chalukya Bhima I granted Chellavva
Attili village and two kandikas of land
Mallappa was Chellavva’s father and was compared to
Tumburu
in the Attili inscription.
The respective royal titles were Kavi Pandita Kamadhenu, Kavigayaka Kalpataru and Kavyageetha Priyudu.

secs.t: Religious sects → royal patronage, popularity and centres

x: Jayasimha I
performed the Ashvamedha, while royal prashastis also boast of several Ashvamedhas.
It was customary for kings to build a temple for each battle fought, and Vijayaditya II built 108 temples.
Kubja Vishnuvardhana built the Kunti Madhava temple at Pithapuram and Danarnava built the Mandavya Narayana temple at Samalkot.

secs.t: Jain basadis and grants → royal donor

x: Vimaladitya built the Ramakonda cave temple for
his Jain guru Trikala Yogi Siddhanta Deva
, as recorded in the Ramateertham inscription.

Potlacheruvu was a leading Jain centre; the Ramakonda cave temple at Ramatirtham is associated with Vimaladitya; and Nedumba Vasati at Vijayawada is associated with Queen Ayyana Mahadevi in the stated attribution.

secs.t: Administration - Ashtadasa tirthas, territorial units, village officers

x: The kingdom followed the Saptanga idea and had Ashtadasa Tirthas, meaning eighteen offices.
The council of ministers was called Tirthulu, and the Samaharta was the chief among its members.
The state was organised into Vishayas or Mandalas under a Vishayapati or Mandaleswara.
The village head was known as
Grameyaka
, Gramani or Urgavunda.
Vanneyus were toll collectors, whereas the Sthanadhipati managed temple affairs.

secs.t: Society - caste groups, Brahmana agraharas

x: Eastern Chalukya society followed a varna-based order with Brahmin privilege, and kings often granted tax-free villages called agraharas to Brahmins.
Brahmins receiving tax-free agraharas performed
Hiranyagarbha and Bahusuvarna
rituals.
Under Jayasimha II, groups such as the Koya Kottalu were assimilated into the Brahmanical fold.
Panduranga
subdued the Boyas, while Jayasimha II is associated with the assimilation of the Koya Kottalu.

secs.t: Economy - land grants, taxes, trade guilds and ports

x: Brahmadeya and agrahara grants came to Andhra from the
Badami Chalukya model
Saktivarma’s coins have been found in Arakan, Burma, and trade with the eastern islands continued under Rajaraja Narendra.
Land revenue was the principal income and could be collected in cash, kind and services; Vatapi and Aihole functioned as urban and trade centres.

secs.t: Education - Ghatikas and agraharas as centres

x: Ghatikas were
advanced Sanskrit schools attached to agraharas or temples
The heads of Ghatikas were called
Ghatika Samanyulu
Mandasharma was the head of the
Asanapura Ghatika in Kammanadu
Ghatikas taught subjects such as Vedas, Vedangas, Dharmashastras, Tarka, Vyakarana, Arthashastra, Dhanurveda and Ayurveda.
Jain pupils began their studies with the expression “
Om Namah Siddham

secs.t: Temple institutions - endowments, servants and dancers

x: The
Sthanadhipati
was the officer who managed temple affairs.
Kings and vassals made land endowments, while musicians and dancers such as Chellavva were attached to temples and courts.
Hallisaka, or Kolatam, was
a popular dance
associated with the cultural life of the period.
Bhairavakona in Nellore preserves sculptures of the
veena, mridangam and cymbals

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Panchadarla temple, housing the Sri Uma Dharmalingeswara shrine, is located at
Dharapalem in Anakapalli district
Sanskrit was the official language, and patronage of Jainism, Buddhism and Hinduism indicates religious tolerance.
The persecution was later associated with the Kalamukha and Virashaiva traditions in the Kakatiya age; Potlacheruvu was among the sites attacked.
Panchadarla temple is at
Dharapalem in Anakapalli
, and its pillars carry Eastern Chalukya inscriptions.

rows.title: Eastern Chalukya art and architecture - Biccavolu, Draksharama and Samalkot temples
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Chalukya-Chola / Vengi style - influences combined, temple exemplifying it

x: The Eastern Chalukyas mainly followed the Dravida style, combining Pallava and Badami Chalukya influences with local Andhra features.
Some accounts describe the style as Vesara or Chalukya style and explain it as a blend of the Dravidian vimana form with Buddhist art.
Local laterite and limestone were used, and construction was concentrated in the Krishna-Godavari delta.

secs.t: Temple-building claims → ruler

x: Vijayaditya II, known as Narendramrigaraja, is credited with constructing 108 Shiva temples, reportedly at his 108 battle sites.
Chalukya Bhima I
is associated with building the Pancharamas or establishing them as Shaiva kshetras.
Rajaraja Narendra is associated with the Kotilingala, Markandeya and Vishnu temples at Rajahmundry, and the Vishnu temple later became the Pedda Masjid under the Tughlaqs.

secs.t: Temples → builder

x: Bhimeswara is at Draksharama, Kumararama at Samalkot, Kumaraswamy at Chebrolu and Someswara at Gunupudi near Bhimavaram.
The Parvateswara temple at Indrakeeladri is attributed to Bhattupu, a commander of Chalukya Bhima I.

secs.t: Pancharama kshetras → location + district

x: Somarama
is located at Gunupudi, near Bhimavaram, in West Godavari.
Ksheerarama is the exception to the two-storeyed form, and the Skanda Purana and Srinatha's Bhimeswara Puranam are associated literary sources.

secs.t: Biccavolu temple group - style influences, dating

x: Mukteswara, Vijayeswara, Chandrasekhara and Golingeswara are all members of the Bikkavolu temple group.
The Bikkavolu temple group belongs to the ninth-century period of
Gunaga Vijayaditya
The Vijayeswara temple contains carvings of the river goddesses
Ganga and Yamuna
Bikkavolu is treated as a
Chalukya-Reddi transition
group because of later Reddi additions.

secs.t: Draksharama vs Samalkot - plan and structural comparison

x: Draksharama and Samalkot share a closely similar two-storeyed plan, while Samalkot's gopuram is a later addition and both were later renovated by the Reddis.
Draksharama is noted for its massive lingam, huge Nandi mandapa and intricate carving.
The Samalkot shrine is known as
Bheemarama or Kumararama
Draksharama is one of
the Trilinga kshetras

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Badami Chalukyas developed Vesara in Karnataka, while the Vengi line transmitted a Dravida-based regional style into the Chalukya-Chola phase.
Rajahmundry
is called the cultural capital of the Andhras.

src: Sources: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.118, 134); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas > Architecture, Religion); CDI (Block09 Eastern Chalukyas > Art and Architecture; Block03 Vengi School; Block10 Reddi Architecture); APHQ (PYQs 2012, 2019, 2025); UPSC (Medieval History p.31); CDCA Aug 2026 p.39

rows.title: Andhra Cholas / Telugu Cholas - Renati Cholas and their inscriptions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Renati Chola inscriptions → ruler, language, date

x: The Kalamalla inscription belongs to Erikal Mutturaju Dhananjaya, also known as Dhanunjaya Varma, and is dated to 575 CE.
The Kalamalla inscription of Dhanunjaya is in Telugu prose, but it is not fully available today.
CDX lists 33 Renati Chola Telugu inscriptions, most of which are donation records or dana sasanalu.

secs.t: Renati Cholas - credited with establishing Telugu in Andhra's history

x: The Renati Cholas gave Telugu official and legislative status, and the period from 575 to 848 CE saw Telugu used in complete prose sentences.

secs.t: Ruler - period - contribution

x: Dhanunjaya Varma was the founder, son of Nandivarma, and ruled from Chimbapuram.
Mahendra Vikramavarman was the grandson of Nandivarma and bore the title Muditha Silakshara Navarama.
Punyakumara's period of rule is given as
Satyaditya
bore the titles Chola Maharaja and Chola Mahadhiraju, and the decline began after his reign.

secs.t: Claimed ancestry and titles of the Renati Cholas

x: Pormukharama, Purushashardula and Uttamottama were titles of Punyakumara.
The Renati Cholas claimed Suryavamsa Kshatriya descent from Karikala Chola, although their culture and administration were Telugu.

secs.t: Territory - Renadu → present districts, capital

x: Renadu was also called Renadu Saptasahasra, referring to
7,000 villages
Renadu lay where
Kadapa, Kurnool and Chittoor
meet, in the upper Pennar basin.
Renadu was situated in the upper Pennar basin and was also known as Renati Cholanadi.
The Renati Cholas ruled from the
fifth to the eighth centuries CE

secs.t: Telugu Choda families → region

x: The Konidena Chodas ruled in Kammanadu, comprising parts of Guntur, Ongole and Bapatla, with Konidena near Narasaraopet as their capital.
The Konidena branch dates from the mid-tenth century and included King Tribhuvana Mallachoda, also known as Tenkanaditya.
The
Nellore Chodas
, associated with Vikrama Simhapuri, were regarded as the foremost Telugu Choda clan.
The Velanati Choda line ended when
Kakatiya Ganapatideva killed Mummadi Rajendra Chola

secs.t: Nellore Chodas - rulers and court poet

x: Bijjana
was the progenitor of the Nellore Choda family, while Manumasiddhi I was its first king.
Tikkana Choda, also called Tikkabhupati, was the son of Manumasiddhi I and took the title Chola Sthapanacharya after helping Rajendra Chola ascend the throne.
Kavi-Brahma Tikkana approached Kakatiya Ganapati for assistance against
Vijayaganda Gopala

secs.t: Relations with Pallavas, Badami Chalukyas and Eastern Chalukyas

x: The Renati Cholas were first feudatories of the Pallavas, later of the Badami Chalukyas; the Pallava–Chalukya conflict produced the three Rayalaseema states, after which the Banas and Vaidumbas ruled the area.
Purushartha Saramu
by Sivadevayya records the Kakatiya-period rule that a woman's property passed to her daughters and daughters' daughters.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 25 inscriptions copied by the ASI Epigraphy Branch date from the 2nd to the 16th centuries CE and span the Satavahana to Vijayanagara periods.
The inscriptions belonged broadly to
the 2nd to 16th centuries CE
, covering a long span of Andhra history.
The inscriptions in question were copied in the Nallamala Tiger Reserve; the Seshachalam reference concerns a separate set of inscriptions.

src: Sources: CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.150-151, 310); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Successor and vassal dynasties); CDI (Block09 The Renati Cholas); APHQ (PYQs 2012, 2019); TH 14 Jun 2026

rows.title: Political overview of Andhradesa, 11th to 16th centuries
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Dynasty succession - chronological order

x: Exam angle: arrange dynasties chronologically; "which dynasty founded Berar" → Imad Shahis.
The
Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
preceded the Kakatiyas, Musunuri Nayakas and Reddis in the stated sequence.
Vijayanagara emerged in 1336, the Bahmani kingdom in 1347, the Gajapatis in 1435 and the Imad Shahis in 1490.
The Kakatiyas had a feudatory phase from 956, Rudradeva asserted independence in 1163, and the Reddi kingdom began in 1325.

secs.t: Dynasty - period - capital

x: Anavema Reddy
shifted the Reddi capital from Addanki to Kondavidu.
Vijayanagara was based at Hampi, and after 1565 its capitals included Penugonda and Chandragiri.
The Qutb Shahi dynasty is dated from 1518 to 1687, had seven sultans, and shifted its capital from Golconda to Hyderabad.
The Qutb Shahi state was Shia, used Persian officially, had Telugu-speaking people, and ended under Abul Hasan Tana Shah.

secs.t: Contest over the Raichur Doab, Krishna-Godavari doab and coastal Andhra

x: The Raichur Doab was agriculturally valuable because of its fertile black soil and strategically important because of its location.
The Krishna-Godavari region and coastal Andhra were contested by the
Reddis, Velamas, Gajapatis, Bahmanis and Vijayanagara
The
Raichur Doab
, also called Raichur Antarvedi, was the principal cause of conflict between the Bahmani Sultanate and Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Feudatory families that became kingdoms

x: The Kakatiyas were feudatories first under the Rashtrakutas and subsequently under the Kalyani Chalukyas before becoming sovereign under Rudradeva in 1163.
The Musunuri Nayakas, Reddis and Velamas were three of Prataparudra's generals who survived the Kakatiya collapse in 1323 and established independent kingdoms.
The Qutb Shahis were Bahmani tarafdars, or governors, of Telangana from 1496 and became independent in 1518.

secs.t: Battles → contending dynasties

x: Rakshasi-Tangadi was fought on 26 January 1565, Raichur in 1520, Muttukur in 1263 and Palnadu in the 12th century.
The Kondavidu and Kondapalli sieges took place in
, during the campaigns of Krishnadevaraya against the Gajapatis.
Palnadu belongs to the 12th century, followed by Muttukur in 1263, the Kondavidu-Kondapalli sieges in 1515–1516, Raichur in 1520 and Rakshasi-Tangadi in 1565.

secs.t: Immediate successor → predecessor in each Andhra region

x: The Telangana sequence was Kakatiyas, Delhi Sultanate in 1323, Musunuri Nayakas, Velamas/Bahmanis and finally the Qutb Shahis.
In Rayalaseema, the sequence was Kakatiyas through Kayastha chiefs, followed by Vijayanagara and then the Qutb Shahis or later powers.
Singama was associated with the Velamas, Prolaya Vemareddy with the Reddis, Harihara-Bukka with Vijayanagara and Hasan Gangu with the Bahmani formation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The year 1323 marked the end of Telugu imperial unity, which continued until the Qutb Shahis reunited the region.
The survey included inscriptions associated with the
Satavahanas, Eastern Chalukyas, Kalyani Chalukyas, Potapi Cholas, Kakatiyas, Reddy rulers and Vijayanagara
The new Seshachalam inscriptions are dated to the 16th century and linked to
the Tuluva or early Aravidu period
of Vijayanagara.

src: Sources: APP (AP History Medieval - Kakatiyas, Vijayanagara, Qutb Shahis); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.174, 209, 246, 282-284); CDI (Block03 Qutb Shahis; Block04 Qutubsahis); APHQ (aph2003_11, aph2005_1, aph2017_2, aph2019_24); TH 14 Jun 2026; APPCA Jun 2026 (Seshachalam)

rows.title: Minor dynasties of Andhradesa - Chalukya-Cholas, Kona Haihayas, Matsyas, Pusapati and others
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-67

secs.t: Minor dynasties → region/capital

x: The Palnadu Haihayas were associated with Gurajala, the Gona Haihayas with Vardhamanapuram, and the Panchadhara Haihayas with the Visakhapatnam-Yelamanchili region.
The Bana kings claimed descent from
Bali
and were associated with Rayalaseema and part of Karnataka.
The Velanati line ended when Kakatiya Ganapatideva killed its last member, Mummadi Rajendra Choda.

secs.t: Palnadu war (Palnati Yuddham) - site, factions, figures

x: The correct order is Kulottunga I’s accession in 1070, the beginning of Bhimaraju I’s period in 1108, the Palnadu war in 1182, and the Padmanabham defeat in 1794.
Brahmanaidu was the minister and leader of the Malideva faction and was known as a social reformer associated with interdining and Chapakudu.
The
Velamas
were described as intruders into Reddi-dominated Palnadu and were driven out in the Battle of Karempudi.

secs.t: Chalukya-Chola viceroys of Vengi - titles, coronation, feudatories

x: Kulottunga I took the Chola throne in 1070 and Vengi in 1075, after the death of Vijayaditya VII, the last Eastern Chalukya.
Jayangondar
wrote Kalingattuparani, which describes Kulottunga I’s conquest of Kalinga by sea.
Velanati Gonka I was the Samasta Senadhipati of Vengi and fought off the Kalyani Chalukyas and Kalingas.

secs.t: Kota and Chagi chiefs - seat, overlords

x: Bhimaraju I ruled from 1108 to 1127 and supported the Chalukya-Cholas in Kalinga campaigns with the Velanati Chodas.
Bhimaraju II was associated with the 1182 Palnadu war, absorbed Kondapadamati, and bore the title Dannala Kota Padaveshtita Kadana.
The Kota chiefs were successively subordinate to the Chalukya-Cholas, the Velanati Chodas and finally the Kakatiyas.

secs.t: Matsyas of Oddadi - origin legend, territory

x: The Matsyas of Oddadi were northern Andhra chieftains of
the upland Srikakulam-Vizianagaram zone
The Matsyas of Oddadi were grouped with
the Ananda Gotrikas
All three statements describe the Matsyas of Oddadi: their early Telugu records, hero-stones and small temples, and bilingual Telugu-Kalinga border culture.

secs.t: Minor dynasty inscriptions → ruler

x: The Draksharama inscription identifies the place as the coronation seat of
a Chalukya-Chola viceroy
The
Taruvariyur inscription
praises Nellore Choda Manumasiddi I as a thunderbolt to his enemies.
The Kalamalla inscription of 575 CE is associated with
Renati Choda Dhanunjaya
Both Amaravati (Dhanyakatakam) and Tripurantakam lay in
Kota
territory.
The Kalamalla inscription of the Renati Chodas, dated to 575 CE, is regarded as the first Telugu inscription.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Post-Eastern Chalukya Andhra was a web of nadus under vassals.
The Velanati Chodas were not related to the Telugu Chodas.

src: Sources: APHQ (2025 aph2025_15; 2011 aph2011_10; 2017 aph2017_21); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.137, 145, 147); APP (Ancient Part 2 Unit 1 - successor dynasties, Eastern Chalukyas); CDI (Block09 Ananda Gotrikas/Matsyas)

rows.title: Kalyani (Western) Chalukyas - Tailapa II, Vikramaditya VI; Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita, Vijnaneswara's Mitakshara

secs.t: Mitakshara - author, patron, Dayabhaga comparison, schools, medieval jurists

x: Mitakshara is a commentary on the
Yajnavalkya Smriti
, composed by Vijnaneshwara.
Mitakshara recognises the sons’ right by birth, whereas Dayabhaga postpones it until the father’s death and was followed mainly in Bengal and Assam.
Rajasekhara was a poet-dramatist, not a jurist.
The Hindu Succession Act still rests largely on the principles of the
Mitakshara
school.

secs.t: Ruler → reign period + achievement

x: Exam angle: reign period of Vikramaditya VI -
Someshvara I killed Rajadhiraja I at Koppam, assumed the title Vengi Purveshwara and granted Hanamkonda to Prola I. The Chalukya-Vikrama era was founded by Vikramaditya VI.
Vikramaditya VI was the greatest Kalyani Chalukya ruler, ruled for 50 years, bore the title Tribhuvanamalla and brought the Vengi feudatories under his authority.

secs.t: Chalukya-Vikrama era - founder, starting year

x: Vikramaditya VI founded the Chalukya-Vikrama era in 1076 CE, the year of his accession, replacing the Saka era in royal records.

secs.t: Bilhana - origin, patron, subject of his work

x: Bilhana’s Vikramankadevacharita is a historical mahakavya dealing with the life and conquests of Vikramaditya VI.
Bilhana claimed that the Chalukyas originated at a place called
Brahmachulakam
Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet at Vikramaditya VI’s court and likened the ruler’s reign to Ramarajya.

secs.t: Someshvara III - Manasollasa contents

x: Someshvara III
, who ruled from 1126 to 1138 CE, was the author of Manasollasa or Abhilashitartha Chintamani.
Manasollasa is regarded as the earliest major record of
South Indian recipes
Vikramankadevacharita was written by Bilhana.

secs.t: Kalyani Chalukya art - Lakkundi, Itagi Mahadeva temple

x: Kalyani Chalukya architecture is associated with the mature Vesara, also called the Gadag style.
Kalyani Chalukya temples used chloritic schist or soapstone, often employed star-shaped plans, and provided a model for later Hoysala architecture.
The Itagi Mahadeva temple is popularly known as the “
Emperor among temples

secs.t: Successor feudatory powers → region

x: The
Hoysalas
were based in southern Karnataka, with Dwarasamudra as their capital.
These powers emerged in different regions after the weakening of Kalyani Chalukya authority.
Kalachuri ruler Bijjala seized the throne at Kalyani around 1156 CE.
The dynasty ended around 1189 CE, while successor powers expanded and the Chalukya–Chola hold over Vengi weakened.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kalyani Chalukyas checked Chola expansion towards the north, while the Mitakshara tradition associated with their court shaped Hindu inheritance law for about a millennium.
The broad periods are Badami from the sixth to eighth centuries, Vengi from the seventh to eleventh centuries, and Kalyani from the late tenth to twelfth centuries.

src: Sources: CDI (Block03 Kalyani Chalukyas - Introduction, Literature, Exam value additions); CDX (pp.122, 136-138, 165); APP (AP History Ancient Part 2 > Eastern Chalukyas); UPSC (Medieval History pp.18, 24, 27, 48)

rows.title: Imperial Cholas - Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I; Gangaikonda title and the naval expeditions
sub: Group-II S1-32: The Cholas - political outline: Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I

secs.t: Founder of the imperial line - capital captured, successor

x: Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur in 850 CE from the
Muttarayars
Aditya I
succeeded Vijayalaya.

secs.t: Ruler → title + achievement (Vijayalaya to Kulottunga I)

x: Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur in 850 CE, followed by Aditya I’s defeat of Aparajita, Parantaka I’s defeat at Takkolam in 949 CE, and the Brihadeshvara temple in 1010 CE.
Maduraikonda was the title of Parantaka I, not Kulottunga I. Rajaraja I was known as Mummadi Chola, Rajendra I as Gangaikondachola, and Rajadhiraja I as Yanai-mel-thunjina Devar.

secs.t: Chola-Eastern Chalukya matrimonial alliances → figure

x: Rajaraja Narendra married Ammanga Devi in
Saktivarman I, the elder brother of Vimaladitya, ruled Vengi with Rajaraja I’s help after
Jatachoda Bhima
was ousted.
Vijayaditya VII died in 1075, after which Kulottunga I, the son of Rajaraja Narendra, merged Vengi into the Chola Empire, creating the Chalukya-Chola line.

secs.t: Chola viceroys of Vengi - titles, coronation sites, Rajamahendravaram

x: Rajaraja III ruled from Jagannathapuram, Vira Chola served twice as viceroy, and Rajaraja Chola Ganga exercised authority up to Mahendragiri.
Amma I made Rajamahendravaram the capital, Rajaraja Narendra made it famous, and it was an important centre in the Vengi administration.
Parantaka Chola
was the last ruler of the Chalukya-Chola line in Vengi.

secs.t: Naval expeditions → ruler + destination

x: Exam angle: "Who led the campaign against Srivijaya?" -
Rajendra I
(asked by UPSC 2025 and the APPSC Group-II papers).
The 1025 CE Kadaram conquest was conducted by Rajendra I. Rajaraja I is associated with the Maldives and the attack on the Chera fleet at Kandalur Salai, while Kulottunga I campaigned in Kalinga.
Rajaraja I attacked the Chera fleet at Kandalur Salai and captured the Maldives; Rajendra I attacked Srivijaya and Kadaram; Kulottunga I campaigned in Kalinga.

secs.t: Rajendra I - Ganga expedition, new capital, Chola Gangam tank, titles

x: In 1022 CE, Rajendra I led a northern campaign, crossed the Ganga and defeated the Pala ruler Mahipala I.
Rajendra I assumed the title Gangaikondachola after his successful northern expedition that reached and crossed the Ganga.
Gangaikondachola was a title of Rajendra I. Kulottunga I was associated with the title Sungam Tavirtta Chola.

secs.t: Capitals and core region (Uraiyur, Tanjore, Gangaikondacholapuram, Coromandel)

x: The
Kaveri delta
formed the core region of the Chola state and supported its agrarian and political strength.
Coromandel is derived from
Cholamandalam
, the traditional name connected with the Chola region.
Rajendra I dug the Chola Gangam tank, and later Cauvery channels were built on the Sangam-era Kallanai of Karikala.

secs.t: Battles → participants + victor (Takkolam, Koppam, Kudalasangamam)

x: The wars arose mainly from succession disputes in Vengi, with each side backing a claimant, and from the wider struggle for supremacy in the Deccan.
Takkolam was won by the Rashtrakutas under Krishna III; at Koppam Rajendra II claimed victory after Rajadhiraja I’s death; Virarajendra won at Kudalasangamam; Rajendra I’s army won at Kalidindi.

secs.t: Kulottunga I - parentage, titles, embassy to China, succession

x: After Virarajendra and Adhirajendra died around 1070–71, Rajendra Chalukya took the Chola throne as Kulottunga I.
After Vijayaditya VII’s death in 1075, Kulottunga I
merged Vengi with his Chola dominions
and ruled both regions, giving rise to the Chalukya-Chola association.
Kulottunga I was the son of Rajaraja Narendra and Ammanga Devi, was also called Rajendra Chalukya, and took the Chola throne in 1070 CE.

secs.t: Chola succession - founder, successors, chronology

x: Exam angle: "Identify the incorrect statement" sets on founder / successor / title pairs.
All three statements correctly describe Rajaraja I, also known as Arumolivarman, whose reign is dated 985–1014 CE and marked major expansion of the Chola state.
The line ended in 1070–71 with Virarajendra followed by Abhirajendra, after which Kulottunga I began the Chalukya-Chola line.

secs.t: Titles → Chola ruler

x: Madurai-konda was associated with Parantaka I's capture of Madurai; Mummudi Chola and Ulakalanda Perumal were titles of Rajaraja I; and Gangaikonda Chola was assumed by Rajendra I after the Ganga expedition.
All four statements describe conquests or political actions attributed to Rajaraja I: the capture of Quilon, the subjugation of the Pandya region, the Maldives conquest and the arrangement in Vengi.

secs.t: Later Cholas - Sri Lanka relations and decline

x: Rajendra I's Ganga expedition took place in 1022 CE; Kulottunga I's China mission occurred later, Vijayabahu I expelled the Cholas around 1070, and Rajendra III was gone by 1279.
The sequence follows the stated associations: Kaveripattinam with Roman trade, Nagapattinam with the vihara, China with Kulottunga I's mission, and the Coromandel coast with Arab horse trade.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed project is a 125-foot Rajaraja Chola statue at the Grand Chola Museum in Thanjavur, spread over 52 acres and costing Rs 56.41 crore.
Vengi was central to Chola–Chalukya rivalry; Kulottunga I united the Tamil and Andhra kingdoms; and the Mandalika Yugam followed from 1076 to approximately 1210.
Vengi was the central arena of succession disputes, and both the Cholas and Kalyani Chalukyas backed rival claimants to gain political control.
