rows.title: Chola local self-government - the Uttaramerur inscriptions, ur, sabha, nagaram, variyams
sub: Group-II S1-34: Chola local self-government - Uttaramerur inscriptions, ur, sabha, nagaram, variyams

secs.t: Terms → meaning (variyam, kudumbu, kudavolai, perumakkal)

x: Exam angle: this exact four-term match was asked in
APPSC-G1 2022 and 2023
- key a-IV, b-I, c-II, d-III.
Kudavolai was the selection procedure in which names written on palm leaves were placed in a pot and drawn by lot.
Kudumbu means ward, perumakkal means a member of the village assembly, and variyapperumakkal means elected committee members.

secs.t: Dynasty-identification - village self-government

x: The
Cholas
are renowned for their elaborate system of village self-government and autonomous local institutions.

secs.t: Uttaramerur inscriptions - ruler, year, contents

x: The two important Uttaramerur inscriptions on village administration belong to the reign of
Parantaka I
The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I are dated 919 CE and 921 CE.
The
Uttaramerur inscriptions
provide detailed information about Chola village government and administration.
Owning a residence
was a qualification, whereas failure to submit accounts, committing sins and stealing property were disqualifications.

secs.t: Variyams (committees) → function

x: Samvatsara variyam dealt with annual works, eri variyam with tanks and water distribution, pon variyam with gold and finance, and thotta variyam with gardens.
Pon variyam
dealt with gold and related financial and currency-checking matters.
Pon variyam dealt with gold, finance and currency checking, not temple worship.
The Uttaramerur record refers to committees dealing with
irrigation, gardens, justice and finance

secs.t: Village assemblies → type (ur, sabha/mahasabha, nagaram)

x: Ur was the general assembly in ordinary non-brahmadeya, or vellanvagai, villages.
Sabha or Mahasabha was the Brahmin-only assembly of agraharas or brahmadeya villages, with membership based on property, family, learning and conduct.
Nagaram was the assembly of merchant groups in market and commercial centres.

secs.t: Election procedure - kudavolai, kudumbu

x: The village was divided into 30 kudumbus or wards for the selection process.
Names of eligible candidates were written on palm leaves, placed in a pot, and drawn by a young boy or girl, generally one from each ward.
Persons who had served on a committee during the previous three years were disqualified from selection.

secs.t: Powers of assemblies - land, tax, justice, temple

x: Chola village assemblies had proprietary rights over communal land, controlled private land and were regarded as the absolute proprietors of newly acquired village lands.
Village assemblies could raise loans, levy taxes and collect royal dues in cash, kind or both.
Rajaraja I directed the Cholamandalam sabhas to serve the
Brihadeshvara temple

secs.t: Comparison with present-day Panchayati Raj

x: The 73rd Amendment does not prescribe Vedic learning; qualifications for PRI elections operate within the constitutional and state-law framework.
The Chola village assemblies had three-year terms, whereas Panchayati Raj Institutions have five-year terms.
The intermediate tier is optional below the twenty-lakh population threshold, Panchayats normally have five-year terms, and elections after dissolution are to be completed within six months.

secs.t: Village autonomy as the hallmark - dynasty comparison

x: The
Cholas
are especially remembered for elected village assemblies, committees and the kudavolai lottery, representing the culmination of local self-government.

Pallava institutions provided an earlier base, the Cholas elaborated them, Badami Chalukya administration was highly centralised, and Rashtrakuta village assemblies had a significant administrative and dispute-related role.
The segmentary-state interpretation stresses the persistence of local autonomy, particularly at the periphery, rather than uniform central control.

secs.t: Nattar and nadu-level assemblies

x: The nattar was the assembly of a nadu, functioning above the village level and dealing with matters such as revenue collection and local disputes.
The nattar consisted of leading peasant landholders, particularly vellalas, of the nadu.
The nattar was the nadu-level assembly of leading landholders, while the nagaram was associated with the nadu’s market town and functioned alongside it.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The kudavolai, or ballot-pot system, was cited as evidence of
India’s early democratic traditions
The system had democratic procedures, but participation was restricted to an educated and propertied elite, especially Brahmins in sabhas.
Kakatiya and Velanati inscriptions
refer to village mahajana assemblies in Andhra, forming a weaker parallel to the Chola institutions.

rows.title: Chola central and provincial administration, land classification, revenue and irrigation
sub: Group-II S1-33: Chola central and provincial administrative system
Group-II S1-35: Chola revenue administration, land classification, army and navy

secs.t: Land and revenue terms → meaning (eripatti, vellanvagai, brahmadeya, devadana, salabhoga, pallichchandam)

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2016 pair-matching - Eripatti (tank land) and Ghatikas (colleges) correct; Taniyurs described as "villages donated to a single Brahmin" is wrong.
Vellanvagai denoted land held by non-Brahmin peasant proprietors, while brahmadeya, devadana and pallichchandam referred respectively to land gifted to Brahmins, temples and Jaina institutions.
Antarayam was a cash rural tax, Eccoru was the obligation to feed officials, Nettal was compulsory labour and Kasu was a gold coin.

secs.t: Chola kingship - succession, titles, rituals, temple role

x: Exam angle: "Which dynasty's king declared his successor during his own tenure?" -
Chola
The Chola king was presented in divine and royal terms: royal images could be placed beside deities, and inscriptions praised his military, cultural and social-religious roles.
The bureaucracy expanded from the reign of Rajaraja I and weakened after
Kulottunga I
as local chieftains gained greater power.

secs.t: Administrative divisions → hierarchy

x: The hierarchy proceeded from Ur at the village level, through Nadu and Kottam or Valanadu, to Mandalam at the provincial level.
Mandalam was the provincial unit, the empire had eight such provinces, and they were administered by viceroys or governors, often princes or nobles.
Chola provincial territories included both annexed principalities and samanta or vassal territories that paid tribute.

secs.t: Officials - perundaram, sirudaram, adhikari, nattar

x: An adhikari was a royal officer supervising local bodies.
Nattar were members of the Nadu assembly.
Hereditary bodyguards were maintained through land assignments yielding revenue.

secs.t: Land survey and revenue - Rajaraja's survey, kadamai, taxes

x: Rajaraja I
conducted a detailed land survey and assessment, and such surveys were repeated periodically.
The Leiden plates record a grant of 8,943 kalam of paddy by Rajaraja I; the other combinations are incorrect.
Perundaram and sirudaram represented higher and lower officials respectively; Shrikaranam was the revenue department and Dharmasana the royal court of justice.

secs.t: Irrigation - tanks, eri variyam, Cauvery channels

x: The
eri variyam
was the tank committee responsible for managing tanks and distributing water to fields.
Eripatti land
was set aside to finance the maintenance and repair of village tanks.
The Grand Anicut on the Kaveri was built by
Karikala, the Sangam Chola
, and was maintained by later Cholas.

secs.t: Army and navy - regiments, cantonments

x: The Chola army included elephants, cavalry and spear-armed infantry.
Kaikkolar referred to royal infantry regiments.
The Velaikkarar were loyal bodyguard troops who were sworn to die with the king.
Kadagams were
military cantonments
Chola naval campaigns extended to the
Maldives, Sri Lanka and Srivijaya

secs.t: Mandalams → region

x: Cholamandalam
referred to the Chola core in the Kaveri delta, particularly the Thanjavur area.
Jayankondacholamandalam referred to Tondaimandalam,
the former Pallava country around Kanchi
Mummudicholamandalam denoted
northern Sri Lanka
and was so named by Rajaraja I.

secs.t: Royal secretaries and officials (tirumandira-olai, olai-nayagam)

x: The
tirumandira-olai
was the royal secretary who recorded the king’s oral orders on palm leaf.
The olai-nayagam, or chief secretary, checked and countersigned royal orders before they were sent to officials.
The royal orders had a Sanskrit preamble containing genealogy and conquests, followed by the Tamil operative portion.

secs.t: Provincial governors - princes as viceroys

x: Each mandalam was governed by
a viceroy or governor, often a royal prince or noble
; offices were paid by land assignments.
Kulottunga I’s sons ruled
Vengi
as viceroys or Rajapratinidhis.
A Samanta was a defeated king restored on condition that he accepted overlordship, paid tribute and provided military help.
Burton Stein’s segmentary model emphasised a strong Kaveri core with continuing local autonomy in peripheral areas.

secs.t: Temple as administrative-economic centre

x: Devadana lands were grants made to temples.
Chola temples were major landholders, employers and lenders, and also served as venues for village assembly meetings.
Rajaraja I directed the Sabhas of Cholamandalam to perform services for the
Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur

secs.t: Royal inscriptions and copper plates as sources (Anbil, Tiruvalangadu, Larger Leiden plates)

x: Anaimangalam village near Nagapattinam was granted to the Chulamanivarma-vihara, built by the Srivijaya king Sri Mara Vijayotunga Varman.
The Chudamani Vihara was built by
Sri Mara Vijayotunga Varman of Srivijaya
, belonging to the Sailendra line.
The larger Leiden plates contain 21 sheets, are attached by a bronze ring bearing the three dynastic emblems, and contain Tamil and Sanskrit text.

secs.t: Navy - ruler credited with it, reach, overseas bases

x: Exam angle: "Which South Indian state was famous for naval power?" -
Chola
; "Which king started the navy?" -
Rajaraja I
Rajendra I’s 1025 CE naval expedition targeted Srivijaya, captured Kadaram in present-day Kedah, and reached parts of Sumatra.
The Kalingattuparani describes Kulottunga I’s conquest of Kalinga as being carried out with
great naval power

secs.t: Famine relief and remission of taxes

x: Kulottunga I
was called Sungam Tavirtta Chola, meaning the Chola who abolished tolls.
The ur was the village assembly involved in land matters, including the granting of tax exemptions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Vengi administration had the Ashtadasha Tirthas, or 18 departments; the Yuvaraja participated as a partner in governance; and councils were called Varagoshti.
Ashtadasha Tirthas means eighteen departments; the Yuvaraja was a partner in governance; Varagoshti denoted councils; and ULPIN was the unique land parcel identification number.

Andhra Pradesh launched the Mee Bhoomi-Blockchain pilot, providing a unique digital ID for each land parcel, with statewide expansion planned from November; the State also runs Mee Bhoomi-Mee Hakku re-survey and passbook camps.

rows.title: Chola economy and merchant guilds - Ayyavole, Manigramam; overseas trade with China and Srivijaya

secs.t: Merchant guilds → base and activities (Ayyavole, Manigramam, Nanadesi, Anjuvannam, Nagaram, Sreni)

x: Exam angle: "Which institution belonged to foreign trade?" - UPPSC 2018 key accepts
Nanadesis or Manigramam
Ayyavole-500 originated from Aihole and operated widely; Manigramam was a foreign-trade corporation; Ubhaya Nanadesi handled both domestic and foreign trade; Nagaram was a market-town assembly.
Manigramam handled foreign or long-distance trade; Ainnurruvar was inter-regional and overseas; Nanadesis represented merchants of many countries; Nagaram was local and domestic.

secs.t: Inscriptions of guilds abroad - Sri Lanka, Sumatra, Myanmar, Thailand

x: The Barus or Lobu Tua inscription in Sumatra is an Ayyavole-500 Tamil inscription dated 1088.
Takua Pa names Manigramam, Pagan has a Nanadesi Vishnu temple inscription, Sri Lanka has many Ayyavole and Nanadesi inscriptions, and Barus has the 1088 Ayyavole-500 inscription.

secs.t: Ports → trade (Nagapattinam, Mahabalipuram, Kaveripattinam, Quilon)

x: Kaveripattinam is identified with the Sangam Chola period, Mahabalipuram with the Pallava era, Nagapattinam with the Chola period and Quilon with later Arab and Chinese trade.
Nagapattinam
was the main Chola port and the location of the Chudamani Vihara.
Mahabalipuram was a Pallava-era port.

secs.t: Items of trade - exports and imports

x: The principal exports included textiles, pepper and precious stones.

secs.t: Temple as economic institution - roles

x: Temples functioned as major economic institutions: they were large landholders, employers and lenders and received guild donations and royal grants.
Devadana holdings, royal and guild donations, and the direction given to sabhas demonstrate the temple’s economic role.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Netherlands formally returned the Anaimangalam or Leiden plates during the Prime Minister’s visit to The Hague.
Ayyavole and Manigramam were active in Andhra, especially around Penugonda, while Nakaras headed by Shreshthis traded under the Eastern Chalukyas.
The guild networks extended Chola commerce and Dravidian cultural influence across the Bay of Bengal.

rows.title: Chola art - Brihadeshwara temple, Dravida style elements, Chola bronzes (Nataraja), Tamil literature
sub: Group-II S1-36: Chola economy, trade guilds, art, architecture and Tamil literature

secs.t: Temple → builder + site + chronological order

x: Exam angle: builder-temple matching and 4-temple chronological order mixing Pallava and Chola monuments.
Exam angle: chronology sets -
Pallava
Mahabalipuram rathas ("Sapta pagoda") →
Shore temple
Brihadeeswara
Gangaikondacholapuram
The
Airavatesvara Temple
at Darasuram is noted for its miniature masterpiece form, stone chariot drawn by horses and Musical Steps.
The concave curvilinear profile of Gangaikondacholapuram is described as having feminine grace, in contrast to the masculine bulk of Thanjavur.
The Chit Sabha of the
Thillai Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram
contains carvings of 108 classical dance poses.

secs.t: Chola bronzes - casting technique, Nataraja iconography, other forms

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2021 - "four hands" and "man's earring right, woman's left" are
both correct
The Cholas perfected the
cire perdue
, or lost-wax, casting technique for bronze icons.
Chola bronzes were worshipped icons, distinguished by fine craftsmanship, intricate jewellery and expressive faces.
The lower left hand directs attention to the raised foot, symbolising
liberation or refuge

secs.t: Dravida style elements - vimana, gopuram, mandapa, garbhagriha, prakara; Dravida vs Nagara pinnacle

x: Nagara temples generally lack large enclosures, Dravida temples emphasise enclosed complexes, and Vesara combines elements of Nagara and Dravida.
Gopuram
refers to the imposing entrance gateway tower characteristic of South Indian temples.
The dominant Dravida tower is the vimana, which is pyramidal and multi-storeyed and rises over the garbhagriha.
Elaborate prakara walls and gateways are characteristic of Dravida temples, whereas Nagara temples usually lack such elaborate enclosures.
Shikhara
denotes the topmost, dome-like crowning portion of the vimana; the monolithic shikhara of the Thanjavur temple is especially noted.

secs.t: Tamil literature → author

x: Kamba Ramayanam or Ramavataram was composed by
Kamban
and is a Tamil adaptation of the Ramayana, not merely a translation of Valmiki.
Kalingattupparani was written by Jayamkondar, Moovar Ula by Ottakuthar, Nalavenba by Pugalendi and Nannul by Pavanandhi.
The Tirumurai is the Shaiva canon containing hymns of the Nayanars, including the Tevaram, and was compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi during the time of Rajaraja I.

secs.t: Great Living Chola Temples - UNESCO listing components

x: The three components are Brihadeeswara at Thanjavur, the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram and Airavatesvara at Darasuram.
The grouping therefore places the original listing before the extension.

secs.t: Chola frescoes - Brihadeshwara paintings

x: The Brihadeeswara frescoes show Shiva as Tripurantaka and royal portraits of Rajaraja I together with his guru Karuvur Thevar.
Murals are known at Gangaikondacholapuram, Narthamalai paintings show Shiva and Parvati, and notable Dakshinamurthy panels occur at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram.
The Thanjavur temple is known for Brihadeeswara frescoes and Dakshinamurthy panels, not exclusively for Jain manuscript illustrations.

secs.t: Temple inscriptions as records of dancers, musicians, donations

x: The inscriptions mention about 400 temple dancing women and also refer to musicians and other staff who were paid through grants.
The Uttiramerur inscriptions, associated with Parantaka I, record the Kudavolai or pot-ballot system used in village assembly elections.
Both statements are true, and the use of mandapas for ceremonial dances and rituals explains the social and cultural role of Chola temples.

secs.t: Foreign trade and embassies - China, Srivijaya, Arabs, ports

x: The
Cholas
were the South Indian dynasty particularly known for maritime trade with Southeast Asia and links with China, Srivijaya, Sri Lanka and the Arab world.
Chola–Srivijaya relations began amicably, but obstruction of Indian traders led to Rajendra I’s 1025 expedition to Kadaram.
Kulottunga I added
4,500 kalam of paddy
to the grant of the Chulamanivarma-vihara.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Chola-era Anaimangalam copper plates were held by
Leiden University
for almost two centuries.
The Draksharama Bhimeswara temple shows an independent Chalukya-Chola style combining
Pallava and early Chalukya elements
Angkor Wat is an example of South-East Asian architecture influenced by the wider transmission of Dravidian art; it is not a monument of Imperial Chola style located in Tamil Nadu.

rows.title: Hoysalas - Vishnuvardhana and Ramanuja; Belur, Halebid and Somanathapura temple architecture

secs.t: Capitals - ancient and modern names

x: Belur
was the earlier capital of the Hoysalas, before Dwarasamudra became their capital.
Halebidu means “old city”; the name was adopted after
Dwarasamudra was sacked by the Delhi armies

secs.t: Temple → builder + deity + site

x: Chennakeshava is at Belur, Hoysaleswara at Halebid, and Keshava at Somanathapura.
Vishnuvardhana built the temple in 1117 after defeating the Cholas at
Talakad
Hoysaleswara was built around 1121 by
Ketamalla, an officer of Vishnuvardhana
The Keshava Temple at Somanathapura is dedicated to Vishnu and was built in 1268 by Somanatha, the general of Narasimha III.

secs.t: Hoysala style - style family, ground plan, stone, pillar type, sculptors' signatures

x: Hoysala architecture is generally classified as
Vesara
in examination keys, although it is also described as an evolution of the Dravida style.
Hoysala temples commonly have stellate plans on raised jagati platforms, and the form reached its peak under the Hoysalas in the twelfth century.
Hoysala temple complexes include open mantapas and several shrines arranged around a central pillared hall.

secs.t: Ruler → achievement

x: Nripa Kama II
was an early Hoysala chief under the Western Chalukyas.
Veera Ballala II
defeated Yadava Bhillama and made the Hoysalas independent; his reign is given as 1170–1220.
Ballala III ruled from 1295 to 1342, defeated Ramachandra’s forces in 1305, and was later defeated by the Kakatiya commander Pedarudru after 1316.

secs.t: Vishnuvardhana - original name, conversion, victories

x: Vishnuvardhana was originally known as Bittideva, also called Bittiga.
Bittideva became a Vaishnava under
Ramanuja
, who had taken refuge in Hoysala territory from Chola persecution.
Although Vishnuvardhana became a Vaishnava, Queen Shantala Devi remained a Jain and the court continued to patronise Jain basadis.
Vishnuvardhana defeated the
Cholas at Talakad
and assumed the title Talakadugonda.

secs.t: UNESCO Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas - components

x: The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage property in 2023.
The three components are Chennakeshava Temple at Belur, Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebid and Keshava Temple at Somanathapura.

secs.t: Decline - invasions, relations with Yadavas and Pandyas

x: The Hoysalas were involved in constant wars with the Yadavas of Devagiri and the Pandyas.
Malik Kafur took Dwarasamudra in 1311, before the Hoysala kingdom’s space passed to Vijayanagara.
Ballala III died in 1342, and the political space of the Hoysala kingdom subsequently passed to Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The hero stone, unearthed on 28 June 2026, may help settle the long-disputed date of Vishnuvardhana’s death.
The Kannada-inscribed veeragallu was found at Neeragunda in Arsikere taluk.
Vijayanagara architecture followed the
Hoysala and Pandya styles
according to the comparative assessment.

src: Sources: UPSC (Art & Culture pp.27, 42, 43); CDI (Block03 Kakatiyas...Qutb Shahis - Hoysala Fine Arts; Block03 Kalyani Chalukyas); CDX pp.169, 274; APP (Indian History Part 1 > Dravida Temple Architecture); TH 7 Aug 2026

rows.title: Yadavas of Devagiri - Bhillama, Singhana, Hemadri and the Hemadpanti style

secs.t: Ruler → achievement

x: Singhana II
, who ruled from 1200 to 1247, was regarded as the greatest Yadava ruler and bore the title ‘Teluguraya Sthapanacharya’.
Ramachandra was defeated in 1295 and became a feudatory, while Harapaladeva’s death during Mubarak Khalji’s invasion marked the end of the Yadava kingdom.
The sequence was the 1295 first invasion, Malik Kafur’s 1307–08 campaign, Shankaradeva’s death in 1313, and Harapaladeva’s death in 1317–18.

secs.t: Singhana - conquests, wars with Hoysalas and Kakatiyas, scholars at court

x: Singhana released Ganapatideva to use him as a counterweight to Veera Ballala’s push into the Krishna–Tungabhadra region.
Sarangapanideva, the son of Singhana II, later served at the court of Rudramadevi.
Sarngadeva was associated with music.
Changadeva
, the astronomer and grandson of Bhaskaracharya, established the school at Patan.

secs.t: Hemadri - office held, works, Hemadpanti style

x: Hemadri served
Mahadeva and Ramachandra
as Shrikaranadhipa, the head of the secretariat or records.
Chaturvarga Chintamani is a Sanskrit encyclopaedia dealing with
dharma, rituals, charity, pilgrimage and vratas
Hemadpanti construction used local black basalt and interlocked dressed stones without mortar, a technique known as dry masonry.
The Yadava court poet Hemadri claimed that Jaitugi captured and sacrificed Kakatiya Rudra.

secs.t: Sangita Ratnakara - author, patron

x: Sangita Ratnakara was written by
Sarngadeva
, the court musician of Singhana II.
The Sangita Ratnakara is considered a basic text for both Hindustani and Carnatic music.

secs.t: Marathi literature of the Yadava period

x: Dnyaneshwar composed the Dnyaneshwari in 1290 during
Ramachandra
’s reign.
The Mahanubhava sect was founded by Chakradhar Swami.
Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, and later Tukaram and Ramdas carried Upanishadic and Gita ideas into Marathi.

secs.t: Delhi Sultanate raids and end of the Yadavas - commanders, years

x: In 1295, Alauddin Khalji, acting for Sultan Jalaluddin, defeated Ramachandra at Devagiri and took Ellichpur.
Alauddin Khalji defeated Ramachandra, took Ellichpur, and reduced the Yadavas to the status of Delhi vassals.
During the 1307–08 campaign, Ramachandra submitted to Malik Kafur and was taken to Delhi.
After 1323, Devagiri’s vizier Malik Burhanuddin was placed in charge of conquered Andhra.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Devagiri was the first southern kingdom to fall to Delhi, opening the road to Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
The rivalry included Jaitugi’s killing of Rudradeva, Singhana’s claim to be the installer of the Telugu king, and Rudramadevi’s repulse of Mahadeva’s attack.

src: Sources: APHQ aph2000_10 (and Q11); CDX pp.169, 209; APP (AP History Medieval > Kakatiyas: Rudradeva, Mahadeva, invasion timeline); CDI (Block05 Maratha background); UPSC (Medieval History p.66)

rows.title: Kakatiyas - origins, Beta I, Rudradeva, Ganapatideva; Kakatiya-Yadava-Hoysala relations
sub: Group-II M1-A-27: Kakatiyas - origin, Beta I, Prola II, Rudradeva and Ganapatideva

secs.t: Capitals → which ruler shifted Hanumakonda to Orugallu

x: Orugallu is the ancient name of Warangal and means ‘
single rock
Andhranagari was used under Ganapatideva, and Sultanpur was the name given after the conquest of 1323.
Prola II developed Hanamkonda.
Rudradeva shifted the capital and began fortifying Orugallu.

secs.t: Ruler → title + achievement

x: Exam angle: match tank → builder and ruler → temple.
Beta II built Shivapura and Betesvaralayam, Durgaraja made donations to the Betesvara temple, and Prola II erected a victory pillar at Srisailam.
Ganapatideva ruled for 63 years, issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam in 1244, and Ramappa temple was built during his reign by Recherla Rudra.
The order is Beta II (1076–1108), Prola II (1116–1157), Rudradeva (1158–1195), and Mahadeva (1195–1199).
Nrittaratnavali is the dance treatise, Jayapa Senani was associated as Ganapatideva's commander, Ramappa is at Palampet, and Ganapatideva was the patron under whom it was built.
The sequence is Ramappa temple in 1213, Singama’s independent kingdom, Bhimavaram in 1367–68, and Sultan Quli’s annexation in 1518–43.

secs.t: Ganapatideva - Nellore Chodas, Velanati Chodas, battles and defeats

x: Mutyalachaundaraya
served as Ganapatideva's general and took Divi during the coastal campaign beginning in 1201.
Ganapatideva married Pinnachodi's daughters Narama and Perama, and appointed their brother Jayapa as Gajasahani, the chief of the elephant forces.
Ganapatideva, along with Akkana and Bayyana, killed
Mummadi Rajendra Chola
in 1257, bringing the final end of the Velanati Chodas.

secs.t: Titles of Kakatiya rulers → ruler

x: Prola I
bore the title Samadhigata Panchamahashabda, along with Arigajakesari.
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Kumara Rudradeva was the title borne by Prataparudra II at his accession.
Mahamandaleswara was a feudatory title used by the Samanta Kakatiyas under the Kalyani Chalukyas.

secs.t: Origin debate - overlords, clan and caste, early religion

x: The progenitor is identified in different traditions as Kakara Gundana of Magallu or Venna Bhupati of Bayyaram.
The Kakatiyas were first under the Rashtrakutas, then the Kalyani Chalukyas; the Samanta phase lasted from 956 to 1162, followed by the sovereign phase from 1163 to 1323.
The early Kakatiya base was
Hanamkonda Vishaya
, corresponding broadly to modern Karimnagar, Warangal and Khammam areas.

secs.t: Inscriptions → ruler + first mention

x: The Draksharamam inscription of 1158 was issued by
Minister Inangala Brahma Reddi
and records Rudradeva's accession.
The
Palampet inscription of 1213
is associated with Recherla Rudra and records the Ramappa temple during Ganapati's reign.
The Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam issued by Ganapatideva in 1244 provided
protection for foreign traders
These inscriptions respectively refer to Jain Juddha Mallajinalaya, the Ramappa temple, Jalakaranda and Kolleru Lake.

secs.t: Kakatiya-Yadava and Kakatiya-Hoysala conflicts

x: Yadava ruler Jaitugi killed Rudradeva and captured Ganapatideva during the Kakatiya-Yadava conflict.
Hoysala Veera Ballala II pushed into the Krishna-Tungabhadra region, compelling Jaitugi to release Ganapatideva.
Rudramadevi repulsed Yadava Mahadeva, and Prataparudra’s commander Pedarudru defeated Hoysala Ballala III after 1316.

secs.t: Kakatiya feudatories → family + title

x: Prasadaditya
of the Kayastha family bore the titles Kakatiya Rajya Sthapanacharya and Raya Pitamahanka.
Kamasani belonged to the
Viriyala
family and made Garuda Beta a Chalukya vassal, as recorded in the Gudur inscription.
Recherla Rudra saved the kingdom during Ganapati’s captivity and is associated with the Ramappa temple and tank at Palampet.

secs.t: Ganapatideva - Nellore Choda intervention, defeats (Pandyas, 1263)

x: Ganapatideva
intervened in Nellore affairs and restored Manumasiddhi II to the throne.
The poet
Tikkana
went as an envoy to request Ganapatideva’s intervention on behalf of Manumasiddhi II.
Ganapatideva bore the title
Andhra Deshadhiswara
and is associated with the unification of Telugudesam.
Ganapatideva was held captive as a boy by Yadava ruler
Jaitugi

secs.t: Wars → opponent

x: The Yadavas captured Ganapatideva.
The Kakatiya conflict with the Yadavas, also called the Sevunas of Devagiri, began during the reign of Prola II.
The
Velanati Chodas
killed Prola II.
In 1159, Rudradeva defeated the Kalachuri confederacy leaders Mailagi, Medaraja of Polavasa and Dommaraja of Nagumuru.
Rudradeva defeated the
Telugu Chodas and Tailapa III

secs.t: Succession after Ganapatideva - daughters, marriages

x: Ganapatideva had no son.
Rudrama Devi succeeded Ganapatideva and ruled from 1262 to 1289.
Kupama Devi
, Rudrama Devi’s mother, guided her training when she was being raised as a son.
Mailamba and Kundamamba married
the sons of Natavadi Buddharaja
, namely Rudra and his brother.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Ramappa Temple at Palampet became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 and is noted for its star-shaped platform and floating bricks.

The first mention at Magallu was in 956, Rudradeva became the first sovereign in 1163, Ganapatideva was defeated at Muttukur in 1263, and Rudrama Devi ruled from 1262 to 1289; in the stated sequence, the intended chronological.

rows.title: Rani Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra; Marco Polo's account; fall to the Delhi Sultanate
sub: Group-II M1-A-28: Rani Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra; the fall of Warangal

secs.t: Rudrama Devi - accession, title, revolts, Yadava invasion, death

x: Rudrama began co-regency in 1258, the 1266 inscription retained the vassal description, and her full coronation followed Ganapatideva’s death in 1262.
The revolt of Harihara and Murari was suppressed with the assistance of Prasadaditya Kayastha, Gona Gannareddy, Jannigadeva and other commanders.
Ganga Narasimhadeva occupied Vengi in 1262; Rudrama’s full coronation followed in 1262 after Ganapatideva’s death; Vengi was recovered in 1278; Rudrama died in 1289.
The
Chandupatla inscription
of Nalgonda district, set up by Puvvula Mummadi, records Rudrama Devi’s death in 1289 while fighting Ambadeva.

secs.t: Tughlaq conquest - Ulugh Khan, renamed city, Prataparudra's fate

x: Exam angle: captor =
Ulugh Khan
(not Malik Kafur, not Alauddin).
The first invasion occurred in 1321–22 under Ulugh Khan; the second occurred in 1323 under Juna Khan; Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur; and Malik Burhanuddin was placed in charge of Andhra.
The order is Malik Kafur’s expedition in 1309–10, Khusrau Khan’s in 1318, Juna Khan’s failed expedition in 1321, and the final conquest in 1323.

secs.t: Khalji invasions of Warangal → commander + year + outcome

x: Exam angle: "first Muslim attack on Orugallu" →
Malik Fakhruddin Juna
commanded Alauddin Khalji’s first expedition against Orugallu in 1303.
The second invasion of 1309–10 was led by Malik Kafur; Prataparudra submitted, paid a large tribute and accepted Delhi’s overlordship.
Alauddin Khalji’s first Deccan raid targeted the Yadavas of
Devagiri
, not Andhra or Warangal.

secs.t: Marco Polo's account

x: Marco Polo described prosperity, efficient administration and a woman ruler of martial ability; his account is regarded as the first foreign reference to a female ruler in India.
Marco Polo described Motupalli as a flourishing sea-trade centre and noted the absence of oppressive merchant taxes, the heat and loincloths, and rice as the only local grain.

secs.t: Prataparudra - reforms, court scholars → work

x: Prataparudra was the grandson of
Rudramadevi
and the son of Mummadamma and Mahadeva.
The Nayankara system assigned principalities and forts to military officers known as Nayakas, who maintained troops and paid fixed tribute.
Prataparudra’s economic measures included land reclamation, waterworks and founding villages; oppressive merchant taxation was contrary to the account of the period.

secs.t: Sources

x: Amir Khusrau’s Khazain-ul-Futuh describes Malik Kafur’s 1310 siege, the double-walled fort with a moat, diamonds and Prataparudra.
Ekamranatha’s
Prataparudra Charitramu
records Kakatiya traditions, including the Jaitugi–Ganapati marriage.
Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi was written by
Barani
and records Delhi’s southern campaigns.
Madhura Vijayam and the Vilasa grant of Prolaya Nayaka describe the hardship after the conquest.

secs.t: Titles → ruler + event commemorated (Rayagajakesari, Rudradeva Maharaja)

x: Amir Khusrau used Ravaddar Dev for Prataparudra II; Ganapatideva was known as Andhra Deshadhiswara; and Rudradeva Maharaja was Rudrama Devi’s male regnal name.
Kakatiya kings used all three styles—Maharaja, Parameshwara and Tirthakrit.

secs.t: Succession from Rudrama to Prataparudra - relationship

x: Prataparudra was Rudrama’s grandson through Mummadamma, was trained by her, and was crowned in 1289.
Prataparudra II faced opposition from Kayastha, Velama and Reddy factions, as well as Tripurari II, the son of Ambadeva.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The fall of Warangal in 1323 ended Kakatiya rule and was followed by the Musunuri-led liberation movement, which produced the Musunuri and Reddi states.
The cited reasons were southern disunity, weak cavalry and internal betrayal associated with Bobbareddi.
The comparative sequence is the Nayankara system, followed by the Vijayanagara Amaranayakas and later the Poligars.

rows.title: Kakatiya administration - Nayankara system, tank irrigation, trade, Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam
sub: Group-II M1-A-29: Kakatiya administration - Nayankara system, revenue and military organisation
Group-II M1-A-30: Kakatiya economy - agriculture, tank irrigation, trade and the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam

secs.t: Trade - routes, merchant guilds and samayas, items

x: The Virabanajam guild was licensed for
Pakanadu, Vengi and Hanumakonda
, as recorded in the Tripurantakam inscription of 1282.
Guilds maintained seals or emblems, settled disputes and kept private military forces, but they did not possess an exclusive royal monopoly over all trade.
Guild members came from several communities, including Settis, Reddis, Nayakulu, Boyas, Dasaris and Vaishyas.

secs.t: Motupalli - alternative name, Abhaya Sasanam

x: Exam angle: "Abhaya" = assurance of safety; issuer Ganapatideva, not Rudrama.
Ganapatideva issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam in
at Motupalli.
The charter protected foreign merchants, remitted arbitrary taxes and promised compensation for losses from shipwreck or theft.
The 1416 Motupalli Dharma Sasanam belonged to Vijayanagara ruler Deva Raya I, not Ganapatideva.

secs.t: Tank irrigation → builder; construction rules (Porumamilla)

x: Samudrams were large tanks, Golusukattu cheruvulu formed linked chains, surplus flowed to lower tanks, and Dashabandhamu was tax-free land for upkeep.
The Porumamilla tank inscription dates to 1369 and was issued by Bhaskara, son of Vijayanagara ruler Bukka I. It belongs to the Vijayanagara period and lists twelve requisites of a good tank.

secs.t: Crafts and industries

x: Ratna kambalu was associated with Warangal, knives with Nirmal and diamonds with the Golconda region.
Marco Polo is said to have described the extremely fine cloth of the region in this manner; the material is identified as
fine muslin
Cotton cultivation and weaving were major activities, fine muslin was exported, and the Golconda region was associated with diamond trade.

secs.t: Nayankara system - origin, obligations, number

x: Exam angle: statement questions on "who introduced the Nayankara system" → Prataparudra II.
A Nayaka retained a share of revenue for maintaining troops, paid a fixed annual sum to the king and remitted the balance.
Nayakas received villages called
Nayakasthalam
instead of a regular salary, drawing revenue from them to meet their obligations.
Baddena's Neeti Sastra Muktavali and Ekamranatha's Pratapa Charitra are cited as sources for the Nayankara system.

secs.t: Administrative terms → meaning

x: Rashtra or Mandala was the largest province, followed by Nadu or Bhumi, Sthala and finally Grama.
Karanam was the
village accountant
The central departments were called 72 Niyogas and were supervised by the
Bahattara Niyogadhipati
Sunkamanya
was a collector of tolls and customs.
Malyala Hemadri Reddi
served as prime minister under Ganapatideva.

secs.t: Taxes - land revenue, sunkam, pullari

x: Land revenue, referred to as bhaga or Ari, was generally
one-sixth
of the produce.
Magani denoted irrigated wet land, generally used for food crops, while Metta denoted rain-fed dry land.
Sunkam was customs or tolls, Angadisunkam a weekly-market tax, Pullari a grazing tax and Pellipannu a marriage tax.
Tax concessions on cleared forest land were intended to
encourage settlement and cultivation

secs.t: Society → ayagars, caste mobility, women donors

x: The twelve Ayagars were paid through
shares of produce and service lands
Mailamba is associated with the Bayyaram tank and Kundamamba with Kunda Samudram.

secs.t: Number of Nayakas and fort bastions under Prataparudra

x: One account gives the number as 72; each Nayankara guarded a fort, and the Nayankaras controlled one-fourth of the kingdom's land.
The three surviving generals named are
Prolaya Nayaka, Racherla Singama and Prolaya Vemareddy

secs.t: Taxes and cesses → meaning

x: Ari denoted land revenue or Bhumi sistu.
Koru
was the tax imposed on wet or Magani land.
Pellipannu was a wedding tax, not a cattle tax.
Pullari, Kanika and Alam are correctly matched.
Siddhayam, Ardhayam and Niruvidi were agricultural levies.
Burra
, Madiga, Gandi and Revu were named as other sunkams.

secs.t: Military organisation - corps, Padmanayaka chiefs, fort types

x: The figures associated with Prataparudra's army were
100 elephants, 20,000 cavalry and 900,000 infantry
Mula Balam was the king's standing army, and the Nayankara army was the other major division.
Jayapa Senani held the position of Gaja Sahini under Ganapatideva.
Padmanayakas were Recherla Velama chiefs and key Kakatiya commanders.
Warangal fort was characterised by concentric walls and a moat.

secs.t: Ports and trade centres → other names, imports and exports

x: Krishnapatnam
was situated on the Nellore coast.
Hamsaladeevi was located in the
Krishna delta
Arabian war horses, silk and perfumes were imports.
Arabian war horses
were imported for the cavalry.

secs.t: Highways and trade routes → towns connected

x: Kakatiya control extended over routes between the
Deccan interior and the eastern coast

secs.t: Agriculture - wet and dry cultivation, crops, tank cesses

x: Maize is excluded because it reached India only after 1500.
Maize was specifically excluded from the medieval crop list, and tea, coffee and tobacco were not included.
Dashabandhamu denoted tax-free land given for the maintenance and upkeep of tanks.

secs.t: Coins → denomination

x: Gadya or Gadyana was a gold coin.
Visa
was described as a small fraction.
Adduga, Padika, Ruka and Visa were all named as coin types or denominations.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Burton Stein’s interpretation is associated with the term ‘segmentary state’, while Romila Thapar used the expression ‘metropolitan state’.
The Kakatiya arrangement was called Nayankara, the comparable Vijayanagara arrangement was Amaranayaka, and the Mughal parallel was the jagir linkage between land and military duty.
Motupalli and Kodur are identified with the Vishnukundin era, while Pulicat, Motupalli and Machilipatnam are identified as Vijayanagara’s Andhra ports.

rows.title: Kakatiya society and religion - Veerashaivism, Jainism, temple institutions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-78

secs.t: Legal work on women's property - Purushartha Saramu (Sivadevayya)

x: Purushartha Saramu was authored by
Sivadevayya
Purushartha Saramu records that a woman's property passed to her
daughters and daughter's daughters
, indicating a comparatively progressive legal outlook.
Niti Shastra Muktavali is associated with Baddena, not Sivadevayya.
Purushartha Saramu also describes the 72 Niyogas, or departments, and the daily routine of the king's council.

secs.t: Castes and caste associations - Samaya

x: Samayas elected senior heads, who settled disputes, and members paid dues to them.
Brahmins were identified as Mahajanas, Komatis as Nakaram, Panchavarmavaru as Saaminumani vaaru, and Panchanamuvaru as the five artisan groups.
Ashtadasha kulas denotes the 18 occupational groups that lived inside Warangal fort, as mentioned in Kreedabhiramam.
Mahajanas
identified Brahmins, whereas Telikas, Gollas and Boyas were among the other castes named.

secs.t: Non-Brahmanical trends - culminating in the Kakatiyas

x: Reddis, Kammas and Velamas
, also referred to as Padmanayakas, emerged as Sudra warrior-peasant groups.
The Kakatiyas, described as Sudras of originally Pulinda origin who adopted the Varna order, represented
the culmination of the non-Brahmanical trend
Pulinda origin, Sudra Nayaka groups and reform sects are central features of the non-Brahmanical trend culminating under the Kakatiyas.

secs.t: Veerashaivism - Basava, Aradhya and Veerashaiva sub-sects

x: The followers of Veerashaivism were Lingayats, its religious teachers were Jangamas, and its texts were the Agamas.
Panditaradhya Charitra records the debate of
Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya
with a Buddhist acharya.
The Kakatiyas supported orthodox Brahmin sects through grants but did not persecute Lingayats and generally did not take sides among these sects.

secs.t: Jainism - early Jain rulers, centres

x: The early Kakatiyas were Jains; they later became Shaivas from the period of Prola II or Rudradeva.
The Padmakshi temple, built by Prola II, was originally
a Jain shrine
The decline of Jainism was associated with hostility from Kalamukha and Veerashaiva groups and persecution by certain Kakatiya authorities.
Visveshwara Shambhu, Brahmayya and Ganapati are associated with actions contributing to the decline of Jainism.

secs.t: Temples as institutions - grants, temple women, festivals

x: Temples functioned as
landed corporations
, possessing lands and employing organised staff.
Temples included monasteries and feeding houses, Kalamukhas supported food charity, and Kalavatis sustained dance and music.
Prataparudra II endowed the Chennakeshava temple in 1321, while his queen Lakshmidevi endowed the Ramanatha temple at Yelledu.
Temple festivals served as
royal occasions
, while temple women and courtesans contributed to their cultural performances.

secs.t: Kalamukha and Pasupata sects - centres, gurus, Kapalikas

x: Exam angle: "Kapalikas arose from which doctrine" and "popular religion of the Reddi Rajas" - both answer Pasupata.
The Kakatiyas patronised the
Pasupata and Kalamukha
sects, which were described as extremist Shaiva sects.
Betaraja and Durgaraja were disciples of a Kalamukhacharya belonging to the Srisailam Shila matha.
Pasupata Shaivism continued as the popular faith into the Reddi period but declined under Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Social customs - hero-stones and self-sacrifice

x: The period witnessed widespread
superstition, animal sacrifice and self-sacrifice by devotees of Shiva
Jain deities were absorbed as Hindu goddesses, including
Kakitamma and Jogulamba
Viragallu were memorial stones for warriors who died in battle or during cattle raids.

secs.t: Royal women's grants - Kuppamamba, Mailama

x: Royal women of the Kakatiya period made donations to
temples and tanks
, contributing to both religious institutions and public water works.
Lakshmidevi
, the queen of Prataparudra II, is cited as an example of a royal woman who donated to temples and tanks.
Kuppamamba and Mailama are associated with the subject of
royal women's grants
in the Kakatiya period.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kakatiya age is called the
Shaiva era
because Shaivism had a prominent position during the period.
The legal framework comprises the AP Endowments Act, 1987 and Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution, in relation to State powers over interim management of old religious endowments.
Srisailam, Alampur and Draksharama
remained important centres of the Shaiva-Shakta axis of Andhra during the period.

rows.title: Kakatiya art - Thousand Pillar Temple, Ramappa/Rudreshwara (UNESCO 2021), Warangal Fort
sub: Group-II M1-A-33: Kakatiya art and architecture - Thousand Pillar Temple, Ramappa, Warangal Fort, Kakatiya Kala Thoranam

secs.t: Ramappa (Rudreshwara) temple - builder, ruler, deity, sculptor, UNESCO, type

x: Exam angle: builder-ruler-place matching, the UNESCO year, and "floating bricks / sandbox" statements.
Ramappa Temple is situated at
Palampet in Mulugu district
of Telangana.
The Ramappa Temple was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on
25 July 2021
The temple has a Nandi facing the sanctum, and Recherla Rudra built the Ramappa tank.

secs.t: Dance sculptures and treatises - author, profession, temple

x: Exam angle: "Jayapa's main profession" has been asked, and the answer is Gajasahini, not dancer.
The madanika poses at Ramappa follow Jayapa Senani's
Nritta Ratnavali
Perini Shiva Tandavam was danced by male warriors
before battle to invoke Shiva
Nataraja Ramakrishna
revived Perini Shiva Tandavam in modern times and also shaped Devadasi Nrityam and Navajanardhanam.

secs.t: Religious patronage, architectural influences, Dharmasagara inscription

x: The conflicts began under Rudradeva, Ganapatideva was a Shaivite, and Gangadhara built the Prasanna Keshava Temple at Hanamkonda.
The recorded figures are 1,300 Vaishnava temples, 2,400 Mallara Devudu temples, 4,400 Bhairava/Durga/Ganesha temples and 52 villages endowed to Srisailam Mallikarjuna.
Kakatiya temple architecture follows the Chalukyan, or Vesara, style and is also described as transitional between early Chalukyan and Vijayanagara styles.

secs.t: Thousand Pillar Temple, Hanamkonda - builder, deities

x: The Thousand Pillar Temple dates to 1163 CE, Ramappa to about 1213 CE, Swayambhu Lingalayam to 1254 CE, and Prasanna Keshavalayam is placed after the earlier constructions in the stated sequence.
The Hanamkonda Thousand Pillar Temple is a Trikuta temple, while the Palampet Ramappa Temple is associated with floating bricks and is named after its sculptor Ramappa.

secs.t: Warangal Fort - Kala Thoranam, walls, Kridabhiramam

x: The Kala Thoranam comprises four ornate stone gateways situated around the Swayambhu Shiva temple inside Warangal Fort.
Kridabhiramam is a Veedhi natakam that describes life inside Warangal Fort and calls Orugallu an abode of drama artists and actors.
The translation titled 'A Lover’s Guide to Warangal' was produced by
David Shulman and Velcheru Narayana Rao

secs.t: Kakatiya style - foundation, bricks, pillars, brackets

x: Floating bricks lighten the tower, stellate plans increase sculptural surface, ekasila refers to monolithic carving, and Kirtimukha means the face of glory.
Kakatiya temples show the influence of the
Western Chalukyas of Kalyani
, especially in carved pillars, star-shaped platforms, ornate doorways and sculptured ceilings.
Kakatiyas used porous, light floating bricks in the Ramappa vimana and black basalt for the Thousand Pillar Nandi and the ekasila Ramappa pillars.

secs.t: Other temples - Ghanapur (Kota Gullu), Pillalamarri, Nagulapadu

x: Ramanujapuram
in Mulugu, near Palampet, is noted for the only Panchakuta temple of the Kakatiya era.
The order is Thousand Pillar Temple, Padmakshi and Siddheshwara temples, Ramappa Temple, and Swayambhu Shiva Temple.
Recherla Rudra is associated with Ramappa in 1213, Ganapatideva with the Swayambhu Shiva Temple in 1254, and Recherla feudatories with Pillalamarri.

secs.t: Architectural features - platform, pillars, brackets

x: Kakatiya temples commonly feature a raised star-shaped platform on a sandbox foundation, polished lathe-turned pillars and projecting madanika or bracket figures in dance poses.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Archaeological Survey of India completed restoration of the Kalyana Mandapam, or dance pavilion, of the Thousand Pillar Temple in May 2026.
Kakatiya painting at Pillalamarri is regarded as having paved the way for the later Vijayanagara painting style seen at Lepakshi.
The sandbox foundation of Ramappa is cited as an example of heritage engineering because it helped the temple withstand earthquakes.

rows.title: Temple architecture styles of Andhradesa between the 11th and 16th centuries
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-79

secs.t: Styles by dynasty - Eastern Chalukya to Vijayanagara compared

x: Vijayanagara architecture drew on Chalukya and Chola styles and featured Sahasra Stambha Mandapas, composite carved pillars and ornate gopurams.
Raya gopuram is the towering gateway; kalyana mandapa is the marriage hall; Amman shrine is the goddess's separate shrine; composite pillars carry yalis and charging horses with riders.
The Vittala Ranga mandapa has 56 musical pillars, Sahasra Stambha means a thousand-pillared hall, and the Hoysala-type pillar has three or four carved sections on one base.

secs.t: Temple components - trikutalaya plan, kalyana mandapa, gopuram evolution

x: The basic components include the garbhagriha, mandapa, northern shikhara or southern vimana, and the axially placed vahana and dhvaja pillar before the sanctum.
Vijayanagara gave prominence to ornate gopurams, and Mangalagiri has a nineteenth-century gopuram about 153 feet high.
The Thousand Pillar Temple dates to 1163, Ramappa to 1213, the Siddhavatam inscription to 1233, and the Mangalagiri gopuram to the nineteenth century.

secs.t: Building materials → dynasty/region

x: The Vishnukundina-period Undavalli caves were cut into a sandstone hillside from top to bottom and contain four storeys.
The five-metre reclining Ananta Padmanabha at Undavalli is a
granite monolith associated with the Vishnukundinas
Kakatiya sandbox foundations used pits filled with sand, stone chips and earth.

secs.t: Nagara, Dravida, Vesara influences → example

x: Nagara architecture is marked by a curvilinear shikhara with the sanctum under the tallest tower; Mukhalingam and Simhachalam represent the Kalinga variant on the north coast.
The Dravida order is marked by a
pyramidal vimana, enclosure walls and gopurams
Vesara represents a blend of Nagara and Dravida features and is associated with the stepped shikharas of Kakatiya temples.

secs.t: North coastal temples → style + dynasty

x: Simhachalam is the temple of Varaha Lakshmi Narasimha, follows the Kalinga style, and is noted as the only Andhra Pradesh temple with two flagpoles.
Krishnadevaraya
gifted a diamond necklace to the deity at Simhachalam.
Srikurmam is dedicated to the Kurma avatar, while Mukhalingam is associated with Madhukeswara and Eastern Ganga temples near their early capital.

secs.t: Pancharama, Jyotirlinga and Shakti peetha temples - dynastic additions

x: Amararama is at Amaravati, Somarama at Bhimavaram, Ksheerarama at Palakollu and Kumararama at Samalkot.
Draksharama is cited as an example of the
Chalukya-Chola style
Draksharama was built by Chalukya Bhima I, later received Reddi renovation and endowments, and is regarded as the most architecturally significant Pancharama.
Kumararama is located at Samalkot and has Reddi sculptural additions.

secs.t: Temple sculpture - bracket figures, dance panels, madanikas

x: Exam angle: treatise → temple → author matching (Nrittaratnavali - Jayapa - Ramappa).
The madanika bracket figures at Ramappa were carved in dance postures based on Jayapa Senani's Nrittaratnavali.

Ramappa was built in 1213, received UNESCO World Heritage status in 2021, and the Nallamala survey and Mangalagiri conservation are recorded in 2026, with the survey preceding the conservation initiative.
Nataraja Ramakrishna
revived the Perini Shiva Tandavam using the dance panels of Ramappa Temple.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The copied inscriptions date from the 2nd to the 16th centuries and span the Satavahana period to the Vijayanagara period, including the Kakatiyas and Reddis.
The survey covered inscriptions ranging from the Satavahanas to Vijayanagara, including the intervening Kakatiya and Reddi periods.
Simhachalam, Annavaram, Srikalahasti and Kanipakam were all among the temples for which master plans had been done.

rows.title: Reddi kingdoms of Addanki, Kondavidu and Rajahmundry - Prolaya Vema Reddi, Kumaragiri Reddi
sub: Group-II M1-A-35: Reddi kingdoms of Addanki-Kondavidu - Prolaya Vema Reddi to Kumaragiri Reddi
Group-II M1-A-36: Rajahmundry Reddis and the end of Reddi rule
Group-II M1-A-37: Reddi society, religion, economy and administration
Group-II M1-A-38: Reddi literature and art - Errana, Srinatha and temple building

secs.t: Reddi rulers in order and their public works

x: The Reddis belonged to the Panta vamsam, were also associated with the Deseti kula, used the Bull as their emblem, worshipped Mula Guramma and used Sanskrit as the royal language.
Anavema Reddi is described as the greatest Reddi ruler because of his widest conquests and large charities, including Brahmanda, Kanakadhara and Gosahasra gifts.
Anavema Reddi
built the Veera Siromandapam, also referred to as the Veerashiro Mantapa, at Srisailam.
Kumaragiri Reddi first set up the Rajahmundry division under
his son Anavota Reddi
; Kataya Vema later succeeded in administering the division.
Kataya Vema Reddi was killed at Kakaraparthi in 1414 by
Gajaraju Tippa
, who was an ally of Pedakomati Vema Reddi.
Vema or Veda Reddi, the brother of Veerabhadra Reddi, served as prime minister and became the de facto ruler of Rajamahendravaram from 1423 to 1448.

secs.t: Ruler-authors, festivals, court dancer

x: Kumaragiri Reddi held the title
Karpura Vasanta Rayalu
in connection with the grand Vasantotsavam celebrations.
Kumaragiri settled the succession opposition by assigning Pedakomati Vema the Chandolu feudatory position and heirship, and later divided the kingdom by creating a separate Rajahmundry division.
Rajahmundry was first placed under Anavota, later under Kataya Vema in 1395, and Pedakomati Vema seized Kondavidu in 1402 before Kumaragiri died in refuge at Rajahmundry.
To settle the opposition to Kumaragiri’s accession, Pedakomati Vema was made a feudatory of Chandolu and designated as heir.
Kataya Vema, Kumaragiri’s brother-in-law and commander, conquered the eastern region up to Cuttack and later took charge of the Rajahmundry division.

secs.t: Taxes - which ruler

x: Anavota abolished the gold tax, while his minister Somaya issued the Abhaya Sasanam at Motupalli to encourage trade.
The 1346 Srisailam record refers to the Patala Ganga steps built by Prolaya Vema Reddi.

secs.t: Reddi queens and tanks

x: Exam angle: read the options. If only one of Govardhana Samudram or Santana Sagaram is offered, that is the answer.
Anitalli, the daughter of Kataya Vema Reddi and wife of Veerabhadra Reddi, was regarded as the rightful heir after her father.
Racha Vema, the son of Surambika, constructed the Jaganobbaganda canals to feed water into the tank dug by his mother.
Reddi royal women took part in welfare works, Surambika was Pedakomati Vema’s wife, and her son Racha Vema provided canal irrigation to her tank.

secs.t: Motupalli sea trade - literary source

x: Motupalli was the chief port of the Reddi kingdom and an important centre of maritime trade.
Anavota developed the Motupalli dock, Somaya was his minister, and Srinatha’s Haravilasam describes Reddi-period imports and exports.
Haravilasam was dedicated to
Tippayya Setti
, who was famous for overseas trade.
Somaya
, the minister of Anavota Reddi, issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam.

secs.t: Titles of Reddi rulers

x: Dharma Pratishtana Nagarudu was Prolaya Vema Reddi’s title; Dweepa Vijetha belonged to Anavota Reddi; Karpura Vasanta Rayalu to Kumaragiri Reddi; and Sarvajna Chakravarti to Pedakomati Vema Reddi.
Veeranna Pothu belonged to Anavota Reddi, Andhra Suratrana and Vasantaraya were associated with Anavema Reddi, Karpura Vasantaraya with Kumaragiri, and Bharatamata Patanga with Sivalinga Reddi.

secs.t: Capitals and forts

x: Rajahmundry, or Rajamahendravaram, was a Reddi seat from 1402 to 1448.
Prolaya Vema Reddi is credited with building 74 forts, including Kondaveedu, Kondapalli and Dharanikota.
Kondaveedu replaced Addanki as the capital and later saw conflict between the Gajapatis and Vijayanagara; Kondapalli was a strategic Krishna-region fort later held by the Gajapatis.
Kondavidu is associated with the Guntur region, not the East Godavari region.

secs.t: Court poets - ruler and work

x: Errana was associated with Prolaya Vema, Bala Saraswati with Anavota, and both Srinatha and Vamana Bhatta Bana were associated with Pedakomati Vema.
Srinatha's period is described as the Kavya Yuga, and his compositions helped prepare the way for the Prabandha style.
Vamana Bhatta Bana held the titles Sahitya Samrajya Dhurandhara and Sahitya Chudamani.
Singabhupala II was a Recherla Velama ruler of Rachakonda, not a Reddi ruler, and he wrote Sangeeta Sudhakaram.
After Kondaveedu fell in 1424, Srinatha joined the Rajahmundry Reddis, whose patron was Veerabhadra Reddi, with the help of
Bendapudi Annamatya
At Vijayanagara, Srinatha defeated Gauda Dindima Bhatta, the court poet of Devaraya II, and received
Kanakabhishekam and the Ganda Penderam

secs.t: Wars with Velamas, Bahmanis, Vijayanagara, Gajapatis

x: The Reddis resisted Bahmani attacks at Motupalli and Kambhammetta, repelled the Kandukur attack in 1398, and later Deva Raya I annexed the Kandukuru Reddis.
These episodes cover Reddi conflicts with Vijayanagara, the Velamas and the Gajapatis or Kalinga forces.
The events occurred in the order Kambhammetta in 1396, the Kandukur attack in 1398, recovery of lost territory in 1404, and the fall of Kondaveedu around 1450.

secs.t: Anavema Reddi - conquests, temple works

x: Anavema Reddi took Nidadavolu, Rajahmundry, Pithapuram, Simhachalam and Konaseema.
After taking Nidadavolu, Anavema Reddi gave it to
Choda Bhima
Anavema Reddi built
the Veerashiro Mantapa
at Srisailam.
Anavema Reddi defeated the Kalinga Gajapatis with assistance from
the Padmanayakas and Vijayanagara

secs.t: Founder Prolaya Vema Reddi - rise, grants

x: Prolaya Vema Reddi had served in Prataparudra's court and expelled Tughluq forces from coastal Andhra around 1325, with one account placing the event in 1324.
Prolaya Vema built steps to Patala Ganga at Srisailam in 1346, constructed steps to Ahobilam hill and restored agraharas to Brahmins.
Mallareddi
, the brother of Prolaya Vema Reddi, took Motupalli from Hasan Gangu of the Bahmani Sultanate.

secs.t: Allada Reddi - wars and opponents

x: Pedakomati Vema Reddi of Kondavidu
was a principal opponent of Allada Reddi and attacked Rajahmundry in 1414.
Deva Raya I of Vijayanagara backed Kataya Vema, making Vijayanagara an ally of Allada Reddi's side.
Pedakomati Vema's campaign and Annadeva's Vengi expansion were significant challenges to Allada Reddi.

secs.t: Relations with the Kondavidu Reddis - division, rivalry

x: Pedakomati Vema resented the creation of Rajahmundry as a separate unit under Kataya Vema.
The 1402 ouster of Kumaragiri shifted the conflict to Rajahmundry, where Kataya Vema ruled independently against Pedakomati.
Although Kondavidu fell in 1424, Rajahmundry continued for another 24 years as a feudatory of Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Gajapati and Vijayanagara rivalry over Rajahmundry

x: The correct sequence is 1420, 1423, 1429 and 1446–48: Ganga Ganapati's capture, recovery by Veerabhadra and Vema, Veerabhanu's occupation, and Kapileswara's annexation.
The Kalinga king
Veerabhanu Deva
occupied Rajahmundry in 1429.
Deva Raya II
expelled Veerabhanu Deva up to Simhachalam and restored the Reddis as Vijayanagara feudatories.
They describe the escalation of Gajapati pressure and the eventual annexation of Rajahmundry after Deva Raya II's death.

secs.t: End of Reddi rule → last ruler + conquering power

x: After the death of Racha Vema Reddi, Kondavidu passed to Vijayanagara under
Deva Raya II
The Rajahmundry branch, ruled at the end by Veerabhadra Reddi and Vema Reddi, was ended by Kapileswara Gajapati of Orissa in 1448.
The Kandukur branch, belonging to Mallareddi's line, was reduced to Vijayanagara feudatory status by
Deva Raya I

secs.t: Taxes and cesses → ruler + meaning (Puriti Pannu, Kanika, Pullari, Illari)

x: Exam angle: "Which Reddi king levied Puriti Pannu?" - Rachavema (not Kumaragiri or Anavema).
Puriti Pannu
was a maternity tax imposed on the delivery of a child.
Kanika meant presents or gifts; Pullari was the cattle-grazing tax; Illari was the house tax; and Ari was the land tax in Kakatiya usage.

secs.t: Festivals at the Reddi court and among people → popularity, royal patron

x: Kumaragiri Reddi
celebrated Vasantotsavams on a grand scale and was associated with the title Karpura Vasantaraya.
The merchant
Avachi Tippayya Setti
funded the Vasantotsavams; this patronage is recorded in Srinatha's Haravilasam.
Lakumadevi was the celebrated Bharatanatyam dancer at
Kumaragiri Reddi
's court.

secs.t: Society - castes (Reddis, Velamas, Kammas, Komatis), Brahmana agraharas

x: The Reddis belonged to the Panta Vamsam, also referred to as the Deseti kula.
The bull was the royal emblem of the Reddis, and Mula Guramma was their family deity.
The
Komatis
were mainly engaged in inland and coastal trade.
The title Nissivu Bhudana Parasurama highlighted Prolaya Vema Reddi's association with gifts of land.

secs.t: Religion - sects patronised, temple endowments (Srisailam, Ahobilam)

x: Bhairava and Mailara worship reflects the wider prevalence of Shaiva religious practices among the people.
The Reddi kings were disciples of
Ghoderayacharulu
, who was associated with the propagation of Shaivism.
The
Vadagalai
sect, belonging to the line of Vedanta Desika, established a matha at Ahobilam.
Reddi donations reached Srisailam, Simhachalam and Ahobilam, and the Pancharama Shiva temples received renovations and land grants.

secs.t: Administration - Nayakas, Karanams, village Ayagars

x: The capitals successively shifted from Addanki to Kondaveedu and later to Rajamahendravaram.
A Reddi village had
twelve
Ayagars, or village servants.
The Karnam was the accountant, the Reddi or Peddakapu was the headman, and the Talari was the watchman.
The
Karnam, Reddi and Talari
collectively held village judicial and police powers, following an inherited Kakatiya administrative pattern.

secs.t: Women - queens' patronage, courtesans and temple women

x: Queens were educated in the arts
Anithalli, wife of
Veerabhadra Reddi
, issued the Kaluvacheru inscription.
Devadasis were trained in music, dance and ritual and were respected performers at Shiva temples, including the Pancharamas.

secs.t: Errana - titles, portion of Mahabharata completed, patron (Prolaya Vemareddy), other works

x: Errana is regarded as a bridge between
Nannaya’s classical style and Tikkana’s style
Errana was the last of the Kavitrayam and completed the Telugu Mahabharata by translating the remaining portion of the Aranya Parva.

secs.t: Temple building → ruler (Srisailam, Ahobilam, Kondavidu)

x: Prolaya Vema Reddi
built the pilgrim rest-houses at Ahobilam and Srisailam and rebuilt the ramparts of Ahobilam and Mahanandi.

The Srisailam Mukha mandapam is associated with Harihara II; the sculptured prakaram with Shanti Lingayya; the earlier steps to Patala Ganga with Prolaya Vema Reddi; and the Tirumala additions with Krishnadevaraya.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Pancharama Shiva temples were renovated and endowed, reflecting the Reddi rulers’ ardent Shaiva faith.
Bikkavolu temples, Draksharama Bhimesvara and Samarlakota Kumararama are identified as Godavari-region sites carrying Reddi-era renovations.
Rajahmundry was associated with all three works: Srinatha’s Kashikhandam, Sivaleka Kommana’s Sivalila Vilasamu and Vinnakota Peddana’s Kavyalankara Chudamani.
Literary patronage gave the Reddis political legitimacy, while their Shaiva devotion was expressed through the restoration and endowment of Pancharama shrines.

rows.title: Musunuri Nayaks and the Velama (Racherla) chiefs of Rachakonda-Devarakonda
sub: Group-II M1-A-34: Musunuri Nayaks - Prolaya Nayaka, Kapaya Nayaka and the recovery of Andhradesa
Group-II M1-A-39: Velama (Racherla) kingdoms of Rachakonda and Devarakonda

secs.t: Musunuri Nayaks - Prolaya, Kapaya, Vilasa grant, liberation leader, Andhra Suratrana

x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq renamed Warangal Sultanpurti and placed Andhra under Malik Burhanuddin, with Malik Maqbul assisting him.
The surname Musunuri was derived from Musunuru village near Vuyyuru in Krishna district.
The Vilasa grant records the sufferings under Tughlaq rule, agrarian relief and the restoration of agraharas to Brahmins.
In 1336 CE, Kapaya Nayaka, together with Prolaya Vema Reddi, Recherla Singama and Hoysala Ballala, took Orugallu from Malik Maqbul.
Kapaya Nayaka appointed his nephew
Anapotha Nayaka
to govern Vengi.
Warangal fell in 1323, the Vilasa grant was issued in 1330, Orugallu was captured in 1336, and the Battle of Bhimavaram occurred in 1367–68.

secs.t: Capitals - dynasty

x: At Bhimavaram, near Orugallu, Kapaya Nayaka was defeated and killed by the Recherla Velamas led by Anapota Nayaka, after which Telangana passed to the Velamas of Rachakonda.
Rekapalli was the capital of the Musunuris under Prolaya; Rachakonda and Devarakonda belonged to the Recherla Velamas; Venkatagiri was associated with the Velugoti family.

secs.t: Velama families - region ruled

x: The Recherla Velamas ruled Telangana from these centres for about
150 years
, approximately from 1325 to 1475.
Velamas are also called Padmanayakas, and their tradition connects their origin with the lotus feet of Vishnu.
The rulers of Rachakonda and Devarakonda belonged to the
Recherla
gotra and had earlier been Kakatiya feudatories.

secs.t: Velama-Reddi conflicts - Palnadu and coastal Andhra

x: The Reddis held coastal Andhra, but the Velama chiefs from the north contested their control.
Kapaya’s decline enabled the Reddis to take coastal Andhra, while the Velamas absorbed Musunuri Telangana.

secs.t: Recherla Velamas - Singama Nayaka I, Anapota, Sarvagna Singa Bhupala

x: Sarvagna Singa Bhupala was a Sanskrit scholar-king and composed
Rasarnava Sudhakara
, a work on dramaturgy.
Sultan Quli Qutb Shah
, who ruled at Golconda from 1518 to 1543, defeated the Velama chiefs and annexed Rachakonda and Devarakonda.
The Recherlas initially served as loyal feudatories of the
early Kakatiyas
; Recherla Rudra belonged to this phase.
Singama Nayaka I was killed fighting the chiefs of Jallipalli, whereas Anapota Nayaka defeated Kapaya at Bhimavaram.

secs.t: Relations with Bahmanis and Vijayanagara - Kapaya's losses, Velama alliances

x: Kapaya Nayaka helped Hasan Gangu, also known as Zafar Khan, establish the Bahmani kingdom at Gulbarga in 1347.
The 1364–65 loss of Golconda Durgam involved 400 elephants, 250 horses and treasure amounting to 33 lakhs.
The Velamas shifted alliances according to circumstances, supporting different powers such as the Bahmanis, Vijayanagara and Gajapatis at different times.

secs.t: Titles → first holder

x: Exam angle: "first borne by" → Kapaya; "popular title of" with Anavema in the options → Anavema Reddi.
Katakachurakara is associated with Kapaya Nayaka, while Bammera Potana held the title Sahaja Panditya.

secs.t: Kapaya Nayaka (1336-1368) - recovery and alliances

x: In 1336, Kapaya Nayaka,
Hoysala Veera Ballala III, Prolaya Vema Reddi and Singama
took Warangal from Malik Maqbul.
Kapaya recovered Warangal, Singama cleared Nalgonda and Mahabubnagar, and Prolaya Vema Reddi cleared Kammanadu and Pakanadu south of the Krishna.
Kapaya ruled the recovered Kakatiya territory from Orugallu, assisted Hasan Gangu in founding the Bahmani kingdom, and later joined Bukka I against the Bahmanis.

secs.t: Sources - Vilasa, Kaluvacheru, Ferishta

x: The Vilasa grant of 1330 records Prolaya Nayaka’s rise and the atrocities committed under the Tughluq rule.
Polavaram, Ganapeshwaram and Palasamarri are associated with
Kapaya Nayaka
Ferishta’s work is a Persian source, calls Telangana ‘Tilang’ and describes the wars between the Bahmanis and Kapaya Nayaka.

secs.t: Conflict with the Bahmanis - terms and territory

x: Muhammad Shah I captured and burnt Vinayaka Deva, the son of Kapaya Nayaka, alive in 1361–62.
Under the truce of 1364–65, Kapaya ceded Golconda fort with huge wealth, and Golconda became the boundary between the powers.
The turquoise throne was among the gifts associated with the truce of 1364–65, under which Golconda was ceded.

secs.t: Devarakonda line - Madanayaka, Pedda Vedagiri

x: Madanayudu and Naganayudu invaded the Reddi kingdom to avenge
Singama
Madanayudu and Naganayudu defeated Anavota Reddi at
Dharanikota
, also called Dannala Kota.
Lingamanidu of Devarakonda
sought Gajapati help against a Bahmani attack.

secs.t: Works composed at the Velama court → author (Rasarnava Sudhakaram, Sangita Sudhakara)

x: Rasarnava Sudhakaram is associated with Sanskrit dramaturgy and poetics.
Sangeeta Sudhakaram is a musical work associated with Singabhupala II and serves as
a commentary on Sarngadeva’s Sangita Ratnakara

secs.t: Battles → opponents and outcome (Bhimavaram, Jallipalli)

x: After the victory over Anavota Reddi at Dharanikota, the titles
Jagadabbaganda and Rayavesa Bhujanga
were associated with the victors.
Singama Nayudu was killed
in the battle of Jallipalli, where the Jallipalli Kshatriyas were aided by the Reddis.
The battle of Bhimavaram took place in 1367–68, where Anapota Nayaka defeated Musunuri Kapaya.

secs.t: Rachakonda and Devarakonda forts - architecture

x: The architecture is associated with high adhisthanas, carved pillars, toranas, and lotus and swan motifs.
Rachakonda and Devarakonda served as the twin capitals and strongholds of the Velamas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The loss of Kakatiya unity gave rise to the Musunuri, Recherla Velama and Reddi successor states.
The Vilasa grant was issued in 1330, Vijayanagara was founded in 1336, the Bahmani kingdom arose in 1347, and the Golconda truce occurred in 1364–65.
Harihara and Bukka founded Vijayanagara in 1336, while Hasan Gangu established the Bahmani kingdom in 1347.

rows.title: Gajapatis of Orissa in Andhra; Bahmani incursions into Andhradesa
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-81

secs.t: Gajapati administration in Andhra - officer titles → function/region (Khandadhipati, Bisayi, Naidu, Pradhan)

x: Exam angle: the title for southern revenue officers is Naidu.
Naidu was the title used for revenue officers in the southern Andhra regions of the Gajapati Empire.
Nayakas and samantas collected revenue and maintained order, and the Reddi-era social order continued.
Devadanas and brahmadeyas were land endowments made to
scholars and temples
, including institutions at Puri, Srisailam and coastal shrines.

secs.t: Bahmani kingdom - founder, year and century of founding

x: The Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347, in the fourteenth century, with Gulbarga as its capital; Kapaya Nayaka helped Hasan Gangu in its foundation.
The Bahmani kingdom later split into Golconda,
Bijapur
, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Berar; Bijapur was the first to break away, in 1489.

secs.t: Gajapati rulers in Andhra → campaigns (Kapilendra, Purushottama, Prataparudra Gajapati)

x: Kapilendra took Bellamkonda, Velugodu, Addanki and Srisailam, besides Kondaveedu.

The Penugonda inscription records Kapileswara's attack on Tiran Andhra in 1448; the Anantavaram inscription records the defeat and tribute of the Virupaksharayas; the Draksharama inscription records Vijayanagara help to the Reddis; and the victory pillars commemorate Krishnadevaraya's triumph over the Gajapatis.

secs.t: Gajapati conquests of Rajahmundry, Kondavidu, Udayagiri - ruler, commander (Hamvira)

x: Kondaveedu was under Vijayanagara until 1449, fell to the Gajapatis around 1450, and was approached by Rajamahendra with Velama support.
In 1471 the Bahmanis briefly installed Hamvira as a puppet ruler; Purushottama subsequently overturned the arrangement.
Hamvira was the son of
Kapileswara
and defeated the Bahmani army after Lingamanidu sought Gajapati assistance.

secs.t: Gajapati-Vijayanagara conflict - forts lost, peace terms

x: Saluva Narasimha
drove the Gajapatis out of south-eastern Andhra by about 1470 and extended his occupation up to the Godavari.
Krishnadevaraya's campaign lasted from 1513 to 1519, and the settlement is best placed around
The campaign proceeded through Udayagiri, Kondaveedu, Kondapalli and Bejawada, followed by the march to Cuttack in 1518.

secs.t: Bahmani incursions → Sultan/commander (Ahmad Shah, Muhammad III, Mahmud Gawan) + places (Rajahmundry, Kondapalli, Warangal)

x: Muhammad Shah I burned Kapaya's son Vinayaka alive in 1361.
Muhammad Shah I forced Kapaya Nayaka to cede
Golconda, 400 elephants and 250 horses
Muhammad III and Mahmud Gawan suppressed Telangana revolts from 1453; Gawan subdued Orugallu and took Kondaveedu, pushing into Odisha in 1471.
The Bahmani kingdom reached its greatest extent under Mahmud Gawan.

secs.t: Sources → content (Madala Panji, Ferishta, Gajapati inscriptions at Srikurmam, Simhachalam)

x: Madala Panji is the temple chronicle of Jagannath at Puri and contains material on Gajapati history.
Ferishta wrote a Persian history of the Deccan sultans, making his account especially significant for the Bahmani side.
The Draksharama inscription, dated 1444, records Vijayanagara assistance to the Reddis.
The victory pillars at Simhachalam and Potnuru commemorate
Krishnadevaraya's triumph over the Gajapatis

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Andhra Pradesh sites associated with the Gajapati wars are
Udayagiri, Kondaveedu, Kondapalli, Rajahmundry and Simhachalam
The Gajapati rule is dated approximately from 1434 to 1541.
Uttarandhra culture shows the influence of the Gajapatis.
