rows.title: Telugu language and literature to the 14th century - Nannaya, Tikkana, Errana, Palkuriki Somanatha
sub: Group-II M1-A-21: Growth of the Telugu language under the Eastern Chalukyas - Nannaya and the Andhra Mahabharatam
Group-II M1-A-24: Origin and evolution of the Telugu language - earliest inscriptions (Kalamalla, Erragudi), scripts
Group-II M1-A-32: Kakatiya literature - Palkuriki Somanatha, Tikkana and the Siva Kavis
Group-II M1-A-48: Growth of Telugu literature, 11th to 16th centuries - Kavitrayam and the Prabandha age

secs.t: Kavitraya - members, parvas, first translator, titles

x: Nannaya was associated with the court of Rajaraja Narendra at Rajamahendravaram and is called the Adi Kavi of Telugu.
Nannaya translated the Adi and Sabha Parvas and 142 padyas of the Aranya Parva.
Tikkana translated 15 Parvas, beginning with Virata and extending to Swargarohana.
Nannaya is associated with Adikavi, Tikkana with Kavibrahma, and Errana with Prabandha Parameswara.
Tikkana called his Bharata rendering
Prabandha Mandali
Tikkana dedicated his work to Hariharanatha, taught the unity of Shiva and Vishnu through Harihara Advaita, and had Ketana as a disciple.
Errana was the court poet of Prolaya Vema Reddi, whose capital was Addanki.
Indra Vijayam and Chamundika Vilasam are associated with Nannaya, while Andhra Shabda Chintamani is the grammar treatise associated with Nannaya.
Nannaya belongs to the eleventh century, Tikkana to the thirteenth century, and Errana to the fourteenth century.
Nannaya pioneered the Champu style, which combines prose and verse.
Nannaya contributed to Telugu grammar, is associated with Akshara Ramyata, and used the Akkara metre borrowed from Kannada.
Nannaya rendered approximately two and a half parvas: Adi, Sabha and a portion of Aranya.

secs.t: Literary work - author

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2019 asked about the woman's-property rule. The answer is Purushartha Saramu by Sivadevayya, not Ketana's Vignaneswaram.
Purushartha Saramu was written by
Sivadevayya
and deals with 72 Niyogas, including the rule concerning women's property.
Nritta Ratnavali was written by Jayapa Senani as a Sanskrit dance treatise containing eight prakaranas.
The stated sequence of literary distinctions is Basava Puranam, Markandeya Puranam, Ranganatha Ramayanam and Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam.
Basava Puranam was composed by Palkuriki Somanatha, is in dwipada form, deals with the life of Basava and is described as the first Telugu Purana.
Ranganatha Ramayanam, by Gona Budda Reddy, is described as the first Telugu Ramayana and the first dwipada kavya.
Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya is associated with Sivatattvasaram, Nannechoda with Kumarasambhavam, and Palkuriki Somanatha with Basava Puranam and Panditaradhya Charitra.

secs.t: Other poets and scholars - work, patron, title

x: Nannechoda composed
Kumara Sambhava
, which is noted for Kannada influence and for beginning the eight descriptions of the prabandha tradition.
Ketana, known as Mula Ghatika, dedicated his work to Tikkana and is credited with the early use of the words Tenugu and Telugu.
Ketana is associated with Dashakumara Charitra, Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam and Vijnaneswariyam, the Telugu rendering connected with the Mitakshara.

secs.t: Srinatha - works and patrons

x: Srinatha was titled
Kavi Sarvabhauma
and is regarded as the bridge between the Kavitraya and the Prabandha age.
Sringara Naishadham
is derived from Sriharsha’s Naishadhiyacharita, which narrates the story of Nala and Damayanti.
Srinatha’s
Palnati Veera Charitra
describes the Battle of Palnadu and mentions instruments including Sannai and Mukha Veena.

secs.t: Epic versions in other Indian languages - composer + language

x: Pampa composed Vikramarjuna Vijaya in Kannada, Kamban composed Ramavataram in Tamil, Sarala Dasa composed the Mahabharata in Odia, and Kasirama Das composed the Mahabharata in Bengali.
Tikkana’s Andhra Mahabharatam covered 15 parvas.

secs.t: Earliest Telugu inscriptions - dynasty

x: The
Erragudipadu inscription
of Punyakumara of the Renati Cholas is regarded as the first fully available Telugu inscription and uses a song or geya style.
The Addanki inscription was issued by Panduranga, the commander of Eastern Chalukya ruler Gunaga Vijayaditya, and is the first Telugu poetic inscription in the Taruvoja metre.

Addanki is linked with Taruvoja and the first Telugu poetic inscription; Bezawada with the first Madhyakkara poem; Sataluru with Champakamala and prasa; and Kandukur–Dharmavaram with Seesa and Ataveladi.
Pitikayagulla is associated with the eighth century and post-Badami Chalukya influence, particularly in relation to early Telugu script; it is not the first Telugu poetic inscription.

secs.t: Early Telugu grammar and prosody - author

x: Andhra Shabda Chintamani is traditionally ascribed to Nannaya; Kavi Vakbandham is by Tikkana; Kavyalankara Chudamani is by Vinnakota Peddana; and Appakaviyam is by Kakunuri Appakavi.

Andhra Shabda Chintamani is traditionally attributed to Nannaya, Ketana used Tenugu/Telugu, Kavyalankara Chudamani is regarded as the first alankara work, and Appakaviyam belongs to the seventeenth century.

secs.t: Veerasaiva literature - author and metre

x: Basava Puranam was composed in the
dwipada
metre.
Somanatha was hailed as Prathama Andhra Viplava Kavi, belonged to the Veerashaiva tradition and was a native of Palakurthi in Janagama district.
Sivatattvasaram was composed by Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya.
His texts record the Brahmin–Veerashaiva conflict and the daily life of commoners.

secs.t: Literary genres - first examples

x: Nannaya's Bharatam uses verse and prose in champu form; Errana is identified as the first prabandha writer, while Nannechoda began the eight descriptions.
Pingali Surana's Raghavapandaviyam is a dvyarthi kavya that conveys
the Ramayana and the Mahabharata
at the same time.
Dasakumara Charitra is a story kavya, Markandeya Puranam is a Purana, Nrusimha Puranam is a Kshetra-mahatmya, and Raghavapandaviyam is a dvyarthi kavya.

secs.t: Grants to poets and scholars → recipient; assistant in the translation

x: Nandampudi agrahara was associated with Narayana Bhattu, while Navakhandavada agrahara was granted to Pavuluri Mallana.
The
Nandampudi donation inscription
is cited as evidence of Narayana Bhattu's assistance in the translation.
Narayana Bhattu was a polyglot familiar with eight languages, held the title Ashtabhasha Kavisekhara, and represented Someshwara I at Rajamahendravaram.
Prathama Andhra Viplava Kavi
was an epithet of Palkuriki Somanatha.

secs.t: Early Telugu mathematical work → author + patron court

x: Sara Sangraha Ganitam is described as the first Telugu mathematics book and scientific kavya, and it derives from Mahaviracharya's Sanskrit Ganita Sara Sangraha.
Pavuluri Mallana is dated to approximately 1100 CE, and his agrahara, Navakhandavada, was granted by Rajaraja Narendra.

secs.t: Official/court language - Sanskrit vs Telugu

x: Sanskrit was the official language, whereas Telugu was the language of the people and the favoured language.
The eulogy was written in Sanskrit, while the details of the grant were written in Telugu.

secs.t: Pre-Nannaya Telugu literature debate - claims and evidence

x: The Renati Chola prose inscription at Kalamalla is dated to
575 CE
and is important evidence of early written Telugu.
The inscriptions demonstrate that written Telugu, including Telugu verse, existed before Nannaya; however, no pre-Nannaya literary text survives in the evidence described.
The statement indicates that Nannaya built on a written Telugu tradition evidenced by about five centuries of inscriptions, rather than creating written Telugu without precedent.

secs.t: Epithets of Telugu → coined by

x: The Venetian traveller
Niccolo de' Conti
, who visited in the fifteenth century, is associated with the epithet “Italian of the East” for Telugu.
Sri Krishnadevaraya used the expression “Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa” in Amuktamalyada, meaning that Telugu is the finest among regional languages.
The epithet is linked to the rounded, vowel-ending and highly phonetic character of Telugu.

secs.t: Earliest Telugu words in Prakrit records → site

x: ‘Vepuru’ appears in the Myakadoni inscription. ‘Andhrapatha’ belongs to the Mayidavolu plates, ‘Nagabu’ to Amaravati, and ‘-ambul’ to Vishnukundin plates.
The
Vishnukundin Chikkulla plates
use the Telugu plural suffix ‘-ambul’, as in ‘Vijayarajya Samvatsarambul’.
‘Andhrapatha’ is first recorded in the
Mayidavolu plates
of Pallava Sivaskandavarman, written in Prakrit around 300 CE.

secs.t: Telugu script evolution - stages from Brahmi

x: The sequence is Bhattiprolu Brahmi variant, common Old Kannada–Telugu script, differentiation during the Rashtrakuta–Eastern Chalukya age, and separate Telugu script in the 11th–14th centuries.
One account places the emergence of distinct Telugu script by the 11th century, while another describes full separation over the 11th–14th centuries.

secs.t: Dravidian family - sub-branch, sister languages

x: Gondi and Kui
are identified among the sister languages of Telugu in the South-Central Dravidian sub-branch.
Telugu is the official language of Andhra Pradesh and one of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages.
The stated theory connects Telugu with the Desi bhasha or Paisachi of Prakrit, and D.C. Sircar observed that Desi words were very close to Telugu.

secs.t: Names of the language - etymology theories

x: The Trilinga theory refers to
Srisailam, Kaleshwaram and Draksharama
as the three Shaiva centres of Trilinga desa.
The material presents Telugu, Andhra, Andhrika and Tenugu as names or theories of origin; it does not support an exclusive Tamil derivation accepted by all scholars.
Shaivism was dominant, included the three named sects, and the three sacred centres gave Andhra the name Trilinga desa.

secs.t: Sanskrit authors at the Kakatiya court

x: Vidyanatha wrote Prataparudra Yashobhushanam; Jayapa Senani wrote the three Ratnavali works; Sakalya Mallabhattu is named among the Sanskrit authors.
Gajasahini means
commander of the elephant corps
Ravipati Tripurantakudu is credited with the Sanskrit Niroshthya Ramayanam, but an APP fragment attributes Niroshtya Ramayana and Udara Raghavam to Takavelli Mallikarju Bhattu.

secs.t: Tikkana - patron, parvas, independent works, philosophy

x: Tikkana was associated with the court of Manumasiddhi II of Nellore and bore the title Ubhayakavimitrudu.
The other works are associated with different authors or literary contexts.
Tikkana propounded Harihara philosophy, described as Harihara Dvaitam, to
reconcile Shaiva and Vaishnava traditions

secs.t: Siva Kavis (Shaiva Kavitrayam) → works

x: The sources differ: one identifies Sivatattvasaram as the first Satakam, while another identifies Vrushadhipa Satakam.
Nannechoda wrote Kumarasambhavam and bore the title Kavirajasekhara.

secs.t: Kreedabhiramam - authorship and city

x: Kreedabhiramam is credited to Vinukonda Vallabharaya, who was also known as
Vallabhamatya
Kreedabhiramam is regarded as a Telugu rendering of Ravipati Tripurantakudu’s Sanskrit play
Premabhiramam
, creating an attribution issue alongside its credit to Vallabharaya.
Kreedabhiramam describes Orugallu, or Warangal, through its markets, nightlife and Kakati Devi temple, and calls it ‘Andhra Nagari’.

secs.t: Early Satakas → author

x: Vrushadhipa Satakam is attributed to Palkuriki Somanatha.
Baddena is associated with Sumati Satakam and
Nitisastra Muktavali

secs.t: Book - author

x: Manucharitra was written by Allasani Peddana, Parijatapaharanam by Nandi Timmana, Panduranga Mahatmyam by Tenali Ramakrishna and Vasucharitra by Ramaraja Bhushana.
Ramaraja Bhushana dedicated Vasucharitra to
Tirumala Raya
Pingali Surana
was the author of both Kalapurnodayam and Raghavapandaviyam.
Tirumalamba
wrote the Sanskrit work Varadambika Parinayam.
Madhura Vijayam was written in Sanskrit by Gangadevi, not by Pingali Surana.

secs.t: Poets' titles - holder

x: Tikkana was Kavibrahma, Errana was Sambhudasa, Allasani Peddana was Andhra Kavita Pitamaha and Srinatha was Kavisarvabhauma.
Potana held the title Sahaja Panditya.
Ketana was called Abhinava Dandi for his Telugu Dasakumara Charitra.

secs.t: Prabandha age - features, first prabandha, leading poets, patronage

x: Nannechoda
's Kumarasambhava introduced the set descriptions associated with the Prabandha tradition.
Errana is credited as the first Prabandha writer in one classification, while Srinatha is identified as a pioneer through works such as Sringara Naishadham and Haravilasam.
The Reddi courts and Vijayanagara Nayaka courts also supported or spread the Prabandha style.

secs.t: Sanskrit works translated into Telugu - translator

x: Errana translated Harivamsa, Marana translated Markandeya Puranam, Srinatha rendered Naishadham as Sringara Naishadham and Ketana translated Dasakumara Charitra.
Errana
translated Harivamsa and dedicated it to Prolaya Vema.
Uttara Harivamsa was written by Nachana Somana.
Marana was a disciple of
Tikkana
Manchena rendered
Viddhasalabhanjika
as Keyurabahu Charitra in Telugu.

secs.t: Periodisation of Telugu literature

x: The Nannaya age belongs to the 11th century, followed by the Tikkana age in the 13th century, the Srinatha age in the 15th century and the Prabandha or Rayala age in the 16th century.
The Srinatha age is followed by the Prabandha or Rayala age in the 16th century, the Dakshinatya or southern Nayaka age in the 17th–18th centuries and the Modern age from the 19th century onward.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Mahabharatamu is identified as the first Telugu book, Andhra Shabda Chintamani as the first Telugu grammar in Sanskrit, and Ganita Sara Sangraha as the first Telugu mathematics book.
Telugu Language Day is observed on 29 August, the birth anniversary of
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy
The ASI survey in the Nallamala Tiger Reserve copied 25 inscriptions dating from the 2nd to the 16th century CE.

Kalamalla is dated to 575 CE, the Addanki poetic inscription belongs later, the Pitikayagulla inscription is from the eighth century, and the surveyed Telugu records extend up to the sixteenth century.
The State honours include the Telugu Language Awards linked with 29 August and Gidugu, revived Kandukuri Veeresalingam awards, and Gurram Jashuva and Boyi Bheemanna awards.

rows.title: Arab conquest of Sindh (712 CE); Ghaznavid and Ghurid invasions - Mahmud, Muhammad Ghori, Battles of Tarain

secs.t: Muhammad Ghori - route, Tarain I and II, Chandawar, reasons for Ghurid success

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2018 asked why Ghori won. Key:
superior war technology of the Turks
. APPSC-G2 2011: Prithviraj defeated Ghori at
Tarain
(the first battle).
Ghori took Multan in 1175, Peshawar around 1179, Sindh around 1182, and Punjab and Lahore around 1190.
The Chaulukya ruler
Bhimdev II
defeated Muhammad Ghori near Mount Abu at Kayadara in 1178.

secs.t: Arab conquest of Sindh - commander, ruler defeated, Chachnama, effects

x: The Thar desert and Aravallis, together with the strong Pratihara, Rashtrakuta and Pala powers, restricted Arab expansion largely to Sindh.
Muhammad bin Qasim defeated
Raja Dahir
in Sindh in 712 CE.
Indian mathematics, especially
the decimal and place-value systems
, along with astronomy and medicine, passed to the Islamic world and later to Europe.

secs.t: Scholars in Mahmud's court - work

x: Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind, also known as Tahqiq-i-Hind.
Firdausi wrote the commissioned Shahnama, Utbi wrote Tarikh-i-Yamini, and Al-Biruni composed an objective account of eleventh-century India.

secs.t: Bakhtiyar Khalji - Bihar and Bengal

x: Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji
was the real founder of Turk rule in Bihar.
Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked the Buddhist centres of
Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri
during approximately 1193–1203.
The Buddhist centres were sacked around 1193–1203; Nadia was attacked in 1204, Lakshmana Sena was driven out, and Bakhtiyar then ruled from Lakhnauti.

secs.t: Causes of Turkish success

x: Turkish armies used
mobile cavalry and mounted archers
, whereas Indian armies relied heavily on elephants.
Both statements are true, and the fragmentation and rivalry of Rajput states explain why political disunity aided Turkish success.
R. S. Sharma associated Indian feudalism with feudal levies, sub-infeudation and a closed village economy.
The historical debate gives greater importance to
military organisation
and less to religious zeal.

secs.t: Mahmud of Ghazni - founder, raids, targets, resisters, motives

x: Mahmud's 17 raids were not aimed at systematic conquest; they exposed India's military weakness and opened the north-west frontier.
Mahmud first encountered the Hindushahis in 1001–1008, attacked Nagarkot in 1009, Thanesar, Mathura and Kanauj in 1014–1018, and Somnath in 1025.
Nagarkot, identified with Kangra, was attacked in 1009 for its
temple treasure

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Arab contact beginning with the conquest of Sindh in 712 CE helped Indian scientific knowledge move westward and subsequently reach the Islamic world and Europe.
Mahmud of Ghazni is characterised mainly as a plunder-seeking raider, while Muhammad Ghori pursued conquest and established a lasting political presence in North India.

src: Sources: CDI (Block04 Advent of Islam, Phases II-IV); UPSC (Medieval History pp.54-55); APP (Indian History Part 1, Mamluk dynasty - Aibak; Delhi before the Sultanate); LENS Jan 2026 p.113

rows.title: Rajput states and society; Chandella (Khajuraho), Solanki (Dilwara, Modhera), Paramara contributions

secs.t: Court literature - author

x: ‘Prithviraj Raso’ was authored by
Chand Bardai
and is associated with Prithviraj Chauhan.
Jagnik
is credited with ‘Alha Khand’, which is associated with Chandela Paramardi.
All four pairs are correct. ‘Bisaldeva Raso’ was written by Narapati, ‘Lalit Vigraharaja’ by Somadeva, ‘Kirtikaumudi’ by Someshvara and ‘Navasahasanka Charita’ by Padmagupta.

secs.t: Rajput society and warfare - clans, feudalism, strategy, women, chivalry

x: These Rajput states rose after the
collapse of the Pratihara Empire
, which led to political fragmentation in North India.
Rajput feudal arrangements involved land grants carrying revenue, judicial and police rights.
Indian feudalism was characterised by sub-infeudation, vishti or forced labour, and closed village economies.
Rajput warfare emphasised direct combat and personal valour, with chivalry and clan honour receiving great importance.

secs.t: Rajput forts and victory towers - builder

x: Rana Kumbha built the Vijaya Stambha at Chittor to commemorate his victory over
Mahmud Khalji of Malwa
The Kirti Stambha at Chittor was constructed in the twelfth century by Jijaji, also known as Jeeja, a Jain merchant.
Kumbhalgarh Fort was built by Rana Kumbha.

secs.t: Rajput dynasties - founder, region, capital, rulers

x: Mahalakadeva
was the last Paramara ruler mentioned here and was killed in 1305 by the forces of Alauddin Khalji.
The founders are Vasudeva of the Chahamanas, Nannuka of the Chandelas, Chandradeva of the Gahadavalas and Kokalla I of the Kalachuris, giving the sequence
B, C, A, D
in the arrangement used here.

secs.t: Temple - dynasty, deity, state

x: Vimal Vasahi was built around 1031 by Vimal Shah, a minister of Solanki ruler Bhima I. It is dedicated to Jain Tirthankara Rishabha or Adinatha.
Luna Vasahi was constructed in 1230 by the Vaghela ministers
Vastupala and Tejapala
and is dedicated to Neminatha.
Udayamati, the queen of
Bhima I
, built Rani-ki-Vav in his memory.

secs.t: Paramara Bhoja - works, prashastis, Bhojshala, Bhojpur

x: Samarangana Sutradhara
’ is Bhoja’s work on architecture. ‘Siddha-Hema’ is associated with Hemachandra, while ‘Alha Khand’ and ‘Kirtikaumudi’ have different authors.
Bhojshala at Dhar is an ASI-protected centre of Sanskrit learning linked with Bhoja and associated with a Saraswati or Vagdevi temple.
Bhojpur, near Bhopal, is known for an unfinished Shiva temple containing a huge linga and the Bhojpur lake.
The Udaipur Prashasti gives the Paramara genealogy and praises King Bhoja.

secs.t: Solanki rulers - contribution

x: Mularaja I founded the Solanki dynasty and established Anahilapataka, identified with Patan, as its capital.
Jayasimha Siddharaja
patronised the Jain scholar Hemachandra and is associated with the Sahasralinga tank at Patan.
Mahmud attacked Somnath in 1025 during the reign of
Bhima I
. Bhima I was also associated with the Modhera Sun Temple and Vimal Vasahi through his minister Vimal Shah.

secs.t: Rajput origin theories - proponent

x: The Agnikula tradition describes the clans as emerging from a sacrificial fire at Mount Abu and is recorded in association with Chand Bardai’s Prithviraj Raso; the four traditional clans are Paramara, Pratihara, Chauhan and Solanki.
James Tod and V.A. Smith advocated the foreign-origin theory of the Rajputs, associating them with Scythian, Huna and Gurjara elements.

secs.t: Nagara style sub-types - region

x: Latina or Rekha-prasada is a single curvilinear tower; Phamsana has a sloping, stepped roof; and Valabhi is barrel-vaulted.
Valabhi is a Nagara shikhara type characterised by a barrel-vaulted form; it is not the name of the Odisha regional school.
Maru-Gurjara is a Solanki-associated Nagara sub-style of Gujarat and Rajasthan, broadly dated to the eleventh–thirteenth centuries, and combines the Maha-Maru and Maha-Gurjara traditions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Madhya Pradesh High Court relied on ASI findings in declaring Bhojshala a Hindu temple; the survey was ordered in 2024, while the 2003 arrangement provided for worship by the two communities on separate days.
Modhera was fully solarised under an MNRE scheme through a 6 MW plant and 15 MWh storage system.

src: Sources: UPSC (Medieval History pp.42, 45); CDI (Block01 Tripartite Struggle impact); APP (Science & Tech Unit 2 Modhera solarisation; Indian History Part 1 Tomara Delhi); LENSD 18 May 2026 (Bhojshala); LENS Jan 2026 p.113 (Somnath, Maru-Gurjara)

units.title: Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara Empire, Mughal Empire, Bhakti Movement and Sufism - Administration, Economy, Society, Religion, Literature, Arts and Architecture

rows.title: Sources for medieval India - Persian chronicles, inscriptions, travellers' accounts

secs.t: Persian and Arabic chronicles → author + reign covered + chronological order

x: Exam angle: match author to work (Al-Biruni: Tahqiq-i-Hind; Minhaj: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Barani: Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; Ibn Battuta: Rihla); arrange the works in chronological order.
Futuh-us-Salatin was written by
Isami
at the Bahmani court around 1350 and covers the period from the Ghaznavids to Muhammad bin Tughlaq, including the Tughlaq campaigns against Warangal.
Amir Khusrau, court poet of Alauddin Khalji, wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh and accompanied Malik Kafur’s 1310 expedition to Warangal.

secs.t: Foreign travellers → country of origin + ruler visited + subject described

x: Exam angle: "who mentioned 300 ports" (Barbosa), "who mentioned sati" (Abdur Razzaq), traveller → country pairs.
Ibn Battuta
’s account of Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign contains observations on espionage, the postal system, sati and slave markets.
Robert Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire draws chiefly on the accounts of
Paes, Nuniz and Abdur Razzaq
Abdur Razzaq
described the sale of diamonds in heaps during his visit to Vijayanagara under Deva Raya II.
Ibn Battuta came to India during
Muhammad bin Tughlaq
’s reign, was appointed qazi of Delhi and was later sent as an envoy to China.

secs.t: Al-Biruni - century, patron, works, views on India

x: Al-Biruni came to India around 1030 CE, during the eleventh century, under Mahmud of Ghazni.
Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and wrote in Arabic on Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy and the caste system.
Al-Biruni recorded
the celebration of Diwali
on Kartika Amavasya.
Al-Biruni observed that Indians were unwilling to share their learning with outsiders.

secs.t: Regional and Sanskrit sources - Rajatarangini, biographies, Vijayanagara and Qutb Shahi works

x: Madhura Vijayam, written by Gangadevi, describes
Kampana’s conquest of Madurai and conditions under Tughlaq rule
Siddhesvara Charitam is a Telugu work by Kase Siddhappa that provides information on
Kakatiya-era society and religion
Firishta was born at Astarabad in Iran in 1552, and his Deccan history refers to Telangana as ‘Tilang’.
Muhammad Qasim Firishta dedicated Tarikh-i-Firishta, or Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi, to
Ibrahim Adil Shah of Bijapur

secs.t: Inscriptions and coins as medieval sources

x: The Vilasa copper plate dates approximately to 1330, the Kaluvacheru record is associated with Anitalli, and Shitab Khan's Warangal inscription dates to 1504–06.
The Lahore dirhams of Mahmud of Ghazni carry an Arabic legend along with a Sanskrit translation written in Sharada script.
The Palam Baoli inscription, dated 1276, praises
Balban
in Sanskrit.

secs.t: Architecture and paintings as sources

x: Sultanate buildings demonstrate the shift from trabeate construction to arcuate construction through the use of
true arches, domes and lime mortar
Naskh was used for Quranic verses, while Nastaliq was used for Persian texts.
The Golconda school of painting was founded by
Mir Hashimi
The Quliyat Quli manuscript contains 14 miniatures.

secs.t: Chronicle writers' biases - court patronage, religious viewpoint

x: Abul Fazl
wrote the official history of Akbar and was one of Akbar's Navaratnas.
Ziauddin Barani wrote from an orthodox Sunni viewpoint and also theorised about kingship.
The Telugu sources Pratapa Charitra, Vilasa and Kaluvacheru record eight invasions of Warangal, whereas Muslim sources associated with Amir Khusrau and Wassaf record five.
Firishta's story that Deva Raya kidnapped Nehal is rejected by modern historians.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Marco Polo is associated with Motupalli, Abdur Razzaq and Barbosa with Vijayanagara, and Tavernier with Golconda.
Al-Biruni, Nicolo Conti and the Ain-i-Akbari are cited as early evidence of Diwali in the referenced UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage discussion.
The Allahabad High Court sought responses from
the Centre and the Archaeological Survey of India

src: Sources: CDI (Block02 Foreign Travellers; Block04 Advent of Islam; Block04 Qutb Shahis; Block03 Kakatiya sources; Block05 Mughal literature); APP (AP History - Medieval, Unit 2 Kakatiya and Qutb Shahi sources; Indian History Part 2 Indo-Islamic architecture); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.173, 234, 238, 282, 295, 300); APHQ (2011 Q24, Q26; 2017 Q33); UPSC (Medieval History p.54); VIS PT365 Apr 2026 p.95; TH 8 Jul 2026
see: See also Group-II S1-44 (Sultanate language and literature - Persian chronicles, Amir Khusrau, regional languages), merged under A-96.

rows.title: Slave/Mamluk dynasty - Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish (iqta, Chalisa, Turkan-i-Chahalgani), Razia Sultan, Balban

secs.t: Qutbuddin Aibak - master, earlier post, titles, capital, monuments, death

x: Qutbuddin Aibak began the Qutb Minar and dedicated it to
Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki
The Second Battle of Tarain occurred in 1192, followed by Ghori's death and Aibak's accession in 1206; Aibak died in 1210.
Qutbuddin Aibak was originally a slave of Muhammad Ghori, rose from Master of Stables to general, and became Sultan after Ghori’s death in 1206.

secs.t: Dynasty names and period - Slave, Mamluk, Ilbari

x: The dynasty is known as the Slave or Mamluk dynasty; the ruling line is also associated with the Ilbari Turks.
The Qutbi line lasted from 1206 to 1211 and the First Ilbari line from 1211 to 1266.
The sequence was Mamluk (1206–1290), Khalji (1290–1320), Tughlaq (1320–1414), Sayyid (1414–1451) and Lodi (1451–1526).

secs.t: Balban - name, theory of kingship, court customs, blood and iron, army, Mongols

x: Balban was captured by the Mongols, bought by Iltutmish, rose from water-carrier to the Forty, and was made Amir-i-Shikar by Razia.
Balban used ruthless suppression, strict court discipline and the policy popularly described as blood and iron.
Balban used forts and a strong army on the north-west frontier, and his son Prince Muhammad was killed fighting the Mongols in 1285.

secs.t: Iltutmish - rivals, capital, legitimacy, institutions, Mongols, monuments

x: Iltutmish was the Iqtadar of Gwalior and later served as governor of Baran and Badaun.
Iltutmish received the investiture, or mansur, from the Abbasid Caliph of Baghdad in 1229.
Under the iqta system, revenue assignments were given to officers called muqtis instead of paying them cash salaries.
Iltutmish built the
Sultan Ghari tomb
and is consequently called the Father of tomb building.

secs.t: Razia Sultan - accession, opposition, Yakut, end

x: Razia discarded purdah, wore male attire and personally led the army.
The Turkish nobles resented Razia's favour towards
Yaqut, an Abyssinian
Altuniya's revolt was followed by Yaqut's death and Razia's imprisonment; Razia then married Altuniya, marched towards Delhi, and was defeated and killed in 1240.
Altuniya
, the governor of Bhatinda or Sirhind, revolted against Razia.

secs.t: Nasiruddin Mahmud and the rise of Balban

x: Nasiruddin Mahmud ruled from 1246 to 1266 and was considered a pious and weak Sultan.
Balban was Nasiruddin Mahmud's principal minister, or naib, and leader of the Forty.
Minhaj-us-Siraj's Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was named after Sultan
Nasiruddin Mahmud

secs.t: End of the dynasty and rise of the Khaljis

x: Balban died in 1286 and was followed by his grandson Kaiqubad, who was murdered.
Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji crowned himself at
Kilokhari
in 1290, thereby ending Mamluk rule and beginning the Khalji dynasty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Slave or Mamluk dynasty
was the first Muslim dynasty to rule North India from Delhi and laid the institutional foundation of the Delhi Sultanate.
The dynasty helped establish the iqta, Forty, tanka-jital and Diwan-i-Arz institutions, while the Qutb complex is now a UNESCO site.
The
Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
is regarded as the first mosque in India in the context of the early Delhi Sultanate.

src: Sources: APP (Indian History Part 1: Mamluk Dynasty; Iltutmish and Razia; Balban and the End of the Slave Dynasty); UPSC (Medieval History pp.2, 58-59); CDI (Block04 Advent of Islam - Ghurid phase, Iqta system); PYQs APPSC G1 2004/2018, GS 2023, UPPSC 2024

rows.title: Khalji dynasty - Jalaluddin; Alauddin Khalji's conquests, Deccan campaigns of Malik Kafur

secs.t: Alauddin Khalji's territorial expansion - order of conquests, commanders, ruler defeated

x: Exam angle: chronological order (UPPSC 2022: Gujarat, Ranthambore, Chittor, Warangal); statements on Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan leading the 1299 Gujarat campaign.
After the conquest of Chittor in 1303, Alauddin Khalji renamed it
Khizrabad
after his son Prince Khizr Khan.
Gujarat was associated with Rai Karan, Chittor with Rana Ratan Singh, Warangal with Prataparudra II, and the Malwa campaign was led by Ain-ul-Mulk Multani.
Alauddin generally pursued annexation in northern territories, whereas southern rulers often retained their thrones after agreeing to pay tribute.

secs.t: Delhi Sultans → reign period

x: Bahlol Lodi ruled from 1451 to 1489, not 1491.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled from 1325 to 1351.

secs.t: Mongol invasions under Jalaluddin and Alauddin - leaders, defence

x: The first Mongol threat came under Iltutmish in 1221, when
Chengiz Khan
was the Mongol leader.
The Mongols who converted and settled in the Sultanate were known as the
New Mussalmans
Zafar Khan was killed in the battle of
Kili
in 1299 while fighting the Mongols.
During the Mongol advance and siege of Delhi, Alauddin Khalji sheltered in
Siri Fort

secs.t: Alauddin's titles, religious ambitions, Shariat, nobles

x: Under Jalaluddin, Alauddin held the office of
Amir-i-Tuzuk
, or master of ceremonies.
Ala-ul-Mulk
, the Kotwal of Delhi and uncle of Barani, advised Alauddin against both ambitions.
Alauddin ruled according to the interests of the state and did not allow the ulema's religious advice to control every state decision.
Ulugh Khan, Ain-ul-Mulk Multani and Malik Kafur served Alauddin Khalji.

secs.t: Chittor and the Padmini legend

x: Alauddin Khalji defeated Raja Ratan Singh at Chittor in 1303, and Rani Padmini and the Rajput women are described as having performed jauhar.
Padmavat was written in 1540.
Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed Padmavat in
Awadhi
Some scholars treat the Padmini motive as a legend rather than an undisputed historical account.

secs.t: Jalaluddin - accession, policy, end

x: Jalaluddin Khalji was the first Sultan described as having a benevolent attitude towards Hindus, and he was lenient towards rebels including Malik Chhajju.
Jalaluddin crowned himself at Kilokhari, failed in his attack on Ranthambore, and was murdered at Kara by Alauddin in 1296.
Alauddin Khalji raided Devagiri during
, before murdering Jalaluddin and becoming Sultan.

secs.t: Successors - Mubarak Shah, Khusrau Khan, end of the Khaljis

x: After Alauddin's death in 1316, Malik Kafur set aside Khizr Khan and placed the minor Shihabuddin Umar on the throne.
Malik Kafur was murdered after Alauddin's death; Mubarak Shah was later murdered by Khusrau Khan, who was then killed by Ghazi Malik in 1320.
Khusrau Khan
murdered Mubarak Shah and briefly succeeded him as Nasiruddin Khusrau Shah.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements correctly describe the major stages of Kakatiya–Delhi relations: the defeat at Upparapalli, the treaty of 1309–10, assistance against the Pandyas in 1311, and the cessation of tribute after 1316.
Alauddin Khalji's reign is called
the imperial period
of the Delhi Sultanate because of its extensive territorial expansion and campaigns.

src: Sources: APP (Indian History Part 1: Jalaluddin Khilji; Alauddin Khilji - Rise and Military Campaigns; Part 2: Decline of the Khiljis); UPSC (Medieval History pp.64-66); CDX (AP History pp.160, 169, 173-174); CDI (Block03 Kakatiya sources); APHQ (2019 Q24); PYQs APPSC G2 2012, GS 2023, UPPSC 2022/2025, BPSC 2024, UPSC 2022
see: See also Group-II S1-38 (Alauddin Khalji - conquests, market control and administrative reforms), merged under A-88.

rows.title: Alauddin Khalji's market control regulations, revenue and military reforms
sub: Group-II S1-38: Alauddin Khalji - conquests, market control and administrative reforms

secs.t: Market reforms - aim, markets, price fixation, rationing, officials

x: Exam angle: UPPSC keys call the market control "highly successful"; Barani is the main source.
Mandi dealt with food grains, Sarai Adl with cloth and other specified commodities, the third market with horses, slaves and cattle, and the fourth market with miscellaneous goods.
The regulations sought to fix prices, guarantee supply, control distribution and end monopolistic practices through official supervision.

secs.t: Delhi Sultanate dynasties → key contribution
Ordinances and social measures - nobles, prohibition, punishments, espionage

x: Barani identified noble wealth, noble intermarriage and gatherings, a weak intelligence system and drinking as four causes of revolt perceived by Alauddin.
Alauddin Khalji required royal permission for gatherings and marriages among nobles, thereby limiting their independent alliances and collective activity.
Alauddin reorganised espionage, prohibited liquor and gambling, and confiscated religious grants and free lands.

secs.t: Revenue reforms - assessment, share, new taxes, khalisa, intermediaries

x: Alauddin Khalji introduced systematic land measurement, with the biswa as the standard unit, and assessed revenue on the measured area and yield.
Unjustified inam and waqf grants were taken back, enlarging the khalisa, or crown-land, area.
Abolition of the headman's cess prevented village intermediaries and rich peasants from shifting the burden of taxation to poorer cultivators.

secs.t: Military reforms - army type, dagh and huliya, payment

x: Dagh referred to branding horses and huliya or chehra to the descriptive roll of each soldier.
Ferishta put Alauddin Khalji’s cavalry at approximately 4,75,000.
The Ariz-i-Mamalik recruited, inspected and paid the army.
Alauddin Khalji
created the first standing army paid in cash and introduced dagh and huliya in military administration.

secs.t: Alauddin's views on kingship and religion - ulema

x: Alauddin openly overrode the ulema and held that state policy should be determined by the needs of the state rather than exclusively by religious advice.
Alauddin did revive a harsh and centralised style of rule, but unlike Balban he did not depend on religious sanction for his policies.

secs.t: Effects and end of reforms after his death

x: Mubarak Shah, who ruled from 1316 to 1320, abolished the price controls, restored confiscated lands and withdrew the harsh regulations.
Mubarak Shah ruled from 1316 to 1320, immediately after Alauddin Khalji’s death in 1316.
The reforms helped maintain low prices and a strong army capable of resisting the Mongols, but repression and espionage created widespread discontent.

secs.t: Deccan campaigns of Malik Kafur, and Kafur's background

x: Pothuganti Maili and Recherla Venna
defeated the expedition led by Malik Fakhruddin Juna at Upparapalli in 1303.
Malik Kafur and Khwaja Haji besieged Warangal, obtained Prataparudra's submission and sent the loot to Delhi on 1,000 camels.
The Deccan expeditions were primarily financial ventures intended to secure plunder and tribute for paying the army, rather than to annex the southern states.
Devagiri was ruled by Ramachandra, Warangal by Prataparudra II, Dwarasamudra by Vira Ballala III, and the Pandya kingdom of Madurai was sacked.

secs.t: Mongol defence - forts, Sikandar-i-Sani, plan for a new religion

x: Alauddin repaired old frontier forts and built new ones, thereby completing Balban’s frontier policy.
Kotwal Ala-ul-Mulk
talked Alauddin out of both the plan for world conquest and the proposal for a new religion.
Alauddin Khalji's victories were at Jalandhar in 1298, Kili in 1299, Amroha in 1305 and Ravi in 1306.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Potuganti Maili and Recherla Venna
defeated Malik Fakhruddin Juna at Upparapalli during the failed 1303 attack on Warangal.
Mahmud Gawan
of the Bahmani kingdom later introduced dagh and chehra, land measurement and a larger khalisa.
The combination of despotism and extensive espionage weakened the state internally, and the dynasty declined soon after Alauddin’s death in 1316.

Sources: Group-II S1-38: APP (Indian History Part 1 & 2 > Alauddin Khilji: Rise; Deccan Campaigns, Market Reforms); UPSC (Medieval History pp.65-66); CDX (AP History pp.160, 173-174, 209); CDI (Block03 Kakatiya sources); APHQ aph2012_20, aph2019_24
see: Group-II S1-38 also overlaps Group-I A-87.

rows.title: Tughlaq dynasty - Ghiyasuddin; Muhammad bin Tughlaq's five experiments; Firoz Shah's reforms
sub: Group-II S1-39: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments and Firoz Shah Tughlaq's reforms

secs.t: Firoz Shah Tughlaq - departments, canals, towns, jizya, charity, translations, autobiography, Ashokan pillars

x: Firoz Shah succeeded
Muhammad bin Tughlaq
at Thatta in 1351 and ruled until 1388.
Diwan-i-Khairat dealt with charity, Diwan-i-Bandagan with slaves, Dar-ul-Shifa was a free hospital, and Diwan-i-Istihqaq provided pensions and grants.
The Employment Bureau arranged work, Diwan-i-Khairat provided charitable assistance, and Diwan-i-Bandagan dealt with slaves.
Important canals of Firoz Shah included those carrying water from the
Yamuna and Sutlej to Hisar
Firoz wrote off taqavi loans and state debts, fixed land revenue, retained the four Islamic taxes, and made iqtas hereditary.
Azizuddin Khalid Khani
translated the Sanskrit texts taken from the Jwalamukhi temple at Nagarkot into Persian.
Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul paid compensation to persons who had suffered during Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rule.
Firoz Tughlaq's period saw the translation of Sanskrit texts from Nagarkot into Dalail-i-Firozshahi and the translation of Ragadarpan.
The translation of Amritakund belongs to the thirteenth century, followed by the translations under Firoz Tughlaq and Sikandar Lodi.
Siri was founded by Alauddin Khalji, Tughlaqabad by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Jahanpanah by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firozabad by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq brought the Ashokan pillars from Topra or Khizrabad and Meerut to Delhi.

secs.t: Muhammad bin Tughlaq - five experiments, causes and results

x: Exam angle: statement questions ("token currency was copper and brass"; "the Doab tax coincided with famine").
The capital was transferred in 1327, token currency was introduced around 1329–30, and the Khurasan and Qarachil experiments followed.
Copper and brass token coins were widely forged, so the Sultan recalled and redeemed them at a heavy cost to the treasury.
The higher Doab taxation aimed at increasing revenue, but it coincided with famine and led to peasant revolts and flight.

secs.t: Delhi Sultans → distinctive measure

x: Iltutmish
established the Chahalgani, while Balban later ended its influence.
Branding of horses
, or dagh, was a measure of Alauddin Khalji.
Alauddin Khalji's military and administrative measures included dagh, huliya, market control and land measurement.
The Zil-i-Ilahi theory was associated with Balban, not Iltutmish.

secs.t: MBT's agrarian measures - department, loans, famine relief

x: Taqavi or sondhar loans were agricultural advances intended to help cultivators purchase seed and dig wells.
The Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi financed the extension of cultivation, provided state loans and encouraged farmers to grow better crops.
During the famine in the Doab, Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted to a camp at Swargadwari near
Kannauj

secs.t: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq - earlier name, agrarian policy, Warangal, Tughlaqabad, death

x: Ghazi Malik had the stated parentage, served as governor of Punjab under Alauddin Khalji, and became Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq Shah in 1320.
Ghiyasuddin became Sultan in 1320, Juna Khan attacked Warangal in 1321–22, Warangal fell in 1323, and Ghiyasuddin died in 1325.
Prince
Juna Khan
led the attack on Warangal in 1321–22 and later succeeded his father as Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

secs.t: Contemporary accounts of MBT - Ibn Battuta, historians' verdicts

x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq appointed Ibn Battuta Qazi of Delhi and later sent him as an envoy to China in 1342.
Ibn Battuta recorded horse couriers called uluq at intervals of four miles and foot couriers called dawa at intervals of one mile.
Ibn Battuta came to India in 1333 during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and was appointed Qazi of Delhi.
Ibn Battuta is identified in this context as the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara during the reign of
Harihara I
The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta’s real name was
Abu Abdullah Muhammad

secs.t: Successors of Firoz and the end of the Tughlaqs

x: Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah Tughlaq
was the last Tughlaq ruler and was on the throne when Timur invaded India in 1398.
Daulat Khan Lodi
was briefly recognised after Sultan Mahmud's death.
The Tughlaq period began with Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in 1320 and ended when Khizr Khan took Delhi in 1414.

secs.t: Revolts under MBT - Madurai, Vijayanagara and Bahmani rise

x: The order is coastal Andhra liberation around 1325, Madurai Sultanate in 1335, Vijayanagara in 1336 and Bahmani kingdom in 1347.
Harihara and Bukka had been sent by Muhammad bin Tughlaq and later founded Vijayanagara under the guidance of Vidyaranya.
The Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347 by
Alauddin Hasan Gangu, who assumed the title Bahman Shah

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Warangal fell in 1323 and became Sultanpur; the Musunuri recovery followed, while Prolaya Vema Reddi expelled Tughlaq forces from coastal Andhra around 1325.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq is regarded as the first Sultan of Delhi to initiate canal digging, while Firoz Shah undertook canal construction on a much larger scale.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq has been judged both a visionary ahead of his time and an eccentric ruler, notably in the accounts of Ibn Battuta and Barani.

rows.title: Timur's invasion; Sayyid and Lodi dynasties; the First Battle of Panipat, 1526

secs.t: Sikandar Lodi - city founded, measurement unit, pen name, tax remissions

x: Sikandar Lodi maintained
systematic audits and a spy network
as part of his administration.
Sikandar Lodi extended his authority from Punjab to Bihar, subdued Jaunpur and defeated Bengal rulers and Rajput chiefs.
Sikandar Lodi was religiously intolerant in several actions, including destruction of images and temples and imposition of jizya, yet he had a Sanskrit medical treatise translated into Persian.

secs.t: Lodi rulers → contribution, succession, contemporary events

x: Bahlol Lodi
ruled from 1451 to 1489 and had the longest reign among the three Lodi rulers.
Bahlol Lodi was succeeded by his son Sikandar Lodi, who was followed by Ibrahim Lodi.
Before becoming Sultan, Bahlol Lodi was the governor of
Punjab
Bahlol Lodi received the throne from
Alam Shah
, the last ruler of the Sayyid dynasty.

secs.t: Sayyid dynasty - founder, rulers in order, relationship with Timur

x: Khizr Khan, Timur’s viceroy, arrested Daulat Khan Lodi, captured Delhi in 1414 and ruled as Timur’s deputy without using the title Sultan.
Mubarak Shah’s octagonal tomb is noted for
blue enamelled tiles and guldasta motifs
Alauddin Alam Shah voluntarily gave up the throne to Bahlol Lodi in 1451.

secs.t: Timur's invasion - year, Sultan, route, effects

x: Timur crossed the Indus, passed through Punjab via Multan and Bhatnair, and sacked Delhi in December 1398.
Jaunpur, Malwa and Gujarat
were among the regional kingdoms that emerged after the weakening and breakup of the Tughlaq state.
Babur was descended from Timur on his father’s side and from Chengiz Khan on his mother’s side.

secs.t: Ibrahim Lodi - Rana Sanga, nobles, invitation to Babur

x: Ibrahim Lodi fought
Rana Sanga of Mewar
at Khatauli in 1517–18 and was defeated there.
Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of Punjab, Alam Khan, Ibrahim’s uncle, and Rana Sanga invited Babur against Ibrahim Lodi.
The political background included Ibrahim Lodi’s unpopularity, strong Mewar and Marwar, five Deccan Sultanates and Vijayanagara in the south.

secs.t: First Battle of Panipat - tactics, consequences

x: Babur’s
field artillery and muskets
were decisive factors in the victory at Panipat.
Tulughma was a
flanking manoeuvre
used by Babur to envelop the opposing army.
Babur chained Araba carts together to create a defensive line, following the Rumi or Ottoman device.
Babur fought Rana Sanga at Kanwah in 1527 and then fought at Chanderi in 1528.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Lodis constituted the first Afghan dynasty and the final ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, while Ibrahim Lodi was its last Delhi Sultan.
The 500th anniversary of the First Battle of Panipat was marked on
21 April 2026
, five centuries after the battle of 21 April 1526.

rows.title: Delhi Sultanate - the five dynasties in outline
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-90

secs.t: Dynasties - founder and period in order; shortest and longest

x: Exam angle: the rule periods are asked as a match (Tughlaqs 1320-1414, Mamluks 1206-1290, Lodis 1451-1526, Sayyids 1414-1451).
The Mamluks ruled from 1206 to 1290, the Khaljis from 1290 to 1320, the Tughlaqs from 1320 to 1414 and the Sayyids from 1414 to 1451.
The Tughlaqs ruled from 1320 to 1414, making theirs the longest dynasty in the Delhi Sultanate, with a duration of
94 years

secs.t: FIRST-LAST - first Sultan, last ruler of each dynasty, ruler at Portuguese arrival

x: Kaiqubad
was the last effective ruler of the Mamluk dynasty and was killed in 1290.
Sikandar Lodi
was the Delhi Sultan when Vasco da Gama arrived at Calicut.
Bahlol Lodi was the first Afghan ruler of Delhi
; the rulers before him were Turks.

secs.t: Succession order within dynasties

x: The succession was Qutbuddin Aibak, Aram Shah, Iltutmish, Ruknuddin Firoz and Razia.
The order was Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji, Shihabuddin, the child set up by Malik Kafur, and Mubarak Shah.
The Sayyid succession was Khizr Khan, Mubarak Shah, Muhammad Shah and Alauddin Alam Shah.

secs.t: Titles and epithets - Lakh Baksh, Zillillah, Ghazi Malik

x: Balban
adopted the titles Zil-i-Ilahi or Zillillah, meaning Shadow of God, and Niyabat-i-Khudai.
Sikandar Lodi
used Gulrukhi as his pen-name for Persian verse.

secs.t: Battles - Tarain, Chandawar, Khatoli; Iltutmish's rivals Yalduz and Qabacha

x: The First and Second Battles of Tarain occurred in 1191 and 1192, Chandawar in 1194, and Khatoli in 1517.
Rana Sanga defeated
Ibrahim Lodi
in the Battle of Khatoli in 1517.
Iltutmish defeated Yalduz at Tarain in 1215–16 and suppressed Qabacha in 1228.

secs.t: Mongol invasions - Chengiz Khan's arrival, Balban's frontier policy

x: Chengiz Khan reached the Indus in 1221 while pursuing the fugitive Khwarezm prince
Jalaluddin Mangbarni
Iltutmish refused shelter to Jalaluddin Mangbarni because granting protection to Chengiz Khan's enemy could have invited a Mongol invasion of his kingdom.
Timur invaded India in 1398 during the reign of
Nasiruddin Mahmud
, the last ruler of the Tughlaq dynasty.

secs.t: Breakaway kingdoms - Bengal, Bahmani, Vijayanagara origins

x: Tughril Khan revolted in 1279, Haji Iliyas later made Bengal independent, the Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347, and Firoz's second campaign occurred in 1359–60.
Harihara and Bukka were sent against Deccan rebels, later returned to Hinduism under Vidyaranya, and founded Anegondi, which developed into Vijayanagara.
Tughril Khan's Bengal revolt occurred in 1279, the Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347, Vijayanagara in 1336, and Jaunpur was re-annexed in 1476.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Rajon ki Baoli is a
four-tier stepwell
located in the Mehrauli Archaeological Park.
Daulat Khan Lodi built Rajon ki Baoli in 1506 during the reign of
Sikandar Lodi
Delhi's first invasion of Andhra occurred in 1303, Prataparudra II was captured in 1323, Vijayanagara was founded in 1336, and the Bahmani kingdom in 1347.

rows.title: Sultanate central administration - Sultan, wazir, the diwans, nobility, theory of kingship
sub: Group-II S1-40: Delhi Sultanate administration - Sultan, wazir, diwans, iqta and the nobility

secs.t: Wazirs and key nobles → Sultan served; heyday of the wizarat

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Junaidi
served as the wazir of Iltutmish.
Imad-ul-Mulk served Balban, Malik Kafur was the Naib Malik of Alauddin Khalji, and Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul was the wazir of Firoz Tughlaq.
The wizarat reached its heyday under
Firoz Tughlaq
, when Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul effectively ran the government.
The Naib ranked next to the Sultan and, in practice, controlled all departments.

secs.t: Central departments → function + founding Sultan

x: Diwan-i-Insha dealt with correspondence, Diwan-i-Risalat with religious affairs and grants, Diwan-i-Arz with the army, and Diwan-i-Mustakhraj with recovery of arrears.
Diwan-i-Arz, the department dealing with army recruitment and inspection, was set up by
Balban
Diwan-i-Bandagan, the department dealing with slaves, was established by Firoz Tughlaq, not Balban.
Diwan-i-Riyasat was the department of
market control
, functioning under the Naib-i-Riyasat, during Alauddin Khalji's reign.

secs.t: Relations with the Caliphate - investiture, titles, self-proclaimed Caliph

x: Exam angle: BPSC 2022 asked who "opposed the Khalifa's power". The key was "more than one of the above".
Iltutmish received a letter of investiture, or mansur, from the Abbasid Caliph of Baghdad in approximately 1229.
Mubarak Shah Khalji
proclaimed himself Caliph.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq sought investiture from the Abbasid Caliph in Egypt.

secs.t: Theory of kingship → Sultan

x: Balban
propounded the concept of the Sultan as Zil-i-Ilahi, or Shadow of God, along with Niyabat-i-Khudai, or divine deputyship.
Balban excluded low-born men from high office, whereas the appointment of non-Turks and low-born men is associated with Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
Both statements are true, and the absence of a fixed succession rule resulted from the decisive role of nobles, ulema and military strength in determining the successor.

secs.t: Officials → duty

x: The
Ariz-i-Mamalik
was the head of the army department.
The Sadr-us-Sudur supervised
religious affairs and endowments
; the Chief Sadr was also the Chief Qazi.
Qazi-ul-Quzat was the Chief Justice, Barid-i-Mumalik headed intelligence, and Wakil-i-Dar supervised the court and royal household.

secs.t: Legal basis and nature of the state - sharia vs zawabit, composite elements

x: Sharia covered the civil matters of Muslims, while royal decrees or zawabit supplemented the legal order.
The title Sultan, the nominal authority of the Caliph and Persian court rituals such as sijda, paibos and Nauroz were Perso-Arabic elements.
The Turko-Mongol elements included decimal military organisation and power based on horse warfare with mounted archers.

secs.t: Nobility - ethnic composition, the Chalisa

x: The Khalji Revolution opened high office to non-Turks and Indian Muslims, breaking the earlier Turkish monopoly.
Lodi rulers dealt with an Afghan tribal nobility that treated the Sultan as first among equals.
Iltutmish created the Forty, Balban destroyed its power, Jalaluddin Khalji came to power in 1290, and Alauddin later imposed restrictions on the nobility.

secs.t: Local and revenue officials → role

x: The muqaddam or chaudhari headed the village, the chaudhari had a major rural revenue role, and Alauddin abolished the khut’s cess.
Mauza was the village unit; the muqaddam or chaudhari was the village headman; and the patwari was the village accountant.
Mir Bakshi
was a Mughal office and did not exist under the Delhi Sultans.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Peshwa was the Prime Minister, was renamed Diwan under Tana Shah, was last held by Madanna, and the Majumdar served as auditor, mostly from the Hindu community.
The Bahmani state and the Qutb Shahis inherited the Delhi model, including institutions such as Wakil-us-Saltanat, Amir-i-Jumla, Peshwa, Mir Jumla and Diwan-i-Insha.

rows.title: Sultanate provincial and military administration - iqta system, dagh and huliya, army organisation

secs.t: Iqta system - introducer, muqti duties, fawazil, transfers, changes by Sultan

x: Amaram or nayankara
was the Vijayanagara system in which land was granted to amaranayakas for maintaining troops.
The surplus remaining after meeting the obligations of the iqta was called
fawazil
and was remitted to the central authority.
Iltutmish
organised the iqta system and assigned iqtas to Turkish officers, who were known as Shamsi officers.
Alauddin Khalji enlarged the khalisa, paid his large standing army in cash, and strengthened the audit of muqtis.
Before Firoz Tughlaq made iqtas hereditary, muqtis were transferred periodically from one iqta to another.

secs.t: Land assignment terms compared → dynasty/region

x: Khalisa
land was under direct crown administration, and its revenue went to the royal treasury, court and household.
Iqta denoted an assignment of land revenue in the Delhi Sultanate and was also used in the Bahmani context as a synonym for jagir.
Khalisa was crown land, iqta was assigned to officials in place of salary, and inam was granted to religious men and institutions.

secs.t: Dagh and huliya and the ariz's department - introducer, purpose

x: Alauddin Khalji
introduced dagh, the branding of horses, and huliya, the descriptive roll of each soldier.
Branding horses and maintaining descriptive rolls helped prevent soldiers from bringing inferior horses or sending proxies in their place during inspection.
Balban did not introduce horse branding.

secs.t: Army organisation - ranks and unit sizes

x: The order was sar-i-khail, sipah-salar, amir, malik and khan.
An Amir commanded ten sipah-salars
Cavalry was the core arm of the army, which also included infantry and elephants.

secs.t: Army pay - cash vs iqta under different Sultans

x: Alauddin Khalji
maintained the first large permanent standing army paid in cash from the royal treasury.
Iltutmish and Balban used iqtas for payment, Alauddin Khalji introduced large-scale cash payment, and Firoz Tughlaq returned to assignment-based payment through the jagir revival.
The jagir revival enabled nobles to control
recruitment, promotion and discipline
, which weakened the efficiency of the army.

secs.t: Postal and intelligence systems - dak chowkis, barids

x: Alauddin Khalji obtained daily market reports from
barids and munhiyans
, the latter functioning as secret spies.
Ghiyasuddin Tughluq
improved the postal system by employing both runners and horsemen.
Ibn Battuta described the horse post as ulaq and the foot post as dawa.
The horse post, called ulaq, was used to bring fruit from Khorasan to Delhi.

secs.t: Military technology - cavalry, war elephants, horse trade

x: The Turks introduced or strengthened horse-based warfare, mounted archery, the iron stirrup, armour and stronger fortifications.
The importance of horses increased with the spread of Turkish horse-based warfare.
War elephants were regarded as a royal preserve.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Vijayanagara had the Siddha Sainyam and Amara Nayankara army; the Qutb Shahis had the Siddha Sainyam and Jagirdar Sainyam; Kakatiya royal bodyguards were Lenkas; and Shivaji maintained a cash-paid standing army.
Shivaji maintained a standing army paid in cash, avoided jagir grants and established the naval bases of Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg.

rows.title: Sultanate economy - kharaj, jizya, zakat, khams; agriculture, urbanisation, trade and craft
sub: Group-II S1-41: Sultanate socio-economic conditions - agriculture, revenue, towns and trade

secs.t: Taxes → nature + payer (kharaj, jizya, zakat, khams, ushr)

x: Exam angle: "Khams = 1/5 of war booty" and "Zakat = tax on Muslims only" are the standard traps.
Kharaj
was a land tax, usually assessed at one-third of the produce, with the rate varying according to crop and region from one-tenth to one-half.
Jizya was a protection tax on non-Muslims, zakat was payable by Muslims, and khams was the state’s one-fifth share of booty and treasure-troves.

secs.t: Trade - overland (Khorasan) and coastal routes, transport, trading groups

x: Textiles, glassware and horses were imported from West Asia, while silk and porcelain came from China.
Multanis and Khurasanis controlled overseas trade and financing; Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants dominated inland trade; and Banjaras carried bulk goods such as grain using oxen.
The horse post, or uluq/ulaq, had royal horses stationed about every four miles.

secs.t: Currency - tanka, jital, shashgani, metals, token currency

x: Iltutmish
first issued the silver tanka and copper jital as standard Arabic coinage.
Around 1329–30, Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced brass and copper token coins at par with the silver tanka.
Firoz Tughlaq introduced the adha, worth one-half of a jital, and the bikh, worth one-fourth of a jital.
The tanka was silver, associated with Iltutmish and weighed 175 grains; the jital was copper; and the shashgani was worth six jitals.

secs.t: Agriculture - crops, irrigation devices, Firoz's canals, taccavi

x: The longest canal of Firoz Tughlaq's extensive canal network ran from the
Yamuna to Hisar
Firoz Tughlaq
built the most extensive canal network, although Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq was the first canal-builder of the fourteenth century.
Ibn Battuta observed two harvests a year, rabi and kharif, and noted that rice was sown three times annually.

secs.t: Additional cesses introduced by Sultans → Sultan + nature

x: Alauddin Khalji
introduced Ghari, the house tax, and Charai, the grazing tax on milch cattle.
Haq-i-sharb was an irrigation cess of about
one-tenth of the produce
on canal-watered land.
Firoz Tughlaq abolished many illegal cesses and retained the four Sharia taxes: kharaj, jizya, zakat and khams.

secs.t: Urbanisation - new towns founded → Sultan

x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
renamed Devagiri as Daulatabad and shifted his capital there.
Alauddin Khalji founded Siri, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded Tughlaqabad, Muhammad bin Tughlaq founded Jahanpanah and Sikandar Lodi founded Agra.
Firoz Tughlaq founded or established Hisar, also known as Hisar Firoza, Firozabad, Fatehabad and Jaunpur.
Broach and Cambay
were important ports, while the other pairs were chiefly inland towns or administrative centres.

secs.t: Crafts and industries - karkhanas, textiles, paper

x: Firoz Tughlaq maintained about 36 royal karkhanas.
The Turks popularised paper-making, glass-making, the spinning wheel, improved looms, the iron stirrup and better armour.
The availability of paper
strengthened bureaucratic record-keeping
in the Sultanate administration.
Leather work, metal-work and carpet-weaving flourished during the Sultanate period, along with textiles and other crafts.

secs.t: Land revenue categories

x: An iqta was a land assignment made to officials instead of paying them a direct salary.
Peasants generally paid
one-third and sometimes one-half
of the produce as land revenue.

secs.t: Social classes - nobles, ulema, peasants, slaves

x: Nobles held iqtas, the ulema interpreted religious law, and khuts and muqaddams were involved in collecting revenue from peasants.
The ulema were the custodians and interpreters of religious law.
Ibn Battuta referred to slave markets, and Firoz Tughlaq maintained a separate department for slaves.
Hindu society retained its caste order, while sati and purdah spread during this period.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Alauddin Khalji's price controls were designed in the context of maintaining the army, showing how military needs shaped economic policy.
Sher Shah's revenue demand ranged from
one-fourth to one-third of the produce
and was based on survey.
Amir Khusrau's account of Warangal's diamonds and wealth helps explain why it attracted invasions from Delhi.
Ibn Battuta described the Malabar
pepper
trade with China and Persia.

rows.title: Sultanate society - nobility, ulema, position of women, slavery; conversion and syncretism
sub: Group-II S1-42: Sultanate religious conditions - ulema, conversion, jizya and syncretism

secs.t: Social group terms → meaning

x: Kulah-daran referred to the Sayyids, who wore the pointed cap called kulah.
Ashraf denoted elite Muslims of foreign descent, including Turks, Persians, Afghans and Sayyids.
Rais, Rana and Rawat were terms used for Hindu chiefs and landed warrior aristocrats in Barani’s vocabulary.
The Hindu caste order, with Brahmins at the top, continued.

secs.t: Ulema and the Islamic character of the state

x: Barani argued that the Sultanate was not purely Islamic because the Sultan supplemented the Sharia with state regulations known as zawabits.
Alauddin Khalji reduced the ulema’s interference in state affairs and told Qazi Mughisuddin that he would decree what he considered good for the state.
Firoz Tughlaq followed the ulema, adopted theocratic principles, respected the Egyptian Caliph and extended jizya to Brahmins.

secs.t: Hindu-Muslim relations - jizya, temple policy, Hindu worship at court

x: Sikandar Lodi was orthodox; he destroyed temples at Mathura, broke the Jwalamukhi images at Nagarkot and imposed jizya.
Firoz Tughlaq
ordered temples to be destroyed, prohibited public idol worship and penalised Hindus and Shias.
They represent the different religious and political approaches of Iltutmish, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Sikandar Lodi and Firoz Tughlaq.

secs.t: Position of women - purdah, sati, jauhar, women rulers

x: Sati was prevalent and had documented instances, including Ibn Battuta’s description.
Purdah was brought by the
Arabs and Turks
and spread particularly among the elite, along with child marriage.
Jauhar was performed at
Ranthambhor in 1301 and Chittor in 1303
during resistance against Alauddin.
Lal Ded
of Kashmir was a female saint who found expression through Bhakti and Sufism.

secs.t: Slavery - sources, slave markets, diwan-i-bandagan

x: Slaves came from war captivity, purchase in markets and among defaulters.
Alauddin Khalji’s third regulated market dealt with horses, slaves and cattle at fixed prices.
Firoz Tughlaq created the Diwan-i-Bandagan to administer
slaves
Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban were themselves slaves, or bandagan, which explains the association with the name Slave or Mamluk Dynasty.

secs.t: Conversion debates - theories

x: Political patronage and state employment could encourage conversion by providing benefits such as
tax relief and access to office
Social liberation was a contributing factor because egalitarian ideals appealed to some groups, but caste-like stratification continued among converts.
Sufi influence was a major factor especially in Bengal and Punjab, and it operated together with agrarian expansion.

secs.t: Syncretism - Bhakti-Sufi interaction, Sanskrit-Persian exchange, new rituals

x: Hamiduddin Nagori's Hindi verses equated the Hindu devotional expression Alakh Niranjan with Khuda.
Sheikh Nuruddin founded Kashmir's Rishi movement, echoing Lalla, adopted vegetarianism and served people of all castes.
The Chishtis made their khanqahs centres of charity, while dargah worship, Urs festivals and qawwali developed as shared rituals and practices.

secs.t: Syncretism - Bhakti-Sufi links, shared shrines, music

x: Sufis, especially the
Chishtis
such as Muinuddin, Nizamuddin Auliya and Baba Farid, communicated with people in Hindavi.
Sufi khanqahs and dargahs drew
Hindus and Muslims alike
, alongside the Bhakti and Nath traditions.
Sufi poetry represented human love as a metaphor for
divine love
, as illustrated by Jayasi's Padmavat.
The sitar is traditionally cited as a Hindu-Muslim fusion instrument, and Amir Khusrau is traditionally credited with the sitar and qawwali.

secs.t: Ulema - role, Sadr-us-Sudur, qazi

x: The ulema interpreted the Sharia and sought influence in state policy.
The Sadr-us-Sudur headed the Diwan-i-Risalat, dealt with religious affairs and grants to mosques and madrasas, and was also the Chief Qazi.
The
Qazi
administered Sharia law in the civil cases of Muslims.

secs.t: Jizya - nature, exemptions, who imposed it

x: Jizya was a protection tax imposed on non-Muslims in place of military service.
Women, children, the old and the disabled
were exempt from jizya.
Brahmins were initially exempt from jizya, but
Firoz Tughlaq
extended its collection to them.
Sikandar Lodi
enforced jizya.
The Qutb Shahis of Golconda never imposed jizya.

secs.t: Conversion - causes and extent

x: Sufi saints reached lower castes and farming communities through
pirs and dargahs
Temple destruction could be motivated by royal legitimacy and the acquisition of temple wealth, in addition to religious considerations.
The Deccan developed a mixed culture in which Hindu Nayakas served Sultans and Sultans patronised temples.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: In Meenakshipuram in February 1981, 558 Dalits embraced Islam, associated with the social-liberation argument of escaping caste oppression.
Gesu Daraz moved to Gulbarga under Firoz Shah Bahmani and wrote in Persian and early Dakhni, including Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq.
The competing framings are 'destruction' and 'liberation', while current scholarship stresses regional variation rather than a single uniform explanation.

rows.title: Indo-Islamic architecture - arcuate style, Qutb Minar, Alai Darwaza, Tughlaqabad, provincial styles
sub: Group-II S1-43: Sultanate art and architecture - Indo-Islamic style, Qutb complex, Tughlaq architecture

secs.t: Qutb complex - UNESCO components, Qutb Minar storeys → builder, Iron Pillar

x: The Qutb complex World Heritage Site includes the Qutb Minar, Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Alai Darwaza, Iron Pillar, tomb of Iltutmish, Alauddin’s tomb and madrasa, and Imam Zamin’s tomb.
The Qutb Minar has five tapering storeys, is about 72.5 metres high and is decorated with bands of Quranic calligraphy.
The Chand Minar at Daulatabad was built in 1435 by the Bahmani Sultan Alauddin Ahmad Shah.

secs.t: Monuments → builder + city + chronological order

x: Exam angle: match building → Sultan (UPPSC 2022 pairs: Sultan Garhi-Iltutmish, Red Palace-Balban, Jamat Khana-Alauddin, mosque-Aibak).
Alauddin Khalji excavated the tank known as Hauz-i-Alai, while Firoz Shah Tughlaq added the madrasa and tomb.
Tughlaqabad was a massive, rugged fort-city built by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq primarily for security.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq’s tomb at Tughlaqabad is noted for its sloping walls and marble dome.
Jamat Khana Masjid was built by Alauddin Khalji at the Nizamuddin dargah in Delhi.
The sequence is Qutb Minar, Tughlaqabad Fort, Lodi Garden tombs and Fatehpur Sikri.

secs.t: Arcuate style features and FIRSTs

x: Indian trabeate construction relied on lintels, pillars and corbelled roofs, while the arcuate system relied on arches, domes and vaults.
The mihrab is a prayer niche, the minbar is a pulpit, the squinch provides the structural transition to a dome, and a minaret is a mosque-associated tower.
Sultan Ghari dates to 1231, followed by Balban’s tomb, Alai Darwaza, and the later octagonal tomb of Khan-i-Jahan Tilangani.

secs.t: Style features → dynasty (sloping walls, octagonal tomb, double dome, lotus-bud fringe)

x: Battered walls belong to the Tughlaqs, octagonal tombs and double domes to the Lodis, the propylon screen to the Sharqis, and the lotus-bud horseshoe arch to the Khaljis.
Sharqi architecture of Jaunpur is especially associated with massive gateway façades or propylon screens and the absence of minarets; Atala Masjid is a major example.

secs.t: Provincial styles → region + monument

x: The
Eklakhi tomb, Dakhil Darwaza and Chota Sona Masjid
are all associated with Bengal.
Bengal architecture is noted for brick construction and curved roofs, with the Adina Mosque and the mosques of Pandua as important examples.
Gujarat
’s provincial style is characterised by strong Hindu-Jain carving, exemplified by the Jama Masjid of Ahmedabad.

secs.t: Deccan architecture - Bahmani and Qutb Shahi monuments in AP/Telangana

x: The Qutb Shahi Tombs at Ibrahim Bagh contain the seven rulers of the dynasty and are characterised by onion domes resting on square bases.
The gateway of the Golconda Jami Masjid carries fine Nastaliq calligraphy, associated with Yazdani; Naskh is used for the Quranic verses around the mihrab.
Golconda served as the Qutb Shahi capital from Sultan Quli, Ibrahim built its high walls, and Hussain Sagar was built by Hussain Shah Wali in 1562 during Ibrahim’s reign.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The minarets of Sultan Quli's Juma Masjid at Golconda are said to have inspired the
Charminar
Rajon ki Baoli, known as the stepwell of the masons, was built by Daulat Khan Lodi in 1506 under Sikandar Lodi at Mehrauli Archaeological Park.
The restoration of Rajon ki Baoli was undertaken by the
Archaeological Survey of India, World Monuments Fund India and TCS Foundation

rows.title: Sultanate literature and culture - Amir Khusrau, Ziauddin Barani, Ibn Battuta, music and Sufi influence
sub: Group-II S1-44: Sultanate language and literature - Persian chronicles, Amir Khusrau, regional languages

secs.t: Authors → works

x: Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi
wrote Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi, associated with the Sayyid period.
Barani wrote on Khalji-Tughlaq history, criticised south Indian kingdoms and authored the political-theory work Fatawa-i-Jahandari.
Ferishta refers to Telangana as ‘Tilang’ and describes the fall of Warangal in 1323.
Both Ziauddin Barani and Shams Siraj Afif wrote works titled Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi.
Ibn Battuta’s Rihla is an Arabic travelogue containing observations on the Delhi Sultanate and the Deccan.

secs.t: Amir Khusrau - titles, works, Sultans, Hindavi/Urdu, Persian style, music

x: Alauddin Khalji
patronised Amir Khusrau and gave him the title ‘Tuti-i-Hind’, meaning Parrot of India.
Amir Khusrau was a disciple of
Nizamuddin Auliya
of the Chishti order.
Khusrau served several Sultans from Balban’s time and was poet laureate under
Ghiyasuddin Tughluq
Khazain-ul-Futuh
describes the conquests of Alauddin Khalji, including his Deccan campaigns.
Ashiqa, or Deval Rani–Khizr Khan, deals with
the romance involving Alauddin Khalji’s son
Amir Khusrau is credited with founding the Indian style of Persian poetry known as
Sabak-i-Hindi
or the Hindustani style.
The sitar is traditionally credited to Amir Khusrau and is described as a combination of the Persian setar and the Indian veena.

secs.t: Music - Indo-Islamic instruments, qawwali, sama, treatises → author

x: Sama is devotional music intended to induce spiritual ecstasy and was a core Sufi practice.
The Chishtis popularised sama, and qawwali was institutionalised in Chishti khanqahs using Indian ragas.
The Bahmanis brought the
rebab and oud
to the Deccan, where they were combined with the veena and mridangam.
Ghunyat-ul-Munya, dated 1375, is identified as
the earliest Persian treatise on Indian music

secs.t: Sanskrit-Persian translations → translator/patron

x: The translation is associated with Ziya Nakhshabi during the time of
Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Zain-ul-Abidin of Kashmir
is associated with translating the Mahabharata and Rajatarangini into Persian.
Razmnama was the Persian translation of the Mahabharata, whereas Suka Saptati was translated as Tutinama.

secs.t: Sufi and premakhyan poetry → author

x: Mrigavati was written by Qutban, Padmavat by Malik Muhammad Jayasi, Padmavati Katha by Damodar Kavi, and Fawaid-ul-Fuad by Amir Hasan Sijzi.
Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed Padmavat in 1540, although some accounts broadly place it in the fifteenth-century tradition.
‘Fawaid-ul-Fuad’ was compiled by
Amir Hasan Sijzi
and records the conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya.

secs.t: Ziauddin Barani - works, patron, views on kingship

x: Barani viewed jahandari on the Persian model and held that kingship required
awe and force
Barani wanted offices to remain with the high-born and opposed promoting
low-born men
Both statements are true, and the gap between the ideal of protecting sharia and the practical use of state laws explains Barani’s assessment.

secs.t: Chronological order of texts

x: Kitab-ul-Hind belongs to about 1030, Prithviraj Raso is traditionally assigned to the late twelfth century, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri to about 1260, and Fatawa-i-Jahandari to the fourteenth century.
Al-Biruni’s Kitab-ul-Hind is generally dated to about 1030.

secs.t: Regional literature - Telugu under Kakatiyas and Reddis

x: Kase Siddhappa
wrote Siddhesvara Charitam, noted for its description of socio-economic conditions.
Errana
completed the Aranya Parva of the Mahabharata during the Reddi period associated with Prolaya Vema.
Srinatha
wrote Kasi Khandam and Sringara Naishadham during the Reddi period associated with Pedakomati Vema.
Kumara Ramana Charitam, associated with Kumara Kampana, describes the south after the Sultanate conquest of Warangal.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Persian became the elite language of administration and culture, while Indo-Persian historiography developed through writers such as Minhaj, Barani, Afif and Isami.
Indo-Persian historiography
constitutes the principal narrative source base for Sultanate and Deccan history.
Abdullah Qutb Shah and Abul Hasan Tana Shah
are identified as the first Qutb Shahi rulers to issue farmans in Telugu.

rows.title: Provincial kingdoms - Bahmani Sultanate and Mahmud Gawan; Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Jaunpur, Kashmir

secs.t: Kashmir - Zain-ul-Abidin (name, epithets, religious policy, translations, monuments), Sikandar Butshikan

x: Sikandar
, who ruled Kashmir from 1389 to 1413, was given the epithet “Butshikan”, meaning idol-breaker.
Sikandar Butshikan destroyed temples, imposed jizya and drove out Brahmins.
Zain-ul-Abidin was called “Bud Shah”, meaning Great King, and the “Akbar of Kashmir”.
The Mahabharata and Kalhana’s Rajatarangini were translated into Persian during Zain-ul-Abidin’s reign.
Zaina Lank is an island in
Wular Lake
in Kashmir.

secs.t: Jaunpur - Sharqi dynasty, rulers, "Shiraz of India", monuments → builder (Atala Masjid)

x: Malik Sarwar, known as Khwaja Jahan, founded the Sharqi dynasty in 1394 after receiving the title Malik-us-Sharq.
Jaunpur city was founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq before the Sharqi dynasty was founded in 1394; Jaunpur fell to Bahlul Lodi in 1479.
Atala Masjid and Jama Masjid were associated with Ibrahim Shah Sharqi, while Lal Darwaza Mosque was built by Bibi Raje.

secs.t: Bahmani Sultanate - founder, capitals in order (Gulbarga, Bidar), wars with Vijayanagara (Raichur Doab)

x: Exam angle: "main cause of conflict" = Raichur Doab; "who shifted to Bidar" = Ahmad Shah I.
The Bahmani kingdom was founded in the Deccan, initially ruled from Gulbarga, and ended in 1527 under its last Sultan, Kalimullah.
Firuz Shah
, who ruled from 1397 to 1422, was regarded as a scholar-king and the Bahmani kingdom reached peak strength during his reign.

secs.t: Malwa - rulers, Mandu monuments → builder (Jahaz Mahal, Hindola Mahal, Jami Masjid), Baz Bahadur and Rupmati

x: Dilawar Khan Ghuri
broke away from Delhi and established the independent Malwa kingdom in 1401.
Hoshang Shah
shifted the capital of Malwa from Dhar to Mandu.
Hoshang Shah began the Jami Masjid, Mahmud Khalji completed it, and Ghiyasuddin Khalji built the Hindola Mahal.
Baz Bahadur’s Palace, Rupmati’s Pavilion and Ashrafi Mahal belong to the late Malwa period.

secs.t: Gujarat Sultanate rulers → contribution (Ahmad Shah, Mahmud Begarha, Bahadur Shah), Mirat-i-Sikandari

x: Zafar Khan, also called Muzaffar Shah I, founded the Gujarat Sultanate; Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad; Mahmud Begarha captured Girnar and Champaner; and Bahadur Shah annexed Malwa.
Bahadur Shah annexed Malwa in 1531, attacked Chittor in 1535, was defeated by Humayun and was killed by the Portuguese at Diu in 1537.

secs.t: Minor regional kingdoms → founder + region (Faruqis of Khandesh, Sisodia and Rathore chiefs)

x: Burhanpur was the capital of the Faruqi kingdom, which lay in Khandesh’s Tapti valley; Akbar took Asirgarh in 1601.
Rana Kumbha
of the Sisodia line is associated with the Vijay Stambha at Chittor and Kumbhalgarh.
Rao Jodha founded Jodhpur in 1459, Rao Bika founded Bikaner, and the Rathores were associated with Marwar.

secs.t: Mahmud Gawan - office, administrative and military reforms, madrasa, end

x: Mahmud Gawan strengthened the centre, curtailed provincial nobles, divided the four tarafs into eight and placed forts under central commanders.
Mahmud Gawan suppressed Telangana revolts from 1453 onward with Velama assistance, and the Bahmanis captured Goa in 1472.
Mahmud Gawan was framed by rival nobles and executed, traditionally dated to 1481; his fall contributed to the break-up of the Bahmani Kingdom.

secs.t: Bengal Sultanate - Ilyas Shahi, Hussain Shahi rulers, patronage of Bengali literature

x: Haji Ilyas, who assumed the title
Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah
, unified Bengal in 1342 and established Pandua as his capital.
Sikandar Shah
built the Adina Mosque at Pandua during the Ilyas Shahi period.
The Hussain Shahi Mosque was at Bagerhat, the Chhota Sona Masjid dates to 1510, and Alauddin Hussain Shah founded the dynasty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Doab was contested in Bahmani-Vijayanagara wars, Telangana saw revolts, and the Qutb Shahi state of Golconda emerged from the Bahmani break-up.
Bidriware developed under the Bahmanis in the fourteenth century, is linked to Bidar, received a GI tag in 2006 and was included among the Prime Minister’s diplomatic gifts on 22 May 2026.
