rows.title: The five Deccan Sultanates - Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar, Bidar, Berar; Golconda and Andhra
sub: Group-II M1-A-47: Qutb Shahis of Golconda - Andhra under Qutb Shahi rule; Telugu patronage

secs.t: Qutb Shahi rulers → reign + contribution (Sultan Quli to Abul Hasan Tana Shah)

x: The Qutb Shahis were Qara Qoyunlu, or Black Sheep, Turkmen originating from Hamadan.
Ibrahim Qutb Shah spent seven years in exile at
Vijayanagara
before becoming ruler of Golconda.
Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was a Dakhni and Urdu poet who used the pen-name
Maani
Muhammad Qutb Shah used Zillullah as his pen-name, Abdullah patronised Kshetrayya, and Abul Hasan made the pact with Shivaji in 1677.
Abdullah Qutb Shah ruled with his mother Hayat Bakshi Begum and had the longest reign among the Qutb Shahi rulers.
Abul Hasan Tana Shah relied on Madanna and Akkanna and concluded a treaty with Shivaji in 1677.

secs.t: Qutb Shahi administration in Andhra - revenue sources, officials → duty (mahasibs, tarafdars, havaldars)

x: Mir Jumla was the finance minister, the Kotwal headed city policing and also ran the mint, and the Havaldar was associated with treasuries and stables.
A Sarkar was headed by a Faujdar, a Pargana by a Tahsildar or Deshmukh, and the village had the Mukaddam as head and Kulkarni as accountant.
Mahasibs or Mustasibs supervised public morals and religious conduct, performing a role comparable to the Mughal Muhtasib.

secs.t: Hyderabad - founder, original name, Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Dakhni poetry

x: Peshwa
Mir Momin Astarabadi
planned Hyderabad after its foundation by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah.
Golconda Fort was famous for its acoustics, including the transmission of a handclap from the gate to Bala Hisar, and also had piped water.
The Qutb Shahi tombs at Ibrahim Bagh are characterised by
onion domes on square bases and charbagh gardens

secs.t: Golconda diamonds and Machilipatnam trade - Tavernier, Kollur mines, European factories

x: Tavernier was a French jeweller and diamond merchant who visited the Andhra mines in the seventeenth century and wrote Six Travels.
The Kohinoor is stated to have been found in 1656 in the Kollur mines, after which
Mir Jumla
presented it to Shah Jahan.
The Dutch factory dates to 1605, the English factory to 1611, and Captain Hippon arrived in the ship Globe.

secs.t: Deccan Sultanates → dynasty + capital + founder

x: Exam angle: "Berar was founded by" = Imad Shahis.
Sultan Quli
founded the Qutb Shahi state of Golconda, the last of the major Bahmani successor states to break away in 1518.
Yusuf Adil Shah founded the Adil Shahi dynasty, Malik Ahmad the Nizam Shahi, Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk the Imad Shahi, and Sultan Quli the Qutb Shahi dynasty.

secs.t: Bijapur - Ibrahim Adil Shah II, Kitab-i-Nauras, Gol Gumbaz

x: Ibrahim Adil Shah II was a Dakhni author, invoked Saraswati, received Firishta’s dedication, and married Chand Sultana, Muhammad Quli’s sister.
Firishta dedicated Tarikh-i-Firishta, also called Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi, to Ibrahim Adil Shah II.
Gol Gumbaz
is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah.
The Bijapur style is associated with
three-arched facades, bulbous domes and cornices

secs.t: Annexation of Deccan Sultanates by the Mughals - rulers, fate of the last rulers

x: Akbar
captured Ahmadnagar city in 1600 and Asirgarh of Khandesh in 1601.
The correct order is Ahmadnagar’s capture in 1600, the end of the Nizam Shahis in 1633, Bijapur’s annexation in 1686 and Golconda’s annexation in 1687.
The gates were opened by the traitor
Abdullah Khan Pani
, also referred to as Abdullah Phani in the accounts.

secs.t: Golconda and Andhra - coastal conquests, Telugu patronage (Malkibharama), Akkanna-Madanna

x: Sultan Quli took Rachakonda, Devarakonda, Warangal, Rajahmundry, Eluru and Kovilakonda.
Ibrahim gained Kondavidu and Machilipatnam after 1565, and coastal Andhra was annexed during
Addanki Gangadhara’s
Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu
is regarded as the first Telugu poem or kavya dedicated to a Muslim ruler.
The Qutb Shahis united the Telugu lands for the third time, following the earlier unifications under the Satavahanas and Kakatiyas.

secs.t: Ahmednagar - Chand Bibi, Malik Ambar's revenue system

x: Chand Bibi defended Ahmadnagar against the Mughals in
Malik Ambar
was an Abyssinian regent of the Nizam Shahis and resisted the Mughal emperor Jahangir.
Malik Ambar revived revenue administration on Todar Mal’s lines through survey and fixed assessment, avoided revenue farming and used Maratha guerrilla cavalry.
Fath Khan
, Malik Ambar’s son, made peace with the Mughals.

secs.t: Revenue - main source and revenue farming

x: The leased diamond mines were called the highest single source, whereas land revenue was the chief general source of income.
Dasabandhu lands paid only
one-tenth
of the produce or assessment as revenue.
The bidders in the revenue-farming auctions were called
Mustajirs
and were mostly Hindus.
The example given for revenue farming is the lease of Machilipatnam for 1,80,000 pagodas annually.

secs.t: Madanna and Akkanna - role and fall

x: Madanna was the Diwan or prime minister, while Akkanna was the Sar Lashkar or army chief.
Podili Linganna was the governor of the Karnatak, while Kancherla Gopanna was the tahsildar of Palvancha.
The brothers were murdered in 1686, shortly before Golconda fell to Aurangzeb in 1687, thereby weakening the state’s administration and defence.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revival of Machilipatnam port is linked with the historical
Gilakaladindi port
, which functioned as a transshipment hub under the Golconda dynasty.
Hussain Sagar was named after Hussain Shah Wali, built under Ibrahim, and received the UNWTO designation ‘Heart of the World’ in 2012.
Murari Rao, Jagadeva Rao and Madanna
are identified as Hindus who held high office under the Qutb Shahis.

rows.title: Foundation of Vijayanagara - Harihara and Bukka, Vidyaranya; the Sangama dynasty
sub: Group-II M1-A-41: Vijayanagara Empire - Sangama, Saluva and Tuluva dynasties in the Andhra context

secs.t: Founders' background - Harihara and Bukka, earlier service theories (Kakatiya/Kampili/Delhi), dynasty name, founding year

x: Exam angle: APPSC treats the Kakatiya link as the correct answer.
Harihara and Bukka were sons of Sangama; Sangama came from Mangalanilaya, and some accounts place the family in the Kuruba clan.
The Kakatiya theory states that Harihara and Bukka served
Prataparudra of Warangal
before being taken to Delhi after 1323.
The Kampili version states that they governed Kampili, were captured by Muhammad bin Tughlaq, converted in Delhi and later returned as Sultanate governors.
The Delhi-service version says that Muhammad bin Tughlaq sent them to crush Deccan rebels, including the forces associated with Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka and Prolaya Vema.
Father Heras
, Rice, S. K. Ayyangar, H. Krishna Sastri and P. B. Desai supported the Kannada or Hoysala theory.

secs.t: Sites associated with the founders → founding legend, capital's river (Hampi, Vijayanagara, Sringeri)

x: Vidyaranya headed the
Sringeri Shankara Math
and is associated with the brothers' return to Hinduism.
Hampi, or Pampa, was the region where Harihara and Bukka met Vidyaranya according to the founding tradition.
The site was considered a place of valour because a hare reportedly
turned on the royal hunting dogs

secs.t: Dynasties of Vijayanagara in order (Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu) - founders

x: Sangama was founded by Harihara I and Bukka I, Saluva by Saluva Narasimha, Tuluva by Vira Narasimha, and Aravidu by Tirumala Raya.
The APPSC-associated account identifies Vira Narasimha as the founder; he was crowned in 1505 after executing Immadi Narasimha.
Tirumala Raya founded the Aravidu dynasty, whose capitals included Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore.
The
Sangama
dynasty was the longest-ruling dynasty; Devaraya II was regarded as its greatest ruler and Praudha Raya as its last ruler.

secs.t: Vedic commentaries - Sayana, Madhava/Vidyaranya, ruler under whom written

x: Gangadevi wrote the Sanskrit work Madhura Vijayam and was related to Kumara Kampana and Bukka I as stated; she was also a disciple of Agastya.
Madhura Vijayam describes Kumara Kampana’s southern campaign, including the defeat of Champaraya of Tondaimandalam, the advance to Kanchi and the conquest of Madurai.
Nachana Somana
, the author of Uttara Harivamsam, was patronised by the first two Sangama kings.

secs.t: Vijayanagara-Bahmani conflicts - Raichur doab, Tungabhadra wars, Goa

x: The Raichur Doab, or Raichur Antarvedi, lies between the
Krishna and Tungabhadra
rivers and was the main cause of the recurring wars.
The 1358 Mudgal conflict occurred under Bukka I, who took Mudgal; it is noted as the first Indian war involving artillery, followed by a truce intended to spare civilians.
The correct sequence is Mudgal in 1358, Goa’s loss in 1472, the capture of Gulbarga in 1523, and Talikota in 1565.

secs.t: Modern histories of Vijayanagara → author (A Forgotten Empire)

x: Kampili and Vijayanagara was written by Nelaturi Venkataramanaiah, not Robert Sewell.
Robert Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire: Vijayanagar is an English translation of the Portuguese accounts of Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz.
Ferishta was a Persian chronicler of the Deccan sultans and provides the Bahmani perspective on the wars.
Cesare Federici visited Vijayanagara during the reign of
Sadasivaraya

secs.t: Sangama rulers → achievement (Harihara I, Bukka I, Harihara II, Devaraya I, Devaraya II)

x: Bukka I completed the city, conquered Madurai and reconciled Jains and Vaishnavas.
Harihara II
, who ruled from 1377 to 1404, was the longest-reigning Sangama king.
Irugappa
, the minister of Harihara II, built the Ganigitti Jain temple and wrote Navaratnamala.
Devaraya I built a dam and canals, fought Firuz Shah and is recorded as the first Sangama ruler to recruit Muslims into the army.
Devaraya I belonged to a period earlier than the Portuguese arrival in India in 1498; therefore, crediting them with his dam is chronologically inconsistent.

secs.t: Bukka I - southern conquest and its literary record (author), foreign embassy

x: Kumara Kampana
, son of Bukka I, overthrew Sambhuvaraya in 1366 and destroyed the Madurai Sultanate.
Kampana led the conquest, while General Saluva Mangu killed the Sultan and received the title ‘Parapakshi Saluva’.
Madhura Vijayam, a Sanskrit work describing the Madurai conquest, was written by
Gangadevi
, the wife of Kumara Kampana.

secs.t: Devaraya II - army reforms, foreign visitors, titles

x: Nicolo Conti’s visit is dated 1420–21, during Devaraya I, although an APPSC association places him under Devaraya II.
Purva-Paschima Samudradhipati
was the title of Harihara I. Devaraya II was known as Gajabetekara, Praudha Devaraya and Ilanti Raikonda.
Devaraya II annexed Kondaveedu, received Sri Lankan tribute through Lakkanna Dandanayaka and repelled the Gajapatis, as recorded at Draksharama.

secs.t: Capital city - river setting, present ruins site, irrigation works on the Tungabhadra → ruler

x: Vijayanagar stood on the
southern
bank of the Tungabhadra.
The ruins of Vijayanagar are located at
Hampi
Devaraya I
built a dam across the Tungabhadra and canals to carry water to Vijayanagar.
After Talikota, the capital moved from Hampi to Penukonda and subsequently to Chandragiri; both later capitals were in present-day Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Saluva Narasimha - home base, seizure of the Sangama throne, contemporary of Annamacharya, Gajapati and Bahmani wars

x: The Saluva clan came from Kalyana and Saluva Mangu served Kumara Kampana.
In 1485, Saluva Narasimha expelled Praudha Raya with the help of
Tuluva Narasa Nayaka
Saluva Narasimha’s seizure of the throne in 1485 is called the
First Usurpation
Annamacharya (1408–1503) was a contemporary of
Saluva Narasimha
and is also placed in his court.

secs.t: Sangama campaigns in Andhra (Bukka I, Devaraya II) - Kondavidu, Udayagiri, Rayalaseema forts, court poets

x: Bukka I captured
Srisailam and Dupadu
, the latter being near Markapur.
Devaraya I’s capture of southern Kondaveedu, including Motupalli, is recorded in the
Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam
Devaraya II sent Mallappa Odayar to help
Rajahmundry
, as recorded in the Draksharama inscription of 1444.
Vinukonda Vallabharaya
wrote Kridabhiramam and was the governor of Vinukonda under Devaraya II.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The copper plates relate to Devaraya I’s coronation, use Sanskrit, Kannada and Nagari, record the grant and renamed village, and contain a full Sangama genealogy.
The copper plates carry a
Vamana
seal, rather than the usual Varaha seal.
Udayagiri, Kondaveedu, Penukonda and Chandragiri
are identified as places linking the empire with Andhra Pradesh.

rows.title: Saluva and Tuluva dynasties; Krishnadevaraya - conquests, Amuktamalyada, the Ashtadiggajas
sub: Group-II M1-A-42: Krishnadevaraya - conquests in Andhra, Amuktamalyada, Bhuvana Vijayam and the Ashtadiggajas

secs.t: Krishnadevaraya's literary works - Amuktamalyada (place, circumstance, subject), Jambavati Kalyanam (language), Sanskrit works

x: Amuktamalyada means “
one who offers the garland she has worn
,” referring to the devotional story associated with Goda Devi or Andal.
Andhra Mahavishnu of Srikakulam
appeared to Krishnadevaraya in a dream and commanded him to write the work.
The work deals with Goda Devi’s marriage to Ranganatha, includes Yamunacharya Charitra and Maladasari Katha, and gives political advice.
Amuktamalyada records the
genealogy from Bukka to Krishnadevaraya
, in addition to its religious and political content.
The famous expression praising Telugu among regional languages occurs in the preface to
Amuktamalyada

secs.t: Krishnadevaraya - campaigns, victory pillars, marriage alliance, court described by travellers (Domingo Paes)

x: During the
Diwani or Kovilkonda campaign
of 1509–10, the Bahmani jihad was crushed and Yusuf Adil Khan was killed.
After taking Raichur and freeing Sultan Mahmud Shah from Ali Barid, Krishnadevaraya acquired the title Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya.
The sequence is coronation in 1509, Ummattur in 1512–13, Udayagiri in 1513–14, and Raichur in 1520.
Barbosa
also visited the court of Krishnadevaraya; Domingo Paes described the Bhuvana Vijayam or House of Victory and the king.

secs.t: Tuluva dynasty - founder, succession, dynasty identification

x: The Tuluva dynasty was named after
Tulunadu
, identified in the material with the Mysore region.
Tuluva Narasa Nayaka
, a Saluva general, was the real ruler under Immadi Narasimha.
Vira Narasimha established Tuluva rule after killing Immadi Narasimha at Penugonda in 1505.
Krishnadevaraya ruled from 1509 to 1529 and succeeded Vira Narasimha.

secs.t: Ashtadiggajas - meaning, poet → work + title

x: Ashtadiggajas means the eight elephants believed to support the eight directions; in Krishnadevaraya's court it referred to eight eminent poets.
The Ashtadiggajas were the eight pillar-poets of Krishnadevaraya's court in the Bhuvana Vijayam hall.
Pingali Surana's Raghava Pandaviyamu is a dvyarthi kavya, employing a double meaning.
Nandi Timmana, known as Mukku Timmana, wrote Parijatapaharanamu and was regarded as the king's favourite.

secs.t: Titles of Krishnadevaraya; towns founded and their namesakes

x: Krishnadevaraya was called
Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya
for restoring the Bahmani Sultan.
Andhra Kavita Pitamaha
was the title conferred on Allasani Peddana.
Nagalapuram was named after Krishnadevaraya's mother Nagalamba.
Hospet, or Tirumaladevi-pattana, was named after
Queen Tirumaladevi
Chintalapudi Ellanarya
received the title Radhamadhava Kavi.
Krishnadevaraya personally fixed the Gandapenderam anklet on Allasani Peddana's foot.

secs.t: Saluva Narasimha - usurpation, reasons, Saluva rule, contemporary of Annamacharya

x: Saluva Narasimha was the lord of
Chandragiri
when he sent Tuluva Narasa Nayaka to seize the throne.
After Devaraya II, weak rulers such as Virupaksha II and Praudha Raya were unable to resist Gajapati and Bahmani invasions, which weakened the kingdom.
Saluva Narasimha imported Arab horses from Ormuz, introduced gunmen called Samugaris, and lost Udayagiri to Gajapati Purushottama.

secs.t: Relations with the Portuguese - Albuquerque, Goa, horse trade

x: Vira Narasimha allied with Viceroy
Francisco de Almeida
for horses and military training.
Krishnadevaraya backed Albuquerque's capture of Goa through the envoy
Luis
Krishnadevaraya received horses and training and permitted the Portuguese to build a fort at Bhatkal.
João de Castro
made peace after the defeat of Martin de Souza, whose actions had included damaging temples.

secs.t: Achyutaraya and Sadasivaraya - Rama Raya's regency

x: Real power during Achyutaraya's reign lay with his brothers-in-law,
the Salakam brothers
Rama Raya killed Salakam Tirumala in 1543, made Sadasiva a figurehead king, was beheaded at Talikota in 1565, and thereafter Sadasiva and Tirumala fled to Penukonda.
Rama Raya used divide and rule against the
Deccan Sultanates
, which eventually united against him.

secs.t: Cities founded → named after (Nagalapura, Hospet)

x: Nagalapuram was named after Krishnadevaraya's mother, Nagalamba.
Hospet, or
Tirumaladevi
pattana, was named after Krishnadevaraya's queen Tirumaladevi.

secs.t: Bhuvana Vijayam - meaning, poets, titles conferred, described by Domingo Paes

x: Bhuvana Vijayam means ‘
conquest of the world
Bhuvana Vijayam was the court hall where the
Ashtadiggajas met
The Tippalur agrahara recorded in the inscription was in
Kadapa
Domingo Paes described the
palace, festivals, army and markets
along with Bhuvana Vijayam.
The Tippalur inscription calls the Ashtadiggajas a
Kavula Samstha
, or institution of poets.

secs.t: Foreign accounts of Krishnadevaraya's reign (Paes, Nuniz)

x: Domingo Paes
described Krishnadevaraya's appearance and the beauty of the city.
Babur
praised Krishnadevaraya in the Tuzuk-i-Baburi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The first usurpation was by Saluva Narasimha in 1485, the second by Vira Narasimha in 1505, and Sadasiva was the last Tuluva ruler.
The Kalinga campaign is associated with the forts of
Udayagiri, Kondaveedu and Kondapalli
The renovation project involves
₹6 crore
and includes restoration of the Sri Krishna Devaraya Mandapam.

rows.title: Vijayanagara administration - Nayankara and Ayagar systems, amaram tenure, revenue and army
sub: Group-II M1-A-43: Vijayanagara administration in Andhra - Nayankara and Ayagar systems, amaram tenure

secs.t: Revenue - land classification, share of produce, taxes → object (navidadere, malavana, maneyana, tudimova, meruka), Krishnadevaraya's tax policy

x: Exam angle: a single-term question ("Meruka was a tax on") or a four-pair match of the tax terms.
Sangoru represented one-half, Mungoru one-third, and Brahmin inam lands paid one-sixth of the produce.
Ganachari Pannu concerned prostitutes, Sampatti covered hidden treasure, cattle and gardens, and Adikasu was a shop tax.
Kanika or Kanuka could denote a levy or present; Kalyanakanikey was a wedding tax on both parties and Putrodaya Kanuka was related to the birth of a son.
The sequence is the remission in some regions by Saluva Narasimha, the recorded attribution to Vira Narasimha, and the empire-wide abolition under Krishnadevaraya.
Adhuvanatantram referred to land-tax documents, rates varied with land quality, and private workshop owners paid an industries tax.

secs.t: Central administration - king, council, pradhani, mahapradhani, departments → function (Kandachara, Athavane)

x: Each Samprati worked from an office called the
Rayasam
, with Karanalu serving as accountants.
Karanikas are identified as scribes, while Karanalu are described as accountants working in the Rayasam offices of the departments.
The obligation to follow Dharma and consider ministerial counsel explains why the king was not viewed as completely unrestricted.

secs.t: Nayankara system - amaranayakas, amaram lands, obligations, comparison with Kakatiya nayankara and Mughal mansabdari

x: Amaram
was land granted to military chiefs, who were known as Amaranayakas, Nayaks, Palaiyagars or Poligars.
Nuniz
recorded about 200 Nayankaras under Krishnadevaraya and 6,00,000 amara troops under Achyutaraya.
The Kakatiya system involved 75 or 77 Nayakas holding mandalams and forts; the Vijayanagara system involved amaram fiefs and about 200 Nayakas; Mughal mansabdars held zat and sawar ranks.
Kakatiya Nayakas retained a share of revenue, Vijayanagara Nayakas retained land revenue while paying tribute, and Mughal mansabdars received cash or transferable jagirs.

secs.t: Ayagar system - number and names of village functionaries, their payment

x: Ayagars received tax-free Ayagar or manyam land together with a share of each harvest instead of cash payment.
Karanam was the accountant, Reddi the village head, Talari the watchman and Purohita the priest.
Ayagars received tax-free Manyam lands, also called Mirasi, Bhattu Vrutti or Jatikattu Manyalu, along with a share of the harvest called Mera.

secs.t: Provincial administration - rajya/mandala, nadu, sthala, grama, governors (princes)

x: The administrative hierarchy was Rajyam or Rashtram (province), followed by Seema or Nadu (district), Sthalam (sub-district), and Gramam (village).
A province was headed by a prince or Durgadhipati, a Nadu by the Nadagauda and Parupatyagar, a Sthala by the Reddi, Gauda or Sthalakaranam, and a village by the Ayagars.
Aravidu inscriptions divide the Udayagiri, Penukonda and Hampi Rajyams into
Vanitas

secs.t: Army - composition, forts (durga dannayaka), cavalry and horse imports

x: The Vijayanagara army included several social groups, including Chenchus, Koyas, Boyas and Muslim troops.
Cavalry was decisive in Vijayanagara warfare, but Arabian and Persian horses had to be imported because adequate local supplies were unavailable.
Portuguese and Arab merchants
conducted the horse trade, and the payment for imported horses caused a drain of bullion from the empire.

secs.t: Political ideas in Krishnadevaraya's Amuktamalyada

x: Amuktamalyada advises improving harbours, encouraging imports and treating foreign merchants generously.
The work combines devotion and practical statecraft, stresses Dharma and protection of subjects, and recommends tanks and irrigation.
Amuktamalyada contains discussion of
political matters
along with devotional content and practical advice on kingship and administration.
Amuktamalyada records the genealogy of the dynasty, but it does not record Krishnadevaraya’s campaigns.

secs.t: Judicial system and punishments (pradvivaka and other officers' duties)

x: Pratishtita was a fixed court, Apratishtita a mobile court, Mudrita a court of a royal appointee, and Shastrita the court of the king.
Death was prescribed for treason, mutilation for theft, and Brahmins received life imprisonment instead of the death penalty.
The Talari served as the village police officer, while the Peta Kavalidaru performed the corresponding function in towns.

secs.t: Palegars - origin in Rayalaseema

x: The
Amara-nayakas
became the Palegars or Poligars when central authority weakened after the Battle of Talikota.
Military officer Campbell
assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the poligars of Rayalaseema.
The Kurnool Nawabs were deposed in 1839, Banganapalle remained semi-independent, and Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy was a Kurnool poligar.
Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy, a Kurnool poligar, revolted in the 1840s, looted the treasury at Koilkuntla and was later hanged.

secs.t: Village officers - duties (Karanam, Talari, Reddi)

x: The Karanam dealt with revenue affairs and maintained village accounts, land and crop registers, and temple accounts.
The Reddi was both village head and revenue collector; under the Kakatiyas, the office also included the function of village judge.
The Talari had no salary and instead collected Merulu, or gifts in grain, from farmers and merchants at harvest.

secs.t: Police - Kavali system

x: The Kavali Daru maintained law and order at the Sthala level, the Peta Kavalidaru watched the towns, and the Talari policed the village.
The
Panchanam
community is mentioned in this context, including in the Vijayanthi Vilasam.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The three inscriptions found at Sadasivakona in the Seshachalam forest are dated 31 July 1554, belong to Sadasiva Raya, and are in Telugu, Tamil and Kannada.
The Nayankara system enabled the empire to maintain a huge army cheaply, but it also facilitated the rise of Nayaka kingdoms that broke away after Talikota.

rows.title: Vijayanagara society, economy and trade; accounts of Nicolo Conti, Abdur Razzak, Domingo Paes, Nuniz
sub: Group-II M1-A-44: Vijayanagara society, economy and religion in Andhradesa; foreign travellers' accounts

secs.t: Foreign travellers → country + ruler visited + observations

x: Exam angle: questions pair a traveller with a fact (Sati, 300 ports, "large as Rome").
All four statements occur in accounts attributed to Abdur Razzaq: the city’s grandeur, Mahanavami celebrations, the prostitution tax and the absence of purdah.
Nuniz recorded dynastic history, the foundation legend, sati, polygamy and an army described as 600,000 amara troops.
Caesar Frederick
, an Italian visitor from Venice, recorded the ruined capital after Talikota and visited during the time of Sadasiva Raya in 1567.
The relevant APPSC key credits
Duarte Barbosa
with the observation regarding 300 port towns.
Nicolo de Conti visited in 1420–21, Abdur Razzaq in 1443–44, Domingo Paes in 1520–22 and Caesar Frederick in 1567.
Nicolo de Conti visited during Devaraya I; Abdur Razzaq during Devaraya II; Paes and Barbosa during Krishnadevaraya; and Nuniz during Achyutaraya.

secs.t: Society - castes and sects → occupation (Vipravinodins, Settis, Vira Panchalas), devadasis, sati, women's roles, poetesses

x: The society is described as having four varnas and about eighteen castes; Brahmins included priests and officials, while many Sudras became amaranayakas.
Settis, Komatis and Balijas
were trading groups, including Arya and Kalinga Vaishyas and Shetti and Veera Balijas.
Accounts describe the absence of strict purdah and women serving as bodyguards, wrestlers, accountants and judges; both kanyasulkam and dowry existed.

secs.t: Economy - agriculture, tank rules (Porumamilla), anicuts, granaries, temple economy, main revenue source

x: Agriculture included paddy, jowar, millets and sugarcane; rice was a luxury, and land tax was the main revenue source.
Devadaya villages and land endowments supported temples, while Sri Bhandara was the temple treasury kept by the Karanam.
The Porumamilla inscription, associated with Bhaskara Mantri, records the construction of
the Porumamilla tank
Portuguese engineers constructed the Nagalapuram tank and Toragallu dam, and Portuguese assistance counted at Raichur in 1520.

secs.t: Trade - number of ports, ports (Honnavar, Bhatkal, Pulicat, Machilipatnam), imports (horses) and exports

x: Devaraya I issued the Motupalli Dharma Sasanam in 1416 after taking Motupalli from Kondaveedu.
The Anantasagaram tank is dated to 1369, the Motupalli Dharma Sasanam to 1416, the Nagalapuram tank belongs to Krishnadevaraya's period, and the Portuguese reached India in 1498.
Merchant guilds, or samayas, met in
temple mandapas
Gutti and Rayadurg supplied silk, Venkatagiri supplied zari, and diamonds from Kurnool and Anantapur were polished at Vajrakarur.

secs.t: Coinage - varaha/pagoda, pratapa, fanam, metals

x: Pratapa was a gold coin equal to half a varaha and was called Mada in Telugu.
Pagoda
was the European name for the varaha, also known as gadyana or honnu.
The panam, or fanam, was equal to
one-tenth of a pratapa
and was the most used coin.
The coin symbols included Hanuman, Venkateswara and Krishna, Garuda, and Varaha under the rulers specified.

secs.t: Right-hand and left-hand caste divisions

x: The two caste divisions clashed mainly over precedence and honours, including the right to participate in processions and use insignia.
The right-hand and left-hand groupings began during
Chola times
and continued under the Vijayanagara Empire.
Vaidikulu were Brahmin priests, Niyogulu were Brahmin administrators, Vipravinodins were Brahmin performers, and some Shudras became Amaranayakas.

secs.t: Festivals - Mahanavami (Mahanavami Dibba), Vasantotsava

x: The Mahanavami Dibba, on which the Dasara celebrations were held, was built by
Krishnadevaraya
Domingo Paes
recorded the sacrifice of 250 buffaloes and 400 goats on the final day of the Mahanavami festival.
Burton Stein compared the importance of Mahanavami to the
Ashvamedha
sacrifice.
Shivaratri, Deepavali, Rathotsavam and Eruvaka Punnami were all among the festivals celebrated in the Vijayanagara period.

secs.t: Christian missions - Jesuit churches permitted by rulers

x: Venkatapati Raya II
allowed a church at Chandragiri and extended protection to the Jesuit mission.
Chevvappa Nayaka
permitted the Portuguese to build a church in Thanjavur.
Veerappa Nayaka admitted Portuguese missionaries to Madurai.
Barbosa recorded that
Christians, Jews and Muslims
lived without interference, indicating a measure of religious tolerance.

secs.t: Women - status and customs recorded by travellers

x: Abdur Razzaq
recorded the practice of Sati.
Lingden noted that widows who did not commit Sati had their heads shaved.
Women moved freely without strict purdah, and respectable women attended the Mahanavami celebrations.
Gangadevi and Tirumalamba
are identified as learned women of the Vijayanagara period.
Prostitution was state-recognised, and each woman engaged in it paid an annual tax of
12,000 panams

secs.t: Performing arts and folk entertainment

x: Burrakatha consists of a lead narrator who plays the burra and is accompanied by
two vantalu or assistants
Tholu Bommalata is leather shadow-puppetry, is mentioned in Panditaradhya Charitra, and later gave rise to Surabhi theatre.
Tholu Bommalata is mentioned in both Palkuriki's Panditaradhya Charitra and
Palnati Veeracharitra
Addanki Gangadhara wrote Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu, Ponnaganti Telaganarya wrote Yayati Charitra, and Kandukuri Rudrakavi wrote Sugriva Vijayam.

secs.t: Religion - sects and temple and goddess centres

x: Kalamukha Kriya Shakti
was the family guru of the Sangama rulers.
From
Venkatapati II
onward, Venkateswara replaced Virupaksha as the main deity.
Srisailam, Tripurantakam and Srikalahasti
were important Shaiva centres.
Draksharama and Amaravati
were centres where Smarta Shaivism was followed.
Tirupati rose under Saluva Narasimha, Achyutaraya was crowned at Tirumala, and Ahobilam and Kadiri had Narasimha temples.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Robert Sewell
translated the accounts of the Portuguese travellers Domingo Paes and Nuniz in A Forgotten Empire.
Andhra Pradesh announced an annual Telugu Mahotsavam and the revival of Tholu Bommalata, Harikatha, Burrakatha and Padya Natakam in July 2026.
All four forms—Tholu Bommalata, Harikatha, Burrakatha and Padya Natakam—were identified for revival under the announced Telugu cultural initiative.
Culture Minister Kandula Durgesh
announced the annual Telugu Mahotsavam at the valedictory programme at the Undavalli Caves.

rows.title: Vijayanagara art and architecture - Hampi, gopurams, kalyana mandapa, Vitthala temple, painting
sub: Group-II M1-A-45: Vijayanagara art and architecture in Andhra - Lepakshi, Tadipatri, Ahobilam, Srisailam, Tirupati

secs.t: Lepakshi - builders, shrines, notable features, murals

x: Veerabhadra Swamy (Papanaseswara) temple
, Lepakshi village,
Sri Sathya Sai district.
Builders: Nayaka brothers
Virupanna and Veeranna
- i.e.
Exam angle: "stone bull / hanging pillar / frescoes" → Lepakshi.
The complex has
Shiva, Veerabhadra and Vishnu
shrines, each with a mukha mandapa.
Its structural marvels are the
hanging pillar
and the
monolithic Nandi.
They represent the peak of the
Vijayanagara school of painting

secs.t: Temples at Hampi - patron + popular name

x: Virupaksha is associated with Pampapati, Vitthala with Saptaswara Devalayam, Krishna with the Bala Krishna idol from Udayagiri, and Achyutaraya with the Tiruvengalanatha temple.
The Vitthala Temple is Vaishnava, contains musical pillars and a stone chariot, and was begun under Devaraya II and expanded by Krishnadevaraya.
The Lotus Mahal, also called Chitrangana or Padma Mahal, is described as a secular building in the
Indo-Arabic style

secs.t: Vijayanagara temples and forts in Andhra - patron

x: Srikalahasti was renovated by Krishnadevaraya and its gali gopuram collapsed in 2010.
The Narasimha Swamy temple at Ahobilam was developed in
the late Vijayanagara phase
Krishnadevaraya's queens
Chinnadevi and Tirumaladevi
installed idols at Tirumala.
Tirumala used Penukonda, while Venkatapati II shifted the capital first to Chandragiri and then to Vellore in 1600.

secs.t: Vijayanagara painting - temples with murals, themes

x: The Veerabhadra temple at
Lepakshi
contains Vijayanagara murals depicting themes from the Shiva Purana.
The Hampi Virupaksha temple murals include
the Dashavatara and Girijakalyana
themes.
Mineral pigments were applied on lime plaster, with bold dark outlines, flat colours, elongated figures and energetic movement.
Stella Kramrisch
wrote A Survey of Painting in the Deccan.

secs.t: Secular structures and Indo-Islamic influence

x: The Elephant Stables and Queen's Bath were located near the
Lotus Mahal in the zenana area
Huzur Daftar or Diwan Khana was a council chamber in Indo-Persian style and had 40 pillars.
The Vijayanagara period introduced secular buildings within temple premises, while also showing Indo-Islamic influence in structures such as the Lotus Mahal and Huzur Daftar.

secs.t: Architectural features → dynasty

x: Percy Brown described Vijayanagara architecture as the
matured state of the Dravidian tradition
Vijayanagara architecture blended
Chola, Hoysala, Pandya and Chalukya
styles.
The kalyana mandapa was a pillared hall used for the divine marriage ceremony.
Composite pillars feature
rearing yalis and charging horses with riders
and are generally 7–8 feet tall.

secs.t: Hampi - UNESCO status, monuments on currency notes

x: The Group of Monuments at Hampi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
The Vittala stone chariot appears on the reverse of the
note of the Mahatma Gandhi New Series.

secs.t: Performing arts - Yakshagana, Veedhi Bhagavatham, Kuchipudi, Tolu Bommalata

x: Tolu Bommalata
, a leather shadow-puppet tradition, was the chief entertainment of rural people.
Tolu Bommalata uses stories from the
Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas
Veedhi Bhagavatham is a street dance-drama regarded as the
forerunner of Kuchipudi
The Machupalli Kaifiyat records a Kuchipudi troupe performing before
Viranarasimharaya
Sangita Suryodaya was written by Lakminatha, identified as a court musician of Krishnadevaraya.

secs.t: Monument feature - site matching

x: "gopurams better than Hampi" = Tadipatri.
The gopurams said by art critics to surpass those of Hampi's Vittala temple are at Tadipatri, not Chandragiri.
Ubattu Shilpalu and the painting of Vatapatra Shayi are associated with
Tadipatri
Srisailam
is identified as the only temple with four entrance gates facing the four directions.

secs.t: Temple - presiding deity

x: Mallikarjuna at Srisailam, Veerabhadra at Lepakshi, and Narasimha at both Ahobilam and Kadiri.
The Chintala Venkataramana temple is dedicated to Venkataramana, not Veerabhadra.

secs.t: Forts and palaces - kingdom

x: Chandragiri shows Hindu and Indo-Saracenic elements, Gooty was Aliya Rama Raya’s base, and Mir Jumla looted the idols of Gandikota in 1657.
Udayagiri in Nellore was built by the Vijayanagara rulers, later taken by Golconda, and is associated with the Panchaloha cannon.
Chandragiri, Penukonda and Lepakshi are important monuments associated with Vijayanagara heritage in the stated districts.

secs.t: Vijayanagara style - distinctive additions

x: Vijayanagara architecture was characterised by large pillared Kalyana mandapas, massive enclosures, towering Raya gopurams, pillared corridors and thousand-pillared halls;
exclusive use of unpillared halls
was not a feature.
Sahasra Stambha Mandapa means a thousand-pillared hall, generally marked by elaborately carved composite pillars in the Vijayanagara style.
The style spread across Andhra through the courts at
Kondavidu, Udayagiri, Chandragiri and Vinukonda

secs.t: Srisailam and Tirupati - Vijayanagara additions and rulers

x: Shanti Lingayya constructed the sculptured prakaram at Srisailam during the reign of Krishnadevaraya.
Krishnadevaraya was associated with the Tirumala Kalyana mandapam, outer prakara and bronze statues of himself with Chinnadevi and Tirumaladevi.
The steps to Tirumala and the Govindaraja temple were associated with
Anantaraju, an Aravidu feudatory
Krishnadevaraya renovated or endowed Srikalahasti, Simhachalam, Amaravati and Kanaka Durga at Bejawada.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Lepakshi is in Sri Sathya Sai district, Tadipatri is in Anantapur, Tirupati belongs to the Tirupati region, and Chandragiri is associated with the Chittoor region.
The authorship of the Hazara Rama temple is debated among Devaraya I, Devaraya II and Krishnadevaraya, while Lepakshi is variously attributed to Krishnadevaraya or Achyutaraya.
The ASI is conserving Udayagiri Fort, and IYB 2026 lists Hampi, Tadipatri and Lepakshi; Tadipatri is identified with the 13th–16th century period.

rows.title: Folk culture of Andhra - Burrakatha, Harikatha, Veedhi Natakam, Oggu Katha, Tolu Bommalata
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-103

secs.t: Folk narrative forms - earlier names, performing community, instruments

x: Exam angle: "which folk form was earlier called Jangam Katha" → Burrakatha.
Burrakatha uses the
Gummata, Burra, Tambura and Ukki
, along with the characteristic chorus phrase ‘Thandana Taana’.
Oggu Katha is a Telangana ballad tradition of rural life and struggle, performed by the Golla/Kuruma shepherd community with a small oggu drum.

secs.t: Folk performance forms - home state, origin period, patrons

x: Tholu Bommalata
, the leather puppet show, was the most popular entertainment among the rural people of Andhra during the Vijayanagara period.
Yakshaganam entertained royal courts and elites, while the leather puppet show was especially popular in rural Andhra.
Sugreeva Vijayam, considered the first published Yakshaganam in Telugu, was written by
Kandukuri Rudra Kavi

secs.t: Harikatha - founder and exponents

x: Narayana Dasu fused music, story-telling, dance, philosophy and literature into Harikatha.
Adibhatla Narayana Dasu was a
multilingual scholar
who developed Harikatha as a composite performance tradition.
Jagajyothi
and Navarasa Tarangini are among the kavyas of Adibhatla Narayana Dasu.
Harikatha has deep roots in Vizianagaram, a region also associated with Adibhatla Narayana Dasu.

secs.t: Burrakatha - troupe roles, famous troupes, political use

x: Sunkara Satyanarayana wrote or performed Burrakathas such as
Kashtajeevi
, Raithu Vijayam, Stalin, Alluri Sitaramaraju and Veeresalingam.
The Praja Natya Mandali used folk plays to communicate
socialist and communist ideals
Burrakatha historical ballads draw upon events such as the
Bobbili War of 1757
, in which Vijayarama Raju of Vizianagaram sought French assistance.

secs.t: Tolu Bommalata - material, region, performing families

x: Tolu Bommalata combines leather shadow figures, sung verses and dialogue, movable puppet heads, and themes drawn from major Hindu epics and Puranic traditions.
Tolu Bommalata presents stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas, and its performances include classical music.
Vanarasa Govinda Rao came from a leather-puppet family and introduced live actors in Keechaka Vadham at a wedding in Sorugu village near Jammalamadugu.

secs.t: Folk artists and awards

x: Sheikh Nazar was a Burrakatha artist, received the Best Artist honour of the Andhra Nataka Akademi in 1981 and the Padma Shri in 1986, and is associated with the biography Pinjari.
Applications for the 2026 Ugadi awards were invited on
19 March 2026

secs.t: Kuchipudi and the Bhagavata Mela tradition

x: Exam angle: Kuchipudi <- Bhagavata Mela <- Siddhendra Yogi; Tana Shah grant.
Kuchipudi grew from the Bhagavata Mela dance-drama of hereditary Brahmin families, illustrating how a village-theatre tradition developed into a classical form.
The tradition emerged from Bhagavata Mela, Siddhendra Yogi is associated with its founding, the village was later gifted to the performers by Tana Shah, and Kuchipudi developed as a classical form.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Telugu Mahotsavam was announced to
revive Tolu Bommalata, Harikatha, Burrakatha and Padya Natakam
All four statements describe identified challenges: inadequate patronage, only three or four performances annually in some cases, youth disinterest and weak welfare support for veteran artists.
The initiatives include annual Telugu Mahotsavam, Telugu Language Day and Awards on 29 August, revival of Nandi Natakotsavams, and the announcement at Undavalli Caves by Minister Kandula Durgesh.

rows.title: Folk arts, festivals and fairs of Andhra Pradesh
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-103

secs.t: Handicrafts and GI-tagged arts → place

x: Farishkhani and Ashunkhani were designs of Eluru carpets that attracted attention at the
London Exhibition of 1851
Lepakshi launched a global e-commerce portal to export GI products such as
Kondapalli toys and Dharmavaram sarees
A 90-foot installation of GI-tagged Etikoppaka toys stands at
the new Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport at Bhogapuram

secs.t: Kuchipudi - village, district, vs Bharatanatyam

x: Kuchipudi village is associated with Krishna district, and the dance is among India’s eight classical forms and is regarded as a global ambassador of Indian culture.
Kuchipudi is an Andhra dance-drama tradition, while Bharatanatyam is associated with Tamil Nadu and a solo temple-dance tradition.
Tarangam is a distinctive Kuchipudi feature in which the dancer performs while
dancing on the rim of a brass plate

secs.t: Crafts of AP vs Telangana - which state

x: Dharmavaram sarees
are an Andhra Pradesh tradition.
The other sets contain Andhra Pradesh traditions or mixed associations.
Hyderabad’s Bidri tradition is derived from Bidar, which is in
Karnataka

secs.t: Folk dances → region + similar dances elsewhere

x: Pennadi leads Kolattam; it was prominent in the Eastern Chalukya era, Annamacharya composed Kolatam kirtanas, and its Karnataka version is Jadakollu.
Shepherd communities perform Tappeta Gullu to
invoke rain and appease Gangamma
The origin of Dhimsa is traced to
Koraput in Odisha
, although it is strongly associated with the tribal women of the Araku and ASR region.

secs.t: Festivals → month, region, dynastic origin

x: Kumaragiri Reddy used the title Karpura Vasantarayalu, and merchant Avachi Tippayashetti headed the Sugandhabhandagara that supplied the festival.
Sankranti occurs in January and is associated with Gangireddulaata, cockfights called Kolla Pandalu and ram fights called Pottella Pandalu.
Bathukamma and Bonalu represent Telangana identity, while Bihu belongs to Assam and Rongali Bihu is celebrated in April.

secs.t: State cultural festivals → theme + city

x: Lepakshi Utsav is held at Lepakshi and reflects Vijayanagara heritage; Visakha Utsav is held in Visakhapatnam, and the Kondapalli Toys Festival is to be held annually.
Bathukamma is a symbol of Telangana identity and is not in that list.

secs.t: Temple towns → epithet

x: Dwaraka Tirumala is known as Dakshina Dwaraka.
Draksharamam is called Dakshina Kasi, while Srikalahasti is called Dakshina Kailasam.

secs.t: Fairs and jataras → place + district

x: Sirimanu utsavam is the distinctive feature associated with
Paidithalli Ammavaru
at Vizianagaram.
Medieval Tirunallu or Jataralu were held at holy sites, with Kotappakonda and Srikakulam in Krishna district cited as examples.
Gangamma Jatara is associated with Tirupati, Paidithalli Ammavaru with Vizianagaram, Mahanandi fair with Shivaratri, and Jola patalu with lullabies.

secs.t: Folk songs → occasion

x: Jola patalu are
lullabies
Kolatam kirtanas are sung for
group dance
and are associated with Annamacharya.
The Gathasaptasati records couple and choir dances of rural folk.
Janapada Kalalu means the arts of the Janapadam, or village folk.
Biruduraju Ramaraju
wrote the first folk-knowledge theory book.
The period 1857–1956 is described as the golden era of dance.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: An Etikoppaka installation was reported at
Bhogapuram airport
in August 2026.
Lepakshi has an e-commerce export portal for promoting crafts, reported in March 2026.
APHDC markets Andhra Pradesh GI crafts through Lepakshi under the theme ‘
Vocal for Local
Kolatam kirtanas
are associated with group dance in the Andhra folk-song context.

rows.title: Battle of Talikota (1565), the Aravidu dynasty and the legacy of Vijayanagara
sub: Group-II M1-A-46: Aravidu dynasty and the Battle of Talikota; the Nayaka successor states

secs.t: Battle of Talikota - combatants, other names, year, commanders, causes, results

x: Aliya Rama Raya
was the de facto ruler and acted as regent for the Tuluva king Sadasiva Raya.
Sadasiva Raya was the nominal Tuluva king, while Rama Raya was his regent; Rama Raya's brothers Tirumala and Venkatadri fought with him.
Bijapur was ruled by Ali Adil Shah, Ahmadnagar by Hussain Nizam Shah, Golconda by Ibrahim Qutb Shah and Bidar by Ali Barid Shah.
The notes attribute the coalition to Rama Raya's diplomacy, interference, earlier attacks and sheltering of Jagadeva Rao; no Bahmani emperor created the coalition.
The battle initially saw Vijayanagara successes, followed by deceptive peace talks, a surprise attack and the withdrawal of Muslim contingents from the Vijayanagara army.

secs.t: Jesuit missions and the grant of Madras - ruler, local Nayaka, company

x: Venkatapati Raya II permitted Jesuit churches and Dutch trade, and allied with Spain and Portugal.
Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka granted Madras in 1639 to
Francis Day of the English East India Company
The site was named Chennapattanam after Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka's father,
Chennappa
Fort St George
followed the acquisition of Madras; the cited account places it in 1641.

secs.t: Nayaka and successor kingdoms → founder + contemporary ruler

x: Madurai was founded by Vishwanatha Nayaka, Tanjore by Sevappa Nayaka, Gingee by Krishnappa Nayaka and Mysore by Raja Wodeyar.
Vishwanatha Nayaka
captured his rebel father Nagama and was granted Madurai.
Vishwanatha Nayaka's son
Krishnappa Nayaka
made Madurai independent around 1565.
Tirumala Nayaka ruled Madurai from 1623 to 1659 and allied with Golconda against Vijayanagara.

secs.t: Deccan Sultanates in the alliance and the one that stayed out

x: Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar formed the alliance;
Berar
, ruled by the Imad Shahi dynasty, stayed out.

secs.t: Aravidu dynasty - rulers and shifting capitals

x: Tirumala Raya
founded the Aravidu dynasty and was crowned at Penukonda in 1570.
Venkatapati Raya II, the greatest and longest-ruling Aravidu ruler, was called the
Second Krishnadevaraya
The Vilapakam inscription of 1601 gives the genealogy of the
Tuluva and Aravidu
dynasties.
Jagga Raya
was killed in the Battle of Toppur in 1616.
Mir Jumla of Golconda
defeated Sriranga Raya III at Vandavasi in 1642.

secs.t: Legacy - temple architecture, Telugu literature, administration models

x: Nayaka courts helped spread
raya gopurams, kalyana mandapas and pillared corridors
across Andhra.
Ramaraja Bhushanudu
authored Vasucharitra, which was dedicated to Tirumala.
Krishnadevaraya’s reign marked the zenith of classical Telugu, while Appayya Dikshita and Ramaraja Bhushanudu are linked with the two named works.
The Nayankara or Amaranayaka system involved the assignment of territories and responsibilities to military-local chiefs.

secs.t: Rediscovery and survey of Hampi - who, when

x: Colin Mackenzie
surveyed and mapped the Hampi ruins in 1800 and later became the first Surveyor General of India.
Robert Sewell’s
A Forgotten Empire
, published in 1900, brought Vijayanagara history to wide notice.
Caesar Frederick
, a Venetian merchant, visited Vijayanagara in 1567 and left an eyewitness account of the ruined capital.

secs.t: Venkatapati Raya II (1585-1614) - capitals, Europeans, missionaries

x: Venkatapati II rejected Akbar’s demand for submission, maintained relations with the Portuguese and Philip II of Spain, and permitted the Dutch factory at Pulicat.
Venkatapati II allowed the Jesuits to build churches at
Chandragiri and Nellore
Venkatapati II gave villages to the Muslim saint
Babanathu
, as recorded in the Penukonda inscription.

secs.t: Rama Raya - regency and policy toward the Deccan Sultans

x: Aliya Rama Raya ruled as regent for the nominal king
Sadasiva Raya
from 1543 onward.
Rama Raya exploited rivalries among the Deccan Sultans, supporting different states at different times for Vijayanagara’s advantage.
All three statements correctly describe Rama Raya’s shifting alliances and territorial policy in the Deccan.
Rama Raya established
a Muslim quarter
known as the Turka Vada.

secs.t: Andhra Nayakas and Palegars after Talikota

x: Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka
, the Kalahasti-Wandiwash chief, arranged the Madras grant.
Velugoti Yachama Nayaka and Raghunatha of Tanjore
won the Battle of Toppur in 1616.
Mir Jumla of Golconda
is recorded as having melted temple idols into cannon at Gandikota in 1657.
The 1605 Siddhavatam inscription records that Matli Ananta built the fort walls during the reign of Venkatapati II.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The correct sequence is Talikota in 1565, Caesar Frederick’s visit in 1567, and Tirumala’s foundation of the Aravidu line and shift to Penukonda in 1570.
Caesar Frederick was a Venetian merchant who recorded an eyewitness account in 1567; Tirumala, not Caesar Frederick, founded the Aravidu line.
All three statements are correct within the stated chronology: Sadasiva Raya is dated to 1542–1570, and Tirumala’s accession is placed in 1570 after Sadasiva’s death.

rows.title: Mughal Empire - Babur: Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra; Tuzuk-i-Baburi

secs.t: Babur after Panipat - territories, extent at death, treasure

x: Babur distributed the treasure so lavishly that he came to be known by the nickname “Qalandar.” The lavish distribution also left the treasury depleted for Humayun.
At his death, Babur’s dominions extended
from Kabul and Badakhshan through Punjab, Delhi and Agra to the borders of Bihar
Babur died at Agra in 1530, and
Humayun
took the throne on 29 December 1530.

secs.t: Establishment of the Mughal Empire - scope and limits

x: Babur did not build an administrative system; his authority had shallow roots and the treasury was empty.
The Mansabdari system was introduced under Akbar, not Babur.

secs.t: Military tactics and technology

x: Tulughma was an Uzbek-origin tactic in which flanking units wheeled around the enemy to encircle it.
The Rumi method involved chaining carts together to form a field defence for matchlockmen and guns.
Ustad Ali and Mustafa were Ottoman gunners who commanded Babur’s artillery.
Babur’s force of about 12,000 defeated approximately 1,00,000 troops of Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat.

secs.t: Babur's background and invitations to invade

x: Babur became ruler of Farghana in 1494, took Kabul in 1504 and made his first Indian raid in 1519 according to the stated chronology.
Daulat Khan Lodi was the
Governor of Punjab
and one of the principal invitees of Babur.
Babur became ruler of Farghana in 1494, experienced repeated success and failure at Samarkand, and captured Kabul in 1504.

secs.t: Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama) - language, translators, observations

x: Baburnama was written in
Chagatai Turki
Leyden and Erskine produced an English translation in 1826.
Babur counted five Muslim and two Hindu powers in India; the two Hindu powers were Vijayanagara and Mewar.
Babur praised
Krishnadevaraya
of Vijayanagara as the most powerful ruler in India.

secs.t: Khanwa (1527) - Sanga's coalition, religious appeal, title

x: Rana Sanga’s coalition included the Afghan
Mahmud Lodi and Hasan Khan Mewati
Babur declared the battle a jihad, renounced wine and remitted the tamgha for Muslims before Khanwa.
After defeating Rana Sanga at Khanwa, Babur assumed the title “
Ghazi
Babur used trenches and barricades against the elephants of Rana Sanga.

secs.t: Babur's gardens, architecture and coinage

x: Shahrukhi was a silver coin in the Timurid style, not a copper coin.
Ram Bagh, also called Aram Bagh, at Agra was the first Mughal garden.
The Kabuli Bagh mosque at Panipat commemorates Babur’s victory in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Panipat I ended the rule of the Lodis, the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, and began Mughal rule in India.
The Mughals did not interfere in the Deccan during Babur’s time
Babur’s authority had shallow roots, and he did not establish a complete administrative system during his short rule.

rows.title: Humayun and Sher Shah Suri - Sur administration, land revenue, sarais, currency, Grand Trunk Road
sub: Group-II S1-45: Mughal Empire - Babur, Humayun, Sher Shah Suri and the Sur interregnum

secs.t: Sher Shah's land revenue administration

x: Sher Shah introduced a uniform system of land measurement using the sikandari gaz, also called
gaz-i-Sikandari
Land was classified as good, middling or bad according to its productivity.
Sher Shah's direct state-peasant settlement is regarded as an early ryotwari-type arrangement and influenced Todar Mal's bandobast.
The system sought to remove illegal demands and recognise the rights of tenants through a direct relationship between the state and cultivators.

secs.t: Sher Shah's roads and sarais

x: Sher Shah's sarais were roadside establishments with shade-giving trees and separate accommodation for Hindu and Muslim travellers.
Sher Shah combined road construction with traveller amenities, including roadside sarais and shady trees.
Sher Shah maintained efficient espionage and policing, including local responsibility for reporting and preventing crime.
Dagh
was the branding of horses, used along with descriptive rolls of soldiers to prevent military fraud.

secs.t: Sher Shah's currency - coins, metals, weights

x: Sher Shah's rupiya was a silver coin weighing approximately
178 grains
The silver rupiya continued as a standard for centuries, the dam was copper, and the mohur or ashrafi was gold.
Sher Shah minted pure gold and silver coins, and the monetary system continued to influence currency after the Sur dynasty ended.

secs.t: Sur monuments → location

x: The tomb at Sasaram is an octagonal monument surrounded by water in a tank.
Rohtas Fort is characterised by
angled walls and bastions
, reflecting its defensive design.
Humayun's Tomb is considered
the first garden tomb of the Indian subcontinent
Humayun's tomb introduced the garden-tomb and double-dome traditions, while Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb was the first Mughal tomb in white marble.

secs.t: Humayun - battles in order, exile, return, death

x: Exam angle: "wrong pair" questions - Jahangir-Chausa is wrong.
At Ghaghra in 1529, Babur fought the
Afghans under Mahmud Lodi
and achieved a Mughal victory.
Chausa was fought in 1539, Kannauj in 1540 and Panipat II in 1556.
Humayun's initial problems included his rival brothers, the Afghans, Bahadur Shah of Gujarat-Malwa and an empty treasury.
Humayun defeated the Afghans at Dourah and drove
Mahmud Lodi
from Jaunpur.
When pressed by Humayun in Gujarat in 1535, Bahadur Shah allowed the Portuguese to fortify Diu.
Safavid ruler
Shah Tahmasp of Persia
helped Humayun retake Kandahar and Kabul.
Humayun exploited
quarrels among Sher Shah's successors
and returned in July 1555.
After returning, Humayun defeated Sikandar Sur at Machhiwara and Sirhind, and then took Delhi and Agra.
Humayun died in January 1556 after falling from the stairs of
the Sher Mandal library in Purana Qila
The Second Battle of Panipat was fought on 5 November 1556, when Akbar and Bairam Khan defeated Hemu, ending Afghan power.
The Battle of Haldighati in 1576, fought between Man Singh and Maharana Pratap, was
not decisive

secs.t: Sher Shah - rise, titles, conquests, Rajput resistance, death

x: Sher Khan served Babur and later became deputy regent and the de facto ruler of
Bihar
After defeating Humayun at
Chausa
in 1539, Sher Khan assumed the title Sher Shah.
The remark referred to the hard-fought Battle of
Samel against Maldeo
of Marwar.
Sher Shah died in 1545 in a gunpowder explosion during the siege of
Kalinjar

secs.t: Sur successors - Islam Shah, Adil Shah, Hemu

x: Jaita and Kumpa were associated with Maldeo of Marwar and fought with great valour against Sher Shah at Samel.
After occupying Agra and Delhi in 1556, Hemu took the title
Vikramaditya
Hemu served Adil Shah, occupied Agra and Delhi, and was captured after being struck in the eye at the Second Battle of Panipat.

secs.t: Sur administration - sarkar, pargana, army, police, dak

x: The pargana had a Shiqdar, Amin, Fotedar and Hindi and Persian-writing Karkuns.
Sur officers were frequently transferred, limiting the growth of local personal power and vested interests.
Dagh was the branding of horses, while chehra or huliya was the descriptive record of soldiers.
The Sur army was regular, directly recruited and strictly disciplined; it also used horse branding and descriptive rolls.

secs.t: Babur - origin, Tuzuk-i-Baburi, cities after Panipat, war tactics

x: Babur was born in Farghana, descended from Timur through his father and Genghis Khan through his mother, and had held Samarkand and Kabul.
Tulughma was a rapid cavalry tactic based on flanking and encircling the enemy.
The Rumi or Ottoman method used linked carts as a protective barrier for matchlockmen and artillery.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sher Shah used three land classes and a one-third rate, while Akbar’s system used ten-year averages and four classes while retaining the one-third share.
The rupiya began with Sher Shah, and Sur coinage formed one of the foundations inherited by Akbar’s administration.
Sultan Quli Qutb Shah ruled Golconda from 1518 to 1543 and was contemporary with the early Mughals and Sher Shah, while Mughal interference in the Deccan had not yet begun.

rows.title: Akbar - conquests, Rajput policy, religious policy, Ibadat Khana, Din-i-Ilahi, Sulh-i-Kul
sub: Group-II S1-46: Akbar - conquests, Rajput policy, religious policy, Mansabdari and revenue system
Group-II S1-50: Mughal religious conditions and policies

secs.t: Mughal emperors' education - literacy, Akbar's reforms, Maktab Khana

x: Akbar
was unlettered, yet he was a great patron of learning, literature and culture.
Humayun learned Persian, Arabic, Turkish, mathematics and astronomy.
Babur's autobiography, the Tuzuk-i-Baburi, was written in
Chaghatai Turkish
Akbar's curriculum included ethics, arithmetic, agriculture, geometry, astronomy, government, medicine, logic and history.
The
Atharvaveda
was also translated under Akbar's translation initiative.

secs.t: Conquests → year + ruler opposed

x: Baz Bahadur opposed Akbar in Malwa, Rani Durgavati in Gondwana, Rana Udai Singh at Chittor, and Surjan Rai at Ranthambore.
Gondwana was conquered in 1564, Chittor in 1568, Gujarat in 1572–73 and Kabul in 1581.
Akbar's last campaign was the conquest of Khandesh in 1601, during which the Asirgarh fort was taken from Miran Bahadur.

secs.t: Rajput policy - marriages, mansabdars, holdouts, Haldighati

x: Exam angle: the counter-intuitive answer "Aurangzeb" is the tested fact.
Akbar followed a twin policy of
conquest and conciliation
, accepting submission while restoring autonomy and honour in suitable cases.
Raja Todarmal
was prominent in revenue administration under Akbar, while Man Singh was a leading Rajput military officer.
Shah Jahan retained many Hindu nobles, and Aurangzeb had the highest absolute number, including Marathas and Rajputs recruited during the Deccan wars.

secs.t: Religious policy - Ibadat Khana, taxes, Mahzar, Sulh-i-Kul

x: The pilgrimage tax was abolished in 1563 and jizya was abolished in 1564 according to the commonly used chronology.
The debates were broadened beyond Muslim scholars and included
Hindus, Jains, Christians and Zoroastrians
The Mahzar of 1579 made Akbar the supreme arbiter in religious disputes and was drafted by Shaikh Mubarak.
Sulh-i-Kul means universal peace or
peace with all
and served as a guiding principle of Akbar's policy.

secs.t: Contacts with Jesuits, Jain, Sikh and Parsi leaders

x: The first Jesuit mission from Goa in 1580 was led by
Rudolf Acquaviva and Antonio Monserrate
The third Jesuit mission, sent in 1595, was under
Jerome Xavier
Hiravijaya Suri was a
Jain scholar who received the title Jagat Guru
from Akbar.
Akbar granted land to the Parsi leader
Dastur Meherji Rana

secs.t: Navratnas and court figures → field + fate

x: Abul Fazl was murdered in 1602 by Bir Singh Bundela at the instance of Prince Salim.
Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan was a poet, son of Bairam Khan and translator of the Baburnama; he was not a Jesuit missionary.
The sequence is abolition of jizya in 1564, construction of the Ibadat Khana in 1575, Mahzar in 1579 and Din-i-Ilahi in 1582.

secs.t: Regency and early reign - Bairam Khan, Panipat II, petticoat government

x: Bairam Khan served as regent from 1556 to 1560 and was dismissed in 1560.
The term refers to the period from 1560 to 1564 when
Maham Anaga and her son Adham Khan
exercised considerable influence.
Bairam Khan's regency came first, followed by his dismissal in 1560, the petticoat government from 1560 to 1564, and his death in 1561.

secs.t: Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi) - members, features, reactions

x: Din-i-Ilahi or Tauhid-i-Ilahi was proclaimed as a
syncretic moral order
Din-i-Ilahi included belief in one God, reverence for the sun and fire, and avoidance of meat-eating.
Badauni and the Naqshbandi scholar Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi criticised Akbar's religious innovations, including Din-i-Ilahi and Sulh-i-Kul.
Both statements are true, and the voluntary nature and small membership of Din-i-Ilahi explain why it did not become a mass religion.

secs.t: Revenue systems → designer and features

x: Batai involved division of the harvested crop, Kankut estimated the standing crop, and Nasaq relied roughly on the peasant's past payments.
Under Zabti/Dahsala, land was measured and the state share was one-third of the average produce of the preceding ten years, commuted into cash as damil.
Nasaq was a rough assessment based on
the village's past revenue record
, whereas Kankut estimated the standing crop by eye or sample.

secs.t: Taxes on non-Muslims → emperor who imposed or abolished (jizya, pilgrim tax)

x: Aurangzeb re-imposed
jizya
Zakat was an alms tax on Muslims, ushr was a land tax on Muslims, khums represented one-fifth of war booty, and jizya was imposed on non-Muslims.
Shah Jahan abolished the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Allahabad after a deputation of Banaras pandits led by
Kavindracharya

secs.t: Sikh Gurus and Mughal relations (Guru Arjan Dev, Guru Hargobind, Guru Tegh Bahadur)

x: Guru Tegh Bahadur founded Anandpur Sahib, contributed 116 hymns and acquired the title Hind-di-Chadar for protecting Kashmiri Pandits.
Banda Singh Bahadur took Samana in 1709, defeated Wazir Khan at Chappar Chiri in 1710 and established Lohgarh as the capital of the first sovereign Sikh state.
Guru Tegh Bahadur was born Tyag Mal in 1621, served as Guru from 1665 to 1675, founded Anandpur Sahib and contributed 116 hymns.
Sis Ganj marks the execution site, Rakab Ganj the cremation site, and Takht Keshgarh Sahib at Anandpur the place where the Khalsa was founded.
Banda Singh Bahadur captured Sirhind from
Wazir Khan
in 1710 to avenge the killing of Guru Gobind Singh's younger sons.

secs.t: Emperor-wise religious policy (Babur, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb)

x: Jahangir broadly continued Akbar's tolerant approach, but Guru Arjan Dev was executed for political reasons related to support for rebel prince Khusrau.
Shah Jahan was slightly more orthodox and destroyed some newly built temples, but he continued to employ many Hindu nobles.
Aurangzeb re-imposed jizya in 1679, banned festivals such as Navroz, patronised the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri and was known as Zinda Pir.

secs.t: Orthodox reaction - Naqshbandi order and its leaders

x: The Naqshbandi order stressed strict adherence to Islamic law, or Sharia.
Sirhindi propounded
Wahdat-ul-Shuhud
, or Unity of Appearance, against Wahdat-ul-Wujud.
Shah Waliullah and Shah Abdul Aziz were later Naqshbandi scholars.
The Qadiri order is associated with Abdul Qadir Jilani and Dara Shikoh, while the Naqshbandi order was founded by Baha-ud-din Naqshband and had an orthodox Wahdat-ul-Shuhud orientation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Aurangzeb reimposed jizya in 1679, reversing Akbar’s policy of abolition.
The jagirdari crisis arose because too many mansabdars chased too few jagirs, which increased pressure on the peasantry.
Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
of Golconda maintained friendly relations with Akbar, who sent Masud Beg with gifts.
Abul Hasan Tana Shah followed religious tolerance and appointed Madanna and Akkanna to high office.
Sirhind Fateh Diwas commemorates
Banda Singh Bahadur’s conquest of Sirhind in 1710
and is observed from 12 to 14 May.

rows.title: Akbar's institutions - Mansabdari system, Todar Mal's bandobast, dahsala, zabti and other revenue systems

secs.t: Revenue systems → meaning + year + region

x: Zabti was used in the core provinces of North India, extending from Lahore to Allahabad and including Malwa and Gujarat.
Batai or Ghalla-bakhshi
involved sharing the crop between the state and the peasant and was used in areas such as Thatta, Kabul and Kashmir.
Nasaq was a rough assessment based on previous revenue records and did not involve fresh measurement; it was mainly used in Bengal.

secs.t: Todar Mal - service, bandobast, jarib, land classes, office

x: Todar Mal had earlier served
Sher Shah
and built upon Sher Shah’s survey-based system.
The jarib was made from bamboo pieces joined with iron rings, avoiding the shrinkage or stretching associated with hemp rope.
Polaj was cultivated every year, Parauti was fallow for one or two years, Chachar for three or four years, and Banjar was uncultivated for five or more years.

secs.t: Revenue and grant terms → meaning; principal state income

x: Madad-i-maash
was a revenue-free grant made to scholars, holy men and needy persons.
Suyurghal was another term for charitable revenue-free grants such as madad-i-maash.
Khalisa was crown land, and its revenue went directly to the imperial treasury.
A jagir was an assignment of the right to collect revenue in lieu of salary; it did not confer ownership of the land.

secs.t: Karori experiment and revenue circles

x: In 1574, the core provinces were divided into revenue circles under karoris.
Each circle was designed to yield
one crore dams
and was placed under a karori.
Karoris collected revenue and reported cultivation data.

secs.t: Administrative structure - subas, sarkars, parganas, officials

x: The administrative hierarchy proceeded from Suba to Sarkar to Pargana and then to the village.
The officials associated with a Suba included the Subedar, Diwan, Bakhshi, Sadr and Qazi.
At the Sarkar level, the Faujdar dealt with law and order and the amalguzar with revenue.
The village officials were the Muqaddam, or headman, the Patwari and the Chowkidar.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The mansabdari and zabti-dahsala arrangements together provided the Mughal state with a salaried, transferable nobility and a predictable stream of cash revenue.
Mughal mansabdars combined civil and military functions, held non-hereditary ranks and were paid through jagirs.
The Khalisa was expanded under
Abdullah and Tana Shah
in the Qutb Shahi kingdom.

rows.title: Jahangir and Nur Jahan; Shah Jahan - Deccan and Central Asian policy, the war of succession
sub: Group-II S1-47: Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb - policies and consequences

secs.t: Events of Jahangir's reign - Sikh Guru, Mewar, Kandahar, rebellions

x: Exam angle: "Which events took place under Jahangir" - Arjan Dev's execution, Mewar's submission and the English arrival are correct; annexation of Kabul-Kandahar is the trap.
Akbar's eldest son Salim was named after Sheikh Salim Chishti and assumed the title
Nur-ud-din Muhammad Jahangir
when he was crowned in 1605.
The execution of the fifth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, in 1606 was connected with his support for the rebel Khusrau and was political in character, rather than a general persecution.
Khurram revolted during 1622–1626, mainly because Nur Jahan supported Shahryar as the prospective heir.

secs.t: War of succession (1657-59) - four princes, battles, fate

x: Exam angle: chronology - Shuja near Banaras, then Dharmat, then Samugarh, then Deorai.
Dara Shikoh was at the imperial court, Shuja governed Bengal, Aurangzeb was in the Deccan and Murad Bakhsh was associated with Gujarat.
In April 1658 at Dharmat near Ujjain, the forces of Aurangzeb and Murad defeated the imperial army led by
Jaswant Singh and Qasim Khan
Murad Bakhsh, initially Aurangzeb's ally, was
imprisoned in Gwalior Fort and executed in 1661
Shuja fled to Arakan, while Shah Jahan remained confined in Agra Fort, where Jahanara cared for him until his death in 1666.

secs.t: Nur Jahan junta - members, coinage, farmans, court politics

x: Mehrunnisa, widow of Sher Afghan, married Jahangir in 1611, received the title Nur Jahan and was later known as Padshah Begum.
Ghiyas Beg was Nur Jahan's father and Jahangir's diwan; Asaf Khan was her brother and Mumtaz's father; Khurram married Arjumand; Nur Jahan's name appeared on coins and farmans.
Nur Jahan's support for Shahryar, who was married to her daughter, divided the junta and helped provoke Khurram's revolt in 1622.

secs.t: European envoys at Jahangir's court - Hawkins and Roe

x: William Hawkins reached Surat in 1608 and proceeded to
Agra
in 1609, where he obtained a mansab and the title English Khan.
Portuguese intrigue
blocked Hawkins from obtaining a trade farman, and he left India in 1611.
Captain Best's victory over the Portuguese in 1612 preceded the establishment of the English factory at Surat in 1613.

secs.t: Central Asian (Balkh-Badakhshan) campaign and Kandahar sieges

x: The Persian governor
Ali Mardan Khan
surrendered Kandahar to Shah Jahan.
The campaign was linked with Shah Jahan's ambition concerning the ancestral lands and ended in withdrawal with heavy losses.
Aurangzeb's sieges in 1649 and 1652 and Dara Shikoh's siege in 1653 all failed; Kandahar was thereafter lost for good.

secs.t: Royal family - relations, titles, fate

x: Dara Shikoh was Shah Jahan's eldest son, was given the title Shah-i-Iqbal, took refuge at Dadar and was eventually buried in Humayun's Tomb.
Before marrying Jahangir in 1611, Mehrunnisa, later Nur Jahan, was the widow of
Sher Afghan
Nur Jahan's junta consisted of Nur Jahan, her father Itimad-ud-Daula, her brother Asaf Khan and Prince Khurram.
The junta broke when Nur Jahan supported Shahryar, her son-in-law, thereby provoking Khurram's revolt during 1622–26.

secs.t: Shah Jahan's Deccan policy - Ahmadnagar, 1636 treaties, Aurangzeb as viceroy

x: The Deccan governor
Khan Jahan Lodi
sought shelter with the Nizam Shah.
Abul Hasan Tana Shah was exiled to Daulatabad, died in 1700, and Qamruddin Chin Qilich Khan played a key role in the annexation.
Sambhaji was captured and executed in 1689; Rajaram continued resistance from Jinji, followed by Tarabai, while Shahu was later released by Bahadur Shah I.
The prolonged war against the Marathas proved unwinnable, drained the Mughal treasury and continued until Aurangzeb's death in the Deccan in 1707.
The 1636 agreements involved suzerainty, indemnity, a two-lakh-hun tribute from Golconda and the khutba in Shah Jahan’s name.
The phases were 1658–68 recovery of Bijapur territory, 1668–84 alliances against the Marathas, 1686–87 annexation, and 1687–1707 war against the Marathas.

secs.t: Shah Jahan's reign - captivity and the "golden age" verdict

x: Shah Jahan remained under guard for about
eight years
, from his deposition in 1658 until his death in 1666.
Shah Jahan's policy was somewhat more orthodox, including the destruction of some new temples, but many Hindu nobles remained in service.
Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra in 1628, faced the stated revolts, and is associated with major architectural works and the Peacock Throne in the Diwan-i-Khas.

secs.t: Revolts against Aurangzeb → region

x: The Jats were associated with Mathura and Gokula; the Satnamis with Narnaul; the Sikhs with Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution; and the Rajputs with Marwar, Mewar and Durgadas Rathore.
The Jat revolt and temple order occurred in 1669, followed by the Satnami revolt in 1672 and Guru Tegh Bahadur's execution in 1675.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Jahangir–Shah Jahan era is regarded as the Mughal high noon, and the 1636 treaties made the Deccan sultanates tributaries, preparing the way for later annexations.
Aurangzeb's Deccan wars, alienation of the Rajputs and the jagir crisis contributed to the later decline of the Mughal Empire.
Jahangir and Shah Jahan broadly continued Akbar's tolerant approach, although Shah Jahan was somewhat more orthodox; Aurangzeb reversed this trend.

rows.title: Aurangzeb - religious policy, Deccan policy; Rajput, Jat, Satnami, Sikh and Maratha resistance

secs.t: Religious taxes and other religious-policy measures

x: Exam angle: identify the tax on non-Muslims (Jizya vs Zakat, Ushr, Khums).
Aurangzeb adopted the title
Alamgir
and was also known as Zinda Pir or Darvesh.
Akbar abolished Jizya in 1564, whereas Aurangzeb reimposed it in 1679.
Aurangzeb
's order of 1669 led to the demolition of the Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai temples.

secs.t: Deccan policy - Bijapur and Golconda conquest

x: The traitor
Abdullah Pani
opened the gates of Golconda Fort on 21 September 1687.
The 27-year Deccan war drained the Mughal treasury and was therefore called the 'Deccan Ulcer', in comparison with Napoleon's Spanish Ulcer.
The last Qutb Shahi ruler, Abul Hasan Tana Shah, was imprisoned first at Bidar and then at Daulatabad, where he died in 1699.

secs.t: Titles - Alamgir, Zinda Pir, double coronation, royal women

x: Aurangzeb had a hurried first coronation in 1658 after Samugarh and a grand second coronation in 1659 after Deorai.
Roshanara was made Padshah Begum, Jahanara was honoured as Sahibat-uz-Zamani, and Alamgir means World Conqueror.
The
Child's War
of 1686–90 was the first conflict between the English and a Mughal emperor under Aurangzeb.

secs.t: Rajput resistance - Marwar and Mewar

x: Prince Akbar rebelled against Aurangzeb and joined the Rajputs in 1681.
The clumsy handling of Marwar and Mewar broke the Rajput alliance that had been a pillar of Akbar's empire and cost the Mughals considerable influence.

secs.t: Jat and Satnami revolts - leaders and region

x: Gokula led the 1669 Jat revolt at Mathura, Rajaram plundered Akbar's tomb, Churaman built Jat power, and the Satnami revolt occurred at Narnaul.
Gokula led the 1669 Jat peasant revolt in the Mathura region, particularly at Tilpat, against
heavy revenue demands
The Satnami revolt of 1672 occurred at Narnaul in Haryana and involved peasants and artisans.

secs.t: Maratha conflict - Shivaji to Tarabai

x: The order is Treaty of Purandar in 1665, Agra visit in 1666, coronation at Raigad in 1674, and Sambhaji's capture and execution in 1689.
During his 1666 visit to Agra, Shivaji was insulted and placed under house arrest, from which he escaped in fruit baskets.

secs.t: Aurangzeb's last years - death and burial

x: Aurangzeb spent approximately 25–27 of his last years camped in the Deccan.
Aurangzeb died in 1707 at
Ahmednagar
Aurangzeb was buried in a simple grave at
Khuldabad, near Aurangabad

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The PIL concerning the removal of the “Maratha Empire” map from NCERT was reported in the
Bombay High Court
The martyrdom of
Guru Tegh Bahadur
continues to be recalled in recent public commemoration.
The conventional criticism refers to the Deccan ulcer and Rajput alienation, while the revisionist view highlights the increased presence of Hindu nobles under Aurangzeb.
