rows.title: Mughal administration - mansab (zat and sawar), jagirdari system and the jagirdari crisis
sub: Group-II S1-48: Mughal administration - mansabdari, jagirdari, zamindari and provincial set-up

secs.t: Mansabdari system - introducing ruler, purpose, model, zat and sawar

x: Exam angle: statement sets on "hereditary?", "introduced by Akbar?", "three classes?", "civil officers also mansabdars?".
Zat represented the mansabdar’s personal rank, status, salary and prestige; sawar indicated the number of cavalrymen to be maintained.
The Mansabdari system theoretically contained 66 grades, 33 were used in practice, and the system followed decimal grading.

secs.t: Central officials - functions

x: These portfolios respectively covered finance, military administration, royal household management, and religious-charitable matters.
The
Mir Bakhshi
headed military and intelligence affairs, supervised recruitment, promotion, pay and musters, and presented candidates to the emperor.
Although the Wakil had traditionally been the chief adviser or regent, the office became largely
symbolic
under Akbar.

secs.t: Sawar sub-categories and conditional ranks - du-aspa sih-aspa, mashrut

x: Exam angle: the system served both army recruitment and revenue/civil administration (BPSC 2019 - "more than one").
Jahangir
introduced du-aspa sih-aspa, under which selected mansabdars maintained additional cavalry without a corresponding increase in zat.
Du-aspa sih-aspa required selected mansabdars to maintain double troopers without increasing their zat, with payment adjusted accordingly.
Akbar’s mansab ranks ranged from 10 to 10,000, the highest were reserved for princes, and the decimal pattern had Central Asian or Mongol origins.
The troopers covered by the du-aspa sih-aspa arrangement maintained
two or three horses each
, and their relevant sawar component was counted double.

secs.t: Army components - ahadis, dakhili, tabinan

x: Ahadis were gentlemen troopers recruited and paid directly by the emperor.
Dakhili troops were recruited and paid by the state but placed under mansabdars.
Tabinan were the personal contingents or retainers maintained by mansabdars.
The Mughal army was not composed exclusively of ahadis.

secs.t: Jagir types - holder

x: A Tankhwah jagir was assigned in lieu of salary, a Watan jagir was hereditary and retained in the homeland, Mashrut was conditional, and Altamgha was a perpetual grant.
Under Aurangzeb, mansabdars multiplied while the supply of jagirs shrank, resulting in intensified and ruthless extraction from the peasantry.
Under Aurangzeb, the number of mansabdars increased, profitable jagirs became scarce, and peasants were subjected to intensified extraction.

secs.t: Jagirdari crisis - historians' explanations

x: Satish Chandra explained the crisis through shortage of jagirs relative to claimants; Irfan Habib stressed agrarian exploitation and revolts; Athar Ali highlighted the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles.
The growth of mansabdars coincided with the reduction of profitable land, encouraging harsher extraction from peasants and contributing to agrarian ruin and decline.

secs.t: Transfer of jagirs and bejagiri - effects on nobility

x: Frequent transfers, usually every three to four years, were intended to prevent mansabdars from establishing local bases and becoming independent feudal lords.
Frequent transfers contributed to short-term extraction; they did not eliminate factionalism at court.
Bejagiri meant that mansabdars remained without jagir assignments.

secs.t: TERMS - dagh, chehra, tashiha and muster rules

x: Dagh was the branding of horses to prevent substitution.
Periodic military musters were conducted under the Mir Bakhshi.

secs.t: Provincial set-up in ascending order and officials

x: Akbar had 12 subahs in 1580, 15 by the end of his reign, and Aurangzeb had 21, with Golconda as the twenty-first.
The subah had the Subahdar and other provincial officers; the city had the Kotwal; the sarkar had the Faujdar and Amalguzar; and the pargana had the Shiqdar, Amil, Qanungo and Chaudhari.

secs.t: Espionage and news-writers (waqia-navis)

x: Waqia-navis, khufia-navis and harkaras formed complementary channels, intelligence came under the Mir Bakhshi, and Sher Shah had earlier operated an efficient espionage system.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The British ICS was purely civil and cash-paid, whereas Mughal mansabdars performed mixed civil-military duties and were paid through jagirs.
In Qutb Shahi Golconda, the Peshwa was the Peshwa, Mir Jumla handled finance, Ain-ul-Mulk handled military affairs and the Majumdar was the auditor.
The Kakatiya Nayankara system is compared with the Delhi Sultanate iqta and the Mughal jagir as systems involving assignments connected with military service and revenue.

rows.title: Mughal provincial and local administration; the mansabdari-jagirdari-zamindari linkage

secs.t: Revenue officials - duties

x: Bitikchi prepared assessment and land records; Qanungo maintained pargana-level revenue records; Potdar was the treasurer; and Patwari was the village accountant.
The Amalguzar collected district revenue; the Karkun recorded cultivation and revenue; the Qanungo maintained pargana records; and the Patwari was the village accountant.
The
Amalguzar
, also called the Amil, was responsible for the assessment and collection of revenue at the Sarkar level.

secs.t: Units - suba, sarkar, chakla, pargana, village

x: Exam angle: ascending order -
Pargana - Sarkar - Suba
; Mughal "district" =
Sarkar
A Suba was headed by the Subedar and provincial Diwan, while a Sarkar had the Faujdar and Amalguzar as its principal officials.
The state's effective administrative reach generally ended at the Pargana; villages retained substantial self-government.

secs.t: Provincial and city officials - functions

x: The provincial Diwan handled revenue and finance independently of the Subedar, thereby acting as a check on the governor.
The
Diwan-i-Tan
dealt with salaries or tankhwah and jagir assignments.
The
Mustaufi
was the auditor in the Mughal administrative structure.
The Faujdar was responsible for Sarkar-level military command and law and order.

secs.t: Mansabdar-jagirdar-zamindar linkage

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2019 - "jagirs in lieu of judicial/police duties" and "jagirs hereditary" are both
wrong
(answer: neither).
The Mansabdar received a rank and was paid through a tankhwah jagir; the jagirdar's agents collected assessed revenue through zamindars, from whom the peasant paid the state demand.
Short tenure encouraged Jagirdars to press for higher collections; Zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants sometimes fled, producing a local face of the jagirdari crisis.

secs.t: Zamindar categories - rights and role

x: Autonomous chiefs
were Rajas who ruled their own territories, paid tribute and could serve as Mansabdars.
Intermediary zamindars collected revenue from primary zamindars on behalf of the state and received a commission for the service.
Primary zamindars possessed proprietary, hereditary rights over cultivated land.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The separation of the Subedar and Diwan and the Zabti revenue system were important models for later revenue administration.
The Sultanate had Iqtas administered by Muqtis, while the British district collector combined revenue, magisterial and police powers that the Mughals kept separate.
The village officials included the Mukaddam and accountant Kulkarni, while the Desai served as the Pargana accounts officer.

rows.title: Mughal economy - agriculture, karkhanas, trade, silver influx, Indian Ocean commerce
sub: Group-II S1-49: Mughal socio-economic conditions - agriculture, trade, karkhanas, classes

secs.t: Trader classes - function (banjaras, beoparis, sarrafs, mahajans, baniks)

x: Exam angle: "traders who carried bulk goods over long distances" =
Banjaras
Marwaris comprised Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals; Chettis were Coromandel merchants; Muslim merchants dominated Malabar trade; and Gujarati merchants included Hindus, Jains and Muslims.
In the earlier Sultanate pattern, Multanis and Khurasanis controlled overseas trade, whereas Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants were important in inland trade.

secs.t: Rural produce marketed - share and commercial crops

x: Exam angle: "approximately what % was marketed?" - 15%.
Jins-i-kamil referred to commercial or superior cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane, indigo, oilseeds and opium.
Polaj was cultivated annually; Parauti remained fallow for one year; Chachar for three to four years; and Banjar was uncultivated.
Patta was a title deed, while Qabuliyat was a deed of agreement issued in the revenue arrangement.

secs.t: Credit instruments - hundi, bima, shroffs

x: Exam angle: distractors are Farman (royal order), Parcha, Rokad (cash).
A
hundi
was a letter of credit issued by a shroff against cash deposited at one place and encashed later or elsewhere.
The English East India Company relied on Indian brokers or dalals, shroffs and banians and thus fitted into the existing credit network.

secs.t: Historians and travellers on the Mughal economy - books

x: Exam angle: book-author matching (APPSC-G1 2022: a-IV, b-I, c-II, d-III).

William Hawkins was associated with Jahangir; Pelsaert came during Jahangir's time in 1620; Peter Mundy visited during Shah Jahan's reign; Tavernier visited during the reigns of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.

Tapan Raychaudhuri was a co-editor, along with Irfan Habib, of the Cambridge Economic History of India, Volume I. Six Voyages was associated with Tavernier, Early Travels in India with William Foster, and Storia do Mogor with Niccolao Manucci.
Manucci was the Italian doctor linked with court intrigues; Thevenot reached Surat in 1666; Pelsaert was the Dutch VOC merchant; and Peter Mundy was the English merchant who recorded a famine.

secs.t: Coins - metal and name

x: The silver rupiya was standardised by Sher Shah at 178 grains, continued by Akbar, while the dam was made of copper.
Sikka denoted the right of coinage in the ruler's name and, together with the khutba, symbolised sovereignty.
Mughal silver coins circulated in Golconda, although Golconda itself minted only copper coins, as noted by Thevenot.

secs.t: Ports and trading centres - epithets, exports, imports

x: Surat
was the chief Mughal port on the west coast and was known as the Gateway to Mecca or Bab-ul-Makka owing to its importance for Haj traffic.
English ships arrived at Surat in 1608, Hawkins obtained a firman in 1609, and Roe secured the factory in 1615.
Shah Jahan granted exemptions to the English in 1652 and the Dutch in 1665, while Farrukhsiyar’s firman of 1716/1717 reduced English duties.

secs.t: Karkhanas - royal workshops

x: Mughal karkhanas supplied courtly luxury goods and continued a tradition inherited from the Sultanate karkhanas.
Artisans worked in both state karkhanas and private enterprises and were often organised into guilds; they were not confined exclusively to royal workshops.
Royal karkhanas produced luxury articles, including costly gold and silver goods, for the court.

secs.t: Silver influx and Indian Ocean commerce

x: India became a ‘sink of precious metals’ because European companies paid for Indian goods with bullion, causing large inflows of gold and silver.
The
English East India Company
, founded in 1600, was one of the European trading groups active in Indian Ocean commerce.
The English East India Company was established in 1600, the Dutch reached Masulipatnam in 1605, the English in 1611, and the French in 1669.

secs.t: Social classes - nobility, zamindars, peasants (khud-kasht, pahi-kasht), artisans

x: Khud-kasht peasants cultivated land in their own village, whereas pahi-kasht peasants cultivated land in another village.
Zamindars were hereditary rural superior-right holders and took a large share along with jagirdars and revenue-farmers.
Artisans and merchants constituted middle and lower urban strata and were associated with guilds and karkhanas.
Eighteenth-century society was characterised by the coexistence of extreme poverty and extreme wealth.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Cash revenue under zabt monetised the rural economy and connected peasants with markets.
Masulipatnam functioned as the
Qutb Shahi gateway for overseas commerce
Machilipatnam
was the first European trade centre in Andhra, established by the Dutch in 1605.
Bernier did express the view that private property in land did not exist.

rows.title: Mughal society - nobility, peasantry, position of women, urban classes

secs.t: Festivals and court customs - origin

x: Nauroz was the Persian New Year adopted from the Zoroastrians.
Aurangzeb
ended Jharokha darshan and stopped the celebration of Nauroz.
Tuladan was a Hindu custom adopted by Akbar in which the emperor was weighed against gold and goods that were given to the poor.
Sijda meant prostration, while paibos meant kissing the feet; Akbar introduced both practices at court.

secs.t: Nobility composition

x: The umara constituted the top mansabdars and formed the Mughal ruling nobility.
Mughal nobles were wealthy but remained wholly dependent on the emperor’s favour.
The
Deccan wars
brought a larger number of Deccanis and Marathas into the Mughal nobility under Aurangzeb.
M. Athar Ali estimated the Hindu share in the Mughal nobility at about
one-third
under Aurangzeb.

secs.t: Peasantry categories

x: Muzarian were tenants who cultivated land held by others.
Peasants, or raiyats, were the backbone of the Mughal economy and carried the burden of land revenue.

secs.t: Position of women

x: Nur Jahan married Jahangir in 1611, became Padshah Begum, had her name inscribed on coins and farmans, and built Itimad-ud-Daula’s tomb.
Jahanara, Shah Jahan’s daughter and Padshah Begum, built the
Jama Masjid at Agra and a sarai at Chandni Chowk
Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb at Agra was built by Nur Jahan for her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, and is popularly called the “Baby Taj”.

secs.t: Urban classes

x: Merchants such as nagarseths, Marwaris, Bohras and Chettis, along with artisans, formed the middle and lower urban strata.
Bernier found no real middle class in Delhi and described a sharp contrast between the very rich and the very poor.
Firangi Mahal in Lucknow was a madrasa associated with
Muslim jurisprudence

secs.t: Slavery and domestic servants

x: Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war in 1562, although slaves and large domestic staffs continued to exist in noble households.
Pelsaert contrasted the luxury enjoyed by nobles with the misery of servants and workmen.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Travellers’ accounts are a major source for Mughal social history, but their observations should be read critically alongside Persian chronicles.
Both statements are true, and the possibility of cultural bias explains why travellers’ accounts must be compared with Persian chronicles rather than used in isolation.
J.B. Tavernier
recorded the presence of 20,000 registered prostitutes in Hyderabad under Abdullah Qutb Shah.

rows.title: Mughal architecture - Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun's tomb, Taj Mahal, Red Fort; garden and tomb traditions
sub: Group-II S1-51: Mughal art and architecture - Fatehpur Sikri, Taj Mahal, gardens and forts

secs.t: Monument → builder and chronological order (Humayun's tomb to Char Minar)

x: Exam angle: "built in Akbar's reign" sets and "not built by Shah Jahan" odd-one-out questions.
Exam angle: "not built by Shah Jahan" =
Buland Darwaza
; "built during Akbar's reign" = Salim Chishti's Tomb, Buland Darwaza, Humayun's Tomb and Jami Masjid (Fatehpur Sikri) - all four.
Humayun’s tomb was the first garden tomb in the subcontinent, introduced the double dome and used red sandstone with white marble inlay.
Char Minar was built at Hyderabad in 1591 by
Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
of the Qutb Shahi dynasty.
The order is Humayun's Tomb (1565–1572), Jami Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri (1571–1574), Tomb of Salim Chishti (1580–1581), and Char Minar (1591).
Akbar's Tomb was completed around 1613, followed by the Taj Mahal (1632–1648), Red Fort (1639–1648), and Jama Masjid of Delhi (1650–1656).
Prince Azam Shah built Bibi ka Maqbara during Aurangzeb's reign for his mother,
Dilras Banu Begum

secs.t: Taj Mahal - architect, marble source, views on style origin

x: The Taj Mahal was built by Shah Jahan at Agra as the mausoleum of Mumtaz Mahal, on the right bank of the Yamuna.
Humayun's Tomb
provided an important design ancestry for the Taj Mahal, particularly through the garden-tomb form and use of a double dome.
Unlike the usual central placement in a charbagh, the Taj Mahal's tomb stands at the river end of the garden, near the Yamuna.
Sulphur dioxide emitted by the Mathura refinery, industries and traffic contributes to yellowing and the deterioration popularly called marble cancer.

secs.t: Tomb traditions → builder (Sher Shah, Itimad-ud-Daula, Bibi ka Maqbara) - Lodi to Mughal evolution

x: Prince Azam Shah
, son of Aurangzeb, built Bibi ka Maqbara for his mother, Dilras Banu Begum, at Aurangabad.
Sayyid-Lodi tombs incorporated Hindu elements such as Hindu-style gates and facades, plaster ornament and drip-stones.
Sher Shah's tomb
at Sasaram marks the Sur transition in the evolution of Indo-Islamic tomb architecture.

secs.t: Emperor → tomb location (Babur to Aurangzeb)

x: Babur's tomb is at Bagh-e-Babur in
Kabul
, although he was first buried at Agra.
Shah Jahan is buried in the Taj Mahal at Agra beside Mumtaz Mahal.
Aurangzeb was buried in
a simple grave at Khuldabad near Aurangabad
Jahangir's tomb is located at Shahdara in Lahore.

secs.t: Fatehpur Sikri buildings → purpose and style influence

x: Buland Darwaza, meaning the “Gate of Magnificence”, commemorated Akbar's
victory in the Gujarat conquest
The
Ibadat Khana
was the House of Worship used for philosophical debates among scholars of various religions.
Jodha Bai's palace combines Hindu trabeate construction, based on beams and lintels, with Islamic arcuate construction, based on arches and domes.
Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's planned capital during 1571–1585 and reflects multiple architectural influences, including the Tudor arch introduced by Akbar.

secs.t: Architectural features - double dome, pietra dura, charbagh, synthesis, sandstone vs marble

x: Pietra dura began during Jahangir's reign, was first used on a large scale at Itimad-ud-Daula and reached its peak at the Taj Mahal.
The Persian-Indian synthesis combined
arches and domes with trabeate forms, chhatris and Hindu motifs
, as seen at Fatehpur Sikri and Akbar's tomb.
Akbar's phase is represented by red-sandstone structures such as Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, while Shah Jahan's phase is dominated by white marble, as in the Taj Mahal.

secs.t: Red Fort and Shahjahanabad - components

x: Agra Fort was begun in 1565, Allahabad Fort was built in 1583, Lahore Fort was rebuilt by Akbar and the Red Fort at Delhi was built by Shah Jahan.
The Jami Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was built by Akbar, while the Jama Masjid of Delhi and Moti Masjid of Agra Fort were built by Shah Jahan.

secs.t: Garden traditions → location (Shalimar, Nishat, Ram Bagh)

x: Nishat Bagh at Srinagar, on Dal Lake, was built by
Asaf Khan
, the brother of Nur Jahan.
The Shalimar Gardens at Lahore were built under
Shah Jahan
Humayun's Tomb is regarded as the first garden tomb, and the Taj Mahal represents the later development of the garden-tomb and charbagh tradition.

secs.t: UNESCO Mughal sites in India

x: Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal were inscribed in 1983, Fatehpur Sikri in 1986, Humayun's Tomb in 1993 and the Red Fort Complex in 2007.
The Taj Mahal was included among the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Mughal architecture is marked by red sandstone and white marble, charbagh layouts, double domes, pietra dura and calligraphic decoration.
The Bahmani Jama Masjid at Gulbarga is notable for its fully covered courtyard, whereas Mughal mosques generally followed an open-court arrangement.
Ram Bagh belongs to Babur's period, followed by Charminar in 1591, the first appearance of pietra dura under Jahangir, and the Taj Mahal's inclusion among the New Seven Wonders in 2007.

rows.title: Mughal painting, music, language and literature; Persian-Sanskrit translation movement
sub: Group-II S1-52: Mughal language, literature and painting; decline of the Mughal Empire

secs.t: Painting - Persian masters, Hamzanama, emperor-wise emphasis, painters → reign

x: Exam angle: statement sets. "Jahangir's reign = golden period" is correct.
Exam angle: statement pairs on Humayun's Persian masters and Jahangir's golden age.
Humayun is associated with the Persian masters; Akbar with illustrated manuscripts; Jahangir with naturalism; and Shah Jahan with formal court scenes and floral decoration.
Jahangir's period represented the zenith of Mughal painting, especially in portraiture, albums, flora, fauna and naturalistic representation.
Jahangir
's painters introduced the halo or nimbus behind the emperor's head, reflecting the period's refined and naturalistic style.
Ustad Mansur, a painter of Jahangir's court, was renowned for depicting
flora and fauna
Manohar, the son of Basawan, worked in the Akbar–Jahangir period and was known for portraits, while Basawan was a leading Akbar-era master.

secs.t: Book → author (Akbarnama to Futuhat-i-Alamgiri)

x: Humayun-nama was authored by
Gulbadan Begum
, the daughter of Babur and sister of Humayun.
Tabaqat-i-Akbari was written by Nizamuddin Ahmad; Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh by Badauni; Padshahnama by Abdul Hamid Lahori; and Alamgirnama by Mirza Muhammad Kazim.
Abdul Qadir Badauni
wrote the Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh, which was critical of Akbar's religious policy.
The Ain-i-Akbari, dated 1590, mentions Diwali and compares it with
Shab-e-baraat
Rekhta developed through the combination of
Persian, Hindi and regional dialects
, contributing to the rise of Urdu.

secs.t: Musicians → patron and facts; music forms → court

x: Baiju Bawra was a Dhrupad singer at
the court of Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior
Tappa was refined by
Shori Miyan
in the late eighteenth-century Awadh–Lucknow milieu.
Although Aurangzeb ended court music, Persian treatises on classical music were produced during his reign, and he played the veena.
Khayal flourished through Sadarang and Adarang, Tappa was refined by Shori Miyan, and Tansen and Baiju Bawra were masters of Dhrupad.

secs.t: Translated works → original, translator, reign; Maktab Khana

x: Badauni translated the Ramayana, Haji Ibrahim Sirhindi the Atharvaveda, Maulana Shah Muhammad Shahabadi the Rajatarangini, and Faizi Lilavati.
The Maktab Khana was created as a translation bureau to
promote cross-cultural understanding among the nobility
Nizamuddin Panipati
translated the Yoga Vasistha, known as Jog Bashisht, for Prince Salim during Akbar's reign.

secs.t: Hindi poets of the Mughal age → works and patron

x: Keshavdas was associated with the
Bundela court of Orchha
and wrote works including Ramchandrika, Kavipriya and Rasikpriya.
Kavindracharya Saraswati obtained Shah Jahan's remission of the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Prayag and wrote Kavindra-kalpalata in Hindi.
Tulsidas belonged to Akbar's age but was not a court poet of Akbar.
Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana composed Hindi dohas and translated the Baburnama into Persian.

secs.t: Dara Shikoh's works - themes

x: Sirr-i-Akbar, meaning ‘The Great Secret’, was Dara Shikoh’s Persian translation of the Upanishads.
Majma-ul-Bahrain, meaning ‘Mingling of the Two Oceans’, explores the
common ground between Sufism and Vedanta
Anquetil-Duperron
prepared a Latin version of Sirr-i-Akbar, helping take the Upanishads to Europe.
Niccolao Manucci served in Dara Shikoh's artillery and later wrote Storia do Mogor.

secs.t: Languages - Persian court language, rise of Urdu/Rekhta

x: Hindavi emerged in the multilingual environment of
camps and bazaars
and later acquired names such as Rekhta, Lashkari and Urdu.
Dakhni Urdu served as the common language of Deccan camps and bazaars, became a literary medium under the Qutb Shahis, and Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah is known for the first Urdu poetic diwan.
Urdu mixes Persian, Arabic, Turkic, local Prakrits and Braj, uses the Perso-Arabic script, and retains an indigenous grammar.

secs.t: Regional painting schools emerging (Rajput, Pahari, Deccani)

x: Rajput paintings are known for bold colours, a flat two-dimensional style, and subjects such as Hindu epics, love legends and daily life.
At Golconda,
Mir Hashim
is identified as the founder of the Deccani painting tradition; he was later invited to the Mughal court.
Mughal painting generally displayed muted naturalistic colours, perspective, shading and a cosmopolitan outlook, while Rajput painting was indigenous, vivid and decorative.

secs.t: Causes of decline - Aurangzeb's policies, jagirdari crisis, Sayyid Brothers as kingmakers

x: The jagirdari crisis involved too many mansabdars and too few revenue-yielding jagirs, a condition described as be-jagiri, which weakened the mansabdari system.
The decline was also accelerated by weak successors, Turani, Irani and Hindustani noble factions, the rise of regional powers and the Marathas, and invasions by Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The interaction of translation, painting and Hindavi-Urdu literature helped create
a composite Indo-Persian culture
Persian served as the official language, Telugu was widely used by the people, and Deccani painting and Deccani Urdu developed under Qutb Shahi patronage.

All four statements describe the stated current debate: the removed NCERT map, the Bombay High Court PIL of 20 May 2026, the Attock-to-Cuttack extent, and Rajputana’s status as a tribute zone rather than an annexed territory.

rows.title: Decline of the Mughal Empire - causes and historiography; the Later Mughals; regional successor states

secs.t: Later Mughals - chronological order, epithets and fate

x: Farrukhsiyar ruled from 1713 to 1719, was controlled by the Sayyid brothers, executed Banda Singh Bahadur in 1716, and granted the English duty-free trade in Bengal.
Jahandar Shah was called Lampat, was backed by Zulfiqar Khan and remained under the sway of his mistress Lal Kunwar.
Farrukh Siyar issued the important farman granting favourable trading privileges to the Company in 1717.
Muhammad Shah eliminated the Sayyid influence with Nizam-ul-Mulk’s help, witnessed the autonomy of major provincial rulers and faced Nadir Shah’s invasion in 1739.
Udham Bai, who controlled affairs during Ahmad Shah’s reign, was honoured with the title
Qibla-i-Alam

secs.t: Regional successor states → founder and position held; Sayyid brothers as king-makers

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah, also known as Chin Qilich Khan or Mir Qamar-ud-din Siddiqi, founded the Asaf Jahi state of
Hyderabad
Saadatullah Khan
, also rendered as Saadullah Khan, founded the Carnatic state of Arcot and named his nephew Dost Ali as successor.
Husain Ali Khan was a Sayyid brother, Murshid Quli Khan was associated with Bengal, Chin Qilich Khan was the Nizam of Hyderabad and Safdar Jung was associated with Awadh.

secs.t: Invasions → invader, year, consequence

x: After defeating Muhammad Shah at Karnal and plundering Delhi, Nadir Shah carried away
the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne
Punjab and Multan were ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali, and his repeated invasions occurred during the reign of Alamgir II.
Both statements are true, and the repeated invasions, military challenges and financial drain explain why Mughal weakness was exposed.

secs.t: Asaf Jahi founding - founder's names and titles, Shakar Kheda, rulers in sequence

x: Aurangzeb conferred the title Chin Qilich Khan, Farrukh Siyar conferred Nizam-ul-Mulk, and Muhammad Shah conferred Asaf Jah in 1725.
The order is Asaf Jah I (1724), Nasir Jung (1748), Muzaffar Jung (1750), Salabat Jung (1751), and Nizam Ali Khan (1762).
Sikandar Jah ruled from 1803–1829, Nasir-ud-Daula from 1829–1857, Afzal-ud-Daula from 1857–1869, and Mir Mahbub Ali Khan from 1869–1911.

secs.t: Historiography of decline → historian and book

x: Irfan Habib
explained the decline through an agrarian crisis in The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963), arguing that over-exploitation of peasants provoked revolts.
Satish Chandra wrote
Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court, 1707–1740
and associated decline with the jagirdari crisis.
Athar Ali argued that the enlarged nobility, including Deccanis and Marathas, intensified the shortage of jagirs.

secs.t: Causes of decline

x: Independent nobles weakened, rather than strengthened, central authority.
Under Aurangzeb the empire reached from Kashmir to Jinji and from the Hindukush to Chittagong.
Religious policies, prolonged warfare, factional noble politics, fiscal crisis and agrarian unrest combined to weaken the empire.
The Maratha rise weakened Mughal authority; it did not restore it.

secs.t: Treaties and titles granted by later Mughals

x: The 1719 grant recognised Shahu's claim to chauth and sardeshmukhi from the six Deccan subas through his agent Balaji Vishwanath.
From 1772 Warren Hastings stopped the annual grant and sold Kora and Allahabad to the Nawab of Awadh.
Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in return for an annual payment of
Rs 26 lakh

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Golconda was incorporated as the 21st Mughal suba in 1687, Hyderabad emerged from the Mughal Deccan, and the Nizam accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
Nadir Shah carried away
the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne
during his raid of 1739.
Ahmad Shah Abdali
's raids, which began from 1748, culminated in the Battle of Panipat in 1761.

rows.title: Rise of the Marathas - Shivaji's career, Ashtapradhan, revenue system, chauth and sardeshmukhi
sub: Group-II S1-57: Shivaji - career, conquests and the Ashtapradhan administration
Group-II S1-58: Shivaji's revenue system, chauth and sardeshmukhi; rise of the Maratha Empire

secs.t: Ashtapradhan → portfolio of each minister, plus Persian titles

x: Exam angle: title-to-portfolio matching. Under the later Peshwas the post became
hereditary and supreme
Amatya, also known as Majumdar, was responsible for the treasury, accounts audit and revenue.
The Peshwa was also called
Mukhya Pradhan
and functioned as the Prime Minister with responsibility for general administration.
The
Panditrao
, also known as Danadhyaksha, handled religious affairs and charitable grants.
The Ashtapradhan model was influenced by the administrative arrangements of the
Deccan Sultanates

secs.t: Shivaji's career - birthplace fort to Agra escape

x: The coronation at Raigad occurred in 1674, the second raid on Surat occurred in 1670, the treaty with Abul Hasan Tana Shah was made in 1677 and Shivaji died in 1680.
In 1677 Shivaji made a treaty with
Abul Hasan Tana Shah of Golconda
, through Akkanna and Madanna, to obtain assistance in his southern campaign.

secs.t: Contemporaries - spiritual guides and generals opposed

x: Samarth Ramdas is traditionally regarded as Shivaji's guru and is identified as the author of
Dasbodh
Samarth Ramdas is traditionally named as Shivaji's guru, but the attribution is disputed by historians.
Tukaram was a
contemporary
of Shivaji and, along with Samarth Ramdas, was associated with the spiritual background of the Maratha movement.

secs.t: Chauth and sardeshmukhi - rate and nature

x: Exam angle: "Maratha revenue claim for protection" =
Chauth
Chauth was levied on
territories outside direct Maratha rule
, including Mughal and Deccan Sultanate territories.
Together, the levies financed military expansion and extended political hegemony without requiring the Marathas to administer every territory directly.
The Nizam was forced to pay chauth
again
after the 1795 war, indicating an earlier concession or payment arrangement.

secs.t: Coronation - place, year, title

x: Shivaji was crowned at Raigad on
6 June 1674
Gaga Bhatt, a learned Brahmin from Banaras or Varanasi, officiated at the coronation with Vedic rites.
Shivaji adopted the title “
Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati
” at his coronation.
Shivaji was also styled
Haindava Dharmoddharak
Shivaji began the
Rajabhisheka Shaka
after his coronation to assert sovereign status.

secs.t: Successors - administrative steps of each

x: Exam angle: order is
Sambhaji - Rajaram - Shivaji II - Shahu
; "Maratha woman who fought the Mughals from 1700" = Tarabai.
Tarabai governed as regent, raided Mughal territory, and her line was later settled at Kolhapur under the Treaty of Warna.
These events mark the transition from Shivaji's leadership to the resistance led by Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai.
Shahu, Sambhaji's son, was released by Bahadur Shah I and represented the Satara line, while Tarabai led the Kolhapur line.

secs.t: Revenue and administrative terms

x: Shivaji paid officials in cash instead of granting jagirs, thereby maintaining direct loyalty to the state.
Saranjam, or service land grants, came back under
Shahu and the Peshwas
Shivaji's system included remission during famine, abolition of illegal cesses and protection against seizure of peasant property.
Kathi was a measuring rod, Jirayat denoted dry land and Bagayat denoted irrigated land.

secs.t: Military organisation - forts, navy, hill troops

x: Raigad, Pratapgad, Torna and Sinhagad
are hill forts, or Giri Durg.
Bargirs were state-equipped cavalrymen, whereas Shiledars supplied their own horses; both were cavalry categories.
The Havaldar commanded the garrison, the Sabnis maintained records and the Sarnobat was the military officer.
Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg served as naval bases guarding the
Konkan coast
Shivaji's standing army was paid in cash rather than jagirs so that loyalty remained directly attached to the state.

secs.t: Conflicts - opponent and the Treaty of Purandar

x: Exam angle: the 2011 APPSC option "1665 - Raja Jai Singh" is the right pairing.
Shivaji killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan with a wagh nakh at the foot of Pratapgad in 1659.
Torna was captured in 1646, Afzal Khan was killed in 1659, Shaista Khan was attacked in 1663 and the Treaty of Purandar was concluded in 1665.

secs.t: Early career - Shivneri, Jijabai, Dadaji Kondadev, Torna, Raigad

x: Shivaji began capturing hill forts from declining Bijapur by seizing
Torna in 1646
at the age of 16.
Shivaji took Raigad from the Mores of Javli in 1656, and it later served as his
capital and coronation site
Ganimi Kava denotes guerrilla warfare, in which Shivaji effectively used the rugged Sahyadri terrain.

secs.t: Karnataka campaign - Jinji, Vellore, alliance with Golconda

x: Akkanna was associated with the position of Sar Lashkar, and Niraj Pant and Prahlad Pant were Shivaji’s envoys.
Shivaji visited Hyderabad on 7 March 1677 and made a treaty with
Abul Hasan Tana Shah
of Golconda.
After its capture, Jinji became Rajaram’s base for resistance against Aurangzeb.
Shivaji took Gingee, Vellore and Ballari and refused to share the spoils.

secs.t: Causes of the Maratha rise

x: The first three statements are correct causes.
Tukaram and Ramdas
are identified with the spiritual and regional unity that aided the Maratha rise.
The prolonged Deccan campaign drained the treasury, while the succession war after 1707 created a political vacuum.

secs.t: Coinage and records - coins, Modi script

x: Shivaji issued the gold Hon and the copper Shivrai.
Marathi and Sanskrit were promoted in official usage over Persian, and the cursive Modi script was used for Marathi administrative records.

secs.t: Revenue officials and units

x: A Prant was administered by a Subedar or Sarsubedar; Pargana and Tarf were associated with Deshmukh and Deshpande; Mauza had the Patil and Kulkarni.
Mauza
was the village-level unit; the Patil was its head and the Kulkarni was its accountant.
Shivaji divided the kingdom into prants and curtailed the hereditary rights of Deshmukhs and Deshpandes.

secs.t: Expansion under Balaji Vishwanath - Mughal grants

x: Balaji Vishwanath backed Shahu during the civil war and brought Maratha chiefs together in his support.
In 1719, Mughal emperor
Farrukhsiyar
granted recognition of Shahu, Swarajya lands, and the rights to chauth and sardeshmukhi in the six Deccan subas.
The period beginning in 1713 saw the gradual transfer of effective power from the Chhatrapati at Satara to the
Peshwa

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Maratha Deccan war, especially Tarabai’s raids, seriously weakened and broke Mughal finances.
Jyotirao Phule initiated the first public celebration in 1870, and
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
later popularised it.
The stated peak extent of the Maratha Empire ran from Attock to Cuttack and from the Gulf of Khambhat to beyond the Kaveri.
After the 1795 war, the Nizam paid chauth to the Marathas; this pressure contributed to his move towards the British Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.

rows.title: Peshwas and the Maratha confederacy; Third Battle of Panipat (1761); three Anglo-Maratha wars
sub: Group-II S1-59: Peshwas, the Maratha confederacy and the Third Battle of Panipat

secs.t: Peshwas → chronological order, key contribution, conquests and treaties

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2024 order - Balaji Vishwanath, Balaji Baji Rao, Narayan Rao, Raghunath Rao; APPSC 2025 - Gujarat under
Balaji Baji Rao
Balaji Vishwanath obtained the 1719 Mughal grant recognising Shahu’s swarajya and granting the Marathas the right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan.
Balaji Baji Rao, or Nana Saheb, was Peshwa from 1740 to 1761, during which Maratha power reached its zenith and Maratha forces reached Lahore and Peshawar.
Madhav Rao I revived Maratha power after Panipat and defeated the Nizam, Mysore under Haidar Ali, Rohillas, Rajputs and Jats.

secs.t: Third Battle of Panipat (1761)

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 - "Third Battle of Panipat was fought between Ahmad Shah Abdali and the Marathas".
Vishwas Rao was Balaji Baji Rao’s son, Sadashiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao were killed, and Ibrahim Khan Gardi led the artillery.
Balaji Baji Rao
, popularly known as Nana Saheb, was the Peshwa when the Third Battle of Panipat was fought.
The battle halted Maratha imperial ambitions in the north and caused heavy losses, but Maratha power was not destroyed and recovered within about a decade.

secs.t: Maratha confederacy → houses → seat of power

x: Raghuji Bhonsle, Pilaji Gaekwad, Malhar Rao Holkar and Ranoji Scindia are associated with the respective houses.
Baji Rao I built the confederacy to maintain unity among Maratha factions and to accommodate older chiefs led by Senapati Dabhade.
Scindia recaptured Delhi in 1771, restored Shah Alam II under Maratha protection and reorganised his army on European lines.

secs.t: Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18)

x: The Third Anglo-Maratha War was fought during the tenure of
Lord Hastings
, also known as the Marquess of Hastings.
The Peshwaship was abolished, Baji Rao II was pensioned at Bithur and a reduced Satara state was created for Shivaji’s descendant.
After his deposition, Baji Rao II was pensioned and sent to
Bithur near Kanpur

secs.t: First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) - Raghunath Rao, Surat, Salbai

x: The Barabhai, a group of twelve chiefs led by Nana Phadnavis, supported
the infant Madhav Rao II
against Raghunath Rao.
Raghunath Rao offered Salsette, Bassein and revenue from Surat and Bharuch to obtain British support in the succession dispute.
The correct sequence is Treaty of Surat (1775), Treaty of Purandar (1776), Convention of Wadgaon (1779) and Treaty of Salbai (1782).

secs.t: Nana Phadnavis - role in the confederacy

x: Nana Phadnavis led the twelve-member Barabhai council, governed for the infant Madhav Rao II, opposed Raghunath Rao and helped preserve Maratha unity during the First Anglo-Maratha War.
Barabhai literally referred to the group of
twelve chiefs
who supported the infant Madhav Rao II against Raghunath Rao.
Madhav Rao I
defeated the Nizam as well as Haider Ali, the Rohillas, the Rajputs and the Jats.

secs.t: Battles and treaties with the Nizam

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2025 - Mungi-Shevgaon was between the
Marathas and the Nizam
At Palkhed in 1728, Baji Rao I defeated the Nizam and secured recognition of Maratha chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan.
The Battle of Udgir in 1760 was fought during the time of
Balaji Baji Rao
, and the Nizam was defeated.

secs.t: Rise of the Peshwa as virtual ruler

x: From Balaji Vishwanath’s appointment in 1713, Shahu’s dependence on him and the hereditary character of the office strengthened the Peshwa.
The Sangola agreement of 1750 followed Shahu’s death in 1749 and left the Chhatrapati nominal, thereby consolidating the Peshwa’s position.
The sequence begins with Balaji Vishwanath’s appointment in 1713, followed by the transfer of effective power, the Sangola settlement of 1750 and the mature confederate form of the monarchy.

secs.t: Baji Rao I - ideology, northern expansion, Nizam

x: The phrase “strike the trunk, the branches will fall” is associated with
Baji Rao I
’s strategic outlook.
Baji Rao I conquered Malwa and Bundelkhand and raided Delhi in 1737.
The battles of Palkhed and Bhopal preceded the Delhi raid of 1737, while Chimaji Appa’s capture of Salsette and Bassein occurred in 1739.

secs.t: Maratha administration - saranjam, Peshwa daftar

x: Saranjam consisted of land assignments made to chiefs for military service and formed the base of the Maratha confederacy.
Saranjam was a Maratha land-assignment system connected with military service; it was not a Portuguese coastal institution.
The Peshwa Daftar at Pune contains Peshwa-era state records that were largely maintained in Modi script.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Nizam’s dissatisfaction, including his blame directed at Sir John Shore’s neutrality, pushed him towards the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
Salbai maintained the status quo in 1782, Bassein placed the Peshwa in a position of subsidiary subordination in 1802, and 1818 marked the extinction of the Peshwaship.
The Marathas repeatedly defeated the Nizam at
Palkhed, Udgir and Kharda
, and extracted chauth from the Nizam’s Deccan territories.

rows.title: Bhakti Movement - origins, Alvars and Nayanars, Nirguna and Saguna streams, social base
sub: Group-II S1-53: Bhakti Movement - origin, Nirguna and Saguna streams, principal saints

secs.t: Nirguna and Saguna streams → saints of each tradition

x: Nirguna worship is directed towards a formless and attributeless God, while Saguna worship accepts God with form, attributes, avatars and personal deities.
Kabir, Guru Nanak, Dadu Dayal and Ravidas
are associated with the Nirguna stream, which worships a formless God.
Both Nirguna and Saguna traditions drew on the Upanishadic doctrine of Advaita, and the Bhakti movement was essentially monotheistic.
Tulsidas was a Rama-oriented Saguna saint; Surdas and Chaitanya were Krishna-oriented Saguna saints; Guru Nanak belonged to the Nirguna tradition.

secs.t: Sacred text → tradition

x: The Tevaram contains the hymns of
Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar
and forms the first seven books of the Tirumurai.
The Tirumurai is the twelve-book Shaiva canon of the Nayanars, compiled by Nambi Andar Nambi and known as the Fifth Veda.
Periya Puranam was written by Sekkizhar under Kulottunga II, narrates the lives of the 63 Nayanars and forms the twelfth Tirumurai.

secs.t: Origins - Gita and Bhagavata roots, Tamil start, revival

x: The movement reacted against ritualism, priestly dominance and caste, while the paths of knowledge and action were considered difficult for ordinary people.
Older historians viewed Bhakti as a reaction to Islam, whereas modern scholars emphasise its indigenous Alvar–Nayanar roots and regard Islam as influencing mainly its later egalitarian character.
Shankaracharya was born in 788, Guru Nanak in 1469, Chaitanya in 1485, while Ramananda belongs between the earlier philosopher and the later fifteenth-century saints in the sequence given.

secs.t: Language - vernaculars by region

x: Bhakti saints commonly preached in regional languages rather than Sanskrit, contributing to the enrichment of Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati and other literatures.
Basavanna and Akkamahadevi composed vachanas in Karnataka; Tukaram composed abhangas in Maharashtra; Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi; and Chaitanya was associated with kirtans in Bengal.
Namdev
was identified as the most influential saint of the Maharashtra tradition; Eknath, Tukaram and Narhari were also associated with it.

secs.t: Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis

x: The Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis made devotional religion popular in
Northern India
Their practices included hatha yoga, meditation and renunciation.
These groups criticised the caste system, ritualism and orthodox religion.
The Panchacharyas were Revana (Renuka), Marula, Ekorama, Panditaradhya and Vishwaradhya.
Udbhata was a
Sanskrit rhetorician
and was not included among the Siddhacharyas.

secs.t: Social base - castes, women, attitude to caste and ritual

x: Ramananda
is described as the first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright and he admitted disciples from all castes.
Dhanna
was a male disciple of Ramananda and a Jat cultivator.
The movement rejected
idol worship, ritual, pilgrimage, fasting and caste
, while emphasising devotion and the guru.
Palnati Brahmanayudu treated the Mala devotee
Kannama Dasu
as his son.

secs.t: Origin - Alvars and Nayanars, Bhagavata tradition, Nathpanthis and Siddhas

x: The roots of Bhakti are traced to the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Bhagavata Purana.
Gyana and Karma margas were considered too hard for ordinary people, making the path of devotion more accessible.
The Nathpanthis and Siddhas of the Gorakhnath tradition rejected caste and ritual, used vernacular languages and influenced Kabir's nirguna idiom.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The movement brought Hindus and Muslims closer and weakened caste bondage, but it did not fully achieve lasting Hindu-Muslim unity or completely abolish caste.

All three statements are correct within the stated first/last distinctions: Andal was the only female Alvar, Ramanuja the first true exponent, and Ramananda the first to denounce caste outright in the north.
Begampura, envisioned by Guru Ravidas, literally represents the ideal ‘
city without sorrow

rows.title: Bhakti saints and their teachings - Ramanuja, Madhva, Nimbarka, Vallabha, Ramananda

secs.t: Acharya → philosophy school and teaching emphasis

x: Exam angle: "which statement is NOT correct" - e.g. Madhva propounded Nirguna bhakti is wrong; Shankara = Advaita.
Ramanuja’s Vishishtadvaita presented dependent souls and universe as related to the Supreme and emphasised devotion over alternative means of salvation.
Madhvacharya’s Dvaita philosophy maintains that God, identified with Vishnu, and individual souls are eternally distinct.

secs.t: Sect founded → acharya

x: Pushtimarga was associated with Vallabhacharya, Ramanandi with Ramananda, Gaudiya Vaishnavism with Chaitanya and Sri Vaishnava with Ramanuja.
Pushtimarga is the Vallabha Sampradaya, means the path of grace and was represented through 84 centres established by Vallabhacharya.
Sri Vaishnavism later split into Vadakalai, associated with the Vedic tradition of Vedanta Desika, and Tengalai.

secs.t: Acharyas in chronological order and contemporaries

x: The sequence is Shankara (788–820), Ramanuja (1017–1137), Madhva in the thirteenth century and Vallabhacharya (1479–1531).
Vallabhacharya visited the court of
Krishnadevaraya
, refuted Shaiva propositions and defeated the Dvaita scholar Vyasaraya, also known as Vyasa Tirtha.
Vyasa Tirtha was a Dvaita scholar, royal guru to Saluva Narasimha and Krishnadevaraya, and author of Nyayamrita.

secs.t: Acharya → birthplace and main centre

x: Ramanuja was born at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu.
Nimbarka is traditionally described as a Telugu Brahmin and is associated with Brindavan.
Ramanuja’s main centre was the Srirangam monastery; Madhva’s was the Udupi Krishna Matha; Nimbarka’s was Brindavan; and Ramananda’s was Varanasi.

secs.t: Ramananda - language, caste dictum, disciples

x: Kabir was a weaver of Muslim background, Raidas a shoemaker or leather worker, Sena a barber and Dhanna a Jat cultivator.
Padmavati was a woman disciple, Pipa was a Rajput ruler and Kabir came from a weaver background associated with Muslims.
Since Ramanuja died in 1137 and Ramananda belonged to a much later period, the description is understood as referring to Ramananda’s following of Ramanuja’s school, not direct contemporaneity.

secs.t: Book → author

x: Sri Bhashya, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, was written by Ramanuja.
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Tattva Teeka and Nyaya Siddhanjanam are works of
Vedanta Desika

secs.t: Deity worshipped by each school

x: Vallabha worshipped child Krishna and Radha-Krishna; Ramananda worshipped Rama; Chaitanya worshipped Krishna; and Nimbarka worshipped Radha-Krishna.
Madhva’s tradition centred on Vishnu, especially Krishna at Udupi; Ramanuja’s on Narayana with Lakshmi; and Chaitanya’s on Krishna.

secs.t: Ramanuja's connection to Andhra/Tirumala

x: Sri Vaishnavism was the most widely spread sect of the Vijayanagara era, with centres at Tirupati, Kanchi, Mangalagiri and Pushpagiri.
Brahmanayudu's Veera Vaishnava movement in Palnadu was inspired by Sri Vaishnavism and aimed at creating
a casteless society
Tradition credits Ramanuja with ordering the worship of the Tirumala temple and installing Govindaraja at Tirupati.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ramanuja's 11th–12th-century influence preceded the Vijayanagara period; Vedanta Desika's Andhra activity belongs to the 14th century, while the Hyderabad statue is a modern development.
The acharyas provided a philosophical basis for Bhakti against Advaita and helped open temple worship to lower groups; their teachings were not confined exclusively to elites.

rows.title: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tukaram, Namdeva, Surdas, Tulsidas

secs.t: Saint → region of activity and royal/family links

x: Mirabai was associated with
Rajasthan
and is described as a Rajput princess of Merta.
Vallabhacharya was associated with Gujarat, Tulsidas with Uttar Pradesh, Chaitanya with Bengal and Tukaram with Maharashtra.
Tulsidas was associated with Akbar’s time; Chaitanya with Prataparudra Gajapati; Tukaram with Shivaji; and Mirabai with the Rajput and Mewar royal houses.
Chaitanya visited Puri during the reign of
Prataparudra Gajapati

secs.t: Kabir - guru, stream, dohas, caste and ritual

x: Tradition holds that Kabir was born to a Brahmin widow and was raised by the Muslim weaver Niru and his wife Nima.
Kabir held that there is one God, referred to by different names including Ram, Rahim, Allah, Khuda, Hari and Govinda.
Kabir condemned rituals and idol worship in both communities, opposed caste, worked for Hindu-Muslim unity and is regarded as the greatest saint of the Bhakti cult.

secs.t: Maharashtra saints - Varkari sect, disciples, Shivaji

x: Ramdas stressed
strength, discipline and devotion to Rama
, and these ideas aided the Maratha political awakening.
The Varkari sect worships Vitthala, also called Vithoba, at Pandharpur and undertakes an annual pilgrimage there.
Tukaram composed abhangas addressed to Vithoba or
Vitthala
, the central deity of the Varkari tradition.
Janabai
was Namdev’s disciple, lived in his home as a servant and composed more than 300 poems.

secs.t: Literary work → saint

x: Ramcharitmanas is by Tulsidas, Sursagar by Surdas, Bijak by Kabir and Gita Govinda by Jayadeva.
Jnaneshwari
, also known as the Marathi Gita, is associated with Jnaneshwar.
Sahitya Lahari is not attributed to Tulsidas in the stated literary associations.
Vinaya Patrika, Kavitavali and Gitavali are associated with Tulsidas, while Sursagar is associated with Surdas.

secs.t: Saint → guru and disciple lineage

x: Ramananda was associated with Kabir, Raidas with Mirabai, Vallabhacharya with Surdas and Guru Nanak with Mardana.
Kabir, Raidas and Pipa are included in the lineage associated with Ramananda.
Amir Khusrau was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.

secs.t: Contemporary ruler and chronological order

x: The correct sequence is Ramananda, Kabir, Guru Nanak, Chaitanya and Tulsidas.
Tulsidas lived from 1532 to 1623.
Vallabhacharya, Chaitanya, Mirabai and Tukaram belong successively to the late fifteenth–early sixteenth, early sixteenth, sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
Chaitanya was associated with Prataparudra Gajapati of Odisha, not Akbar.
Tulsidas and Surdas are associated with the period of
Akbar

secs.t: Chaitanya - sankirtan, sect, Bengal and Puri

x: Chaitanya founded or is chiefly associated with
Gaudiya Vaishnavism
and preached passionate devotion to Krishna.
Sankirtan means
collective devotional singing
Chaitanya spread Bhakti in
Bengal and Odisha
and visited Puri during the reign of Prataparudra Deva.
Chaitanya
, born in Bengal in 1485, preached passionate devotion to Krishna.

secs.t: Saint → language used

x: Jnaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram used Marathi; Namdev also composed in Hindi.
Mirabai’s poetry is associated with Rajasthani, with elements of Braj.
Tulsidas is associated with Awadhi, Surdas with Braj Bhasha and Guru Nanak with Punjabi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Vemana and Potuluri Veerabrahmam
are identified as Andhra parallels to Kabir in their attack on caste.
These saints enriched several regional literatures and contributed to the early stirrings of both Maratha and Sikh awakening.
Kabir, Guru Nanak and Guru Ravidas are associated with the Nirguna tradition, which emphasises devotion to the formless divine.

rows.title: Bhakti in Andhra - Annamacharya, Bammera Potana, Vemana, the Tallapaka poets
sub: Group-II S1-54: Bhakti Movement in the South and in Andhra; its social impact
Group-II M1-A-49: Telugu literature - Srinatha, Potana, Annamacharya and the Bhakti stream

secs.t: Vemana - collector/translator, verse form, social themes

x: Exam angle: Vemana is paired with Potuluri Veerabrahmam (Kaalagnanam) as Andhra's anti-caste voices.
Vemana criticised superstition, empty ritual, idol worship and hypocrisy; he advocated humanism, inner wisdom and equality.
C.
P. Brown
collected Vemana's verses from manuscripts, edited them and published an English translation titled Verses of Vemana.
Vemana mainly used the Ataveladi metre, and his verses commonly conclude with the refrain “Vishwadabhirama Vinura Vema.”.

secs.t: Telugu women poets → literary work

x: Molla wrote
Molla Ramayanam
in simple and elegant Telugu and is noted as the first Telugu woman poet to translate the Ramayana.
Oduva Tirumalamba
wrote Varadambika Parinayam, which describes the marriage of Achyuta Deva Raya and Varadambika.
Tarigonda Vengamamba wrote Venkatachala Mahatyamu and was an eighteenth-century poet-devotee of Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala.

secs.t: Tallapaka poets → family members and works

x: Annamacharya
is identified as the founder of the Tallapaka line of poets.
China Tirumalacharya, the eldest son of Peda Tirumalacharya, was given the title
Ashtabhasha Kavi Chakravarti
China Tirumalacharya wrote
Ashtabhasha Dandakam
and Sankirtana Lakshanamu.
Chinnanna wrote
Annamacharya Charitra
, a biography of Annamacharya in the Dvipada form, along with Paramayogi Vilasam, Ashtamahishi Kalyanam and Usha Kalyanam.

secs.t: Annamacharya - sankirtanas, deity, copper plates, title, form, rulers

x: The CDI dates Annamacharya to
, while CDX gives the alternative dates 1424–1508.
About 12,000 surviving songs of Annamacharya were preserved on copper plates kept at
Tirumala
Veturi Prabhakara Sastry
excavated and edited Annamacharya's copper-plate songs and stated that Annamacharya created the science of sankirtana.
Arudra
praised Annamacharya by describing him as “Incarnated Telugu.”.

secs.t: Bammera Potana → works and attitude to royal patronage

x: Tradition states that Potana refused to dedicate the Andhra Maha Bhagavatam to
Sarvajna Singa Bhupala
and instead dedicated it to Lord Rama.
Veerabhadra Vijayam
is identified as another work of Bammera Potana.
Potana was known by the titles
Sahaja Panditudu and Nigarva Chudamani
Potana wrote his first work, Veerabhadra Vijayam, for his guru
Ivaturi Somanaradhyudu

secs.t: Other Andhra bhakti figures - Kshetrayya, Ramadasu, Tyagaraja

x: Kshetrayya composed Shringara padams dedicated to
Muvva Gopala
, a form of Krishna.
Kshetrayya composed over a thousand Movva Gopala padams and is associated with Abdullah Qutb Shah’s court.
Ramadasu, or Kancharla Gopanna, served under Tana Shah, built the Bhadrachalam temple and was imprisoned for it.
The Carnatic Trinity consists of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami
Dikshitar and Syama Sastri
Pedda Tirumalacharya
, one of the Tallapaka poets, wrote Venkateshwara Satakam.

secs.t: Kannada-Telugu Virashaiva links - Palkuriki Somanatha

x: Somanatha championed Desi kavita, using
simple native metres such as Dwipada, Ragada, Manjari and Kanda
against the Sanskritised Marga style.
Aradhya Saivism was the moderate Andhra Shaiva tradition associated with Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya; it retained Vedic learning and varna while preaching devotion to Shiva.
Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya wrote Sivatattvasaram, consisting of about 400 kanda poems, and is regarded as the originator of the Sataka form.

secs.t: Temple → saint

x: Tirumala is associated with Annamacharya and the Tallapaka family.
Tarigonda Vengamamba is included among the saints associated with
Tirumala
and the Venkateswara tradition.
Narahari Tirtha is associated with Srikurmam and spread the
Dvaita
tradition.

secs.t: Acharyas → philosophy preached (Shankaracharya, Ramanuja, Madhvacharya, Nimbarka, Basavanna)

x: Shankaracharya is associated with Kaladi and is generally dated to
Basavanna founded the Virashaiva movement, and its theology was termed Shakti Vishishtadvaita, according to which the soul and Shiva are fundamentally identical.
Shankaracharya was associated with Advaita; Ramanuja was the first true exponent of Vishishtadvaita and worshipped Narayana and Lakshmi; Ramananda brought the movement to the north.

secs.t: Alvars and Nayanars - sect, number, women saints, names, canons

x: Parantaka I
installed statues of the Nayanar saints Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in temples.
Tevaram is the earliest and most sacred part of the
Tirumurai
, the Tamil Shaiva canon.
The Alvars and Nayanars used Tamil devotional hymns, while Tirumurai became the major Shaiva canonical collection.
Rajaraja I
consecrated bronzes of all 63 Nayanars at Chidambaram.

secs.t: Virashaiva/Lingayat movement - founder, Anubhava Mantapa, spread into Andhra

x: Anubhava Mantapa functioned as an early
religious parliament
where ideas were discussed by the Sharanas.

Basavanna first led the Sharana movement; the tradition entered Andhra through Mallikarjuna Panditulu, was propagated by Palkuriki Somanatha, and later had an Andhra parallel in Brahmanayudu’s Veeravaishnavism.
Brahmanayudu’s movement in Palnadu was known as
Veeravaishnavism
, or “heroic Vaishnavism,” and was inspired by the Veerashaiva example.

secs.t: Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna) - temple and kirtanas

x: Bhakta Ramadasu was
Kancherla Gopanna
, a prominent devotee and composer associated with Bhadrachalam.
Ramadasu was born at Nelakondapalli in 1620, studied under Raghunatha Bhattacharya, was related to Akkanna and Madanna, and used revenue for the Bhadrachalam temple.
Bhakta Ramadasu was imprisoned for
12 years
in Golconda Fort by Abul Hasan Tana Shah.

secs.t: Veerabrahmendra Swamy - work and social message

x: Potuluri Veerabrahmam’s prophecies are contained in
Kalagnanam
Veerabrahmendra Swamy strongly condemned caste differences and accepted disciples from different castes and faiths, including Siddaiah, a Muslim.

secs.t: Social impact - caste critique, use of vernaculars, women saints (Atukuri Molla, Akka Mahadevi)

x: Akka Mahadevi belonged to the 12th-century Karnataka Sharana or Vachana tradition.
Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam
became important vernacular vehicles that carried Bhakti ideas to common people instead of relying exclusively on Sanskrit.
The
satakam and dwipada
forms helped communicate Bhakti ideas to common people in Telugu-speaking regions.
These traditions challenged caste and Brahmanical dominance rather than uniformly upholding it.

secs.t: Book → author (Srinatha's works and look-alikes)

x: Exam angle: "not written by Srinatha" lists; know both the attribution in your notes and the key APPSC used.
Sivaratri Mahatmyam narrates the story of the Brahmin Sukumara and was dedicated to Mummadi Santayya of the Bhikshavritti matha.
Veerabhadra Vijayam is regarded by the cited accounts as Potana's first work, written at the request of his guru Ivaturi Somanaradhya, though an older APPSC key attributed it to Srinatha.

secs.t: Palnadu socio-economic life in literature → poet + work

x: Palnati Veera Charitra is a heroic dvipada narrative of the Palnadu war, dated to 1182.
The text records houses decorated with Rama and Krishna avatars and refers to 1,500 painters' houses at Orugallu, making it a source for social life.
After Rajahmundry fell in 1448, Srinatha lived in poverty in Palnadu.

secs.t: Srinatha - life, patrons, courts, titles, paper

x: After Kondaveedu fell in 1424, Srinatha went to Rajahmundry under Veerabhadra Reddy through Bendapudi Anantamatya.
At Vijayanagara, under Devaraya II, Srinatha defeated Gauda Dindima Bhatta and received Kanakabhishekam, Ganda Penderam and the title Kavi Sarvabhauma.
The sequence is Kondaveedu, Rajahmundry, Vijayanagara and finally poverty in Palnadu after Rajahmundry fell.
Srinatha is regarded as a pioneer of the Prabandha style, and his period is called the Kavya Yuga.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Telugu Bhakti poets carried devotional expression through
padams, keertanas, satakas and dvipada compositions
, helping establish the Telugu base of the Carnatic music repertoire.
Pro-Basava groups protested against the
manipulation of Sharana Vachanas and claims that Basava endorsed Brahmanical traditions
C. P. Brown printed
Srinatha's Bhimeswara Puranam
, Kasi Khandam and Palnati Veera Charitra, in addition to the Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu and Tallapaka works.

rows.title: Sufism - doctrines, khanqah, sama; silsilas - Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri, Naqshbandi
sub: Group-II S1-55: Sufi Movement - doctrines, silsilas and major saints

secs.t: Silsila → saints belonging to it

x: Exam angle: "which saint belongs to the Chishti order" (Gesudaraz - yes; Bahauddin Zakariya = Suhrawardi; Sirhindi and Baqi Billah = Naqshbandi).
Moinuddin Chishti was associated with Ajmer, Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki and Nizamuddin Auliya with Delhi, and Baba Farid with Pakpattan.
Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi, Burhanuddin Gharib, Gesudaraz and the Chishti Hamiduddin of Nagaur are all associated with the Chishti order.
Miyan Mir and Dara Shikoh belonged to the Qadiri order, while Shah Abdul Aziz and Shah Waliullah belonged to the Naqshbandi order.
The Chishti Hamiduddin of Nagaur was a disciple of Moinuddin Chishti, whereas Qazi Hamiduddin Nagori was a Suhrawardi.
Muhammad Ghaus of Gwalior belonged to the
Shattari
order and is identified as Tansen's guide.
Bahauddin Zakariya introduced the
Suhrawardi
order in India, and its major khanqah was at Multan in the region of Punjab and Sindh.

secs.t: Silsila → founder in India, region and centre

x: The Chishti order developed around Ajmer and Delhi, later reached Deccan centres such as Gulbarga and Bijapur, and gained popularity by adapting to local traditions and vernacular languages.
Abdul Qadir Jilani founded the Qadiri order; it reached India in the fourteenth century in the stated account, and Miyan Mir and Dara Shikoh were Qadiri figures.

secs.t: Attitude to state patronage, sama and orthodoxy

x: Bahauddin Zakariya received the title
Shaikh-ul-Islam
after backing Iltutmish against Qabacha.
The Naqshbandis were regarded as the most orthodox, adhered strictly to the Shariat and condemned innovations or bid'at.
Ahmad Sirhindi criticised Akbar’s Sulh-i-Kul and was imprisoned during the reign of
Jahangir
Abul Hasan Tana Shah was a disciple of the Chishti saint
Shah Raju Qattal

secs.t: TERMS - khanqah, sama, pir, murid, etc.

x: A khanqah was a Sufi hospice for the residence and training of disciples, and it also provided food and shelter to the poor.
Ba-shara Sufis follow the Shariat, whereas Be-shara Sufis remain outside it; qalandars are given as an example of the latter.
The maqamat proceed from Tauba through Wara, Zuhd, Faqr, Sabr, Shukr, Khauf, Raja and Tawakkul to Riza.
Sufis accepted the Quran and the Prophet while also absorbing ideas associated with Vedanta, Yoga and Neo-Platonism.
The pir or murshid is the spiritual master, the murid is the disciple, tariqa is the spiritual path or order, and zikr is a practice of remembrance of God.

secs.t: Sufi practices - meditation, breath control, yogic borrowings

x: Zikr, meditation, fasting, asceticism, sama and solitude or chilla were Sufi practices.
Amritakund was translated into Arabic and Persian in the
13th century
, after which breath control became important in almost every Sufi order except the Naqshbandis.
Breath control entered almost every Sufi order except the Naqshbandis, and interaction with Nath yogis contributed to the adoption of yogic meditation.

secs.t: Doctrines - Wahdat-ul-Wujud vs Wahdat-ush-Shuhud

x: Wahdat-ush-Shuhud, or Unity of Appearance/Witness, was associated with
Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi
of the Naqshbandi order.
Wahdat-ush-Shuhud means Unity of Appearance or Witness: creation reflects God but is not identical with the Creator.
Wahdat-ul-Wujud was associated with Ibn Arabi and followed by Qadiris and Chishtis, while Sirhindi represented the Naqshbandi-associated Wahdat-ush-Shuhud.

secs.t: Sufi texts → author

x: ‘Siyar-ul-Auliya’ was written by Mir Khwurd Kirmani and ‘Akhbar-ul-Akhyar’ by Abdul Haqq Muhaddis Dehlavi. ‘Fawaid-ul-Fuad’ was associated with Amir Hasan Sijzi, not Ahmad Sirhindi.
Salim Chishti was associated with Fatehpur Sikri, whereas Gesudaraz was also known as Muhammad Banda Nawaz and Bande Nawaz.
Nasiruddin Mahmud, known as Chiragh-i-Dehlavi
, was the last great Chishti saint of Delhi.

secs.t: Sufis in the Deccan

x: The event is dated to the
14th century
, although some UPSC notes mention the 13th century.
The
migration of Chishtis to Gulbarga
followed Burhanuddin Gharib’s transmission of the order to the Deccan.
The dargah of Gesudaraz or Bande Nawaz is at
Gulbarga
, where he settled under the Bahmanis.
Golconda witnessed the settlement of Sufi gurus, widespread popularity of Sufism and the development of khanqahs as higher-education centres.

secs.t: Chishti saints - dargah locations

x: Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki
lived from 1173 to 1235 and his dargah is at Delhi, specifically Mehrauli.
Amir Khusrau was a
famous disciple
of Nizamuddin Auliya and is credited here with introducing Qaul, the opening hymn of qawwali.
The birth years are Moinuddin Chishti, 1143; Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, 1173; Baba Farid, 1178; and Nizamuddin Auliya, 1238.

secs.t: Ba-shara vs be-shara orders

x: Ba-shara orders followed Sharia, while Be-shara orders were not bound by Islamic law.
Naqshbandi and Firdausi are Ba-shara orders, while Madaris and wandering Qalandars are Be-shara groups.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sufism gave Islam in India a tolerant and vernacular character, while khanqahs served as welfare centres.
The adaptation of Chishtis to local language and music helped Sufism serve as a bridge for Indo-Islamic composite culture.
Ali Hujwiri is identified as the first prominent Sufi in India, while Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehlavi is the last great Chishti saint of Delhi.

rows.title: Sufi saints - Moinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya, Baba Farid, Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi

secs.t: Saint → contemporary ruler and relations

x: Moinuddin Chishti came with Muhammad Ghori in 1192 and settled at
Ajmer
Bahauddin Zakariya supported Iltutmish and was appointed Shaikh-ul-Islam.
The statement ‘Hunuz Dilli dur ast’ is associated with
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
in connection with Nizamuddin Auliya.
The Chishtis generally kept away from political power; however, later Chishtis in the Deccan accepted grants.

secs.t: Malfuzat (Fawaid-ul-Fuad) → saint and compiler

x: Fawaid-ul-Fuad records the conversations of
Nizamuddin Auliya
Fawaid-ul-Fuad was compiled by
Amir Hasan Sijzi

secs.t: Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi - order, opposition to Akbar, letters

x: Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi belonged to the
Naqshbandi
order and was a disciple of Khwaja Baqi Billah.
Sirhindi criticised Akbar’s Sulh-i-kul and Din-i-Ilahi and opposed sama and visits to saints’ tombs.
Maktubat-i-Imam Rabbani is the collection of letters written by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi.
Jahangir imprisoned Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi at
Gwalior Fort

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four statements correctly express the contrast: Nizamuddin was a Chishti associated with sama and aloofness from court, while Sirhindi was a Naqshbandi orthodox critic.
The calendar covers the Annual Urs of Garib Nawaz, the Mini-Urs of Baba Farid and the Urs of Usman Harooni and Bakhtiyar Kaki.
The Chishti dargahs at Ajmer and Delhi developed as shared shrines visited by both Hindus and Muslims.

rows.title: Interaction and impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements on society and language
sub: Group-II S1-56: Impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements on Indian society and languages

secs.t: Principles common to Bhakti and Sufi

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2022 and 2023 both keyed
I, II and III only
(monotheism, asceticism, tolerance) - "accepted idol worship" is the trap.
Bhakti traditions placed devotion above Vedic ritual and priestly mediation, while Sufism emphasised inner spiritual experience rather than merely formal observance of the Shariat.
The guru was central to Bhakti, the pir-murid bond to Sufism, and both traditions promoted accessible vernacular preaching and spiritual equality beyond caste distinctions.

secs.t: Nathpanthi Hath Yoga - practitioners and Sufi borrowings

x: Exam angle: "Hath Yoga practised by Nathpanthis and adopted by Sufis" -
both correct
The Kanphata Yogis followed the Nath tradition of
Gorakhnath
and were practitioners of Hath Yoga.
The interaction involved spiritual dialogues, meditation and breath-control techniques; it was not confined exclusively to temple rituals.
Nizamuddin Auliya
noted the yogic Siva-Sakti division of the body while discussing ideas encountered from Nath yogis.

secs.t: Music - Persian translations, qawwali, bhajan and kirtan

x: Exam angle: UPPSC A-R - both true, but Chishti love of music is
not
the explanation for the translations.
Amir Khusrau
is credited with introducing the Qaul, which became associated with qawwali traditions around Sufi shrines.
Ghunyat-ul-Munya is dated 1375, Raga Darpan was Faqirullah’s rendering of Man Kautuhal, and Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi is associated with Sikandar Lodi.

secs.t: Impact on caste and gender

x: All four occupational or caste backgrounds are correctly matched: Kabir was a weaver, Ravidas a leather worker, Sena a barber and Dhanna a Jat cultivator.
Mirabai, Andal, Lal Ded, Janabai and Bahinabai
are the women named for expressing their devotion openly.
Basava’s Veerashaivism condemned caste and child marriage and supported widow remarriage and gender equality.

secs.t: Growth of vernacular literature by region

x: Ramcharitmanas, composed by Tulsidas, belongs to the Hindi literary tradition, particularly Awadhi.
Punjabi is associated with Baba Farid’s verses, Marathi with Jnaneshwari, Bengali with Padavali kirtans and Telugu with Annamacharya’s sankirtanas.
Vemana
, associated with the seventeenth century, used satire in common Telugu against birth-based inequality.
The use of people’s speech helped regional languages develop and laid foundations for
modern Indian literature

secs.t: Syncretic traditions - Kabirpanth, Sant tradition, dargah worship

x: The Rishi movement served all castes, emphasised universal love and adopted vegetarianism, although the Shariat permitted meat.
Sufi shrines became
shared religious and cultural centres
, attracting people across social and religious boundaries.
Alberuni observed parallels between Sufi ideas and both
the Yoga Sutra and the Bhagavad Gita
Bhakti-Sufi interaction produced
a composite Indo-Islamic culture
, with shrines and vernacular traditions acting as shared spaces.

secs.t: Akbar's Sulh-i-kul and Din-i-Ilahi

x: Sulh-i-kul means
universal peace
and represented Akbar’s attempt to harmonise diverse beliefs.
Akbar revered Salim Chishti and undertook pilgrimages to Ajmer, reflecting the Sufi influence on his religious outlook.
Ahmad Sirhindi
, associated with the Naqshbandi order, opposed Akbar’s syncretic policies.
Dara Shikoh carried forward the syncretic line associated with the interaction of Bhakti and Sufi ideas.

secs.t: Limitations - persistence of caste, later sectarianisation

x: In some phases, Veerashaivism spread through physical force, described as the “Sivapasa”, meaning the
sword
The movements later hardened into separate sects and panths, despite their earlier emphasis on broad spiritual and social interaction.
Medieval norms became more restrictive, particularly through purdah and limited access to education and work for women and lower castes.

secs.t: Rise of new sects

x: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, in the Punjab region.
Kabirpanth is associated with North India, Dadupanth with Rajasthan, Mahanubhava with Maharashtra and the Rishi movement with Kashmir.
Basaveswara founded or led the Lingayat/Veerasaiva tradition, which was associated with Karnataka and Andhra.
Sheikh Nuruddin founded or led the
Rishi movement in Kashmir

secs.t: Women in the movements

x: Mirabai is linked with Rajasthan and Krishna devotion, Andal was the only woman Alvar, and Lal Ded of Kashmir inspired the Rishi movement.
Molla
was an Andhra woman poet associated with the Telugu Molla Ramayanam of the sixteenth century.
The Bhakti and Sufi movements created space for women’s open spiritual expression; Veerabrahmam also admitted women to his order.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Bulleh Shah prioritised Tariqat over rigid Shariat, followed Wahdat-al-Wujud, used the Kafi form and regarded Shah Inayat Qadiri as his guide.
The Andhra pre-colonial reform line included
Veerashaivism and Srivaishnavism
, along with figures such as Brahmanayudu, Vemana, Veerabrahmam and Nasaraiah.
The movements revived devotional Hinduism, weakened priestly dominance and contributed to composite culture, but they did not completely abolish caste distinctions.

rows.title: Sikhism - the ten Gurus, Guru Granth Sahib, the Khalsa; Banda Bahadur and Ranjit Singh

secs.t: Founder, meaning of 'Sikh', the ten Gurus in order - contribution, successor, birthplace

x: Exam angle: founder, meaning of 'Sikh', successor of Nanak, Guru → contribution matching.
Kabir taught belief in one God known by many names and condemned the rituals of both faiths, advocating Hindu–Muslim unity.
Guru Nanak’s teachings included
Nirguna devotion, Ek Onkar, Naam Simran and Sangat
, while rejecting rituals of both religions.
Guru Hargobind militarised the Panth and was released from Gwalior Fort in 1619 along with 52 prisoners, an event associated with Bandi Chhor Divas.

secs.t: Ranjit Singh - misl, capital, Treaty of Amritsar, Kohinoor, Adalat-i-Ala, successors

x: Exam angle: capital and Treaty of Amritsar are the most-asked facts.
The Treaty of Amritsar, concluded in 1809 with Lord Minto, fixed the
Sutlej
as the boundary between the British and Ranjit Singh's territories.
The order was Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh, Sher Singh and finally the minor Dalip Singh, with Rani Jindan as regent.

secs.t: Guru Granth Sahib - compiler, contributors including non-Sikh saints

x: Kabir
was a non-Sikh contributor to the Guru Granth Sahib.
Sheikh Farid, Namdev and Ravidas contributed to the Guru Granth Sahib.
The Guru Granth Sahib is written in the
Gurmukhi
script.
Anand Karaj includes
four
circumambulations of the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan hymns are sung.

secs.t: Khalsa - founding Guru, year, place, five Ks, Panj Pyare

x: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa on Baisakhi, 13 April 1699, at Takht Keshgarh Sahib in Anandpur.
The Five Ks are Kesh, Kangha, Kara, Kachera and Kirpan.
The Panj Pyare were the five volunteers whom Guru Gobind Singh baptised with sacred nectar at the founding of the Khalsa.

secs.t: Banda Bahadur - original name, appointment, campaigns, coins, end

x: Guru Gobind Singh commissioned Banda Bahadur at Nanded in 1708.
The eight-month siege of Gurdas Nangal took place in 1715, after which Banda Bahadur was captured.
Banda Bahadur minted coins in the names of
Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh
Banda Bahadur was executed at Delhi by Farrukhsiyar in 1716 for refusing to convert.

secs.t: Sikh misls - names and consolidation

x: After Banda Bahadur, the Khalsa was organised into 12 misls, including Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Ramgarhia, Kanhaiya, Sukerchakia and Phulkian.
Ranjit Singh
, belonging to the Sukerchakia misl, unified the misls into the kingdom of Lahore.
After 1708, the Khalsa established an autonomous administration in the region between the
Sutlej and Jamuna

secs.t: Sacred places → Guru

x: Amritsar was founded by Guru Ram Das and the Golden Temple was built by Guru Arjan.
Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib at Nanded is associated with the final resting place of Guru Gobind Singh.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Akal Takht asked for the re-amendment of the
Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026
The 350th martyrdom year of Guru Tegh Bahadur was observed in 2026.
Andhra Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister
Pawan Kalyan
paid tribute at Hazur Sahib, Nanded, during the Shaheedi Samagam.
Banda Bahadur
established the first sovereign Sikh state at Sirhind in 1710.
