units.title: European Trading Companies in India - Struggle for Supremacy (Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Mysore, Andhra, Nizam); Governors-General and Viceroys

rows.title: Age of discovery and the sea route to India - Vasco da Gama; motives of European expansion

secs.t: Vasco da Gama - arrival, route, ruler, voyages

x: Exam angle: CGPSC 2022 - only "Zamorin ruled Calicut" was correct; he did not stay a year in India.
Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon on
8 July 1497
, beginning the voyage that culminated in his arrival at Calicut in 1498.
Vasco da Gama was piloted with the help of the trader
Abdul Majid
on his voyage to Calicut.

secs.t: Motives of European expansion

x: Spices, silk, religion, wealth, prestige, rivalry and the desire to break Arab control were stated motives.
Demand for spices, silk and Indian textiles, together with the Arab trading monopoly and Italian distribution network, encouraged European expansion.
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453, closing the main overland route through Constantinople and Central Asia to India.

secs.t: Explorers → discovery and sponsoring country

x: Bartholomew Dias
reached the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms.
Bartholomew Dias and Vasco da Gama were sponsored by Portugal, whereas Christopher Columbus was sponsored by Spain.
Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, referred to in the account as the West Indies.
Cabral reached Brazil and India in 1500 and established factories at Calicut, Cannanore and Cochin.

secs.t: Treaty of Tordesillas and papal bulls

x: Pope Alexander VI
issued Inter caetera in 1493, dividing newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal.
The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 divided newly claimed lands along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, assigning the eastern sphere to Portugal and the western sphere to Spain.

secs.t: Navigational advances

x: The
caravel and astrolabe
are identified as navigational advances that made long voyages safer.
Prince Henry the Navigator established naval training centres and was the first European identified here as actively promoting navigation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, two years after Vasco da Gama's 1498 arrival in India, and this historical link was recalled in the context of the Prime Minister's visit for the 17th BRICS Summit.
The years 1453 and 1498 are treated as marking the beginning of the Modern Age for India and Andhra, linking the disruption of old routes with the opening of the sea route.

rows.title: Advent of Europeans - Portuguese, Dutch, English, French and Danish
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-128

secs.t: European companies - formation, charter, first factory, headquarters

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 asked the EIC year thrice -
. APPSC 2024 keyed the 1600 Charter as "exclusive trading rights" - not territorial or legislative powers.
The English East India Company received a fifteen-year monopoly for trade between
the Cape of Good Hope and the Magellan Straits
The States-General granted the VOC sovereign powers, including making war, constructing forts and concluding treaties.
Francis Day
obtained the site from the Raja of Chandragiri and built Fort St. George at Madras in 1639.
Job Charnock settled at Sutanuti in 1690; the three zamindaris were bought in 1698, and Fort William was built in 1700.

secs.t: Portuguese governors - policy

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 twice - Blue Water Policy =
Portuguese
Almeida
Francisco de Almeida
, the first Portuguese viceroy in India, followed the Blue Water Policy, which emphasised naval mastery rather than territorial expansion inland.
Cartaz was a naval-pass system used to regulate shipping and enforce the Portuguese maritime monopoly, along with convoys and customs duties.
Albuquerque reversed Almeida's exclusively naval approach and pursued territorial conquest, including Goa, Malacca and Hormuz.
Francisco de Almeida served first from 1505–09, followed by Afonso de Albuquerque from 1509–15, and then Nino da Cunha.

secs.t: European settlements in Andhra - company and grant

x: Pulicat was initially Portuguese, was captured by the Dutch and became the Dutch headquarters in 1610; pepper and cloth were important commodities there.
Abdullah Qutb Shah of Golconda
issued the Golden Farman in 1636, granting trade concessions to the English.
The Dutch established the trade centre at Machilipatnam in 1605, Bangaru Farmana was issued in 1636, and the import-duty increase occurred in May 2026.

secs.t: Portuguese contributions - crops, printing press

x: The Portuguese introduced the printing press at Goa in 1556.
The Portuguese were the first Europeans to arrive and the last colonial power to leave India.
The Portuguese
introduced these crops and fruits, including tobacco, potato, maize, red chilli, groundnut, pineapple, papaya and cashew.
Portuguese and Arab traders supplied
horses
to the Deccan.

secs.t: English envoys and travellers at the Mughal court

x: Hawkins visited Jahangir’s court in 1608–09, led the first English trade mission there and faced Portuguese pressure resulting in refusal.
Sir Thomas Roe’s mission in 1615 secured the right for the English to
establish factories across the Mughal Empire
Ralph Fitch visited Akbar in the 1580s, William Hawkins was at Jahangir’s court from 1608 to 1611, Sir Thomas Roe arrived in 1615, and Edward Terry accompanied Roe as chaplain.

secs.t: Indian rulers' dealings with the Portuguese

x: The correct sequence is Goa in 1510, Diu in 1535, expulsion from Hooghly in 1632, and the Maratha capture of Salsette and Bassein in 1739.
Bombay came to Charles II as Catherine of Braganza’s dowry in 1661, was handed to the Company in 1668, and subsequently replaced Surat as the chief west-coast settlement.

secs.t: Battles among Europeans - participants

x: The English fought the Portuguese at Jask in 1620 and Ormuz in 1622 and emerged victorious; Ormuz was taken for the Shah of Persia.
Travancore, under
Marthanda Varma
, defeated the Dutch at Colachel in 1741.
The English, led by Eyre Coote, defeated the French under Lally at Wandiwash in 1760.
The sequence is Swally (1612), Colachel (1741), Bedara (1759) and Wandiwash (1760).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The British benefited from the steady finances of a private joint-stock company and from using the rivalries among Indian rulers.
The Portuguese naval monopoly ended with the emergence of the Dutch and English as competing maritime powers.
The Portuguese were the first Europeans to come to India and remained until 1961, making them the last European power to leave.

rows.title: Portuguese in India - Almeida's Blue Water Policy, Albuquerque, Estado da India, Cartaz system, decline

secs.t: Contributions - New World crops, printing press, churches, Jesuits, Inquisition

x: Tobacco, potato, lady's finger and chilli are included among the crops introduced through Portuguese contacts.
Kannada and Malayalam Bible printing is associated with the Portuguese, Xavier reached Goa in 1542, and his remains are at the Basilica of Bom Jesus.
The Goa Inquisition in the sixteenth century acted against religious dissent and used state machinery for conversions.

secs.t: Cartaz system - meaning, purpose, enforcement

x: A Cartaz was a Portuguese naval trade licence or pass required for ships sailing in the Indian Ocean.
Ships without the required Cartaz could be
confiscated or sunk
by the Portuguese.
The Cartaz system was backed by the Caes convoy system and customs duties.

secs.t: Settlements and forts → year and grantor

x: Cochin and Cannanore were bases from 1503; the Zamorin had earlier welcomed the Portuguese at Calicut.
Goa was taken from Bijapur in 1510, Bassein was obtained in 1534, Diu was secured by treaty in 1535 and conquered in 1546, and Daman was obtained in 1559.
Akbar granted the Portuguese permission to establish themselves at
Hugli

secs.t: Hugli base - piracy and Mughal response

x: Shah Jahan
captured Hugli in 1632 in response to Portuguese piracy and related activities.
During Aurangzeb's reign, Bengal governor
Shaista Khan
captured Sondip and Chittagong and suppressed the Arakanese pirates.

secs.t: Battles - Diu, Gujarat, Zamorin, Bijapur

x: Almeida defeated the combined fleet of
Gujarat, the Egyptian Mamluks and the Zamorin
at Diu in 1509.
Pressed by Humayun, Bahadur Shah of Gujarat permitted Nino da Cunha to build the Diu fort in 1535.
The Portuguese suffered defeat at Swally in 1612, off Jask in 1620, and lost Ormuz in 1622 to the English and the Shah of Persia.

secs.t: Decline - causes and territories lost

x: Dutch and English competition contributed to Portuguese decline rather than supporting Portugal.
All four statements describe factors associated with Portuguese decline in India.
The Portuguese lost
Cochin
to the Dutch in 1663.
Goa attained statehood in May 1987; Portuguese rule had ended earlier through Operation Vijay on 19 December 1961.

secs.t: Portuguese in Andhra coast and Bay of Bengal trade

x: Portuguese posts existed at
Masulipatnam, Pulicat and San Thome
on or near the Andhra coast.
The Portuguese obtained permission from Abdullah Qutb Shah and established their first Andhra factory at Machilipatnam in 1670.
Portuguese religious intolerance alienated the Golconda Sultans, contributing to the waning of their influence by the mid-seventeenth century.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Portuguese
were the first Europeans to arrive in India and were the last European power to leave, in 1961.
Tomato, chilli and groundnut
were among the New World crops introduced by the Portuguese into the Telugu country.
The Portuguese left India in 1961; 1510 is associated with Goa becoming the first European territory in India since the time of Alexander.

rows.title: Dutch in India - VOC, factories (Pulicat, Machilipatnam, Nagapattinam), Battle of Colachel

secs.t: Dutch factories in Andhra → year and order; earlier Portuguese presence

x: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
of Golconda permitted Van der Haghen to establish the Dutch factory at Machilipatnam.
Bheemunipatnam, Palakollu, Jagannathapuram and Koringa are associated respectively with 1641, 1652, 1736 and 1802.
Draksharama
was one of the subordinate Dutch factories in the Krishna–Godavari weaving belt; the other places are associated with Dutch activity outside that factory network.

secs.t: Coromandel textile ports and trade items

x: Silk and porcelain
were imported, whereas gems, diamonds, indigo, cotton, Kalamkari and cloth were among the exports.
The Dutch carried textiles from the Coromandel in exchange for
spices
from the East Indies.
The Dutch trade network carried saltpetre from Bihar, opium and rice, and pepper from Malabar in addition to Coromandel textiles.

secs.t: Dutch factories elsewhere → year; earliest and chief factory

x: The correct sequence is Surat (1616), Karaikal (1645), Chinsura (1653) and Nagapattinam (1658).
Pulicat
was the chief Dutch centre until 1690, after which Nagapattinam became the chief factory.
Mahe
was a French centre, although it is sometimes incorrectly included in lists of Dutch centres.

secs.t: Terms of Dutch settlement; later fate of Cochin

x: The Dutch took Cochin from the Portuguese in 1663; it later passed to the British in 1795.

secs.t: VOC - formation, charter, headquarters in Asia

x: The VOC received sovereign powers to wage war, build forts and sign treaties; it had no power to crown the British monarch.
The VOC primarily focused on the
Spice Islands
, while India was not its central strategic focus.
Jan Huyghen van Linschoten
’s *Itinerario* of 1595–96 provided important information that assisted Dutch expansion.

secs.t: Battles of Colachel and Bedara/Chinsura

x: Travancore under Marthanda Varma defeated the Dutch at Colachel in 1741, ending Dutch ambitions in Malabar.
The English defeated the Dutch at Bedara/Chinsura in 1759, with Francis Forde as commander, after which the Dutch withdrew to Indonesia.
J.B. Russell
commanded the Dutch forces at the Battle of Bedara/Chinsura in 1759.

secs.t: Decline of the Dutch in India - causes

x: The Dutch prioritised their spice monopoly in Indonesia, while Malabar was less profitable to them than the Coromandel cloth trade.
The conferences of 1613 and 1615 failed to settle the fierce Anglo-Dutch rivalry.
All four factors contributed to Dutch decline: military defeats, loss of Andhra strongholds and the prioritisation of the Indonesian spice monopoly.

secs.t: Monuments of Dutch presence in AP

x: Bheemunipatnam is associated with a
Dutch cemetery
, while Fort Geldria is located at Pulicat.
Fort Geldria was established at
Pulicat
, the major Dutch centre on the Coromandel Coast.
Palakollu and
Draksharama
are identified as old Dutch settlements in Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Dutch network in Andhra extended from Machilipatnam in the south-western part of the network to Bheemunipatnam in the north-east.

rows.title: English East India Company - Charter of 1600, Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta; Farman of 1717

secs.t: Charter of 1600 - monarch, powers, Mughal emperor, monopoly period

x: The Company was run by a Governor and a 24-member committee, later known as the Court of Directors.
Courten’s rival association was licensed by Charles I and merged in 1649; Cromwell’s 1657 charter created permanent joint stock; the Company merged into the United Company in 1708.
Charles II and James II delegated powers including coining money, exercising jurisdiction, and making war and peace with non-Christians.

secs.t: English on the Andhra coast - Globe, Hippon, Qutb Shahi permission, Golden Farman, Armagaon

x: The Globe reached Machilipatnam in 1611 under
Captain Anthony Hippon
, marking the establishment of the first English factory in Andhra.
Pulicat was the second settlement, was abandoned due to Dutch hostility, Visakhapatnam was established in 1682, and Bhimili became the first municipality in Andhra in 1861.
The Golden Farman gave the English trading privileges in Golconda's ports on payment of 500 pagodas annually, helping them return to Machilipatnam.

secs.t: Factory / Presidency → year and founder

x: Exam angle: first English factory - Surat (India) vs Machilipatnam (Andhra).
Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta are associated respectively with 1612–13, 1639, 1668 and 1690/1700 in the early English settlement chronology.
Francis Day founded Madras in 1639 after obtaining a grant from the Chandragiri ruler Venkatapati Raya III, with the efforts of the Damerla brothers, Venkatadri and Ayyappa.

secs.t: Trade of early settlements → goods and source

x: Silk and cotton piece-goods were obtained from Bengal, not Gujarat.
The main sources of indigo mentioned are
Gujarat and the Coromandel region
Dubashes
served as intermediaries in the Company’s commercial transactions.
Imported bullion
was used to pay for Indian goods in the early period of Company trade.

secs.t: Early conflicts - Swally, Child's War

x: The Swally victory occurred in 1612, Jahangir’s farman followed in 1613, and further English victories occurred in 1615, off Jask in 1620 and at Ormuz in 1622.
Aurangzeb
defeated the Company during Child’s War and pardoned it after payment of a fine.
Shivaji sacked Surat twice and threatened the English factory located there.

secs.t: Farman of 1717

x: The Farman of 1717 was issued by Mughal emperor
Farrukhsiyar
and substantially enhanced the Company’s trading privileges.
The Company’s mission to Farrukhsiyar’s court was led by
John Surman
The Farman granted the Company the right to issue
dastaks
, or passes for duty-free trade in Bengal.
Company servants misused dastaks for private trade, depriving the Nawab of Bengal of revenue.

secs.t: Bombay - acquisition from the Portuguese

x: In 1668, Bombay was transferred to the East India Company for an annual rent of

secs.t: Job Charnock and the three villages of Calcutta

x: Job Charnock founded the English settlement at
Sutanuti
In 1698, the Company bought the zamindari rights of
Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata
The settlement formed from the three villages was fortified as
Fort William
The imperial order of 1691 allowed the Company to trade in Bengal for
annually in lieu of dues.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Company was established as a trading company in 1600 and emerged as a territorial ruling power after the Battles of Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764.
The correct order is establishment of the Company in 1600, Plassey in 1757, Buxar in 1764 and the end of Company rule in 1858.

src: Sources: CDI (Block05 Advent of Europeans - English, Trade Practices; Block06 Rise of British Rule; Block11 European Trade Establishments); UPSC (Modern History pp.26-27); APP (Indian History Part 2 - English EIC, British EIC; AP History Modern-3, Modern-4); APHQ (aph2025_31, aph2025_46, aph2025_62); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.349-350)

rows.title: French in India - Colbert, Compagnie des Indes, Pondicherry, Dupleix and his policy

secs.t: French settlements → chronological order

x: Surat
was the site of the first French factory in India, established in 1667 under François Caron.
Masulipatnam
was established in 1669 by François Caron with Marcara under a patent from the Sultan of Golconda.
Shaista Khan permitted the French presence at Chandernagore in 1673, and it was settled in 1690.

secs.t: French in Andhra - Yanam, Machilipatnam, Bussy, Northern Circars, Bobbili

x: Following Muzaffar Jang’s murder at Rayachoti, Bussy helped establish
Salabat Jang
as Subedar of the Deccan.
The Northern Circars granted in 1753 comprised Mustafanagar or Kondapalli, Eluru, Rajahmundry and Chicacole or Srikakulam.
The battle took place on 24 January 1757; French forces under Bussy supported Vijayaramaraju, Ranga Rao was killed, and Vijayaramaraju was later killed by Ranga Rao’s brother-in-law Tandra Papayya.
Salabat Jang granted Mustafanagar, Eluru, Rajahmundry and Chicacole to the French in 1753 to meet the expenses of Bussy's troops.

secs.t: Pondicherry - founder, changes of control, restoring treaty

x: Sher Khan Lodi
, the Bijapur governor of Valikondapuram, gave the land to François Martin in 1673.
François Martin built
Fort St. Louis
at Pondicherry, which became the headquarters of the French in India.
The sequence is 1693, 1697, 1761 and 1763: Dutch capture, Treaty of Ryswick restoration, British capture and Treaty of Paris restoration.

secs.t: Dupleix - intervention policy, titles and jagirs

x: Dupleix intervened in the Hyderabad succession between Nasir Jang and Muzaffar Jang and in the Carnatic succession between Anwaruddin and Chanda Sahib.
At Ambur, Anwaruddin was killed; Muzaffar Jang was made Subedar and Chanda Sahib became Nawab.
Dupleix was declared Nawab of the coastal region of the Krishna, with
Valapadu
as his jagir.

secs.t: French East India Company - minister, king, state control, last to arrive

x: Jean-Baptiste Colbert, minister of
Louis XIV
, founded the French East India Company in 1664.
The company received a 50-year monopoly in the Indian and Pacific Oceans together with rights over Madagascar.
The French East India Company was state-owned and depended on subsidies, making it vulnerable when sustained state support was lacking.

secs.t: French governors in order

x: François Martin was followed by Dumas, Dupleix and Count de Lally.
François Martin
was the first French governor and built Pondicherry.
Dumas
, who served from 1735 to 1741, acquired Karaikal.
Dupleix served from 1742 to 1754, Godeheu replaced him and was recalled at the start of the Third Carnatic War, while Lally lost at Wandiwash to Eyre Coote.

secs.t: Later French possessions and merger with India

x: After Wandiwash and the Treaty of Paris of 1763, the French retained only the trading enclaves of Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore.
Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam
transferred de facto in 1954 and de jure in 1962, becoming part of the Union Territory of Puducherry.
The Danish company was founded in 1616; Tranquebar was established in 1620, Serampore was another Danish settlement, and the settlements were sold to the British in 1845.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The French challenge weakened because they lacked naval supremacy and consistent state support.
Yanam
was the last French enclave on Andhra soil and remained French de facto until 1954 and de jure until 1962.

rows.title: Danish and other minor European settlements (Tranquebar, Serampore)

secs.t: European settlements → power and order of arrival (Pondicherry, Goa, Tranquebar, Serampore, Chinsura)

x: Exam angle: match-the-settlement-to-power (UPPSC 2016: Pondicherry-French, Goa-Portuguese, Tranquebar-Danish, Sadras-Dutch).
The Portuguese were the first among these powers to arrive, followed by the Dutch, British, Danish and French.
Pondicherry was founded as a French headquarters in 1673–74 by
Francois Martin
Chinsura was a Dutch settlement, not a Danish one.

secs.t: Danish East India Company - formation, first settlement

x: Tranquebar is situated near Tanjore on the south-eastern
Coromandel coast
Serampore
, established in 1699 near Calcutta, became the second major Danish settlement and the focus of Danish activity in Bengal.
The commercial impact of the Danish settlements was negligible, but
their Protestant missionary, educational and linguistic work
was historically important.

secs.t: Danish settlements → present state

x: Tranquebar is in Tamil Nadu, Serampore is near Kolkata in West Bengal, and Balasore is in Odisha.

secs.t: Serampore Mission - Carey, Marshman, Ward; press; college

x: The Serampore Trio consisted of the Baptist missionaries
William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward
Carey, Marshman and Ward operated from Danish Serampore to bypass the early bans imposed by the East India Company on missionary activity.
The Telugu Bible was printed at the Serampore press during
, making it the first Telugu Bible printed in India.

secs.t: Sale of Danish settlements - to whom and when

x: The sale of Serampore and Tranquebar to the British in 1845 took place under Governor-General
Hardinge I

secs.t: Ostend Company and Swedish company - brief presence

x: The Ostend Company had a small post at Banquibazar in Bengal and another at Covelong near Madras.
The Ostend Company’s Indian activities were suspended within a decade under British-Dutch pressure.
The Swedish East India Company was established in 1731, focused mainly on trade with China, and had only a negligible presence in India.

secs.t: Tranquebar - Ziegenbalg, first Protestant mission, Tamil and Telugu Bible

x: Exam angle: "Who translated the Bible into Telugu in 1746-47?" - Benjamin Schulz.
Founded in 1706, the Danish-Halle Mission at Tranquebar was the earliest sustained Protestant mission in
South India
Ziegenbalg’s method combined learning the local language, producing a vernacular Bible and establishing schools.
Besides his Bible work, Schulz prepared
a Telugu grammar and a dictionary
, contributing to the development of early Telugu prose.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Danish legacy was primarily educational and linguistic, reflected in printing, vernacular Bible translation and Serampore College, rather than commercial dominance.
The Danish East India Company was founded in 1616, Tranquebar was established in 1620, the Danish-Halle Mission began in 1706, and Serampore became a major settlement in 1699.
The Danes left in 1845, while the French were the last to arrive in 1664.

rows.title: Advent of Europeans in Andhra - Portuguese, Dutch, French and English
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-133

secs.t: Europeans → first factory in Andhra + year; factories by district (Nellore)

x: Abdullah Qutb Shah
permitted the French to establish their factory at Machilipatnam in 1669.
The order was Dutch in 1605, English in 1611, French in 1669 and Portuguese in 1670.
Armagaon was located at
Durgarajapatnam
, about 35 miles north of Pulicat.
The Masulipatnam factory of 1611 marked the beginning of the Company's territorial expansion in the south.

secs.t: French in Andhra - settlements, Bussy, Bobbili War

x: After Eyre Coote defeated Count de Lally at Wandiwash, the French retained
Pondicherry, Karaikal, Yanam, Mahe and Chandernagore
Eyre Coote
defeated the French commander Count de Lally at Wandiwash in 1760.
The French established themselves at Surat in 1668, Machilipatnam in 1669 and Pondicherry during 1673–74.
Bussy obtained the Northern Circars from Salabat Jung in 1753 for maintaining the French troops.

secs.t: Missionaries in Andhra - Bible translation, schools

x: Christian missionaries contributed significantly to education in Andhra and established schools, including the school founded by Rev.
Benjamin Schultze
, a German Lutheran missionary, completed the first Telugu Bible translation around 1732.

secs.t: Policies → European power

x: The Blue Water Policy belonged to the Portuguese, spice monopoly and own coins to the Dutch, and dadni advances and dubashes to the English.
The Blue Water Policy, associated with Francisco de Almeida, aimed at controlling maritime trade and the sea rather than acquiring extensive land territories.
The Portuguese held the Arabian Sea trade monopoly until the seventeenth century
, and their decline began with the Dutch arrival in 1605.

secs.t: Anglo-French rivalry in Andhra - Carnatic Wars, Battle of Chandurthi

x: Colonel Forde
, who was sent from Bengal, defeated the French forces commanded by Conflans at Chandurthi in 1758.
The correct order is the grant of the Circars to the French in 1753, the Bobbili War in 1757, the Battle of Chandurthi in 1758, and the fall of Masulipatnam in 1759.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Portuguese
are identified as the last of the four European powers to establish a factory in Andhra, in 1670.
The Dutch, Portuguese and French advanced money and paid fairly, whereas the English paid less while demanding high-quality goods, causing weavers to avoid them.
Machilipatnam attracted all four European powers because of its important chintz and diamond trade.

rows.title: Trade centres of coastal Andhra - Masulipatnam, Nizampatnam, Bheemunipatnam, Yanam
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-133

secs.t: Exports from coastal Andhra → centre; dominant pre-colonial industry

x: Saltpetre was exported from Machilipatnam, Narsapur and Pulicat; diamonds came from Golconda and Kollur; indigo from Nagulavancha and Nalgonda; and salt from Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam.
Textiles
were the dominant pre-colonial industry and stood second only to diamonds in the Qutb Shahi economy.
Kalingapatnam, Srikakulam, Vizag and Bhimunipatnam
were among the textile ports shipping to England, France and Holland.

secs.t: Masulipatnam - ruler controlling the port, merchant communities, textiles

x: Under
the Qutb Shahis of Golconda
, Masulipatnam was the Sultanate’s main maritime gateway, and its customs revenue contributed to Golconda’s wealth.
The bans imposed by England in 1700 and 1721 did not seriously affect Andhra because other markets remained open.
The earlier lighthouse was at Tavisipudi in 1858, followed by Campbelpeta in 1903, while the present lighthouse near Manginapudi dates from 1984.

secs.t: Shipbuilding centres of coastal Andhra

x: Narasapuram and Machilipatnam built ships and boats.
The term
odaberam
was used for sea-going ships in the Shuka Saptati.

secs.t: Trade centres → European power + factory year

x: The Dutch established a factory at Pulicat in 1610.
All four statements are correct according to the recorded European factory dates for Pulicat, Vizagapatnam and Yanam.
Madapollam was associated with the English, not the French.

secs.t: Imports into Andhra ports - commodities and source regions

x: Bullion
brought from Europe financed English purchases of chintz, calico and muslin.
Horses came through
Portuguese and Arab traders
The Dutch traded Coromandel textiles in exchange for spices from the East Indies.
Colonial-era imports included metals, minerals, porcelain, liquor, drugs, iron, steel and medicines.

secs.t: Yanam - European owner, merger, present status

x: Yanam merged into the Indian Union in 1954, while the de jure transfer occurred in 1962.

secs.t: Bheemunipatnam - surviving European-period monuments

x: A Dutch cemetery
survives at Bheemunipatnam.
Bheemunipatnam had a Dutch subordinate factory, later an English factory, and Bhimili became Andhra’s first municipality in 1861.

secs.t: Other historic ports and centres

x: Motupalli
was an important Kakatiya port, and Ganapatideva’s Abhaya Sasanam protected foreign traders there.
Somaya, a minister of the Reddi period, issued another record concerning sea trade.
Ghantasala, also called Kantakasela, and Koddura were ancient east-coast ports associated with the Satavahana period.
Tirupati, Srisailam, Srikurmam and Srikalahasti
were pilgrim centres that developed into trade centres.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the high Company-era duties explain the adverse effect on Andhra’s domestic and foreign trade.
Andhra Pradesh covers about 1,62,970 square kilometres, is ranked eighth by area, has a coastline of about 1,053.07 km in the 2025–26 survey analysis and had 28 districts in 2025.

rows.title: First Carnatic War - causes, Battle of St. Thome, Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle

secs.t: First Carnatic War - belligerents, immediate cause, European link

x: The English navy seized French ships; France retaliated, and the French, using a fleet from Mauritius, captured Madras in 1746.
France used its fleet from Mauritius to capture Madras, and the war was an extension of the War of Austrian Succession.

secs.t: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle - territorial exchanges

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2020/2025 - "war ended" and "English got back Madras" are both correct.
Madras was restored to the English in exchange for
Louisbourg in North America
, which was given back to the French.
The treaty restored the pre-war position and did not permanently end French political power in India.

secs.t: Battle of St. Thome / Adyar (1746) - belligerents, significance

x: The Battle of St. Thome or Adyar was fought in 1746 during the First Carnatic War.
A small French force under
Captain Paradis
defeated the army of the Nawab of Carnatic at St. Thome.
The battle showed the superiority of disciplined European infantry over a much larger Indian army and opened the way for European interference in Indian politics.

secs.t: Lessons of the war - European discipline vs Indian armies

x: The war demonstrated that small, disciplined European forces using artillery could defeat much larger Indian cavalry armies.
The war showed that
naval power
was decisive in the Anglo-French contest on the Coromandel coast.
Despite Dupleix’s victories, the political result of the war was nil.

secs.t: Nawab of Carnatic - Anwaruddin's role

x: Nizam-ul-Mulk
sent Anwaruddin to act as guardian of the minor Nawab Syed Ali.
Anwaruddin opposed fighting in his territory, supported the English, suffered defeat at St. Thome, and was later killed at Ambur in 1749 during the Second Carnatic War.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The war first revealed the military weakness of Indian rulers when facing disciplined European-trained troops.
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle restored the pre-war position, while the Treaty of Paris in 1763 marked the end of French political power in India.

src: Sources: CDI (Block06 Rise of British Rule - Three Carnatic Wars, French Rivalry); UPSC (Modern History p.29); CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.353); APP (Indian History Part 2 - French and the Carnatic; AP History Modern-3 Anglo-Carnatic Wars)

rows.title: Second Carnatic War - Anwaruddin, Chanda Sahib, Muhammad Ali; Robert Clive at Arcot

secs.t: Succession disputes - Hyderabad and Carnatic - side each company backed, rewards to Dupleix

x: Muzaffar Jang's concessions included Dupleix's governorship, Valapadu, Villianur, Bahur, Diviseema and Machilipatnam.
Muzaffar Jang was killed at Rayachoti in 1751 by
the Nawabs of Kadapa, Kurnool and Nayanur
Bussy immediately installed
Salabat Jang
, the fourth son of Nizam-ul-Mulk, after Muzaffar Jang was killed.
Anwaruddin was killed at Ambur; Chanda Sahib was installed as Nawab of the Carnatic and Muzaffar Jang as Subahdar of the Deccan.

secs.t: Battle of Ambur - year, participants, outcome

x: Exam angle: CGPSC 2023 - a statement that Ambur was fought in 1752 is wrong; it was
Anwaruddin was killed at Ambur, after which Chanda Sahib became Nawab of the Carnatic.
Muhammad Ali fled to Tiruchirappalli, also known as
Trichinopoly
, after the Battle of Ambur.

secs.t: Robert Clive at Arcot - siege, relief of Trichinopoly

x: Clive captured Arcot in 1751 with a very small force, described as about 210 men.
Clive defeated Raja Sahib at
Arni and Kaveripak
after resisting the siege of Arcot.
Robert Clive and Stringer Lawrence
relieved Trichinopoly.
Law first surrendered; Chanda Sahib surrendered in June 1752, was executed, and Muhammad Ali subsequently became Nawab of the Carnatic.

secs.t: Dupleix's recall - reasons and successor

x: The French Company became alarmed by the heavy expense and failures of Dupleix's interventionist policy, particularly the defeat at Trichinopoly, and recalled him in 1754.
Godeheu
succeeded Dupleix in 1754 and made peace with the English.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The war centred on Indian political disputes, demonstrated the territorial and revenue advantages of backing claimants, and brought major French gains on the Andhra coast.
Dupleix succeeded in the Deccan, particularly through influence at Hyderabad, but lost the Carnatic struggle at Arcot and Trichinopoly.
The main French territorial gains on the Andhra coast were
Machilipatnam, Diviseema and the Northern Circars

src: Sources: CDI (Block06 Rise of British Rule - Three Carnatic Wars, French Rivalry); UPSC (Modern History p.29-30); CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.353-355); APP (AP History Modern-3 Anglo-Carnatic Wars; Indian History Part 2 French and the Carnatic)

rows.title: Third Carnatic War - Battle of Wandiwash, Treaty of Paris (1763); reasons for English success

secs.t: Treaty of Paris (1763) - territories restored, fortification ban

x: Exam angle: "Third Carnatic War concluded by the Treaty of ___ in 1763" - Paris.
Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore were retained as French enclaves.
The Treaty restored the French settlements as demilitarised trading posts; fortification was prohibited.

secs.t: Battle of Wandiwash - year, belligerents, commanders, outcome

x: The Battle of Wandiwash was fought on
22 January 1760
at Wandiwash, also known as Vandavasi, in present-day Tamil Nadu.
Eyre Coote led the English victory over Count de Lally at Wandiwash, where Bussy was taken prisoner.
The English victory at Wandiwash, along with Plassey, removed the last serious European rival to British political supremacy in India.

secs.t: Reasons for English success and French failure

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2016 - both "Bengal wealth and manpower" and "naval superiority" are correct reasons.
The English company was privately organised, with a yearly elected board and relatively quicker decision-making.
Both statements are true, and dependence on royal subsidy and a state-controlled structure directly contributed to French financial weakness.
Lally's quarrels with his officers and inadequate understanding of Indian conditions weakened the French effort.

secs.t: Seven Years' War link and Bengal resources

x: The Third Carnatic War was the Indian theatre of the Seven Years' War, fought from 1756 to 1763.
After Clive's victory at Plassey in 1757 and the capture of French Chandernagore, Bengal revenue helped finance the English Carnatic campaign.
Plassey occurred in 1757, the capture of Chandernagore followed in the same period, and the Third Carnatic War extended to 1763.

secs.t: Battle of Condore/Chandurti and capture of Machilipatnam - Andhra theatre

x: Forde came from Bengal, joined Ananda Gajapati's Vizianagaram force, and defeated the French under Conflans.
The victory at Chandurti
drove the French out of the Northern Circars
and was later described as a small battle with great results.
Machilipatnam was taken by the English in
April 1759
after the victory at Chandurti in December 1758.
Ananda Gajapati
defeated Peddapuram's Jagapati Raju at Konduru.

secs.t: Siege and fall of Pondicherry

x: Lally captured Fort St. David at Cuddalore in 1758 but failed before Madras because he lacked money and naval support.
After Wandiwash, Lally held Pondicherry for
eight months
before surrendering on 16 January 1761.
Lally surrendered Pondicherry on 16 January 1761 after an eight-month hold; Jinji and Mahe also fell.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The treaty settled the Anglo-French contest in favour of British political supremacy.
The victories at Chandurti and Machilipatnam gave the English their first foothold in the Northern Circars.
Chandurti is described as the foundation of British rule in Andhra, in a parallel often drawn with
Plassey
as the foundation of British rule in India.

src: Sources: UPSC (Modern History p.30-32); CDI (Block06 Three Carnatic Wars; French Rivalry); APP (AP History Modern-3 Anglo-Carnatic Wars; Modern-3 European settlements; Indian History Part 2 Governors of Bengal); CDX (AP History Complete Notes p.350, 355, 364-365)

rows.title: Anglo-French rivalry - the three Carnatic Wars and the English ascendancy
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-136

secs.t: Carnatic Wars → treaty ending each (Aix-la-Chapelle, Pondicherry, Paris)

x: Exam angle: match-the-pair of war and treaty; "Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle ended the First war and returned Madras" - both correct.
Madras was captured in 1746, the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was signed in 1748, the Treaty of Pondicherry followed in 1754, and the Treaty of Paris was concluded in 1763.
The First, Second and Third Carnatic Wars respectively occurred during 1746–48, 1749–54 and 1756–63.

secs.t: Commanders and governors → war and role

x: Exam angle: Count de Lally = Third Carnatic War; defeated at Wandiwash.
Count de Lally, the French commander and Governor in the Third Carnatic War, captured Fort St. David in 1758 and surrendered Pondicherry on 16 January 1761.
Clive led the siege of Arcot in 1751 and won at Arni and Kaveripak during the Second Carnatic War.

secs.t: Causes and participants of each war

x: The First Carnatic War was
an extension of the War of Austrian Succession in Europe
, bringing the British and French into conflict in India.
The Second Carnatic War arose from succession disputes in Hyderabad after the death of Nizam-ul-Mulk and in the Carnatic after 1749.
The Third Carnatic War was connected with the
Seven Years’ War
of 1756–63 and began before the Treaty of Pondicherry could be ratified.

secs.t: Battles → war + victor

x: During the Second Carnatic War, Clive defeated
Raja Sahib and Chanda Sahib
at Arni and Kaveripak in 1751–52.
Chendurthi was fought on 7 December 1758, Wandiwash on 22 January 1760, Ambur in 1749 and Arcot in 1751.
Eyre Coote defeated Lally at Wandiwash on 22 January 1760 during the Third Carnatic War, and Bussy was taken prisoner.

secs.t: Reasons for English success over the French

x: The English navy defeated
d’Aché’s fleet off Masulipatnam
, after which he withdrew to Mauritius.
French difficulties included the recall of Dupleix, Lally’s quarrels and unpaid troops, failures at Madras and Thanjavur, and the withdrawal of Bussy from Hyderabad.
Robert
Clive, Stringer Lawrence and Eyre Coote
were identified as better English commanders who contributed to English success.

secs.t: French in Andhra - Bussy in Hyderabad, Masulipatnam, Yanam

x: The Northern Circars were granted to the French in 1753, the Treaty of Charmahal followed the Tumnapalem victory in 1756, the Battle of Bobbili occurred on 24 January 1757, and Chendurthi was fought in 1758.
Yanam is a French-origin enclave situated inside the Godavari delta in Andhra Pradesh and is administered as part of the Puducherry Union Territory.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The wars showed the military effectiveness of disciplined European infantry and established the English as kingmakers of South India.
Both statements are true, and the military events at Bobbili and Chendurthi and the fall of Machilipatnam explain why the Andhra struggle decided control over the Northern Circars.
Yanam, one of the French settlements retained after 1763, is still part of the Union Territory of Puducherry.

src: Sources: APP (AP History Modern-3 > Unit 3 > Anglo-Carnatic Wars; Indian History Pt 2 > French and Carnatic Wars; Europeans' decline); CDI (Block06 Rise of British Rule > French Rivalry & Carnatic Wars); CDX (AP History Complete Notes pp.353-355, 364-365); UPSC (Modern History pp.29-30)

rows.title: Bengal - Murshid Quli Khan to Siraj-ud-Daula; Black Hole episode; Battle of Plassey (1757)

secs.t: Murshid Quli Khan - capital shift, revenue reforms (mal jasmani, ijaradari)

x: Under ijaradari, contractors called ij aradars collected land revenue.
The term mal jasmani is used for the contract-based revenue-collection arrangement associated with ijaradari.
Conversion of jagir land into khalisa brought the land under direct state control for revenue purposes.
Murshid Quli Khan wanted the English to pay customs duties, but the English increased their military establishment instead.

secs.t: PERSON - called as / known as

x: Mir Jafar was the puppet Nawab installed after Plassey.

secs.t: Nawabs of Bengal in order → key act and Mughal status

x: Shuja-ud-din
was the son-in-law of Murshid Quli Khan.
Alivardi Khan seized the throne after killing Sarfaraz Khan in the
Battle of Giria
Alivardi Khan was Deputy Governor of Bihar, opposed the fortification of Calcutta and Chandernagore, and was succeeded by his grandson Siraj-ud-Daula.
Siraj-ud-Daula obtained an imperial farman as Subahdar of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

secs.t: Significance of Plassey - battle chronology, "first decisive" debate

x: Plassey is generally viewed as a victory of treachery and a political-financial arrangement rather than a prolonged contest between equally matched armies.
Buxar
, fought in 1764, is regarded as the real military test and confirmed the political result achieved at Plassey.
Plassey is commonly called the foundation of British rule, but Buxar is treated in some examination assessments as the most significant or decisive battle.

secs.t: Causes of conflict - dastak misuse, fortification of Calcutta, fugitives

x: The 1717 farman allowed duty-free Company trade, but Company servants misused dastaks for private trade, causing the Nawab to lose revenue.
All three developments intensified the conflict: unauthorised fortification, English refusal to stop it, and asylum to Krishna Das.
Ghaseti Begum and Shaukat Jang of Purnea
were court factions whom the English were perceived to support against Siraj-ud-Daula.

secs.t: Black Hole episode - narrator, historiographical debate

x: The episode is traditionally said to have occurred on
20 June 1756
after Siraj-ud-Daula captured Fort William.
J.Z. Holwell
, one of the survivors, gave the principal account on which the story of the Black Hole largely rests.
The traditional account states that 146 English prisoners were confined in a small cell and about 120 died.

secs.t: Siraj's capture of Calcutta, Clive-Watson recapture, rewards of Plassey

x: Kasimbazar was seized in May 1756, Calcutta fell in June 1756, Clive and Watson recaptured it in January 1757, and the Treaty of Alinagar followed in February 1757.
Governor Drake fled to Fulta, while Holwell surrendered when Calcutta fell to Siraj-ud-Daula.
The Company received
the Zamindari of the 24 Parganas
, along with duty-free trade privileges and monetary payments.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Plassey is characterised as a conspiracy, whereas Buxar is described as an open military victory.
The deal associated with Clive's conspiracy at Plassey involved Jagat Seth, Omichund and Mir Jafar.
The numbers associated with the Black Hole episode remain a subject of historical criticism and debate.
The 269th anniversary of Plassey was noted in
June 2026

rows.title: Mir Jafar, Mir Qasim and the Battle of Buxar (1764); Treaty of Allahabad (1765) and Diwani
sub: Group-II S1-62: Rise of British power - Battle of Plassey, Battle of Buxar and the Diwani of Bengal

secs.t: Diwani - date, grantor, Governor of Bengal, terms

x: Under the Dual Government, the Company enjoyed the financial power of Diwani, while the Nawab formally retained Nizamat and associated responsibilities.
Muhammad Reza Khan served Bengal, Raja Shitab Rai served Bihar, Robert Clive was the Governor associated with the grant, and Warren Hastings ended the Dual Government.
Warren Hastings
ended the Dual Government in 1772, stopped the tribute to Shah Alam and removed the remaining façade of Mughal sovereignty.

secs.t: Mir Qasim - capital shift, army modernisation, trade duties, conflict

x: Mir Qasim, the son-in-law of Mir Jafar, was placed on the throne in 1760 by
Governor Vansittart
The Treaty of 1760 involved the cession of the three districts, a half share in the Sylhet chunam trade and Rs 5 lakh for the Company’s southern wars.
By abolishing internal duties, Mir Qasim placed Indian merchants on an equal footing with English merchants and removed the advantage that Company servants obtained through misuse of dastaks.

secs.t: Battle of Buxar - allies, British commander, Nawab at the time, outcome

x: Mir Qasim was the deposed Nawab of Bengal, Shuja-ud-Daulah was Nawab of Awadh, Shah Alam II was the Mughal Emperor, and Hector Munro commanded the British forces.

All four statements describe the consequences recorded after the English victory at Buxar: Shuja fled, sought assistance, surrendered, Awadh and Allahabad were occupied, and Shah Alam II joined the English.

secs.t: Buxar vs Plassey - "most decisive battle"

x: The battle was fought on 23 June 1757 at Plassey, also called Palashi, on the Bhagirathi River in present-day Nadia district of West Bengal.
Siraj captured Qasim Bazar and then Calcutta, Governor Drake fled to Fulta, and Holwell was among the prisoners confined in the small cell.
The British used the deaths of prisoners in the Black Hole episode as a pretext for launching war against Siraj-ud-Daulah.
After Plassey, the Company obtained the zamindari of the 24 Parganas, duty-free trade in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and resources to fight the French.

secs.t: Treaty of Allahabad (1765) - separate terms; chronology

x: Exam angle: "Which treaty followed Buxar?" The answer is Allahabad, not Salbai, Bassein or Sugauli.
Robert Clive returned as
Governor of Bengal for the second time
in May 1765 and concluded the Treaty of Allahabad later that year.
The
Treaty of Salbai
was concluded in 1782; the treaties of Allahabad, Madras and Mangalore were concluded in 1765, 1769 and 1784 respectively.

secs.t: Mir Jafar - two tenures, Dutch intrigue, concessions

x: Mir Jafar served as Nawab from 1757 to 1760 and again from 1763 to 1765, after the fall of Mir Qasim.
Mir Jafar plotted with
the Dutch
against the English, but Clive defeated the Dutch at Chinsura or Bidara in 1759, after which the Dutch left India.
During his second tenure, Mir Jafar accepted restrictions on the size of his army, reflecting the Company's control over Bengal's political and military affairs.

secs.t: Najm-ud-Daula - Company control

x: Najm-ud-Daula
, the son of Mir Jafar, became Nawab of Bengal from 1765.
Najm-ud-Daula handed defence and administration to the Company-nominated Naib Subahdar, Muhammad Reza Khan, while retaining the Nizamat only nominally.
Najm-ud-Daula was left with the Nizamat in name only, since defence and administration were placed under a Company-nominated official.
In 1772, Warren Hastings ended the Mughal pretence and ruled Bengal by right of conquest.

secs.t: Nawabs of Bengal in sequence

x: Shuja-ud-din was too powerful to heed the court orders of 1735; Sarfaraz Khan was killed by Alivardi; Alivardi stopped the fortifications; and Siraj-ud-Daulah killed Shaukat Jang at Manihari.
Mir Jafar ruled from 1757 to 1760 and again from 1763 to 1765.
Mir Qasim was regarded as a reformer, ruled Bengal from 1760 to 1763 and fought at the Battle of Buxar.

secs.t: Farman of Farrukhsiyar and dastak system

x: Farrukhsiyar's 1717 farman allowed the Company to trade in Bengal without customs duties for a fixed payment of Rs 3,000 a year.
The 1717 farman granted important trading privileges to the Company and is popularly called the
Magna Carta of the Company
Private misuse of duty-free passes reduced the Nawab's revenue and caused disputes with Siraj-ud-Daulah and Mir Qasim.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 269th anniversary of Plassey was recalled on
28 June 2026
, along with issues such as misuse of the dastaks, the Black Hole and Mir Jafar's bribe.
All four items were associated with the anniversary recall: dastak misuse, the Black Hole, Mir Jafar's bribe and the treatment of Mir Madan as loyal.

rows.title: Dual Government in Bengal and its consequences; the Bengal Famine of 1770

secs.t: Dual Government - architect, Diwani vs Nizamat

x: Exam angle: "The dual system was enforced by" - Robert Clive (not Warren Hastings, who abolished it).
Robert Clive
introduced the Dual Government in Bengal during his second term as Governor of Bengal from 1765 to 1767.
The Second Treaty of Allahabad in 1765 enabled Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II to grant the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company.

secs.t: Naib Diwans and Naib Nazim - Muhammad Reza Khan, Shitab Rai

x: Muhammad Reza Khan was Naib Diwan at Murshidabad, Shitab Rai was Naib Diwan in Bihar, Clive introduced the system, and Hastings abolished it.
Muhammad Reza Khan served as Naib Diwan at Murshidabad and also as Naib Nazim for the minor Nawab of Bengal.
Both Muhammad Reza Khan and Raja Shitab Rai were removed and tried when the Dual Government ended in 1772.

secs.t: Abolition of Dual Government - Governor, year, treasury

x: Exam angle: BPSC 1996 asked "who abolished Dual Government" - Warren Hastings.
The state treasury was shifted from Murshidabad to
Calcutta
after Warren Hastings abolished the Dual Government.
All three measures followed the abolition: direct revenue collection began, the payment to Shah Alam II ended, and Allahabad and Kora were returned and sold to the Nawab of Awadh.

secs.t: Consequences - revenue extortion, weavers, private trade

x: Company agents forced weavers to sell their products at low prices, contributing to the decline of handicrafts.
Mir Qasim abolished internal duties for all traders in protest against the Company servants’ misuse of duty-free dastaks.
In under two decades, Bengal was reduced to
acute poverty, famines and epidemics
despite its earlier wealth.

secs.t: Bengal Famine of 1770 - areas, mortality, Company response

x: Exam angle: "Governor during the 1770 famine" - John Cartier; "Famine and Dual Government" - direct cause-effect.
The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 occurred during
John Cartier
's term as governor, which lasted from 1769 to 1772.
Different sources give different estimates: about 10 million in UPSC notes and about two million lives in the APP Governors’ table.

secs.t: Anandamath and the Sanyasi-Fakir rebellion

x: The revolt was caused by
the famine of 1770, Company insensitivity and restrictions on pilgrims
visiting holy places.
The participants included Hindu Sanyasis, Muslim Fakirs, dispossessed zamindars and peasants.
Majnum Shah, Bhawani Pathak and Devi Chaudhurani were associated with the revolt;
Shah Alam II
was not a leader of it.
The song
Vande Mataram
appears in Anandamath.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Both statements are true, and the Company's formal control over revenue provides the basis for tracing the drain of wealth and deindustrialisation to the arrangement.
The Guntur famine of 1832–33 and the Kurnool famine of 1866 were separate Andhra famines, distinct from the Bengal Famine of 1770.
Warren Hastings was the last Governor of Bengal from 1772 to 1773 and became the first Governor-General of Bengal in 1773.

rows.title: Anglo-Mysore Wars I-IV - Haidar Ali, Tipu Sultan, Treaty of Mangalore and Srirangapatnam

secs.t: Tipu Sultan - embassies, navy, reforms, Jacobin Club, capital

x: Exam angle: statement questions on "French embassy + navy" point to Tipu, not Haidar or the Wodeyars.
Tipu Sultan sent envoys to
Turkey
, whose capital Constantinople was an important diplomatic destination.
Tipu Sultan supported the Jacobin Club at Seringapatam, became a member, used the title ‘Citizen Tipu’ and planted a Tree of Liberty.

secs.t: Haidar Ali - rise, Dindigul, alliances

x: Haidar Ali was appointed Faujdar of Dindigul in 1755 under the Mysore minister
Nanjaraja
Haidar Ali adopted Western military techniques and established a modern arsenal at Dindigul with French help.
Haidar Ali used diplomacy to win over the Marathas and detach the Nizam from the British during the First Anglo-Mysore War.

secs.t: Battles - victor and British commanders

x: At the Battle of
Pollilur
in 1780, Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan defeated Colonel Baillie's force.
Cornwallis's coalition won at Seringapatam in 1792, causing Tipu Sultan to sue for peace.
In 1790, Tipu Sultan defeated the British army under
General Meadows
during the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
Hector Munro and Sir Eyre Coote were British commanders in the early wars, and Thomas Munro served under both of them.

secs.t: Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) - territories ceded and to whom

x: Tipu Sultan ceded about half his territory, paid a war indemnity of ₹3 crore and gave two sons as hostages under the Treaty of Seringapatam.
Bellary, Gurramkonda, Gandikota and Kadapa were among the territories in the Nizam's share, which included about half of Rayalaseema.
The British received Malabar, Coorg as a protectorate, Dindigul and the Bara Mahal.

secs.t: Fourth war - battle sites and the settlement of Mysore

x: After the Fourth War, Mysore was partitioned, the Hindu Wodeyar dynasty was restored, the boy ruler Krishnaraja Wodeyar III was installed, and the state was placed under a Subsidiary Alliance.
Arthur Wellesley served in
the campaign of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War
and later became known as the Duke of Wellington.

secs.t: Nizam and Marathas - side in each war

x: In the First Anglo-Mysore War, the Nizam initially joined the British but was subsequently detached from them by Haidar Ali.
The Marathas had earlier attacked Haidar Ali and concluded peace with the British at Salbai in 1782.
Both the Nizam and the Marathas were with the British in the
Third Anglo-Mysore War
, forming part of the grand alliance.

secs.t: Tipu - titles and Srirangapatna monuments

x: Tipu Sultan was associated with the titles ‘Tiger of Mysore’, ‘Citizen Tipu’ and ‘Padshah’. ‘Lion of Mysore’ is not among the stated titles.
Daria Daulat Bagh was a summer palace with war murals, the Gumbaz is the mausoleum of Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, and Jamia Masjid is also known as Masjid-e-Ala.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Third Anglo-Mysore War ended Tipu Sultan's supremacy in the south.
The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War removed the French-backed threat and brought Mysore and Andhra, through the Ceded Districts, under the Company.
The Ceded Districts were
Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary
The Ceded Districts came to the British in 1800 as a direct result of the Mysore Wars.

rows.title: The Nizam of Hyderabad, Subsidiary Alliance, and the cession of the Northern Circars
sub: Group-II S1-64: Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Lapse; annexation policy

secs.t: Subsidiary Alliance - Governor-General, terms, aims, order of signing, refusals

x: Exam angle: "First Indian state to sign the Subsidiary Alliance" = Hyderabad.
Wellesley designed the system to counter French influence and establish British paramountcy without assuming the cost of direct administration.
In return for the subsidiary force and other concessions, the Company undertook to protect the ruler's borders.
Hyderabad accepted in 1798, Awadh in 1801, the Peshwa in 1802 and Scindia in 1804.
Mysore accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799.
The Treaty of Bassein was concluded on
31 December 1802
Tipu Sultan
refused the Subsidiary Alliance, and this resistance led to the Fourth Mysore War.
Holkar resisted the system for the longest period and continued fighting during the Second Maratha War.
Holkar, Bharatpur, Jodhpur, Jaipur and Bundi
entered into the arrangement in 1818.

secs.t: Nizam Ali Khan - capital shift and treaties with the British

x: After joining the British against Tipu Sultan during 1790–1792, Nizam Ali Khan obtained lands from
the Krishna to beyond the Pennar
After the defeat at Kharda in 1795, Nizam Ali Khan blamed Sir John Shore's neutrality, dismissed his British battalions and relied on French troops under Raymond.
Resident Kirkpatrick
reported the Nizam's reliance on French troops under Raymond, which contributed to Wellesley's pressure for the alliance.

secs.t: Later Nizams - events of reign and British contemporaries

x: Afzal-ud-Daula
, or Asaf Jah V, ruled from 1857 to 1869, was the Nizam during the Revolt of 1857 and received the title “Star of India” for his loyalty.
Mir Turab Ali Khan became Diwan on 31 May 1853 after Siraj-ul-Mulk's death, took the title Salar Jung I, served three Nizams and died in 1883.
Salar Jung I served
Nasir-ud-Daula, Afzal-ud-Daula and Mir Mahbub Ali Khan
, dying in 1883 during the period of the latter's reign.

secs.t: Northern Circars - grants, lease talks, Andhra negotiator, Guntur

x: Exam angle: "Area of conflict between Nizam Ali and the British" =
Guntur Circar
, not the Northern Circars as a whole.
The Mughal firman granting the Circars to the East India Company was issued by
Shah Alam II
in 1765, though some sources date it to 1766.
Nizam Ali initially refused to accept Shah Alam II's firman and agreed to lease the Circars in 1766.
Jogipantulu was respected by Ruknudaula, used the Gollapudi pay mutiny in negotiations, proposed ₹15 lakh annually, and the final treaty fixed ₹9 lakh.
Nizam Ali made Jogipantulu the Majumdar of
Rajamahendravaram
, while the British gave him the title Raja Bahadur.

secs.t: Ceded Districts - territories and treaty

x: The Treaty of Hyderabad of 1798 was followed by the treaty of 1800, under which the Nizam ceded territories to meet the cost of the subsidiary force.
The ceded territories of Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary were known as Dattamandalalu, or the Ceded Districts.
The Andhra Mahasabha at Nandyal, presided over by
Dr S. Radhakrishnan
, approved the name Rayalaseema proposed by Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao.
The 1801 acquisition of Nellore and Chittoor completed Company control over the Andhra region, which Wellesley merged into the Madras Presidency.

secs.t: Hyderabad Residency and the British Resident

x: Resident
James Kirkpatrick
reported the Nizam's French battalions in the 1790s and pushed him into the Subsidiary Alliance of 1798.
James Kirkpatrick built the Hyderabad Residency building, which was popularly known as the
Koti
Turrebaz Khan attacked the Residency on 17 July 1857 in an attempt to free Chida Khan, but Davidson repulsed the attack.

secs.t: States annexed under Doctrine of Lapse - order, and states taken on other grounds

x: Punjab annexed 1849
(the key there is blank, but 1849 is correct per CDI and IYB).
Baghat
was annexed in 1850; Udaipur, Jhansi and Nagpur followed in 1852, 1853 and 1854 respectively.
Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of
misgovernment
, based on reports by Residents Sleeman and Outram against Wajid Ali Shah.
Jaitpur and Sambalpur were annexed in 1849, Baghat in 1850, the small state of Udaipur in 1852, and Jhansi in 1853, all under the Doctrine of Lapse.

secs.t: Annexation policy - names and authors

x: Lord Hastings
pursued subordinate isolation during 1813–1823, binding each princely state separately to the paramount Company.
Lord Dalhousie
pursued annexation for misgovernment, including the annexation of Awadh in 1856.
After 1858, subordinate union developed under the
Crown through the Queen's Proclamation
All four changes formed part of the post-1858 policy of subordinate union and the altered relationship with the princely states.

secs.t: Paramountcy over princely states - grounds for intervention, subordinate isolation

x: The British claimed intervention to fulfil international commitments and also intervened in succession disputes and cases of misgovernment.
Subordinate isolation bound each state separately to the paramount Company and isolated it from other princely states.
After 1858, the princes were described as “breakwaters to the storm” under the policy of subordinate union.

secs.t: Subordinate alliances with Rajput states - negotiator and aims

x: Charles Metcalfe
negotiated the treaties with the Rajput states in 1818 under Lord Hastings.
The alliances aimed to protect the Rajput states from the Marathas and Pindaris, bring them under British paramountcy and isolate them from Maratha powers.

secs.t: Wellesley - Subsidiary Alliance objectives and effects

x: Wellesley sought to exclude French influence seen in the Nizam's French battalions under Raymond and Tipu Sultan's French connections.
The alliance reduced sovereignty, imposed financial burdens, caused territorial cessions such as the Nizam's Ceded Districts and increased dependence on the Company.
The subsidy drained allied states and could lead to territorial cessions, as happened with the Nizam's Ceded Districts.

secs.t: Ring-fence policy - author and buffer states

x: The Ring-fence policy sought to guard the Company's own frontiers by defending the borders of neighbouring states.
Awadh acted as a buffer protecting Bengal from the Marathas and Afghans.
Awadh was developed as a buffer after Buxar in 1765, and Hastings sold Kora and Allahabad to its Nawab.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Telangana
remained under the Nizam, whereas the Northern Circars and Ceded Districts together broadly correspond to Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema.
The discontent of rulers, taluqdars and sepoys, intensified by the lapse annexations and the takeover of Awadh, led to the abandonment of the policy after 1857.
Hyderabad was the first state to sign the Subsidiary Alliance, doing so in 1798.

rows.title: Andhra region under the Company - Machilipatnam, Ceded Districts, early administration and revenue
sub: Group-II M1-A-54: Andhra under the Company - acquisition of the Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts
Group-II M1-A-55: Company administration in Andhra - districts, revenue and judicial arrangements

secs.t: Chronology of Andhra colonial events

x: The firman was issued in 1765, the treaty transferring the Circars was concluded in 1766, and the Treaty of Masulipatnam settled the dispute in 1768.
The correct order is Treaty of Masulipatnam (1768), Guntur handed over (1788), Battle of Padmanabham (1794), and Subsidiary Alliance (1798).
The events occurred in 1788, 1794, 1820 and 1948 respectively: Guntur, Padmanabham, extension of Ryotwari, and abolition of zamindari.

secs.t: Collectorates/districts - formation, Masulipatnam Council, Committee of Circuit

x: Exam angle: year of a district's creation (Kadapa 1911 trap), and the count of collectorates by 1856.
Before acquiring the Circars, the East India Company maintained factories at
Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam
The Northern Circars were governed by a
Chief-in-Council at Masulipatnam
until the earlier administrative arrangement was replaced.
The Collector was responsible for land revenue, law and order, and acted as District Magistrate or Judge.
The Collector’s judicial powers were withdrawn in 1816, although revenue and administrative responsibilities continued.
The initial eight collectorates included Ganjam, Bellary and Kurnool, but not Chittoor.

secs.t: Revenue terms and taxes - Moturpha, peshkash, Haveli

x: The Permanent Settlement introduced
a fixed revenue demand
in place of the auctioning of zamindaris.
Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793, and it was applied in Andhra in 1802.
Permanent Settlement was applied in Andhra in 1802, while Ryotwari was applied in the Ceded Districts.
Nine-tenths
of the estimated revenue went to the government and one-tenth went to the zamindar.

secs.t: Revenue system - Permanent Settlement areas vs Ryotwari areas

x: Zamindari applied to estates such as Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram; Ryotwari dealt directly with the ryot; and Mahalwari involved collection through village headmen.
Ryotwari areas experienced heavy assessment, often exceeding 50 percent of the produce, along with dependence on moneylenders and alienation of land.
Ryotwari was first introduced in
Baramahal in 1792
, the area now comprising Salem and Krishnagiri in Tamil Nadu, under Captain Alexander Read with Munro.

secs.t: Ceded Districts - region, old name, Rayalaseema, headquarters

x: The Ceded Districts comprised Kadapa, Kurnool and Anantapur in present-day Andhra Pradesh, together with Bellary, now in Karnataka.
The region was known as
Dattamandalam or Dattamandalalu
, meaning the ceded lands, until 1928.
The territories changed hands during the Mysore conflicts and were finally ceded by the Nizam in 1800 under the Subsidiary Alliance arrangement.
The Ceded region functioned as one collectorate centred at
Anantapur
under Munro until 1808.

secs.t: Company officials - Munro, Cotton and his assistant, C.P. Brown

x: Thomas Munro
became the first Collector of the Ceded Districts in 1800, with sub-collectors stationed at Harpanahalli, Kadapa, Adoni and Kurnool.
C.P. Brown studied Telugu thoroughly and published Vemana’s verses as well as a Telugu-English dictionary.

Arthur Cotton built the major anicuts; C.P. Brown contributed to Telugu revival and manuscript work; Colin Mackenzie preserved records; and Thomas Munro introduced ryotwari and suppressed the palegars.

secs.t: Zamindaris - Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram, Venkatagiri; battles

x: After the British defeated and killed Chinna Vijayaramaraju at Padmanabham, his minor son Narayana Babu was made zamindar.
George Russell
took charge of the forts of Vizianagaram after the minor Narayana Babu became zamindar.
Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram were pre-existing estates brought under the Permanent Settlement
The hereditary zamindari families of the Northern Circars included
Velamas, Reddis and Kshatriya Rajus

secs.t: Northern Circars → districts, stages of acquisition, Mughal grant

x: The Northern Circars corresponded to the Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, East Godavari, West Godavari and Krishna regions, with Guntur added to the group.
Robert Clive secured the firman from
Shah Alam II
; the firman is dated 1765 in the detailed chronology.
Since the Nizam initially refused to accept the firman, the Company negotiated a lease of the Circars from him in 1766.

secs.t: Intermediaries in the Circar lease - Kandregula Jogipantulu

x: Jogipantulu secured the lease of the Circars to the Company for an annual payment of
15 lakh rupees
When the Nizam was at Rajamahendravaram, his army at Gollapudi mutinied over unpaid pay.
Kandregula Jogipantulu was a prominent dubashi and envoy who acted between the Nizam's court and the Company's men at Machilipatnam.

secs.t: Carnatic districts (Nellore, Prakasam area, part of Chittoor) - year, ruler

x: Nellore and Chittoor were once under
Aravidu Sriranga Raya III
and later formed part of the Carnatic.
After the Second Carnatic War, the British installed
Muhammad Ali
as Nawab of the Carnatic, though his position became secure only after 1763.
The British shielded Muhammad Ali from
Najibullah of Nellore, the Marathas and Hyder Ali

secs.t: Treaties with the Nizam - terms, peshkash, Subsidiary Alliance

x: Salabat Jung's grant belongs to 1759, the Circar lease to 1766, the Treaty of Masulipatnam to 1768 and the Treaty of Hyderabad to 1798.
The Treaty of Masulipatnam allowed the Company to retain the Circars for a reduced annual peshkash of 9 lakh rupees, along with military assistance to the Nizam.

secs.t: Company taxes - Moturpha, Sayer, Abkari, Peshcush

x: Exam angle: statement pairs. "Moturpha is a salt tax" is false; "Peshcush is the revenue collected from zamindars" is true.
Sayer
was the tax imposed on inland transit and customs duties on goods.
Moturpha was imposed on trades and occupations, including looms, shops and artisans.
The Madras Native Association's petition of 1861 complained about the burden of
Moturpha

secs.t: Chiefs and Councils system - Masulipatnam, Vizagapatnam

x: The Company maintained factories and godowns at
Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam
before acquiring the Circars.
Provincial Chiefs and Councils
at Masulipatnam and Vizagapatnam governed the Circars before the district Collector system replaced them.
The station-level Chiefs and Councils were also described as the Board of Revenue, and district Collectors replaced them in 1794.

secs.t: Circuit Committee - purpose, findings

x: The Circuit Committee recommended against the highest-bidder auction system because it harmed both the government and the ryots.

secs.t: Judicial courts hierarchy - Munsiff, Zilla, Sadr Adalat

x: Provincial appellate powers were expanded in 1820, while the Sadar Adalat and Sadar Faujdari Adalat were the civil and criminal apex courts for natives at Madras.
The Madras Supreme Court, established in 1801, dealt with
British subjects in Madras town
British judicial procedure displaced village panchayats and was criticised as slow and costly.

secs.t: Munro's judicial reforms - Indian officials, village courts

x: Munro presided over the Judicial Commission in 1814, whose report was submitted in April 1816 and was largely accepted.
The Madras Regulations of 1816 established Munsiff courts and Panchayat courts in every large village and district as courts of first instance.
Village officials handled
petty thefts
under the reformed arrangements.

secs.t: Police administration - Daroga system, village watch

x: Cornwallis created thanas under darogas, who were Indian officers assisted by constables.
The daroga system placed Indian officers in charge of thanas with constables assisting them, but abuse of authority was a recognised criticism.
Traditional village watchmen continued but were
supplemented by a central police force under a District Superintendent
Munro's changes in 1816 transferred police supervision from
judges to Collectors

secs.t: Board of Revenue - establishment, functions

x: The Board of Revenue was at the state level, the Collector at the district level, the Tahsildar at the taluk level and the Karanam and Munsab at the village level.
The hierarchy placed the Collector at the district level, Sub-Collector or Revenue Officer at the divisional level and Deputy Tahsildar or Firka Revenue Inspector at the firka level.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Circars came under Company control in 1766, Guntur in 1788, the Ceded Districts in 1800 and Nellore-Chittoor in 1801.
The contrasting development of the Circars and the Ceded Districts later shaped the
Sri Bagh Pact
debate.
The plea invoked
Article 14
and argued that officers without legal training should not adjudicate land-title disputes.

rows.title: Establishment of British rule in Andhra - administrative consolidation and its effects
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-142

secs.t: Anicuts - Dowleswaram, Vijayawada, Sangam; Cotton, Veeranna, Ramapada Sagaram

x: The
Guntur famine of 1832–33
prompted the proposal for an anicut near Rajahmundry.
The main work was completed in April 1852 at a cost of Rs 1.5 lakh, with Veenam Veeranna serving as Indian assistant.
Charles Orr built the Krishna anicut on
Arthur Cotton
's plan.
Arthur Cotton suggested renaming
Rajahmundry and Machilipatnam
districts as Godavari and Krishna respectively.

secs.t: Economic impact - handicrafts, commercial crops, land revenue burden

x: Deindustrialisation occurred because artisans lost traditional patronage and British goods entered duty-free.
Since land revenue had to be paid in cash, farmers increasingly cultivated commercial crops such as tobacco, indigo, cotton and oilseeds.
The shift from food crops to commercial crops reduced food availability and made the region more vulnerable to famines.

secs.t: Railways, roads, telegraph and canals - first lines, Buckingham Canal

x: Vizagapatnam port developed for the movement of iron ore and agricultural exports.
The Buckingham Canal was a salt-water navigation canal along the coast, passing through Pulicat Lake.
The Buckingham Canal is now part of
NW-4
, the Kakinada–Puducherry waterway, along with the Eluru and Kakinada canals.
The Buckingham Canal was extended as famine relief during

secs.t: British administrators - contribution

x: C.P. Brown served as the Collector of
Kadapa
C.P. Brown contributed to Telugu revival, edited the Madras Literary Journal and served as Curator of the Madras Manuscript Library.
Colin Mackenzie was the first Surveyor General in 1815 and also preserved manuscripts and records.
G.N. Taylor, Rajahmundry Sub-Collector, started Anglo-Vernacular schools across Andhra.

secs.t: Telugu journals on British rule - criticism voiced

x: Linked PYQ:
M.G. Ranade
called
Veeresalingam
"South India's Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar".

secs.t: Madras Presidency districts of Andhra - reorganisation

x: In 1859, Rajahmundry and Machilipatnam were reorganised into Godavari and Krishna districts respectively.
The correct order is 1802, 1859, 1904 and 1925: union of collectorates, reorganisation into Godavari and Krishna, formation of Guntur and East Godavari, and formation of West Godavari.

secs.t: Madras Presidency governance - Collector's powers, gazetteers

x: From 1819, the Collector in Ganjam also acted as Agent to the Governor for the Agency tracts.

x: The foundation for replacing the gates of the Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage was laid on
13 July 2026
The project involves replacing 117 gates of the Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage.
The barrage is 5.837 kilometres long, was rebuilt in 1969, and irrigates about 10 lakh acres.

in February 2026.
