rows.title: Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh wars; conquest of Sindh; Doctrine of Lapse and annexations
sub: Group-II S1-63: Consolidation of British power - Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh wars

secs.t: Anglo-Maratha Wars - Governor-General, treaties, parties

x: Exam angle: the Treaty of Salbai was between the
British and the Marathas
Chronology item: Wandiwash (1760), Nand Kumar hanged (1775), Salbai (1782), death of Tipu (1799).
Baji Rao II accepted the
Subsidiary Alliance
through the Treaty of Bassein after fleeing from Holkar’s attack.
The stated causes were British commercial interest in Malabar pepper and cardamom, Mysore's threat to Madras, and Mysore's French alliances.
The British broke the Treaty of Madras by not helping Haidar Ali against the Marathas, and they also captured Mahe, contributing to the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
The sequence was the Treaty of Surat in 1775, Treaty of Purandar in 1776, Convention of Wadgaon in 1779 and Treaty of Salbai in 1782.
The Treaty of Surji-Arjangaon was concluded with Scindia in 1803 and gave the British
Delhi and control over the Mughal emperor
The Third Anglo-Maratha War was set off by Lord Hastings' campaign against the
Pindaris
, followed by the rising of the Peshwa, Bhonsle and Holkar.
The Bhonsle of Nagpur and the Holkar of Indore
joined Baji Rao II after his attack on the British Residency at Poona.
The Treaty of Salbai restored the status quo, allowed the British to retain Salsette and ushered in approximately twenty years of peace.

secs.t: Anglo-Sikh Wars I-II - battles, treaties, annexation

x: Lord Hardinge
was the Governor-General during the First Anglo-Sikh War, fought in 1845–46.
The First Anglo-Sikh War began when the Sikh army crossed the Sutlej, whose boundary had been fixed by the Treaty of Amritsar of 1809.
Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal and Sobraon
were the principal battles of the First Anglo-Sikh War.
The British Resident became the virtual ruler under the Treaty of Bhairowal, not as a result of the First War's battles themselves; Bhairowal was a subsequent treaty of December 1846.
Mudki and Sobraon belonged to the First Anglo-Sikh War, while Chillianwala and Gujrat belonged to the Second.

secs.t: Paramountcy - grounds for intervention; Rajputana alliances

x: Misgovernance was cited as a ground for intervention and annexation in
Coorg and Awadh
Lord Hastings
developed subsidiary alliances into the system of British paramountcy and imposed humiliating treaties on the Peshwa and Scindia.
The Rajputana states accepted British protection and surrendered control over their external relations under subordinate alliances in 1818.

secs.t: Conquest of Sindh - Napier, Amirs, Miani

x: The conquest and annexation of Sindh took place in 1843 under
Lord Ellenborough
The stated objectives were recovery of prestige after the First Afghan War, countering Russia and securing Indus trade.
Sir Charles Napier
used coercive diplomacy against the Amirs and annexed Sindh after the battles of Miani and Dabo.

secs.t: Wars of expansion - chronological order

x: The
Carnatic Wars
were fought during the period 1746–1763.
The British effectively took control of India from the Marathas; the Mughal emperor no longer represented the main political power being conquered.
The Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–1799) preceded the Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818), which in turn preceded the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–1849).
The statement emphasises that the Marathas were the principal major Indian power whose political and military position the British had to break in their expansion.

secs.t: Other annexations - Coorg, Sikkim, Karnataka titles, pensions

x: Coorg was taken in 1834 by
Lord William Bentinck
on the plea of misgovernance, along with Central Cachar.
Dalhousie annexed parts of Sikkim in 1850 after two British doctors had been detained.
Nana Sahib, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, was denied continuation of the Peshwa pension after Baji Rao II died in 1851.

secs.t: Dalhousie's imperialism - a cause of 1857

x: All four developments contributed to the growth of resentment.
Awadh’s cotton market and agrarian wealth were important motives, while misgovernance was used as the formal justification.
By 1856, British India stretched from the
Hindukush to Burma
Expansion created geographical unity and a basis for common resistance.

secs.t: Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan - modernisation, capital, embassies, French links

x: Tipu Sultan sent ambassadors to France in an effort to
obtain European technology
and modernise his state.
Tipu Sultan is said to have joined the Jacobin Club and planted a Tree of Liberty at Srirangapatnam.
Lord Wellesley feared Tipu Sultan's alliance with Napoleon
, which contributed to the decision to wage the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

secs.t: Governor-Generals → wars fought

x: Warren Hastings
was Governor-General from 1772 to 1785 and his tenure included the Rohilla War, the First Anglo-Maratha War and the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
Sir John Shore
, Governor-General from 1793 to 1798, followed a policy of neutrality at Kharda, where the Marathas defeated the Nizam.
The First Anglo-Burmese War occurred from 1824 to 1826 during
Amherst
’s tenure, and the Treaty of Yandabo transferred Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim to the British sphere.

secs.t: Battles → war and British commander

x: Porto Novo was commanded by Eyre Coote, Assaye by Arthur Wellesley, and both Mudki and Chillianwala by Sir Hugh Gough.
Porto Novo was fought in 1781 during the
Second Anglo-Mysore War
Assaye, Delhi and Laswari were important battles of the
Second Anglo-Maratha War
Chillianwala was fought in 1849 during the Second Anglo-Sikh War.

secs.t: Nizam of Hyderabad's alliances and territories ceded (Ceded Districts - Rayalaseema)

x: In the First Anglo-Mysore War, the Nizam, the Marathas and the British formed an alliance against
Haidar Ali
The Nizam blamed Sir John Shore's neutrality at Kharda and hired French battalions under Raymond.
In 1800, the Nizam ceded
Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary
The territories ceded by the Nizam in 1800 were known as the Ceded Districts or
Dattamandalalu

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The classification is: conquest for Sindh and Punjab, Doctrine of Lapse for Satara to Nagpur, misgovernance for Awadh and Coorg, and abolition of titles for Carnatic and Tanjore.
Nellore and Chittoor were taken from the Carnatic Nawab in 1801 on the charge of
collusion with Tipu Sultan
, an early pretext annexation.

rows.title: Governors-General of Bengal and of India - Warren Hastings to Dalhousie: key measures

secs.t: Governor-General - key measure

x: Warren Hastings shifted the treasury to Calcutta, stopped the ₹26 lakh tribute to Shah Alam and established Diwani and Fauzdari Adalats.
Minto I
concluded the Treaty of Amritsar with Ranjit Singh in 1809.
The Mahalwari system was introduced in 1822 through Holt Mackenzie during the tenure of Marquess Hastings.
The Act provided for a four-member council, subordinated Bombay and Madras to Bengal, and led to the establishment of the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774.

secs.t: Governors-General in chronological order

x: Sir John Shore served from 1793 to 1798, and
Wellesley
succeeded him in 1798.
Wellesley served before Cornwallis’s second term; Cornwallis’s second term was followed by Sir George Barlow and then Minto I.
Marquess Hastings served as Governor-General from 1813 to 1823.
Bentinck served from 1828 to 1835; after the Charter Act of 1833, he held the title Governor-General of India from 1833 onward.

secs.t: Events during tenure - which Governor-General

x: The suppression of Thuggee, with Sleeman’s assistance, took place during
William Bentinck
’s tenure.
Sir Charles Metcalfe
is associated with the liberation of the press during his brief tenure in 1835–36.
The Charter Act of 1813 was passed at the transition between
Minto I and Marquess Hastings
, whose tenure began in 1813.

secs.t: FIRST - Governor, Governor-General, Acts that changed the title

x: Before 1773 the office was titled Governor of Bengal (1757-1772), and Bentinck was the first GG of India.
Bentinck was also the
last GG of Bengal

secs.t: PERSON - titles and real names

x: Lord Wellesley
described himself as the "Bengal Tiger".
All four pairs are correctly matched.

secs.t: Impeachment of Warren Hastings - charges and outcome

x: Warren Hastings was impeached in 1787 by Edmund Burke and the Whigs in the British Parliament.
The impeachment trial of Warren Hastings ran from 1788 to 1795 and ended in his acquittal.
The charges included the Rohilla War, the treatment of Chait Singh, the plunder of the Begums of Awadh and the judicial murder of Nand Kumar.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Under Wellesley, the Subsidiary Alliance with the Nizam was concluded in 1798, the Ceded Districts followed in 1800, and Andhra was merged into Madras in 1801.
The prohibition of human sacrifice in 1845 is associated with Hardinge I. Dalhousie is associated with caste disabilities legislation in 1850 and widow remarriage in 1856.

rows.title: Viceroys of India - Canning to Mountbatten: key measures, acts and events

secs.t: Capital shift to Delhi, Delhi Durbars, summer capital, Partition of Bengal, Bihar reorganisation

x: Exam angle: A-R pairs - the 1911 Durbar was for George V; the Edward VII coronation Durbar was 1903 (true, but not the reason for 1911).
In 1912, Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal attempted to assassinate Lord Hardinge II during his state-entry procession into Delhi.
The anti-partition
Vande Mataram movement
contributed to the revocation of the Partition of Bengal, which was announced through King George V in 1911.

secs.t: Viceroy → key measure/event and memoirs

x: Lord Ripon's Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882 is described as the Magna Carta of Local Self-Government.
Both the Third Burma War of 1885 and the foundation of the Indian National Congress in 1885 occurred during
Lord Dufferin
's tenure.
Rand and Ayerst were killed by the Chapekar brothers in 1897 during the tenure of
Lord Elgin II
The Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh tragedy occurred during Lord Chelmsford's tenure.
The Wavell Plan and Simla Conference were held in 1945 and failed largely because of disagreement over Jinnah's position.
The Cabinet Mission consisted of Stafford
Cripps, A. V. Alexander and Pethick-Lawrence
The Royal Titles Act was passed in 1876, followed by the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act in 1878.
The Police Commission of 1902 was appointed by Lord Curzon and functioned under
Andrew Frazer

secs.t: Archaeology and census firsts

x: Alexander Cunningham
was the founder of the Archaeological Survey of India, which was set up in 1861 under Lord Canning.
The motto of the Archaeological Survey of India is '
Pratnakirti Apavarini
The first census was conducted in 1872 during Lord Mayo's tenure.
The first census was non-synchronous and the first regular synchronous census was held in 1881.

secs.t: FIRST - first Viceroy, only Viceroy assassinated and assassin

x: Sher Ali Afridi, a convict, murdered Lord Mayo in
the Andamans in 1872
while Mayo was on tour.
The Government of India Act, 1858 created the designation Viceroy, and
Lord Canning
became its first holder.
After 1858, the Governor-General of India was also styled the Viceroy, signifying his role as the representative of the Crown.

secs.t: Viceroy → Act passed

x: Exam angle: "match the Act with the Viceroy" - Lytton owns three (Royal Titles, VPA, Arms), Ripon repealed VPA.
The Royal Titles Act was passed in 1876 during
Lord Lytton
's viceroyalty and recognised Queen Victoria as Empress of India.
The Ilbert Bill was introduced in 1883 during
Lord Ripon
's viceroyalty.

secs.t: Viceroys and their Acts in chronological order

x: The correct order is Canning's Indian Councils Act of 1861, Mayo's 1870 resolution, Lytton's Royal Titles Act of 1876 and Ripon's First Factory Act of 1881.
The sequence is Canning, Lawrence, Mayo, Northbrook, Lytton and Ripon.
The correct order is Curzon, Minto II, Hardinge II, Chelmsford and Reading.
The correct sequence is Willingdon, Linlithgow, Wavell and Mountbatten.

secs.t: Viceroy → commission appointed

x: The Durand Commission, appointed in 1893 during Lord Lansdowne's viceroyalty, dealt with
the Afghan boundary
The Lyall Commission was appointed in 1897 during Lord Elgin II's viceroyalty to examine famine-related matters.
The Royal Commission on Labour was appointed in 1929 during
Lord Irwin
's viceroyalty.
The famine commission chain was Strachey under Lytton, Lyall under Elgin II and MacDonnell under Curzon.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gadicherla and Bodi Narayana Rao
are identified as the first Telugu political prisoners on 18 July 1908, during Minto II's tenure.
Lytton's reactionary policies, including the Durbar during famine conditions, the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act, fuelled early nationalist criticism.
The Ilbert Bill controversy revealed the racial discrimination involved in preventing Indian judges from exercising jurisdiction over European British subjects on equal terms.

rows.title: Company's constitutional framework - Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Act of 1786

secs.t: Pre-1773 Parliamentary control - 1760s Acts, Select and Secret Committees

x: After the Battle of Buxar in 1764, Shah Alam granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company in 1765.
In 1772, Parliament appointed a Select Committee headed by Burgoyne and a Secret Committee to investigate the Company's affairs.
The reports of the two committees investigating Company affairs formed the basis for the
Regulating Act

secs.t: Regulating Act 1773 - GG of Bengal, subordination of presidencies, Supreme Court, defects

x: Exam angle: "incorrect statement" - it did
not
abolish the Court of Directors.
The Supreme Court at Calcutta, established in 1774, consisted of one Chief Justice and three judges and exercised civil and criminal jurisdiction.
The Court of Directors had to report on the Company's
revenue, civil and military affairs
to the British Government.

secs.t: Act of 1786 - power of the Governor-General over his council and why

x: The Act of 1786 was passed to meet Lord Cornwallis's condition for accepting the office of Governor-General.
The Act of 1786 allowed the Governor-General to override his Council in special cases and combined the office with that of Commander-in-Chief.
The Act of 1786 addressed the defect under which the Governor-General, including Hastings, could be repeatedly outvoted by his Council.

secs.t: Amending Act 1781 - jurisdiction changes

x: The correct sequence is Regulating Act of 1773, Amending Act of 1781, Pitt's India Act of 1784 and Act of 1786.
The Act exempted the Governor-General, the Council and Company servants from Supreme Court jurisdiction for acts done in their official capacity.
The Act directed the Supreme Court to respect the personal laws of
Hindus and Muslims

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sadar Adalat and Sadar Faujdari Adalat dealt with
persons other than British subjects
in the Madras Presidency.
The Ministry of Law and Justice traces its origin to the
Charter Act of 1833
, which introduced the Law Member and the first Law Commission.
The Ministry of Law and Justice is traced to the Charter Act of 1833, which centralised legislative authority in the Governor-General-in-Council.

rows.title: Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853 - provisions and significance

secs.t: Charter Act 1853 - open competition, separate legislative functions, territories held in trust

x: Exam angle: the "held in trust" line is fill-in-the-blank bait: answer
Charter Act
(not Regulating Act).
Charles Trevelyan and Robert Lowe
supported the introduction of open competitive examination for the civil services.
The
Charter Act of 1853
continued the Company's authority over its Indian territories in trust for the British Crown, its heirs and successors.

secs.t: Trade monopoly - Act ending it in India, Act ending tea and China trade

x: Exam angle: CGPSC 2022 - "the 1813 Act abolished the Company's trade monopoly" is marked
not true
because tea and China trade were kept.
The Act ended the general trade monopoly in India but retained the Company's exclusive trade in
tea and with China
The
Charter Act of 1833
removed the Company's remaining monopoly over tea trade and trade with China.

secs.t: Charter Act 1813 - education grant, missionaries' entry, significance statements

x: The Charter Act of 1813 provided one lakh rupees, or
, annually for education-related purposes.
Under Evangelical pressure and the influence of figures such as William Wilberforce and Charles Grant, the Act allowed missionaries to enter India and propagate Christianity.
The missionary provision reflected Evangelical pressure, including that of William Wilberforce and Charles Grant, as well as Utilitarian influence.

secs.t: Charter Act 1833 - title changes, end of commercial functions, Law Member, Law Commission, Agra Presidency

x: Exam angle: "final step towards centralisation" =
The
Governor-General-in-Council
received exclusive legislative power for all British India, and the presidencies lost their law-making powers.
Section 87 declared that
religion, place of birth, descent or colour
should not bar an Indian from holding office.
The separated territory was placed under the Agra Presidency in 1834 and was renamed the
North-Western Provinces

secs.t: Macaulay - Law Member, remarks on the Company

x: Macaulay was the head of the first Law Commission, and the Indian Penal Code emerged from his draft.
Macaulay made this observation in his speech in the House of Commons on the Bill that became the
Charter Act of 1833
The Macaulay Committee of 1854 dealt with the ICS after the Charter Act of 1853.

secs.t: Centralisation trend - Governor-General's legislative power across Acts

x: The measures of 1773, 1784 and 1786 successively strengthened central supervision and the authority of the Governor-General.
The
Charter Act of 1833
marked the peak of centralisation by vesting exclusive legislative power in the Governor-General-in-Council.
The Indian Councils Act of 1861 marked decentralisation by restoring legislative power to the Bombay and Madras presidencies.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Charter Act of 1853 opened the way for a legislature and merit-based recruitment to the ICS; the transfer to the Crown came later through the Government of India Act of 1858.
The Charter Act of 1853 was the last Charter Act, and the Government of India Act of 1858 ended the East India Company's rule by transferring authority to the Crown.

rows.title: Land revenue systems - Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari; areas and effects
sub: Group-II S1-70: Land revenue systems - Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari; economic impact
Group-II M1-A-56: Revenue settlements in Andhra - Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari system of Thomas Munro

secs.t: System → originator + year + areas

x: The Ryotwari System was introduced in Baramahal and later in the Madras Presidency; the Mahalwari System covered the North-Western Provinces; and the Permanent Settlement extended to the Northern Circars.
The correct sequence is Permanent Settlement in 1793, Mahalwari proposal in 1822, Ryotwari introduction in the Madras Presidency in 1820, and Mahalwari revision in 1833.
The Mahalwari System was associated with the North-Western Provinces, Punjab, the Gangetic valley and Central India, not Bengal and the Northern Circars.

secs.t: Features of each system - ownership, settlement period, intermediaries (comparison)

x: Revenue was fixed permanently under the Permanent Settlement, whereas assessments under the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems were periodically revised.
The zamindar was the collector under the Permanent Settlement, the individual farmer under the Ryotwari System, and the village headman or lambardar under the Mahalwari System.
All four statements describe features of the Ryotwari arrangement: individual settlement, land-based assessment, periodic revision and supervision through village officers under the Collector.

secs.t: Ryotwari - first area in Madras Presidency, Read and Munro

x: Exam angle: "Ryotwari first introduced in Andhra" = Rayalaseema. "In the Madras Presidency" = Baramahal. A 2018 PYQ stem gave the date as 1808. The answer is still Munro.
The first experiment was conducted in
Baramahal
, comprising areas such as Salem, Krishnagiri, Dharmapuri and Tiruvannamalai.
Munro distrusted Palegars and big intermediaries and therefore favoured settling revenue directly with the cultivator.
Munro considered the system suitable because the Ceded Districts lacked strong zamindars and he did not want to strengthen the Palegars.
The Northern Circars were mainly zamindari areas, whereas Haveli lands under direct British control later came under Ryotwari.
Ryotwari revenue was linked to
the actual area cultivated
, so the amount could rise or fall accordingly.

secs.t: Mahalwari - areas and officials → role

x: Holt Mackenzie devised the system, R.M. Bird revised it through survey-based settlement, and James Thomason carried on Bird's settlement in the NWP.
Bird's major contribution was
the survey-based revision of the Mahalwari settlement
in north India.
Baramahal came under Company control in 1792, the Permanent Settlement became permanent in 1793, Regulation VII was issued in 1822 and Regulation IX in 1833.

secs.t: Permanent Settlement - high revenue demand, Sunset Law, litigation, zamindari sales

x: Many old zamindars lost their estates for arrears, which were purchased by urban merchants and moneylenders, creating a new landed class.
The regulations of 1799, known as Haftam, and 1812, known as Panjam, enabled zamindars to seize tenants' property.
The decennial settlement made permanent in 1793 recognised zamindars as proprietors, with rights that were
alienable, rentable and heritable
The rationale included assured income, lower collection costs, a loyal landlord class and the hope that zamindars would improve the land.

secs.t: Ryotwari in Andhra - first region, later coastal extension

x: The Ceded Districts were ceded by the Nizam in 1800, after which Munro became principal collector and introduced Ryotwari there in 1802.
Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer
Campbell
before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.
Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram were old estates brought under the Zamindari arrangement.
The
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
provided for the abolition of estates and their conversion into Ryotwari holdings.

secs.t: Effects - indebtedness, absentee landlordism, revenue rigidity

x: Tenants-at-will were vulnerable to
rack-renting
, as landlords or their agents could demand excessive rents and threaten eviction.
The inflexible cash demand continued even during crop failures, forcing ryots to borrow from Mahajans and often mortgage or lose their land.
The Mughal zabt is described as involving a one-third share and taccavi loans, whereas the British demand was rigid and offered no famine remission.

secs.t: Andhra estates and Sarkar areas - settlement timeline

x: The correct sequence is Guntur acquired in 1788, Battle of Padmanabham in 1794, Ceded Districts obtained in 1800, and the 1802 settlements.
In the Battle of Padmanabham in 1794,
Vijayarama Gajapati Raju, the Vizianagaram zamindar
, was defeated.
The Company obtained the Northern Circars in 1765–66 through
a Mughal farman and a treaty with the Nizam
Moturpha was a tax on
professions, trades and looms
, affecting weavers, artisans and merchants in the Madras Presidency.

secs.t: Mahalwari - proposer, unit, periodic revision, regions

x: Mahalwari
revenue was periodically revised
, and each cultivator remained liable for his share of the village assessment.
Common ownership arrangements under the Mahalwari framework were called
Bhai Chara or Mahali
The Mahalwari-type arrangement is placed in
Nellore and Chittoor
in the relevant regional account; in some accounts, Nellore alone is specifically mentioned.

secs.t: Economic impact - commercialisation, moneylenders, land alienation, indebtedness

x: The need to meet cash revenue demands encouraged cultivation of commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute.
Merchant-landlords became prominent in Zamindari areas, while moneylender-landlords emerged particularly in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.
Under Zamindari, the profit from agriculture went to
the zamindars
rather than to the cultivators, contributing to agrarian inequality and indebtedness.

secs.t: Thomas Munro - posts, tenures, Rayalaseema legacy, philosophy

x: Munro served in the Mysore wars from 1780 to 1792, assisted Read in the Baramahal from 1792 to 1799, and became Collector of South Canara in 1798.
Munro served as Assistant to Read in the Baramahal, Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, President of the Judicial Commission, and finally Governor of Madras.

secs.t: Zamindari vs Ryotwari compared

x: Under the Permanent or Zamindari Settlement, the zamindar was treated as proprietor; under Ryotwari, the cultivator was treated as owner.
Permanent Settlement fixed the revenue demand permanently.
Default under Zamindari could result in forfeiture of the estate under the Sunset Law, while default under Ryotwari could lead to auction of the land.

secs.t: Mootah / village lease settlements

x: After 1802, mootahs were auctioned to mootahdars, who held them in the manner of
proprietary estates
Village-lease settlements, in which village headmen acted as lessees, replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts after Munro's departure from 1808 onward and lasted until about 1820.
In Nellore, village headmen collected and remitted the tax under an arrangement resembling the Mahalwari system.

secs.t: Impact on peasantry and zamindars

x: Ryotwari suffered from over-assessment, inadequate records and unclear boundaries.
Heavy assessments pushed peasants towards moneylenders; defaults could lead to land auctions and alienation.
Zamindari was associated with rent-racking of tenants and absentee landlordism.

secs.t: Inam Commission - year, purpose

x: The Madras Inam Commission was constituted in 1858 to investigate rent-free inam titles.
Valid rent-free inam titles were confirmed subject to payment of a quit-rent.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The three settlements made land transferable, helped create a loyal landlord class and contributed to rural indebtedness, which in turn fed peasant revolts.
Munro is remembered as the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and for establishing its direct relationship between the ryot and the state through ryotwari administration.
The three settlements shaped agrarian class relations and structures, which post-1947 land reforms sought to dismantle or modify.
The residential portion of Pulladigunta was reclassified from '
Thopu Poramboke
', enabling 201 families to receive ownership after nearly a century.

rows.title: Economic impact of colonial rule - drain of wealth, deindustrialisation, commercialisation of agriculture
sub: Group-II S1-71: Economic impact of colonial rule - drain of wealth, deindustrialisation, famines

secs.t: Drain of wealth theory → proponents, books and metaphors

x: Exam angle: "popularised by" = Naoroji; reason-for-drain options.
Dadabhai Naoroji
popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory and was known as the Grand Old Man and the father of Indian Nationalism.
Naoroji first stated the drain argument in
England's Debt to India
Dadabhai Naoroji
coined the expression 'moral drain' while explaining the economic consequences of colonial rule.
The drain is traced to the grant of the Diwani of Bengal in 1765, after which Indian resources were transferred to England without economic return.
The drain reduced the resources available for domestic investment, thereby stifling capital formation and industrialisation.

secs.t: Indian economy on the eve of independence - sectors, world income share, capital goods

x: More than 75 percent of the workforce depended on agriculture, but the sector contributed only about 50 percent of GDP, indicating low productivity and disguised unemployment.
India exported primary products such as raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo and jute.
The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 shortened the sea route and tightened British control over India's trade and economy.
British policy contributed to deindustrialisation, industry declined through loss of markets and agriculture remained stagnant with low productivity.
The export surplus generated by India was used for Britain’s office expenses and war expenses, contributing to the drain of wealth.
Large foodgrain imports and inflation led the First Plan to give top priority to
agriculture, irrigation and power
Nearly
97 per cent
of British capital before 1914 went to government projects, plantations and financial houses.

secs.t: Drain components - home charges, interest, salaries, pensions, railway returns, military

x: The guaranteed return was payable even when the railway lines did not earn the assured interest, placing the burden on Indian revenues.
Profits earned by British capitalists, merchants and banks in India and sent home constituted another component of the drain.
The Moderates opposed the financial burden of imperial wars, especially those in
Afghanistan and Burma

secs.t: Andhra textiles - employment rank, piece-goods trade, famous centres

x: Srikakulam is associated with muslin, Machilipatnam with dyed clothes, Nellore with towels and Eluru with carpets.
Nellore was famous for towels, whereas silk clothes were associated with Peddapuram, Dharmavaram, Adoni and Bellary.
Uppada was known for jamdani silk, while Ponduru was known for fine hand-spun khadi and is associated with Srikakulam.
High Company duties reduced the earlier textile trade to small boats carrying
salt and groceries

secs.t: Deindustrialisation - handloom decline, Charter Act 1813, one-way free trade, tariffs

x: The
Charter Act of 1813
ended the Company's monopoly, after which British machine-made goods entered India at low duty.
British goods entered India almost duty-free, whereas Indian manufactures faced heavy duties in Britain.
The sequence is coercion by Company agents in 1772, the Charter Act in 1813, Lancashire cloth in Bengal in 1786, and displacement by 1793.
The collapse of handicrafts pushed artisans onto the land, producing overcrowding in agriculture and disguised unemployment.
The cotton excise duty of 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was imposed to offset the import duty and is a classic example of tariff policy.
The 1793 Act and famines pushed weavers into
agriculture or wage labour
, increasing pressure on land.

secs.t: Commercialisation of agriculture - cash crops, regions, triangular trade, famines

x: Cotton was associated with the Deccan, Gujarat and Berar; jute with Bengal; opium with Bengal-Bihar and Malwa; and tea with Assam.
Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti reported Andhra famines in his paper The Crescent and founded the Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam.
Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti founded the Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam in 1852.

secs.t: Rise of modern industries - firsts

x: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was established in 1854 by
Cowasji Nanabhai Davar
The first
jute mill
was established at Rishra in Bengal in 1855.
TISCO, the Tata Iron and Steel Company, was incorporated in 1907 at
Jamshedpur
Jute mills were at Chittivalasa and Nellimarla, cotton ginning occurred in several districts, and the first railway was Puttur-Renigunta.

secs.t: Currency policy - rupee-sterling ratio and the Hilton Young Commission

x: The Hilton Young Commission was the
Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance
, appointed in 1926.
Both statements are true, and cheaper British imports increased competitive pressure on Indian producers and exporters, explaining the adverse effect.
Purshottamdas Thakurdas
was associated with the Indian business demand for a ratio of 1 shilling 4 pence.

secs.t: Famines → commission appointed, Famine Code, Andhra famines

x: The Guntur famine of 1832–33 was regarded as the worst in the south and caused about two lakh deaths, though one account gives the death share as 40 per cent.
The decline in cotton demand after the American Civil War contributed to the Ganjam famine, after which people migrated to Mauritius and Sri Lanka.
Budda Vengalareddy of Uyyalawada
fed people during the 1866 Kurnool famine and received a gold medal from Victoria on 1 January 1877.
The Guntur famine was also called Nandana Karuvu, caused very high mortality—reported as about two lakh or nearly half the population—and was marked by bodies being thrown into rivers.

secs.t: Peasant protection laws - against whom

x: The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act of 1879 protected peasants against
moneylenders
after the Deccan riots of 1875.
The Act aimed to prevent transfer of agricultural land from agriculturists to non-agriculturist moneylenders.

secs.t: Stages of colonialism - mercantile, industrial capital, finance capital

x: The mercantilist stage from 1757 to 1813 was marked by the Company's trade monopoly, direct plunder and the use of Bengal revenue for purchasing export goods.
From 1858 onwards, the finance-capital stage involved British capital in
railways, plantations and banks
R.P. Dutt proposed the three-stage interpretation in India Today, drawing on Karl Marx.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Colonial economic change involved the decline of India's manufacturing export position and its transformation into a supplier of raw materials.
The drain theory and the wider economic critique were major contributions of the Moderates and helped provide the basis for Swadeshi and early nationalism.
The comparison holds that IMF–World Bank structural adjustment programmes caused deindustrialisation through sudden tariff removal, reflecting a one-way free-trade logic comparable to colonial India.

rows.title: Famines under colonial rule and famine policy; Famine Commissions

secs.t: Major famines → year + region + mortality and epithets

x: The Doji Bara famine, also called the skull famine, occurred in 1791–92 and affected the Deccan, Hyderabad and the Northern Circars.
The correct sequence is Great Bengal Famine (1770), Doji Bara (1791–92), Orissa and Ganjam (1865–66), and Great Famine (1876–78).
The Richard Strachey Commission was appointed in 1880 after the
Great Famine of 1876–78
, during the viceroyalty of Lytton.

secs.t: Famine Commissions → chairman + Viceroy

x: Campbell was associated with John Lawrence, Strachey with Lytton, Lyall with Elgin II and MacDonnell with Curzon.
The
Lyall Commission
assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures to prevent or mitigate future famines.
The MacDonnell Commission was appointed in 1901 during Curzon’s tenure in relation to the famine of 1899–1900.

secs.t: Famine Code - year, drafting commission, provisions

x: The Famine Code of 1883 was framed on the recommendations of the
Strachey Commission
The Famine Code provided for stages of scarcity and famine, relief works for able-bodied persons, gratuitous relief for the old and infirm, and suspension or remission of revenue.
During the Company period, the government never adopted a famine code and provided only minimal relief.

secs.t: Famine relief policy - Temple wage, public works

x: The Temple wage provided about 1 pound of grain per day on relief works and was criticised as a starvation wage.
Sir Richard Temple
fixed the relief ration known as the Temple wage during the Madras famine of 1877.
Kautilya’s famine duties included supplying seeds and food, granting tax exemption and undertaking public works.

secs.t: Arthur Cotton's irrigation response in Godavari-Krishna

x: Arthur Cotton’s Godavari anicut project was reported in 1844, sanctioned in 1846, begun in 1847 and had its main structure completed in April 1852.
The Krishna anicut at Bezwada was proposed by Colonel Henry Atlock Lake and supervised by
Charles Orr
The Penna anicut at Nellore, dating from 1860, was constructed according to
Arthur Cotton
’s plan.

secs.t: Nationalist critique of famine policy

x: Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt
connected famines with the burden of high land revenue and the drain of wealth.
R.C. Dutt’s work titled Open Letters to Lord Curzon was associated with the year 1900.
Commercialisation, illustrated by cotton cultivation in Ganjam, and laissez-faire relief deepened the disasters caused by famine.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The five phases progress from Phase 1 Minimal through Phase 2 Stressed, Phase 3 Crisis and Phase 4 Emergency to Phase 5 Catastrophe/Famine.
The Guntur famine occurred in 1833, followed by the Campbell Commission in 1866, the Ganjam famine in 1865–66, and the Woodhead Commission in 1944.
Modern food security through the PDS is based on
availability, accessibility and affordability
of food.

rows.title: Education policy - Orientalist-Anglicist debate, Macaulay's Minute, Wood's Despatch 1854, Hunter Commission

secs.t: Institutions - founder and year

x: Exam angle: institution-founder pairs; "first educational institution in British India" = Calcutta Madrasa (Warren Hastings).
Lord Richard Wellesley
established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 to train Company civil servants.
The institutions were founded in the order Calcutta Madrasa (1781), Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784), Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791), and Fort William College (1800).

secs.t: Wood's Despatch 1854 - epithet, provisions, first universities

x: Sir Charles Wood drafted the 1854 Despatch as
President of the Board of Control
The Despatch proposed a hierarchy beginning with vernacular primary schools and progressing through Anglo-vernacular high schools and affiliated colleges to universities.
Wood's Despatch recommended supervision of vernacular education, teacher training, and a differentiated language policy using English at higher levels and vernacular languages at lower levels.

secs.t: Later commissions and plans - year, Viceroy, focus

x: The Hunter Commission recommended handing schools to local boards and municipalities and encouraged private enterprise.
The Indian Universities Commission was appointed in 1902 during
Lord Curzon
's Viceroyalty.
The 1913 Resolution responded to Gokhale's demand for
compulsory primary education
and provided funding for primary education.
The Sadler Commission recommended a 12-year school course, an intermediate stage, and a three-year degree.

secs.t: Steps introducing English education - 1813, GCPI, 1835 Act

x: The Charter Act was passed in 1813, the General Committee was established in 1823, the English Education Act followed in 1835, and Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854.
The 1835 resolution dealt a fatal blow to the district and tahsildari vernacular schools of the Madras Presidency.
Dalhousie's Minute of 1853 backed vernacular education, and Wood's Despatch followed in 1854.

secs.t: Education in Andhra - Presidency College, Machilipatnam, Rajahmundry, missionaries

x: Elphinstone's scheme dates to 1839, the regional school to 1854, the second-grade college to 1873 and the degree college to 1877.
Mission schools admitted Sudras and Panchamas, thereby extending education to social groups that had often been excluded from traditional educational institutions.
The correct order is Central Collegiate Institute (1841), Noble School (1843), Madras University (1857), and the grants-in-aid system linked to results (1877–78).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: English education contributed to the emergence of a reformist middle class in coastal Andhra, represented by Kandukuri Veeresalingam, and also helped create a pan-Indian educated elite.
The
downward filtration
approach was criticised because it prioritised educating a limited section and neglected mass literacy.
The
Hunter and Hartog Commissions
repeatedly emphasised the importance of primary education, especially against the limitations of downward filtration.

rows.title: Development of railways, telegraph, post and the press; the Vernacular Press Act
sub: Group-II S1-72: Changes in the social and cultural sphere - education policy, press, railways and telegraph

secs.t: Newspapers - founder/editor

x: Desamata
, associated with Chilakamarti, was among the press publications supportive of the Home Rule movement, along with Andhra Patrika and Krishna Patrika.
Sitarama Sastri of Guntur
wrote the series ‘Telugu Prajala Prasthuta Paristhiti’ in ‘The Hindu’.

Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh; The Hindu by G. Subramania Iyer, M. Veeraraghavachariar and others; The Bengalee by Surendranath Banerjee; and Kesari by Tilak.

secs.t: Press laws in sequence - provisions

x: Charles Metcalfe’s Press Act of 1835 repealed the 1823 restrictions and earned him the description ‘
liberator of the Indian press
The Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act of 1908 was associated with Minto II and enabled magistrates to seize presses of papers inciting violence.
Metcalfe’s 1835 measure brought relative freedom, the 1878 Act imposed restrictions, it was repealed in 1882, and repression returned through the 1908 and 1910 measures.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao received a heavy sentence for revolutionary editorials such as 'Veerabali' during the era of the
Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act, 1908

secs.t: Vernacular Press Act 1878 - Viceroy, provisions, targets, repeal

x: The Act was passed by Lord Lytton amid public anger over the 1876–77 famine and the lavish Delhi Durbar held in 1877.
District magistrates could require printers and publishers to sign bonds undertaking not to publish seditious matter.
Som Prakash
was one of the newspapers targeted by the Vernacular Press Act, along with Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash and Samachar.

secs.t: Act/policy - year and Viceroy

x: Wood’s Despatch was issued in 1854, the First Factory Act in 1881, the Famine Code in 1883, and the Resolution on Local Self-Government in 1882.
The First Factory Act concerning child labour is placed in 1881 and was enacted during Ripon’s tenure.

secs.t: FIRST - newspaper, press, railway, telegraph, Post Office Act

x: Portuguese Jesuits
introduced the first printing press in India at Goa in 1556.
The Post Office Act of 1854, associated with Dalhousie, introduced uniform postage rates and postage stamps.
The trunk telegraph network linking Calcutta, Peshawar, Bombay and Madras was established by the
mid-1850s
Lord Mayo
introduced state railways in India.

secs.t: Andhra railway and telegraph firsts

x: The first railway in South India ran from Royapuram in Madras to Wallajah Road near Arcot on 1 July 1856.

secs.t: Railways - guarantee system, Dalhousie's minute, famine and drain

x: The guarantee system assured private British companies about 5 percent interest from Indian revenues even when the railway lines did not make a profit.
Guaranteed interest was paid from Indian revenues to British private companies whether or not the railway lines earned profits, and nationalists treated this as a drain of wealth.

secs.t: Education policy milestones → purpose and epithet

x: The Charter Act of 1813 allowed missionaries, while the money earmarked for education was released only in the 1830s.
Wood's Despatch of 1854 is known as the
Magna Carta of English Education in India
Wood's Despatch envisaged vernacular primary schools, Anglo-vernacular high schools and universities, along with grants-in-aid.
The Hunter Commission dealt with primary and secondary education and recommended
handing schools to local boards and municipalities

secs.t: Macaulay's Minute and Downward Filtration Theory - Anglicist-Orientalist debate

x: Munro's 1826 survey found
a wide network of vernacular village schools in the Madras Presidency
Macaulay's Minute of 1835 was approved by
Lord William Bentinck
, who is associated with modern Western education in India.
The theory proposed educating a small upper class first, expecting knowledge to descend or filter down to the wider population.
Macaulay made the well-known comparison that
a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia
Macaulay aimed to create a class
Indian in blood and colour but English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect

secs.t: Telegraph and postal system - Dalhousie's reforms

x: Lord Dalhousie’s reforms included the Post Office Act of 1854, which introduced uniform low postage throughout British India.
John Lawrence opened telegraph communication with Europe during the period
The integrated postal and telegraph network helped integrate markets, eased travel across caste lines and facilitated pan-Indian mobilisation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 was repealed with effect from
1 March 2024
English education, the press, railways and the telegraph helped create an educated middle class and an all-India public sphere in which nationalism developed.
Telugu journalism is traced to 1835, and Machilipatnam and Rajahmundry were important early centres of education and public activity.
Raja Ram Mohan Roy is associated with Atmiya Sabha in 1814, Hindu College in 1817, an English school in 1822 and Vedanta College in 1825.

rows.title: Administrative changes - civil services, army reorganisation, police, judiciary, local self-government (Ripon)
sub: Group-II S1-69: Changes in administration - civil services, police, judiciary, army and local self-government

secs.t: Local self-government - first corporation, Cantonments Act, Mayo, Ripon

x: Exam angle: statement sets combining Madras 1688 + Cantonments Act 1924 + Ripon's epithet (all correct in APPSC-G2 2025).
Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 statement set - Cantonments Act 1924, Madras corporation 1688, Ripon as father of LSG -
all three correct

Mayo's Resolution dealt with financial decentralisation; Ripon's Resolution was regarded as the Magna Carta of local self-government; the 1907 Royal Commission stressed village panchayats; and the 1919 Act made local self-government a transferred provincial subject.
The correct sequence is Madras Corporation in 1688, Bombay and Calcutta Corporations in 1726, Lord Mayo’s resolution in 1870, and Lord Ripon’s resolution in 1882.

secs.t: Civil services - Cornwallis, Haileybury, ICS age, simultaneous exams, commissions

x: Cornwallis established a merit-based covenanted civil service, prohibited private trade and acceptance of gifts, and introduced promotion substantially based on seniority.
The Charter Act of 1853 abolished appointments by patronage of the Company's Directors and introduced open competitive examination for the civil services.
The Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 allowed limited Indian entry, mainly into uncovenanted posts, with conditions including seven years' residence and an examination in the local language.
The Aitchison Commission dropped the covenanted–uncovenanted terminology, proposed the three-level classification of services and raised the age limit to 23 years.
Lytton's statutory civil service scheme reserved one-sixth of covenanted posts for Indians of high families; it was later abolished.

secs.t: Judiciary - Hastings, Cornwallis, Bentinck, High Courts Act 1861, Ilbert Bill

x: Warren Hastings
established the district Diwani Adalats for civil cases and Faujdari Adalats for criminal cases in 1772.
Under
Cornwallis
, the Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats at Calcutta were presided over by the Governor-General in Council.
The correct sequence is Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), Charter Act and Law Commission (1833), Code of Civil Procedure (1859), and Indian High Courts Act (1861).
The Ilbert Bill sought to empower
Indian judges and magistrates to try Europeans in criminal cases
The violent protest by Europeans against the Ilbert Bill was popularly described as the
White Mutiny

secs.t: Police - darogas, kotwal, Police Act 1861, Police Commission

x: Cornwallis divided districts into thanas, each placed under an
Indian daroga
assisted by constables.
The daroga represented the “
aura and authority of Company Bahadur
” at the local level.
The colonial police force created under the Police Act of 1861 was modelled on the
Royal Irish Constabulary
and was intended to suppress dissent.

secs.t: Munro and the Madras judicial/police system

x: Thomas Munro returned in June 1814 as President of the
Judicial Commission
, which reviewed judicial and police administration in Bengal and Madras.
Munro recommended police supervision under the Collector and trial of minor crimes by village officers.
Munro recommended that minor crimes could be tried at village level by a
village munsif or panchayat

secs.t: Ilbert Bill controversy - aim, opposition, outcome

x: The Ilbert Bill sought to allow Indian
district magistrates and sessions judges to try European British subjects
, removing the racial judicial privilege enjoyed by Europeans.
European residents opposed the Bill because it would permit Indian district magistrates and sessions judges to try European British subjects, who had previously been tried only by European judges.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The ICS is the direct ancestor of the IAS, codified laws of IPC-era codes, the 1861 police model of modern police institutions, and Ripon's local bodies of PRIs and ULBs.
The colonial justice system was criticised as costly, slow and racially unequal; these inequalities were highlighted in the context of the Ilbert Bill debate.

units.title: Indian War of Independence 1857; Religious and Social Reform Movements of the 19th Century; India's Freedom Movement; Revolutionaries in India and Abroad

rows.title: Revolt of 1857 - political causes (annexations, Doctrine of Lapse, subsidiary alliance)

secs.t: Annexation of Awadh - ground, summary settlement, taluqdars and sepoys

x: Nawab
Wajid Ali Shah
was deposed after Awadh was annexed and was exiled to Calcutta.
The settlement was made directly with village proprietors, while taluqdars lost their estates, were disarmed and had their forts demolished.
The Bengal Army drew heavily from Awadh, and the new revenue burden directly affected the families of its sepoys.

secs.t: Doctrine of Lapse - Dalhousie, states and heirs affected

x: The Doctrine of Lapse was the policy of
Lord Dalhousie
, who served as Governor-General from 1848 to 1856.
Nana Saheb, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, was denied the pension of his adoptive father.
Queen Victoria’s Proclamation, read by Canning at the Allahabad Durbar on 1 November 1858, abolished the policy and recognised adoption.

secs.t: Subsidiary alliance - loss of sovereignty, first state (Hyderabad)

x: Mysore accepted the alliance in 1799, Tanjore in October 1799, Awadh in November 1801 and the Peshwa in December 1801.
Awadh accepted the alliance in November 1801, the Peshwa in December 1801, Bhonsle of Berar in December 1803 and Scindia in February 1804.
The Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema districts in 1800 to meet the cost of the subsidiary force; these became known as the
Ceded Districts

secs.t: Mughal succession - Dalhousie and Canning

x: Dalhousie declared that Bahadur Shah’s successors would have to leave the
Red Fort and move to the Qutub at Mehrauli
Canning announced that after Bahadur Shah Zafar, his successors would lose the imperial title and would be treated merely as princes.

secs.t: Abolition of titles and pensions

x: The titles of the Carnatic Nawab and the Tanjore Raja
were abolished in 1855.
The
disbanding of Pindaris and irregular troops
increased unemployment and contributed to discontent.

secs.t: Leaders → personal political grievance

x: Denial of Baji Rao II’s pension was Nana Saheb’s grievance.
Khan Bahadur Khan
, a Rohilla chief at Bareilly, proclaimed himself Nawab Nizam.
Begum Hazrat Mahal led at Lucknow, proclaimed Birjis Qadr ruler of Awadh, and the administration included both Hindus and Muslims in offices.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Fear of further annexations encouraged princely and aristocratic participation and helped transform the sepoy mutiny into a wider revolt.
After 1858, princely states were guaranteed in return for accepting British
paramountcy

rows.title: Revolt of 1857 - economic, socio-religious, administrative and military causes
sub: Group-II S1-65: Revolt of 1857 - political, economic, socio-religious, administrative and military causes

secs.t: Immediate cause - Enfield rifle, greased cartridges, rumours, chapatis

x: The 19th Native Infantry acted at Berhampur in February, Mangal Pandey acted at Barrackpore on 29 March, and the Meerut rising began on 10 May 1857.
The 85 sepoys of the 3rd Cavalry were court-martialled on 9 May 1857 and given
ten years' imprisonment
, helping precipitate the rising on 10 May.

secs.t: Military grievances - GSEA, bhatta, discrimination, troop ratio

x: Orthodox Hindus believed that crossing the sea resulted in loss of caste, making the overseas-service requirement deeply unpopular.
Bhatta was the
foreign service allowance
paid to soldiers serving outside their ordinary area.
Racial discrimination restricted the highest rank ordinarily attainable by an Indian soldier to
Subedar
European troops had been drawn away for the
Crimean and Persian wars
, contributing to the imbalance in troop strength.

secs.t: Contemporary Indian writings on the causes - author and book

x: V.D. Savarkar wrote *The Indian War of Independence*. *Majha Pravas* was written by Vishnubhat Godse, *Rebellion 1857: A Symposium* by P.C. Joshi, and *Eighteen Fifty-Seven* by S.N. Sen.

P.E. Roberts was associated with the description of the revolt as “just a sepoy mutiny,” not with a work titled *The Causes of the Indian Revolt*. *Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind*, meaning “The Causes of the Indian Revolt,” was written by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan.
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies was written by S.B. Chaudhuri; The Great Rebellion by Ashok Mehta; The Peasant and the Raj by Eric Stokes; and Awadh in Revolt 1857-58 by Rudrangshu Mukherjee.

secs.t: Earlier sepoy mutinies - causes and dates

x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
The correct sequence is Vellore mutiny in July 1806, Barrackpore mutiny in November 1824, Berhampur in February 1857 and Mangal Pandey’s attack on 29 March 1857.

secs.t: Socio-religious causes - social laws, missionaries

x: The abolition of Sati in 1829 was carried out during the tenure of
Lord William Bentinck
The Act enabled converts to Christianity to inherit ancestral property, which was viewed as an incentive for conversion.
Missionary activity under official protection and the spread of Western institutions created apprehensions about religious conversion and the loss of caste identity.

secs.t: Economic causes - revenue settlements, taluqdars, Inam Commission, artisans

x: High land revenue was collected rigidly under the Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements, placing severe pressure on peasants.
Cheap British machine-made goods entered India with favourable treatment, while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs, contributing to deindustrialisation.
Annexations ended princely patronage, while British machine-made goods, particularly textiles, damaged Indian handicrafts; statement 3 reverses this effect.

secs.t: Administrative causes - exclusion from high posts, corrupt courts and police

x: Indians were excluded from high civil and military posts, producing resentment against the colonial administrative structure.
Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
The administration was inefficient and prejudiced; corruption was widespread in the police and lower courts, while Indians were excluded from high posts.

secs.t: Political causes - Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh, the Mughal emperor

x: The adopted son of Rani Lakshmibai was refused succession to the throne of Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse.
Canning announced that the successors of Bahadur Shah Zafar would lose the royal title, in addition to being removed from the Red Fort.
The disbanding of the Pindaris and irregular soldiers, along with the displacement of established political and military interests, contributed to the perception of absentee sovereignty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Enfield rifle was introduced in 1853, Awadh was annexed in 1856, Mangal Pandey attacked at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857, and the Crown’s promise of religious neutrality followed after 1858.

Mangal Pandey was born on 19 July 1827, attacked Lieutenant Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 in the context of the Enfield rifle controversy, and was subsequently hanged.

rows.title: Outbreak and spread - Mangal Pandey, Meerut; centres and leaders of the revolt
sub: Group-II S1-66: Revolt of 1857 - outbreak, centres, leaders and suppression

secs.t: Centre → leader

x: General Bakht Khan
was the real military leader at Delhi, whereas Bahadur Shah Zafar was the nominal leader.
Bakht Khan led
a 10-member Court of Soldiers
at Delhi.
Rani Lakshmibai was proclaimed head of state at Jhansi on
4 June 1858
Rani Lakshmibai and Tantia Tope captured Gwalior, while Scindia fled to Agra.
Khan Bahadur Khan proclaimed himself
Nawab Nizam
at Bareilly and commanded an army of about 40,000.

secs.t: Outbreak - first outbreak, Barrackpore, march to Delhi

x: Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857 and his regiment, the 34th Bengal Native Infantry, was disbanded.
Eighty-five sepoys of the 3rd Light Cavalry were jailed for refusing the cartridges, provoking their comrades to revolt.
At Meerut, the sepoys shot their officers, broke into the jails, freed the prisoners and then marched to Delhi.
The Meerut rebels marched towards Delhi shouting “
Dilli Chalo
The sequence was Gwalior and Jhansi in June 1857, Delhi recaptured in September 1857, Kanpur retaken in December 1857, and Lucknow recaptured in March 1858.
Jhansi was recaptured and Kunwar Singh led a fresh rising in Bihar in April 1858, while Bareilly was recaptured in May 1858.

secs.t: Lesser-known and local leaders

x: Jhalkari Bai was Lakshmibai's lookalike and commanded her women's wing at Jhansi.
Dandasena was the Savara chief of Paralakimidi; Captain Wilson crushed his resistance, and Dandasena was hanged on 9 August 1857.
Shah Mal mobilised the chaurasee des, meaning the area of 84 villages, in the Baraut region of Uttar Pradesh.

secs.t: Centre → date the rising began

x: The rising began at Barrackpore on 29 March, Delhi on 11 May, Lucknow on 4 June and Kanpur on 5 June 1857.
The rising began in the
Kolhapur area
in October 1857.

secs.t: Spread - affected vs unaffected; Rajputana and Central India centres

x: By May 1857 the revolt had reached
Ferozepur, Aligarh, Etawah, Bulandshahar, Nasirabad, Bareilly, Moradabad and Shahjahanpur
The revolt was mostly confined to northern India, particularly the Doab, Awadh, Bihar and Central India, extending from near Patna to the Rajasthan border.
Hyderabad's Nizam and Scindia were loyal, while Scindia's troops defected and the troops of Tonk and Bhopal rebelled despite their rulers' loyalty.

secs.t: Symbolic leader - Bahadur Shah Zafar's proclamation

x: The sepoys proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar as
Shahenshah-e-Hindustan
, making him the symbolic leader of the revolt.
The proclamations in Bahadur Shah Zafar's name stressed Hindu-Muslim unity, including measures such as a ban on cow slaughter and joint commands, and called for restoration of the Mughal order.
Most princes ignored his appeals rather than responding positively to them.

secs.t: Revolt in Andhra and Hyderabad → leaders and places

x: Dandasena rose at Paralakimidi on 9 August 1857 after
the ban on selling forest produce
Dandasena’s rising was suppressed by Captain Wilson, and Dandasena was hanged.
Afzal-ud-Daula remained pro-British, and the Nizam’s loyalty helped keep the Deccan quiet.
Dandasena led the rising at Paralakimidi, while Korukonda Subba Reddy led the rebellion at Errannagudem; both occurred in August 1857.

secs.t: Contemporary accounts and advisers

x: W. H. Russell
, correspondent of The Times, reported on the revolt and British reprisals in My Diary in India.
Azimullah Khan, Nana Saheb’s adviser, went to London to plead Nana Saheb’s pension case.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The heroes of 1857 entered folklore and were invoked during the Quit India and Indian National Army phases.
Participation by all major princes and urban elites was not a limitation because many big princes and urban elites stayed away from the revolt.
The Hindu-Muslim unity associated with the revolt was later cited against the
two-nation theory
Tantia Tope
is regarded as the last major leader of the Revolt of 1857 to be executed.

rows.title: Suppression of the revolt; why it failed; areas that stayed loyal

secs.t: Fate of leaders - Bahadur Shah Zafar, Tantia Tope, Nana Saheb, Rani Lakshmibai, Kunwar Singh

x: Exam angle: "Bahadur Shah was exiled to - Rangoon".
Khan Bahadur Khan operated in Rohilkhand, Ahmadullah in Faizabad, Kunwar Singh in Bihar, and Tantia Tope continued guerrilla warfare in Central India.
Rani Lakshmibai captured Gwalior with Tantia Tope and died fighting near Gwalior on 17 June 1858 against Sir Hugh Rose's force.

secs.t: Reasons for failure - leadership, unity, plan, arms, communication, British strength

x: Exam angle: statement sets (military superiority, no unified programme, lack of support from all sections) - all three correct.
The rebels generally used
swords, spears and old muskets
, whereas the British had Enfield rifles and the electric telegraph.
The revolt suffered because several princes and big zamindars remained loyal and it lacked adequate support from the martial races of the north.

secs.t: Rulers' stand during the revolt and the presidency armies

x: The revolt was chiefly of the
Bengal Army
; the Madras and Bombay armies largely remained loyal, while a Gorkha regiment assisted Campbell.
Scindia of Gwalior
was regarded as most loyal to the British, but his troops deserted to Rani Lakshmibai.
The phrase “breakwaters to the storm” is attributed to
Lord Canning
, although some accounts credit Lord Elgin.

secs.t: Indian classes that stayed aloof or took part

x: The educated middle class generally saw the revolt as
a backward-looking feudal reaction
and therefore remained neutral.
Big zamindars and moneylenders
acted as “breakwaters” because they sought to protect their class interests.
Merchants and the urban elite
generally did not support the revolt.

secs.t: Recapture - centres retaken and British officers who fell

x: Exam angle: "Which centre was recaptured by the English?" - Delhi.
Colin Campbell recaptured Kanpur in December 1857, Lucknow in March 1858, Hugh Rose recaptured Jhansi in April 1858 and Gwalior in June 1858.
Maulvi Liyakat Ali led the rebellion at Allahabad and Banaras, which were recaptured by Colonel Neill.

secs.t: Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief during suppression

x: Sir Colin Campbell
was the Commander-in-Chief during the suppression and later became known as Lord Clyde.
Lord Canning served as Governor-General from 1856 to 1858 and became the first Viceroy in 1858, serving until 1862.
Lord Canning served during the period
, becoming the first Viceroy after the transfer of administration to the Crown.

secs.t: Repression measures - executions, Delhi's aftermath

x: The repression was harsh;
thousands of rebels were publicly executed after mock trials
, and British troops also committed atrocities.
The Mughal line ended after Bahadur Shah was tried and deported and his sons were shot by Hodson.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revolt was suppressed by mid-1858, but its impact was profound because it shook British rule in India to its foundations.
Rani Avantibai Lodhi of Ramgarh defeated Charles Waddington’s force at Kheri near Mandla and died fighting in 1858.
Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Salar Jung I stayed loyal, and the Hyderabad Residency attack of 17 July 1857 was repulsed.

rows.title: Nature of 1857 - the historiographical debate (mutiny, feudal reaction, first war of independence)
sub: Group-II S1-68: Nature of the 1857 Revolt - historiographical debate

secs.t: Interpretations and famous verdicts → historian

x: Exam angle: "Who first described 1857 as the First Indian War of Independence?" - V.D. Savarkar.
Exam angle: "Who first called it the First Indian War of Independence?" -
Savarkar
, with Tilak and Majumdar as distractors.
Sir John Lawrence
, along with J.R. Seeley and Charles Raikes, regarded the uprising primarily as a sepoy mutiny and denied it a popular or national character.
Jawaharlal Nehru
described the uprising as essentially a feudal rising in The Discovery of India.

secs.t: Centenary histories - S.N. Sen and R.C. Majumdar

x: R.C. Majumdar's own verdict was that the revolt was neither the first nor national nor a war of independence, despite some classifications placing him in a broader nationalist school.
*Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind* appeared in 1858–59, followed by *Majha Pravas*, then Savarkar's work in 1909, and S.N. Sen's *Eighteen Fifty-Seven* in 1957.
The Indian War of Independence, 1857 was published in 1909; the Marx-Engels compilation covers 1857-1859; and both Majumdar's and Sen's books were published in 1957.

secs.t: British vs Indian historians - labels

x: British or imperialist historians
commonly used the labels Sepoy Mutiny or Indian Mutiny and denied the revolt a national character.
The feudal-reaction interpretation highlights dispossessed princes and taluqdars such as Nana Saheb, Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal, who sought to recover lost positions.
The
elite and urban classes
were largely uninvolved, which is one reason historians question whether the revolt can be called a fully national movement.

secs.t: Contemporary views - Disraeli, Marx, Syed Ahmad Khan

x: Disraeli questioned whether the event was merely a military mutiny or a national revolt, and viewed it as
a national rising
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan argued that
the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council
caused the rulers to misunderstand the ruled.
The work attributed the revolt mainly to the absence of Indian representation in the Legislative Council, which led to misunderstanding between rulers and ruled.

secs.t: Subaltern and peasant perspectives - Eric Stokes, Rudrangshu Mukherjee

x: Eric Stokes emphasised local agrarian studies and interpreted the revolt as multiple peasant and elite risings, not as one centrally directed movement.
*Awadh in Revolt* focuses on the popular resistance of peasants and taluqdars in Awadh.

secs.t: Statement-type judgments - participation, national character, outcome

x: The revolt began among soldiers but quickly drew in rulers, peasants, soldiers and common people, becoming a wider popular rebellion.
The revolt was not a modern nationalist movement with a common future-oriented programme, making statement 2 incorrect.
Although the revolt failed, it shook British rule and later became a source of inspiration for Indian nationalism.

secs.t: Participation and attitude of social groups

x: Nana Saheb was associated with Kanpur, Lakshmibai with Jhansi, Begum Hazrat Mahal with Lucknow and Khan Bahadur Khan with Bareilly.
The
taluqdars and zamindars of Awadh
joined the revolt in large numbers, unlike the big zamindars of Bengal who remained loyal.
Merchants and moneylenders, most princes, and the educated middle class did not generally join the revolt; the middle class remained aloof because it saw British rule as modernising.

secs.t: Hindu-Muslim unity in the revolt

x: Bahadur Shah II was accepted as the symbolic head by both Hindu and Muslim rebels.
The greased cartridges offended the religious sentiments of both Hindus and Muslims, creating a common grievance.
After 1857, the British increasingly pursued a policy of divide and rule in response to the cooperation between Hindus and Muslims.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The revolt damaged the belief in British invincibility and helped create the conditions for later nationalism, although it did not end British rule.
The RIN revolt began at HMIS Talwar in Bombay on
18 February 1946
The 80th anniversary of the RIN revolt of 1946 was marked on
18 February 2026

rows.title: Consequences of 1857 - Queen's Proclamation, Government of India Act 1858, army reorganisation
sub: Group-II S1-67: Impact of the 1857 Revolt - Government of India Act 1858 and army reorganisation

secs.t: Government of India Act 1858 - transfer of power, Secretary of State, India Council, Viceroy

x: Exam angle: options mix Charter Acts 1833/1853, Pitt's Act and Indian Councils Act 1861 - only the 1858 Act transferred power.
Exam angle: "which Act transferred power to the Crown" with the Charter Acts of 1833/1853 and ICA 1861 as distractors.
Exam angle: APPSC G2 2024 and G2 2025 asked "GG of Bengal designated GG of India by?" The answer is the
Charter Act 1833
Robert Clive was the first Governor of Bengal, Warren Hastings the first Governor-General of Bengal and Lord Canning the first Viceroy and Governor-General.

secs.t: Queen's Proclamation - date, venue, reader, promises, which were kept

x: The Proclamation promised respect for the rights, dignity and honour of the native princes and declared that Company treaties would be honoured.
The Proclamation promised equal opportunity in public service on the basis of merit and qualifications, without discrimination of race or creed.
The period 1858–1885 is commonly described as the
Era of Broken Promises
because the assurance of equal employment was not implemented in practice.
The Queen’s Proclamation is often called the
Magna Carta of the Indian people
because of its wide-ranging assurances concerning rulers, religion, public service, property and land rights.

secs.t: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

x: Exam angle: "divide and rule" inside the army - the counterpoise principle.
The British retained artillery and heavy weapons for Europeans and organised other regiments to restrict unity and fraternisation among Indian soldiers.
The British increasingly recruited
Sikhs, Gurkhas and Pathans
, describing them as martial races, while reducing dependence on recruits from Awadh and Bihar.

secs.t: Policy towards princes - adoption rights, end of annexation

x: The British recognised the right of childless rulers to adopt heirs, thereby withdrawing the Doctrine of Lapse and ending the annexation policy associated with Dalhousie.
The princes retained their states subject to British paramountcy and were converted into loyal subordinate allies of the Crown.
Lord Elgin
described the loyal Indian princes as “breakwaters to the storm,” reflecting their role as supports of British rule after 1857.

secs.t: Divide-and-rule and racial attitudes - Hindu-Muslim policy shift

x: The British initially held Muslims chiefly responsible for the revolt and adopted anti-Muslim measures, but later cultivated Muslim support against the rising educated Hindu middle class.
The British first adopted an anti-Muslim posture, later cultivated Muslims against educated Hindus, protected landed interests and withdrew from social reform and interference.
In Awadh, zamindars and taluqdars were restored to proprietary rights and became a conservative and loyal landed class supporting British rule.

secs.t: End of the Mughal dynasty and East India Company

x: Bahadur Shah II was tried and exiled to
Rangoon
after the Revolt of 1857, where he died in 1862.
The Government of India Act, 1858 ended the Company’s political rule, while the East India Company was formally dissolved in 1874.
The rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan, after which the British tried and exiled him to Rangoon, ending the Mughal dynasty in practice and form.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The submarine cable introduced in 1870 facilitated faster communication between India and London, strengthening control from Britain.
Gandhi referred to Queen Victoria’s Proclamation of 1858 as a “
Magna Carta
” because of its assurances concerning governance, religion and the Indian princes.
Rani Avantibai Lodhi opposed the Doctrine of Lapse and won the Battle of Kheri during the Revolt of 1857.

rows.title: Andhra and South India in 1857 - limited response; earlier local uprisings (Rampa, Palegar revolts)
sub: Group-II M1-A-57: Early resistance to British rule - Poligar/Palegar revolts and the Vizianagaram rising of 1794
Group-II M1-A-58: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt, 1846-47
Group-II M1-A-59: 1857 Revolt and its impact on Andhra - response, repression and consequences

secs.t: Hyderabad in 1857 - Residency attack, Turrebaz Khan, Maulvi Allauddin, Nizam and Salar Jung

x: The 1st Cavalry came under suspicion and was disarmed; Mir Fida Ali was hanged, whereas Maulvi Allauddin was transported to the Andamans.
Mubariz-ud-Daula was arrested in 1839, the Aurangabad episode occurred in June 1857, Chida Khan was then detained, and the Residency was attacked on 17 July 1857.
Dandasena rose at Paralakimidi, Korukonda Subba Reddy led the rebellion at Errannagudem, Turrebaz Khan attacked the British Residency, and Mubariz-ud-Daula was imprisoned in Golconda Fort.

secs.t: Chronology of rebellions in Hyderabad State and Andhra

x: The Rampa rebellion occurred in 1879, whereas Mubariz-ud-Daula was associated with the 1839 Wahabi conspiracy.
The 1801 Taranikallu disturbance in Adoni was associated with Patel Mutakuri Goudappa, who was hanged.
Korra Mallayya and Chinna Bhupathi
were associated with the Gulugonda/Ganjam Agency rising of 1845–48.
Ganjam was associated with the 1845–48 Agency rising, not the list of other 1857-era Hyderabad State risings.

secs.t: Reasons for limited response in Andhra (assertion-reason)

x: The Nizam and Salar Jung remained pro-British, while the Madras Presidency was generally quiet.
Local leaders and disturbances, including Turrebaz Khan, Korukonda Subba Reddy and Dandasena, did exist.
The major background grievances identified were the 1800 cession, the Wahabi conspiracy of 1839 and the 1853 Berar treaty, involving Berar, Raichur and Osmanabad/Dharashiv.

secs.t: Andhra leaders of 1857 → area of operation

x: Exam angle: matching a leader to an area. A 2024 A/R on Sheikh Peer Sahib's jihad was keyed "both true, R not the explanation".
Captain Wilson
suppressed the uprising led by Radhakrishna Dandasena at Paralakimidi and Dandasena was subsequently hanged.
Buttaigudem Munsab Shankar Swamy
helped the British suppress Korukonda Subba Reddy's rising in the Godavari Agency.
Sheikh Peer Sahib preached jihad at Cuddapah on 28 August 1857 and prayed for the success of the Mughal Emperor; he was later arrested.

secs.t: Vizianagaram vs the Company - Battle of Padmanabham (1794)

x: Exam angle: "Padmanabham decided whose defeat?" = Vijayarama Raju of Vizianagaram, not Bobbili.
Colonel Pendergast
commanded the English East India Company forces at the Battle of Padmanabham.
On 2 August 1793, the British seized the Vizianagaram fort, divided the estate into three parts and ordered the Raja to reside at Machilipatnam on a pension of Rs 1,200.
The battle was fought between the English East India Company and Pusapati Chinna Vijayarama Gajapati Raju II, the Vizianagaram zamindar.
Narayana Babu had hidden at
Makkuva
before receiving the Vizianagaram estate back under the Permanent Settlement.

secs.t: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt - district, cause, end

x: His estate was taken over under Munro, he was offered only a meagre pension, and he was ordered to lay down arms and pay peshkash.
All four events are associated with the revolt in July 1846: nine sepoys were killed, Rudravaram and the Koilakuntla treasury were looted, and Collector Cochrane pursued him.
Narasimha Reddy was the younger son of Pedda Mallareddy, Palegar of Uyyalawada, and was the maternal grandson of Nosam Palegar Jayarama Reddy.

secs.t: Palegar/Polygar revolts - Rayalaseema palegars, Kattabomman, Marudu brothers, Velu Thampi

x: The Company's 1781 arrangement allowed the Nawab of Arcot to manage the revenues of Tirunelveli and the Carnatic, affecting the rights of the Poligars.
Kattabomman was hanged in 1799, the Marudu brothers were executed in 1801, and Velu Thampi Dalawa was associated with the Kundara Proclamation.
Velu Thampi Dalawa was the
Diwan
of Travancore and led the revolt of 1808–09.

secs.t: Vellore Mutiny - cause and consequence

x: The new uniform regulations, including changes concerning the turban and a ban on caste marks, hurt the caste and religious sentiments of the sepoys.
Tipu Sultan's family was lodged in Vellore Fort, which was an associated factor in the mutiny.
Following the mutiny, Madras Governor William Bentinck and the Commander-in-Chief Cradock were recalled.

secs.t: Rampa and agency rebellions - phases, leaders, places

x: Exam angle: the year of the Rampa revolution is 1879, not Alluri's 1922.
The correct order is Vizianagaram–Visakhapatnam hill unrest in the 1830s, Korra Mallayya and Chinna Bhupathi in 1845–48, Korukonda Subba Reddy in 1857–58, and the Rampa rebellion in 1879.
The Gulugonda revolt occurred in 1845–48, Phadke’s revolt in 1879, Khudiram Bose’s episode in 1908, and Alluri’s Rampa rebellion in 1922–24.

secs.t: Palegars - nature of the office, revolts in the Ceded Districts

x: Palegars were fortified military chiefs who exercised autonomous power under the nominal suzerainty of the Nizam.
There were dozens of Palegars in
Kurnool, Cuddapah, Bellary and Anantapur
Village Patel
Mutakuri Goudappa
attacked the Sub-Collector's office at Taranikallu in 1801.
The Palakonda Poligars rebelled against
heavy taxes
and were brutally suppressed.

secs.t: Causes of resistance - revenue demands, palegar policy, Wahabi movement

x: Heavy revenue and peshkash demands, estate forfeiture and the order to disarm Palegars were causes of resistance.

After the revolt, the Army was recast on the 'martial races' theory.
