The Scientific Society began in 1864, the MAO school in 1875, the Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886, and the United Indian Patriotic Association in 1888.

secs.t: Movement → founder pairs

x: Exam angle: "correctly matched" pairs - Gangohi belongs to Deoband, not to the Taiyuni movement.
Patna was a principal centre of the Wahabi movement, Qadian was associated with the Ahmadiya movement, Nadwatul Ulama was located at Lucknow, and Deoband lay in Saharanpur district.
The Faraizi Movement dates from 1818, Deoband from 1866, Ahmadiya from 1889 and Nadwatul Ulama from 1894.

secs.t: Deoband Movement - founders, year, state, stance on Congress

x: Qasim Nanotavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi
led the establishment of the Deoband movement at Darul Uloom in 1866.
The Deoband Movement aimed at religious revival, training religious leaders and resistance to foreign rule; replacing Islamic learning with exclusively Western education was not its objective.
Shibli Numani founded
Nadwat al-Ulama
at Lucknow in the 1894–96 period and supported the teaching of English and European science.

secs.t: Sayyid Ahmad Khan - books, journal, stand on Congress

x: Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind, written by Sayyid Ahmad Khan in 1859, examined
the causes of the Indian Revolt of 1857
Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq
was the journal associated with Sayyid Ahmad Khan's reformist and rational interpretation of Islam.
Sayyid Ahmad Khan lived from 1817 to 1898 and promoted English education and rational religious interpretation after 1857.
The
Hindi-Urdu controversy of 1867
contributed to the change in Sayyid Ahmad Khan's political outlook.

secs.t: Faraizi Movement - founder, later leader, region

x: The Faraizi Movement sought to enforce religious duties, or faraiz, and remove un-Islamic practices.
Haji Shariatullah
founded the Faraizi Movement in East Bengal in 1818.
Dudu Miyan, the son of Haji Shariatullah, converted the Faraizi Movement into a peasant movement against
zamindars and indigo planters

secs.t: Aligarh Movement - initial objective, MAO College year and principals, later leaders, AMU conversion

x: The Aligarh institution began as a school in 1875, college classes started in 1877, and it became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.
The movement sought Muslim social and educational uplift through modern education, rational religious interpretation and cooperation with the British.
Theodore Morison
was another British principal of the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College.

secs.t: Wahabi Movement - Indian founder, chief centre, trials, Andhra leader, anti-British stance

x: Exam angle: character of the Wahabi movement →
anti-British
The movement was named after
Abdul Wahab of Arabia
, although its Indian founder was Syed Ahmad Barelvi.
Mubariz-ud-Daula was arrested in 1839, followed by the Ambala trial in 1864, the Patna trial in 1865 and suppression of the movement by 1870.

secs.t: Book → author on Muslims under British rule

x: W.W. Hunter wrote The Indian Musalmans in 1871.
Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind was written by
Sayyid Ahmad Khan

secs.t: Ahmadiya Movement - founder, place, beliefs

x: The Ahmadiya Movement promoted liberal and universal religious ideas, opposed jihad and supported Western liberal education.
Qadian is in
Gurdaspur district of Punjab

secs.t: Sikh reform - Kuka, Singh Sabha, Akali movement, Gurdwara Act

x: Nirankari was associated with Baba Dayal Das and the formless God; Namdhari with Baba Ram Singh and Bhaini; Singh Sabha with Gurmukhi and Punjabi literature; and Akali with removal of corrupt mahants.
Khalsa College was established in 1892, the SGPC was formed in 1920, Guru-ka-Bagh became a flashpoint in 1922, and the Sikh Gurdwaras Act was enacted in 1925.

secs.t: Muslim reform in Hyderabad and Andhra

x: Nasaraiah, a Sayyid Muslim who died in 1825, preached belief in one God and opposed idol worship.
Nasaraiah was associated with the Vinukonda–Narasaraopet area of Guntur.
Osmania University, established in Hyderabad in 1918, conferred an honorary D.Litt. on B.R. Ambedkar in 1953.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Aligarh promoted Western education and was broadly pro-British and anti-Congress, whereas Deoband preserved an orthodox, anti-British and pro-Congress strand.
A criticism of Sayyid Ahmad Khan’s later political conservatism is that it sowed the seeds of communal division.
One criticism holds that Deoband supported Congress more as a means of opposing Sir Syed than from an independently developed positive political creed.

rows.title: Sikh, Parsi and other reform movements - Singh Sabha, Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha

secs.t: Kuka (Namdhari) movement - founder, region, boycott methods, suppression

x: The Kuka movement was begun in Punjab in the 1840s by
Bhagat Jawahar Mal
The Kukas rejected idol worship, worship of tombs, trees and snakes, and Brahmin-led rituals.
Satguru Ram Singh
is regarded as the first to use boycott and non-cooperation against British rule as political weapons.
After the 1872 Malerkotla clash, dozens of Kukas were blown from cannons and Ram Singh was deported to Rangoon in Burma.

secs.t: Reform body → community it reformed

x: Exam angle: "Mazdayasnan Sabha was started to reform ___" → Parsees.
Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha reformed the Parsis; Singh Sabha and Kuka/Namdhari were Sikh movements; Deoband was associated with Muslims.

secs.t: Other reform bodies → founder

x: The Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was founded by Anandamohan Bose and Sivanath Sastri; Seva Sadan by Behramji Malabari; Deva Samaj by Shiv Narayan Agnihotri; and Dharma Sabha by Radhakant Deb.
Deva Samaj was founded by Shiv Narayan Agnihotri, Seva Samiti by Hriday Nath Kunzru, Social Service League by N.M. Joshi, and Sharada Sadan by Pandita Ramabai.

secs.t: Parsi reformers - Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha

x: Rast Goftar means “
Truth-teller
.” It was the organ of the Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha and was edited by Dadabhai Naoroji.
The Parsi Religious Reform Association was founded in Bombay in 1851 by
Naoroji Furdonji, Dadabhai Naoroji and S. S. Bengalee
Behramji M. Malabari campaigned against
child marriage
, a campaign associated with the Age of Consent Act, 1891.

secs.t: Akali Movement - Gurdwara Reform, SGPC, Gurdwaras Act 1925

x: The Akali movement sought to free Sikh gurdwaras from corrupt Udasi mahants.
Kartar Singh Jhabbar
was a leader of the Akali or Gurdwara Reform Movement during 1920–25.
The Nankana Sahib massacre of 1921 was one of the flashpoints of the Akali movement.

secs.t: Nirankari Movement - founder and teachings

x: The Nirankari movement was founded by
Baba Dayal Das
Nirankari teaching emphasised worship of God as Nirankar, meaning formless.
The Nirankari movement issued hukamnamas on correct practice and developed its own network of worship places and priests.
The Nirankari movement grew by cooperating with the British and subsequently became a separate group within Sikhism.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kuka boycott anticipated the later
Swadeshi and non-cooperation
methods used in the national movement.
Namdhari practices included white dress and carrying a lathi, while Nirankari teaching centred on worship of the formless God.
The Kuka methods foreshadowed later nationalist techniques, Sikh reform encouraged political mobilisation, and the Akali movement later developed into the Akali Dal.

rows.title: Anti-caste and non-Brahmin movements - Jyotiba Phule and Satyashodhak Samaj, Narayana Guru, Periyar, Justice Party
sub: Group-II S1-77: Anti-caste and non-Brahmin movements - Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar, Ambedkar
Group-II M1-A-64: Justice Party in Andhra - formation, programme and impact
Group-II M1-A-65: Self-Respect Movement and the non-Brahmin movement in Andhra

secs.t: Justice Party - founders, aims, reforms in Madras, universities

x: Exam angle: "Justice Party Government helped create which university?" →
Andhra University (1926)
(APPSC G2 2025, asked three times).
A.
Subbarayalu Reddiar
became the first Chief Minister of the first Justice Party ministry on 17 December 1920; he was later succeeded by the Raja of Panagal.
The Andhra University Act and Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act were in 1926, the women’s franchise resolution was in 1921, and Annamalai University was founded in 1929.

The first ministry was led by the Raja of Panagal after Subbarayalu Reddiar; the later ministries were associated with B. Munuswami Naidu and the Raja of Bobbili, while Panuganti Ramarayaningar was the Raja of Panagal and party president.
All four statements describe important factors in the Justice Party’s decline: lack of mass support, regional rifts, leadership losses, and defeat by the Congress in 1937.

secs.t: Satyashodhak Samaj - founder, year, books, aims

x: The Satyashodhak Samaj opposed Brahminical dominance and priestly monopoly; it did not seek to strengthen them.
Vithalrao Krishnaji Vandekar
gave Jyotiba Phule the title ‘Mahatma’ in 1888.
Gulamgiri, meaning
Slavery
, compared the condition of lower castes to slavery and criticised social oppression.
Satyashodhak Samaj means Society of Truth Seekers; Gulamgiri means Slavery; Sarvajanik Satyadharma concerns public true religion; and Shetkaryacha Asud means The Cultivator’s Whipcord.

secs.t: Adi-Andhra and Adi-Hindu movements - sessions, venues, leaders, bodies

x: Exam angle: "district of the first Adi Andhra session" →
Krishna
; "chairman of the first Panchama Mahajana Sabha" → Bhagya Reddy Varma (2019).
Madari Bhagya Reddy Varma
popularised both terms and is regarded as the father of the Dalit movement in Hyderabad and Andhra.
Bhagya Reddy Varma was president, Guduru Ramachandra Rao organiser, Sundru Venkayya reception chairman, and Chilukuri Venkataswamy presided over the 1919 conference.
Kusuma Dharmanna
urged Dalits towards socialism at the 1936 Adi Andhra Mahasabha held in Vizianagaram.
The conference was held at Lucknow in 1930 under the presidency of Bhagya Reddy Varma and selected Ambedkar as the Dalit representative for the Round Table Conferences.
Jagan Mitra Mandali was established in 1906, the first Adi-Andhra session was held in 1917, the Amalapuram Sadassu in 1921, and the Lucknow conference in 1930.
The 1917 resolution sought the replacement of “Panchama” by regionally appropriate names, representation in local bodies and councils, special schools, and access to wells in Dalit wadas.
Medida Narayana Murthy worked at Tuni in 1936, Bojja Appala Swamy established a school at Kandipappu in West Godavari, and Pandu Lakshmanaswamy was associated with Rajolu.
Din Bandhu was founded by Krishnarao Bhalekar, Kudi Arasu by Periyar, Adi Hindu by Bhagya Reddy Varma, and Jai Bheem by Jala Rangaswamy.

secs.t: Reformer → movement or organisation

x: Sri Narayana Guru founded the SNDP Yogam, Periyar led the Self-Respect Movement, and Ayyankali established the Sadhu Jana Paripalana Sangham.
Gopal Baba Walangkar published the journal
Vital-Vidhvansak
and worked among the Mahars.
B.R. Ambedkar established the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in 1924, the Independent Labour Party in 1936 and the Scheduled Castes Federation in 1942.

secs.t: Caste movements → region and caste group

x: The Justice Party represented
non-Brahmin castes
in the Madras Presidency, including Reddys, Kammas, Kapus, Vellalas and Chettis.
Madiga welfare in Andhra was associated with the Arundhatiya Yuvajana Sangham, and the Adi-Andhra movement was associated with Bhagya Reddy Varma and Jala Rangaswamy.
The Nadar Mahajana Sangam was formed in 1910 and was associated with Nadars of Tamil Nadu and Travancore.

secs.t: Vaikom Satyagraha - issue, leaders, Gandhi's role

x: Exam angle: "Vaikom Satyagraha was associated with" → Temple Entry Movement.
After the Mahad Satyagraha, the INC reconstituted its Anti-Untouchability Subcommittee under
Madan Mohan Malaviya
The satyagrahas brought untouchability into sharper focus, and the INC reconstituted its Anti-Untouchability Subcommittee under Malaviya.

Mahad is associated with the public tank at Mahad in 1927; Manusmriti Dahan occurred on 25 December 1927; Kalaram Temple Entry was at Nashik in 1930; and Guruvayur Satyagraha occurred in Kerala in 1931–32.

secs.t: Self-Respect Movement - founder, journals, Periyar's Congress years

x: Periyar served as president and secretary of the provincial Congress and left it in 1925 over the issue of non-Brahmin communal representation and related caste discrimination.
The Self-Respect Movement was launched in 1925, the anti-Hindi agitation occurred in 1937, the Dravidistan demand was made in 1940, and the DMK was formed in 1949.
In Andhra, the movement influenced
Bhagya Reddy Varma and Jala Rangaswamy
to adopt the 'Adi' identity and demand temple entry.
The Self-Respect Movement's rejection of caste hierarchy and Brahmanical dominance fed the Justice Party's non-Brahmin political orientation.

secs.t: Depressed-class journals → founder

x: Vital-Vidhvansak was founded in 1888 by
Gopal Baba Walangkar
Din Bandhu was founded in 1877 by Krishnarao Bhalekar of the Satyashodhak tradition and was later associated with N.M. Lokhande.
Mooknayak was published in 1920, Bahishkrit Bharat in 1927, and Harijan was Gandhi's weekly journal from 1933.

secs.t: Chronology of social reformers' major contributions

x: The organisations were established in 1873, 1903, 1916 and 1925 respectively.
The Madras Communal G.O. was issued in 1921, not 1937.
The Mahad Satyagraha took place in 1927, while the Kalaram Temple Satyagraha is associated with 1930.
The Madras Communal G.O. was issued in 1921 and was associated with the Justice Party's policy of communal representation.

secs.t: Organisations → founder

x: The Justice Party was founded in Madras in 1916 as the
South Indian Liberal Federation
The
SNDP Yogam
was founded in Kerala in 1903 under the inspiration of Sree Narayana Guru.
The Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha organised the Mahad Satyagraha at the
Chawdar Tank
on 20 March 1927.
The Adi Hindu Social Service League opposed the Devadasi system, child marriage and liquor consumption; it did not promote the Devadasi system.

secs.t: Books → author

x: Annihilation of Caste dates to 1936, and The Untouchables and The Problem of the Rupee are also works of B.R. Ambedkar.

Ambedkar criticised Gandhi’s approach, including in Annihilation of Caste, and rejected the term ‘Harijan’. ‘Modern Manu’, ‘Messenger of Dalits’ and ‘Educate, Agitate, Organise’ are associated with him.
Nimna Jatula Charitra was written by Jala Rangaswamy, not B.R. Ambedkar.

secs.t: Ambedkar - satyagrahas, journals, honorary degrees, Neo-Buddhism, Poona Pact

x: Ambedkar accepted the change from separate electorates to reserved seats in joint electorates reluctantly in order to
save Gandhi’s life
The sequence is Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in 1924, Kalaram Temple Satyagraha in 1930, Independent Labour Party in 1936 and Scheduled Castes Federation in 1942.
Ambedkar has been referred to as the ‘
Modern Manu
’, besides being called the Father or chief architect of the Indian Constitution and the Messenger of Dalits.

secs.t: South Indian Liberal Federation - founding and aim

x: Around 30 non-Brahmin leaders met at Victoria Memorial Hall, Madras, on
20 November 1916
and formed the South Indian People's Association.
The English daily Justice was launched on
26 February 1917
, after which the South Indian Liberal Federation became popularly known as the Justice Party.
C. Natesa Mudaliar, T.M. Nair and P. Thyagaraya Chetty were founders of the South Indian Liberal Federation.

secs.t: Elections and ministries under dyarchy

x: A.
Subbarayalu Reddiar
was the first Premier, serving from 17 December 1920 until July 1921 because of ill health.
Panagal Raja
, also known as P. Ramarayaningar, served as Premier from 1921 to 1926 and headed two ministries.
P.T. Rajan
acted as Premier from April to August 1936 during the period of the Bobbili Raja ministry.

secs.t: Andhra leaders of the party - office held

x: Panagal Raja was party president, served as Premier from 1921 to 1926, was associated with Andhra University in 1926 and died on 16 December 1928.
Ramakrishna Ranga Rao was the
13th Raja of Bobbili
and served as Premier from 1932 to 1937.
M. Suryanarayana
moved the separate Andhra resolution in 1922, and it was withdrawn at the urging of A.P. Patro.

secs.t: Decline and later transformation

x: The party suffered from Andhra–Tamil rivalry, lacked a mass base in Andhra and opposed both the freedom struggle and the Andhra movement.
After the 1937 defeat, Periyar became dominant, and the stream later developed into the Dravidar Kazhagam.
C.
Natesa Mudaliar
criticised the Justice Party for neglecting the poor and Harijans.
P. Thyagaraya Chetty died on 25 April 1925, while Panagal Raja died on 16 December 1928.

secs.t: Relations with Congress and the Swaraj Party

x: The government used the Justice Party against the Home Rule movement and Gandhi’s movements.
C.R. Reddy
moved the no-confidence motion against Panagal Raja on 26 November 1923.

secs.t: Aim and social base of the non-Brahmin movement

x: The movement aimed to end Brahmin dominance in jobs, education, politics and religion, besides safeguarding the interests of non-Brahmins.
Reddys, Kammas and Kapus formed the principal intermediate landed-caste base of the movement.
The Andhra Mahasabha met at
Vijayawada in 1917
and sought reserved seats for non-Brahmins.
Ponaka Pattabhirama Reddy and Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary echoed the demand.

secs.t: Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary

x: Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary was popularly known as ‘
Kavi Raju
His rationalist writings and dramas attacked caste stories found in Puranic traditions.
The song was associated with the
Civil Disobedience Movement

secs.t: Works - author

x: Nimna Jatula Charitra was written by Jala Rangaswamy, whereas Boyi Bhimanna wrote works such as Paleru and Gudiselu Kalipotunnai.

secs.t: Caste associations and their journals

x: Prabhodini was associated with the Viswa Brahmana Sangham in 1907 and with Vaddipati Niranjanasastri of Duggirala.
Panchanana was associated with the Viswa Brahmana Sangham in 1914 at Sompet and with K. Ramamurthy.

secs.t: Rationalist and atheist leaders

x: Goparaju Ramachandra Rao was popularly known as
Gora
Gora founded the Atheist Centre at Mudunuru in 1940; it moved to Vijayawada in 1947, and Positive Atheism is associated with him.
The temple-entry campaign took place at Siddhantam in Krishna district in 1933.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
began the two-year nationwide celebration, marked on 11 April 2026.
The Justice Party was criticised for being pro-British and landlord-led, and for having a weak base among the Andhra masses.

All four statements accurately describe the contrast: Gandhi defended varna as division of labour while opposing untouchability, whereas Ambedkar sought caste annihilation, legal rights and separate electorates.
Periyar’s movement was strongly anti-religious, while the Andhra movement was mostly reformist and education-led.
Sree Narayana Guru’s 172nd birth anniversary was observed on
28 August 2026
Sree Narayana Guru consecrated Shiva at Aruvippuram in 1888.

rows.title: Social and religious reform in Andhra - Kandukuri Veeresalingam, Gurajada Apparao, Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu
sub: Group-II S1-78: Social and religious reform in Andhra - Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Venkataratnam Naidu
Group-II M1-A-61: Socio-cultural awakening in Andhra - Kandukuri Veeresalingam and social reform
Group-II M1-A-62: Reform organisations and reformers in Andhra - Brahmo Samaj, Theosophical Society, Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu
Group-II M1-A-63: Gurajada Apparao, Gidugu Ramamurthy and the movement for modern Telugu prose

secs.t: Journals → founder

x: Satyaduta
, published by the Bellary Christian Mission in 1835, is identified as the first Telugu journal and was issued from Bellary.
Vivekavardhini attacked corruption and superstition, while Satyasamvardhini printed a biography of Raja Rammohan Roy.
Satyasamvardhini was a monthly associated with the Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj and was published in 1891.
Satyasamvardhini was edited by
Rayasam Venkata Siva
and included a biography of Raja Rammohan Roy.

Satyaduta was issued by the Bellary Christian Mission; Satyasamvardhini was associated with the Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj; Janana Patrika concerned women's education; and Chintamani was the first Telugu political journal.
The first girls' school was established in 1874, Vivekavardhini began in 1874, the printing press was set up in 1876, and Satihitabodhini began in 1883.
Chintamani was jointly edited by Veeresalingam and Nyapati Subbarao, Satyasamvardhini was linked with the Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj, and Janana or Zenana Patrika promoted women's education.
Veeresalingam's
Hasyasanjeevani
, started in 1876, was a satirical reply to Kokkonda Venkataratnam's Hasyavardhini.
Brahma Vivaham was a satire, not a historical chronicle of the Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj.
Telugu was associated with Gidugu in 1919, Janavani with Tapi Dharma Rao, and the Andhra Sahitya Parishad magazine with Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu.
Satyavahini, also referred to as Satyavadini, was Veeresalingam's reply to Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri's Arya Mata Bodhini and is associated with 1905.

secs.t: Andhra reform firsts → person and place

x: Kandukuri Veeresalingam
conducted the first widow remarriage in Andhra involving Sitamma and Gogulapati Sriramulu.
By 1892 Veeresalingam had arranged 20 widow remarriages, established widow homes at Madras and Rajahmundry, and promoted co-education in Andhra.
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham
founded the Ram Mohan Roy School in 1909 to provide education for children from backward communities.
The correct order is Rajahmundry Social Reform Association (1875), Prarthana Samaj (1878), Widow Remarriage Association (1880), and Hitakarini Samajam (1905).

secs.t: Called as / known as

x: Kandukuri Veeresalingam
was known by several titles, including Gadya Tikkana and Andhra Vaitalikudu.
M. G. Ranade
called Veeresalingam the ‘Vidyasagar of South India’ in 1898, when Veeresalingam presided over the Indian Social Reform Congress at Madras.
The sequence is Hitakarini Samajam (1905), Rao Bahadur title (1893) is actually earlier; therefore the chronological order is A (1893), B (1898), D (1905), C (1919).

secs.t: Plays, novels and songs → author

x: Brahma Vivaham was written by
Kandukuri Veeresalingam
and is identified as a satire.
Kanyasulkam was written by Gurajada Apparao, dealt with bride-price and the plight of widows, and used spoken Telugu.
The line from Gurajada Apparao’s poem Desamunu Preminchumanna expresses that a nation consists of its people rather than merely its soil.

secs.t: Brahmo Samaj / Prarthana Samaj in Andhra - founders, anti-nautch leader

x: The Brahmo Trinity of Andhra comprised
Veeresalingam, Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu and Desiraju Peda Bapaiah
Chembeti Sridharulu Naidu
, the secretary of Madras Veda Samajam, renamed it Dakshina Bharata Brahmo Samaj.
The Brahmo movement in Andhra reached its peak during 1870–1935, with Rajahmundry and Kakinada as its main centres, and upheld monotheism without idol worship.
The correct chronological order is Rajahmundry Prarthana Samaj (1878), Machilipatnam Brahmo Samaj (1882), Kakinada Samaj (1888) and Guntur Samaj (1898).
The anti-nautch campaign opposed
the Bhogam or Devadasi custom
Desiraju Peda Bapayya
of Bapatla was the first practising, or Anushtanika, Brahmo in Andhra.
Desiraju Peda Bapayya led the boycott of Bhogam melas through the Temperance and Social Purity Sangham.
Rajahmundry was the first Renaissance centre, Dowlaiswaram had the first girls' school, and Kakinada became another important centre.
Chembeti Sridharulu Naidu translated Debendranath Tagore's Brahma Dharmam into Telugu in 1875.

secs.t: Region where Andhra social reform began - district and town

x: Reform began at Rajahmundry and subsequently developed in Kakinada, Bapatla and Guntur.
The reform movement began in Rajahmundry under the leadership of
the English-educated middle class
The reform movement began at Rajahmundry in
Godavari district
, corresponding broadly to present-day East Godavari.
Atmuri Lakshmi Narasimham
is identified as the first guru of the early Andhra social reform movement.

secs.t: Young Men's Literary Associations and reform bodies in Andhra towns

x: Stree Punarvivaha Sangham was associated with Kandukuri Veeresalingam.
The Madras Native Association dates to 1852 and was associated with Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty; the Madras Mahajana Sabha was formed in 1884.

secs.t: Other Andhra reformers

x: Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led the movement for Vyavaharika Bhasha, opposing
the Sanskritised grandhika style
The song 'Veeragandhamu techinaramu' is associated with the
Civil Disobedience Movement
Rajyalakshmamma, or Bapamma, married Veeresalingam in 1860 and supported widows and couples involved in the remarriage movement.
Gurajada Apparao used literature to criticise bride-price and the exploitation of widows.

secs.t: Reform institutions → founder

women's homes and schools

Komarraju Lakshmana Rao, Ravichettu Ranga Rao and Nayani Venkata Ranga Rao

secs.t: Gurajada Appa Rao - plays, social themes, modern Telugu literature

x: Kanyasulkam attacked bride-price and child marriage, Mutyala Saralu introduced a new metre, and Desamunu Preminchumanna is a patriotic song associated with Gurajada Appa Rao.
Gurajada Appa Rao worked alongside
Kandukuri Veeresalingam
's reform activities, contributing to literary and cultural renaissance.
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy
and Gurajada Appa Rao were prominent champions of vyavaharika, or spoken, Telugu.

secs.t: Women reformers of Andhra - organisations and journals

x: Acchamamba founded Stree Samajam in 1902, Hindu Sundari was associated with Ramabai and Shantabai, and Rajyalakshmamma provided shelter and organised marriages.
Bhandaru Acchamamba founded
Stree Samajam at Brundavanapuram
in Machilipatnam in 1902.
Acchamamba wrote Abala Sachcharitra Ratnamala, Ramabai and Shantabai were associated with Hindu Sundari, and Muthulakshmi Reddy and Chodagam Ammannaraja worked for the Devadasi Bill.

secs.t: Library movement and spoken-Telugu (vyavaharika) movement - leaders

x: 29 August is observed as Telugu Language Day in recognition of
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy
, a major champion of vyavaharika Telugu.
The first widow remarriage occurred in 1881, Stree Samajam and Hindu Sundari date to 1902, and the Andhra Desa Library Association was founded in 1914.

secs.t: Veeresalingam's literary works - genre and "firsts"

x: Abhijnana Sakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram and Ratnavali were among the translations through which Veeresalingam rendered classical Sanskrit drama into Telugu for the first time.
Rajasekhara Charitra carried the reform themes of
widow remarriage and education
and helped establish the pattern of Telugu social fiction.
Satyaraju Purvadesayatralu was based on Jonathan Swift’s
Gulliver’s Travels

secs.t: Widow remarriage - first marriage and the 1856 Act

x: Exam angle: year (1881) and Act (1856) are asked directly; Ranade/Vidyasagar title with Mrs Manning as distractor.
Paidah Ramakrishnayya supported remarriages at Kakinada, Vedam Venkataraya Sastri wrote the anti-remarriage work, and Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri was associated with Aryananda Brundavani Sabha.
Vedam Venkataraya Sastri wrote
Stree Punarvivaha Durvada Nirvaranam
in 1883, described as the first major anti-remarriage book.

secs.t: Social evils campaigned against - list and methods

x: Expansion of scientific education
was a reform objective, not a social evil.
Veeresalingam's reform methods included journals, satire, public lectures, schools, co-education, remarriages at his own expense and widow homes.
Nautch
, or the Bhogam system, was one of the social evils targeted by reformers in Andhra.

secs.t: Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu (1862-1939)

x: Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu joined the Brahmo Samaj under the inspiration of
Pandit Sivanath Sastri
The Temperance and Social Purity Sangham at Rajahmundry was associated with Desiraju Peda Bapayya.
People's Friend
was associated with Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu's anti-Devadasi campaign.

secs.t: Reform associations - founder and year

Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu founded the Social Purity Association in 1891.

secs.t: Reformers' journals and institutions

x: Vivekavardhini was associated with Rajahmundry in 1874.
Dharmajyoti was associated with Kakinada and appeared in 1939.
Manavaseva was associated with Madras and appeared in 1911.

secs.t: Christian missions in Andhra - year and centre

x: The American Baptist mission was active in Rayalaseema and had schools in Guntur, Gurazala, Palnadu, Ongole and Nellore.
The Church Mission Society operated in the Krishna-Godavari region from 1841, and its Machilipatnam school of that year became a college in 1864.
Christian mission schools admitted Sudras and Panchamas, thereby extending education beyond the traditional upper-caste groups.

secs.t: Zamindari patrons of reform

x: The Pithapuram Raja established
Karunalayam
at Kakinada in 1909 in association with reform and welfare activities.
Karunalayam was described as
the only orphanage in Andhra
and also provided vocational education.
The Pithapuram Raja supported orphan and vocational schools, Brahmopasana Mandiram and the Brahma Dharma Prachara Nidhi.
The second edition of Kanyasulkam, published in 1909, was dedicated to
Ananda Gajapati

secs.t: Gurajada Apparao's literary works - genre and social theme

x: Exam angle: assertion-reason - "Kanyasulkam written by Kommaraju Lakshmana Rao" is false; "it is a satirical play on social evils" is true.
Kanyasulkam is a social play written in vyavaharika Telugu and deals with social evils such as bride-price, child marriage and the plight of widows.
Kanyasulkam uses the Srikakulam dialect, presents Soujanya Rao as a reformer and Ramappa Pantulu as a hypocrite.

secs.t: Vyavaharika vs granthika bhasha - positions, participants, associations

x: Granthika Telugu is classical, archaic and Sanskritised, while Vyavaharika Telugu is the spoken form, also called Gramya or Janapada bhasha.
Navya Sahitya Parishat functioned as a youth organisation that spread Gidugu’s cause of spoken Telugu.
P. T. Srinivasa Ayyangar
wrote *Life or Death: A Plea for Vernaculars* in support of vernacular language use.

secs.t: Early modern Telugu prose, travelogues and the first novel

x: Kandukuri Veeresalingam’s *Rajasekhara Charitra* was based on Oliver Goldsmith’s *
The Vicar of Wakefield
Veeresalingam is credited with writing the first autobiography in Telugu.
*Kasiyatra Charitra* was authored by Enugula Veeraswamayya, not C. P. Brown.
C. P. Brown, Collector of Cuddapah, prepared the first Telugu-English dictionaries and edited Vemana’s verses.

secs.t: Gidugu Ramamurthy - tribal-language work and titles

x: Gidugu was born in 1863, founded the organisation in 1910, received Kaisar-e-Hind in 1934, and died in 1940.
Gidugu created a script, prepared bilingual dictionaries and wrote *A Manual of Savara Language*.
Gidugu was known as Vyavaharika Bhashodyama Pitamaha and Abhinava Vaganushasanudu, and received the titles Rao Saheb and Kaisar-e-Hind.

secs.t: Gurajada - metre, patron court, famous lines

x: Gurajada was associated with the court of
Ananda Gajapati
at Vizianagaram, and his play was staged by the Vizianagaram troupe.
The line expresses the idea that a nation is its people rather than merely its soil or territory.
Gurajada Apparao, associated with 1861–1915, and Gidugu Ramamurthy, associated with 1863–1940, are described as twin pioneers.

secs.t: Supporters and opponents of spoken-Telugu prose

x: Gidugu, Gurajada, Tapi Dharma Rao and the Navya Sahitya Parishat all supported the movement for spoken-Telugu prose.
Kokkonda Venkataratnam was an orthodox editor of *Andhra Bhasha Sanjeevini* and opposed the reform towards spoken Telugu.
Jayanti Ramaiah Pantulu led the classical side through the
Andhra Sahitya Parishad

secs.t: Madras University textbook language controversy
Telugu Language Day

x: Telugu Language Day is observed on 29 August, the birth anniversary of
Gidugu Ramamurthy
Telugu was granted classical language status by the Government of India in 2008.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Kasibhatta Brahmayya Sastri
criticised Rajasekhara Charitra by calling it a mere translation.
Veeresalingam is linked with the Prarthana Samaj and widow remarriage, while Venkataratnam Naidu was associated with the Brahmo Samaj, anti-nautch and social purity reforms.
The reform movement became institutional through
samajs, homes and journals
, enabling it to outlive its individual founders.
The sequence is Atmiya Sabha in 1814, Brahmo Sabha in 1828, Brahmo Samaj in 1828 as the developed institutional form, and abolition of sati in 1829.
The Prarthana Samaj did not reject idol worship or caste outright, whereas the Brahmo Samaj took a more categorical position against them.

wrote Seesari Charitra, a Telugu rendering of Julius Caesar, in 1875.
The standard answer is Kandukuri Veeresalingam’s Rajasekhara Charitram, although some scholars have proposed Kokkonda Venkataratnam’s Mahasweta.
Erramalli Mallikarjunudu
translated Char Darvesh into Telugu as Nagu Pakirula Charitra.
Carey's Telugu Bible was published at Serampore during 1812–1819, and it represents missionary publishing.

secs.t: Colonial scholars of Telugu → contribution

x: C.P. Brown prepared
Telugu-English and English-Telugu dictionaries in 1853
The phrase “Italian of the East” was first used by
Nicolo de Conti
, though it is associated in later discussions with Telugu scholarship.
The Kavali brothers
—Borraiah, Venkataramaiah and Lakshmaiah—assisted Colin Mackenzie in collecting Kaifiyats.
1797 marked Mackenzie’s first visit to the stupa; the marbles reached London decades later.

secs.t: Modern Telugu works → author

x: Musalamma Maranamu was written by Gurajada Apparao, not Tripuraneni Gopichand.
Gabbilam, published in 1941, presents
a bat carrying a Dalit’s prayer to God
Gurajada Apparao’s Kanyasulkam was first staged in 1893.
Kandukuri Veeresalingam
is known as the Father of the Telugu Renaissance.
Veeresalingam was the first to render Kalidasa’s Shakuntalam and Malavikagnimitram into Telugu.

secs.t: Literary associations → members

x: Kokkonda Venkataratnam
presided over the Andhra Sahitya Parishat meetings at Rajahmundry on 23 April 1912 and 22 April 1913.

The correct sequence is founding of Andhra Sahitya Parishat in 1911, Vijnana Chandrika Mandali in 1905, followed by the Rajahmundry meetings in 1912 and 1913; therefore, by the dates supplied, the chronological.

secs.t: Collection and publication of classical works → editor

x: C.P. Brown edited works of Nannaya, Tikkana, Pothana and other classical poets, helping rescue palm-leaf texts through missionary presses.
The manuscripts and Kaifiyats collected by Mackenzie and the Kavali brothers were preserved by
C.P. Brown

secs.t: Andhra Parishat and Kakinada/Rajahmundry cultural bodies

x: The Andhra Sahitya Parishat was founded in Madras in 1911 and later based at
Kakinada
Rajahmundry was Veeresalingam’s reform base, associated with Vivekavardhini, and has been regarded as a cultural capital since the Eastern Chalukya period.

secs.t: Printing presses, missionary publishing, first magazines

x: Schultze's Telugu books were printed at Halle in Germany in 1747.
Ginnekasu and Dinavartamani were Madras publications, while Hitavadi was associated with Masulipatnam and J. Edmund Sharky.
The correct order is Adams Regulation in 1823, Vernacular Press Act in 1878, Press Acts in 1908 and 1910, and the declaration of Telugu as a Classical Language in 2008.

x: Telugu Language Day falls on 29 August, marks Gidugu's birth anniversary, and is associated with Telugu Language Awards.
Andhra Pradesh re-introduced Vemana Suktulu lessons in schools, and a Telugu Bhavan was planned in Mumbai.

were re-introduced in Andhra Pradesh schools in March 2026.
A Telugu Bhavan
was planned in Mumbai as a recent Telugu-related initiative.

secs.t: Social-reform Acts → year, Governor-General, minimum ages

x: Exam angle: Act-year-Governor-General matching, and ages under the 1872, 1891 and 1929 Acts.
Exam angle: "Sati was abolished by" → Bentinck; "Widow Remarriage Act passed in" → 1856.
Regulation XVII of 1829, associated with William Bentinck, prohibited sati and treated participation in it as culpable homicide.
Behramji Malabari
, a Parsi reformer from Bombay, advocated the Age of Consent law.
The correct sequence is the Caste Disabilities Removal Act of 1850, Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act of 1856, Age of Consent Act of 1891, and Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929.
The Lex Loci Act protected the right of a convert to inherit ancestral property; abolition of sati was dealt with by the 1829 Sati Regulation.
The correct sequence is Abolition of Sati Regulation (1829), Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act (1856), Female Infanticide Prevention Act (1870), and Child Marriage Restraint Act (1929).
The Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act, Act XV, was enacted in 1856 and was associated with Lord Canning and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

secs.t: Reform institutions → founder

x: Exam angle: institution-founder matching; the 2023 key differs from the textbooks.
Poona Seva Sadan was founded by
Ramabai Ranade and G.K. Devadhar
Pandita Ramabai founded
Sharada Sadan
in Bombay in 1889; it was later shifted to Poona.
Sarada Niketan was established at Guntur in 1922 by Unnava Lakshminarayana with his wife Lakshmibayamma.

secs.t: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar - campaigns, books, Bethune School, title

x: Exam angle: statement pairs "upliftment of women" + "movement for Widow Remarriage Act" → both correct.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar served as
Head Pandit at Fort William College
As Principal of Sanskrit College, Calcutta, Vidyasagar opened the institution to non-Brahmin students.
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
sent a message of support for Veeresalingam’s third widow remarriage.
Barnaparichay was a Bengali alphabet primer written by Vidyasagar.
Vidyasagar helped
J.E.D. Bethune
establish the Bethune School in 1849, one of the earliest girls’ schools in India.

secs.t: Women's organisations → year

x: Arya Mahila Samaj was established in 1882, Ladies’ Social Conference in 1904, Bharat Stree Mahamandal in 1910 and the Women’s Indian Association in 1917.
The Ladies’ Social Conference, also called Bharat Mahila Parishad, was associated with Ramabai Ranade in Bombay in 1904 and functioned under the National Social Conference.
Bharat Stree Mahamandal, founded by Sarala Devi Chaudhurani, is regarded as
the first major all-India women’s body founded by a woman

secs.t: Age-of-consent debates - Rakhmabai, Phulmoni, Malabari, Tilak

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2020 asked what the Rakhmabai case was about (age of consent + restitution of conjugal rights).
Behramji Malabari published Notes on Infant Marriage and Enforced Widowhood in 1884 while campaigning against child marriage and enforced widowhood.
The Phulmoni Dasi case occurred in
and preceded the Age of Consent Act of 1891.
The 1891 Act raised the age of consent from 10 to 12, dealt with consummation rather than directly regulating marriage, and was enacted during Lord Lansdowne’s tenure.
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
opposed the Bill, including through Kesari, on the ground that it was foreign interference in Hindu custom.

secs.t: Women reformers - FIRSTs and works

x: Exam angle: matching "Sharda Sadan → a home for widows".
Tarabai Shinde wrote
Stri Purush Tulana
in 1882, an early feminist critique of patriarchy.
D.K. Karve founded the Widow Marriage Association, Pandita Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj, and Jyotiba and Savitribai Phule established a girls' school for untouchables.
The Phules opened a girls’ school at Pune in 1848, Savitribai is regarded as India’s first woman teacher, and a home for upper-caste widows was established in 1854.

secs.t: Andhra women reformers (Bandaru Achamamba, Kandukuri Rajyalakshmamma)

x: Kandukuri Rajyalakshmamma hosted widow remarriages and inter-caste marriages at her home, which also became a shelter for widows and destitute women.
Bandaru Achamamba wrote
Abala Sachcharitra Ratnamala
, dealing with the lives of notable women.
The widow homes were established at Madras in 1897 and Rajahmundry in 1905, while Unnava Lakshmibayamma's Guntur asylum of 1902 later merged into Sarada Niketan.

secs.t: Child Marriage Restraint Act - ages fixed and mover

x: The Sarda Act was moved by
Har Bilas Sarda
during the period of Lord Irwin.
The 2021 proposal to raise the women's age to 21 had not become law by January 2026, when the legal age remained 18.
The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 provides a minimum marriageable age of
18 years for women and 21 years for men

secs.t: Bentinck-era reforms - sati, thuggee and its officer, other measures

x: Colonel
William Sleeman
led the suppression of thuggee in the 1830s.
The English Education Act of 1835, associated with Macaulay's Minute, belongs to the Bentinck-era reform context.

secs.t: Native Marriage Act (Civil Marriage Act), 1872 and Brahmo marriages

x: The Act permitted inter-caste marriage, prohibited polygamy and prescribed minimum ages of 14 for girls and 18 for boys.
The Act was passed at the urging of
Keshab Chandra Sen
for the regulation of Brahmo marriages.
The 1878 Brahmo split followed Keshab Chandra Sen's marriage of his minor daughter to the Cooch Behar prince, contrary to the spirit of the Act he had supported.

secs.t: Female infanticide laws - Bengal Regulations, Female Infanticide Prevention Act

x: Bengal Regulations XXI of 1795 and III of 1804 declared infanticide, including female infanticide, to be murder.
The order is Bengal Regulation XXI of 1795, the Sagar Island measure of 1802, the Female Infanticide Prevention Act of 1870, and the Native Marriage Act of 1872.

secs.t: Abolition of slavery - Act V of 1843

x: The Charter Act of 1833 directed abolition, Act V of 1843 under Ellenborough made slavery illegal, and the IPC of 1860 made the slave trade an offence.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court flagged the misuse of POCSO provisions in cases involving consensual adolescent relationships, thereby reopening the debate on the age of consent.

The Supreme Court's observation concerns POCSO and consensual adolescent relationships, while the Rajasthan High Court criticised 'Atta Satta' and noted its possible violation of the PCMA, 2006 when minors are involved.

The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act was enacted in 1856, the first widow remarriage in Bengal took place on 7 December 1856, the Andhra event occurred in 1881, and the Supreme Court observation is contemporary.

founded the Madras Native Association and served as its first president.
Gazula Lakshmi Narasu Chetty started the newspaper
Crescent
P. Rangaiah Naidu
was the president of the Madras Mahajana Sabha, while P. Anandacharlu was its secretary.
The conferences were held at Guntur in 1892, Machilipatnam in 1893, Eluru in 1894 and Angalur in 1900.
S. N. Banerjee toured in 1878 on behalf of the
Indian Association
, stimulating political sentiment.

secs.t: Nationalist literature → author and year

in 1882 and was set against the background of the Sannyasi Rebellion.

founded Crescent, an English newspaper of Madras, in 1844.

secs.t: Surendranath Banerjee - ICS episode, Indian Association, National Conference

x: The reduction from 21 to 19 was viewed as a measure to exclude Indians from the ICS, and Surendranath Banerjee campaigned against it.
Surendranath Banerjee convened the Indian National Conference in 1883 and 1885; it subsequently merged with the Indian National Congress.
Lytton’s policies, including the two Acts, the Delhi Durbar and the reduction in the ICS age limit, intensified criticism of colonial rule.

secs.t: Factors of nationalism - western education, press, history-writing, economic critique

x: British rule produced political, administrative and economic integration through railways, telegraph, post and uniform laws, but economic exploitation ruined many artisans rather than bringing them prosperity.
Veeresalingam’s Vivekavardhani, published in 1874, represented the contribution of socio-religious reform and the press to nationalism.
Economic exploitation, racial arrogance, Lytton’s policies, the Ilbert Bill controversy and foreign nationalist movements stimulated nationalism.

secs.t: Lytton's resented measures (1876-80)

x: Exam angle: "Which was NOT a measure of Lytton?" (the Ilbert Bill was Ripon's).
The Delhi Durbar of 1877
proclaimed Queen Victoria as Empress of India
, even as millions were suffering in the famine of 1876–78.
The Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act were enacted in 1878, the Second Afghan War lasted from 1878 to 1880, and the Delhi Durbar took place in 1877.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: These associations trained educated Indians in constitutional political methods such as petitions and memorials and promoted all-India coordination, leading to the formation of the INC in 1885.
The Madras Native Association was founded in 1852, the Madras Mahajana Sabha in 1884, the Krishna District Association in 1892, and the Indian National Congress in 1885.

secs.t: PERSON - Called as/Known as (Grand Old Man of India) and number of presidencies

x: Naoroji presided three times—in Calcutta 1886, Lahore 1893 and Calcutta 1906—while Bonnerjee presided twice, at Bombay 1885 and Allahabad 1892.
Pherozeshah Mehta was known as the “Lion of Bombay.” Dadabhai Naoroji was the “Grand Old Man of India,” and Surendranath Banerjee was known as “Rashtraguru.”.
Surendranath Banerjee presided at Poona in 1895 and Ahmedabad in 1902; Rash Behari Ghosh at Surat in 1907 and Madras in 1908; Pherozeshah Mehta at Calcutta in 1890.

secs.t: Safety-valve theory → proponents, critics and first user

x: R.P. Dutt gave the conspiracy interpretation, while Bipan Chandra criticised the theory as a colonial myth and described Hume as a lightning conductor; Gokhale made the related point about official hostility.
Dufferin may have suggested an annual forum of educated Indians, but there is no proof that he proposed the establishment of the INC itself.
Bipan Chandra
regarded the safety-valve theory as a colonial myth because Indians were already organising through bodies such as the Indian Association.

The safety-valve view presents the Congress as an outlet for discontent, while the lightning-conductor view presents Hume as a British intermediary who protected the infant organisation from official suppression.

secs.t: INC sessions by region → venue and president

x: Sarojini Naidu presided at Kanpur in 1925, R.N. Mudholkar at Bankipore in 1912, C.R. Das at Gaya in 1922 and Maulana Azad at Ramgarh in 1940.
The presidents were Badruddin Tyabji in 1887, Alfred Webb in 1894, Ananda Mohan Bose in 1898 and Lalmohan Ghosh in 1903.
Rash Behari Ghosh presided in Madras in 1908, Bhupendranath Basu in 1914, M.A. Ansari in 1927 and Maulana Mohammad Ali at Kakinada in 1923.

secs.t: A.O. Hume - background, Viceroy Dufferin's attitude

x: Hume was a retired ICS officer, had strained relations with Lytton, was demoted in 1879, retired in 1882 and then settled at Shimla.
A.O. Hume is known as the
Father of Indian Ornithology
, in addition to his political role in the formation of the INC.
Dufferin initially encouraged the idea of an annual forum but later mocked the Congress as a microscopic minority in 1888.

secs.t: Pre-Congress associations - founder and founding order

x: The Landholders' Society was founded in 1838 to represent zamindar interests, with Dwarkanath Tagore, Prasanna Kumar Tagore and Radhakant Deb among its founders.
George Thomson
founded the Bengal British India Society along with Dwarkanath Tagore, Chandra Mohan Chatterjee and Parmananda Maitra.
Pherozeshah Mehta and K.T. Telang
established the Bombay Presidency Association in 1885 to promote political thinking among western Indian youth.
The Landholders’ Society was founded in 1838, the East India Association in 1866, the Indian Association in 1876 and the Madras Mahajana Sabha in 1884.
The sequence is Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha (1836), Bengal British India Society (1843), British Indian Association (1851), and Madras Native Association and Bombay Association (1852).

secs.t: Causes of the rise of nationalism

x: Colonial economic exploitation, including the conversion of India into a raw-material supplier and captive market, became a major basis of nationalist criticism.
Lord Lytton
was Viceroy from 1876 to 1880 and enacted both the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act in 1878.
The European ‘White Mutiny’ against the Bill and its subsequent dilution revealed the racial discrimination embedded in colonial administration.

secs.t: Nationalist literature - author

x: Anandamath, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1882, is the source of the hymn ‘Vande Mataram’.
Dinabandhu Mitra’s Neel Darpan portrayed
the oppression of indigo cultivators

secs.t: Viceroy at the founding and official attitude

x: Dufferin initially showed official tolerance towards the Congress, but later criticised it as representing a ‘microscopic minority’.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The East India Association was founded in 1866, the Indian Association in 1876, the Madras Mahajana Sabha in 1884 and the INC in 1885.
The INC provided the English-educated class with its first all-India political forum, although its early social base was narrow.
Neel Darpan was written by Dinabandhu Mitra, whereas Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote Anandamath.

secs.t: Economic critique books → author

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2018 - author of *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* = Naoroji (not R.C. Dutt).
Naoroji’s work dates to 1901, Ranade’s to 1898 and G. Subramania Iyer’s to 1903.
Dadabhai Naoroji
used the expression “bleeding India white” while explaining the colonial economic drain.
The Moderates demanded cuts in military expenditure, along with lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax and tariff protection for Indian industries.

secs.t: Gokhale - Servants of India Society, political guru relationships

x: Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society at Poona on 12 June 1905.
The Society trained dedicated public workers and responsible leaders and promoted India’s interests through constitutional means.
M.G. Ranade
was Gokhale’s political and intellectual guru.

secs.t: Dadabhai Naoroji - presidencies, title, British Parliament, drain theory

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2019 keyed "Naoroji founded the INC with Hume and Wacha" as wrong - Hume is the founder.
Dadabhai Naoroji helped found the INC, presided over it three times and became the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons.
In 1892, Dadabhai Naoroji was elected from Central Finsbury as a Liberal Party candidate.

secs.t: Moderate leaders → title and books

x: Surendranath Banerjee wrote *A Nation in Making*. *The Bengalee* was associated with Banerjee, *Rise of the Maratha Power* with Ranade, and *Economic History of India* with R.C. Dutt.
M.G. Ranade was a
judge, economist and social reformer associated with the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha
G. Subramania Iyer founded
*The Hindu* and *Swadesamitran*
and was associated with the Madras Mahajana Sabha.

secs.t: Andhra leaders in the early Congress - sessions presided

x: Nyapathi Subbarao
founded the monthly *Vaijayanti* and edited *People’s Magazine*.
Nyapathi Subbarao was associated with the titles Rajabahadur and Padyavinoda.
After 1908,
Konda Venkatappayya and B.N. Sarma
came to the forefront among the Andhra Moderates.
Anandacharlu was Secretary of the Madras Mahajana Sabha in 1884, while Pattabhi Sitaramayya presided over the Jaipur session in 1948.

secs.t: British Committee of INC and Indian Parliamentary Committee

x: The Committee was formed in London in 1889, was associated with Wedderburn and Naoroji, and published India.
The Indian Parliamentary Committee was set up by
William Wedderburn and W. S. Caine
William Wedderburn
wrote Hume’s biography, published in 1913.
William Wedderburn was President of the INC at its Bombay session in 1889.

secs.t: Demands - councils, ICS, military expenditure, Indianisation, tax relief

x: The Moderates demanded simultaneous examinations, a higher ICS age limit and separation of the judiciary from the executive.
Holding the examination in India as well as England was intended to make entry into the higher services more accessible to Indians and promote Indianisation.
The Moderates expressed outrage at
Tilak’s arrest and the deportation of the Natu brothers without trial

secs.t: Methods and limitations

x: The Moderates believed that British rule was providential and initially placed faith in
British justice and fair play
The Moderate movement had a narrow social base consisting largely of the urban educated elite.
The
Partition of Bengal in 1905
exposed the limitations of the Moderate faith in British justice and fair play.
The Moderates fostered national identity, economic critique and democratic training, but they did not achieve complete independence.

secs.t: Official attitude to the Moderates

x: Lord Curzon made this remark in 1900 while expressing his hostile attitude towards the Congress.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Although the Moderates were criticised for relying on petitions, their supporters argued that this approach created realistic political groundwork for the later national struggle.
The Kakinada Literary Association’s memorandums belong to 1884–1885, Anandacharlu’s presidency was in 1891, and Gandhi’s return on Gokhale’s advice occurred later.
Nyapathi Subbarao was associated with the monthly Vajayanti and was known by the title Rajabahadur.

secs.t: District associations of Andhra

Nyapathi Subbarao
presided over the Krishna District Association conference, which attracted approximately 223 delegates.
The order is Krishna (1892), Vizag (1893), Nellore (1908) and Kurnool (1914).
The Vizag District Association was formed in 1893, not 1907.

secs.t: Early nationalist newspapers of Andhra

x: The pairing of Andhra Prakasika with
P. Anandacharyulu
is accepted as correct.
Nyapathi Subbarao was associated as editor with the monthly publications
Vyjayanti and People's Magazine
By 1905, there were approximately 20 Telugu journals, including Deshabhimani, Sasilekha, Rasikollasini and Gowtami.
These journals criticised administrative failures and helped spread nationalism and democratic ideas.

secs.t: Moderate demands and economic critique

x: The early demands included simultaneous ICS examinations, elected legislative councils and reduction of military expenditure.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
presented the data-led drain critique at the 7th Andhra Mahasabha in Guntur in 1919.
The Andhra opposition to the transfer of Ganjam to Orissa was regarded as the
first victory
of the Andhra political movement.

secs.t: Municipal and local-board politics

x: Paidah Ramakrishnayya
served as the municipal president of Kakinada.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Moderate leaders, district associations and nationalist newspapers collectively built Andhra's political base before the Vande Mataram phase of 1905.
The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded in 1884, the first INC session was held in 1885, the Krishna District Association was formed in 1892, and Krishna Patrika appeared in 1902.

secs.t: Partition of Bengal - Viceroy, dates, stated vs real motives, annulment

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2022 A-R - 1911 Durbar true; Edward VII's coronation (celebrated at the 1903 Durbar ) is not its explanation.
The Moderates’ campaign from 1903 to 1905 was associated with S.N. Banerjee, K.K. Mitra and Prithwishchandra Ray, and used petitions and meetings.
Lord Curzon
described Bengal as “the nerve centre of Indian nationalism,” reflecting the political significance he attached to the province.
The partition separated Bengali-speaking areas and altered the demographic balance so that Bengalis became a minority in their own province, thereby weakening the nationalist centre in Bengal.

secs.t: Swadeshi (Vandemataram) movement in Andhra - Pal's tour, Bala Bharati Samiti, incidents, Andhra Patrika

x: Exam angle: the APPSC 2025 key paired Pal's tour with July 1907 and the Kakinada riots case with April 1907; APP dates Pal's tour to April 1907 - learn the key's pairing for that match.
The arrest of
S.N. Banerjee
in 1906 led to protests and the slogan “Vandemataram — Manade Rajyam.”.
The Bala Bharati Samiti was formed at Rajahmundry in February 1907 by local youths and was supported by Karanam Guneswara Rao.
The formulation “Swaraj the goal, boycott the weapon” was associated with Pal’s
Kakinada
lectures on 17 April 1907.
Principal Mark Hunter banned students from wearing
Vandemataram badges
, leading to defiance and punishment.
The Kakinada case followed the assault of Kompelli Krishna Rao by Dr Kemp after the boy shouted Vande Mataram, after which the European Club was attacked.
Tanguturi Prakasam
defended Chukkapalli Ramayya and the other accused in the Tenali Bomb Case.
Tanguturi Prakasam and Panchumarti Ramachandra Rao
were members of the Bala Bharathi Samiti; the other named founders were Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao, Gante Lakshmanna and Unguturi Sriramulu.
The Young Men's Swarajya Samiti was formed at Machilipatnam during Bipin Chandra Pal's visit in 1907.
Student
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
presented the address against Principal Mark Hunter’s ban on Vande Mataram badges.

secs.t: Swadeshi enterprises → founder

x: Bengal Chemicals was founded by
Acharya P.C. Ray
as a Swadeshi enterprise.
V.O. Chidambaram Pillai established the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin in 1906.
Munagala Raja’s textile unit at Vijayawada, established in June 1906, was the first of its kind in the Madras Presidency.
Malladi Venkata Subbarao trained in pencil production, while S. Ramarao trained in glass and clock manufacture; both were sent to Japan for industrial training.

secs.t: Impact on art, literature and science

x: Rabindranath Tagore
wrote ‘Amar Sonar Bangla’, which later became Bangladesh’s national anthem.
Bankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote ‘Bande Mataram’, which became the anthem of the Swadeshi movement. ‘Desher Katha’ was written by S.G. Deuskar.
S.G. Deuskar’s ‘Desher Katha’ warned against
the British ‘hypnotic conquest of the mind’
Abanindranath Tagore’s Bharat Mata represented nationalist art and marked a break with Victorian naturalism.

secs.t: Chronology - partition to annulment, Handloom Day

x: On 7 August 1905,
the boycott resolution was passed at Calcutta Town Hall and Swadeshi was formally proclaimed
16 October 1905 was marked by mourning, Raksha Bandhan observances and a vow to follow Swadeshi.
In December 1906, the Muslim League was formed at Dacca and the Calcutta Congress under Dadabhai Naoroji adopted Swaraj.
National Handloom Day has been observed on 7 August since 2015, commemorating the Swadeshi proclamation at Calcutta Town Hall.

secs.t: Techniques and programme - boycott, national education, samitis, Town Hall, Calcutta 1906

x: The boycott targeted foreign cloth, salt and sugar;
indigenous handloom products
were encouraged through the Swadeshi programme.
Jatras, folk songs, melas, volunteer corps and physical-training institutions such as akharas and lathi clubs were all used for mobilisation.
The early Moderate phase was associated with petition-based politics under leaders such as S.N. Banerjea, K.K. Mitra and Prithwishchandra Ray; Extremist control emerged from 1906.

secs.t: Leaders → region

x: Aurobindo Ghosh, Bipin Chandra Pal and Ashwini Kumar Dutt were associated with Bengal.
Syed Haider Raza
was identified with the Swadeshi movement in Delhi.
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was associated with Vijayawada.
Chilakamarti was associated with Rajahmundry.

secs.t: Extremist leaders - groups, titles, journals, slogans, trials

x: Bal Gangadhar Tilak served a six-year imprisonment at
Mandalay
Bipin Chandra Pal undertook an Andhra tour in 1907 and was subsequently arrested.
Aurobindo Ghosh was acquitted in the Alipore case and later retired to Pondicherry.
Extremist Swaraj meant complete freedom, not colonial self-government.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sumit Sarkar authored
The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal
, dealing with the 1905 partition and its movement.
Japan’s victory over Russia in 1904–05
inspired Asian and Indian nationalist sentiment and contributed to anger against the partition.
Plays, novels and pamphlets
were used to spread nationalist ideas during the Swadeshi movement.
The movement was regarded as the first mass movement, fostered mass nationalism and popularised boycott, Swadeshi and national education as methods of struggle.

Japan's victory over Russia inspired many young Andhras to seek industrial training in Japan and influenced Munagala Raja, the play Japaniyam and Adipudi Somanatha Rao's Japan Charitra.

secs.t: Bipin Chandra Pal's tour of Andhra - towns, year, organisers, hosts

x: Exam angle: pairing a town with its host or organising body.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
welcomed Pal at Rajahmundry, where Pal stayed at Madella Sourayya's house and delivered five lectures.
Munagala Raja and Nayani Venkata Rangarao
hosted Pal at Vijayawada on 24 April 1907.
Pal delivered his final speech, titled
Matru Murthi
, at Machilipatnam on 27 April 1907.

secs.t: Seditious writings and trials - author and sentence

x: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
started the Telugu weekly Swarajya in 1908.
His article Viparita Buddhi led to a sedition charge and a sentence of
three years
' rigorous imprisonment.

secs.t: Rajahmundry college student incident

x: Mark Hunter, principal of the Rajahmundry Arts and Teachers Training College, banned Vandemataram badges and the slogan in April 1907.
Gadicherla defied Principal Mark Hunter by presenting an address to Bipin Chandra Pal.
A total of
138 students were debarred from examinations for two years
after the incident.
The incident marked the active entry of Andhra students into the freedom struggle.

secs.t: Kakinada riots, Kotappakonda riots, Tenali bomb case

x: Chinnapa, also known as Chennappa Reddy, was sentenced to death and was described as the only person in India sentenced to death in the Vandemataram movement.
The Tenali bomb case occurred in April 1909, involved a bomb aimed at the Howrah passenger, and had Y. Jagganna as a witness.
The accused were
Chukkapalli Ramaiah, Lakkaraju Basavaiah and K. Venkatarayudu
T. Prakasam
successfully secured the release of the accused in the Tenali bomb case.

secs.t: Popular Andhra name - Vandemataram slogan, protests, songs

x: The arrest of Surendranath Banerjee in 1906 triggered protests at
Rajahmundry, Kakinada, Vizianagaram and Gooty
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham
translated Pal's speeches and composed the poem beginning “Bharata khandambu chakkani paadi yaavu.”.
Hinduvulara ennaall ee gati
” is identified as the first Telugu national song, while Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham is regarded as the first Telugu national poet.

secs.t: Leaders of Swadeshi in Andhra - role

x: Mutnuri Krishna Rao
was the editor of Krishna Patrika at Machilipatnam.
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham was the editor of Desamata at Rajahmundry and translated Bipin Chandra Pal's speeches.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao edited Swarajya, was a leader at Bandar, and led the Rajahmundry student protest.
C.Y. Chintamani led in Vizag/Vizianagaram, Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao in Vijayawada, and Konda Venkatappaiah in Guntur.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The movement was connected with national education, Swadeshi stores and student politics.
The movement fed into the Andhra Mahasabha era and the Home Rule branches led by the same men, including Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao and Konda Venkatappaiah.
Chinnapa Reddy
is identified with the only death sentence in India associated with this movement; he was connected with Kotappakonda.

rows.title: Extremists - Lal-Bal-Pal and Aurobindo; ideology; Surat Split 1907

secs.t: PERSON - Called as/Known as (Lokmanya, Punjab Kesari, Father of Indian Unrest, Mahatma of Revolution)

x: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
was popularly known as ‘Lokmanya’, meaning ‘beloved of the people’.
Chirol used the phrase in his book
Indian Unrest
, published in 1910.
Aurobindo Ghosh
was regarded as the chief ideologue of the Extremist wing.
Deshbandhu was the title of C.R. Das.
Lala Lajpat Rai was Punjab Kesari and Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya was Andhra Ratna.

secs.t: Moderate vs Extremist classification; regional extremist groups

x: The Maharashtra extremist group was led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak; Bengal was associated with Pal and Aurobindo, and Punjab with Lala Lajpat Rai.
The Moderates followed the three Ps—prayers, petitions and protests—whereas the Extremists emphasised the three Ss and mass agitation.
The Moderates were generally pro-reform, while the Extremists were comparatively orthodox; Tilak opposed the Age of Consent Bill.

secs.t: Chronology - Swadeshi, Surat Split, Minto-Morley, Lucknow Pact, Home Rule

x: The correct order is Surat Split (1907), Tilak's Home Rule League (1916), Lucknow Pact (December 1916), and Montagu Declaration (20 August 1917).
Tilak's League was formed in April 1916, Besant's in September 1916, the Lucknow Pact was concluded in December 1916, and the Montagu Declaration was issued in August 1917.

secs.t: Extremist leaders → newspapers, books and slogans

x: Tilak published
Kesari
in Marathi and Mahratta in English; both newspapers began in 1881.
Aurobindo Ghosh’s New Lamps for Old appeared during 1893–94 in the Bombay newspaper
Indu Prakash
Bipin Chandra Pal
is commonly identified with Aurobindo Ghosh as a co-editor of Bande Mataram.
Lala Lajpat Rai is associated with the slogan ‘
Go back Simon
The Arctic Home in the Vedas was written by
Bal Gangadhar Tilak

secs.t: Surat Split (1907) - president, issues, Calcutta 1906 background

x: The Calcutta session of 1906 passed resolutions on
Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education
as a compromise between Moderates and Extremists.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta represented the Moderates, while Bal Gangadhar Tilak represented the Extremists in the Surat conflict.
The Extremists wanted the boycott extended throughout India, while the Moderates wanted the movement restricted to Bengal and sought to drop the 1906 resolutions.

secs.t: Tilak - festivals, sedition trials, imprisonment, books

x: Tilak worked with Agarkar in establishing the New English School, and the Deccan Education Society founded Fergusson College; the standard dates are 1880 and 1884.
Tilak received 18 months in the 1897 sedition trial, six years in Mandalay in 1908, and was acquitted in the 1916 case.
Tilak was released from Mandalay prison on
16 June 1914
after his six-year imprisonment beginning in 1908.

secs.t: Lajpat Rai and Bipin Pal - writings, biographies, stay abroad, Brahmo links

x: Bipin Chandra Pal was a member of the
Brahmo Samaj
, whereas Lajpat Rai was associated with the Arya Samaj.
Bipin Chandra Pal was arrested in 1907
for refusing to testify in the Bande Mataram case
The correct order is 1907 deportation of Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh, 1908 deportation of Tilak, Aurobindo's acquittal in 1909 and his retirement to Pondicherry in 1910.

secs.t: Ideology - swaraj, self-reliance, passive resistance, spiritual nationalism

x: For the Extremists, Swaraj meant
complete freedom from British control
, not merely colonial self-government.
All four were part of the Extremist programme, along with self-sacrifice and a rejection of dependence on British generosity.
Spiritual nationalism represented the nation as
a mother goddess
, an idea expressed through symbols such as Bande Mataram and Bhavani Mandir.
Cooperatives
were cited as an example of constructive work associated with Atmashakti or self-reliance.

secs.t: Government repression - Newspapers Act 1908, deportations

x: The
Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act
was enacted in 1908.
Bipin Chandra Pal was arrested in 1907 for refusing to testify in the Bande Mataram case; he was not deported to Mandalay.
The Moderates dominated because Tilak was in jail, Aurobindo had retired, Pal was arrested and Lajpat Rai had left by 1910.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Extremists were criticised for using religious symbolism that alienated Muslims and for being socially orthodox.
Lokmanya Tilak's birth anniversary is observed on
23 July
, and the Prime Minister paid tribute to him on that occasion.
Students of the Machilipatnam National College wore
Besant lockets
after Annie Besant was arrested on 15 June 1917.

rows.title: Morley-Minto Reforms 1909; formation of the Muslim League 1906; Lucknow Pact 1916

secs.t: Act → electoral feature introduced

x: Exam angle: "Which Act introduced the communal electorate?" → Morley-Minto 1909; match-the-list of Acts with separate electorates / dyarchy / federation / provincial autonomy.

The 1935 Act supplied the federal scheme, the Instrument of Instructions influenced the Directive Principles, the 1919 Act provided for central bicameralism, and the 1909 Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

secs.t: Indian Councils Act 1909 - name, electorates, first Indian on Executive Council

x: Satyendra Prasanna Sinha
became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council and held the Law portfolio.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
met Morley in England in 1906 and advocated self-government for India.
Morley and Minto sought to
rally the Moderates and reward Muslim loyalty

led the Shanti Sena in the firka and was also associated with the no-tax campaign.
The Guntur District Congress Committee decided to form the Shanti Sena in
December 1921

secs.t: Government response - officials, arrests, withdrawal

x: Collector A.
Gellatly
attributed the resignations to low pay and workload.
Konda Venkatappayya and Gollapudi Sitarama Sastri backed the campaign, whereas Nyapathi Subbarao urged restraint.
Gandhi’s message to suspend the campaign reached the Guntur District Congress Committee on
11 February 1922
, after which the campaign ended with the Non-Cooperation Movement.

secs.t: Link with Bezawada AICC decisions and NCM programme

x: The Delhi AICC permitted provincial committees to undertake
civil disobedience, including no-tax campaigns
The Palnadu forest satyagraha was also a local expression of the same Non-Cooperation call.

secs.t: Madras Forest Act - year and provisions

x: The Madras Forest Act was enacted in 1882.
The Act restricted tribal access to podu cultivation and minor forest produce, and curbed grazing; it did not recognise unrestricted access.
Begar meant forced unpaid labour, including work imposed on roads.

secs.t: Rampa rebellion chronology - start, police stations, end

x: Chintapalli was attacked on 22 August 1922, Annavaram was raided on 18 April 1923, Mallu Dora was arrested on 17 September 1923, and the Assam Rifles and Gurkhas reached Narsipatnam on 27 January 1924.
Bastian’s local excesses contributed to the grievance, Keirns arrested Mallu Dora, and Scott Coward and Heiter were killed at Damanapalli.

secs.t: Rebellions in chronological order - Phadke, Khudiram Bose, Alluri

x: The Gulugonda tribal revolt took place in the Vizag region during 1845–48 under Chinna Bhupathi.

secs.t: Associates of Alluri - role

x: Gam Gantam Dora was killed on 7 June 1924.
Aggiraju
was arrested at the Maddaru river on 6 May 1924.

secs.t: British officers involved - post

x: Rutherford
served as Special Commissioner to crush the revolt and ordered the exile of 55 helpers; warrants were issued for 183 persons.
Goodall
was the Major in whose presence Alluri Sitarama Raju was shot.

secs.t: Agency tribes and grievances - podu, muttadars, forced labour

x: Begar meant forced unpaid labour, not voluntary paid labour.
The Muttadari system generated resentment through extortion and forced labour, adding to the grievances caused by forest restrictions and begar.

secs.t: Earlier 19th-century Rampa rebellions - causes, leaders

x: Madhava Bhupati was made Munsubdar in 1848, after which his exploitation of the tribal population became a major cause of the Rampa rebellion.
Dwarabandala Chandrayya, Pulikanta Sambaiah and Karu Tammanna Dora led the Rampa rebellion.
The Rekapalle rebellion was triggered by
the increase of the axe tax on podu from 4 annas to 4–12 annas during a famine

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The period 1921–31 is called the “
Glorious Decade
” of Andhra because of mass movements such as Chirala–Perala, Palnadu and Pedanandipadu.
Chirala–Perala, Palnadu and Pedanandipadu demonstrated mass non-cooperation, while the Rampa movement represented tribal armed resistance.
Guntur witnessed mass exodus, resignations by officials and a no-tax campaign, making it one of the most innovative centres of the Non-Cooperation Movement in Andhra.
A 30-foot bronze statue of Alluri Sitarama Raju was unveiled by the Prime Minister at Bhimavaram to mark his 125th birth anniversary.

rows.title: Growth of nationalist poetry in Telugu - Gurajada, Rayaprolu, Garimella Satyanarayana
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-180

secs.t: Nationalist songs → poet + collection

x: Gurajada Apparao’s poem was published in
Andhra Bharati
and came to be regarded as the national anthem of the Telugu people.
“Veera gandham tecchinaramu” was written by Tripuraneni Ramaswamy during
the Salt Satyagraha era
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham improvised the song
during Bipin Chandra Pal’s speeches at Rajahmundry in April 1907

secs.t: Poets' popular titles → poet

x: The accepted examination answer is
Rayaprolu Subbarao
Gurram Jashuva was given the title Navayuga Kavi Chakravarti in 1946.
Kavi Kokila is associated with
Duvvuri Ramireddy
Sri Sri
is popularly known as 'Maha Kavi'.
Gurram Jashuva's recorded titles include Kavi Kokila, Navayuga Kavi Chakravarti, Viswa
kavi Samrat
and Madhura Kavi Srinatha. 'Kavi Samrat' is associated with Viswanatha Satyanarayana.

secs.t: Poets → works (match format)

x: Rayaprolu wrote Andhravali, Gurajada wrote Kanyasulkam, Viswanatha wrote Veyipadagalu, and Unnava wrote Malapalli.
Matru Desa Sankeertanam
was written by Duvvuri Ramireddy.
Kanyasulkam was written by
Gurajada Apparao
and was staged in 1893.
Veyipadagalu received Sahitya Akademi recognition, while Ramayana Kalpavrikshamu won the Jnanpith and was the first such award for a Telugu writer.

secs.t: Patriotic plays and verse inspired by world events → author

x: Japaneeyamu was written by
Sriram Veerabrahmam
of Bandar and celebrated Japan’s victory over Russia in 1905.
The play concerned Jallianwala Bagh, cast Dyer as Duryodhana, was discussed in the British Parliament, and led to the arrest of 25 Vizag students who staged it.
Kanyasulkam was staged in 1893, Japan’s victory occurred in 1905, Mahabharata Kaurava Rangam was written in 1916, and Padmavyuham in 1919.

secs.t: Rayaprolu Subba Rao - works, genre, new poetic concept

x: Rayaprolu pioneered
Bhava Kavitvam
, or poetry centred on emotion, drawing on Shelley and Keats.
Rayaprolu broke with the translation of Sanskrit epics and brought original, emotive verse into Telugu.
Progressive writers such as Sri Sri
criticised Rayaprolu’s romanticism as escapist, even though he had an important role in freeing Telugu verse from rigid prosody.

secs.t: Garimella Satyanarayana - song banned, imprisonment, collections

x: He was jailed in 1922 for
one year
for the song “Maakoddee Tella Doratanamu.” A later sentence involved two and a half years of rigorous imprisonment.
The song belonged to the Non-Cooperation era, he later received two and a half years of rigorous imprisonment, and three close family members died during his imprisonment.

secs.t: Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham - patriotic verse, occasion, consequence

x: Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham translated Bipin Chandra Pal’s 1907 speeches and improvised the verse at Rajahmundry.
At Rajahmundry, Chilakamarti translated Bipin Chandra Pal’s speeches and improvised the patriotic verse “Bharata khandambu...”.
The verse literally presents the Indian subcontinent as one large prison, conveying the reality of British colonial rule.
Hinduvulara ennaallee gati
” is recognised as the first Telugu national song, while Chilakamarti is recognised as the first Telugu national poet.

secs.t: Bhavakavitvam - founder, features, main poets

x: Rayaprolu Subbarao
is regarded as the founder of Bhavakavitvam.
Bhavakavitvam emphasised romantic and personal emotion, nature, love and freedom from classical prosody, and it also contained patriotic strands.
Ekanta Seva
, associated with the Venkata Parvateeswara Kavulu, is described as the “Telugu Gitanjali”.

secs.t: Proscribed Telugu literature → author + year

x: Chicharapidugu was serialised in Congress from 1927 to 1929, and its editor Madduri Annapurnaiah was jailed.
Performers of Panchala Parabhavam by Damaraju Pundarikakshudu were arrested in Vizag.
Roshanara was the earliest item identified as the first banned play, followed by Maakoddee Tella Doratanamu in 1922, Chicharapidugu in 1927–29 and Veerabali in 1931.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Songs in spoken Telugu could reach villagers more effectively than pamphlets, thereby widening nationalist communication.
Gurajada helped make vyavaharika bhasha, or spoken Telugu, a normal literary medium.
Chief Minister Naidu recalled Gurajada, Sri Sri and the Jnanpith winners
Viswanatha, C. Narayana Reddy and Ravuri Bharadwaja
at the World Telugu Mahasabhalu.
