rows.title: Revolutionary literature in Telugu - Sri Sri, Abhyudaya movement
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-180

secs.t: Works → author

x: The preface to *Mahaprasthanam* was written by
Chalam
, whereas the work was dedicated to Kompella Janardhana Rao.
*Gabbilam* was written by Gurram Jashuva, not Sri Sri. *Firdausi* was also written by Jashuva, while *Asamarthuni Jeevayatra* was written by Tripuraneni Gopichand.
*Firdausi* is described as a
laghu kavyam
by Gurram Jashuva.

secs.t: Telugu translations of world progressive literature → translator

x: Krovvidi Lingaraju
translated Gorky's *The Mother* into Telugu as *Amma* in 1934.
*Neti Russia* was written by
Narla Venkateswara Rao
Arudra translated *Veera Telangana Viplava Geethalu*, while the Mahidhara brothers and Gadde Lingayya's organisations published progressive and world literature.

secs.t: Abhyudaya Rachayitala Sangham (Arasam) - founding year, venue, first president

x: Arasam, the Telugu Progressive Writers' Association, was formed in 1943.
Arasam
organised the Abhyudaya current that Sri Sri's poems initiated.

secs.t: All India Progressive Writers' Association - founding session, link to Arasam

x: The All India Progressive Writers' Association was founded at Lucknow in 1936.
Premchand
presided over the founding session of the All India Progressive Writers' Association at Lucknow.

secs.t: Abhyudaya writers → works

x: Arudra
wrote *Tvamevaham*, associated with the Telangana struggle and dated 1948–49.
Arudra, whose original name was Bhagavatula Sadasiva Sankara Sastri, was
Sri Sri
's nephew.
*Pandita Parameswara Sastri Veelunama*
by Tripuraneni Gopichand received the Sahitya Akademi recognition referred to here.
Boyi Bhimanna
wrote *Gudisale Kalipotunnayi*, which won the Sahitya Akademi award in 1975.

secs.t: Praja Natya Mandali and progressive songs → writers

x: Praja Natya Mandali staged *Maa Bhoomi*, written by
Sunkara Satyanarayana and Vasireddy Bhaskara Rao
Art Lovers became Jana Natya Mandali in 1971; Art Lovers itself is associated with 1970.
Praja Natya Mandali was a communist cultural front that spread its ideas through drama, songs and folk forms.
Burrakatha
was the main folk form used by Praja Natya Mandali.

secs.t: Sri Sri's titles, awards and later organisations

x: Sri Sri received the National Award for Best Lyricist for
*Telugu Veera Levara*
from the film *Alluri Seetharama Raju*.
CDX dates Sri Sri's National Award for Best Lyricist to 1974.
Sri Sri
was the founding President of Virasam, the Viplava Rachayitala Sangham or Revolutionary Writers' Association.
Sri Sri co-founded Sahiti Samiti at Vizag with
Puripanda Appalaswamy

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The broad path ran from Abhyudaya literature through Arasam in the 1930s–40s to Viplava literature through Virasam in 1970, with Telugu poetry moving from nationalism towards class struggle.
Traditionalists argued that Sri Sri's free verse destroyed the 'sweetness' of Telugu, while his supporters credited him with making Telugu poetry modern.

rows.title: Nataka Samasthalu - theatre companies and their nationalist role
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-180

secs.t: Nationalist and reformist plays → playwright

x: Exam angle: four-pair play-author matching.
Kanyasulkam attacks bride-price and uses spoken Telugu, Varavikrayam opposes dowry, and Prataparudriyam deals with Prataparudra historically.
Drama companies initially carried social-reform themes, including Kanyasulkam and Veeresalingam’s drama, before taking up nationalist themes.
The Rajahmundry Hindu Nataka Samajam staged plays written by
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham and Toleti Venkata Subbarao

secs.t: Plays banned by the British → author + movement

x: Exam angle: "banned during which movement" plus "who wrote it".
Theatre could communicate political ideas before thousands of illiterate people in a single evening, making drama companies an influential medium of nationalist mobilisation.
Gollapudi Sitarama Sastri was among the Andhra leaders who supported the Non-Cooperation Movement boycott of elections in 1920.

secs.t: Theatre companies → founder + town

x: Surabhi was founded by Vanarasa Govinda Rao, Sarasa Vinodini Sabha by Dharmavaram Ramakrishnamacharyulu, Guntur Hindu Nataka Samajam by Kondubhatla Subramanyasastri, and Amateur Nataka Sabha by Erugudipati Gopalakrishnarao.
Surabhi was founded in 1885, Sarasa Vinodini Sabha in 1886, Amateur Nataka Sabha in 1896, and the first Mahasabha of Andhra Nataka Kala Parishad was held in 1929.

secs.t: Stage actors → famous roles

x: Sthanam Narasimha Rao was famed for female roles such as Madhuravani in Kanyasulkam and Satyabhama.
Tanguturi Prakasam and Durga Gopalakrishnayya
acted main roles for the Hindu Nataka Samajam at Rajahmundry.
Bellary Raghava, the celebrated stage actor, was a relative of
Dharmavaram Ramakrishnamacharyulu

secs.t: Titles of playwrights and actors → person

x: Dharmavaram Ramakrishnamacharyulu
was known as Andhra Nataka Pitamaha, meaning ‘Grandfather of Andhra Drama’.
Dharmavaram Ramakrishnamacharyulu was born in January 1853 at Dharmavaram, Anantapur, died on 30 November 1912, and wrote more than 30 plays.

secs.t: Bellary and Rayalaseema theatre - playwrights and companies

x: Kolachalam Srinivasa Rao was a Bellary playwright known for
historical plays
Lalita Kala Parishad at Anantapur was inaugurated by the Governor on 11 February 1956, and its land was donated by freedom fighter Kalluru Subbarao.

secs.t: Padya natakam vs social drama - features

x: Padya natakam deals mainly with mythological or epic themes, whereas social drama focuses on contemporary social evils.
Surabhi repertoire and Gayopakhyanam are associated with Padya natakam.
Gurajada made spoken Telugu the norm for writing.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Drama companies were the main mass entertainment of the time.
Nataka Vidyalayam was started at Vijayawada on 1 August 1964 and trained students in the dramatic arts.
Surabhi marks the shift
from Tholu Bommalata puppets to live Telugu family theatre

rows.title: Women's participation in the national movement in Andhra - Durgabai Deshmukh, Unnava Lakshmibayamma, Duvvuri Subbamma
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-180

secs.t: Women's organisations and journals → founder + year

x: Exam angle: "Who founded Andhra Mahila Sabha?": Durgabai Deshmukh, not Sarojini Naidu or Duvvuri Subbamma.
Zenana Patrika was founded by Kandukuri Veeresalingam in 1894, and Sati Hitabodhini by him in 1883.
The Nizam's Andhra Mahasabha conducted parallel Andhra Mahila Sabha conferences, including one at Devarakonda in 1931 under the presidency of T. Varalakshmamma.

secs.t: Durgabai Deshmukh - institutions, CDM role, posts after independence

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2023 asked which statements on her were NOT true; the key rejected "Iron Lady" and "Tamrapatra and Paul Hoffman award".
At Kakinada in April 1921, Durgabai
collected and donated Rs 5,000, arranged Gandhi's meeting with Devadasis and Muslim women, and translated his speech
Durgabai Deshmukh participated prominently in the Salt Satyagraha in
Madras city
, alongside K. Nageswara Rao and T. Prakasam.

secs.t: Other women freedom fighters → district + distinctive sacrifice

x: Ravuri Alivelu Mangatayaramma, an elderly woman from the Chirala-Perala area, was one of twelve women jailed in 1921.
Bharati Devi Ranga

was among the other women associated with the Civil Disobedience Movement in Andhra, along with Vallabhaneni Sitamahalakshamma, Digumarti Janakamma, Gadicherla Seshabai and Tallapragada Viswasundaramma.
Dodla Ramireddy
formed the Nellore Zilla Zamindari Rytu Sangam in 1929 in connection with the Venkatagiri struggle.

secs.t: Books on women in the Andhra freedom struggle → author
Sarada Niketanam (Guntur) → founders + year

x: Sarada Niketanam was founded as a women's Gurukulam in 1922.
Sarada Niketanam was founded by Unnava Lakshminarayana together with his wife Unnava Lakshmibayamma.
Sarada Niketanam was a women's Gurukulam that sheltered and educated vulnerable girls and became a hotbed of the freedom movement.

secs.t: Unnava Lakshmibayamma - movements joined, imprisonment

x: In 1902, Unnava Lakshmibayamma ran the widow asylum and held the first widow remarriage there.
She led the Guntur hartals after her husband was arrested over the Palnadu forest, or pullari, satyagraha.
On 9 April 1930, Unnava Lakshmibayamma led women in
Krishna and Guntur districts
along with Rukmini Lakshmipathi.

secs.t: Duvvuri Subbamma - titles, movements, imprisonment

x: Duvvuri Subbamma founded the national school called
Sanatana Vidyalayam
at Rajahmundry.
The Vijayawada AICC was attended in 1921, followed by the Neil statue satyagraha, the Salt Satyagraha at Chollangi in April 1930, and the Quit India Movement lathi charge at Peddapuram in 1942.
After making salt at Chollangi, Duvvuri Subbamma was arrested at Rajahmundry and sent to
Nellore jail

secs.t: Women in Salt Satyagraha and QIM in Andhra → place

x: On 6 April 1930 at Chollangi in East Godavari, Duvvuri Subbamma was among the women participating in salt-making activities.
During the 1942 Quit India Movement, Duvvuri Subbamma faced a lathi charge at Peddapuram.
In the Palnadu forest satyagraha, eight women were arrested along with twenty-eight men.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Pawan Kalyan referred to Durgabai Deshmukh as a founding mother of the Constitution while welcoming the Bill, which concerns 33 per cent reservation and was introduced in the Lok Sabha; the report was dated 17 April 2026.
Annie Besant became the first woman President of the INC at the Calcutta session in 1917.

rows.title: Prominent Andhra leaders - Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Tanguturi Prakasam, Bulusu Sambamurthy
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-180

secs.t: Leaders' popular titles → person + episode behind the title

x: Exam angle: "After which movement was Prakasam called Andhra Kesari?" = Simon Go Back.
Tanguturi Prakasam came to be known as Andhra Kesari for his role in
the Simon Go Back protest at Madras in 1928
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao earned the title ‘Andhra Tilak’ for his
courage during the Vande Mataram era

secs.t: Posts held → leader

x: Bezawada Gopal Reddy
was the second and last Chief Minister of Andhra State, holding office from 28 March 1955 to 31 October 1956.

Tanguturi Prakasam was the Chief Minister of Andhra State in 1953, Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy led united Andhra Pradesh in 1956–1960, and N. Chandrababu Naidu became Chief Minister of residuary Andhra Pradesh in 2014.

secs.t: Pingali Venkayya - flag design, Congress sessions, early career

x: Pingali Venkayya showed the flag to Gandhi at the Vijayawada AICC meeting held on 31 March–1 April 1921.
The venue of the Vijayawada AICC meeting was named ‘
Gandhi Nagar
Pingali Venkayya was born at
Bhatlapenumarru near Machilipatnam
Pingali Venkayya was known as ‘Patti Venkayya’ for his study of cotton varieties.
Pingali Venkayya published a book on national-flag designs in 1916.

secs.t: Books written → author

x: Feathers and Stones
’, described as an Ahmednagar Fort prison diary, was written by Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Chenna Nagaramu Andhra Nagaramae
’ was written by Tanguturi Prakasam.
‘Naa Jeevita Yatra’ is Prakasam’s autobiography and consists of four parts.
Andhrudyamam
’ was written by Konda Venkatappayya.
Pattabhi Sitaramayya wrote articles in The Hindu advocating the need for
linguistic states

secs.t: Tanguturi Prakasam - Simon protest, Swarajya, Madras premiership

x: Tanguturi Prakasam was born on 23 August 1872 at Vinodarayunipalem, in the area now forming Prakasam district.
In 1951, Tanguturi Prakasam left the Congress with N. G. Ranga and founded the
Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party
Tanguturi Prakasam was a coastal signatory to the Sribagh Pact, concluded on
16 November 1937

secs.t: Konda Venkatappayya - Andhra Mahasabha, Congress offices, CDM dictator

x: The correct order is Tenali Swadeshi meeting (1907), Nidadavolu standing committee (1912), Bapatla session (1913), and Nellore session (1917).
Konda Venkatappayya presided over the fifth session of the Andhra Mahasabha held at
Nellore
The Non-Cooperation resolution at the Calcutta Special Session of 1920 was passed by 1,886 votes to 884, despite Konda Venkatappayya’s opposition.

secs.t: Bulusu Sambamurthy - Congress session role, posts held

x: Bulusu Sambamurthy toured Andhra calling for a
boycott of the Simon Commission
Sambamurthy supported the 1920 election boycott, attended the Vijayawada AICC meeting in 1921 and signed the Sribagh Pact as a coastal representative.
The correct order is the 1920 election boycott, the 1921 Vijayawada AICC meeting, the 1923 Kakinada session and the 1937 speakership.

secs.t: Pattabhi Sitaramayya - presidential contest, session presided, first Telugu INC president

x: Exam angle: book-author, title-person and post-person matching.
Pattabhi Sitaramayya contested the 1939 Tripuri presidential election as Gandhi's candidate and was defeated by Subhas Chandra Bose.
The JVP Committee, comprising Nehru, Patel and Pattabhi, initially rejected the demand for linguistic States.
The JVP Committee consisted of
Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.

These four leaders collectively guided Andhra's political activities connected with the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience Movements, Simon Commission boycott, Sribagh Pact and the demand for Statehood.
Prakasam district
is named after Tanguturi Prakasam.
Andhra Bank, founded in 1923, represented the spirit of
Swadeshi enterprise
in Andhra.

rows.title: Peasant movements - Indigo, Deccan Riots, Moplah, Bardoli, Tebhaga, Telangana armed struggle

secs.t: Telangana armed struggle - Komaraiah, Ailamma, Andhra Mahasabha presidents, leaders and memoirs

x: The struggle in Hyderabad State was directed against the Nizam’s feudal order, particularly the power of jagirdars and deshmukhs and the practice of Vetti.
The Andhra Mahasabha evolved from cultural activity into a left-oriented agrarian organisation and became the CPI’s organisational front in the struggle.
Doddi Komaraiah was shot at Kadavendi in Jangaon on 4 July 1946 by the men of
the Visnur deshmukh
Chakali Ailamma, a washerwoman from Palakurthi,
defended her land against the Visnur deshmukh
and became a symbol of the revolt.

secs.t: Kisan movement in Andhra - pioneer, Nidubrolu, Ryots' Associations

x: The Andhra Pradesh references name
Kommareddy Satyanarayana Murthy and Chalasani Vasudeva Rao
as the leaders of the march, dated 1937–38.
The Political Summer School was at Kothapatnam in 1937, Rajakeeya Pathashala at Kankipadu in 1939, and Andhra Rythu Vidyalayam at Madanapalle in May 1938.
The Peasant Institute or Ramanayidu Rythu Vidyalayam was established at Nidubrolu in
and was regarded as India’s first Kisan School.

secs.t: Andhra anti-zamindari struggles - district and leaders

x: The Permanent Settlement, introduced by Cornwallis in 1793, made zamindars owners while cultivators became tenants, creating the structural basis for later anti-zamindari opposition.
The Munagala estate was then in Krishna and is now in Nalgonda; Nayani Venkataranga Rao was its zamindar, and Batchala Jagannadh Das was associated with its peasant association.

secs.t: Indigo Revolt - Nil Darpan, region

x: The Indigo Revolt of 1859–1860 occurred chiefly in Nadia region of Bengal.
Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas
were leaders associated with the Indigo Revolt in Bengal.
The Tinkathia system required indigo cultivation on three-twentieths, or 3/20, of the peasants’ land, generally at poor prices.

secs.t: Peasant movements - region, year and chronology

rows.title: Government of India Act 1919 - dyarchy, Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms; Rowlatt Act
sub: Group-II S1-88: Constitutional developments - GoI Act 1919, Simon Commission, GoI Act 1935

secs.t: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - dyarchy, subjects, central legislature, electorate

x: The reforms were named after Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State for India, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy of India.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Report was announced in
July 1918
; it subsequently formed the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919.
Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces, provincial subjects were divided into reserved and transferred categories, and the provincial budget was separated from the central budget.
Education
was a transferred subject administered by a Governor's minister drawn from the elected legislature and answerable to it.
The Act introduced a bicameral central legislature comprising the Council of State as the upper chamber and the Legislative Assembly as the lower chamber.
Local self-government
was among the transferred subjects administered by the Governor with ministers.

secs.t: GoI Act 1919 - sections and bodies, first ministries

x: The
Chamber of Princes
, also known as Narendra Mandal, was created as a consultative body of rulers under the 1919 reforms.
The Chamber of Princes was set up in 1921 by royal proclamation under the framework of the 1919 reforms.
The Congress boycotted the 1920 Madras elections as part of the Non-Cooperation movement, while the Justice Party won 63 seats.

secs.t: Direct elections - first Act and franchise

x: The Act introduced direct elections, but the franchise remained limited by
property, tax and educational qualifications
The
Indian Councils Act, 1909
introduced elected non-official members, largely through indirect and separate electorates.
The
Government of India Act, 1919
introduced direct elections.

secs.t: Central Legislative Assembly elections under the 1919 Act

x: The Swaraj Party, led by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, entered the legislatures in order to obstruct colonial governance from within.
The Swarajists secured about 40 per cent of the seats in 1923 and demanded a review of the Government of India Act, 1919.
Vithalbhai Patel
became the President, commonly described as the Speaker, of the Central Legislative Assembly.

secs.t: Montagu Declaration 1917

x: The
Home Rule Leagues
created political pressure that contributed to the British declaration recognising self-government as an objective.
Montagu and Chelmsford toured India in December 1917 as part of the process of consulting Indian opinion on constitutional reforms.
The Andhra delegation led by Nyapati Subbarao sought the creation of
a separate Andhra province

secs.t: Moderates' exit - Indian National Liberal Federation

x: Following the split over the Montagu-Chelmsford proposals, the Moderates under Surendranath Banerjee formed the
Indian National Liberal Federation

The Surat split occurred in 1907, the reunion at Lucknow in 1916, the Montagu Declaration was issued in 1917, and the Indian National Liberal Federation was formed after the 1918 split over the proposals.

secs.t: Statutory review clause

x: The Act required a statutory commission to review its working after
ten years

secs.t: Simon Commission - composition, arrival, boycott and protests

x: Lahore was associated with Lala Lajpat Rai, Madras with Tanguturi Prakasam, Lucknow with Jawaharlal Nehru and G.B. Pant, and Tenali–Guntur with G.V. Unnayya Sastri.
Tanguturi Prakasam bared his chest before the police during the anti-Simon Commission protest at Madras and became known as Andhra Kesari.
The report recommended abolition of provincial dyarchy, provincial autonomy and retention of separate electorates.
The Simon Commission was appointed on
8 November 1927
by the Conservative Government headed by Stanley Baldwin, two years ahead of schedule.
The Madras Congress session under M. A. Ansari resolved to boycott the Simon Commission at every stage and in every form.
Lala Lajpat Rai led a peaceful protest at Lahore on
30 October 1928

secs.t: Chronology of constitutional milestones

x: The Rowlatt Act and the Government of India Act were both associated with 1919.
The Nehru Report was issued in 1928, followed by Jinnah's Fourteen Points in 1929.

secs.t: Nehru Report and Jinnah's Fourteen Points

x: The Nehru Report was prepared in reply to Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead's challenge to Indians to frame their own constitution.
Jinnah's Fourteen Points demanded a federal constitution with residuary powers to the provinces and separate electorates.
The Nehru Report demanded Dominion Status, and the one-year ultimatum issued at Calcutta in 1928 had expired.

secs.t: Government of India Act 1935 - federation, autonomy, Federal Court, RBI, elections, ministries

x: The Act contained
321 sections and 10 schedules
; it is also described in some references as having 14 parts and 321 articles.
The correct sequence is Hilton Young Commission in 1926, RBI operations in 1935, provincial autonomy in April 1937, and RBI nationalisation in 1949.
The Muslim League observed the Day of Deliverance on 22 December 1939; B. R. Ambedkar also joined the observance.

secs.t: Borrowed features from GoI Act 1935 - constitutional provision

x: The Instrument of Instructions corresponds to the Directive Principles, the Federal Court to the Supreme Court, emergency powers to emergency provisions, and the federal scheme and PSCs to the Union-State structure and present PSC system.
The 1935 Act is considered the largest single source of the structural provisions of the Constitution of India.
Section 63 enabled the Governor to address the provincial legislature in his discretion.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Dyarchy was criticised because ministers controlled transferred subjects while finance remained among the reserved subjects.
The first Justice Party ministry in Madras was associated with
Subbarayalu Reddiar and Panagal Raja
In the context of the 1928 Trade Disputes and Public Safety Bills, Motilal Nehru called one the “Slavery of India Bill”.

rows.title: Simon Commission, Nehru Report, Jinnah's Fourteen Points, Round Table Conferences

secs.t: Simon boycott in Andhra - Prakasam, Andhra Kesari

x: During the Simon protest, Prakasam bared his chest and challenged the police to shoot, earning the title ‘Andhra Kesari’.
Police firing during the Madras protest killed
Parthasarathi
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao sent a cover bearing only the words ‘
Simon Go Back
The municipalities of Vijayawada, Tirupati, Kurnool, Eluru and Srikakulam passed resolutions supporting the boycott.

secs.t: Nehru Report - chairman, demand, recommendations, reactions

x: Birkenhead challenged Indians to prepare an agreed constitutional scheme, leading to the All Parties Conference and the Nehru Report committee.
The seven-member committee was formed by the All Parties Conference presided over by Dr M. A. Ansari, with Motilal Nehru as chairman and Jawaharlal Nehru as secretary.
The Nehru Report recommended ending dyarchy, establishing responsible government and a Supreme Court, and creating linguistic provinces including Andhra.

secs.t: Round Table Conferences - dates, venue, participants, Congress attendance

x: Exam angle: matching - 1st RTC = no Congress; Gandhi-Irwin Pact = Gandhi agrees to attend; 2nd RTC = disputes with League and Ambedkar; 3rd RTC = Congress absent again.
Exam angle: APPSC 2025 match - First RTC = no Congress; Pact = Gandhi to attend next; Second = disputes with League and Ambedkar; Third = Congress absent again.
All three Round Table Conferences were held in London under British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald to discuss the Simon Report and a federal constitution.

secs.t: Butler Committee - purpose

x: The Butler Committee, appointed in 1927 under Harcourt Butler, examined relations between
the Indian princely states and the Paramount Power

secs.t: All Parties and Muslim conferences, Delhi Proposals, Fourteen Points

x: The Delhi Proposals offered joint electorates in return for safeguards including one-third Muslim representation at the centre, separation of Sindh, reforms in the North-West Frontier Province and Baluchistan, and population-based representation in Punjab and Bengal.

All four were among the major demands associated with Jinnah's Fourteen Points: provincial residuary powers, one-third central representation, separate electorates and safeguards for Muslim-majority provinces.

secs.t: Deepavali Declaration

x: Lord Irwin issued the Deepavali Declaration on
31 October 1929
The declaration described dominion status as the natural goal of India’s constitutional progress and promised a Round Table Conference after the Simon report.

secs.t: Simon Commission report and the 1935 Act

x: The report recommended abolition of dyarchy, separation of Sindh from Bombay, separation of Burma from India, and creation of an Orissa province.
The report recommended abolition of dyarchy, provincial autonomy and continuation of separate communal electorates.
The Simon Commission report and the Round Table Conferences contributed to
the Government of India Act, 1935

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Lala Lajpat Rai presided over the first session of the All India Trade Union Congress in 1920.
Lala Lajpat Rai led the anti-Simon protest in Lahore and was fatally injured during the agitation.
The neglect of Andhra’s demand by the Simon Commission and Prakasam’s political role fuelled
the demand for a separate Andhra Province

rows.title: Government of India Act 1935 - provisions, provincial autonomy, 1937 elections and Congress ministries

secs.t: Congress ministries - provinces formed, resignation year and reason

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 asked the reason: protest against making India a party to the war with Germany.
The Congress ministries resigned in
October-November 1939
, following the unilateral declaration of India's participation in the Second World War.
Linlithgow made the declaration without consulting Indian leaders, and the League observed the Congress resignations as Deliverance Day on 22 December 1939.

secs.t: Madras after the 1937 elections - party, premier, Andhra ministers

x: The campaign was led by
Tanguturi Prakasam
, then President of the Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee, and Bulusu Sambamurthy.
Tanguturi Prakasam held Revenue, Bezawada Gopala Reddy held Local Self-Government, V.V. Giri held Labour and Industries, and Bulusu Sambamurthy was Speaker.
Rajaji introduced Hindi in Madras schools, but Periyar's anti-Hindi agitation in 1937 led the government to withdraw the policy.

secs.t: Features borrowed into the Constitution

x: The
Instrument of Instructions
under the Government of India Act, 1935 served as the model for the Directive Principles of State Policy.
The Government of India Act, 1935 contributed the
federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary and Public Service Commissions
, among other administrative features.

secs.t: Critiques of the 1935 Act and Congress rejection

x: Congress rejected the Act and demanded a Constituent Assembly elected on adult franchise
M.N. Roy first raised the Constituent Assembly demand in 1934, Congress adopted it officially in 1935, Lucknow rejected the Act, and Faizpur decided to contest the elections.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah
used the description “thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable” for the Act.

secs.t: 1937 elections - results by province, League performance

x: The elections were held in the winter of 1936-37 in eleven provinces.
In Bengal, Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party formed a coalition.
A coalition under Allah Baksh was formed in
Sindh
The Muslim League performed poorly even in Muslim seats.

secs.t: Schedules and Lists - three lists, Governor's discretion

x: The Federal List contained 59 subjects, the Provincial List 54 subjects and the Concurrent List 36 subjects.
The Government of India Act, 1935 assigned residuary powers to the
Governor-General
The Governor-General could stop discussion and suspend proceedings relating to a Bill.
The separate electorate system was extended further to
depressed classes, women and labour

secs.t: Congress ministries' legislative record

x: All four measures formed part of the civil-liberties record of the Congress ministries: emergency powers were lifted, prisoners released, bans on leftist bodies removed and press freedom restored.
Begar referred to forced or compulsory labour, and its abolition was an agrarian and social measure of the Congress ministries.
Free education
and other upliftment measures for Harijans formed part of the social-welfare programme of the Congress ministries.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Contemporary rows concerning Governors' addresses in Opposition-ruled States are traced to Section 63 of the 1935 Act and Article 175 of the Constitution.
The Coastal-Rayalaseema rift
had to be closed before the 1937 elections in order to consolidate the Andhra position.
The Sri Bagh Pact of 1937 was associated with resolving the
Coastal-Rayalaseema rift
in the Andhra context.

rows.title: Growth of communal politics - separate electorates, Two-Nation theory, Lahore Resolution 1940

secs.t: Lahore Resolution - president, drafter, mover, year, demand

x: The Lahore Resolution demanded independent states in the Muslim-majority areas of the north-western and eastern zones of India.
The Lahore Session of 1940 formally set out
the Two-Nation Theory
, treating Hindus and Muslims as separate nations.
The Lahore Resolution was adopted on
23 March 1940
The Lahore Resolution soon came to be known as the
Pakistan Resolution

secs.t: Pakistan name - coiner and pamphlet

x: Chaudhry Rahmat Ali, a Cambridge student, coined the term in 1933 in Now or Never.
The acronym was explained through Punjab, Afghan or NWFP, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan.

secs.t: Separate Muslim homeland idea - first proponents

x: Sayyid Ahmad Khan
, along with Raja Shiv Prasad of Bhinga, promoted an anti-Congress front in 1887.
In his 1930 Allahabad address, Iqbal advocated a consolidated Muslim state in the north-western region.
The sequence is Sayyid Ahmad Khan in 1887, Iqbal in 1930, Rahmat Ali in 1933 and Jinnah in 1940.

secs.t: League's tactics and slogans

x: The slogan 'Divide and Quit' was raised by
M.A. Jinnah
The League's campaigns alleged that Muslims were being subjected to '
Hindu Raj
' under the Congress ministries.
The League campaigned in the 1946 elections with the slogan, '
A vote for the League was a vote for Islam

secs.t: Reports on Congress ministries - order and authors

x: The Pirpur Report appeared first in 1938, followed by the Sharif Report and then Fazlul Huq's Muslim Sufferings under Congress Rule in 1939.
The Pirpur Report was authored by
Raja Syed Mohammad Mehdi of Pirpur
The reports alleged that Muslims suffered cruelties in provinces governed by Congress ministries.

secs.t: Hindu Mahasabha and RSS - founders

x: The RSS was founded in 1925 at Nagpur by K.B. Hedgewar.
The claim that India was Hindu territory reinforced the communal conception underlying
the Two-Nation Theory
Golwalkar's writings attacked nationalists for
embracing Muslims
The All-India Hindu Mahasabha was founded in 1915 under the
Maharaja of Kasim Bazar

secs.t: Books and quotations on communalism

x: The quotation appears in
W.W. Hunter
's The Indian Musalmans, published in 1871.
All three pairs are correctly matched.
The statement identifies the continuing presence of England as a factor that sustained communal differences.

secs.t: Two-Nation theory - proponents and origin

x: The Nehru Report rejected separate electorates, and Jinnah responded with his Fourteen Points, marking a parting of the ways.
The Pact produced temporary Congress-League unity, but Congress’s acceptance of separate electorates and weightage also legitimised communal political arrangements.
The criticism was that acceptance of separate electorates and weightage legitimised communal politics and ultimately provided part of the groundwork for Partition.

secs.t: Separate electorates - chronology across Acts

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 - "Which Act introduced the communal electorate?" =
Morley-Minto Reforms
The Lucknow Pact accepted separate electorates, weightage and a communal veto requiring a three-fourths rule.
The system of separate electorates continued until the
Constituent Assembly
dealt with the constitutional framework of independent India.
The 1909 Act legally institutionalised communal representation, thereby strengthening communal politics and contributing to the emergence of the Two-Nation Theory.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The imperialist interpretation regards Partition as inevitable; the nationalist interpretation emphasises divide and rule and League intransigence; the Marxist interpretation views it as an elite deal.
The op-ed revisited the fact that the 1946 provincial elections were conducted along communal lines, raising the contemporary concern of a return of separate-electorate politics.

rows.title: Gandhi - early life, South African phase, the making of satyagraha; Hind Swaraj

secs.t: Return to India - date, Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, Gokhale's advice, Kaisar-i-Hind

x: The Kaisar-i-Hind gold medal was awarded to Gandhi in 1915 for
his ambulance work in South Africa
Gandhi returned the Kaisar-i-Hind medal in 1920 during the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation campaign.
Champaran concerned indigo, Ahmedabad concerned mill wages, and Kheda concerned remission of land revenue.
Champaran was in 1917, Ahmedabad involved the first hunger strike, and Kheda sought revenue remission.

secs.t: Journals and writings - language and place

x: Anasakti Yoga is Gandhi’s Gujarati rendering of the Bhagavad Gita with commentary.
Songs from Prison contains
English translations of ancient Indian religious lyrics made in Yerwada jail
The Publications Division brought out the 100-volume English Collected Works and the Hindi Sampoorna Gandhi Vangmaya, while the e-version is associated with Gujarat Vidyapith.

secs.t: Settlements and ashrams in order

x: Phoenix Settlement dates to 1904, Tolstoy Farm to 1910, Sabarmati Ashram to 1917, and Sevagram to 1936.
Potti Sriramulu
worked at Sabarmati Satyagraha Ashram.
Kochrab Ashram was established in 1915, Sabarmati Ashram in 1917, and Sevagram at Wardha in 1936.
After reading Unto This Last in 1904, Gandhi
founded the Phoenix Settlement
soon afterwards.

secs.t: Early life - birth, education, Bar, practice

x: Gandhi studied at
Samaldas College
in Bhavnagar.
Gandhi studied law in London from 1888 to 1891 at the Inner Temple and was called to the Bar in 1891.
Gandhi’s early practice in Rajkot and Bombay was unsuccessful, he went to South Africa in 1893 for Dada Abdullah’s case, and Karamchand Gandhi was Diwan of Porbandar.

secs.t: Influences - book and author

x: From Ruskin’s Unto This Last, Gandhi drew the ideas of
dignity of labour and Sarvodaya
Gandhi associated the Bhagavad Gita with
Nishkama karma
, or action without attachment to the fruits of action.
Jainism influenced Gandhi through the five vows; Tolstoy through love and non-violence; Ruskin through dignity of labour and welfare of all; and Thoreau through civil disobedience.

secs.t: Titles - who gave them and when

x: Subhas Chandra Bose used the title ‘Father of the Nation’ for Gandhi in
a radio address from Singapore in 1944
Winston Churchill
used the expression ‘half-naked fakir’ for Gandhi in 1931.

secs.t: South Africa - years, Pietermaritzburg, NIC, campaigns, indentured labour

x: The 1913 Great March opposed the £3 poll tax and the invalidation of non-Christian marriages; miners and plantation workers joined it.
The two phases were moderate petitioning from 1894–1906 and passive resistance or satyagraha from 1906–1914; the Natal Indian Congress was founded within the first phase, not between the two phases.

secs.t: Hind Swaraj - year, language, themes, ban

x: Mahatma Gandhi wrote *Hind Swaraj* in 1909 on board the ship *
Kildonan Castle
* during his journey from London to South Africa.
*Hind Swaraj* criticised modern Western civilisation, industrialisation, railways, lawyers and doctors.
*Hind Swaraj* critiques industrialisation rather than endorsing it without qualification.
Mahatma Gandhi
himself translated *Hind Swaraj* from Gujarati into English.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gandhi's first satyagraha was launched in
Transvaal
Andhra Pradesh Assembly Speaker Ch.
Potti Sriramulu is associated with Sabarmati, while Mukunda Ramarao's Telugu book *Agamya Gamyaalu* traces Andhra indentured migrants to South Africa.
Gandhi translated the work, the Bombay Government banned it in 1910, Mukunda Ramarao wrote *Agamya Gamyaalu*, and Ch.

rows.title: Gandhian philosophy - truth, ahimsa, satyagraha, means and ends

secs.t: Gandhian quotations and principles

x: Gandhi described the persistence of poverty as the cruellest or worst form of violence.
Gandhi held that means are everything and that the end reflects the means used to attain it.
The Talisman advises recalling the face of the poorest and weakest person and asking whether the proposed step will help that person.

secs.t: Gandhi's view of politics - religion, ethics, welfare, authority

x: Gandhi used religion in this context to mean morality founded on truth and non-violence, not sectarian affiliation.
Gandhi maintained that politics without religion, understood as morality, becomes a death-trap.
Truth, non-violence, compassion, simplicity, Sarvodaya and purity of means and ends are Gandhian values.
Gandhi favoured decentralisation, with power located close to the people and decisions taken by local communities.

secs.t: Gandhism compared - Marxism, socialism, anarchism, individualism

x: Trusteeship is Gandhian, whereas Marxism seeks abolition of private property; economic determinism is Marxist rather than Gandhian.
Gandhi's ideal of enlightened anarchy and his view of the State as violence in concentrated form led to his description as a philosophical anarchist.
Gandhian individualism treats the individual and conscience as the basic unit and places self-rule before rule by the State.

secs.t: Satyagraha - meaning, forms, final step, rules

x: Satyagraha combines satya, meaning truth, and agraha, meaning insistence or eagerness.
Satyagraha was rendered in English as
passive resistance
, although Gandhi's concept gave it a distinctive emphasis on truth and soul force.

Champaran and the Salt March illustrate civil disobedience; Ahmedabad illustrates fasting; Rowlatt Satyagraha involved hartal; and boycott and picketing were used in the Non-Cooperation and Swadeshi movements.

secs.t: Truth and ahimsa - Truth is God; ahimsa of the brave

x: Gandhi initially used the formulation ‘God is Truth’ and later expressed the idea as ‘Truth is God’, giving truth an independent and central status.
Gandhi regarded truth as the ultimate end and non-violence as the means for realising it.
Gandhi regarded non-violence as the quality of the strong, not a sign of weakness.

secs.t: Swaraj concept - self-rule and political freedom

x: For Gandhi, Swaraj meant not merely political freedom but also self-rule, self-control and the ability of people to govern themselves without coercion.
Swadeshi, ahimsa, Satyagraha, decentralisation and education for all are included among the interrelated principles of Swaraj.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gandhian non-violence substituted moral force for physical force and enabled broad mass participation in the national movement.
Gandhian non-violence inspired the Baltic Way and the Singing Revolution, which contributed to Baltic re-independence in 1991.
NSE launched the Nifty 500 Ahimsa Index for companies free of animal cruelty, while BSE had earlier launched the Saatvik 100 Index.

rows.title: Gandhian social and economic thought - trusteeship, sarvodaya, swadeshi, village republic, bread labour

secs.t: Book → Gandhi's translated title

x: *Unto This Last* was written by John Ruskin, not H.D. Thoreau.
Ruskin's
*Unto This Last*
inspired Gandhi's ideas concerning the dignity of labour and Sarvodaya.
Gandhi took the ideas of
love and non-violence
from Leo Tolstoy’s The Kingdom of God is Within You.

secs.t: Sarvodaya - meaning, who used it, later movement

x: Sarvodaya means the welfare, uplift or progress of all, with attention reaching the last person.
Vinoba Bhave
made Sarvodaya central to his work and associated it with the Bhoodan, or land-gift, movement.
The Bhoodan movement began at
Pochampalli
Jayaprakash Narayan's Sarvodaya Plan dates to 1950, and 30 January is also observed as Sarvodaya Day.

secs.t: Rural reconstruction - Gram Swaraj, panchayats, Article 40, constructive programme

x: Ambedkar viewed the village as a seat of caste domination and described it as a sink of localism, ignorance and communalism.
Article 40 is a non-justiciable Directive Principle and directs the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government.
The constructive programme included khadi, removal of untouchability and Hindu-Muslim unity, among other rural and social initiatives.

secs.t: Gandhian economy - statement type

x: Gandhi advocated a non-violent, decentralised and self-reliant economy, with production directed toward need rather than profit.
All three statements describe Gandhian economic thought.
The incorrect statement is that Gandhi did not favour mechanisation in the United States.
Gandhian innovation means producing more from less input for the benefit of more people.

secs.t: Trusteeship - meaning and application

x: Trusteeship does not seek expropriation of the wealthy in the Marxist sense; it expects them to hold wealth in trust for social welfare.
The Ahmedabad Mill Strike took place in 1918 and involved a 35 per cent wage rise.
The trusteeship idea drew on
the Gita's principle of non-possession and the English law of trusts

secs.t: Swadeshi and khadi

x: Swadeshi and khadi promoted rural employment, self-reliance and a bridge between towns and villages.
The All India Spinners' Association was established in 1925, while the All India Village Industries Association was established in 1934.
Ponduru in Srikakulam is noted for producing the finest khadi in India.
The Khadi Development Centre at Guravareddypalem received Rs 10,000 from the All India Spinners' Association.

secs.t: Bread labour - source of idea

x: Bread labour holds that every person must earn his or her bread through physical labour.
The idea came from Tolstoy, who had taken the term from T.M. Bondaref, and was also associated with Ruskin's *Unto This Last*.
Gandhi linked bread labour with the Gita's concept of
yajna
, understood as work performed as an offering or duty.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gandhian ideas influenced the Directive Principles, the panchayat framework associated with the 73rd Amendment and policies supporting cottage industries.
Tummala Sitaramamurthy
wrote *Sarvodaya Ganam*, inspired by Vinoba, and translated Gandhi's autobiography into Telugu.
Gandhian trusteeship has been cited in connection with owners funding fire-safety systems, while Gandhian civil resistance has been credited as an influence in the Baltic freedom struggle.

rows.title: Gandhi on caste, untouchability, religion, women and education (Nai Talim)

secs.t: Harijan Sevak Sangh - founder, former name, president, year

x: Amritlal Thakkar, popularly known as Thakkar Bapa, was the
secretary
of the Harijan Sevak Sangh.
The organisation was founded in September 1932; one record specifically gives
30 October 1932 at Mumbai
as the date and place of establishment.
The Sangh worked for access to wells, schools and temples, and promoted schools, hostels, cooperatives, inter-dining and inter-caste marriage.

secs.t: Nai Talim - Wardha Scheme, Zakir Hussain Committee

x: Gandhi's Basic Education was vocational and craft-centred, sought to make villages self-sufficient and aimed to dignify manual labour.
The scheme was adopted in 1937, drafted by the Zakir Hussain Committee, and envisaged seven years of free and compulsory education.
Nai Talim emphasised the mother tongue, productive craft and dignity of manual labour; it did not prescribe
exclusive reliance on classical languages

secs.t: Harijan weekly and Harijan tour

x: Gandhi's Harijan tour ran from November 1933 to July 1934, covered about 20,000 km, began from the Wardha Ashram and collected funds for the Harijan Sevak Sangh.
Gandhi adopted the term ‘Harijan’, meaning ‘children of God’, from the Gujarati saint
Narsi Mehta

secs.t: Gandhi on untouchability - quotations, route to uplift

x: Gandhi called untouchability ‘
a blot on Hinduism
’ and advocated reform from within Hindu society.
Gandhi's approach combined
moral persuasion, temple entry, funds, schools and hostels, and constructive work
After 1937, Congress ministries provided free education to Harijans as part of their social reform measures.
Bhagya Reddy Varma considered the Sangh paternalistic and criticised it for being weak on civil rights.

secs.t: Women - satyagraha, purdah, child marriage, widows

x: Gandhi brought women into public action through activities such as picketing liquor shops, making salt and facing lathis.
Gandhi opposed
purdah, child marriage and dowry
, and supported the remarriage of child widows.
Desasevikalu was a women's wing.

secs.t: Religion - sarva dharma samabhava, unity, prayers

x: Sarva dharma samabhava means
equal respect for all religions
Gandhi regarded Hindu-Muslim unity as the bedrock of nationalism and supported the Khilafat movement.
Gandhi fasted during communal disturbances in
Calcutta and Noakhali

secs.t: Gandhi in Andhra - Harijan and khadi tours

x: Kolla Tayaramma led Harijan schools and hostels at Tenali, while Alladi Annapurna Devi was associated with similar work at Nellore.
Gandhi toured Andhra extensively for Harijan uplift and anti-untouchability work, visited Machilipatnam for Swaraj Nidhi and was associated with Ponduru khadi.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gandhi's campaign made untouchability a national issue, and Article 17 of the Constitution abolished untouchability.
Justice B.V. Nagarathna stated that untouchability cannot be practised ‘three days a month’ in the Sabarimala reference.
Ambedkar and Dalit leaders rejected the term ‘Harijan’ and criticised what they regarded as caste-Hindu paternalism.
Potti Sriramulu undertook temple-entry fasts in Nellore in 1946.

rows.title: Champaran, Ahmedabad Mill and Kheda Satyagrahas
sub: Group-II S1-84: Gandhian era - Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad; Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh

secs.t: Champaran (1917, Bihar) - inviter, associates, issue, outcome

x: Exam angle: statement pairs on "who invited" and "which state" (Champaran is in Bihar, not Gujarat).
Rajkumar Shukla was a
local indigo cultivator
and agriculturist of Champaran who persuaded Gandhi to investigate the peasants’ condition.
Gandhi defied the official order to leave Champaran and toured villages with his lawyers to record complaints against forced indigo cultivation.

secs.t: Kheda (1918) - district, state, grievance, calling off

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2019 - Champaran was the first mass movement (1917) but in
Bihar
, not Gujarat.
The Kheda peasants suffered crop failure caused by drought or famine and sought remission or suspension of land revenue, which the government initially refused.
The 1918 movement occurred in Kheda, Gujarat; peasants resisted revenue payment despite threats, and Vallabhbhai Patel gave field leadership.
The Kheda campaign of 1918 arose from crop failure, with peasants refusing to pay revenue.

secs.t: Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) - dispute, employer, mediators, outcome, TLA

x: The workers demanded a 50 per cent wage increase because of wartime inflation, while the mill owners offered only 20 per cent.
Ambalal Sarabhai represented the mill owners, Gandhi advised a 35 per cent demand, and the tribunal awarded a 35 per cent increase.
The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, or Majoor Mahajan Sangh, was founded in 1920 by
Anusuya Sarabhai with Gandhi’s guidance

secs.t: Significance - national leader, leaders recruited

x: The three struggles connected Gandhi with peasants in Champaran and Kheda and with labour in Ahmedabad.
Vallabhbhai Patel
provided field leadership in Kheda and thereby began the important Gandhi–Patel alliance.
Ambalal Sarabhai
led the Ahmedabad mill owners.
All three struggles occurred during the viceroyalty of
Lord Chelmsford
, who served from 1916 to 1921.

secs.t: Champaran Agrarian Enquiry Committee - appointment, members

x: The Champaran Satyagraha began in 1917, the inquiry committee was appointed during the same inquiry, the Agrarian Act followed in 1918, and the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association was founded in 1920.
The recommendations led to the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918, which abolished Tinkathia and secured a partial refund—25 per cent—of illegal exactions.

secs.t: Indigo system in Champaran - Tinkathia

x: Sharahbeshi was enhanced rent, while tawan was lump-sum compensation extracted when indigo became less valuable.
The Bengal Indigo Revolt of 1859
preceded and served as an important precursor to the later indigo-related mobilisation in Champaran.

secs.t: Chronological order

x: Exam angle: arrange Champaran - Ahmedabad - Kheda - Rowlatt; Gandhi returned to India in 1915.
The Ahmedabad Mill Strike took place in
February–March 1918
The all-India hartal and Satyagraha against the Rowlatt legislation took place on
6 April 1919

secs.t: Jallianwala Bagh - Dyer, Viceroy, Hunter Committee, renunciations

x: The Hunter Committee was appointed after the massacre and condemned Dyer’s conduct, while the House of Lords backed him.
Damaraju Pundarikakshudu
wrote the Telugu play ‘Panchala Parabhavam’ on Dyer.
Tagore renounced his Knighthood, C. Sankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council, and Gandhi returned the Kaiser-i-Hind medal.
Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal
were arrested for organising anti-Rowlatt protests.
Dyer blocked the only exit and fired without warning for about ten minutes, using 1,650 rounds.

secs.t: Gandhi in South Africa and return

x: Tolstoy Farm was established in 1910 near
Johannesburg
Indian Opinion
was the journal associated with Gandhi’s South African period.
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas
commemorates Gandhi’s return to India from South Africa on 9 January 1915.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
advised Gandhi to tour India for a year without taking political positions, enabling him to understand the country’s conditions.

secs.t: Gandhi's newspapers, writings and ashrams

x: Mathrubhumi
was not associated with Gandhi.
Hind Swaraj was written in 1909.
The Satyagraha Ashram at Kochrab was established in 1915, Sabarmati Ashram in 1917 and Sevagram in Wardha in 1936.
Rabindranath Tagore
is credited with giving Gandhi the title ‘Mahatma’.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Champaran, Ahmedabad and related struggles between 1917 and 1919 established Gandhi as a national leader and Satyagraha as an important method of anti-colonial struggle.
The Hindu
traced the connection from the Bengal indigo refusal of 1859 to Champaran nearly sixty years later, presenting Champaran as a launch pad for a new anti-colonial method.
The LENS profile repeated the triad of Gandhi’s
first civil disobedience, first hunger strike and first non-cooperation
, associated respectively with Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda in the stated sequence.

rows.title: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh; Hunter Committee

secs.t: Chronology from Swadeshi to Quit India

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2003 key - Swadeshi, Jallianwala Bagh, Dandi, Quit India.
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was concluded in 1931.
The Simon Commission arrived in 1928.

secs.t: Hunter Committee - event probed, members, minority report

x: The committee was appointed to investigate the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the disturbances in Punjab.
Chimanlal Setalvad, Jagat Narayan and Sultan Ahmed Khan were among the Indian members of the Hunter Committee.
The Indian members submitted a minority report that was more critical of Dyer's conduct.
The committee censured Dyer, who was relieved of command, but he did not receive real punishment.

secs.t: Rowlatt Act and Satyagraha

x: The Act permitted arrest and detention without warrant or trial, in-camera trials by a three-judge High Court panel and suspension of habeas corpus.
The Act permitted detention without trial for up to two years and suspended habeas corpus, giving rise to the description ‘No Vakil, No Dalil, No Appeal’.
The Act extended extraordinary wartime powers, including detention without trial up to two years, suspension of habeas corpus, special tribunals and press restrictions.
The phrase expressed opposition to the denial of ordinary legal safeguards under the
Rowlatt Act
, popularly called the Black Act.
The movement turned violent in Punjab and Ahmedabad, prompting Gandhi to call it a Himalayan blunder and withdraw it on 18 April 1919.

secs.t: Congress inquiry committee - members

x: The Punjab Sub-Committee included Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Abbas Tyabji, M.R. Jayakar and Gandhi.
The Congress inquiry condemned Dyer's firing as inhuman and considered the martial law measures
disproportionate
; it demanded action against Dyer.

secs.t: Martial law in Punjab and crawling order

x: Martial law included public floggings, aircraft strafing of protestors and the humiliating crawling order.
The order was imposed in the Amritsar lane where
Marcella Sherwood, an English woman missionary
, had been assaulted.
Gandhi was stopped from entering Punjab during the disturbances.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The massacre severely damaged Indian faith in British justice and contributed directly to the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements.
Prakasam demanded fundamental rights at the Nellore meeting in September 1919.
The Prime Minister recalled C.
Sankaran Nair
's resignation from the Viceroy's Executive Council on the 106th anniversary in April 2025.
K. Kamaraj joined the freedom struggle after the
Jallianwala Bagh massacre

rows.title: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement - programme, spread, Chauri Chaura and withdrawal
sub: Group-II S1-85: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement

secs.t: Non-Cooperation - launch, Calcutta and Nagpur sessions, programme, withdrawal

x: Exam angle: statement pairs - NCM made nationalism a mass movement (true); withdrawn after Jallianwala (false - after Chauri Chaura).
The Nagpur session unanimously ratified the programme, defined Swaraj in peaceful and legitimate terms, and reorganised Congress units on linguistic lines with committees extending to village level.
The Nagpur session fixed the Congress membership fee at
one-fourth of an anna
Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, C.R. Das, C. Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel, Asaf Ali, T. Prakasam and Rajendra Prasad were among the lawyers who gave up practice.
Although Swaraj was not achieved within one year, the Non-Cooperation Movement became the first nationwide mass movement and transformed the Congress into a mass force.
The Bardoli resolution of
11–12 February 1922
turned the Congress towards constructive work after the movement was withdrawn.
Subhas Chandra Bose criticised the withdrawal as the equivalent of sprinkling cold water on national enthusiasm.

secs.t: Chauri Chaura - date, place, events, defence

x: Chauri Chaura occurred in Gorakhpur district of the United Provinces after police action against a procession, following which the crowd burnt the police station.
Bhagwan Ahir
was among those beaten by the police before the crowd attacked and burnt the Chauri Chaura police station.
The Moplah uprising occurred in August 1921, the Prince of Wales boycott on 17 November 1921, Chauri Chaura in February 1922 and the Swaraj Party was formed in 1923.

secs.t: National institutions - founding year

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2023 - of Jamia, Kashi Vidyapith and AMU, only Jamia and Kashi Vidyapith are NCM-era.
Aligarh Muslim University developed from the MAO College, established in 1875 by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.
Acharya Narendra Dev, C.R. Das, Lala Lajpat Rai, Zakir Hussain and Subhas Chandra Bose were among the leaders associated with the national institutions of the period.

secs.t: Khilafat Movement - objective, Ali brothers, committee, Gandhi

x: The
Treaty of Sevres
, signed in May 1920, threatened the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and intensified the Khilafat agitation.
Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali were the leading Ali brothers, the Khilafat Committee emerged in 1919, and Turkey abolished the Caliphate in 1924.
The sequence was the failed deputation in February 1920, the Allahabad conference in June 1920, the Karachi conference in July 1921 and abolition of the Caliphate in 1924.

secs.t: Leaders - region and stance

x: C.R. Das was associated with Bengal, Motilal Nehru with the United Provinces, Rajagopalachari with Madras and Lala Lajpat Rai with Punjab and opposition to school boycott.
Konda Venkatappayya
initially opposed the resolution but subsequently resigned from the Madras Legislature.
C.R. Das later became a Swarajist and Rajagopalachari a No-Changer.

secs.t: Gandhi's arrest - place, charge, trial, sentence

x: In April 1919 Gandhi was stopped and detained at
Palwal
while proceeding towards Punjab; the incident contributed to riots.
Gandhi’s 1922 Ahmedabad trial concerned sedition under Section 124A in relation to his Young India articles and resulted in a six-year sentence.
The trial before Judge C.N. Broomfield on 18 March 1922 was called the Great Trial; Gandhi pleaded guilty and requested the highest penalty.

secs.t: NCM in Andhra

x: Unnava Lakshminarayana and Madabhushi Vedanta Lakshmi Narasimhachari were arrested during the Palnadu forest satyagraha.
The venue of the Vijayawada meeting was named
Gandhinagar
; Addepati Ramaseshaiah was its reception chairman.
The satyagraha was led by Kanneganti Hanumanthu and involved refusal of the grazing tax, boycott of forest officials and the stated arrests.
Maganti Annapurnamma and Yamini Purna Tilakam contributed jewellery to the Tilak Swaraj Fund.
Kanneganti Hanumanthu led the Palnadu forest satyagraha, Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya led Chirala-Perala, and Parvataneni Veeraiah Chowdary led the Pedanandipadu no-tax movement.
“Ma Koddi Telladoratanam” was a song of
Garimella Satyanarayana
used in the nationalist propaganda context.

secs.t: Character of NCM - social groups, banned plays and songs

x: Students, teachers, lawyers and merchants
were important participants in the urban phase of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
Peasants joined no-tax campaigns, forest users opposed pullari, women participated in large numbers, and Desasevikalu was an Andhra organisation of women volunteers.
Viplava Parivarthanam was written by Gollapudi Sitarama Sastri, Veeragandhamu Techhinaramu by Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Chowdary, and Makoddi Telladoratanam by Garimella Satyanarayana.

secs.t: Parallel struggles - Prince of Wales, Moplah, Akali

x: The Prince of Wales landed at Bombay on
17 November 1921
, leading to hartals and clashes in the city.
The Moplah uprising took place in Malabar, Kerala, and began as an agrarian conflict involving Muslim tenants and Hindu landlords before turning communal.
The Akali Movement of 1920–25 sought reform of Sikh gurdwaras and culminated institutionally in the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925.

secs.t: Congress sessions of the NCM period - venue and president

x: The Belgaum Congress Session was held in 1924, not December 1925.
Mahatma Gandhi presided over the Belgaum Session in 1924, which was his only presidency of the Indian National Congress.
The AICC was expanded to 350 members, not reduced to exactly 100.
At the 1921 AICC meeting at Bezawada, Pingali Venkayya presented his flag design to Mahatma Gandhi.

secs.t: Swaraj Party - founders, council entry, pro-changers vs no-changers

x: The Swarajists entered the councils to expose them as sham parliaments and obstruct their functioning from within, a strategy expressed as “End or Mend.”.
The Gaya session occurred in December 1922, the party was announced on 31 December 1922, it was formally founded on 1 January 1923, and the Delhi special session followed in September 1923.
The No-Changers opposed council entry, supported continuation of the boycott and concentrated on preparing the country for civil disobedience.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Marxist interpretation argued that Gandhi halted the movement to prevent it from taking a radical anti-landlord direction.
Vijayawada, Pingali Venkayya, Chirala-Perala, Pedanandipadu and Palnadu
are the Andhra-related references highlighted for this period.
The Rajaji Utsav and the bust unveiled at Rashtrapati Bhavan were associated with C.
Rajagopalachari
, popularly known as Rajaji.

rows.title: Andhra in the Home Rule Movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-195

secs.t: Palnad forest satyagraha - district, grievance, year, leaders

x: The Pullari tax was 12 annas per cow and Rs 1.50 per buffalo, while goats were prohibited from grazing in the reserved forests.
Forest reservation, corrupt forest officials and the fodder shortage caused by failed 1921 rains intensified the grievance against the Pullari system.
The satyagrahis boycotted officials at Macherla, drove 300 cattle into the forest without paying Pullari and had the cattle impounded at Minchalapadu.

secs.t: AICC meeting at Bezawada - year, decisions, targets

x: The targets were one crore members, one crore rupees for the Tilak Swaraj Fund and twenty lakh charkhas by 30 June 1921.
Mahatma Gandhi
endorsed Pingali Venkayya's flag design, which included the charkha, at the 1921 Vijayawada session.
The January 1921 APCC meeting at Vijayawada established Congress committees at the
district, taluk and village levels

secs.t: Kanneganti Hanumanthu - district, movement, event

x: Kanneganti Hanumanthu was shot dead during
the cattle-rescue action at Minchalapadu
on 26 February 1922.

secs.t: Chronology - Home Rule, NCM, Chauri Chaura, suspension

x: The Delhi AICC of 5 November 1921 permitted provinces to launch
civil disobedience, including no-tax campaigns
C.R. Das’s resolution supporting council entry was
defeated
at Gaya in December 1922, leading to the subsequent formation of the Swaraj Party.
At Gaya, C.R. Das’s council-entry resolution was rejected, after which Das and Motilal Nehru resigned and announced the new party on 31 December 1922.

secs.t: Gandhi's visits to Andhra during NCM - towns, year

x: Gandhi's April 1921 coastal tour included
Kakinada, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Machilipatnam, Chirala and Nellore
In October 1921, Gandhi visited
Kurnool, Kadapa, Tirupati and Tadipatri
, when the movement was at its peak in Andhra.
Ponduru
became famous for its Khadi during the nationalist movement.
Duvvuri Subbamma, Ponaka Kanakamma and Unnava Lakshmibayamma
emerged prominently after Gandhi’s 1921 coastal tour.

secs.t: Boycott of courts and colleges - lawyers and national schools

x: Andhra followed the Nagpur and Calcutta programme by boycotting courts, colleges and councils.
The Eluru National College and Duggirala's Andhra Vidyapeetha Goshthi at Chirala were among the national educational institutions established during the movement.
Tanguturi Prakasam
gave up his lucrative legal practice as part of the boycott of courts.
The Prince of Wales hartal at Vijayawada was
total

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Prime Minister paid tribute to Pingali Venkayya on 3 August 2026, marking his 150th birth anniversary.
Konda Venkatappaiah was known as Desabhakta, Duggirala as Andhra Ratna, Prakasam as Andhra Kesari, and Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao as Desoddharaka.
The withdrawal after Chauri Chaura dismayed Andhra satyagrahis in the middle of the struggle, particularly in the context of Pedanandipadu and Palnadu.

rows.title: Swarajists and No-Changers; constructive programme in the 1920s

secs.t: Swarajists in the Central Legislative Assembly

x: The Nationalist Party brought together the
Swarajists, Jinnah’s Independents and Malaviya’s group
The Nationalist Party used its numerical strength to outvote the government and block the Finance Bill.
Frederick Whyte was the first President, Sachchidananda Sinha the first Deputy President, and Vithalbhai Patel the first elected Indian President.
Vithalbhai Patel
became the first elected Indian President of the Legislative Assembly in 1925.

secs.t: Constructive programme - khadi, unity, untouchability, schools

x: The constructive programme included khadi and spinning, removal of untouchability, Hindu-Muslim unity, prohibition, national schools and village panchayats.
All four statements correctly describe components of the constructive programme.
Ponduru in
Srikakulam
was nationally famous for khadi.
Women in Andhra participated in
picketing and prohibition work
as part of the constructive programme.

secs.t: Decline of Swarajists - C.R. Das's death, Responsivists

x: C.R. Das died in
June 1925
The Responsivists favoured
cooperation with the government
All four statements are correct descriptions of factors and events associated with the decline of the Swarajists.

secs.t: Andhra Swarajists and Kakinada session

x: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was President, Unnava Lakshminarayana Secretary, Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao Treasurer and V. Ramadas an additional associated leader.
The Kakinada Congress session of 1923 was held in
Andhra

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Swarajists kept the national movement active through council work, while the No-Changers sustained constructive work.
The Swarajists favoured entry into the councils, while the No-Changers concentrated on constructive work and continued the boycott.

src: Sources: CDI (Gandhian Phase Pt 1 Part 6; programme of NCM); UPSC Modern History p.234, p.237-238; APP (AP History Modern-3 Swaraj Party; Indian History Pt 2); CDX AP History p.445, p.453

rows.title: Civil Disobedience Movement - Lahore Session and Purna Swaraj, Dandi March, spread and phases
sub: Group-II S1-86: Civil Disobedience Movement - Dandi March, Round Table Conferences, Poona Pact

secs.t: Lahore Session (Dec 1929) - president, Purna Swaraj, Independence Day

x: The committee that prepared the Nehru Report was chaired by
Motilal Nehru
Bulusu Sambamurthy
of East Godavari was associated with the first district-level Purna Swaraj resolution in Andhra Pradesh.
Lord Irwin
was the Viceroy of India during the Lahore Session of December 1929 and during the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

secs.t: Dandi March - dates, ashram, route, marchers, Viceroy

x: Gandhi sent the letter containing eleven demands to Irwin on
2 March 1930
Abolition of the salt tax
was a central demand in Gandhi's eleven-point letter to Viceroy Irwin.
Yerneni, also written Erneni, Subrahmanyam of Krishna district was the only Telugu marcher among Gandhi's followers in the Dandi March.
Salt was consumed by both rich and poor, and the salt tax and monopoly made it a visible symbol of colonial economic exploitation.

secs.t: Chronology - Simon to later events

x: The Simon Commission was appointed in November 1927, the Lahore Session was held in December 1929, 26 January 1930 was observed as the first Independence Day, and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.
The sequence is Partition of Bengal (1905), Simon Commission (1927–28), Nehru Report (1928), Fourteen Points (1929), and Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931).

secs.t: Women in CDM - role

x: Sarojini Naidu led the raid at the
Dharasana Salt Works
after Gandhi's arrest.
The Civil Disobedience Movement marked the first occasion on which women participated in massive numbers.
Duvvuri Subbamma was an Andhra woman leader from East Godavari who was jailed during the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Women participated on a large scale and undertook picketing of liquor and foreign-cloth shops.

secs.t: Salt Satyagraha centres - leaders, eyewitnesses

x: Sarojini Naidu led the raid on the Dharasana Salt Works after Abbas Tyabji was arrested.
Babu Genu was crushed by a lorry carrying foreign cloth in Bombay on 12 December 1930 while protesting against foreign cloth.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
was popularly known as the ‘Frontier Gandhi’ and was associated with the Khudai Khidmatgars.

secs.t: Martyrs and CDM incidents

x: All four pairs are correctly matched.
The Garhwal Rifles, associated with Chandra Singh Garhwali,
refused to fire on the crowd at Peshawar
Sholapur
witnessed a textile workers’ rising in 1930, following which martial law was imposed.

secs.t: Salt Satyagraha in Andhra - dictator and camps

x: Konda Venkatappayya
was the dictator of the Andhra Salt Satyagraha and had met Gandhi at Jambusar.
Pattabhi Sitaramayya
suggested the organisation of one satyagraha camp, with a dictator and war council, in each district.
Tanguturi Prakasam and Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
led the first salt squad from the Swarajya office at Madras on 13 April 1930.
Rayalaseema had no coast
, so Kalluri Subbarao led the activity at Bellary instead of a coastal salt-making centre.

secs.t: Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirts)

x: The Khudai Khidmatgars, or Red Shirts, led non-violent protests in Peshawar and the North-West Frontier Province.
The Qissa Khwani firing in Peshawar occurred in
April 1930
during the non-violent protests of the Khudai Khidmatgars.

secs.t: Patriotic songs - authors

x: Jagganna Sastri
wrote ‘Bharata Swarajya Yuddham’.
Adavi Bapiraju wrote patriotic songs while in jail.

secs.t: Gandhi-Irwin Pact - terms, mediator, Karachi session

x: Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar
acted as mediators in the negotiations leading to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
Irwin agreed to release non-violent political prisoners, remit fines, return unsold lands and permit limited salt-making.

Gandhi made the first two observations, while Subhas Chandra Bose made the comparison concerning the Dandi March.

secs.t: Leaders and poets - region

x: V.O. Chidambaram Pillai founded the
Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company
at Tuticorin.
V.O. Chidambaram Pillai participated in the 1908 Coral Mill strike along with
Subramania Siva
Lala Lajpat Rai belonged to Punjab, formed part of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio and presided over the Congress in 1920.
Subramania Siva was from Tamil Nadu, regarded as the first political prisoner of the Madras Presidency, and worked with VOC and Bharati.

secs.t: Positions held by leaders

x: Gandhi presided at Belgaum in 1924, Sarojini Naidu at Kanpur in 1925, M.A. Ansari at Madras in 1927 and Nehru at Lahore in 1929.
Surendranath Banerjee
was associated with the National Liberal Federation formed by moderates who had left the Congress.
Tej Bahadur Sapru and V.S. Srinivasa Sastri were among the presidents of the National Liberal Federation.

secs.t: Leaders from Andhra - contributions

x: Prakasam participated in the Simon boycott in Madras, led the salt satyagraha at Devarampadu and became the first Chief Minister of Andhra State in 1953.
The Constituent Assembly adopted the present national flag on 22 July 1947, with the Ashoka Chakra replacing the
charkha
The Rampa rebellion of 1922–24 was connected with opposition to the
Madras Forest Act of 1882 and forced labour

secs.t: Peasant and tribal leaders - organisations and movements

x: N.G. Ranga
was associated with the Andhra kisan movement and the Andhra Socialist Party; he also resigned his professorship in 1930.
Birsa Munda led the Munda Ulgulan, Alluri Sitarama Raju was associated with the Rampa movement, Komaram Bheem with the Gond movement and Sahajanand Saraswati with the Bihar Kisan Sabha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Events marking Tanguturi Prakasam’s 154th anniversary were held at
Visakhapatnam and Ongole
in August 2026.
The Chief Minister recalled Alluri Sitarama Raju and Pingali Venkayya on the 80th Independence Day.
The comparative assessment is that
southern leaders such as Rajaji, Prakasam and EMS had less national presence than Gandhi, Nehru, Bose and Patel

rows.title: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel - Bardoli Satyagraha, organisational role, Deputy Prime Minister

secs.t: Bardoli Satyagraha - year, leader, issue, women, inquiry and outcome

x: Exam angle: "who led Bardoli" and "which satyagraha was not led by Gandhi".
The Bardoli movement opposed an approximately 30 per cent increase in land revenue imposed despite floods and famine.
Patel organised a disciplined no-tax campaign and maintained a village intelligence network during Bardoli Satyagraha.
The government suspended the enhanced assessment and ordered a fresh survey; the Maxwell-Broomfield inquiry reduced the increase to about 6 per cent.

secs.t: Titles → who conferred them and when

x: The title ‘Sardar’ became associated with Patel at Bardoli in 1928; accounts variously credit the women and peasants, Sarojini Naidu and the masses, or Gandhi.
Patel is popularly called the Iron Man of India for his role in integrating approximately 565 princely states.
The description refers to Patel’s role in creating the All India Services and supporting their importance in administration.

secs.t: Kheda, Borsad and Sarabandi campaigns

x: Gandhi acted as the spiritual head, while Patel, Mohanlal Pandya and Narahari Parikh led the mobilisation among the peasants.
The government suspended revenue collection for poor peasants and returned confiscated property in the Kheda campaign.
The Borsad Satyagraha took place in 1923 under Patel’s leadership and opposed a punitive tax.
The correct sequence is Kheda (1918), Sarabandi (1922), Borsad (1923) and Bardoli (1928).

secs.t: Organisational role - Gujarat PCC, Parliamentary Board, 1937 elections

x: Patel served as President of the Gujarat PCC for
over two decades
All three statements correctly describe Patel’s organisational role as head of the Congress Parliamentary Board.
The statement contrasts Gandhi’s moral vision with Patel’s strong organisational and administrative machinery within the Congress.

secs.t: Posts in the Interim Government and first cabinet

x: In the Interim Government under Nehru, Patel held the
Home and Information & Broadcasting
portfolios.
Patel was the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister and handled the States Department with V.P. Menon as Secretary.
Patel chaired the
Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, Tribal and Excluded Areas
, as well as the Provincial Constitution Committee.

secs.t: Patel on civil services - All India Services speech

x: Patel stated that if the civil service steel frame bends, the whole structure will collapse, stressing its importance to national administration.
Patel addressed the first IAS probationers at Metcalfe House, Delhi, on
21 April 1947
; the date is now observed as Civil Services Day.
Patel played a key role in creating the IAS and IPS, and his 21 April 1947 address is commemorated as Civil Services Day.

secs.t: Patel-Nehru relations - Kashmir, China, Hyderabad

x: Nehru referred the Kashmir issue to the UN, influenced by idealism and Mountbatten’s advice, while Patel was sceptical and preferred a military solution.
Patel pressed for and ordered Operation Polo in September 1948 after diplomacy failed to resolve the Hyderabad issue.
Patel warned Nehru about China after Tibet in his letter of
7 November 1950

secs.t: Commemoration - Statue of Unity, National Unity Day

x: National Unity Day is observed on 31 October, the birth anniversary of Vallabhbhai Patel, who was born on 31 October 1875 at Nadiad.
Instituted in 2019, the award recognises unity and integrity; it includes a medal and citation, carries no cash, and is limited to not more than three recipients annually.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The two-year commemoration of Patel’s 150th birth anniversary was launched on 31 October 2024 at the Statue of Unity and includes the ‘Amrit Parampara’ festival series.
Sardar Gouthu Latchanna of Srikakulam
is said to be the only other person in India to receive the title ‘Sardar’.
