rows.title: Integration of princely states - instrument of accession, Junagadh, Hyderabad (Operation Polo), Kashmir
sub: Group-II S1-91: Post-independence consolidation - integration of princely states, Hyderabad and Junagadh

secs.t: Hyderabad integration - Operation Polo, commanders, Nizam, Razakars

x: Exam angle: "Operation Polo" vs Blue Star/Meghdoot/Vijay; Asaf Jahi vs Qutb Shahi; Razakar leader = Kasim Razvi.
Operation Polo was conducted from 13 to 17 September 1948, ending with the surrender and accession of the Nizam.
The Nizam’s forces and the Razakars were defeated in approximately
four to five days
during Operation Polo.
The Razakars were a militant volunteer force associated with the Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen.
Mir Osman Ali Khan was the seventh Nizam, the ruling house was Asaf Jahi, and Asaf Jah I founded it in 1724.
On 1 November 1956, the Telugu-speaking districts were transferred to Andhra Pradesh, Marathwada to Bombay State, and Raichur and Gulbarga to Mysore State.

secs.t: Hyderabad after independence - Standstill Agreement, independence, dynasty

x: Mir Osman Ali Khan wanted Hyderabad to remain independent or accede to Pakistan, while India suspected secret dealings between Hyderabad and Pakistan.
The Nizam’s government banned Indian currency, imported arms from Pakistan and sought an independent Dominion of Hyderabad.
Hyderabad remained outside India from 15 August 1947 until 17 September 1948, a period of approximately thirteen months.

secs.t: Praja Mandals and the States' People's movement

x: Swami Ramananda Theertha
led the Join Indian Union movement through the Hyderabad State Congress.
Vijay Singh Pathik was associated with Rajasthan, Sewa Singh Thikriwala with Punjab, Sarangadhar Das with Orissa, and Swami Ramananda Tirtha with the Hyderabad State Congress.
Congress first followed non-interference in the 1920s, adopted the Haripura position in 1938, and at Tripuri in 1939 openly backed the movements in the states.

secs.t: States → method and timing of integration

x: Shah Nawaz Bhutto
was the Dewan of Junagadh under Nawab Mahabat Khanji III.
Junagadh acceded to Pakistan in
September 1947
; the plebiscite favouring India was held later, in February 1948.
Bhopal merged in 1949, Manipur and Tripura merged in October 1949 through merger agreements, and Travancore joined India without conditions.
The standard account identifies
Kashmir, Hyderabad and Junagadh
as the states that had not signed accession by 15 August 1947.

secs.t: States Department - Patel and V.P. Menon

x: The States Department used persuasion and patriotic appeals, along with the threat of popular uprisings or force where necessary.
The rulers were offered
privy purses and internal autonomy
in return for accession, while Defence, External Affairs and Communications were ceded to the Centre.
Dewan C.P. Ramaswami Iyer declared Travancore’s independence, partly in the context of its thorium wealth.

secs.t: Privy purses and Rajpramukhs

x: Menon’s four phases were extinction, consolidation into unions, democratisation and finally abolition of privy purses.
Rajpramukhs were the heads of
Part B states
, which consisted of former princely states or unions.
The
Twenty-sixth Amendment Act, 1971
, abolished privy purses and royal titles.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment omitted
Articles 291 and 362
, which were associated with privy purses and the privileges of former rulers.

secs.t: Instrument of Accession; Part A, B, C, D states

x: Part A comprised former Governor’s provinces; Part B comprised former princely states or unions headed by Rajpramukhs; Part C included former Chief Commissioners’ provinces and some princely states; Part D consisted of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

secs.t: Hyderabad's UN appeal and accounts

x: Moin Nawaz Jung
led the Nizam’s delegation to the United Nations Security Council in 1948.
Laik Ali was the
last Prime Minister of Hyderabad
and authored Hyderabad in Retrospect.

secs.t: Liberation of Goa, Daman and Diu - Operation Vijay, colonial powers left after 1947

x: Exam angle: Operation Vijay (Goa 1961) vs Operation Polo (Hyderabad 1948) - both asked by APPSC.
The Portuguese surrender in December 1961 marked the
end of European colonial rule in India
France possessed Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore, which were handed over in 1954.

secs.t: Telangana armed struggle and Hyderabad's integration

x: The killing of
Doddi Komaraiah
in 1946 helped set off the Telangana armed struggle.
The revolt was led by the
Communists and the Andhra Mahasabha
against the Nizam’s order, the deshmukhs and later the Razakars.
The unrest and Razakar violence in Hyderabad contributed to the Indian military intervention known as Operation Polo in 1948.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Junagadh was resolved through a plebiscite, Hyderabad through police action, and Kashmir through an Instrument of Accession followed by war.
Pondicherry was transferred in 1954, Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated in 1961, Pondicherry became a Union Territory in 1962, and Goa attained statehood in 1987.
Yanam is a French-origin enclave located inside Andhra Pradesh’s Godavari delta, but it is administered as part of the Puducherry Union Territory.

rows.title: Wavell Plan and Simla Conference; Cabinet Mission Plan 1946; Interim Government
sub: Group-II S1-90: Towards independence - Cripps Mission, Cabinet Mission, Mountbatten Plan and Partition

secs.t: Cabinet Mission - members, purpose, three-tier structure, groupings (A, B, C), Constituent Assembly method

x: Exam angle: "The Constituent Assembly was formed under which plan?" -
Cabinet Mission Plan
(not Cripps, not Mountbatten). "Not a member" questions list a fake name.
The Cabinet Mission was sent by
Clement Attlee
's Labour Government after the Second World War.
Group B consisted of Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province and Sindh, forming the Muslim-majority north-western group.
The proposed Constituent Assembly had
389 members
: 296 from British India and 93 from the princely states.
Provincial assembly members elected representatives through community-wise voting using proportional representation by the single transferable vote.

secs.t: Interim Government - date, plan that envisaged it, head, portfolios, League's entry

x: As Finance Member, Liaquat Ali Khan introduced the 'poor man's budget' in 1947, which heavily taxed Indian business and embarrassed Congress members.
M.N. Roy raised the demand in 1934, Congress adopted it in 1935, the August Offer accepted the idea in 1940, and the Cabinet Mission Plan provided the formation scheme.
The Interim Government was proposed by the
Cabinet Mission
, comprising Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander.

secs.t: Chronology (1944-1946)

x: The Red Fort trials began in November 1945, the RIN revolt began on 18 February 1946, the Cabinet Mission arrived on 24 March 1946, and the Plan was issued on 16 May 1946.
The Desai-Liaquat Pact was made in 1945 between Bhulabhai Desai and Liaquat Ali Khan.
The Simla Conference was abruptly closed by Wavell on
14 July 1945
after the disagreement over Muslim representation.
The Cabinet Mission accepted the ideas of a Constituent Assembly, an Interim Government and provincial grouping, but rejected the demand for
a fully sovereign Pakistan
The Plan Balkan envisaged the fragmentation of India into
independent successor states formed by the provinces
The
Dickie Bird Plan
proposed independent successor states for the provinces and was rejected by Nehru as a plan for Balkanisation.

secs.t: Wavell Plan - year, Executive Council proposals, reason for Simla failure

x: The Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief were exceptions, so the Executive Council was not entirely an elected body without a special Viceroyal position.
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad represented the Congress, while Muhammad Ali Jinnah represented the Muslim League at the Simla Conference.
Jinnah insisted that all Muslim members should be nominated only by the Muslim League, denying the Congress and Punjab Unionists the right to nominate Muslim members.

secs.t: C.R. Formula and Desai-Liaquat Pact - author, proposals

x: The C.R. Formula proposed a plebiscite and joint agreements after separation, but Jinnah demanded that only Muslims should vote and that there should be no common centre.
The Pact proposed equal numbers of Congress and Muslim League nominees, along with 20 per cent representation for minorities.
Bhulabhai Desai was a Congress leader in the Central Legislative Assembly and negotiated with Liaquat Ali Khan for the Pact.

secs.t: League's acceptance and withdrawal from the Cabinet Mission Plan

x: On 10 July 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru stated that Congress could modify the scheme through its majority in the Constituent Assembly.
The Muslim League observed 16 August 1946 as Direct Action Day, which resulted in the
Great Calcutta Killings
Gandhi walked from village to village in Noakhali from
November 1946 to March 1947
to promote peace, though he could not stop the violence completely.

secs.t: Provincial and Constituent Assembly elections after the war

x: Congress dominated the general seats, the League dominated Muslim seats, and the Communists performed poorly in the elections.
In the Constituent Assembly elections, Congress won 208 of the 296 British Indian seats, while the Muslim League won 73 and other groups won 15.
The Muslim League adopted the slogan “Divide and Quit” at its Karachi session in December 1943.
In the July 1946 results, the Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League 73 and other parties won 15 seats.

secs.t: Partition boundaries - Radcliffe award, referendums

x: Exam angle: "referendum" provinces are only
NWFP and Sylhet
Sir Cyril Radcliffe
, a British lawyer unfamiliar with Indian conditions, chaired both Boundary Commissions.
Although independence took place on 15 August 1947, the Radcliffe Award was announced two days later, on
17 August 1947
Referendums were held in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Wavell's concessions at Simla were criticised for handing Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League an effective veto in the negotiations.
The ambiguity regarding the compulsory nature of provincial grouping created conflicting interpretations and contributed substantially to the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan.
The sequence from the Cripps Mission through the Cabinet Mission to the Mountbatten Plan culminated in Indian independence accompanied by partition.

rows.title: Direct Action Day, Mountbatten Plan, Indian Independence Act 1947; partition and its consequences

secs.t: Heads at independence → person

x: M.A. Jinnah
became the first Governor-General of Pakistan in August 1947.
Lord Mountbatten was Governor-General during Kashmir’s accession in October 1947 and Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination on 30 January 1948.
Mountbatten became Governor-General in 1947, India became a Dominion on 15 August 1947, Rajagopalachari assumed office in June 1948, and India became a Republic on 26 January 1950.

secs.t: Direct Action Day - date, city of riots, League's call

x: The Muslim League called for Direct Action on 29 July 1946 after withdrawing its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Jinnah condemned
Wavell’s invitation to the Congress to form the interim government
, in the context of the League’s Direct Action call.
The violence that began in Calcutta spread to Noakhali, Bihar and other parts of north India, causing deaths in both communities.

secs.t: Boundary Commission - chairman, Radcliffe Line, share of territory and assets

x: The armed forces were divided between India and Pakistan as part of the partition arrangements.
Separate Commissions were formed for Punjab and Bengal, and both were chaired by Sir Cyril Radcliffe.
Sir Cyril Radcliffe was a
British lawyer
who had little knowledge of India when he was appointed to chair both Boundary Commissions.

secs.t: Indian Independence Act 1947 - features, dominions, lapse of paramountcy

x: With the lapse of paramountcy, the 565 princely states were free to accede to India or Pakistan.
The Act abolished the two offices, provided for Governors-General acting on cabinet advice, and made the Constituent Assemblies sovereign law-making bodies.
The
Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted
, continued to govern the dominions until their new constitutions were framed.
The Act transferred power to the two dominions but left the framing of their constitutions to their respective Constituent Assemblies.
The Constituent Assemblies had sovereign constitutional authority; they were not required to retain British laws permanently.
The interim law for each Dominion was the
Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted
, until its new Constitution came into force.
Attlee's declaration was made on 20 February 1947, the Mountbatten Plan was announced on 3 June, royal assent was given on 18 July, and the dominions came into being on 15 August.

secs.t: Gandhi in 1946-47 - Noakhali and Bihar, Independence Day, tributes

x: Gandhi undertook the Noakhali peace mission from
November 1946 to March 1947
, moving from village to village.
Gandhi spent 15 August 1947 at Beliaghata in Calcutta, fasting and praying, rather than attending the Delhi celebrations.
Lord Mountbatten
described Gandhi as a ‘one-man boundary force’ because of his efforts to restrain communal violence.

secs.t: Partition accounts → author

x: India Divided was written by Rajendra Prasad; India Wins Freedom by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad; Freedom at Midnight by Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre; and Train to Pakistan by Khushwant Singh.

secs.t: Mountbatten Plan (3 June Plan) - provisions, referendums, advanced date

x: V.P. Menon
suggested immediate transfer of power on dominion status without waiting for a new constitution.
The North-West Frontier Province joined
Pakistan
after the referendum, which was boycotted by the Khudai Khidmatgars led by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan.
Congress accepted partition to avoid Balkanisation, establish a strong Centre and bring an end to communal bloodshed.
The two provincial Assemblies met in separate sections, and a simple majority in either section led to partition; both provinces voted for partition.

secs.t: Alternative schemes and deadlines - Plan Balkan, United Bengal plan, Attlee's deadline

x: The Attlee Statement of 20 February 1947 declared that British rule would end by
30 June 1948
, even if no agreement among Indian political parties was reached.
The statement fixed 30 June 1948 as the outer deadline, hinted at transfer to provincial governments and was followed by Mountbatten replacing Wavell.
The sovereign undivided Bengal proposal was a separate United Bengal plan advanced by Sarat Chandra Bose and H.S. Suhrawardy.

secs.t: Consequences - refugees, rehabilitation, division of forces and assets

x: An estimated
10–15 million
people crossed the new borders during Partition.
The Government of India established the
Ministry of Relief and Rehabilitation
The Ministry dealt with refugee camps, resettlement and evacuee property.
Armed forces, services and assets were divided.
The UN ceasefire in the first Kashmir conflict came into effect on
1 January 1949

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Dominion status enabled India and Pakistan to become free before their constitutions were written.
The haste associated with advancing the date of transfer and the late announcement of the Radcliffe Award are criticised as factors that aggravated Partition violence.
C. Rajagopalachari gave assent to
the Madras Estate Abolition Act
on 2 April 1949.

rows.title: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar - life, Mahad and Kalaram Satyagrahas, writings, Round Table Conferences

secs.t: Journals → founder and year

x: Mooknayak was founded by
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Bahishkrit Bharat
was founded by Ambedkar in 1927 and focused on Dalit rights and social reform.

secs.t: Organisations and parties → year

x: Samata Samaj was founded in 1927 to promote
coordination between Dalits and caste Hindus
The Republican Party of India was planned by Ambedkar but was formed in 1957, after his death.
The Independent Labour Party worked for the rights of
labourers, Dalits and peasants

secs.t: Books → author (all Ambedkar)

x: The Problem of the Rupee
, published in 1923, contained ideas that formed the basis for Ambedkar’s thinking behind the Reserve Bank of India.
Servants of India
is not a work of Ambedkar.
Who Were the Shudras?
, published in 1946, examined the origin of the Shudras.
The Buddha and His Dhamma was written by Ambedkar and published in 1957.

secs.t: Education - universities, degrees, honorary doctorates

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2025 asked the honorary D.Litt of 1953 -
Osmania University
Ambedkar studied at Columbia University, where he obtained an M.A. and Ph.D. Gray’s Inn awarded the qualification of Barrister-at-law, while Osmania University conferred an honorary D.Litt.
Ambedkar studied at the
London School of Economics
and obtained the MSc and DSc qualifications; his thesis was related to The Problem of the Rupee.

secs.t: Round Table Conferences - attendance, demands, Communal Award, Poona Pact

x: The Communal Award provided a separate electorate along with a general vote, whereas the Poona Pact replaced this with joint electorates and reserved seats.
Madan Mohan Malaviya
acted as mediator in the negotiations between Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar that led to the Poona Pact.
The Poona Pact provided 148 reserved seats for the depressed classes in the provincial legislatures, compared with 71 under the Communal Award.
Gandhi undertook the fast unto death at
Yerwada Jail
, opposing separate electorates because he feared a permanent division in Hindu society.

secs.t: Remarks exchanged

x: What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables
was written by Ambedkar in 1945 and expressed his criticism of Congress and Gandhi’s treatment of the Untouchables.
Gandhi opposed separate electorates because he feared that they would create a permanent split in Hindu society, leading to his fast at Yerwada Jail.

secs.t: Mahad Satyagraha - year, issue, symbolic act

x: The Mahad Municipality opened the
Chavdar Tank
to untouchables in 1924, but the decision was not effectively implemented in practice.
On 20 March 1927, Ambedkar led the Water Satyagraha at the Chavdar Tank to assert the right of untouchables to use a public water source.
The Mahad Satyagraha was organised by the
Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha
, Ambedkar’s organisation founded in 1924.

secs.t: Kalaram Temple Satyagraha - place and year

x: The Khoti movement was directed against the landlord system in the
Konkan
region.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: 'Kula Nirmoolana' is the Telugu rendering of Ambedkar's work '
Annihilation of Caste
The comparative formulation associated with Mahad is that water came before salt, highlighting the earlier importance of access to water in the struggle for social equality.
The Social Justice Ministry began a two-year celebration of
Mahatma Jyotirao Phule
's 200th birth anniversary.

rows.title: Ambedkar's contribution to the making of the Constitution - Drafting Committee and key interventions

secs.t: Drafting Committee - date, chairman, members, sittings

x: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar was a jurist, while K.M. Munshi chaired the Order of Business Committee and was originally the only Congress member of the Drafting Committee.
The Drafting Committee sat for only
141 days
and completed its draft in under six months.
B.N. Rau’s initial draft of October 1947 was built on
the reports of the Constituent Assembly committees

secs.t: Constituencies Ambedkar represented

x: Before Partition, Ambedkar was elected from Bengal’s Jessore-Khulna area with the support of Jogendra Nath Mandal.
The Jessore-Khulna districts, from which Ambedkar had been elected, went to East Pakistan after Partition, causing him to lose that seat.
Ambedkar was re-elected from Bombay in 1947 to the seat vacated by
M.R. Jayakar

secs.t: Key interventions and replies

x: Ambedkar favoured a strong Centre as a means of protecting weaker sections while retaining a constitutional system capable of functioning in federal or unitary conditions.
The constitutional framework combined equality provisions, welfare directions, reserved representation and universal adult suffrage including women from the outset.
Articles 82 and 170 provide for readjustment relating to Parliament and State Assemblies, while Articles 330 and 332 concern SC/ST seat reservation.

secs.t: Final speech in the Constituent Assembly

x: Ambedkar warned against violent and extra-constitutional methods, hero-worship in politics, and the failure to establish social democracy.
‘The grammar of anarchy’ referred to the continued use of bloody revolutionary methods and civil disobedience when constitutional methods were available.
Ambedkar warned that placing liberties at the feet of a great man, or political hero-worship, could lead to
dictatorship

The Untouchables
, published in 1948, dealt with the origin of untouchability and advanced the theory of “broken men.”.
The Buddha and His Dhamma was published posthumously in 1957 and provided Ambedkar's rational and social interpretation of Buddhism, forming the basis of Navayana.

secs.t: State socialism - States and Minorities memorandum

x: States and Minorities was a 1947 memorandum submitted to the Constituent Assembly on behalf of
the Scheduled Castes Federation
The proposals included state ownership of key industries and agricultural land, collective farming through village collectives and nationalised insurance.
Ambedkar wanted State socialism entrenched in the Constitution so that a temporary legislative majority could not reverse it.

secs.t: Views on the village, Gandhism and Congress

x: In the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948, Ambedkar sharply criticised the village as

Because of his criticism of the village's localism and social narrow-mindedness, Ambedkar preferred
the individual
rather than the village as the unit.
Ambedkar rejected Gandhi's ideas of Gram Swaraj and trusteeship, favouring a strong, centralised constitutional democracy to protect minorities.

secs.t: Views on women's rights, labour and education

“Educate, Agitate, Organise” was Ambedkar's well-known slogan expressing the importance of education and organised social and political action.

secs.t: Ambedkar-Gandhi debate on untouchability and caste

x: Gandhi used the term Harijan and stressed moral persuasion and temple entry, while Ambedkar preferred Dalit or Scheduled Castes and emphasised legal, constitutional and political rights.
Gandhi viewed varna as an ideal division of labour and untouchability as a corruption, while Ambedkar considered the entire caste system oppressive and sought its annihilation.

Ambedkar suggested

secs.t: Post-war Congress Working Committee on linguistic provinces

x: The Constituent Assembly retained
the pre-Independence provinces
rather than immediately implementing linguistic reorganisation.
The JVP Committee postponed linguistic reorganisation, while allowing that Andhra could be formed if the claim to Madras city was given up.
The committee was formed after the April 1949 JVP report, constituted by the Madras Cabinet on 7 December 1949, chaired by Kumaraswamy Raja, and reported on 4 January 1950.

secs.t: Leaders - contribution

x: The Balabharati Samithi was established by Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao in
February 1907
Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao
founded the Vijnana Chandrika Mandali in 1906 with Komarraju Lakshmana Rao.
Konda Venkatappayya was the first secretary, Nyapati Subba Rao the first president, Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao wrote Andhrula Charitra, and B.N. Sarma moved the linguistic-provinces resolution.
The phrase appeared in Krishna Patrika on
13 July 1918
as a criticism of the Montagu-Chelmsford scheme.
B. N. Sarma moved the resolution for the
creation of linguistic provinces
in the Imperial Legislative Council on 6 February 1918.

secs.t: Popular titles - person

x: Exam angle: "incorrectly paired" title questions (APPSC G2 2002: Desoddharaka - Pattabhi is the wrong pair).
Desoddharaka was the title of Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao, not Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Kalluri Subbarao
was known as Rayalaseema Kuruvriddhudu or Pitamaha.
Thota Narsayya Naidu
was popularly known as Jenda Narsayya.
Swami Sitaram was the popular name of
Gollapudi Sitarama Sastri

secs.t: Leaders who opposed separate Andhra - reason

x: Nemali Pattabhi Rama Rao
of Cuddapah initially opposed the demand in 1916 but changed his position and supported it at Cuddapah in 1918.
Jinnah and V.S. Srinivasa Sastri
opposed the demand in the Imperial Council in 1918.
The new Rayalaseema Mahasabha leaders R. Suryanarayana Rao and N.M. Sastry opposed the demand because they feared Circars domination.

secs.t: Leaders of the post-1947 phase - role

x: Swami Sitaram ended his fast on the appeal of
Vinoba Bhave
T. Prakasam served on the Partition Committee, formed the Kisan Mazdoor (Praja) Party with Ranga in 1951, and became the first Chief Minister of Andhra State on 1 October 1953.
N.G. Ranga, supported as Prakasam’s candidate, lost to N. Sanjiva Reddy by
5 votes

secs.t: Leaders - newspapers founded (Swarajya)

x: The Vijayawada Swarajya of the Vandemataram era had
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
as its editor.
Desamata was founded at Rajahmundry by
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham
Deshabhimani
was an early Anglo-Telugu paper associated with the Andhra cause and was published from Guntur.
Krishna Patrika dates to 1902, Andhra Kesari to 1904, Vijnana Chandrika Mandali to 1906, and Swarajya at Madras to 1922.

secs.t: Andhra University - establishment, Act, first headquarters, shift

x: The Governor-General gave assent to the Madras Act II of 1926 on
13 January 1926
Education Minister
A.P. Patro
of the Justice Party introduced the Andhra University Bill on 20 August 1925.
At its establishment on 26 April 1926, Andhra University had its headquarters at Vijayawada and its teaching centre at Rajahmundry.

secs.t: Recommendation behind the shift of the seat

x: C.R. Reddy chose Waltair for its
climate and setting

secs.t: Founding Vice-Chancellors - tenure

x: Cattamanchi Ramalinga Reddy was the first Vice-Chancellor from 1926 to 1931 and again from 1936 to 1949.
S. Radhakrishnan was Vice-Chancellor of Andhra University from 1931 to 1936.

secs.t: Rival claims for the seat

x: The Senate voted
in favour of Anantapur, reflecting the Rayalaseema claim.
An amendment excluded Rayalaseema from Andhra University's jurisdiction, and its colleges went back to Madras University.
The Circars–Rayalaseema dispute over the university's seat and jurisdiction led Andhra members to support a no-confidence motion against Subbaroyan in August 1927.

secs.t: Rayalaseema's grievance and Sri Venkateswara University

x: The Sri Bagh Pact of 1937 promised Andhra University centres at Waltair and Anantapur.

secs.t: Telugu identity symbols - Telugu Talli song, Andhra Parishat

x: “Maa Telugu Talliki” was written by
Sankarambadi Sundarachari
and is the State song of Andhra Pradesh.
The Andhra Week was conducted by students under the Vice-Chancellor C.R. Reddy during the Waltair Andhra Varotsavalu in December 1937.

secs.t: Madras Chief Ministers before Andhra State - stand on separation

x: T. Prakasam
, Chief Minister during 1946–47, was the leading champion of Andhra separation and submitted a separate report to the Partition Committee.
P.S. Kumaraswamy Raja
, Chief Minister of Madras from 1949 to 1952, chaired the Partition Committee.
The Andhra members were
T. Prakasam, Kala Venkatrao, Bezawada Gopala Reddy and Neelam Sanjiva Reddy
The committee agreed on the formation of Andhra on 26 January 1950, but T. Prakasam submitted a separate report reflecting his distinct position.

secs.t: Congress Working Committee decisions after the JVP report

x: The Andhra Mahasabha demanded the formation of Andhra State by
26 January 1950
The CWC report divided Andhra leaders into the Prakasam–Ranga group and the Pattabhi–Sanjiva Reddy group.
The JVP Committee stated that Andhra could be formed if the claim to
Madras city
was relinquished.
The Congress Working Committee recommended the
formation of Andhra without Madras city

secs.t: Demand - territorial scope and the Madras city question

x: The three conditions concerned immediate announcement, unity among Andhra leaders and making Madras a Chief Commissioner's State by agreement.
The proposed “free state” referred to
Madras city
being constituted as a separate Chief Commissioner's or C-class State by agreement.
On the fiftieth day, Nehru offered to form Andhra without Madras, provided all parties agreed.

secs.t: Association with Gandhi - ashram life, constructive work

x: He left his railway employment after the deaths of his wife and mother and subsequently devoted himself to Gandhian constructive work.
Potti Sriramulu worked in the Komaravolu and Angaluru ashrams and in the Village Seva Sangam as part of his constructive activities.
Gandhi reportedly said that with
selfless workers like Potti Sriramulu, he would have won Swaraj long before.

secs.t: Public reaction after his death

x: His death led to hartals, demonstrations and riots across Andhra.
Police firing at Anakapalli killed seven persons during the disturbances following his death.
MLA Tenneti Viswanatham and MLC P. Sitaramayya resigned in protest.
The editor of
The Madras Mail
compared Potti Sriramulu's sacrifice to the sacrifice of Christ.

secs.t: Earlier fasts - causes and outcomes

x: The 19-day fast in 1946 was connected with the demand for a law permitting temple entry for Harijans.
The Wardha fast in 1948 was associated with the observance of
Harijan Day and a grant of one crore rupees
The 28-day fast in January 1949 was associated with the observance of
Gandhi Smarak Din

secs.t: Commemoration - district, university, titles

x: Nellore district was renamed Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore District in 2008 by the government headed by Chief Minister Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy.
Potti Sriramulu is known by the title
Amarajeevi
, meaning Immortal Martyr.
The memorial park covers 6.80 acres, and the statue uses 26 tonnes of bronze and 42 tonnes of iron.

secs.t: First government - Chief Minister, Governor, Speaker, budget

x: Tanguturi Prakasam Pantulu
was the first Chief Minister of Andhra State and headed a coalition government.
C.M. or Chandulal Madhavlal Trivedi was the Governor.
The Andhra Assembly consisted of members elected to the Madras Assembly in 1952.
The advisory committee to Special Officer C. M. Trivedi included
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy and Tenneti Viswanatham

secs.t: Chief Ministers of Andhra State 1953-56 in order

x: Prakasam became Chief Minister on 1 October 1953, his ministry fell in November 1954, the mid-term poll followed in 1955, and Gopala Reddy then became Chief Minister.
Immediately before the 1956 merger, B. Gopala Reddy was Chief Minister and Laxmi Narasimham was Speaker of Andhra State.

secs.t: Andhra State Act 1953 - Madras city, Bellary question

x: The single-member committee headed by Justice K.N. Wanchoo was appointed on
7 February 1953
The Andhra State Act received the President's assent on
14 September 1953
The Centre accepted Justice Mishra's report: Bellary taluk went to Mysore, Rayadurg was added to Anantapur, and Adoni and Alur were added to Kurnool.

secs.t: High Court of Andhra State - Guntur

x: The High Court was at
Guntur
(Coastal Andhra) and the capital at Kurnool (Rayalaseema), following the Sreebagh Pact balance.
The Madras High Court served Andhra until it was set up in
, on
5 July 1954
Exam angle: "capital Kurnool, High Court Guntur" pair.

secs.t: 1955 mid-term election - parties, alliances, results

x: The election followed the fall of Prakasam's ministry, and the Congress, Krishikar Lok Party and Praja Socialist Party formed the United Congress front against the Communists.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Although the Dhar Commission and JVP Committee were cautious about linguistic states, the Andhra exception paved the way for the SRC and broader linguistic reorganisation.
The sequence was Dhar Commission in 1948, JVP Committee in 1948–49, Wanchoo in 1953 for Andhra, and the Fazal Ali SRC in 1953–55 for all India.
The period 1913–1920 was the propaganda phase, with four broad objectives: Andhra State, Andhra University, Telugu development and cultural revival.
Rayalaseema and Nellore leaders criticised the Andhra Mahasabha as a Circars- or Brahmin-led body; district-wise voting was adopted in response.
Nidadavolu in 1912 saw the first formal resolution, Bapatla in 1913 was the first numbered Andhra Conference, and Vijayawada in 1914 was the first session called Andhra Mahasabha.
Factional divisions between regions and leaders, notably Circars versus Rayalaseema and Prakasam versus Pattabhi, repeatedly weakened the movement.
The struggle over Andhra University helped build a distinct Telugu intellectual identity and is regarded by many as a forerunner of the Andhra State movement.
Potti Sriramulu’s death forced the Centre to respond to the Andhra demand and helped initiate the process that led to the SRC and later reorganisation.
The loss of Madras left the new Andhra State administratively and economically weak, requiring it to use the relatively undeveloped town of Kurnool as its capital.
Telugu Ganga was intended to irrigate
2.75 lakh acres
and provide water to Chennai, although the reported present irrigation reach is much lower.
Cattamanchi Ramalinga Reddy
was credited as the founding Vice-Chancellor of Andhra University.
The Madras Presidency organisation began at Bapatla in 1913 under B.N. Sarma, while the Nizam Andhra Mahasabha began at Jogipet in 1930 under Suravaram Pratapa Reddy.
Chief Minister
N. Chandrababu Naidu
unveiled the statue on 16 March 2026, the 125th birth anniversary of Potti Sriramulu.

rows.title: Wanchoo Committee and the problems of the new Andhra State
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Wanchoo Committee - chairman, year, terms of reference

x: The Wanchoo Committee was a single-member committee headed by
Justice Kailas Nath Wanchoo
, then Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court.
Justice Kailas Nath Wanchoo, Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court, constituted the single-member committee in 1953.
The committee dealt with boundary division, financial settlement, asset distribution and administrative arrangements.

secs.t: Financial problems - revenue deficit, assets and liabilities with Madras

x: The new state lacked both developed capital infrastructure and a commercial centre and was described as administratively and economically orphaned.
The
Partition Committee
of 1949–50 was first entrusted with working out the division of assets between Andhra and residual Madras.

secs.t: Capital and secretariat - temporary arrangements

x: Because Andhra lacked capital infrastructure, Wanchoo recommended that the Andhra Government work temporarily from Madras city for three to five years.
The Andhra Assembly was formed from members elected to the Madras Assembly in 1952, and the new state had no Legislative Council.
C.
M. Trivedi
served as the Special Officer.

secs.t: High Court location and Bellary district dispute

x: Siruguppa, Hospet, Sandur, Harpanahalli and Hadagali
went to Mysore.
The Bellary district court was temporarily to serve
Adoni, Alur and Rayadurg
, as stated in Nehru’s 25 March 1953 announcement.
Justice Mishra, who was Chief Justice of the Hyderabad High Court, conducted the hearings on the Bellary question from 1 to 15 May 1953.

secs.t: Tungabhadra project - sharing of works and waters

x: The Sreebagh Pact promised priority for irrigation in Rayalaseema and Nellore on the
Tungabhadra, Krishna and Penna
for ten years or as needed.
The Pact provided priority
for ten years or as needed
, rather than prescribing either a permanent arrangement or a fixed five-year period.
After Bellary was divided, the Tungabhadra works became shared between Andhra and Mysore.

secs.t: Services and employees allocation

x: The Partition Committee of 1949–50, associated with administrative arrangements for the new state, was chaired by
Kumaraswamy Raja

secs.t: Recommendations on Madras city and interim arrangement

x: Exam angle: "Wanchoo = single member, Rajasthan HC Chief Justice, 1953". Remember his Madras recommendation was
not
accepted.
The Andhra PCC demanded half of Madras town, while Wanchoo recommended Madras as the temporary headquarters for three to five years.
The JVP Committee held that Andhra could be formed only if the Telugus relinquished their claim to Madras.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sheela Bhide Committee dealt with Schedule IX institutions, the Kamalanathan Committee with employees, and a separate Section 6 expert committee examined the capital issue.
Union Jal Shakti Minister C. R. Patil
opened 33 new gates of the Tungabhadra dam on 26 June 2026, in the presence of the three Chief Ministers.

rows.title: Role of the press and newspapers in the Andhra Movement - Krishna Patrika, Andhra Patrika, Andhra Prabha, Zamin Ryot
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Newspapers - founder, year, place

x: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao was associated with the Telugu Swarajya of Vijayawada, while Tanguturi Prakasam's Swarajya was a separate English daily from Madras.
Swadesamitran was a Tamil paper of G. Subramania Iyer; Krishna Patrika had the stated founders and editor; and Andhra Patrika was founded by Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao.
Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao started Andhra Patrika as a Bombay weekly on 9 September 1908; it became a daily in 1914.

secs.t: First Telugu newspapers and journals - year and place

x: Satyadoota
, established in Bellary in 1835, was the first Telugu newspaper and was run by Christian missionaries.
Vartamana Tarangini was a weekly begun at Madras in 1842 by Syed Rahamatullah, the first Telugu paper started by a Muslim, and later passed to Puvvada Seshagiri Rao.
By 1905, there were about 20 Telugu journals, including Andhra Prakasika, Sasilekha, Krishna Patrika, Desabhimani and Rasikollasini.

secs.t: Newspaper statements for a separate Andhra - which paper

x: The opposing letter in The Hindu on 29 August 1912 was signed or identified as 'Viswamitra' and questioned where Andhra would find officers.
The cartoon depicted Rayalaseema as an iceberg blocking the ship labelled 'Andhra Movement'.
Janmabhumi's special article of 25 August 1920 stated that the Andhra movement strengthened
national unity

secs.t: Journals and magazines - editor

x: Bharati, a literary monthly started in 1924, was associated with
Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
Andhra Bhasa Sanjivani was associated with Kokkonda Venkataratnam, who introduced the editorial column.
Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham
was associated with Manorama, started in 1906, and Desamata, started in 1910.
Gurajada Appa Rao attempted
Prakasika

secs.t: Newspapers that moved their city of publication

x: Andhra Patrika
moved from Bombay to Madras and became a daily in 1914.
After 1843, Vartamana Tarangini passed to Puvvada Seshagiri Rao, and the change gave it its own press.

secs.t: Press Act prosecutions

x: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878, popularly called the Gagging Act, was repealed by Ripon in 1882.

secs.t: Newspapers backing specific movements

x: The Vandemataram/Swadeshi movement was supported by Krishna Patrika, Swarajya, Desamata, Andhra Kesari and Navayuga.
Zamin Ryot was associated with the peasant or anti-zamindari movement, while Navasakthi held the distinction of being the first fully socialist Telugu journal.
Hindu Sundari was associated with the year 1902, while Sri Savitri was associated with 1904.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Jaya Bharat was the first Telugu journal published after independence.
The press performed a dual role: it spread the national movement and also built support for the separate-Andhra demand.
Newspapers gave rise to reading rooms and libraries.

rows.title: Journalists and editors of the Andhra Movement - Mutnuri Krishna Rao, Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Editors - newspaper and period
Mutnuri Krishna Rao - editorial style, imprisonment, works

x: Krishna Patrika became a political weekly and a hub for freedom fighters under Mutnuri Krishna Rao.
Mutnuri Krishna Rao called upon extremist leaders to visit Andhra in 1907.
Pal spoke at Kakinada on 17 April and delivered five lectures at Rajahmundry between 19 and 24 April 1907.

secs.t: Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao - businesses, publications, titles, libraries

x: The Sreebagh Pact was signed on
16 November 1937
at Sreebagh, the Madras house of Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao.
Nageswara Rao sent his newspaper, books and Bharati free to any group of ten youths that opened a village library.
Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
completed and published the catalogue of printed Telugu books begun by Velidanda Hanumantha Rao.
The Granthalayodyama Trimurthulu included Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao, Ayyanki and
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao

secs.t: Editors who founded other institutions

x: Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao
, along with Kaderbad Narasinga Rao, founded the Edward Corporation Library at Nandyal, now known as the Victoria Reading Room.
Chilukuri Veerabhadra Rao co-founded the Bala Bharati Samithi at Rajahmundry in February 1907 with Gante Laxmanna and Unguturi Sriramulu.
Gadicherla signed the Sreebagh Pact, linked the movement with the Home Rule League and founded the library now known as the Victoria Reading Room.

secs.t: Editors jailed under press laws

x: Navayuga of Chilakaluripet
was shut down by government restrictions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The feature film is titled
Viswadata
and is being made in connection with Nageswara Rao Pantulu’s 160th birth anniversary.
Sivalenka Pavani Prasad is the great-grandson of
Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao
Pantulu.
These editors made journalism an instrument of political awakening while also funding and publicising the library movement.

rows.title: Library Movement in Andhra - origin, growth and role in awakening
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I A-212

secs.t: Andhra Desa Library Association - year, venue, first president, periodical, "first"

x: Exam angle: statement sets built on Grandhalaya Sarvasvam 1915, Andhra Patrika 1908, SKDABN 1901 in Hyderabad (not Kovvur 1916), and the 1918 boat library.
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya became Secretary of the Ramamohan Charitable Library, Vijayawada, in 1911.
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya and Suri Venkata Narasimha called for the conference through
Andhra Patrika

secs.t: Earliest libraries - founder, city, year

x: The Vijnana Chandrika Mandali published
Andhrula Charitramu
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao was blacklisted after the Rajahmundry College incident of 1907.
The respective libraries and their places and years are Hyderabad 1901, Rayakuduru 1894, Rajahmundry 1898 and Ongole 1890.
Gautami Granthalayam was formed by the merger of
Vasuraya Granthalayam and the Town Hall Library

secs.t: Madras and AP Public Libraries Acts

x: The Act was influenced by the Andhra movement, created local library authorities and used a library cess for funding.
The Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act, 1960 created district library bodies known as Zilla Grandhalaya Samsthas.
Pathuri Nagabhushanam
served on the drafting committee of the Andhra Pradesh Public Libraries Act, 1960.

secs.t: Library movement innovations - pioneer

x: Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya
pioneered the library pilgrimage, consisting of village tours.
Pathuri Nagabhushanam
pioneered the boat library on the Bank Canal during 1935–1942 and also undertook a Buckingham Canal tour.
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao
undertook the 1918 boat tour or padava yatra in West Godavari.
Velaga Venkatappayya
was known as the “Library Gandhi” and conducted village tours in Bhimavaram, Tadepalligudem, Kovvur and Guntur.

secs.t: Grandhalaya Sarvasvam and library journals - editor

x: After closing, Grandhalaya Sarvasvam was revived in January 1948 as the Telugu-English quarterly
Andhra Granthalayam
P. Rajasekharam
was the editor of Andhra Granthalayam after its revival.
A.
Srinivasa Rao
was the publisher of Andhra Granthalayam.
Dharma Granthalaya was associated with Yatagiri Lakshmi Venkataramana.
Suri Venkatasastri wrote pamphlets for the library movement.

secs.t: Links to the Nizam Andhra Mahasabha and the Telangana library movement

x: The Hyderabad State libraries shared the revival, delegates attended the Vijayawada conference, and Telangana libraries supported Telugu awakening.
The sequence is the Vijayawada conference in 1913, Andhra Desa Library Association in 1914, All India Public Library Association in 1933 and Andhra Mahasabha session at Jogipet in 1930.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The National Mission on Libraries functions under the Ministry of Culture, has RRRLF as its nodal agency, and aids one State Central Library and one District Library in each State or Union Territory.
Libraries served as legal centres of political education under colonial curbs and helped build Telugu identity, which supported the demand for statehood.

secs.t: Paturi Nagabhushanam - innovations, titles

x: Paturi Nagabhushanam
started the Bala Saraswati Bhandaramu library in his village while he was still a schoolboy.
The Buckingham Canal tour was undertaken for the
Pedapalem Sevakrama Vani Mandiram
Karunasri, the pen name of Jandhyala Papayya Sastri, gave Paturi Nagabhushanam the titles “University of Humanity” and “Walking Library.”.
Paturi Nagabhushanam also received the
Yarlagadda Rajyalakshmi Venkanna Choudary Kala Peetham Award

East Godavari
district on 24 July 1890.
The title Granthalaya Pitamaha was conferred on Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya by the
Maharaja of Baroda
, CDI.
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya was associated with the journal
Grandhalaya Sarvasvam
, published in 1915.
These facts describe Ayyanki’s awards, library philosophy, training activities and professional standing.

Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao became president of the library association in 1946.
The building was named Sarvottama Bhavan in honour of Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao and opened in 1949.

was associated with Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao was imprisoned for editorials such as “Veerabali” published in
Swarajya

taluks.

was the first president of the ADLA.
Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao supplied free papers and books to village libraries and published the catalogue of printed Telugu books.

donated the building that was named Sarvottama Bhavan in honour of Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao.

Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao founded the
SKDABN
Vavilala Ramaswamy Sastrulu & Sons and Nageswara Rao’s Andhra Granthamala supported libraries by supplying books and free copies.

Sarvottama Bhavan came through the

in 1946 and was opened in 1949.
Ayyanki Venkata Ramanayya’s birth anniversary is marked every year in
Vijayawada
Paturi Nagabhushanam received the title
Kala Prapoorna
from Andhra University in 1975.

Ayyanki Murali Krishna
, the grandson of Ayyanki Venkataramanaiah, recalled the slogan “Public libraries are temples of knowledge.”.
Ayyanki Venkataramanaiah built institutions, Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao mobilised people, and Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao provided financial and political backing.

rows.title: States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali) and the States Reorganisation Act 1956
sub: Group-II S1-92: Reorganisation within the country - Andhra State 1953, SRC and the States Reorganisation Act 1956
Group-II M1-A-104: States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali Commission) - appointment and terms of reference
Group-II M1-A-105: SRC recommendations on Andhra and Telangana and the reaction to them

secs.t: SRC - date set up, chairman, members, report

x: Exam angle: Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru was
not
a member (RPSC trap).
Exam angle: chairman (Fazl Ali) and the three-member set are asked most; the RPSC trap adds Tej Bahadur Sapru.
The Commission was announced on 22 December 1953, formally constituted on 29 December 1953, submitted its report in 1955, and the States Reorganisation Act came into force on 1 November 1956.

The S.K. Dhar Commission preferred administrative convenience, the JVP Committee rejected language as the basis, and the States Reorganisation Commission treated language as important but not the sole factor.
All three were recognised arguments in favour of linguistic states: governance in the people's language, preservation of cultural identity and easier administration.

secs.t: States Reorganisation Act 1956 - states, UTs, amendment

x: The reorganised units included merged Andhra Pradesh, bilingual Bombay and Punjab, enlarged Madras, Mysore and Kerala.
The
Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956
abolished the Part A, B, C and D classification and created the categories of States and Union Territories.
The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 later amended
Section 15
of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 to read 'Andhra Pradesh and Telangana'.

secs.t: SRC recommendations - Hyderabad/Telangana, Vidarbha, Bombay

x: Raichur and Gulbarga were assigned to Mysore, Marathwada to Bombay, and the Telugu districts were to remain as a separate Hyderabad State.
The residual Hyderabad State was to consist of the Telugu-speaking districts of the former Nizam's state, with Hyderabad city as its capital.
The plea to keep Hyderabad undivided was made to preserve the 200-year-old Deccani culture, but the Commission did not accept that plea.

secs.t: SRC on Visalandhra - conditions and time-frame

x: The SRC recommended that Telangana remain separate initially, with a possible merger after the 1961 elections if the Telangana Legislature approved it by a two-thirds majority.
The Chief Ministers of Andhra and Hyderabad agreed to merge at
Hyderabad House, New Delhi
, on 22 October 1955.
The Congress sub-committee comprised Jawaharlal Nehru, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and G.B. Pant.

secs.t: Principles of reorganisation

x: National unity and security, people’s welfare and the national plan, and geographical contiguity were among the factors considered.
A holistic approach required balancing linguistic considerations with administrative efficiency, economic viability, geographical contiguity, national unity and public welfare.
The SRC was not solely a Linguistic States Commission; it could divide areas sharing a language into more than one State when other considerations required it.

secs.t: Andhra State formation - Potti Sriramulu's fast, capital, Partition Committee, first CM

x: Exam angle: G2 2025 key "Andhra State formed on 1 October 1953" (not 1 Nov 1956).
The JVP Committee comprised Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
The JVP Committee rejected language as the immediate basis of reorganisation and advised postponement.
Potti Sriramulu died on
15 December 1952
after fasting for 58 days for a separate Telugu state.

secs.t: Andhra Mahasabha and Andhra movement milestones - Sri Bagh Pact

x: Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma
presided over the first Andhra Mahasabha at Bapatla in 1913.
Suravaram Pratapa Reddy
led the first Nizam Andhra Mahasabha at Jogipet in 1930.
The pact provided for irrigation priority, university centres and equal legislative representation for Rayalaseema, but it did not provide for the
immediate merger of Telangana with Andhra

secs.t: Seventh Constitutional Amendment (1956) - categories abolished

x: Articles 350A and 350B
concern mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage and the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities, respectively.
The amendment dealt with the composition of the House of the People and readjustment after each census, besides other reorganisation-related matters.
The States Reorganisation Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on
10 August 1956

secs.t: Report submission and states/UTs recommended

x: The Commission proposed abolishing the Part A, Part B and Part C classification, while the broader reorganisation replaced the old Part A–D arrangement with states and Union Territories.
The report was submitted in 1955 and proposed 16 states and 3 Union Territories along with abolition of the Part A, B and C classification.

secs.t: SRC paragraphs on Telangana - recommended arrangement, review mechanism

x: Exam angle: "two-thirds" and "after 1961 elections" are the testable numbers.
Paragraphs
dealt with the division of Hyderabad.
Paragraphs
set out the case for Visalandhra.
The Telangana Legislative Assembly could reconsider the merger after
the 1961 general elections
The proposed review mechanism required support from
two-thirds
of the elected members of the Telangana Legislative Assembly.

secs.t: Arguments the SRC gave for and against Visalandhra

x: The SRC noted that Visalandhra would be a large state of about 3.2 crore people with considerable raw materials and mineral resources.
Protection of Telangana's revenue surplus was an apprehension of opponents of immediate merger, not an advantage of Visalandhra.
The SRC observed majority support for Visalandhra among Telangana legislators but gave serious consideration to grievances relating to
finance and education

secs.t: Reaction in Andhra - Assembly, Congress, Communists

x: Tenneti Viswanatham described the report as
self-contradictory
Andhra Chief Minister
Bezawada Gopala Reddy
moved the resolution containing guarantees for Telangana.
The resolution covered jobs, education, irrigation and development, with priority and shares linked to population.
The resolution guaranteeing safeguards for Telangana was passed
unanimously
The Communist movement consistently supported integrated linguistic states and specifically backed Visalandhra.

secs.t: Reaction in Telangana - Hyderabad Assembly vote, Burgula government

x: Of the members who voted, 103 supported Visalandhra, while 29 opposed it and 15 remained neutral.
The Hyderabad Assembly had 174 members; the recorded vote was 103 in favour, 29 against and 15 neutral, with 147 members voting.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, then Chief Minister, acted
on the direction of the Congress High Command
to reduce Telangana's apprehensions.

secs.t: Nehru's "matrimonial alliance" remark - context

x: In 1956 Nehru likened the merger to a matrimonial alliance, adding that there could be a provision for divorce if the partners could not get along.
The remark referred to the Andhra-Telangana merger, which proceeded politically despite the SRC's advice and was based on safeguards.
Separate-Telangana advocates later invoked the remark as evidence that the merger was conditional rather than irrevocable.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Linguistic reorganisation raised concerns about national unity, but improved administration through people's languages; disputes such as Belgaum nevertheless continued.
The departure from
paragraph 386
was identified as a central grievance in the Telangana movements of 1969 and 2001-14.
BRS leader
K. T. Rama Rao
invoked the Fazal Ali Commission recommendation in January 2026 while criticising the Congress over the merger.

secs.t: Formation of Andhra Pradesh - date, basis, regions, capital, Governor, Speaker

x: Andhra Pradesh was formed by merging the 11 districts of Andhra State with the nine Telugu-speaking districts of Hyderabad State, while the Kannada and Marathi areas went to Mysore and Bombay respectively.
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy became the first Chief Minister and C.M. Trivedi was the first Governor of Andhra Pradesh after its formation in 1956.
The draft Bill initially used ‘Andhra Telangana’; the Communists proposed ‘Visalandhra’; and the Seventh Amendment Bill finally settled on ‘Andhra Pradesh’.
The Lok Sabha settled on the name ‘Andhra Pradesh’ through the Seventh Amendment Bill on
10 August 1956
Tanguturi Prakasam's ministry lost its majority over the prohibition issue, leading to mid-term polls in 1955.

secs.t: Gentlemen's Agreement - date, signatories, safeguards, cabinet ratio

x: The agreement provided proportionate sharing of common expenditure, exclusive use of Telangana's surplus in Telangana and a review after five years.
The education safeguard
dealt with admission priority for Telangana students or at least one-third of seats in technical institutions, whichever was more favourable.
The services safeguard provided for recruitment according to population ratio under domicile rules and proportionate retrenchment from both regions.
The agreed safeguard referred to Mulki or domicile rules requiring
12 years
of residence for recruitment in Telangana.
Urdu was to continue in Telangana's administration and courts for five years, after which the matter could be reviewed by the Regional Council.
The question of prohibition in Telangana was left to
the Telangana legislators
The finally agreed cabinet share was
between Andhra and Telangana.
The Andhra Assembly resolution supported Telangana priority and population-based allocations in
jobs, education, irrigation and development

Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was Deputy Chief Minister of Andhra State; Gouthu Latchanna was a minister and peasant leader; Alluri Satyanarayana Raju was Andhra PCC President; Marri Chenna Reddy was a Telangana minister.

secs.t: Visalandhra Movement - supporters, opponents, Mahasabhas

x: In
October 1953
, Nehru described Visalandhra as ‘Andhra imperialism’, strengthening the separate-Telangana position.
The Visalandhra Mahasabha was founded at Vijayawada on 26 November 1949 under the leadership of
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao
All four—Swami Ramananda Tirtha, Burgula Ramakrishna Rao, Mandumula Narsing Rao and Pandit Narendraji—supported Visalandhra.
The Socialists held meetings at
Gudivada and Kurnool
in 1954 in support of the Visalandhra idea.
Hayagreevachari
presided over the first Visalandhra Mahasabha at Warangal on 12–13 February 1950.
Tanguturi Prakasam
gave the slogan “Visalandhra nirmanam…” at the Warangal meeting.
The correct sequence is Dhar Commission (1948), Visalandhra Mahasabha (1949), Swami Sitaram's fast (1951), and Andhra State (1953).

secs.t: Chief Ministers of early Andhra Pradesh - chronology

x: Kasu Brahmananda Reddy
served as Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh from 1964 to 1971, with a second term beginning on 6 March 1967.
The Telugu Desam Party was founded on 29 March 1982 during the tenure of
Bhavanam Venkatarami Reddy
Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy
served from 20 September 1982 until January 1983, immediately before N.T. Rama Rao became Chief Minister.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao
had the shortest tenure, lasting 31 days from 16 August to 16 September 1984.
N. Chandrababu Naidu
had the longest continuous tenure as Chief Minister of united Andhra Pradesh, from 1995 to 2004.
Jalagam Vengala Rao assumed office in 1973, followed by M. Chenna Reddy in 1978, T. Anjaiah in 1980 and Bhavanam Venkatarami Reddy in February 1982.

secs.t: Hyderabad State - period, Burgula ministry, merger debate, 1954 shift

x: Exam angle: "In which year did Burgula change his stand?" - key answer 1954.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao
headed the first elected ministry of Hyderabad State, which assumed office in 1952.
B. Ramakrishna Rao changed his position in 1954 and advocated the early merger of Telangana with Andhra; he later kept Delhi informed in favour of Visalandhra.
At Warangal on 8 July 1954, he stated that the Hyderabad Government had no official opinion before the SRC report and that ministers had expressed only personal views.
The Warangal meeting was on 8 July 1954, the Chief Ministers met at Hyderabad House on 22 October 1955, and the agreement was signed on 20 February 1956.

secs.t: Telangana Regional Committee and Mulki Rules

x: The Committee represented Telangana legislators, included Telangana ministers other than the Chief Minister ex officio, referred disputes to the Centre and was subject to review after ten years.
The Mulki Rules originated in the Nizam’s era in 1919 and required about 15 years of residence for eligibility for local jobs.
The Committee was extended for five years in 1968 and was subsequently wound up after the 32nd Amendment in 1973 removed Andhra Pradesh from Article 371(1).

secs.t: Deputy Chief Minister post - clause and fate

x: The agreement provided that the Deputy Chief Minister should come from
Telangana
when the Chief Minister came from Andhra, and vice versa.
Sanjiva Reddy did not appoint a Deputy Chief Minister and dismissed the post as a “sixth finger”.

secs.t: Wanchu Committee - mandate

x: The Pataskar Award was concerned with settling the Andhra–Madras border.

secs.t: Nizam Andhra Mahasabha - founding, first session

x: The Nizam Andhra Mahasabha grew out of the
Andhra Jana Sangham
, which was founded in 1921.
The Nizam Andhra Mahasabha became a vehicle for Telugu cultural and political awakening in the Nizam’s State and later divided along moderate and Communist lines.

secs.t: Visalandhra - origin of the term, first advocates, other names

x: Visalandhra, or Greater Andhra, envisaged one state for Telugu-speaking people living in the Madras region and Nizam’s Hyderabad.
Sundarayya’s 1946 book was titled
Visalandhralo Prajarajyam
, meaning ‘People’s Rule in Greater Andhra’.
The early proposal emerged in 1912, covered the three specified regions, and was advanced further at the second Andhra Mahasabha in 1914.
The correct sequence is 1912 proposal, 1914 Andhra Mahasabha proposal, 1936 manifesto and 1946 publication of Sundarayya’s book.

secs.t: Arguments for Visalandhra → proponent

x: Supporters argued that a united state would permit integrated planning of the Krishna and Godavari river basins from upper Telangana to the coastal delta regions.
Swami Ramananda Tirtha
argued that Telangana would develop within Visalandhra and that a separate Telangana would be weak.
The Communist agrarian argument held that unification could promote land reform and weaken feudal structures.

secs.t: Arguments against → opponent

x: The principal fear was that Telangana would lose employment opportunities and educational seats to the better-educated people of Andhra.
The Mulki rules were
domicile
rules that protected local residents in employment and related opportunities.
The SRC recommended that Telangana remain separate initially, that the issue be reconsidered after the 1961 elections, and that merger require a two-thirds majority in the Telangana legislature.

secs.t: Leaders for and against → stand

x: All three statements describe Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao’s role in the Visalandhra movement.
K.V. Ranga Reddy
initially supported Visalandhra but later supported separate Telangana after becoming president of the Telangana Congress.
Marri Chenna Reddy
demanded a separate Telangana and opposed the Visalandhra resolutions along with K.V. Ranga Reddy.
Tanguturi Prakasam
used this expression while supporting the construction of Visalandhra.

secs.t: Parties' positions on Visalandhra

x: The Communist Party started the Visalandhra movement, won many seats in both regions in 1952 and expected to secure a majority in a united state.
The 1950 position treated Madras as temporary and Hyderabad as permanent, while the 1953 Kurnool meeting demanded Visalandhra with Hyderabad as capital under Neelam Sanjiva Reddy’s association.

secs.t: Visalandhra in literature and press

x: Visalandhra
was a Communist daily that began publication in June 1952.
The press-literary contribution included the Communist daily Visalandhra, Narayana Rao’s book, Ramanuja Rao’s pamphlets and Sri Sri’s presidency of the 1954 Mahasabha.

secs.t: Communist Party role - leaders, slogans, election use

x: The Communist Party of India demanded Visalandhra from 1946 and subsequently popularised the demand through various forms of publicity.
The Communist Party propagated Visalandhra through songs, poems, books, pamphlets and its press.
The Communists made substantial gains in both Telangana and Andhra in the 1952 elections and believed that a united state would provide them a majority.
Puchalapalli Sundarayya, Ravi Narayana Reddy and Arutla Ramachandra Reddy were leaders of the Telangana struggle.

secs.t: Visalandhra Mahasabha - founding year, venue, president, secretary

x: The Visalandhra Mahasabha was founded at Vijayawada on 26 November 1949.
Hayagreevachari
presided over the 1950 session of the Visalandhra Mahasabha.
Sri Sri
was the president of the 1954 session of the Visalandhra Mahasabha.

secs.t: Leaders → role

x: Puchalapalli Sundarayya
coined the expression ‘Visalandhra’ and authored Visalandhralo Prajarajyam.
Kodati Rajalingam, Hayagrivachari, Devulapalli Ramanuja Rao and Paga Pulla Reddy
explained the benefits of Visalandhra through books, pamphlets and tours.
Mir Mohammed Ali Khan was a Deputy Mayor and, along with Makhdoom Mohiuddin and Mehdi Nawaz Jung, helped educate Muslim opinion in Hyderabad.

secs.t: Visalandhra newspaper → year + editor

x: The daily Visalandhra began publication in
June 1952
on the initiative of Puchalapalli Sundarayya.
The Communist Party organ Visalandhra and Sundarayya’s Visalandhra Prajarajyam campaigned for the merger of Telugu-speaking areas.

secs.t: Representations to the SRC

x: Paragraph 386 recommended that Telangana remain a separate state initially, with reconsideration of merger after 1961 subject to a two-thirds vote.
The Commission recommended that Raichur and Gulbarga go to Mysore and that Marathwada be detached from Hyderabad State.
The Visalandhra Mahasabha was founded in 1949, followed by Nehru’s announcement on 22 December 1953, constitution of the Commission on 29 December 1953 and its report in 1955.

secs.t: Andhra Legislative Assembly resolution on Visalandhra → year

x: Related resolutions in your notes: APCC Kurnool (
, on Andhra State's inauguration);
Telangana convention
Nov 1955
where Harishachandra Deda backed a separate Telangana;
Feb 1956
agreement.

secs.t: Apprehensions of Telangana leaders → area

x: Telangana leaders feared that the Mulki or domicile Rules protecting local jobs would be weakened in a larger united state.
The apprehensions concerned the use of Telangana’s revenue surplus, widening regional disparities and weakening of local employment protections.
The recommendation reflected Telangana leaders’ concerns regarding Mulki Rules, domination of public services, diversion of revenue surplus and widening development disparities.

secs.t: Hyderabad Legislative Assembly debate on the SRC report

x: The Assembly had 174 members, 147 voted, 103 supported Visalandhra, 29 opposed it and 15 were neutral.

secs.t: Hyderabad PCC and Hyderabad State Congress resolutions

x: In June 1953 the Hyderabad Congress Committee proposed three divisions; in 1954 that resolution was rejected; on 8 July 1954 the PCC delegation met the SRC; and in November 1955 Harishchandra Heda supported separate Telangana.

The Visalandhra Mahasabha was founded in 1949; the APCC Kurnool resolution occurred on 30 September 1953; the Hyderabad PCC delegation met the SRC on 8 July 1954; and the Telangana convention took place in November 1955.

secs.t: Mulki agitation and City College firing → year + outcome

x: The Nizam's farman of 1919 tightened the Mulki rules, which had originated in 1888.
The agitation occurred under the Burgula ministry, the City College firing killed students, and domicile protection became a central Telangana demand reflected in the Agreement.

secs.t: Signatories → region + post held

x: Bezawada Gopala Reddy was the Chief Minister of Andhra State.
Tanguturi Prakasam
was not a signatory.
Burgula Ramakrishna Rao served as Governor of Kerala from 1956 to 1960 and later as Governor of Uttar Pradesh from 1960 to 1962.

secs.t: Violations alleged later → clause

x: The allegation concerned violation of the
domicile and employment protection
promised to Telangana.
The alleged method of bypassing the Mulki rules was to reclassify local posts as state-cadre or unreserved posts.
The Agreement promised that Telangana's revenue surplus would be spent only on Telangana, but this political assurance was alleged to have been ignored.
The alleged violations, especially concerning employment, domicile and revenue surplus, contributed to the
Jai Telangana agitation of 1969

secs.t: Article 371(1)/371D link and Presidential Orders

x: The 1975 Presidential Order was the AP Public Employment (
Organisation of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment
) Order.
Article 371D was inserted by the Thirty-second Amendment in 1973 and is linked to equitable opportunities, local cadres and related administrative arrangements.
The AP Personnel Department was reported to be finalising the
mapping of zones and multi-zones
under the AP Public Employment Order.

secs.t: First government - CM, Deputy CM, Governor, Speaker

x: Kalluri Subbarao
was the first Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of the newly formed Andhra Pradesh.
Puchalapalli Sundarayya
was the first Leader of the Opposition in the newly formed Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
The Congress had 40 seats from Hyderabad in 1952 and 119 from Andhra in 1955, giving a total strength of 159.

secs.t: Capital of the new state → reasons, earlier capital

x: Hyderabad
became the capital of Andhra Pradesh in 1956, replacing Kurnool, which had served as the capital of Andhra State from 1953 to 1956.
The SRC noted that Hyderabad could solve Andhra's permanent-capital problem, and it was the largest city with ready administrative infrastructure.

secs.t: First Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council → year

x: The second general elections in 1957 were held only in
the Telangana region
, where 79 members were elected.
The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council was constituted in 1958 with
90 members
during the tenure of N. Sanjiva Reddy.

secs.t: High Court of AP - establishment, seat

x: With the formation of the new state, the High Court of Andhra Pradesh sat at Hyderabad from
5 November 1956
After bifurcation, the Andhra Pradesh High Court moved to Amaravati on
1 January 2019

secs.t: Nehru's inaugural visit and remarks

x: Prime Minister
Jawaharlal Nehru
inaugurated Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956, with Hyderabad as its capital.
Dasarathi's song celebrating the event was titled “
Enni Naalla Swapnamidi
Dasarathi wrote “Enni Naalla Swapnamidi”, while Kaloji wrote “Emaanandam.

secs.t: Founding of the Telugu Desam Party - year, founder, CM then, first win

x: The Telugu Desam Party won 202 seats in the 1983 election and formed the first non-Congress government in Andhra Pradesh.
N.T. Rama Rao was sworn in on 9 January 1983 at Lal Bahadur Stadium, with an initial cabinet of 15 members.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao
served as Deputy Chief Minister in N.T. Rama Rao’s initial cabinet.

secs.t: AP leaders in national office → post

x: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was President of India, P.V. Narasimha Rao was Prime Minister, Damodaram Sanjivayya was AICC President, and N.T. Rama Rao was Chairman of the National Front.
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was the only Janata candidate to win in Andhra Pradesh in the 1977 election.

secs.t: 1983 and 1984 political crises - Governor's role, restoration

x: The dismissal by Governor Ram Lal led to Nadendla Bhaskara Rao’s short-lived ministry and NTR’s restoration after Nadendla resigned.
Nadendla Bhaskara Rao was sworn in on 16 August 1984, Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October, mid-term polls were held on 28 December, and NTR was sworn in again on 9 March 1985.

secs.t: Coalition and split events → year

x: The Telangana Praja Samithi was formed in 1969, not 1972.
Indira Gandhi
formed Congress (I) on 1 January 1978, while Brahmananda Reddy led the rival Reddy Congress.

secs.t: Panchayat Raj and local body reforms → CM + year

x: The three-tier Panchayat Raj system was implemented in Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1959 under
N. Sanjiva Reddy
The Balwant Rai Mehta report, considered by the National Development Council in 1958, was associated with the three-tier Panchayat Raj system.
NTR introduced the Mandal system from 1985 and, in 1983, permitted a simple majority for no-confidence motions against Zilla Parishad vice-chairmen instead of the earlier two-thirds majority.

secs.t: Elections → year + winning party

x: The 1957 elections were held only in Telangana and covered 79 seats.
All four statements correctly state the recorded election outcomes for 1962, 1978, 1985 and 1989.

secs.t: NTR-era reforms → initiative + first office holder

x: N. Vittal
was the first holder of the Dharma Mahamatra office associated with the anti-corruption initiative.
The foundation of Sri Rama Pada Sagar Stage II took place on 5 May 1983, not 5 April 1983.
Tirupati had the first Women’s University referred to in the NTR-era reforms.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Gentlemen's Agreement followed the Sribagh Pact's approach of addressing regional fears through a moral and political understanding rather than through a constitutional settlement.
The Andhra Mahasabha broadened the idea of Visalandhra by transforming a Communist slogan into an all-party demand that influenced the 1956 merger.
The SRC is associated with a wait-till-1961 formula, reflecting the apprehension that an immediate merger could intensify regional tensions.
The Deputy Chief Minister provision, protection of surplus funds and the Mulki rules were among the safeguards regarded as inadequately enforced.
The local-cadre and zonal recruitment arrangements under Article 371D are regarded as a later institutional expression of the domicile safeguard associated with the Agreement.
The Public Employment Order zones and multi-zones were reported as being re-mapped in 2026, showing the continuing administrative relevance of regional employment safeguards.
The material identifies the 1984 dismissal as a textbook case of misuse of gubernatorial discretion but does not identify the Governor by name.
The 1984 dismissal is cited as a classic instance of gubernatorial discretion being misused, and it contributed to later debate examined by the Sarkaria Commission.
